title: B0001 – Driver Frontal Stage 1 Deployment Control
text: B0001: Driver Frontal Stage 1 Deployment Control. The supplemental restraint system (SRS) module has detected a fault in the deployment control circuit for the first stage of the driver frontal airbag. The SRS warning lamp illuminates and airbag deployment may be impaired in a crash event. Common causes: Clock spring (spiral cable) damaged in steering column (high likelihood); Loose or corroded airbag connector under steering wheel (medium likelihood); SRS control module internal fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light or symbol related to the affected system; Comfort or safety function impaired. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: B0002 – Driver Frontal Stage 2 Deployment Control
text: B0002: Driver Frontal Stage 2 Deployment Control. The SRS module has detected a fault in the deployment control circuit for the second stage of the driver frontal airbag. Dual-stage airbags use two charges for severity-dependent deployment — this code indicates the high-severity stage cannot be triggered reliably. Common causes: Clock spring damaged or worn (high likelihood); Stage 2 squib circuit open or shorted (medium likelihood); SRS control module fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light or symbol related to the affected system; Comfort or safety function impaired. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: C0021 – ABS Pump Motor Circuit Range/Performance
text: C0021: ABS Pump Motor Circuit Range/Performance. The pump motor responds, but its current draw or run time is outside the expected range. title: P0001 – Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open
text: P0001: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open. The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0001 is set when the control module detects that the control circuit of this valve is open, i.e. no plausible current flows when the valve is driven. Rail pressure can then no longer be controlled as intended. Whether the valve is open or closed without current depends on the design, so the same fault can cause excess pressure in one system and no pressure in another. Common causes: Connector at the regulator loose, corroded or unplugged (high likelihood); Solenoid coil of the regulator open (medium likelihood); Broken wire in the harness, e.g. chafing or rodent damage (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Engine cranks but does not start, or stalls (normally closed valve); Loss of power or limp mode (normally open valve); Additional rail pressure codes possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0002 – Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0002: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Range/Performance. The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. With P0002 the circuit is electrically intact, but command and effect do not match: the measured current does not fit the duty cycle, or rail pressure does not follow the regulator position plausibly. The cause is often mechanical, for example a sticking valve, rather than the wiring. Common causes: Regulator sticking or worn due to dirt, debris or water in the fuel (high likelihood); High resistance at connector or wiring causing wrong current (medium likelihood); Low-pressure supply problem: clogged filter or air in the fuel (medium likelihood); Rail pressure sensor reading wrong values (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode; Jerking or unstable idle; Hard starting or stalling. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0003 – Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Low
text: P0003: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Low. The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0003 means the control module measures a voltage or current below the expected range on the control circuit, typically because of a short to ground. On some output stages an open circuit is also reported as low. A short on the switched ground side can keep the valve permanently energised. Common causes: Harness chafed through, short to ground (high likelihood); Shorted turns in the regulator coil (resistance too low) (medium likelihood); Water or corrosion in the connector (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard starting or stalling; Loss of power or limp mode; Low rail pressure code possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0004 – Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit High
text: P0004: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit High. The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0004 means the voltage on the control circuit stays too high for the commanded duty cycle, typically because of a short to battery voltage, or, with a switched ground side, an open circuit. The valve can then not be energised; a normally open design delivers maximum fuel and rail pressure rises. Common causes: Short to battery voltage in the harness (high likelihood); Open coil or wire, reported as high with ground-side switching (medium likelihood); Connector fault at the regulator (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode; Rough running or diesel knock possible; Excess rail pressure codes possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0005 – Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open
text: P0005: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open. The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. On diesel engines it is usually closed without current, so that the engine stops reliably when switched off. The engine control module energises it to let fuel flow and monitors its control circuit continuously. P0005 is set when this control circuit is open. A normally closed valve then cannot open, so the engine does not start or cuts out while driving. Which vehicles use this valve and code varies by manufacturer. Common causes: Wire or connector interrupted or corroded (high likelihood); Valve coil open (medium likelihood); Fuse or relay in the valve supply faulty (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine cranks but does not start; Engine cuts out suddenly; Check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0007 – Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit High
text: P0007: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit High. The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. title: P0008 – Engine Position System Performance Bank 1
text: P0008: Engine Position System Performance Bank 1. The engine control module learns how far each camshaft of bank 1 is offset from the crankshaft and compares this with a reference. P0008 is set when both camshafts of this bank are shifted in the same direction beyond a threshold. That points to the drive shared by the bank: a stretched primary timing chain, a worn tensioner, an idler gear or a crankshaft reluctor wheel that has slipped. A single faulty camshaft phaser does not set this code, because it affects only one camshaft. Common causes: Primary or timing chain stretched (high likelihood); Chain tensioner worn or loose (medium likelihood); Timing drive fitted incorrectly after an engine repair (medium likelihood); Crankshaft reluctor wheel slipped (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Timing chain rattle, especially at cold start; Loss of power or rough running; Often stored together with P0016 to P0019. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P000A – A Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1
text: P000A: A Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1. This monitor does not judge the end position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. The adjustment speed depends directly on oil flow, so worn or wrong oil and a partly clogged screen are the usual causes. Drivability is often hardly affected; the fault is an early warning before the camshaft misses its target position altogether. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1. Common causes: Oil too thick or too thin, sludged, or oil level low (high likelihood); Screen at the oil control valve partly clogged (high likelihood); Oil control valve sluggish (medium likelihood); Cam phaser leaking internally or worn (medium likelihood); Generally weak oil pressure, e.g. worn oil pump or bearings (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Slight hesitation when accelerating; Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P000E – Fuel Volume Regulator Control Exceeded Learning Limit
text: P000E: Fuel Volume Regulator Control Exceeded Learning Limit. The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. To compensate for tolerances and wear, the control module learns a long-term correction of the regulator control. P000E is set when this correction leaves its calibrated range. The regulator is electrically fine, but the system needs an unusually large correction all the time, which points to wear or contamination of regulator or pump, a weak low-pressure supply, or a missing calibration after a pump replacement. Common causes: Fuel volume regulator worn or contaminated (high likelihood); High-pressure pump worn, delivering less (medium likelihood); Low-pressure side: clogged filter, weak lift pump or air in the fuel (medium likelihood); Not calibrated after pump or regulator replacement (medium likelihood); Rail pressure sensor drifting (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often hardly noticeable at first, later loss of power; Hard starting if rail pressure is wrong; Additional rail pressure codes possible. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P000F – Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Activated
text: P000F: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Activated. On common-rail diesel and some gasoline direct-injection systems a spring-loaded pressure relief valve protects the rail and injectors: if pressure rises too far, it opens and returns fuel to the tank, often holding a reduced pressure for limp-home operation. The control module recognises the opening from the rail pressure signal and stores P000F. The code reports an event, not a defect of the relief valve itself; the actual cause usually lies in pressure control, for example a regulator that delivers too much fuel. Common causes: Fuel volume regulator stuck open or without current, pump over-delivers (high likelihood); Rail pressure sensor reading wrong, control runs into overpressure (medium likelihood); Pressure control valve faulty, where fitted (medium likelihood); Fuel return line blocked or kinked (low likelihood); Relief valve itself leaking or fatigued (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Sudden loss of power or limp mode; Engine may stall; Excess rail pressure code possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0016 – Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 1 Sensor A)
text: P0016: Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation (Bank 1 Sensor A). The engine control module checks whether the signal of the intake camshaft on bank 1 (sensor A) arrives at the expected crankshaft position, usually while the camshaft phaser is in its rest position. P0016 is set when the deviation stays outside a calibrated window. The camshaft is then out of step with the crankshaft: a timing belt or chain has jumped a tooth, the chain is stretched, the phaser is stuck at an end stop, or a reluctor wheel has slipped. On engines with a single camshaft, sensor A is simply the only camshaft sensor. Common causes: Timing chain stretched, or belt or chain jumped a tooth (high likelihood); Camshaft phaser stuck at an end stop, oil control valve or oil pressure faulty (medium likelihood); Incorrect assembly after a belt or chain replacement (medium likelihood); Camshaft or crankshaft sensor signal disturbed (low likelihood); Reluctor wheel on crankshaft or camshaft slipped (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Long cranking or hard starting; Rough idle and loss of power; Chain rattle at cold start on chain-driven engines; Risk of valve damage on interference engines if the timing has jumped. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P001A – A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
text: P001A: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1. A camshaft profile actuator switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between two or more fixed cam profiles with different valve lift and duration, for example by shifting a cam piece axially or by locking rocker arms or tappets with oil pressure. Unlike a camshaft phaser it does not shift the timing continuously. The second letter "A" in the title numbers the actuator on this camshaft. This code is set when the control circuit of the actuator is open: no current flows when it is driven, because of a broken wire, an unplugged connector or an open coil. The engine usually stays on one profile, typically the base profile with low lift. Some manufacturers report these faults with their own codes instead. Common causes: Connector at the actuator corroded, oil-soaked or loose (high likelihood); Wire broken, e.g. at the valve cover (medium likelihood); Actuator coil open (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Less power at high engine speed because the profile does not switch; Higher consumption or uneven part-load running, depending on the profile; Engine speed may be limited. Repair difficulty: medium.

text: P0025: "B" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Retarded (Bank 2). The engine control module compares the commanded position of the exhaust camshaft on bank 2 with the actual position from the camshaft and crankshaft sensors. This code is set when the camshaft stays further retarded than commanded for longer than a calibrated time. Usually the phaser does not move far enough out of its rest position, because oil pressure is too low to release the locking pin, the oil control valve does not open, or the oil screen is blocked. A stretched timing chain also shifts the camshaft towards retarded. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines; it is the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. Common causes: Oil pressure or oil level too low, oil worn out (high likelihood); Oil control valve sticking closed or its screen blocked (high likelihood); Cam phaser defective or seized in its rest position (medium likelihood); Timing chain stretched or jumped a tooth (medium likelihood); Wear debris in the oil circuit, e.g. from a thrust bearing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Noticeably less torque and pulling power; Higher fuel consumption; Harder starting in some cases; Rattle from the timing drive if the chain is stretched. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0026 – Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
text: P0026: Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1). A solenoid valve routes engine oil to a valve control element on the intake side of bank 1. Depending on the manufacturer this is a valve lift changeover or a camshaft phaser. P0026 is a plausibility fault: the electrical control is in order, but the expected effect does not occur or comes too late. The control module recognises this from feedback such as an oil pressure switch or the camshaft sensor. Pure circuit faults of the same solenoid have their own codes. The engine usually remains drivable, but with less power and higher consumption. Common causes: Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludged oil (high likelihood); Feedback oil pressure switch faulty or leaking (systems with switch) (high likelihood); Screen in front of the solenoid clogged, or solenoid sticking (medium likelihood); Mechanical fault in the valve train, e.g. locking pin or phaser sticking (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in wiring or connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, no extra pull at higher engine speed; Higher fuel consumption; Rough idle possible if a phaser is affected. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P002A – B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
text: P002A: B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1. A camshaft profile actuator switches the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) on bank 1 between two or more fixed cam profiles with different valve lift and duration, for example by shifting a cam piece axially or by locking rocker arms or tappets with oil pressure. Unlike a camshaft phaser it does not shift the timing continuously. The second letter "A" in the title numbers the actuator on this camshaft. This code is set when the control circuit of the actuator is open: no current flows when it is driven, because of a broken wire, an unplugged connector or an open coil. The engine usually stays on one profile, typically the base profile with low lift. Some manufacturers report these faults with their own codes instead. Common causes: Connector at the actuator corroded, oil-soaked or loose (high likelihood); Wire broken, e.g. at the valve cover (medium likelihood); Actuator coil open (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Less power at high engine speed because the profile does not switch; Higher consumption or uneven part-load running, depending on the profile; Engine speed may be limited. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0030 – HO2S Heater Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
text: P0030: HO2S Heater Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1). The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) only delivers a usable signal once its ceramic element is hot. A heating element inside the sensor gets it there quickly after a cold start. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse or relay, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while comparing the commanded state with the measured voltage or current. P0030 is the general circuit fault: the measured state does not fit the command, most often because the circuit is interrupted. Which physical fault sets P0030, P0031 or P0032 is defined by each manufacturer. Without heating, closed-loop mixture control starts late and cold-start emissions rise. Common causes: Heater circuit interrupted, e.g. broken or chafed wire near the exhaust (high likelihood); Heating element inside the sensor burnt out (high likelihood); Connector corroded or terminal pushed back (medium likelihood); Heater supply fuse or relay faulty (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable drivability problem; Closed-loop control starts late after a cold start; Emissions test or readiness check failed. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0032 – HO2S Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
text: P0032: HO2S Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1). The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) only delivers a usable signal once its ceramic element is hot. A heating element inside the sensor gets it there quickly after a cold start. title: P0033 – Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit
text: P0033: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit. The turbocharger bypass valve A is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve: it connects the pressure side of the compressor with the intake side upstream of the turbocharger. It opens when the throttle closes quickly at high boost, so the compressor does not surge and the compressor wheel keeps its speed for the next acceleration. It is not the wastegate, which bypasses exhaust gas around the turbine and has its own codes. The valve is either electric or a vacuum unit controlled by a solenoid. P0033 is the general circuit fault, usually an open circuit: the voltage at the control output does not match the command. Common causes: Wire or connector interrupted, corroded or chafed (high likelihood); Solenoid coil or electric bypass valve faulty (high likelihood); Supply missing, e.g. fuse or main relay (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fluttering or hissing when lifting off the throttle if the valve stays closed; Weak response after gear changes; Too little boost if the valve stays open. Repair difficulty: medium.

text: P0036: HO2S Heater Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2). The heated oxygen sensor on bank 1 is the downstream sensor 2 behind the (first) catalytic converter, used mainly to monitor the converter. title: P0039 – Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0039: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Range/Performance. title: P003A – Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
text: P003A: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Position Exceeded Learning Limit. The electric boost actuator A positions the variable turbine vanes or the wastegate and reports its position through a sensor. In a learning run, for example with the engine warm at idle or after switching off, the control module drives the actuator to its mechanical end stops and stores the sensor values as reference. P003A is set when a learned end position or the total travel lies outside the permitted limits. Typical reasons are worn or sticking vanes or linkage, a faulty actuator, a broken actuator lever, or a replacement actuator that has not been learned in. A usually denotes the first turbocharger in the exhaust flow. Common causes: Electronic actuator or its control module faulty (high likelihood); Vane mechanism, sector gear or linkage worn or sticking (medium likelihood); Replacement not learned in, or learning run aborted (e.g. low voltage) (medium likelihood); Actuator lever broken (low likelihood); Position sensor or its wiring faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power mode; Underboost or overboost codes possible; Sometimes no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P003C – A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
text: P003C: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1. The camshaft profile actuator A switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed. Common causes: Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludged oil, so switching pressure is missing (high likelihood); Profile switching solenoid sticking or its screen clogged (high likelihood); Oil supply to the switching elements leaking or restricted, e.g. worn seals (medium likelihood); Locking pin in tappet or rocker arm, or sliding cam piece, sticking (medium likelihood); Consequence of a circuit fault of the same actuator (low likelihood). title: P003D – A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Stuck On Bank 1
text: P003D: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Stuck On Bank 1. The camshaft profile actuator A switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. Common causes: Profile switching solenoid stuck open, oil pressure is not released (high likelihood); Locking pin does not return (weak spring, burr or dirt) (medium likelihood); Oil pressure too high or drain from the switching gallery blocked (medium likelihood); Sliding cam piece stuck in the high-lift position (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle and jerking at low engine speed; Poor running when cold; Misfire codes possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0040 – O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 2 Sensor 1
text: P0040: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 2 Sensor 1. On engines with two exhaust banks, the control module checks whether the upstream oxygen sensors are assigned to the right bank. It changes the mixture on one bank only, actively or as part of normal bank-wise control, and watches which sensor responds. If the sensor that should sit on the other bank reacts, the signals are swapped. This logic is documented for the manufacturer-specific predecessor codes; the usual cause is connectors plugged in crosswise after a repair. If the swap remains, each bank is controlled by the other bank's signal, so fuel trims drift towards their limits. Common causes: Sensor connectors plugged in crosswise after a repair (high likelihood); Harness routed wrongly or pins swapped in a connector (medium likelihood); Wrong harness, control module or calibration after a replacement (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fuel trim and mixture codes possible; Unstable idle or higher consumption possible. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0042 – HO2S Heater Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
text: P0042: HO2S Heater Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3). The heated oxygen sensor on bank 1 is the third sensor further downstream, which exists only on systems with two catalyst stages. Its heating element brings it quickly to operating temperature. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while checking that the circuit state matches the command. P0042 is the general circuit fault: the measured state of the heater circuit does not fit the command, most often because the circuit is interrupted. Which physical fault sets the general, low or high code is defined by each manufacturer. Without heating, the sensor becomes ready late and catalyst monitoring may not complete. Common causes: Heating element inside the sensor burnt out (high likelihood); Wire or connector damaged by heat or road spray (high likelihood); Heater fuse blown; a shared fuse can set several heater codes (medium likelihood); Output driver or software of the engine control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable drivability problem; Catalyst monitor does not complete; Emissions test or readiness check failed. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0045 – Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit/Open
text: P0045: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit/Open. "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. The letters A and B denote two separate actuators, for example on the low- and high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system, not the cylinder banks. This code is set when the control circuit is open: with the driver switched off no load can be measured, or the measured state does not match the command. Without control the actuator usually falls back to its rest position, which on most engines means low boost; depending on the design too much boost is also possible. Common causes: Connector at the actuator corroded or loose (high likelihood); Wire broken or chafed through (high likelihood); Solenoid coil in the actuator burnt out (medium likelihood); Fuse or ignition supply faulty (medium likelihood); Engine control module or separate actuator control unit faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag; Overboost possible in rare cases. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0046 – Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0046: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Circuit Range/Performance. title: P0049 – Turbocharger/Supercharger A Turbine Overspeed
text: P0049: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Turbine Overspeed. The control module has detected that turbocharger A runs above its permitted maximum speed. Engines equipped for it measure turbine speed with a dedicated sensor on the shaft; while the fault is active some systems continue with an estimated speed and reduce power. Real overspeed arises when too much exhaust energy reaches the turbine, for example because the wastegate or the turbine vanes stick closed, or because the turbocharger has to compensate for a charge-air leak or high altitude. Since a damaged turbocharger can fail completely, the cause should be found before driving on. Turbocharger B has its own code. Common causes: Wastegate or turbine vanes stuck closed, boost control fails (medium likelihood); Turbocharger speed sensor or its wiring faulty (medium likelihood); Charge-air leak forcing the turbocharger to higher speed (low likelihood); Engine control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power or limp mode; Whistling from the turbocharger; Risk of turbocharger damage. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0053 – HO2S Heater Resistance Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0053: HO2S Heater Resistance Bank 1 Sensor 1. On bank 1, this monitor checks the heating element of the upstream sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) not for an open or short circuit, but for its resistance. Many systems measure it once after a genuine cold start, when coolant and intake air temperatures show that the sensor is at ambient temperature, and correct the value for temperature; some manufacturers evaluate the heater current instead. The code is set when the value lies outside the limits for this sensor type, typically because the element has aged. Since the test often runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to confirm or clear. Common causes: Heating element aged or partly damaged (high likelihood); Contact resistance or corrosion at connector or pins (medium likelihood); Replacement sensor with a different heater type fitted (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, sometimes only after a cold start; Readiness for the sensor heater stays incomplete; Usually no drivability symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P005A – B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
text: P005A: B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1. The camshaft profile actuator A switches the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed. Common causes: Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludged oil, so switching pressure is missing (high likelihood); Profile switching solenoid sticking or its screen clogged (high likelihood); Oil supply to the switching elements leaking or restricted, e.g. worn seals (medium likelihood); Locking pin in tappet or rocker arm, or sliding cam piece, sticking (medium likelihood); Consequence of a circuit fault of the same actuator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power at higher engine speed; Reduced power mode on some vehicles. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P005E – Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control B Supply Voltage Circuit Low
text: P005E: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control B Supply Voltage Circuit Low. "Boost control B" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. B is the second actuator, for example on the high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system or on the second turbocharger; it does not denote cylinder bank 2. This code concerns the supply voltage that the control module switches to the actuator (high side): it is too low, for example because of a short to ground or an open circuit. Without control the actuator usually falls back to its rest position, which on most engines means low boost; depending on the design too much boost is also possible. Common causes: Supply wire shorted to ground or interrupted (high likelihood); Fuse or relay of the supply faulty (medium likelihood); Internal short in the actuator (medium likelihood); High-side driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag; Overboost possible in rare cases. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0065 – Air Assisted Injector Control Range/Performance
text: P0065: Air Assisted Injector Control Range/Performance. Air-assisted injectors have an air sleeve around the nozzle tip: air flowing past at high speed breaks the fuel spray into finer droplets, which improves combustion and cold starts and lowers hydrocarbon emissions. On port-injected engines this air is taken upstream of the throttle and dosed by a pulse-width modulated bypass solenoid; because it bypasses the throttle, it is part of the idle air. The system is rare and mainly found on older engines. P0065 means the control is electrically in order, but the effect is implausible. One documented method compares the idle speed controller correction with the air assistance switched on and off during stable idle; if the difference is too large, the code is set. Common causes: Air-assist solenoid sticking or dirty (high likelihood); Air hoses to the injectors leaking, disconnected or blocked (high likelihood); Air passages at the injectors coked (medium likelihood); Air leak distorting idle control (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough or unstable idle; Poorer cold starting. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0068 – MAP/MAF - Throttle Position Correlation
text: P0068: MAP/MAF - Throttle Position Correlation. The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the manifold pressure and/or mass air flow sensor with the quantity the throttle position leads it to expect. P0068 is set when they do not match, typically because more air arrives than the nearly closed throttle allows, i.e. an air leak behind the throttle, or because the throttle body is dirty or a sensor reads wrong. On engines with electronic throttle this check protects throttle control, so the engine often goes into reduced power. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own. Common causes: Air leak behind the throttle: intake manifold, vacuum or MAP hoses (high likelihood); Throttle body dirty (high likelihood); Mass air flow or manifold pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Engine control software (manufacturer updates exist) (medium likelihood); Camshaft timing out of position (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power mode; Rough or unstable idle; Jerking. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0069 – Manifold Absolute Pressure - Barometric Pressure Correlation
text: P0069: Manifold Absolute Pressure - Barometric Pressure Correlation. With the ignition on and the engine stopped, the intake manifold is at ambient pressure, so the manifold pressure sensor and the barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) must read almost the same. P0069 is set when they differ by more than a threshold. Some systems also compare the barometric reading with a value estimated from manifold pressure at wide-open throttle while driving. Altitude and weather shift both values equally and do not cause the code. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own. Common causes: Manifold pressure sensor drifting (high likelihood); MAP sensor hose blocked, kinked or leaking (high likelihood); Barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or connector faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no further symptoms; Mixture or power deviations possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P006A – MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 1
text: P006A: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 1. The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the mass air flow sensor with the quantity it calculates from manifold pressure, engine speed and temperature. P006A is set when the two deviate too far. A typical cause is an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close: recirculated exhaust raises manifold pressure without passing the air flow sensor. Air leaks, a leaking crankcase ventilation hose or a dirty sensor have the same effect. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own. Common causes: EGR valve dirty or sticking open (high likelihood); Air leak or crankcase ventilation hose leaking (medium likelihood); Mass air flow sensor dirty or manifold pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Air filter or intake restricted (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running; Slight hesitation when accelerating. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P006B – MAP - Exhaust Pressure Correlation
text: P006B: MAP - Exhaust Pressure Correlation. On engines with an exhaust pressure sensor, mostly turbocharged diesels, the control module checks whether manifold pressure and exhaust back pressure fit each other, for example with the engine stopped, when both should be at ambient pressure. P006B is set when they do not. No manufacturer description of this code was found; the explanation follows the general rule for plausibility checks of input sensors. Suspects are the exhaust pressure sensor or its sooted hose, and the manifold pressure sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own. title: P006C – MAP - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation
text: P006C: MAP - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation. title: P006D – Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 1
text: P006D: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 1. Without boost, for example with the engine stopped or at low load, the pressure sensor ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger must read about the same as the barometric pressure sensor. Typical causes are a faulty inlet pressure sensor, a faulty barometric sensor (often inside the control module) or a wiring or reference-voltage fault. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own. title: P006E – Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Supply Voltage Circuit Low
text: P006E: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Supply Voltage Circuit Low. "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure, for example a wastegate solenoid, the control valve of variable turbine vanes or an electric actuator. Some engines supply it through two driver stages in the control module: a high side that switches the supply voltage and a low side that switches ground. The low side is covered by P0045 to P0048; this code concerns the high side. P006E is set when the switched supply voltage is too low, typically because the supply wire is shorted to ground or interrupted. Without supply the actuator stays in its rest position, which on most engines means low boost and reduced power. Common causes: Supply wire shorted to ground or interrupted (high likelihood); Connector at the actuator corroded or loose (medium likelihood); Internal short in the actuator (medium likelihood); High-side driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0070 – Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit A
text: P0070: Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit A. The ambient air temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. Its value is used by the climate control, the outside temperature display and the engine control module, which needs it to enable other diagnostics and to correct its maps. Depending on the vehicle the engine control module reads the sensor directly, or the instrument cluster or another module sends the value over the data bus; some vehicles have no sensor and estimate ambient temperature from intake air temperature. P0070 is the general circuit fault or an invalid signal, for example when the instrument cluster reports the value as invalid or the reading is implausibly low. Common causes: Sensor faulty (exposed to spray and stone chips at the front) (high likelihood); Connector corroded or wire damaged, e.g. after front-end damage (high likelihood); Instrument cluster or data transmission faulty (vehicles with bus-supplied value) (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Wrong or missing outside temperature display; Climate control regulates incorrectly; Check engine light on (manufacturer-dependent); Other monitors may not complete. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0071 – Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit A Range/Performance
text: P0071: Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit A Range/Performance. The ambient air temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. Its value is used by the climate control, the outside temperature display and the engine control module, which needs it to enable other diagnostics and to correct its maps. P0071 is a plausibility check: after a long standstill (several hours) ambient, intake air and coolant temperatures should be close together. Symptoms: Wrong or missing outside temperature display; Climate control regulates incorrectly; Check engine light on (manufacturer-dependent); Other monitors may not complete. title: P0075 – Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Bank 1
text: P0075: Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Bank 1. A solenoid valve on the cylinder head controls oil flow for the variable valve control on the intake side of bank 1. Depending on the manufacturer it drives a camshaft phaser (for example on Nissan engines) or a valve lift changeover (for example on Subaru engines). This code family reports electrical faults in its control circuit; P0075 is the general circuit fault: open circuit or short, without distinguishing between them. Some manufacturers use only this code for all electrical faults of the valve. Other manufacturers report the same valve under the "camshaft position actuator" codes instead. Valve control is then switched off or stays in its base position. Common causes: Solenoid coil open or shorted (high likelihood); Wiring or connector interrupted, chafed or corroded (high likelihood); Oil at the connector, e.g. from a leaking valve O-ring (medium likelihood); Output driver or supply in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Less power, especially at high engine speed with lift changeover; Rough idle possible; Follow-up codes for camshaft timing or misfire possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P007A – Charge Air Cooler Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 1
text: P007A: Charge Air Cooler Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 1. The charge air cooler temperature sensor (an NTC thermistor) measures the temperature of the compressed charge air at the charge air cooler, depending on the manufacturer upstream or downstream of it, and is often combined with the boost pressure sensor. The engine control module uses it for the air mass calculation, boost control, component protection and to monitor cooler efficiency. P007A is the general circuit fault of the bank 1 sensor; low and high signals have their own codes. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. Common causes: Connector or wiring faulty, oil in the connector from crankcase vapours (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (high likelihood); Ground or 5 V supply disturbed (often shared with the boost pressure sensor) (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power possible, especially on diesels; Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0087 – Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low
text: P0087: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low. On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0087 is set when the actual pressure stays below the target by more than a threshold for some time. It is a system code: it does not say which component is at fault. Typical causes are a weak low-pressure supply, a worn high-pressure pump, a sticking control valve, a leak or a drifting pressure sensor; the engine usually goes into reduced power. Common causes: Low-pressure supply too weak: lift pump, clogged filter, low tank level or waxing (high likelihood); High-pressure pump worn (high likelihood); Pressure control or metering valve sticking (medium likelihood); High-pressure leak or excessive injector return flow (medium likelihood); Rail pressure sensor drifting (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Hard starting or stalling; Jerking under load. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0088 – Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High
text: P0088: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High. On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0088 is set when the actual pressure stays above the target by more than a threshold for some time. On many gasoline systems the pump can only raise pressure, which is then reduced only by injecting. Typical causes are a sticking pressure control or metering valve, a drifting pressure sensor or, on diesels with a pressure control valve, a blocked return. Real overpressure can cause harsh combustion noise and smoke. Common causes: Pressure control or metering valve sticking (high likelihood); Rail pressure sensor drifting (medium likelihood); Fuel return blocked (diesel with pressure control valve) (medium likelihood); Engine control software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Harsh combustion noise; Smoke from the exhaust. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0089 – Fuel Pressure Regulator A Performance
text: P0089: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Performance. On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. The fuel pressure regulator A is the actuator the manufacturer designates for this: depending on the system a pressure control valve that releases fuel from the rail, or the control valve on the high-pressure pump. Some manufacturers report the pump valve under the "fuel volume regulator" codes instead. P0089 is a function check: pressure may still be plausible, but the regulator works at its limit, needs too much correction, or pressure does not follow its control signal. Typical causes are a sticking or worn regulator, a weak pump or a faulty pressure sensor. Common causes: Pressure regulator or pump control valve sticking or worn (high likelihood); High-pressure pump weak (medium likelihood); Rail pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Low-pressure supply too weak (medium likelihood); Engine control software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Jerking or hesitation; Loss of power, reduced power mode possible. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P008A – Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low
text: P008A: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low. Some engines, mainly gasoline direct injection with a demand-controlled in-tank pump, have their own pressure sensor in the low-pressure line between the tank pump and the high-pressure pump. The engine control module compares this supply pressure with its target. P008A is set when the supply pressure stays too low. Besides a weak tank pump or its control unit, a clogged filter or a faulty sensor, simply running the tank empty can set this code. Common causes: Tank run empty or very low fuel level (high likelihood); In-tank pump or its control unit faulty (high likelihood); Filter or line restricted (medium likelihood); Low-pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard starting; Jerking under load; High-pressure codes may follow. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P008C – Fuel Cooler Pump Control Circuit/Open
text: P008C: Fuel Cooler Pump Control Circuit/Open. On some common-rail diesels, fuel returning from the injection system is cooled in a heat exchanger connected to a low-temperature coolant circuit. An electric coolant pump, switched by the engine control module depending on fuel temperature, drives this circuit. P008C reports an open control circuit of this pump or its relay. If the pump fails for long, the fuel runs hotter; some systems then limit power to protect components. Common causes: Connector or wiring faulty (high likelihood); Fuel cooler pump faulty (high likelihood); Relay or fuse faulty (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no further symptoms; Reduced power when fuel gets hot possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P008F – Engine Coolant Temperature/Fuel Temperature Correlation
text: P008F: Engine Coolant Temperature/Fuel Temperature Correlation. After the engine has been switched off long enough, coolant and fuel should have approached the same temperature. The engine control module compares the coolant temperature sensor with the fuel temperature sensor at the next cold start and sets P008F if they differ too much. From this alone it cannot tell which sensor is wrong, so both have to be checked. Regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors; the exact conditions are manufacturer-specific. Common causes: Coolant temperature sensor drifting (high likelihood); Fuel temperature sensor drifting (high likelihood); Contact resistance at a connector (medium likelihood); Values distorted, e.g. by an auxiliary heater (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no drivability symptoms; Cold-start behaviour may be affected. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0090 – Fuel Pressure Regulator A Control Circuit/Open
text: P0090: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Control Circuit/Open. On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. The fuel pressure regulator A is the actuator the manufacturer designates for this: depending on the system a pressure control valve that releases fuel from the rail, or the control valve on the high-pressure pump. Some manufacturers report the pump valve under the "fuel volume regulator" codes instead. P0090 is the general circuit fault, usually an open circuit: the driver voltage or current does not fit the command. Rail pressure can then no longer be controlled as intended, and the engine usually runs in reduced power. Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power mode; Hard starting or stalling. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0093 – Fuel System Leak Detected - Large Leak
text: P0093: Fuel System Leak Detected - Large Leak. A leak in the high-pressure fuel system is not measured directly but inferred from a pressure and volume balance. P0093 means the pump is already delivering at its limit and rail pressure still stays well below target. The leak can be external (line, rail) or internal (injector return, relief valve). An external leak is a fire hazard: stop the engine and inspect it. Common causes: High-pressure line or rail fitting leaking (high likelihood); Injector with excessive leak-off (high likelihood); Pressure relief or control valve leaking (medium likelihood); Weak pump or low-pressure supply mistaken for a leak (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or reduced power mode; Long cranking; Fuel smell or visible leak. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0094 – Fuel System Leak Detected - Small Leak
text: P0094: Fuel System Leak Detected - Small Leak. A leak in the high-pressure fuel system is not measured directly but inferred from a pressure and volume balance. P0094 is typically detected when rail pressure drops too fast during overrun with injection cut off, or when more pump delivery than expected is needed at idle. Possible leaks are injectors with too much leak-off, fittings or relief valves; internal leakage can dilute the engine oil with fuel, so a rising oil level is a warning sign. Common causes: Injector with excessive leak-off (high likelihood); High-pressure fitting slightly leaking (high likelihood); Pressure relief valve leaking (medium likelihood); Engine control software (manufacturer updates exist) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Long cranking; Rising engine oil level from fuel dilution; Slight loss of power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0095 – Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Bank 1
text: P0095: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Bank 1. Intake air temperature sensor 2 is the second air temperature sensor in the intake path. On many turbocharged engines it sits in the intake manifold behind the compressor and charge air cooler, often combined with the manifold pressure sensor, and is used to calculate cylinder filling and ignition timing. The numbering is not standardised, so its position can differ between manufacturers. P0095 is the general circuit fault; low and high signals have their own codes. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. Common causes: Connector or wiring faulty (high likelihood); Sensor or combined sensor faulty (high likelihood); Supply or ground disturbed (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms; Slightly changed power or retarded ignition possible. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0096 – Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
text: P0096: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1. Intake air temperature sensor 2 is the second air temperature sensor in the intake path. title: P009A – Intake Air Temperature/Ambient Air Temperature Correlation
text: P009A: Intake Air Temperature/Ambient Air Temperature Correlation. After a long standstill with the engine cold, intake air temperature and ambient air temperature should be about the same. P009A is set when the two sensors disagree by more than a threshold at the next start. A detected engine block heater usually suspends the test. Several manufacturers perform this comparison under other codes; no manufacturer description naming P009A itself was found. Suspects are both sensors, an ambient sensor in a heat-affected position and contact resistance at a connector. Common causes: Intake air temperature sensor drifting or contaminated (high likelihood); Ambient temperature sensor faulty or in a heat-affected position (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at a connector (medium likelihood); Engine block heater or auxiliary heater distorting the comparison (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P009B – Fuel Pressure Relief Control Circuit/Open
text: P009B: Fuel Pressure Relief Control Circuit/Open. The fuel pressure relief control is an electrically controlled valve on the fuel rail that the engine control module opens to reduce rail pressure deliberately, for example on overrun, on load drops or when the engine is switched off. It differs from the purely mechanical pressure relief valve, which opens passively at overpressure, and from the pressure regulator, which controls pressure continuously. Manufacturer documents show this code mainly on heavy-duty diesel engines. P009B reports an open control circuit of this valve. Rail pressure can then not be reduced as intended, and the engine may be derated. Common causes: Wire broken or connector corroded (high likelihood); Valve coil faulty (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power (derate) possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00A0 – Charge Air Cooler Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 2
text: P00A0: Charge Air Cooler Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 2. The charge air cooler temperature sensor for bank 2 (an NTC thermistor) measures the charge air temperature in the second charge-air path, for example on V engines with two charge air coolers. The engine control module uses it for the air mass calculation, boost control and component protection. For P00A0, this is the general circuit fault; low and high signals have their own codes. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. Bank 2 codes occur only on engines with two separate intake or charge-air paths, one per cylinder bank. Common causes: Connector or wiring faulty (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (high likelihood); Supply or ground disturbed (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms; Emissions test or readiness check may fail. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00AF – Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Module Performance
text: P00AF: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Module Performance. Boost control A here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. P00AF is set when actuator A reports such an internal fault. Manufacturer bulletins recommend checking the vane mechanism for free movement and, if it moves freely, replacing only the actuator rather than the whole turbocharger. Common causes: Electronics or motor inside the actuator faulty (high likelihood); Sector gear or vane mechanism sticking (soot, coking), causing overcurrent (medium likelihood); Weak supply or ground, corroded connector (medium likelihood); Software of actuator or control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode with reduced boost; Often stored with actuator position or boost codes. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P00B1 – Radiator Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P00B1: Radiator Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit. The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. P00B1 is the general circuit fault; low and high signals have their own codes. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. Common causes: Connector or wiring at the radiator corroded or damaged (exposed front position) (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (high likelihood); Loose contact in the circuit (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Thermostat and coolant flow diagnostics are suspended; Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00B6 – Radiator Coolant Temperature/Engine Coolant Temperature Correlation
text: P00B6: Radiator Coolant Temperature/Engine Coolant Temperature Correlation. The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. After a long standstill (eight hours in a documented case) engine and radiator should be at the same temperature. P00B6 is set at the next start when the engine and radiator coolant temperature sensors differ by more than a threshold that may depend on intake air temperature. A detected engine block heater cancels the test. From this alone the control module cannot tell which sensor is wrong. Common causes: Radiator coolant temperature sensor drifting (high likelihood); Engine coolant temperature sensor drifting (high likelihood); Contact resistance at a connector (medium likelihood); Retrofitted engine preheater or auxiliary heater not detected by the system (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00B7 – Engine Coolant Flow Low/Performance
text: P00B7: Engine Coolant Flow Low/Performance. When the engine is hot, the thermostat should be open and coolant should flow through the radiator. P00B7 is set when the engine coolant temperature is very high (above about 117 to 119 °C in documented cases) while the radiator side stays much colder, so too little coolant flows through the radiator. The usual cause is a thermostat stuck closed; low coolant, air in the system, a pump that delivers too little or a blocked radiator have the same effect. If the temperature keeps rising, stop driving to avoid engine damage. Common causes: Thermostat stuck closed (high likelihood); Low coolant level or air in the cooling system (high likelihood); Coolant pump delivering too little (impeller, drive; known cases on some engines) (medium likelihood); Radiator or hoses blocked (medium likelihood); One of the temperature sensors reading wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Coolant warning light; High engine temperature up to overheating; Weak or fluctuating cabin heating. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00B8 – MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 2
text: P00B8: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 2. On engines with two intake paths, the control module compares the manifold pressure of bank 2 with the measured or calculated air quantity of that bank. P00B8 is set when the two do not fit together; the code does not say which value is wrong. As with its bank 1 counterpart, typical causes are an air leak, an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close, or a dirty or drifting sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart. Common causes: Air leak in the intake of bank 2 (high likelihood); EGR valve dirty or sticking open (medium likelihood); Manifold pressure sensor or air flow meter dirty or drifting (medium likelihood); Wiring or connector faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running; Mixture codes possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00B9 – Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low. Low Ambient Temperature
text: P00B9: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low. Low Ambient Temperature. This code reports too low a pressure in the low-pressure fuel supply between the lift pump and the high-pressure pump under the additional condition of low ambient temperature. It separates cold-related supply problems from the general case. A typical mechanism, documented for diesel engines, is wax separating from insufficiently winterised fuel at sub-zero temperatures and clogging the filter or tank strainer. No manufacturer description naming this exact code, its thresholds or the vehicles using it was found. Common causes: Wax separation from summer or insufficiently winterised diesel in frost (high likelihood); Fuel filter clogged or water in the filter frozen (medium likelihood); Fuel filter heater faulty (medium likelihood); Lift pump weak (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard or no cold start; Jerking or loss of power after starting. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00BA – Low Fuel Pressure - Forced Limited Power
text: P00BA: Low Fuel Pressure - Forced Limited Power. "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. Regulations require the check engine light to come on within seconds when such an emissions-relevant limp-home mode is active. These codes report the reason for the limitation; usually further codes point to the actual cause. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. P00BA: power has been limited because fuel pressure is too low, which protects the engine and the pump against running lean or losing rail pressure. Common causes: Fuel filter clogged, suction-side leak or air in the system (high likelihood); Lift pump or high-pressure pump weak (medium likelihood); Pressure regulator or relief valve leaking (medium likelihood); Tank run empty (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Marked loss of power, limp mode; Hard starting or jerking. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P00BC – Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too Low
text: P00BC: Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too Low. The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BC concerns air flow meter A. Typical causes are air entering behind the meter, a charge-air leak, a dirty meter or a restricted intake. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart. Common causes: Air leak behind the meter or charge-air leak (high likelihood); Air flow meter dirty (medium likelihood); Air filter or intake restricted (medium likelihood); Wiring or connector faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power; Lean mixture codes possible. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00C0 – Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit
text: P00C0: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit. Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C0 is the general circuit fault, usually an open circuit in the control circuit of this valve; the circuit is monitored continuously. Common causes: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat (high likelihood); Valve coil open or shorted (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle; Boost fluctuations, loss of power. Repair difficulty: medium.

text: P00C2: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High. Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C2 reports too high a voltage, typically a short to battery voltage in the control circuit of this valve; the circuit is monitored continuously. Common causes: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat (high likelihood); Valve coil open or shorted (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle; Boost fluctuations, loss of power. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00C5 – Turbocharger/Supercharger B Turbine Overspeed
text: P00C5: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Turbine Overspeed. The control module has detected that turbocharger B runs above its permitted maximum speed. Speed is measured by a dedicated sensor per turbocharger where fitted, or estimated from a model of pressure ratio and air mass. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in series systems or the one on bank 2 in parallel systems. Typical causes are sticking boost control of this turbocharger or a charge-air leak; find the cause before driving on, as overspeed can destroy the turbocharger. title: P00C6 – Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking
text: P00C6: Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking. Direct-injection engines release injection only once the rail has reached a minimum pressure. P00C6 is set when this pressure is not reached quickly enough while cranking, or, in another documented variant, when it drops below the minimum again right after the high-pressure start. Cranking then takes longer or the engine does not start. The check runs once per start; some manufacturers only enable it above a minimum tank level. Common causes: High-pressure pump weak, or its drive cam or follower worn (high likelihood); Lift pump or low-pressure supply too weak (medium likelihood); Control valve on the pump faulty (medium likelihood); Leak or check valve fault letting pressure bleed off after shutdown (medium likelihood); Very low fuel level (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Long cranking; No start; Jerking after starting. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P00C7 – Intake Air Pressure Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
text: P00C7: Intake Air Pressure Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1. With the engine stopped, all pressure sensors in the intake system (manifold pressure, boost pressure, barometric pressure) should read ambient pressure; some diesels also compare them at idle. The control module compares them: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own code. P00C7 is set when the readings disagree but no single sensor can be identified as faulty, which points to a fault affecting several sensors, such as a shared reference voltage or ground. Common causes: Shared 5 V reference or ground of the pressure sensors disturbed (high likelihood); Two sensors drifting at the same time (contamination, oil mist, ageing) (medium likelihood); Pressure hose to a sensor leaking or blocked (medium likelihood); Engine control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no further symptoms; Substitute values with loss of power possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00C8 – Fuel Pressure Regulator A Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open
text: P00C8: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open. Some engine control modules switch the solenoid of fuel pressure regulator A on both sides: the ground side is monitored by P0090 to P0092, the supply side (high-side driver) by P00C8 to P00CA. On gasoline direct injection the regulator is typically the control valve on the high-pressure pump. P00C8 reports an open circuit on the supply side. Rail pressure can then not be controlled, causing starting problems, stalling or reduced power. Common causes: Supply wire or connector to the pump solenoid damaged by heat or chafing (high likelihood); Solenoid coil open (medium likelihood); High-side driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard starting or stalling; Loss of power or limp mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00CB – Fuel Volume Regulator Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open
text: P00CB: Fuel Volume Regulator Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open. The fuel volume regulator is the solenoid valve that meters how much fuel the high-pressure pump delivers (metering unit on diesels, pump control valve on some gasoline direct-injection engines). Many control modules switch such solenoids on both sides; P0001 to P0004 cover the control side, while these codes cover the supply side (high-side driver). P00CB reports an open circuit on the supply side. Rail pressure may then deviate, with reduced power or hard starting. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors. Common causes: Supply wire broken or connector corroded (high likelihood); Regulator coil open or shorted (often built into the pump) (medium likelihood); High-side driver in the engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode; Hard starting or jerking. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00CE – Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
text: P00CE: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1. After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code. This code is set when no pair agrees, so no single sensor can be identified as faulty. A detected engine preheater suspends the test. Since it runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to return after being cleared. Some vehicles also disable start-stop while this code is stored. Common causes: One temperature sensor drifting without setting its own code (medium likelihood); Uneven cooling, undetected preheater or strong sunshine (medium likelihood); Shared ground or reference line disturbed, falsifying several sensors (medium likelihood); Engine control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Start-stop disabled on some vehicles; Usually no drivability symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00CF – Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Correlation
text: P00CF: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Correlation. With the engine stopped or without boost, the boost pressure sensor A (between compressor and throttle) must read practically ambient pressure.
