title: P00D1 – HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P00D1: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1. This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor upstream of the catalytic converter (sensor 1) on bank 1. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit. For this sensor position no manufacturer description of the test was found; the code appears in a manufacturer's code list, and the explanation follows the documented counterpart for sensor 2. Common causes: Heating element aged, resistance increased (high likelihood); Corrosion or contact resistance at connector or harness of the heater circuit (high likelihood); Too low supply voltage at the sensor connector, e.g. poor ground (medium likelihood); Diagnostic software (manufacturer updates exist for some vehicles) (medium likelihood); Replacement sensor with a different heater (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable drivability problem; Oxygen sensor heater readiness stays incomplete. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00D5 – HO2S Sensor Correlation Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P00D5: HO2S Sensor Correlation Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 1 Sensor 2. During fuel cut-off on overrun the exhaust gas is pure air, so the oxygen sensors before and behind the catalytic converter must both report the same lean value. A documented method averages and normalises the signals of both sensors during fuel cut-off and sets the code when they differ by more than a limit; it runs once per drive cycle and needs several overrun phases. The code points to one of the sensors having drifted, not to the catalytic converter. The manufacturer documenting it uses wide-band sensors in both positions. Common causes: Upstream sensor aged or shifted (high likelihood); Downstream sensor aged or shifted (high likelihood); Air or exhaust leak between the sensors falsifying the lean signal (medium likelihood); Retrofitted sensor with wrong characteristic, or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable drivability problem; Catalyst readiness may stay incomplete. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00D7 – Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Temperature Too High
text: P00D7: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Temperature Too High. Bypass valve A is the electric compressor recirculation valve, mounted close to the hot compressor and turbine housing. This code reports that its temperature is too high. How the temperature is detected is not described in published manufacturer documents; a documented principle for comparable turbocharger solenoids estimates the coil temperature from current, supply voltage and duty cycle and protects the coil by limiting or switching it off. With the valve switched off, the compressor may surge when lifting off the throttle. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors. Common causes: Valve energised for unusually long periods, e.g. due to boost control problems (medium likelihood); Coil with shorted turns or aged (medium likelihood); Heat shield missing or exhaust leak near the turbocharger (medium likelihood); Contact resistance or supply fault distorting the estimate (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (manufacturer-dependent); Whistling or fluttering when lifting off the throttle; Slight loss of power. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00E3 – Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Stuck Open
text: P00E3: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Stuck Open. Some engines, mainly hybrids and fuel-saving designs, have an exhaust heat exchanger behind the catalytic converter that transfers exhaust heat into the coolant for faster warm-up of engine and cabin. A bypass valve sends the exhaust either through the heat exchanger or around it. Documented diagnostics compare the coolant temperature rise at the heat exchanger with the commanded mode: if it behaves like bypass while recovery is commanded, or the other way round, the valve is considered stuck. P00E3 reports the valve stuck open. How "open" and "closed" map to bypass and recovery is not publicly documented, so both possible effects should be considered: slow warm-up and weak heating, or excessive coolant heat. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors. Common causes: Valve flap coked or corroded and sticking (high likelihood); Actuator faulty (electric or vacuum) (medium likelihood); Linkage or return spring broken (medium likelihood); Heat exchanger temperature sensor faulty, simulating a stuck valve (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Slow warm-up and weak heating in winter; Or high coolant temperature and long fan run-on. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P00E5 – Intake Air Temperature/Fuel Temperature Correlation
text: P00E5: Intake Air Temperature/Fuel Temperature Correlation. After a long standstill, intake air and fuel should be at about ambient temperature. title: P00E6 – Intake Air Pressure Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2
text: P00E6: Intake Air Pressure Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2. This is the bank 2 counterpart of the multiple pressure sensor check for engines with separate pressure measurement per bank, such as twin-turbo V engines. title: P00E7 – Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2
text: P00E7: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2. After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code. This code is set when no pair agrees, so no single sensor can be identified as faulty. A detected engine preheater suspends the test. Since it runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to return after being cleared. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; bank 2 codes are intended for engines with two separate intake paths. Common causes: One temperature sensor drifting without setting its own code (medium likelihood); Uneven cooling, undetected preheater or strong sunshine (medium likelihood); Shared ground or reference line disturbed, falsifying several sensors (medium likelihood); Engine control module or software (low likelihood). text: P00F7: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 2. This is the bank 2 counterpart of the comparison between barometric pressure and the pressure ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger. At low air flow the inlet pressure sensor reads close to ambient pressure, minus the small loss across the air filter, so it must match the barometric reading. The code is set when the difference is too large; a clogged air filter or a leaking intake hose on bank 2 can cause it as well as a drifting sensor. title: P00F9 – Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Range/Performance
text: P00F9: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Range/Performance. The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. It is a separate code family from the boost pressure sensor, which usually measures the pressure just ahead of the throttle; engines use it where the pressure behind the compressor is needed in addition, for example to judge the pressure loss across the charge air cooler or to protect against compressor surge. One manufacturer documents it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. P00F9 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible. In a documented case the cause was a sensor not seated properly and a connector not fully engaged; securing them solved it without parts. Common causes: Connector loose or not fully engaged, or sensor not seated properly (high likelihood); Sensor oil-coated from turbocharger oil mist or characteristic drifted (medium likelihood); Leak at the sensor flange or seal (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode with boost limitation; Jerking under load possible. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00FB – Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
text: P00FB: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High. The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FB means the signal voltage is above its valid range: typically a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, an open ground, or a failed sensor. It does not mean the boost really is too high – that would be P0234. The circuit is monitored continuously from key-on; comparable GM pressure sensors fail above 86–97 % of the reference for about 4 s. The engine then works with a substitute value and may limit boost. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage (high likelihood); Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (oil mist, heat at compressor outlet) (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode with boost limit; Further pressure plausibility codes possible. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00FC – Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
text: P00FC: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic. The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FC covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal that are each too brief for the low or high code, or changes faster than real pressure can move. Comparable intermittent monitors count range violations per drive cycle – Ford's MAP check, for example, sets after 25 events. The FCA case for the sibling code P00F9 was a sensor not fully seated with an unlatched connector, exactly the kind of fault that produces erratic signals; heat and vibration near the turbocharger add to it. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found. Common causes: Connector loose, not latched, or terminals corroded or spread (high likelihood); Harness chafed or broken near the turbocharger (heat, vibration) (medium likelihood); Sensor with internal dropouts (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, possibly only after several drives; Occasional hesitation or brief loss of power under load; Fault comes and goes. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00FD – Battery B State of Charge Performance
text: P00FD: Battery B State of Charge Performance. 'Battery B' here is not a hybrid high-voltage battery (those have codes from P0B27) but, in the only documented use by FCA/Stellantis, the 12 V auxiliary battery of the start-stop system. When the engine restarts automatically, a relay separates main and auxiliary battery so that the auxiliary one keeps the control units stable while the main battery cranks. The engine module sets P00FD if the auxiliary battery is disconnected on the first start, drops below about 8 V during an auto-start, or repeatedly falls below 10.3 V (counter reaches ten). Start-stop is then disabled; often it follows a jump start or many short trips. Whether the MIL comes on is not stated in the sources. Common causes: Auxiliary battery discharged or aged (high likelihood); Loose or corroded positive or ground connections at either battery (high likelihood); 150 A fuse or fuse array in the power distribution centre open or poorly contacting (medium likelihood); Battery separation relay stuck (low likelihood); Main battery faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Start-stop out of service, 'Service Start/Stop' message; Engine does not crank once; 'Service Shifter' message with electronic gear selector. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P00FE – EVAP System Tank Vapor Line Restricted/Blocked
text: P00FE: EVAP System Tank Vapor Line Restricted/Blocked. The evaporative emission system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister and later purges it into the engine. P00FE means the vapour path between tank and canister is restricted or blocked. That matters because a blocked line can hide the tank side from the leak test and disturb tank venting and refuelling. Ford, where P00FE replaces its own code P144A, checks this once per drive cycle during the cruise leak test, while purging with the vent valve closed, and confirms suspicious pressure responses with an intrusive test. VW used the same code on the 2013–2019 Golf, where the diagnosis covers the purge valve and the leak detection module. Typical causes are kinked or pinched lines and charcoal grains from a broken canister. Common causes: Kinked, pinched or misrouted vapour line between tank and canister (high likelihood); Charcoal canister broken down, grains blocking lines or valves (medium likelihood); Rollover or fill-limit valve at the tank stuck closed (e.g. after overfilling) (medium likelihood); Purge valve or leak detection module faulty (low likelihood); Tank pressure sensor reading wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fuel nozzle clicks off early when refuelling; Hiss or vacuum when opening the fuel cap; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P00FF – Body Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
text: P00FF: Body Control Module Requested MIL Illumination. P00FF is an information code in the engine control module: the body control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks over the data bus for the check engine light. The engine module stores P00FF so that a generic OBD scanner can see why the MIL is on; the actual fault is stored in the body control module as B or U codes and must be read there. GM documents two cases – a 2020 Cadillac CT5 with climate flap actuator codes and 2025 full-size SUVs with U1962 – both cured by reprogramming the body control module, not by replacing parts. The mechanism matches other 'module requested MIL' codes such as P069E. P00FF itself causes no limp mode. Common causes: Emissions-relevant fault in the body control module or its sensors/actuators (own B/U codes) (high likelihood); Software or calibration fault in the body control module (medium likelihood); Communication fault on the data bus (low likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on without an engine fault; Other messages depending on the body module fault; Driving behaviour unchanged. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0100 – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit
text: P0100: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit. The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0100 means the control module gets no usable signal at all. Ford uses it for a broken sensing element on digital sensors (period longer than 1.3 ms, i.e. below about 0.78 kHz, for half a second); on GM's 3.0 V6 in the Saab 9-4X it is set at 0 Hz. Many systems with voltage sensors skip P0100 and report low or high directly. The engine then runs on air mass calculated from manifold pressure, throttle angle and speed; Ford also disables start-stop. Common causes: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open (high likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics) (high likelihood); Supply fuse or relay failed (medium likelihood); Control module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value); Hard starting or stalling; Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0101 – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0101: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0101 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the engine's state. GM petrol engines model the expected air flow from manifold pressure, throttle, speed and boost and blame the MAF if it is off by more than 20 g/s; GM diesels check the measured-to-estimated ratio (0.8–1.2) with EGR closed; Bosch ME9 compares it with the throttle angle. Common causes are air leaks after the sensor, a soiled element (oiled sport filters) or a disconnected crankcase vent; GM also documents a bad crimp in the fuse box. Ford uses P0068 instead. Two trips are needed. Common causes: Air leak between sensor and engine (cracked or loose intake duct, boost leak) (high likelihood); Contaminated sensing element (oil from oiled sport filter, dust) (high likelihood); Leaking or disconnected crankcase ventilation (medium likelihood); Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake (medium likelihood); Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, often without driveability problems; Hesitation, flat spot, poor throttle response; Rough idle or stalling; Higher consumption, often with lean codes P0171/P0174. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0102 – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0102: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low. The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0102 means the signal is below its electrical lower limit – a frequency that is too low or a voltage that is too low. Documented limits: GM petrol 450 Hz or less, GM diesel below 276 Hz, Ford digital below 1.5 kHz for 5 s, Ford analogue below 0.244 V. 'Low' describes the signal: typically an open or grounded signal wire, missing supply voltage or failed electronics. Saab notes that a large leak between sensor and throttle can also cause it. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine runs on a calculated substitute value. Common causes: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded or loose (high likelihood); Sensor electronics failed (high likelihood); Missing supply voltage (fuse, relay) or poor ground (medium likelihood); Large leak or disconnected duct between sensor and throttle (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power, hesitation, substitute value mode; Rough idle or stalling; Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0103 – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0103: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit High. The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. title: P0104 – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0104: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. In Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary the code is set once more than 25 short open or short-circuit events have been counted. GM and Saab do not list P0104 in the documents checked; there such dropouts end up under P0102/P0103 or P0101. The trip count is not stated by Ford. title: P0105 – Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit
text: P0105: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit. The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0105 is the general circuit fault and is rarely used today: most petrol engines report low, high and intermittent separately (P0107–P0109). It appears mainly where the fault cannot be broken down further – Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the digital SENT sensor reports a bad status or an out-of-limit value for 5 s (lost communication is a separate U code), and Bosch EDC16 diesels use it with a fault type byte, for example signal below 0.2 V. Saab then substitutes 101.3 kPa, limits torque and switches off EGR and boost control. Common causes: Connector or wiring to the sensor open, shorted or loose (high likelihood); MAP sensor faulty (oiled, failed internally, SENT status fault) (medium likelihood); Sensor hose disconnected, vacuum or boost leak (medium likelihood); 5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same circuit (low likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit (diesel); Rough idle, hard starting, higher consumption (petrol); Smoke possible on diesels. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0106 – Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0106: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0106 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or drifting. Two tests are common. With the engine stopped, all pressures equalise, so MAP must match ambient (and boost) pressure; Ford allows 1.5–3 inHg. While running, MAP is compared with a value modelled from air mass, throttle and speed – GM blames the MAP sensor above about 23–30 kPa error, with two trips on petrol and one on diesel. Turbo engines with three sensors find the odd one out by majority. Besides the sensor, intake or boost leaks often cause it. Common causes: Vacuum leak at the intake manifold or boost leak (hose, clamp, charge air cooler) (high likelihood); Sensor oiled or sooted, port blocked (EGR soot), characteristic drifted (high likelihood); High resistance in signal, reference or ground wire (medium likelihood); Comparison sensor wrong, or mechanical cause (dirty throttle, EGR stuck open) (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle, hesitation, poor response; Higher consumption, black smoke possible on diesels; Loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0107 – Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0107: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Low. The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0107 means the signal voltage is below its lower limit. 'Low' refers to the voltage, not to a real low pressure: typically the signal wire is grounded, the signal or 5 V reference is open, or the sensor has failed. A short on another sensor sharing the same reference can pull it down too, so GM often sees several codes at once. Documented limits: GM below 3.3 % of 5 V (about 0.17 V), GM/Saab 2.0T below 0.19 V for 4 s, Ford petrol below 0.19 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.1 V. GM petrol needs two trips, GM diesel one. A modelled value replaces the reading. Common causes: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open (high likelihood); Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing) (high likelihood); 5 V reference shorted by another faulty sensor on the same circuit (medium likelihood); MAP sensor failed internally (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard starting, rough idle, stalling possible; Wrong mixture from substitute value, higher consumption; Loss of power or limp mode on turbo and diesel engines. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0108 – Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit High
text: P0108: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit High. The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. Common causes: Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded (high likelihood); Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage (medium likelihood); MAP sensor failed internally (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rich mixture, sooting, higher consumption; Rough idle, loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0109 – Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0109: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent. The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. title: P010A – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit
text: P010A: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit. Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010A is the general circuit fault of sensor B: no usable signal at all, just like P0100 for sensor A. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary lists it for a broken element of digital sensor B, with the same limit as sensor A (period above 1.3 ms for half a second); which engines carry sensor B is not stated. GM's twin-turbo V6 only uses the other sensor B codes. The engine can run on values calculated from manifold pressure, throttle and the remaining sensor. Common causes: Connector or wiring of sensor B open (high likelihood); Sensor B faulty internally (broken element) (high likelihood); Supply of sensor B missing (fuse, relay) (medium likelihood); Control module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power, hesitation (substitute value); Rough idle; Start-stop may be disabled. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P010B – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

title: P010F – Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A/B Correlation
text: P010F: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A/B Correlation. Engines with two intake paths have two mass air flow sensors, A and B. On a symmetrical V engine both sides should draw about the same amount of air, so the readings can be compared with each other. P010F is set when both signals are electrically valid but differ by more than allowed; the code does not say which side is wrong. No manufacturer document using exactly this code or its threshold was found: GM's twin-turbo V6 and Nissan's VR30DDTT assess each sensor separately against a model (P0101/P010B). The description therefore rests on the CARB requirement for plausibility checks and on component sources for engines with two sensors. Typical causes are a leaking intake pipe or a soiled sensor on one side. Common causes: Air leak or loose intake pipe on one side (high likelihood); One of the two sensors contaminated or aged (high likelihood); Air filter on one side clogged or wrongly fitted (medium likelihood); Turbocharger or boost problem on one bank (low likelihood); Contact resistance in connector or wiring (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power, uneven running; Mixture codes for one bank (P0171/P0174) possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0110 – Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Bank 1
text: P0110: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Bank 1. Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0110 is the general circuit fault. With a conventional analogue sensor most manufacturers report low and high signals separately (P0112/P0113), so P0110 mainly appears in two cases: with digital (SENT) sensors that combine air mass and temperature, where it stands for lost communication or an implausible status (Ford diesel 2023, after about 5 s), and in some Bosch systems as a collective code whose fault type byte tells open circuit from short to ground. The control module then uses a substitute temperature; some systems also limit torque. Common causes: Connector or wiring to the sensor open or corroded (high likelihood); Sensor or mass air flow sensor with built-in temperature sensor faulty (high likelihood); Sensor supply or ground disturbed (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power or torque limitation on some systems; Otherwise usually inconspicuous; cold start may be slightly worse. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0111 – Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
text: P0111: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1. Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0111 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit. The usual test runs at key-on after a long soak (Ford 6 h, GM 8 h): the intake air sensor is compared with other temperature sensors such as coolant, cylinder head, charge air cooler or IAT2, which should all read about the same. GM flags it above about 25 °C deviation, Ford above about 17 °C; Ford first confirms with a drive above 40 mph because sunshine can warm a sensor, and also sets P0111 if the air reads over 66 °C while driving. A detected block heater suspends the test. Two consecutive trips are needed. Common causes: Sensor drifting or stuck at one value (ageing, oil from crankcase ventilation) (high likelihood); Contact resistance at connector or wiring distorts the reading (medium likelihood); Comparison sensor (coolant, IAT2, charge air cooler) wrong (medium likelihood); Undetected preheater, heat soak or sensor mounted near a heat source (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms; Slightly changed idle, power or cold start possible; Code often returns only after an overnight soak. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0112 – Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low Bank 1
text: P0112: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low Bank 1. title: P0113 – Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High Bank 1
text: P0113: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High Bank 1. title: P0114 – Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 1
text: P0114: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 1. Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0114 covers an unsteady signal. Air temperature changes slowly, so rapid jumps point to the wiring rather than the air. Ford counts short excursions out of range that are each too brief for P0112/P0113 and sets the code after ten of them in one drive cycle. GM evaluates noise within the valid range: if the readings taken every 100 ms add up to more than 80 °C of movement within one second, in four of five seconds, the sample counts as failed. GM needs two trips. Typical culprit is a loose contact that opens with engine movement. Common causes: Loose contact at the connector (corrosion, weak terminal tension) (high likelihood); Partly broken wire that opens with engine movement (high likelihood); Sensor with internal contact problem (medium likelihood); Electrical interference or ground fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms; Occasional brief stumble or rough idle possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0115 – Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
text: P0115: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit. The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0115 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. Today it has largely been replaced by P0117, P0118 and P0119; GM and Ford do not set it in the tables checked. Older or individual systems still use it as a collective code, for example Saab Trionic T5 (1998). The circuit is monitored continuously; when it fails, the module uses a substitute value and many systems run the radiator fan permanently. Common causes: Connector corroded or loose, terminal spread (high likelihood); Broken or chafed signal or ground wire (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (short, open, coolant inside) (medium likelihood); Control module input or 5 V supply faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Poor cold or hot starting; Radiator fan runs constantly; Higher consumption, rough idle; Temperature gauge implausible or dead. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0116 – Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0116: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance. The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0116 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but not believable. Most often it checks for a sensor stuck too warm. After a long soak (GM 8 h, Ford 6 h) coolant must be close to intake air temperature; GM fails it above about 19 °C difference without a detected block heater, Ford if it reads over 110 °C or sits at 79–110 °C. Ford diesels instead check whether coolant warms fast enough in frost. A sensor stuck warm suppresses cold-start enrichment and can defeat the thermostat monitor, which is why CARB requires this test. GM uses one or two trips depending on the engine. Common causes: Sensor drifting and reading too warm (ageing, coolant ingress) (high likelihood); Corrosion or contact resistance in connector or wiring (medium likelihood); Block heater or preheater not detected (medium likelihood); Comparison sensor (intake air, ambient) wrong (low likelihood); Control module calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Poor cold start (too little enrichment); Higher consumption or idle problems; Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0117 – Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low
text: P0117: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low. The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0117 means the signal voltage is too low, so the sensor would report an implausibly hot engine (around 140–160 °C). Mitsubishi then calculates with 80 °C; GM/Saab switch the radiator fan on and the A/C compressor off. GM needs two trips. On Ford engines with a head temperature sensor the equivalent is P1290. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing, pinched harness) (high likelihood); Sensor shorted internally or coolant inside the sensor (high likelihood); Moisture or coolant in the connector (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Radiator fan runs constantly; Hard cold start (no enrichment, engine reported hot); Temperature gauge at hot end; A/C may be switched off. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0118 – Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High
text: P0118: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High. The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. title: P0119 – Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0119: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. Coolant temperature can only change slowly because of the thermal mass involved. P0119 is set when the reading jumps faster than physically possible. GM calculates, every second, a window for the next valid value from the previous reading and a sensor time constant of 13 s; readings outside it in three of four samples count as a fault, monitored continuously over two trips. GM/Saab set it after more than 4 s of abrupt changes and then run the radiator fan. Typical causes are loose contacts or a harness chafing as the engine moves. Common causes: Loose contact or corroded connector pins (high likelihood); Harness chafing that briefly grounds or opens with engine movement (medium likelihood); Sensor with internal crack or contact fault (medium likelihood); Air pockets at the sensor (poorly bled cooling system) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Temperature gauge jumps; Radiator fan switches on for no reason; Occasional rough running or idle fluctuation. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P011A – Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation
text: P011A: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation. Some engines have two coolant temperature sensors that check each other. P011A is set when both are electrically fine but their readings differ more than a calibrated amount under conditions where they should agree. Mazda documents the code for the 2013–2016 CX-5 and 2014–2016 Mazda6: sensor 2 sits in the heater hose, and a clogged heater core keeps it noticeably colder, so P011A often comes with weak cabin heat although both sensors are good. Mazda's check is to compare both sensors with ambient temperature after an overnight soak and then the temperature difference across the heater hoses. A block heater used below 0 °C can also trigger it. Common causes: Clogged heater core or restricted coolant flow at sensor 2 (high likelihood); One of the two sensors drifting (medium likelihood); Air in the cooling system or low coolant level (medium likelihood); Block heater use in frost (low likelihood); Contact resistance at one sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Weak cabin heating (typical on Mazda); Otherwise often no driving symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P011B – Engine Coolant Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation
text: P011B: Engine Coolant Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation. After a long standstill the coolant and the intake air should both have settled close to ambient temperature. P011B compares the two sensors at start-up and is set when they disagree without either sensor showing a circuit fault. In the documented GM/Saab version the engine must have been off for more than 10 hours with no preheater detected; the fault counts if coolant reads at least 20 °C above intake air, or intake air at least 30 °C above coolant, and the coolant reading barely moves (2 °C or less) in the first 45 s. The code does not say which sensor is wrong – that has to be found by comparing both with the actual ambient temperature. Toyota resolved false settings on some 2015 V6 engines with new software. Ford and GM report the same idea under the individual sensor codes. Common causes: Coolant temperature sensor stuck or drifting (high likelihood); Intake air temperature sensor drifting or heat-soaked (medium likelihood); Undetected preheater or uneven cooling (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at a sensor connector or ground (medium likelihood); Control module software (false setting, update available) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving; With a wrong coolant reading: poor cold start, higher consumption or odd fan behaviour; Code often returns only after an overnight soak. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P011C – Charge Air Cooler Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation Bank 1
text: P011C: Charge Air Cooler Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation Bank 1. On turbocharged engines a charge air cooler temperature sensor sits downstream of the compressor, usually after the charge air cooler, and intake air temperature sensor 1 sits upstream near the air filter. While driving they differ by design, because compression heats the air. After a long standstill, however, both should read nearly the same, so the check runs at start-up. P011C is set when the two bank 1 sensors disagree there, without naming the faulty one. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Ford performs the same comparison after 6 hours (tolerance about 17 °C on petrol, 16 °C on the 2023 diesel) but reports the outlier as P007B, P0111 or P00CE. Common causes: Charge air cooler temperature sensor drifting, oily or stuck (high likelihood); Intake air temperature sensor 1 drifting (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at connector or shared ground (medium likelihood); Undetected preheating or uneven cooling (sun, residual heat) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving; Code often returns only after an overnight soak. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P011E – Engine Coolant Temperature 1 / Ambient Air Temperature Correlation
text: P011E: Engine Coolant Temperature 1 / Ambient Air Temperature Correlation. title: P0120 – Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit
text: P0120: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit. Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open). Electronic throttles have two sensors sharing a 5 V reference and ground, usually running in opposite directions – on GM throttle sensor 1 falls from 3–4 V at idle to below 1 V at full throttle. P0120 is the general circuit fault, used when the fault cannot be classed as low or high or when the sensor is digital. Ford sets it on digital SENT throttle sensors when the sensor reports an error for more than 4 s, together with the MIL and wrench lamp; Saab Trionic used it as a collective code. GM and Ford's analogue throttles report P0122/P0123 instead. Electronic throttles then fall back to a spring-loaded limp position with limited power. Common causes: Connector at the throttle body corroded or loose, broken wire (high likelihood); Sensor or throttle body with integrated sensor faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference disturbed (short on another sensor of the same circuit) (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp; Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles; Raised or unsteady idle (cable systems); Poor throttle response, jerky driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0121 – Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance

title: P0124 – Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0124: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Intermittent. Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open). Electronic throttles have two sensors sharing a 5 V reference and ground, usually running in opposite directions – on GM throttle sensor 1 falls from 3–4 V at idle to below 1 V at full throttle. P0124 covers short, recurring dropouts of sensor A. The only manufacturer source naming it is Ford's 2020–2023 summary for digital SENT throttle sensors: an error lasting more than 0.4 s sets P0124, one lasting more than 4 s sets P0120, so brief dropouts are kept apart from lasting faults; MIL and wrench lamp come on. GM does not use P0124 in the tables checked – its low/high monitors already catch intermittent shorts. For analogue sensors the description rests on CARB and component information. Typical causes are loose contacts, a chafed harness or a worn potentiometer track. Common causes: Loose contact in the connector (spread terminals, corrosion) (high likelihood); Chafed or partly broken wire in the harness (medium likelihood); Worn potentiometer track (dropout at a certain position) (medium likelihood); Sensor electronics faulty (SENT) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly only intermittently; Brief hesitation or power drop; Limp mode that disappears after restart; Rough idle. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0125 – Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Closed Loop Fuel Control
text: P0125: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Closed Loop Fuel Control. Closed-loop mixture control using the oxygen sensors is only released once the coolant has reached a minimum temperature. CARB requires that this happens within set times – from 2006 two minutes if the engine starts up to 8 °C below the release temperature, five minutes if 8–19 °C below. P0125 means it took too long. Ford checks once per cold start and fails if coolant is still below 10 °C while its model already expects over 27 °C; Mitsubishi expects about 7 °C within 90–300 s and also fails if coolant drops back below 40 °C. Long idling suspends the test. Usual causes are a thermostat stuck open or a sensor reading too cold. GM does not use this code in the tables checked. Common causes: Thermostat stuck open (especially in cold weather) (high likelihood); Coolant sensor reading too cold or slow (drift, contact resistance) (high likelihood); Low coolant level or air at the sensor (medium likelihood); Much idling or coasting in frost (low likelihood); Engine control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Engine warms up slowly, heater stays cold for a long time; Higher consumption during warm-up; Temperature gauge reads low. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0126 – Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Stable Operation
text: P0126: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Stable Operation. The generic title refers to a coolant temperature that is not reached for stable operation, i.e. for releasing further functions and diagnostics; how manufacturers implement it differs. The only implementation documented in a manufacturer source is Subaru's (via the Saab 9-2X service information): there P0126 is a stuck-sensor check – if the coolant signal changes by less than 5 mV during 20 s of driving or idling after start, the sensor counts as frozen. It runs once per drive cycle, lights the MIL after two consecutive cycles and has no fail-safe mode. Other interpretations, closer to a thermostat check, could not be verified in a manufacturer document. Common causes: Coolant sensor frozen or faulty (resistance does not change) (high likelihood); Thermostat stuck open or low coolant (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in connector or wiring (low likelihood); Engine control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Idle speed stays raised; Engine and heater warm up slowly; Higher consumption. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0127 – Intake Air Temperature Too High
text: P0127: Intake Air Temperature Too High. P0127 is not a circuit fault but a functional check of the air path: the measured intake air temperature is too high for the operating state. The logic is documented for a Bosch EDC16 diesel (Saab 9-3): if the intake air exceeds 130 °C and does not fall below it within 45 s after the exhaust gas recirculation valve is closed, hot exhaust gas is evidently still entering or the sensor is wrong. The engine then disables EGR and runs in limp mode with reduced torque. GM has the code in its diesel software but disabled for US OBD II; Ford reports an overly hot intake air reading as P0111 instead. On other engines a hot reading can also come from warm under-bonnet air being drawn in. Common causes: EGR valve stuck open or not sealing (diesel) (high likelihood); EGR cooler clogged or bypass flap stuck in bypass (medium likelihood); Charge air cooler dirty or airflow through it blocked (medium likelihood); Sensor reading wrong, or hot engine-bay air drawn in (loose intake duct) (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit; EGR switched off; Knock tendency and retarded ignition on petrol engines. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0128 – Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)
text: P0128: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature). After a cold start the thermostat stays closed so the engine warms up quickly. CARB requires the coolant to reach a temperature at most 11 °C below the thermostat's rated value within a set time. GM models the heat put in (fuel energy minus losses to ambient, cabin heater and coasting) and fails if enough energy has gone in without coolant reaching about 65 °C (55 °C in cold weather). Ford compares the measured value with a modelled one, typically failing below 78 °C with an 89 °C thermostat. The test runs once per drive cycle, pauses with much idling or below about −7 °C, and needs two trips. Usually the thermostat is stuck open; a sensor reading too low is the other suspect. Common causes: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early (high likelihood); Coolant sensor reading too low, or corrosion and resistance in its circuit (medium likelihood); Low coolant level or air in the system (medium likelihood); Radiator fan running constantly (relay stuck, wrong control) (low likelihood); Driving pattern or conditions (much idling, extreme cold, strong heating) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Temperature gauge stays low or drops while driving; Heater does not get properly warm; Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0129 – Barometric Pressure Too Low
text: P0129: Barometric Pressure Too Low. The engine control module needs the ambient air pressure for mixture, altitude correction and boost limits. It comes either from a dedicated barometric sensor or from the MAP sensor, read at key-on with the engine stopped and updated at wide-open throttle. P0129 means this value is lower than physically possible – even on the highest drivable passes air pressure stays around 50 kPa, and GM and Ford use 50 kPa as their lower plausibility limit. Usual causes are a MAP or baro sensor reading too low, a blocked sensor port or high resistance in the wiring. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found: GM and Ford file the same finding under P2227. Common causes: MAP or baro sensor reading too low (dirty, oiled, drifted) (high likelihood); High resistance or corrosion in signal wire or connector (medium likelihood); Sensor port or hose blocked (medium likelihood); Control module (baro sensor often built in) or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rich mixture, higher consumption, rough idle; Loss of power (altitude-corrected boost limits). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P012A – Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit
text: P012A: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit. The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012A is the general circuit fault. Ford's 2023 diesels use a digital SENT sensor here and set P012A when its error flag is raised or the value exceeds a limit for 5 s; lost communication is reported separately (U068B). FCA's 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo could set P012A, P012C and P012D falsely and was fixed with new engine software, so the software level is worth checking before replacing parts. GM's supercharged V8 uses only P012B–P012D. A substitute value, usually ambient pressure, is used. Common causes: Connector or wiring open, corroded or shorted (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (SENT sensor reports internal error) (medium likelihood); Control module software (false setting) (medium likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no noticeable symptoms; Power limitation possible. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P012B – Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P012B: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012B is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but stuck or offset. On GM's supercharged 6.2 V8 the sensor must read 50–115 kPa and agree within 10 kPa with MAP and ambient pressure after the engine has been off for more than 8 s; while running, it is compared with modelled values (fault above about 25–30 kPa). GM normally needs two trips, one in some 2019 applications. In operation inlet pressure is slightly below ambient because of filter losses, so a clogged filter or blocked intake lowers it further. Common causes: Sensor oiled (crankcase vent often joins before the compressor) or drifted (high likelihood); Air filter heavily clogged or intake blocked or collapsed (medium likelihood); Leak in the intake pipe between filter and compressor or at the sensor flange (medium likelihood); High resistance in the wiring (medium likelihood); Comparison sensor (MAP, baro, MAF) wrong or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or boost limitation; Possibly no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P012C – Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P012C: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low. The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012C means the signal voltage is below its lower limit – typically a signal wire shorted to ground, an open signal or 5 V reference wire, or a failed sensor. GM's supercharged V8 sets it below 3 % of the 5 V reference (about 0.15 V), with 320 of 400 samples failing, continuously monitored; two trips are normal, one in some 2019 applications. FCA documented false settings on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo that were cured by a software update. A substitute value is used and power may be limited. Common causes: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open (high likelihood); Signal wire shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Sensor failed internally (medium likelihood); Control module software (false setting) (low likelihood); 5 V reference shorted by another sensor (low likelihood). title: P012D – Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
text: P012D: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High. The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors. P012D means the signal voltage is above its upper limit – typically the signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or an open sensor ground that lets the signal rise to the reference. GM's supercharged LT4/LT5 sets it above 97 % of the reference (about 124 kPa) with 320 of 400 samples failing, monitored continuously; two trips on the LT4, one on the 2019 LT5. FCA documented false settings on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo, fixed by new engine software. The control module substitutes a modelled or ambient value and may limit boost. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage (high likelihood); Sensor ground open or connector corroded (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); Control module software (false setting) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power or limp mode possible; Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P012E – Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P012E: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors. P012E covers a signal that jumps or drops out briefly without staying below or above the circuit limits – typically a loose contact. Such intermittent monitors usually count short limit violations or changes faster than real pressure can move. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found: GM handles jumps of this sensor through its range check P012B and the counting windows of P012C/P012D, and Ford's 2023 diesels report their digital sensor under P012A. The description therefore rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information. A substitute value is used while the fault is present. Common causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector (high likelihood); Broken or chafed wire making intermittent contact (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (erratic output) (medium likelihood); Control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Occasional power reduction or boost fluctuation; Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P012F – Engine Coolant Temperature / Engine Oil Temperature Correlation
text: P012F: Engine Coolant Temperature / Engine Oil Temperature Correlation. P012F compares the coolant temperature sensor with the engine oil temperature sensor. The documented user is Ford's Power Stroke diesel. After a calibration update for the 6.0 litre engine, Ford uses it to monitor oil cooler efficiency: if the oil gets much hotter than the coolant at certain speed and load, the oil-to-coolant heat exchanger is probably clogged, and P012F sets together with the wrench lamp. On the 6.7 litre (2015–2018) several bulletins treat P012F as a false setting – partly below 5 °C ambient – cured by reprogramming the engine module. Ford's 2023 diesels run the cold-start comparison of coolant against oil temperature (35 °C limit after 6 h) under P0196 instead. GM does not use the code, and the code does not say which sensor or which system is at fault. Common causes: Oil cooler (oil-to-coolant heat exchanger) clogged – oil much hotter than coolant (high likelihood); Engine module software (false setting, especially in cold weather) (medium likelihood); Coolant or oil temperature sensor inaccurate, or its wiring faulty (medium likelihood); Thermostat stuck open or low coolant (low likelihood); Block heater in use (only coolant preheated) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light and/or wrench lamp (Ford); Raised oil temperature with a clogged oil cooler; Often no driving symptoms when software is the cause. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0130 – O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0130: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1. The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0130 is the general circuit code, and manufacturers fill it very differently. Ford used it up to 2010 as the collective code for all wiring faults reported by the wide-band interface chip and has split it into specific codes since 2011. Subaru sets it when the interface voltages leave their range for 5 s, with immediate MIL. GM calls it 'closed loop performance': cross-talk from the heater (signal rises above 2 V with the heater off) or disagreement with the downstream sensor, two trips. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring. Common causes: Wiring or connector of the bank 1 upstream sensor damaged, corroded or wet (high likelihood); Oxygen sensor faulty internally (high likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or mixture fault (plausibility versions) (medium likelihood); Wrong or aftermarket sensor type (low likelihood); Control module or sensor interface chip faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control); Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure; Sensor and catalyst readiness not set. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0131 – O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0131: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1. The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. On switching sensors it means the signal stays below about 40–60 mV (GM, two trips; some GM engines also require the downstream sensor to read rich at the same time, since a genuinely lean mixture would show there too). On wide-band sensors (Ford from 2011, GM) it has nothing to do with the mixture: the interface chip reports one of the sensor wires shorted to ground. A really lean mixture leads to P0171/P2195 rather than this code. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring. Common causes: Signal wire (or a wide-band sensor wire) shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on exhaust or gearbox (high likelihood); Sensor faulty or poisoned (permanently lean signal) (high likelihood); Large exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or misfires (medium likelihood); Connector wet or corroded (medium likelihood); Control module or interface chip faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control); Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure; Possibly with P0171/P2195. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0132 – O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0132: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1. The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. On switching sensors the signal is above what the sensor can physically produce (about 1 V): Ford above 1.1 V for 10 s, GM above 1050 mV, Saab Trionic above 1.5 V for 5 s. The cause is almost always electrical – the heater supply or battery voltage on the signal wire, or a heater-to-signal short inside the sensor; some GM modules also read an open wire this way. On wide-band sensors the interface chip reports a sensor wire shorted to voltage. If P0132 and P0138 appear together, a shared short in the harness is likely. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to the heater supply or battery voltage (melted or chafed harness) (high likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short) (high likelihood); Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire (GM reads its bias voltage) (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (medium likelihood); Sensor contaminated by silicone, coolant or oil (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Higher consumption, possibly soot or fuel smell; Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure; Often with P0138 or heater codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0133 – O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0133: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 1. The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0133 means the sensor does not react fast enough to mixture changes. Methods differ fundamentally: GM measures passively how long the signal takes to cross 400–600 mV in each direction, averaged over 60 s; Ford forces the mixture to swing at 1.5 Hz and fails a switching sensor whose amplitude stays below 0.5 V, or evaluates response times of a wide-band sensor against a no-fault area; Subaru compares controller activity with measured lambda over 210 s. The test runs once per drive at warm part load; two trips. Mixture control usually stays active, but worse. Common causes: Aged, sooted or poisoned upstream sensor (oil, silicone, coolant, additives) (high likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold gasket, crack) (medium likelihood); Sensor heater weak or intermittent (sensor too cold) (medium likelihood); Mixture fault: air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor (medium likelihood); Wiring resistance or aftermarket sensor with different characteristics (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Slightly higher consumption; Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure; P0420 may follow. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0134 – O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0134: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 1. The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0134 means the sensor delivers no moving signal, typically because the circuit is open or the cell is cold or dead. The control module feeds a bias voltage, and that is all it sees: GM fails a signal stuck at 350–550 mV (or above 1700 mV with a 1.9 V bias) after warm-up, within about 15 s, or a cell resistance above 20 kΩ in hot exhaust; two trips. Subaru's wide-band sensor fails above 500 Ω cell impedance with immediate MIL. Ford's Bosch wide-band systems have used P2237 for this since 2011. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring. Common causes: Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire, connector loose or corroded (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (cell high-resistance, worn out) (high likelihood); Sensor heater faulty – sensor does not get hot enough (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or cracked sensor (low likelihood); Control module bias or measuring circuit faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; No mixture control (open loop), higher consumption; Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0135 – O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0135: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1. The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1) has an electric heater so that it reaches its working temperature of about 300 °C soon after a cold start. The control module switches the heater on the ground side and checks driver voltage and heater current: GM fails it outside 0.3–2.5 A (or 3.1 A) and calls it 'heater performance', Ford outside roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A, Saab Trionic outside 0.5–2.3 A for 5 s. Manufacturers split heater faults differently between P0030–P0032, P0053 and P0135. With the heater dead, closed-loop control starts late after a cold start. If P0135 and P0141 appear together, check the shared fuse. Common causes: Heater element of the sensor burnt out (sensor must be replaced) (high likelihood); Fuse or relay of the heater supply faulty (medium likelihood); Heater wiring or connector open, corroded or shorted (medium likelihood); Unsuitable replacement sensor (different heater resistance) (low likelihood); Heater driver in the control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cold-start phase without mixture control, more fuel and emissions; Follow-up codes P0133/P0134 possible (cold sensor). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0136 – O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P0136: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2. The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0136 is the general circuit code, and its exact meaning varies by manufacturer. Ford sets it as 'no activity' in a functional check: if the sensor never swings beyond about 0.42/0.48 V despite rich and lean phases – if needed after forced enrichment and leaning – once per drive cycle. Opel/GM Europe set it if the average voltage stays outside 400–500 mV after 10 min of closed loop; older Bosch Motronic if it stays at 0 V for 200 s despite heating. GM North America does not use P0136. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Downstream sensor aged or poisoned (stays in the middle band) (high likelihood); Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded (medium likelihood); Sensor heater failed (sensor stays cold) (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (low likelihood); Control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; Slightly higher consumption possible without downstream trim. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0137 – O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P0137: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 2. The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0137 means the signal stays below the lower limit. Documented limits: GM below 40–60 mV (two trips); Ford switches in a pull-up and reads open above 1 MΩ (20 kΩ from 2020) or short to ground below 10 Ω, within 10 s. Subaru uses the code as a functional test instead: the sensor never reaches 550 mV within 200 s after fuel cut-off, i.e. it behaves as if permanently lean – so a real exhaust leak can also trigger it there. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground or melted against the exhaust (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (cracked element, thermal shock from water) (high likelihood); Signal circuit open (counts as low on Ford) (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (lean reading) (medium likelihood); Signal and ground wires swapped after a repair (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0138 – O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P0138: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 2. The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0138 means the signal stays above the upper limit. A zirconia sensor can hardly produce more than about 1 V, so readings above 1.05–1.15 V point to an outside voltage such as the heater supply on the signal wire; GM also sees an open circuit here because of its bias voltage. Ford: above 1.1 V for 10 s; GM: above 1050 mV. Subaru again uses a functional test: the minimum voltage never falls below 250 mV within 200 s after fuel cut-off, so the sensor looks permanently rich. Monitored continuously, two trips. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage (high likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short) (medium likelihood); Signal circuit open or high-resistance (GM bias logic) (medium likelihood); Genuinely rich exhaust or oil/coolant contamination (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0139 – O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P0139: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 2. The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0139 means the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes. Subaru measures it around fuel cut-off: rich to lean from 500 to 300 mV must take no more than 0.51 s, lean to rich from 300 to 500 mV no more than 2 s; two drive cycles set the MIL. CARB requires such a test because a sluggish downstream sensor could let a worn converter pass. Since about 2009–2011 GM and Ford report this as direction-specific codes P013A–P013F instead; P0139 remains in use on older, Asian and Jaguar Land Rover systems. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Sensor aged or contaminated (oil ash, silicone, additives) (high likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (medium likelihood); Sensor heater weak, sensor too cold (medium likelihood); High-resistance ground or connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; P0420 may follow. Repair difficulty: easy.
