title: P013A – O2 Sensor Slow Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P013A: O2 Sensor Slow Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 2. The downstream oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) is used for fine mixture trim and to monitor the converter. 'Slow response' means the signal transition itself is too sluggish – it takes too long to pass between two voltage levels. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, usually tested during deceleration fuel cut-off. GM forces the test itself and measures how quickly the signal passes from 450 to 150 mV relative to air flow; a filtered value above its limit sets the code after one trip (fallback: target not reached before about 60 g of air). Ford measures the slew rate during fuel cut-off, normalised to the converter's stored oxygen. Lexus traced one case to a leaking manifold gasket ahead of the sensor; on Ram diesels it is soot-related. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors). Common causes: Downstream oxygen sensor aged or contaminated (soot, oil, silicone, coolant) (high likelihood); Exhaust leak between manifold/turbo and the sensor (medium likelihood); Converter faulty or non-original with different oxygen storage (low likelihood); Control module software too sensitive (update available) (low likelihood); Sensor connector or wiring with contact resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable change in driving; Catalyst monitor may stay incomplete (inspection readiness missing); With a converter cause, P0420/P0430 may follow. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P013E – O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P013E: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 2. The downstream oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) is used for fine mixture trim and to monitor the converter. Common causes: Downstream oxygen sensor aged or contaminated (soot, oil, silicone, coolant) (high likelihood); Exhaust leak between manifold/turbo and the sensor (medium likelihood); Converter faulty or non-original with different oxygen storage (medium likelihood); Control module software too sensitive (update available) (low likelihood); Sensor connector or wiring with contact resistance (low likelihood). title: P0140 – O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P0140: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 2. The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0140 means the sensor produces no voltage of its own and the control module only sees its own reference (bias) voltage. GM's V6 sets it when the signal sits at 401–548 mV or the sensor's internal resistance exceeds 40 kΩ when it should be hot; newer GM systems apply 1900 mV and read above 1700 mV as an open circuit. Two trips. Ford reports 'no activity' under P0136 instead. A cold sensor with a failed heater can also cause it. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Signal or ground wire open, connector off or corroded (high likelihood); Sensor heater failed, sensor never becomes active (medium likelihood); Sensor worn out (no longer produces voltage) (medium likelihood); Control module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; Live data: sensor 2 stuck at about 450 mV (or 1.9 V). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0141 – O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2
text: P0141: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2. The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 2) has an electric heater so it reaches its working temperature quickly. The control module switches the heater on the ground side and checks both the driver voltage against the commanded state and the heater current. GM fails it outside 0.3–2.5 A (two trips; pure circuit faults are P0036–P0038 there); Ford uses P0141 as its general heater circuit code with a current window of roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A maximum depending on sensor supplier. Without heat the sensor signal is useless, so converter monitoring and trim are suspended. Common causes: Heater element in the sensor burnt out (replace sensor) (high likelihood); Heater supply (fuse, relay) or control wire open (medium likelihood); Short in the heater (current too high) (medium likelihood); Connector corroded, contact resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; Follow-up codes P0140/P0136 possible. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0142 – O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 3
text: P0142: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 3. Sensor 3 is a third oxygen sensor on bank 1, behind a second converter or converter brick. It only exists on some vehicles – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's 3.0 V6 supercharged (2013–2016, where sensor 2 is 'mid-cat' and sensor 3 'post-cat') and Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0142 is the general circuit code of this sensor. Jaguar Land Rover lists it with P0143, P0144 and P0147 for the post-cat sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes. No published thresholds exist for sensor 3; the logic follows the sensor 2 checks (P0136). When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Sensor 3 faulty (thermal shock, ageing) (high likelihood); Wiring or connector under the car damaged or corroded (medium likelihood); Engine module software (Jaguar Land Rover) (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3 (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0148 – Fuel Delivery Error
text: P0148: Fuel Delivery Error. P0148 is an early, rather unspecific OBD II code: the control module finds that the fuel delivered does not match what was requested. Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel (Isuzu) uses it for leak detection: from the balance of quantity and rail pressure it recognises a leak of 90 mm³ per crankshaft revolution, monitored continuously up to 6,400 rpm, and then shuts the engine off – a restart is only possible in the next drive cycle. Ford lists P0148 in the fuel monitor of its 2020–2023 petrol engines, alongside P0171/P0172, without describing the logic. Newer systems usually report such faults more precisely as P0087/P0088 (rail pressure) or P0093 (large leak). Common causes: Fuel leak in the high-pressure or return section (line, rail, injector leakage) (high likelihood); Fuel filter clogged or lift pump weak (medium likelihood); High-pressure or injection pump worn (medium likelihood); Pressure or volume control valve faulty (low likelihood); Air in the fuel system (tank run dry) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Engine stalls or will not restart (Saab: shut-off until next drive cycle); Loss of power, stumbling; Fuel smell with an external leak. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0149 – Fuel Timing Error
text: P0149: Fuel Timing Error. P0149 is a diesel code for a deviation of the actual from the target start of injection. On distributor pumps such as the Bosch VP44, a timing device sets the delivery start, and the pump control unit compares the actual position with the target. On the 2003 Saab 9-3 2.2 TiD (GM/Opel engine) P0149 means injection too early – too late is the manufacturer code P1149; it is monitored continuously above 600 rpm and leads to limp mode with limited fuel quantity. CARB has required injection timing monitoring for all diesels since model year 2010. On common-rail systems timing is mostly covered by injector-related codes, so P0149 is rare there. Common causes: Injection pump wrongly set or drive (belt, key) shifted (high likelihood); Timing device or timing solenoid of the pump faulty (medium likelihood); Air in the fuel or low supply pressure (medium likelihood); Pump control unit faulty (low likelihood); Crankshaft or camshaft signal disturbed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Limp mode with power limitation; Starting problems up to no start; Smoke, knocking, rough running. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P014C – O2 Sensor Slow Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1

title: P0150 – O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 1
text: P0150: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 1. The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. If P0130 and P0150 appear together, look for a shared cause such as supply, ground or the control module. title: P0155 – O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 1
text: P0155: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 1. The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 (sensor 1) has its own electric heater. P0155 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0135: the heater current is outside its window or the driver voltage does not follow the command. title: P0156 – O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2
text: P0156: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2. The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0156 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0136. Ford sets it as 'no activity' when the downstream sensor on bank 2 never swings outside a narrow band around 0.45 V in its functional check, if needed after forced mixture changes, once per drive cycle. Exhaust systems with a Y-pipe have only one downstream sensor, which counts as bank 1. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Downstream sensor aged or poisoned (stays in the middle band) (high likelihood); Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded (medium likelihood); Sensor heater failed (sensor stays cold) (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness not set; Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P015A – O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P015A: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1. The upstream oxygen sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) is the main control sensor for the air-fuel mixture. title: P015E – Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Fuel Timing Control
text: P015E: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Fuel Timing Control. Diesel fuel systems correct injection timing and quantity in closed loop, often with learning routines that run during suitable overrun phases. CARB requires a fault when such feedback control does not start within a manufacturer-defined time. P015E is the code of this kind for injection timing control: the closed-loop correction does not become active in time, or does not learn. It belongs to a family of similar codes – Ford's 2023 diesels, for example, set the sister code P016D when rail pressure adaptation has learned nothing after 300 s. No manufacturer document describing P015E itself, or its threshold, was found; the description rests on CARB and the sister code. Frequent causes are learning conditions that occur too rarely, software, or injectors outside tolerance. Common causes: Learning conditions (overrun phases, temperatures) met too rarely (high likelihood); Control module software (medium likelihood); Injectors outside tolerance or unstable fuel pressure (medium likelihood); Injector wiring or sensors faulty (low likelihood); Engine control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no driving symptoms; Possibly louder combustion noise or uneven running with unlearned injectors. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P015F – Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Cylinder Balance Control
text: P015F: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Cylinder Balance Control. Cylinder balance control evens out the contribution of individual cylinders – on diesels by adjusting each injector's quantity based on crankshaft speed fluctuations. P015F, by its title, is set when this closed-loop control does not become active within the expected time after starting, for example because the crankshaft wheel has not been learned or the conditions are missing. No manufacturer using P015F was found: Ford's 2023 diesels run cylinder balancing (maximum correction 3.5–15 mg per stroke) but report problems as P0263–P0284. The description therefore rests on CARB's requirement for feedback controls and that comparable function; causes are derived, not documented. Common causes: Crankshaft wheel adaptation not learned or speed signal disturbed (medium likelihood); Injector deviating strongly or injector circuit fault (medium likelihood); Control module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly rough idle; Often no symptoms. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0160 – O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 2
text: P0160: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 2. The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor used for converter monitoring and downstream mixture trim; it exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0160 means the sensor shows no change in voltage although it is heated and the engine is in closed loop; the control module only sees its own bias voltage, so the circuit is open or high-resistance or the sensor is dead. On GM's 3.0/3.6 V6 the code sets within 15 s after more than 150 s of running; newer GM systems apply 1900 mV and treat above 1700 mV as open; two trips. Ford does not use P0160 and reports 'no activity' as P0156. A failed heater (P0161) can also cause it. The previous obdex title mixed in 'Slow Response', which is P0159. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded (high likelihood); Sensor dead, poisoned or damaged by thermal shock (high likelihood); Heater failed or fuse blown by a heater short (medium likelihood); Signal wire shorted to voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness for bank 2 not set; Often with P0161 or P0157/P0158. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0161 – O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2
text: P0161: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2. The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 (sensor 2) has an electric heater so that it reaches working temperature quickly. P0161 concerns this heater circuit and its performance. GM measures the current through its low-side driver and fails it outside 0.3–2.9 A on the supercharged V8 (8 of 10 samples, two trips). Ford checks the driver voltage continuously and the current once per drive cycle once the sensor is estimated above about 120 °C; the lower limit is 0.22–0.55 A depending on sensor type, the upper 3 A. Without heat the sensor becomes active late or not at all, so P0159/P0160 can follow; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Heater element of the sensor burnt out (high likelihood); Heater wiring, connector or fuse open or corroded (medium likelihood); Short in the heater circuit (current too high) (low likelihood); Driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Follow-up codes P0159/P0160 possible; Catalyst monitor readiness for bank 2 not set. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0162 – O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 3
text: P0162: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 3. Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode. title: P0165 – O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 3
text: P0165: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 3. Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0165 means sensor 3 reacts too slowly to mixture changes, typically measured around fuel cut-off as for the downstream sensor 2 (Subaru limits for P0139: 0.51 s rich to lean, 2 s lean to rich). No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0162–P0164 and P0167 for this sensor. The description rests on CARB's response requirement for downstream sensors and the sensor 2 logic. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Sensor aged or contaminated (high likelihood); Sensor heater weak (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (medium likelihood); Wiring or connector high-resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst readiness incomplete; Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0166 – O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 3
text: P0166: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 3. Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0166 means sensor 3 shows no voltage change or stays in the control module's bias band – an open or high-resistance circuit, or a cold or dead sensor. For downstream sensor 2 GM sets the equivalent code when the voltage does not change after heater warm-up (within 15 s) or sits at 401–548 mV. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Jaguar Land Rover does not list it and Ford uses only heater codes for sensor 3. A failed heater (P0167) can cause it. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Signal or ground wire open, connector corroded (high likelihood); Sensor dead (high likelihood); Heater failed (sensor stays cold) (medium likelihood); Engine control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Often together with P0167; Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0167 – O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 3
text: P0167: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 3. Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0167 concerns its heater. Ford checks the driver voltage continuously and the heater current once per drive cycle when the sensor is estimated above about 120 °C and has heated for 30 s; below 0.22–0.55 A (depending on sensor type) or above 3 A is a fault, and the heater resistance has its own code (P0061). Jaguar Land Rover lists P0167 for its post-cat sensor of the second bank. A cold sensor can lead to P0165/P0166. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode. Common causes: Heater element burnt out (high likelihood); Heater wiring, connector or fuse (medium likelihood); Short circuit (current above 3 A) (low likelihood); Engine module driver or software (Jaguar Land Rover) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); P0165/P0166 may follow; Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0168 – Fuel Temperature Too High
text: P0168: Fuel Temperature Too High. P0168 is not a sensor fault but an operating condition, almost only on diesels: the fuel temperature sensor reports fuel hotter than a protective limit. The fuel heats up through the return flow from the high-pressure pump and injectors, especially with little fuel in the tank, at idle after full load, in hot weather or with a failed fuel cooler; one manufacturer patent names about 80 °C as the upper limit to protect seals, against a normal range of roughly 5–60 °C. On Saab's Bosch EDC16 diesels the code means an engine protection function is active and injection quantity is reduced. No manufacturer threshold was found, and GM's and Ford's diesel summaries do not use P0168. Whether the warning light comes on depends on the manufacturer. Common causes: Fuel cooler (air or water cooler in the return) dirty or faulty, coolant circuit disturbed (high likelihood); Very little fuel in the tank at high load or heat (medium likelihood); Excessive return flow from worn high-pressure pump or injectors, or faulty overflow valve (medium likelihood); Fuel temperature sensor drifting and reading too high (medium likelihood); Engine overheating or overload (trailer, gradient) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode (reduced injection quantity); Warning light depending on manufacturer; Occurs in heat, at full load, with little fuel in the tank. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0169 – Incorrect Fuel Composition
text: P0169: Incorrect Fuel Composition. According to its title, P0169 means the control module has detected a fuel composition outside what is expected – wrong fuel or an impermissible ethanol or water content – while the composition sensor itself works. None of the manufacturer OBD documents checked (GM, Ford) uses the code: GM reports water or conductive fuel via the ethanol sensor frequency as P2269, and Ford has had no composition sensor since 2000. Claims that diesel makers use it for misfuelling or water could not be verified. The description therefore rests on CARB, which lists the fuel composition sensor as a monitored component, and on component information. Unrecognised fuel usually also shows up as mixture adaptation codes. Common causes: Wrong fuel (E85 in a non-flex-fuel vehicle, ethanol content outside calibration) (high likelihood); Water or contamination in the fuel (medium likelihood); Fuel composition sensor drifting (value in range but wrong) (medium likelihood); Control module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Poor cold start, stumbling, loss of power; Mixture adaptation codes (P0171/P0172); Higher consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P016A – Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control
text: P016A: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control. With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. Closed loop needs a heated, working oxygen sensor and plausible engine data. P016A means the mixture control did not switch to closed loop within the calibrated time after starting; the engine then runs on map values with higher emissions but no actual limp mode. CARB requires this check, and since 2019 also after every automatic restart in start-stop systems. Bentley and other VW group petrol engines set it together with oxygen sensor heater codes when the heater fuse holder was damaged; Ram's 3.0 EcoDiesel listed it in bulletins fixed with new software and sensors. Time limits are not public. Common causes: Oxygen sensor heater not working (fuse, fuse holder, wiring, heater element) (high likelihood); Oxygen sensor sluggish or aged (medium likelihood); Control module software (false setting) (medium likelihood); Engine not warming up (thermostat open, coolant sensor) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Higher consumption after cold start; Often with oxygen sensor or heater codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P016B – Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Rich
text: P016B: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Rich. With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016B means the mixture control as a whole has reached its lower limit: it already removes as much fuel as allowed and the mixture is still rich. In substance it matches P0172, but without a bank reference – for manufacturers whose strategy evaluates the control loop as a whole. CARB requires a fault once the adaptation has used up its range. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Hyundai documents the lean counterpart P016C. Typical causes are those of a rich mixture: excessive fuel pressure, leaking injectors or an open purge valve. Common causes: Fuel pressure too high / high-pressure pump or regulator fault (direct injection) (medium likelihood); Leaking injectors (medium likelihood); Purge valve open (medium likelihood); Oxygen sensor or air flow/pressure sensor offset, control module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Poor cold start, rough idle; Higher consumption, fuel smell; Often together with P0172. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P016C – Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Lean
text: P016C: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Lean. With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016C means the mixture control as a whole has reached its upper limit: it already adds as much fuel as allowed and still cannot reach lambda 1. In substance it matches P0171, without a bank reference. Hyundai documents it on the 2021 Elantra 2.0: if the fuel adaptation was learned wrongly after starts below −10 °C, the engine could stall when stopping or at idle and set P016C; new engine software changed the learning logic. Otherwise the usual lean causes apply: air leaks, low fuel delivery or an air flow sensor reading low. Common causes: Air leak (intake, crankcase ventilation) (high likelihood); Fuel pressure or delivery too low (medium likelihood); Wrongly learned adaptation / control module software (medium likelihood); Air flow or pressure sensor reading low, injectors clogged (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Stalling when stopping or at idle; Rough idle, hesitation; Often together with P0171. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P016D – Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control
text: P016D: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control. Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016D means the pressure control has not settled into closed loop, or has not learned, in the time allowed. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) set it when, within the learning conditions – target rail pressure 600–1300 bar, fuel at most 40 °C – no new adaptation factor has been learned after 300 s; the check only runs while the rail pressure sensor and its supply are fault-free. Ford reports adaptation at its limit separately as P228E/P228F. Use on petrol engines was not found. Often there are no noticeable symptoms. Common causes: Rail pressure sensor drifting (wrong slope) (high likelihood); Volume or pressure control valve sticking or worn (medium likelihood); Unstable low-pressure supply (filter, lift pump, air in system) (medium likelihood); Fuel leak or high injector return flow (low likelihood); Control module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no noticeable symptoms; Occasional power reduction or rough idle. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P016E – Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too High
text: P016E: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too High. Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016E means the controller is already at its limit in the 'reduce pressure' direction and the measured pressure is still above target. That can be real overpressure – a control valve that lets too much through or a blocked return – or a falsely high reading. Volvo and Mack document P016E on their 11 and 13 litre truck diesels together with P0194, caused by corroded contacts at the rail pressure sensor; the fix is a new sensor and internal harness. No public thresholds exist; Ford reports the comparable condition as P228F. Use on passenger-car diesels or petrol engines was not documented. Common causes: Rail pressure sensor or its contacts/wiring (corrosion) giving a falsely high signal (high likelihood); Pressure or volume control valve sticking (lets too much through) (medium likelihood); Return line from control valve or rail blocked or kinked (medium likelihood); Control module software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard combustion noise, knocking; Power reduction (limp mode); Sometimes no symptoms (intermittent sensor fault). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P016F – Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too Low
text: P016F: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too Low. Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016F means the controller is at its limit in the 'more pressure' direction and the actual pressure still stays below target. Which circuit is meant depends on the manufacturer: Volvo and Mack use it for rail pressure, for example as a follow-up when their electronic pressure relief valve stays open (P009B); on FCA's 3.0 EcoDiesel it concerns the regulated low-pressure supply via the fuel pump control module and appears with P025C and P01C6, partly fixed by new engine software. No public thresholds exist. Weak supply pumps, clogged filters and corroded connectors or grounds are typical causes. Common causes: Weak low-pressure supply: lift/tank pump, pump control module, clogged filter (high likelihood); Connector or ground problems (corrosion, water) at pump module, low-pressure sensor or ground point (high likelihood); Pressure relief valve open or its control circuit interrupted (medium likelihood); Worn high-pressure pump or internal leak (medium likelihood); Engine control module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, sluggish acceleration; Hard starting, long cranking, stalling after start; Rough cold idle. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0170 – Fuel Trim Bank 1
text: P0170: Fuel Trim Bank 1. With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0170 is the older, direction-neutral code for 'mixture adaptation of bank 1 out of range'; whether lean or rich has to be read from the trim values. Users are Mercedes-Benz petrol engines, which often set P0170/P0173 instead of P0171–P0175 – a Mercedes-Benz magazine for independent workshops reports that cleaning or replacing the air flow sensor most often cures it – and Ford's 6.7 litre diesel, where it flags a fuel quantity error above 15 % in either direction from its fuel mass observer. GM and Ford petrol engines do not use it. Two trips. Common causes: Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (high likelihood); Air leak or crankcase ventilation leaking (medium likelihood); Injection quantity error (diesel: injector drift, rail pressure sensor; petrol: injectors, fuel pressure) (medium likelihood); Oxygen or NOx sensor offset (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Rough idle or hesitation; Higher consumption; Often no symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0171 – System Too Lean Bank 1
text: P0171: System Too Lean Bank 1. With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0171 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its upper limit: the module already adds the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays lean. GM sets it at a long-term factor of about 1.30–1.36 (+30–36 %, engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; it needs two trips and is suspended during heavy purge flow or intrusive tests. GM bulletins repeatedly trace it to leaking crankcase ventilation hoses or pipes on V6 and V8 engines; Ford found leaking direct injectors. P0171 together with P0174 points to a shared cause. Diagnosis hint: trims very high only at idle and normal under load point to an air leak; trims rising with load point to fuel shortage or an air flow sensor reading low. The oxygen sensor only reports what is in the exhaust and is rarely the cause. Common causes: Air leak after the air flow sensor (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line) (high likelihood); Crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick) (high likelihood); Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air) (medium likelihood); Fuel pressure or delivery too low (weak pump, clogged filter, regulator, tank nearly empty) (medium likelihood); Injectors clogged, or exhaust leak ahead of the oxygen sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Rough or unsteady idle, possibly stalling; Hesitation or lack of power when accelerating; Hissing or whistling from the engine bay (air leak, PCV). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0172 – System Too Rich Bank 1
text: P0172: System Too Rich Bank 1. With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0172 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its lower limit: the module already removes the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays rich. GM separates purge influence carefully: before the first purge it evaluates passively (factor 0.70 or below, i.e. −30 %), afterwards it closes the purge valve briefly for an active test, so a full charcoal canister is not counted as a fault. Ford only evaluates with purge off, at −25 %. Two trips. Bulletins name an open purge valve, leaking direct injectors and, on flex-fuel vehicles, a wrongly learned ethanol content. A permanently rich mixture can overheat the converter and dilutes the oil. Common causes: Purge valve stuck open or charcoal canister saturated (high likelihood); Leaking or dripping injectors (also direct injection) (medium likelihood); Fuel pressure too high (faulty regulator, blocked return, regulator vacuum hose) (medium likelihood); Fuel in the engine oil (short trips, leaking injectors), vapour via crankcase ventilation (medium likelihood); Clogged air filter or intake, air flow sensor reading high; flex-fuel: wrongly learned ethanol content (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Higher consumption, fuel smell; Black smoke, sooted spark plugs; Rough idle or starting problems after refuelling; converter damage possible later. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0174 – System Too Lean Bank 2
text: P0174: System Too Lean Bank 2. With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0174 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0171 and only exists on V and boxer engines with separate mixture control per bank. The limits match: GM a long-term factor of about 1.30 (engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; an older Saab V6 flagged more than 25 % deviation for 20 s. title: P0175 – System Too Rich Bank 2

title: P0176 – Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit
text: P0176: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit. The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0176 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. GM's current documents use P0178/P0179 instead, so P0176 is mainly to be expected on older flex-fuel vehicles or other makes. GM issued a special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models (10 years/150,000 miles) because road salt could make the sensor fail electrically, turning on the MIL and disabling remote start. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information. Common causes: Flex-fuel sensor electrically failed (corrosion from road salt) (high likelihood); Connector or wire corroded, open or shorted (high likelihood); Supply (relay, fuse) missing (medium likelihood); Engine control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Ethanol content in scan data implausible or frozen; Starting problems on E85. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0177 – Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0177: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0177 means the signal lies within the valid frequency range but is implausible – it jumps, changes without a refuelling event or does not match the mixture adaptation. Such sensors measure permittivity, conductivity and temperature and compare them with tables of known blends. GM's documents only list low, high and P2269, so no manufacturer threshold for P0177 was found; the description rests on CARB's rationality requirement and component information. Common causes: Sensor drifting or dirty inside (high likelihood); Water or contamination in the fuel (medium likelihood); Loose contact in the connector (medium likelihood); Control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Wrong ethanol value, stumbling or starting problems; Adaptation codes P0171/P0172. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0178 – Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0178: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Low. The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0178 means the frequency is too low. GM sets it below 45 Hz with 50 of 63 samples failing at 100 ms intervals (about 6 s), monitored continuously with the powertrain relay above 11 V; two trips. 'Low' refers to the frequency, not to the ethanol content: an open wire, missing supply or short to ground gives 0 Hz. The control module then uses a learned or substitute ethanol value. GM's road-salt special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models concerns exactly this kind of electrical failure. Common causes: Signal wire open or shorted to ground (high likelihood); Sensor without supply (relay, fuse, ground) (high likelihood); Sensor electrically failed (corrosion) (high likelihood); Engine control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Ethanol value 0 % or frozen; Starting problems on E85; GM: remote start disabled. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0179 – Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit High
text: P0179: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit High. The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0179 means the frequency is above the physically possible range for E100 plus tolerance. GM sets it between 155 and 185 Hz (50 of 63 samples, two trips); above 185 Hz it sets P2269 instead, because such a high value indicates water or conductive fuel rather than a sensor fault. Typical causes of P0179 are failed sensor electronics or interference on the signal wire. With a falsely high ethanol value the mixture tends to run rich. Common causes: Sensor electronics faulty (high likelihood); Interference or short on the signal wire (medium likelihood); Water or conductive fuel near the P2269 limit (medium likelihood); Engine control module (low likelihood). title: P017A – Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P017A: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit. The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. title: P017B – Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
text: P017B: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance. title: P017F – EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Module Air Filter Restricted
text: P017F: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Module Air Filter Restricted. Leak detection pump modules in the evaporative emission system (for example Bosch's DM-TL, used by VW, BMW, Porsche, Volvo, Mini, Land Rover and Kia/Hyundai) draw fresh air through their own filter, often mounted separately via a hose; at rest the charcoal canister is also vented through it. P017F means this filter is restricted – by dust, mud or water when fitted near a wheel arch. The reference measurement of the pump and the venting are then distorted, and the tank can pull a vacuum. A GM patent describes detection via the pressure difference across the filter during purge (above about 8 inH2O for 10–20 s). No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's requirement to monitor evaporative system components and these component sources. Common causes: Leak detection pump filter dirty or blocked (high likelihood); Moisture or ice in filter or hose (medium likelihood); Hose between filter and pump kinked or blocked (medium likelihood); Pump module faulty (wrong reference) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EVAP readiness not set; Possibly refuelling difficulties (venting); Usually no noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0180 – Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit

title: P0181 – Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0181: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0181 is the plausibility check: after a long standstill fuel temperature must be close to another temperature sensor. Ford's 2023 diesels compare it after 6 h with the charge air cooler outlet temperature (limit 40 °C, or 20 °C without a block heater); GM diesels compare it after 8 h with a reference sensor (20 °C, two trips). Bulletins show other causes: Ford may set P0181 during a running self-test with fuel below 10 °C and warns against replacing parts without a confirmed fault; Nissan Rogues set it because of misrouted wires at the pump unit; Ford's 2018 6.7 diesel needed new software. title: P0184 – Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0184: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. title: P018A – Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit
text: P018A: Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit. Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). Sensor A is the high-pressure rail sensor (P0190–P0194). P018A is the general circuit fault for when a manufacturer does not distinguish low from high. GM and Ford, whose sensor B functions are documented, use P018C/P018D instead, so no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and the component information. When the sensor fails, the control module uses a pre-set value and usually runs the supply pump with fixed control. Common causes: Connector corroded or loose, broken wire (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference disturbed (shared with other sensors) (medium likelihood); Engine or fuel pump control module, or CAN transmission (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no noticeable change in driving; Starting problems or hesitation with fixed pump control. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P018B – Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
text: P018B: Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance. Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). GM checks actively whether the sensor responds: if the pump duty sits at its limit for 5 s or the pressure error varies too little, the module changes pump output and fails the sensor if pressure moves 30 kPa or less – a 'frozen' sensor; two trips. Ford checks the deviation from target instead: more than 20 psi (about 1.4 bar) for 8 s with a plausible target of 35–60 psi, which can also be a genuine pressure problem. A fault-free P018B is a precondition for GM's pump output check (P2635) and Ford's supply checks (P008A/P008B). Common causes: Sensor drifting or stuck (diaphragm, electronics) (high likelihood); Genuine low-pressure fault: weak pump, clogged filter, faulty regulator (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at connector or ground (medium likelihood); Fuel pump control module or its control (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard starting or hesitation when accelerating; Stumbling under load; Often no symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P018F – Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Frequent Activation
text: P018F: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Frequent Activation. Common-rail diesels have a pressure relief valve in the rail – usually a spring-loaded valve, on some truck engines electronically controlled. It opens on overpressure and then holds a low limp-home pressure; every opening wears the seat, and after many openings it may no longer close tightly. P018F means the valve has opened too often: the control module recognises openings from the rail pressure trace (overshoot, then a steep drop to the limp-home level) and counts them. The code therefore usually points to an underlying problem – the pressure control repeatedly lets overpressure build up. No manufacturer document describing P018F was found; the function and counting logic come from patents on large engines (example: opening at about 1950 bar, then about 800 bar). Common causes: Volume control valve sticking – repeated overpressure (high likelihood); Rail pressure sensor reading wrong (controller targets too high) (medium likelihood); Relief valve fatigued, opening too early (medium likelihood); Return blocked or pressure control valve faulty (low likelihood); Load changes or overrun steps with software faults (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Sudden loss of power (limp mode with low rail pressure); Starting problems once the valve no longer seals; Smoke or harsh combustion noise beforehand. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0190 – Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit
text: P0190: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit. The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines – a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference. P0190 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not split low and high; GM and Ford use P0192/P0193 instead. Bosch EDC16 diesels (Saab/Opel 1.9) report P0190 with a fault type byte, and a Saab bulletin traces it to corrosion in the sensor connector, sometimes with no restart for up to 15 minutes. On a sensor fault the engine runs on a calculated pressure in limp mode – on Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel with at most 40 MPa rail pressure and 20 % pedal. Common causes: Connector corroded or water ingress at the rail pressure sensor (high likelihood); Rail pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Harness damaged (heat, chafing) (medium likelihood); 5 V reference disturbed (low likelihood). title: P0191 – Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0191: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines; it is either a three-wire sensor (5 V reference, ground, signal rising with pressure, about 0.5 V at 0 bar) or a digital SENT sensor with two measuring channels. The engine module uses it as the feedback signal for rail pressure control. P0191 means the signal is electrically valid but not believable – stuck, offset or drifting. Manufacturers check it differently: Ford's 2023 diesels and GM's diesels test the offset with the system depressurised (Ford before starting after 10 min and 12 s after switch-off, window about 0.25–0.38 V; GM 6.5–14 % of supply); GM petrol direct injection compares the two SENT channels (limit 1.0 MPa); Saab's V6 diesel flags a large target deviation while the signal barely moves. GM treats it as a one-trip fault. Ford petrol direct injection uses P0087/P0088 instead. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power. Common causes: Rail pressure sensor drifting or stuck (wrong offset at 0 bar) (high likelihood); Genuine pressure fault: high-pressure pump, pressure or volume control valve, tank pump (medium likelihood); Connector corroded, contact resistance in signal or ground (medium likelihood); Fuel shortage or clogged filter (low likelihood); Control module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Limp mode or 'Reduced Engine Power'; Hard starting, stalling; Rough running. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0195 – Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0195: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit. The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0195 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. With analogue sensors most manufacturers use P0197/P0198 instead. The documented use is Ford's 2023 diesels with a digital SENT oil temperature sensor: P0195 is set when the sensor reports a status or data fault for 5 s, while a complete loss of communication is U0667. The module then uses a substitute value (Saab: 100 °C), and functions relying on oil temperature are restricted. Common causes: Connector or harness damaged, corroded or oil-soaked (high likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (electronics fault on SENT sensors) (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or ground problem in the sensor circuit (medium likelihood); Control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer); Oil temperature display missing or fixed; Restricted cam timing, slightly reduced power; Oil life calculation less accurate. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0196 – Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
text: P0196: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance. The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. title: P019A – O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 3
text: P019A: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 3. Sensor 3 on bank 1 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick; it exists on Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (on both banks) and on Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late after a mixture change – unlike 'slow response' (P0145/P0165), where the transition itself is too flat. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, tested during forced fuel cut-off. For sensor 2, GM checks whether the signal falls below 450 mV before a calibrated air mass has passed; behind two converters their oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0142ff/P0162ff for sensor 3 – so the description rests on CARB's response requirement and the sensor 2 logic. There is no limp mode; the converter monitor cannot complete. Common causes: Sensor 3 aged, sooted or oil-poisoned (high likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3 (medium likelihood); Converter with strongly differing oxygen storage (aftermarket or new) (low likelihood); Sensor 3 heater weak (low likelihood); Control module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; No noticeable change in driving; Catalyst readiness not set (emissions test). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P019E – Alternative Fuel Tank A Pressure Sensor Circuit
text: P019E: Alternative Fuel Tank A Pressure Sensor Circuit. These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. CNG is stored at up to about 250 bar (3600 psi); a regulator reduces it to a few bar for the gas rail and injectors. The tank pressure sensor A sits at or in the regulator; together with the tank temperature it gives the gas level, and it decides whether gas operation is possible. P019E is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. Ford's earlier bi-fuel CNG system showed the gauge as empty on a tank pressure sensor fault. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found; GM's bulletins only state that faults are reported like on petrol models. The description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design. Common causes: Connector or harness at the tank pressure sensor (at the regulator) corroded, loose or chafed (high likelihood); Tank pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or ground disturbed (medium likelihood); Engine or alternative fuel control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Gas level gauge wrong, jumping or showing empty; Gas operation blocked or automatic switch to petrol; Dedicated gas engines: limp mode or starting problems possible. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P01A3 – Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit

title: P01A8 – Alternative Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low
text: P01A8: Alternative Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low. These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. P01A8 is not a sensor fault but the gas counterpart of P0087: the measured rail or system pressure stays below target. Typical reasons are a nearly empty tank close to the regulator's minimum inlet pressure, a shut-off valve that does not open fully, clogged high- or low-pressure filters, or a regulator that sticks or ices up when its coolant heating fails. Symptoms: Check engine light on; Automatic switch to petrol or gas operation not possible; Loss of power or hesitation under load in gas mode; Possibly lean codes (P0171/P0174) in gas mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P01A9 – Alternative Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High
text: P01A9: Alternative Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High. These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. title: P01AA – Alternative Fuel Tank Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P01AA: Alternative Fuel Tank Temperature Sensor Circuit. These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. The tank temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor: with CNG there is no float, so the gas level is calculated from tank pressure and tank temperature (GM: full at about 3600 psi at 21 °C, empty at about 400–500 psi). On GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel the sensor is built into the tank and cannot be replaced separately. P01AA is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design. Common causes: Connector or wiring of the tank temperature sensor open, corroded or chafed (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Gas module, CAN link or engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Stored fault code (warning light depending on system); Gas level display wrong; Gas operation blocked, switch to petrol. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P01AF – Alternative Fuel Tank A Level Sensor Circuit

title: P01B4 – Alternative Fuel Rail Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P01B4: Alternative Fuel Rail Temperature Sensor Circuit. These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. The gas rail temperature sensor, often combined with the rail pressure sensor, measures the gas temperature at the injectors: gas cools strongly when it expands in the regulator, and the injected mass depends on density, i.e. on rail pressure and temperature, so the module corrects injection time with it. A Ford patent describes plausibility checks against engine bay temperature at idle and an expected cold rail at full load with a full tank. Roush propane systems report rail temperature faults as P0181–P0183; no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found. P01B4 is the general circuit fault of this sensor. Common causes: Connector or wiring of the rail temperature sensor open, corroded or chafed (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Gas module, CAN link or engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Gas operation blocked or switch to petrol; Mixture errors or stumbling in gas mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01BE – Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 2
text: P01BE: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 2. The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail. P01BE is the general circuit fault of the bank 2 sensor, the counterpart of P0190. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the logic follows the bank 1 sensor and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power. Common causes: Connector or harness of the bank 2 sensor corroded or wet (high likelihood); Bank 2 rail pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or ground disturbed (medium likelihood); Control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Limp mode or 'Reduced Engine Power'; Rough running. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01C3 – Fuel Pressure Sensor A Circuit
text: P01C3: Fuel Pressure Sensor A Circuit. Fuel pressure sensor A is a fuel pressure sensor without 'rail' in its name and without a bank – unlike the rail pressure sensors P0190–P0194 and P01BE–P01C2; which sensor it is depends on the manufacturer. title: P01C8 – Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low Bank 2
text: P01C8: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low Bank 2. Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01C8 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0087: the actual pressure stays below target over time. Typical causes are a weak high-pressure pump on bank 2, a faulty volume control valve, low supply pressure or a leak. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found; the logic follows P0087 and CARB's requirement for pressure control. Not every two-rail engine uses them: GM's LT6 reports bank 2 pressure problems under other codes. Common causes: High-pressure pump of bank 2 weak or worn (high likelihood); Volume control valve faulty or its control disturbed (medium likelihood); Supply pressure too low (lift pump, filter) (medium likelihood); Leak in the bank 2 high-pressure circuit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode; Hard starting, misfires on bank 2. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P01CB – Cylinder 1 Injection Timing Performance - Over Retarded
text: P01CB: Cylinder 1 Injection Timing Performance - Over Retarded. Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor. From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 1 needs clearly more energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too late – GM sets it above 80 µs of extra time, after two trips. Documented users are GM's 6.6 litre Duramax (LML, L5P) and FCA's 3.0 litre EcoDiesel; Ford reports the same function under P2B11ff. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps. Common causes: Injector worn, coked or sticking (opens late, delivers too little) (high likelihood); False setting from software or vehicle vibration (e.g. off-road tyres) (medium likelihood); Wrong injector correction code stored after an injector replacement (medium likelihood); Boost leak or loose injector clamp (low likelihood); Contaminated fuel (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Louder combustion noise or knocking; Rough idle; Possibly smoke. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P01E2 – Cylinder 12 Injection Timing Performance - Over Advanced
text: P01E2: Cylinder 12 Injection Timing Performance - Over Advanced. Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor. From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 12 needs clearly less energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too early or delivers too much – GM sets it below −90 µs, after two trips. No manufacturer document using the codes for cylinders 9–12 was found; the description follows CARB's requirement and the documented measuring principle (Bosch patent, GM tables for cylinders 1–8). Such codes can only appear on engines with at least that many cylinders. Common causes: Injector worn or leaking (delivers too much in small quantities) (high likelihood); False setting from software or vehicle vibration (e.g. off-road tyres) (medium likelihood); Wrong injector correction code stored after an injector replacement (medium likelihood); Boost leak or loose injector clamp (low likelihood); Contaminated fuel (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Louder combustion noise or knocking; Rough idle; Possibly smoke. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P01E3 – Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit
text: P01E3: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit. Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold. CARB requires such additional sensors to be monitored from model year 2019 onwards. P01E3 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; it is described by analogy with its documented sibling codes and the NTC principle. Common causes: Open circuit or loose contact at connector or wiring of sensor 3 (high likelihood); Sensor open or shorted (high likelihood); Short to ground or voltage in the harness (medium likelihood); Control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Coolant temperature or cooling fan behaviour possibly affected; Often no change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01E8 – Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open
text: P01E8: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open. Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports an open control circuit – the module detects missing continuity, typically with the driver switched off. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown. Common causes: Control wire or connector to the heater or relay open (high likelihood); Heater element burnt out or relay coil open (high likelihood); Fuse in the load circuit blown (medium likelihood); Control module output stage faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer warm-up, cabin heat slower in winter; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01F0 – Coolant Temperature Relapsed Below Diagnostic Monitoring Temperature
text: P01F0: Coolant Temperature Relapsed Below Diagnostic Monitoring Temperature. Since model years 2019–2021 CARB requires petrol engines to detect a thermostat fault not only during warm-up but also when the coolant, after reaching operating temperature, drops back below the temperature needed for other diagnostics. P01F0 is this check. GM sets it when coolant falls below 64 °C with a conventional thermostat or 70.5 °C with an electrically heated one (2019 Corvette: 65/78.5 °C) after having been above it, with at least 0.8 km driven, ambient above −7 °C, enough heat input and no long overrun downhill; two trips. GM also uses it on the 6.6 litre Duramax diesel as a 'stuck open thermostat' check. Ford does not use the code in the documents checked. Usual cause is a thermostat stuck open. Common causes: Thermostat stuck open or not sealing (high likelihood); Heated map thermostat, thermal management valve or switchable water pump faulty (medium likelihood); Radiator fan running constantly (relay stuck) (medium likelihood); Coolant sensor drifting cold (medium likelihood); Low coolant or air in the system (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles); Temperature gauge drops while driving; Weak cabin heating, higher consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01F1 – O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 4
text: P01F1: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 4. Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F1 is the general circuit code of this sensor, the counterpart of P0136/P0142 for sensors 2 and 3. Typical causes are an aged sensor, open or high-resistance wiring and a failed heater. Common causes: Sensor 4 aged or poisoned (high likelihood); Wiring or connector open, high-resistance or corroded (medium likelihood); Sensor heater failed (medium likelihood); Control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles); Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P01F5 – O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 4

title: P01F8 – Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
text: P01F8: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High. The engine module switches an electric coolant heater A through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater A are P01E8–P01EB. Common causes: Short or partial short in heater element A (high likelihood); Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated (low likelihood); Heater running without coolant (low level, air pocket) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or warning message (manufacturer-dependent); Slow warm-up, little heat in cold weather; Further heater codes possible (P01E9). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01F9 – Engine Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
text: P01F9: Engine Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High. The engine module switches an electric coolant heater B – a second heater or heating stage – through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater B are P01EC–P01EF. Common causes: Short or partial short in heater element B (high likelihood); Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or warning message (manufacturer-dependent); Slow warm-up, little heat in cold weather. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01FA – Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit
text: P01FA: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit. Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FA is the general electrical fault that the module does not classify as low or high. Without a plausible actual pressure, boost control usually limits boost. Common causes: Connector or pins at sensor B loose or corroded (high likelihood); Harness damaged (5 V reference, signal, ground) (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Engine module or 5 V supply disturbed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, boost limited; Limp mode possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P01FF – Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation
text: P01FF: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation. Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. title: P0200 – Injector Circuit/Open
text: P0200: Injector Circuit/Open. P0200 is the injector circuit fault without a cylinder assignment. The large US manufacturers do not use it – GM and Ford report injector faults per cylinder (P0201 ff) or as faults of the shared injector supply (P062D/P062E, P2146 ff). Saab documents it on the 3.0 V6 diesel of the 9-5, whose injectors are driven by a separate power stage behind the glovebox: there P0200 means an electrical fault in that power stage or its wiring, and the engine is shut down. Generally the cause lies in something all injectors share – supply, fuse, relay, ground or driver stage – so several cylinders are affected at once. CARB does not require separate codes for each kind of circuit fault. Common causes: Shared injector supply open (fuse, relay, harness connector) (high likelihood); Separate injector power stage or its wiring faulty (diesel) (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the engine module faulty (low likelihood); Ground fault of the module or power stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Engine does not start or shuts down; Severe misfire on several cylinders; Limp mode, loss of power. Repair difficulty: medium.
