title: P02EC – Diesel Intake Air Flow A Control System - High Air Flow Detected
text: P02EC: Diesel Intake Air Flow A Control System - High Air Flow Detected. Ford's 6.7 and 3.0 diesels control the air mass through the EGR valve and the intake throttle. P02EC means the measured air mass stays above target with the control at its limit – too little EGR, or the throttle cannot restrict enough – for 10 s (6.7) or 5 s (3.0). Typical causes are a stuck-closed EGR valve or clogged EGR cooler, a throttle stuck open or a mass airflow sensor reading too high. NOx rises; driving is usually unaffected. Other manufacturers using this code were not found. Common causes: EGR valve stuck closed or EGR cooler clogged (high likelihood); Intake throttle stuck open (P02E4) (medium likelihood); Mass airflow sensor reading too high (medium likelihood); Boost too high (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Higher NOx; Often no change in driving. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P02EE – Cylinder 1 Injector Circuit Range/Performance
text: P02EE: Cylinder 1 Injector Circuit Range/Performance. P02EE reports an electrically implausible response of the cylinder 1 injector – not an open or short circuit (those are P0201, P0261, P0262), but a current or voltage pattern outside the expected range. GM's 8-cylinder diesel checks the time the current takes to fall from hold to zero (outside 20–50 µs in 10 of 20 samples, two trips); GM's petrol direct injection evaluates the voltage feedback of the opening and closing; Ford's diesels flag the injector's voltage or charge regulator at its limit (90 s), Ford's petrol direct injection its controlled-valve-operation adaptation at its limit. The injector may be shut off, causing misfire. Common causes: Injector electrically aged (piezo capacitance, coil resistance) (high likelihood); Contact resistance in the injector 1 connector or wiring (medium likelihood); Injector mechanically sticking (valve lift) (medium likelihood); Injector driver stage in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running, misfire on cylinder 1; Loss of power, smoke (diesel). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P02F5 – Cylinder 8 Injector Circuit Range/Performance
text: P02F5: Cylinder 8 Injector Circuit Range/Performance. P02F5 reports an electrically implausible response of the cylinder 8 injector – not an open or short circuit (those are P0208, P0282 and P0283), but a current or voltage pattern outside the expected range. GM's 8-cylinder diesel checks the time the current takes to fall from hold to zero (outside 20–50 µs in 10 of 20 samples, two trips); GM's petrol direct injection evaluates the voltage feedback of opening and closing; Ford's diesels flag the injector's voltage or charge regulator at its limit (90 s), Ford's petrol direct injection its controlled-valve-operation adaptation at its limit. The injector may be shut off, causing misfire. Common causes: Injector electrically aged (piezo capacitance, coil resistance) (high likelihood); Contact resistance in the injector 8 connector or wiring (medium likelihood); Injector mechanically sticking (valve lift) (medium likelihood); Injector driver stage in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running, misfire on cylinder 8; Loss of power, smoke (diesel). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P02FA – Diesel Intake Air Flow Position Sensor Minimum/Maximum Stop Performance
text: P02FA: Diesel Intake Air Flow Position Sensor Minimum/Maximum Stop Performance. The diesel intake throttle learns the position sensor values of its end stops, as a Toyota patent describes for the closed stop at engine stop. P02FA means a learned end-stop value is implausible. Ford's 6.7 and 3.0 diesels check it once after each learning run and set the code when the learned minimum offset is outside ±10 (6.7) or ±6.7 (3.0) – Ford only evaluates the minimum stop. Typical causes are soot and oil deposits at the flap and stop, a worn or shifted sensor, mechanical damage or a replacement part that has not been learned. EGR control may be restricted. Common causes: Soot and oil deposits at flap and stop (EGR, crankcase ventilation) (high likelihood); Position sensor in the throttle unit worn or shifted (medium likelihood); Flap or shaft bent, stop worn, gear worn (medium likelihood); Wrong or not learned replacement part (low likelihood); Engine software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no noticeable driving problems; EGR control restricted, filter regeneration hindered. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P02FB – Cold Start Fuel Injection Control Circuit/Open
text: P02FB: Cold Start Fuel Injection Control Circuit/Open. Cold start fuel injection is an extra injection system for cold starts – for example on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends, where a Hyundai patent describes a small auxiliary tank, a cold-start injector and a heater. CARB lists such heated fuel preparation systems among the monitored output components. P02FB means the control circuit of the cold-start injection is open or has a general fault – a broken coil, a loose or corroded connector or a broken wire. The engine then starts poorly or not at all in the cold; once warm it runs normally. No manufacturer document using this code was found; unlike the older P0213/P0214, these codes separate the fault types. Common causes: Coil of the cold-start injector or valve open (high likelihood); Connector loose, corroded or pin pushed back (medium likelihood); Broken wire in the harness (medium likelihood); Fuse or relay of the cold-start system (low likelihood); Driver stage in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard or no start in cold weather (especially with high ethanol); Rough running right after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P02FF – Propulsion System Inactive Timer Performance
text: P02FF: Propulsion System Inactive Timer Performance. Many diagnostics need to know how long the engine – or, on hybrids, the whole propulsion system – has been off: thermostat and evaporative checks and the cold-start strategy, for which CARB requires at least 6 hours of standstill. A timer measures this time, and the engine module checks its plausibility, for example against coolant cooling – a GM patent describes such a check. P02FF means that timer is implausible. Mercedes documents it on M256, M260, M264 and M274 engines of around 2020: after an internal reset the instrument cluster clock ran wrong; the fix is a software update for engine, transmission and instrument cluster modules. Readiness of standstill-dependent monitors may stay incomplete. Common causes: Time source in another module (instrument cluster, body module) gives an implausible time after a reset or voltage loss (high likelihood); Software level of engine, transmission or instrument cluster module (high likelihood); Battery discharged or disconnected, voltage dips (medium likelihood); Instrument cluster or timer in the engine module faulty (low likelihood); Coolant temperature sensor distorting the cooling check (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, otherwise usually nothing noticeable; Clock in the instrument cluster wrong or reset; Readiness of standstill-dependent monitors incomplete. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0300 – Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected
text: P0300: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected. The engine module detects misfire from crankshaft speed: a cylinder that does not fire gives no acceleration impulse. At a catalyst-damaging rate (CARB: at least 5 % per 200 revolutions) the warning light flashes; at an emissions-relevant rate (at least 1 % per 1,000 revolutions – GM about 2–5 %, Ford 0.9–1.5 %) it comes on after two trips. Ford and GM may shut off a misfiring cylinder's injector to protect the catalyst. P0300 sets when the misfire cannot be assigned to one cylinder: several cylinders each account for more than 10 %, the cylinder changes randomly, or – at Ford – the cylinder cannot be identified at high speed. It often appears together with cylinder codes. Causes are usually systemic: false air, worn plugs on several cylinders, fuel pressure or fuel quality, valve timing – and false detection from a damaged tone wheel, rough roads or vibration. Bulletins name coils, cracked plug insulators and wrong plug gaps. Common causes: False air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket) (high likelihood); Worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils (high likelihood); Fuel pressure too low or high, contaminated fuel (medium likelihood); Valve timing (stretched chain), valves, compression on several cylinders (low likelihood); False detection: tone wheel or pulley, rough road, vibration, software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate; Rough idle, jerking, vibration; Loss of power, hesitation; Smell of unburnt fuel, higher consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0301 – Cylinder 1 Misfire Detected
text: P0301: Cylinder 1 Misfire Detected. The engine module detects misfire from crankshaft speed: a cylinder that does not fire gives no acceleration impulse. At a catalyst-damaging rate (CARB: at least 5 % per 200 revolutions) the warning light flashes; at an emissions-relevant rate (at least 1 % per 1,000 revolutions – GM about 2–5 %, Ford 0.9–1.5 %) it comes on after two trips. Usual causes are the ignition coil or spark plug of that cylinder, its injector, or low compression; a quick test is to swap coil or plug with a neighbouring cylinder and see whether the misfire moves. title: P030A – Ignition A Control Signal Circuit/Open
text: P030A: Ignition A Control Signal Circuit/Open. Ignition A is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P030A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff (open above 30 kΩ, first trip), so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst. Common causes: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin) (high likelihood); Ignition module or coil with integrated driver of this group faulty (medium likelihood); Supply or ground of the ignition module faulty (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Misfire, jerking, rough idle; Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off; Additional misfire codes P0300 ff. Repair difficulty: medium.

The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P030B means the control line reads low – typically shorted to ground. title: P0310 – Cylinder 10 Misfire Detected
text: P0310: Cylinder 10 Misfire Detected. The engine module detects misfire from crankshaft speed: a cylinder that does not fire gives no acceleration impulse. At a catalyst-damaging rate (CARB: at least 5 % per 200 revolutions) the warning light flashes; at an emissions-relevant rate (at least 1 % per 1,000 revolutions – GM about 2–5 %, Ford 0.9–1.5 %) it comes on after two trips. Ford and GM may shut off a misfiring cylinder's injector to protect the catalyst. P0310 means more than 90 % of the detected misfires fall on cylinder 10. Usual causes are the ignition coil or spark plug of that cylinder, its injector, or low compression; a quick test is to swap coil or plug with a neighbouring cylinder and see whether the misfire moves. Cylinder 10 exists on ten-cylinder engines such as Ford's 6.8 litre V10; there an under-torqued crankshaft pulley bolt and engine software caused false misfire codes on all cylinders. Common causes: Ignition coil of cylinder 10 faulty (coil, connector, ground) (high likelihood); Spark plug of cylinder 10 worn, sooted, cracked or wrongly gapped (high likelihood); Injector of cylinder 10 clogged or leaking, or its control (medium likelihood); Low compression on cylinder 10 (valve, rings, head gasket) or local false air (low likelihood); Water or oil in the plug well (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate; Rough idle, jerking, vibration; Loss of power, hesitation; Smell of unburnt fuel, higher consumption. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0313 – Misfire Detected with Low Fuel
text: P0313: Misfire Detected with Low Fuel. When the tank is nearly empty the fuel pump can draw air in corners or on gradients, which causes misfires. CARB allows misfire detection to be switched off at 15 % fuel or less; some manufacturers instead report misfires detected in this state under P0313 rather than P030x. Ford's normal misfire monitor runs from 15 % fuel, Saab's ME9 from 12 %; Saab's T8 sets P0313 below 5 litres with the same tests as P0300 (3 % per 1,000 revolutions, flashing light at a catalyst-damaging rate). GM petrol engines simply suspend the monitor without their own code. After refuelling the symptoms usually disappear – if not, look for a real misfire cause. Common causes: Tank nearly empty – the fuel pump draws air (corners, gradients, braking) (high likelihood); Actual misfire cause (ignition, injector, false air) that happened at low fuel (medium likelihood); Weak fuel pump, clogged strainer or filter, faulty swirl pot (medium likelihood); Fuel level sender reading too low (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate); Jerking or power loss with an almost empty tank, especially in corners or uphill; Usually no symptoms after refuelling. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0314 – Single Cylinder Misfire (Cylinder Not Specified)
text: P0314: Single Cylinder Misfire (Cylinder Not Specified). P0314 means the misfire is attributable to a single cylinder, but the module does not say which one. CARB generally requires cylinder-specific codes and allows a general code only with approval where the cylinder cannot be identified reliably; for diesels identification is required only where possible without extra hardware. GM and Ford do not use P0314. It is documented on Saab's 2.2 TiD diesel with a Bosch distributor pump, as a mechanical misfire fault in two speed and quantity windows with the warning light and limp mode limiting injection quantity; the cylinder can still be read out with a scan tool. Typical causes are a faulty injector, leaking high-pressure lines, air or water in the fuel, or low compression. Common causes: Injector of one cylinder clogged or leaking (diesel), or coil/plug (petrol) (high likelihood); Leaking high-pressure line, fuel bridge or injector washer (medium likelihood); Air, water or petrol in the diesel, clogged filter, low supply pressure (medium likelihood); Compression loss (valve, piston) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, limp mode with quantity limit (Saab diesel); Rough running, vibration. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0315 – Crankshaft Position System Variation Not Learned
text: P0315: Crankshaft Position System Variation Not Learned. Manufacturing tolerances of the crankshaft tone wheel distort the speed fluctuations misfire detection relies on, so the engine module learns a correction for each tooth or segment. P0315 means these values have not been learned or are invalid. GM checks that the learned tooth angles add up to 360° (deviation above 0.001° sets the code in the first trip) and learns them with a scan tool: brakes held, full throttle in park until fuel cut-off. Ford learns the profile during up to three overrun phases from 60 to 40 mph and sets P0315 when that fails. Until relearned, misfire detection is suspended – at GM above 1,000 rpm – and misfire readiness stays incomplete. The relearn is needed after replacing the engine, engine module, crankshaft, damper or crankshaft sensor. Common causes: Relearn not performed after replacing sensor, crankshaft, damper, engine or engine module (high likelihood); Learned values lost through voltage loss (battery disconnected) (medium likelihood); Tone wheel damaged or shifted, crankshaft runout, dirt on the sensor (medium likelihood); Interference in the crankshaft sensor circuit (low likelihood); Engine module memory faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (GM; Ford depending on application); Driving usually unaffected; Misfire readiness not set – emissions test fails. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0316 – Engine Misfire Detected on Startup (First 1000 Revolutions)
text: P0316: Engine Misfire Detected on Startup (First 1000 Revolutions). P0316 concerns misfire within the first 1,000 revolutions after start. CARB requires a pending code here after the first exceedance of the emissions-relevant rate (later in the drive only after the fourth) and the warning light if it recurs at the next start. Ford sets P0316 in addition to the cylinder code; GM evaluates the start within P0300–P0308 without its own code. Typical causes are water in the plug wells (Mazda Tribute bulletin: blocked drain in the valve cover channel), coils that arc when cold and damp, injectors that drip after switch-off and over-rich starting – Ford traced cases on the 2.7 EcoBoost to engine software or leaking direct injectors. Common causes: Moisture or water in the plug wells, coils arcing when cold or damp (high likelihood); Leaking injectors (fuel drips after switch-off, over-rich start) (medium likelihood); Worn or sooted spark plugs that only fire cleanly when warm (medium likelihood); Wrong temperature sensor value or engine software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (usually with P0300/P030x); Rough running right after a cold start, then normal; Delayed start, fuel smell at start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0317 – Rough Road Hardware Not Present
text: P0317: Rough Road Hardware Not Present. Misfire detection works from crankshaft speed fluctuations, which rough roads also cause. CARB therefore allows misfire detection to pause on rough roads; many engines take a rough-road signal from the wheel speeds of the ABS module, a Ford patent describes such a detector. P0317 means the engine module is calibrated for an external rough-road signal but does not find the hardware: the supplying module does not respond on the data bus, or the configuration does not match the equipment – for example after replacing the engine or ABS module. Without the signal misfire detection cannot separate road bumps from misfires. No manufacturer document using P0317 was found; the description follows CARB and GM's rough-road sources in its misfire monitor. Common causes: Module configuration does not match the equipment (after engine or ABS module replacement) (high likelihood); ABS/ESP module not responding (supply, CAN line) (medium likelihood); Separate rough-road sensor missing or unplugged, where fitted (low likelihood); Engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light (manufacturer-dependent); Misfire readiness not set; Possibly false misfire codes on rough roads. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0318 – Rough Road Sensor A Signal Circuit
text: P0318: Rough Road Sensor A Signal Circuit. Misfire detection works from crankshaft speed fluctuations, which rough roads also cause. CARB therefore allows misfire detection to pause on rough roads; many engines take a rough-road signal from the wheel speeds of the ABS module, a Ford patent describes such a detector. P0318 means rough-road signal A is missing or invalid. On GM engines (documented in Saab service information for the 1.6 turbo) the brake control module sends wheel speed over the data bus; the code sets between 1,520 and 4,000 rpm when that module reports a wheel speed sensor fault or no signal arrives for more than 5 s. GM files it without the warning light. Misfire detection then runs without its rough-road filter. ABS or stability warnings and further codes often appear at the same time. Common causes: Wheel speed sensor or wiring faulty – the brake module passes on the fault (high likelihood); Communication between engine and brake module lost (CAN, connector, supply) (medium likelihood); Brake control module faulty (low likelihood); Separate rough-road sensor faulty, where fitted (low likelihood). Symptoms: Service message (GM without warning light); Often ABS or stability warning at the same time; Driving unaffected. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0320 – Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit
text: P0320: Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit. P0320 originally covered the engine speed signal from the distributor or ignition module to the engine module (early OBD II); today Ford's engine module evaluates the crankshaft sensor directly and uses this code for it. Ford checks continuously from 200–500 rpm and sets it within 5 s when the number of teeth after the gap is wrong, the tooth time is implausible (below 30 or above 9,000 rpm) or the gap appears in the wrong place; fuel and spark are then cut briefly to resynchronise, and on electronic throttle P2106 limits power. Some Ford engines use P0339 instead. Typical causes are a faulty crankshaft sensor, interference in the wiring or a damaged tone wheel. Common causes: Crankshaft or distributor speed sensor faulty or wrong air gap (high likelihood); Wiring, connector or shielding disturbed (loose contact, interference from ignition or radios) (high likelihood); Tone wheel damaged or dirty (missing tooth, metal chips) (medium likelihood); Ignition module faulty on older vehicles (medium likelihood); Engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Engine dies or stumbles briefly; Starting problems, tachometer twitching; Reduced power on electronic throttle (Ford P2106). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0321 – Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0321: Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit Range/Performance. P0321 belongs to the same signal as P0320 and P0322: the speed and reference input of the ignition, formerly the distributor's Hall pickup, today practically always the crankshaft position sensor. Range/Performance means a signal is present but implausible – wrong number of teeth between the reference gaps, erratic tooth times, or a speed that does not fit the camshaft signal. No manufacturer document available to us describes P0321 by code: Ford runs these tooth checks under P0320 or P0339 (wrong tooth count after the gap, tooth time outside 30 to 9,000 rpm, gap at the wrong position) and GM under P0336. The description therefore follows that logic and CARB's rationality requirement for crank angle sensors. Common causes: Crankshaft position sensor faulty or aged (weak, noisy signal) (high likelihood); Sensor loose or air gap wrong (medium likelihood); Tone wheel damaged or clogged with metal chips (medium likelihood); Interference, poor ground or damaged wiring (medium likelihood); Engine module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Jerking, misfire or brief stalling; Hard starting, long cranking; Tachometer flickers or drops out. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0322 – Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit No Signal
text: P0322: Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit No Signal. P0322 means the speed and reference input of the ignition – today the crankshaft position sensor – delivers no signal although the engine is turning. Ford proves the rotation with the camshaft sensor: if it shows more than one engine revolution without a crank signal (from 500 rpm, detected within 5 s), Ford sets P0322 or, depending on the engine, P0335; with electronic throttle the throttle software adds P2106 and goes into limp mode. Without a crank signal there is no ignition or injection, so the engine stalls or does not start. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) sets P0322 when the engine fails to start; its inductive sensor should measure 500–600 Ω and give 2–5 V AC while cranking. Systems without a camshaft-based check may store no code at all on a total failure. Common causes: Crankshaft position sensor failed (often heat-related) (high likelihood); Open or short in signal, ground or 5 V supply, corroded connector (high likelihood); Sensor loose, air gap too large or tone wheel damaged (medium likelihood); 5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same supply (low likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine cranks but does not start; Engine stalls while driving; Tachometer shows zero; Check engine light on, with electronic throttle limp mode (P2106). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0323 – Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit Intermittent
text: P0323: Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit Intermittent. P0323 stands for a speed and reference signal at the ignition input – today the crankshaft position sensor – that drops out or is disturbed for moments and then recovers. None of the manufacturer documents available to us (GM 2014–2019, Ford 2012 and 2020–2023, Saab workshop information) uses P0323; the sporadic crank sensor check runs under P0339 at Ford and under P0336 at GM. Ford's logic shows what is evaluated: teeth missing or extra for a moment and the reference gap appearing at an unexpected position, after which the module briefly cuts fuel and spark and resynchronises. Typical causes are a loose contact, chafed wiring and electrical interference. The code itself is described only by its J2012 name and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. Common causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector (high likelihood); Chafed wiring, break under vibration (medium likelihood); Sensor dropping out when hot (medium likelihood); Interference from neighbouring wires (low likelihood). Symptoms: Brief stumbling or stalling, then normal again; Sporadic misfire; Tachometer flickers; Check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0324 – Knock/Combustion Vibration Control System Error
text: P0324: Knock/Combustion Vibration Control System Error. P0324 concerns the knock control as a whole rather than a single sensor circuit. GM and Saab's GM-based engines set it when excessive knock persists on one cylinder – knock despite ignition retard, or mechanical noise taken for knock – for more than 8–10 s; GM's 2018 engines in the first trip, older ones after two. Older GM calibrations also flag an abnormally low or flat signal per cylinder here. Ignition is retarded. Typical causes are low-octane fuel, carbon deposits, high intake or coolant temperature, lean running, or loose parts and valve train noise. Ford does not use this code; GM reports internal processor faults separately (P06B6/P06B7). Common causes: Genuine knock: low-octane fuel, carbon deposits, high intake or coolant temperature, lean mixture (high likelihood); Mechanical noise taken for knock (loose parts, brackets, valve train, bearings) (medium likelihood); Knock sensor damaged, wrongly torqued or mounted with sealant (medium likelihood); Engine software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power from ignition retard; Audible pinging or knocking under load; Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0325 – Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor A Circuit
text: P0325: Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor A Circuit. The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor A is the first sensor (bank 1 or a single sensor). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P0325 means the sensor circuit is open or the signal stays below the noise threshold. GM feeds a 20 kHz test signal into the circuit and detects an open circuit when it does not cancel out, setting the code in the first trip; Ford sees any open or short as a knock signal that is too small compared with the speed- and load-dependent noise level (at least 1,500 rpm, 35 % load, warm engine). Bulletins name moisture in the sensor (VW Touareg 3.6), engine software (GM Malibu 1.5) and chafed wiring (FCA). Common causes: Wiring or connector chafed, broken or corroded (sensor often under the intake manifold) (high likelihood); Knock sensor faulty (cracked piezo, moisture, heat damage) (medium likelihood); Sensor loose or wrongly torqued (medium likelihood); Engine software or diagnostic calibration (low likelihood); Engine module input stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard; Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P032F – Combustion Engine Producing Insufficient Torque
text: P032F: Combustion Engine Producing Insufficient Torque. P032F is a plausibility code: the engine module compares the torque the combustion engine actually delivers with the expected or requested torque. On hybrids the actual torque can be measured precisely through the generator; if it stays too low for a calibrated time, the code sets. Ford uses it on the 2.5 litre Escape, Corsair and Maverick hybrids: after recall 23V-380 the software detects internal engine damage such as connecting rod bearing failure and can then shut the engine down – P032F appears together with Ford's P1061; another bulletin fixes false setting by software. Stellantis lists it on the Ram 6.7 Cummins for engine stall detection. Thresholds are not published. Common causes: Internal mechanical engine damage (connecting rod bearings, crank drive) (high likelihood); Engine software (false setting) (medium likelihood); Poor combustion (misfire, fuel or air shortage, low compression) (medium likelihood); Increased internal friction (wrong oil, seizing parts) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light and warning (Ford: wrench, stop safely); Reduced power, combustion engine shut off; Knocking or metallic noise from the engine. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0335 – Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit
text: P0335: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit. The crankshaft position sensor reads a tone wheel with a reference gap (GM 58X, i.e. 60-2; Ford 36-1, 40-1 or 60-2) and gives the engine module speed and crank angle for injection and ignition. P0335 means it delivers no pulses although the engine demonstrably turns. GM proves the rotation via starter, camshaft pulses or airflow above 1.5 g/s and sets the code after at least 4 s of cranking or 0.3 s while running without a crank pulse (2 of 10 revolutions); petrol engines after two trips, the LML diesel in the first. Ford compares with the camshaft: more than one revolution without a crank signal, detected within 5 s. Without the signal the engine stalls or does not start; GM Global A engines (Saab 9-5 2010) keep running only with learned cam positions. A hot sensor that fails and recovers after cooling is typical. Common causes: Crankshaft position sensor faulty (heat, age – typical hot-start failure) (high likelihood); Connector or wiring corroded, chafed, oil-soaked or open (high likelihood); 5 V reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply (medium likelihood); Tone wheel damaged, loose or clogged with chips; air gap wrong after engine work (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine cranks but does not start; Engine stalls while driving or at idle; Hot-start problem: starts again after cooling down; Tachometer drops out, check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0336 – Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0336: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. P0336 means the crankshaft position sensor delivers pulses, but their pattern is implausible: the reference gap is missing or in the wrong place, the number of teeth between the gaps is wrong (58 on a 60-2 wheel) or the module keeps losing synchronisation. GM sets it after at least 4 resynchronisations in under 5 s, a gap not found within 0.4 s running or 1.5 s cranking, or a wrong tooth count in 8 of 10 revolutions, after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesel sets it when the gap of the 60-2 wheel is not recognised for 3 revolutions; GM's LML diesel uses a fault counter over tooth times. Ford petrol engines use P0320 or P0339 for the same checks. Result: misfire, jerking, brief cut-outs while the module resynchronises, and misfire detection is suspended. Common causes: Tone wheel damaged, bent, loose or teeth clogged with chips (high likelihood); Sensor signal weak or noisy (air gap, ageing) (high likelihood); Interference, poor ground or shielding (medium likelihood); Wrong tone wheel or flywheel fitted after a repair (medium likelihood); Loose contact in the connector (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Misfire, jerking, rough running; Engine stalls sporadically; Hard starting; Check engine light on, misfire codes may be added. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0337 – Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0337: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Low. By its J2012 name P0337 means the crankshaft position signal stays at a low level without changing state – signal wire shorted to ground, missing supply on a Hall sensor or a sensor stuck low. Few manufacturers use the code. GM 2014–2019 and Ford report all crank sensor faults under P0335/P0336 or P0320/P0339. GM's Global A engines (Saab 9-5 1.6 LLU, 2011) define P0337 as a low duty cycle: fewer than 200 reference pulses in 10 consecutive revolutions, caused among other things by an open or high resistance in the signal or ground wire, set after two trips. Older Bosch diesels (Saab 9-5 EDC16) use it differently for crank pulses missing while cam pulses are present, and shut the engine down. The consequence is as for P0335: stalling or no start. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground or open (high likelihood); Crankshaft position sensor faulty (output stuck low) (high likelihood); Sensor supply missing or shorted (medium likelihood); Connector corroded or pin pushed back (medium likelihood); Engine module input (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine cranks but does not start; Engine stalls while driving or at idle; Tachometer drops to zero or flickers; Check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0338 – Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0338: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit High. By its J2012 name P0338 means the crankshaft position signal stays at a high level – signal wire shorted to supply, or an open signal output that the module's pull-up holds high on a Hall sensor. GM 2014–2019 and Ford do not use the code. GM's Global A engines in the Saab 9-5 (2010/11) and 9-4X define it as a high duty cycle, i.e. too many pulses or teeth between the reference gaps: on the 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) a deviation of more than 8 teeth, checked once per revolution and set in the first trip; on the 1.6 (LLU) more than 200 reference pulses in 10 revolutions, and on the 2.0 turbo (LDK) a large tooth deviation over 4 revolutions, both after two trips. Behind this are usually interference pulses or a gap that is not recognised. Result: misfire, stalling, limp mode. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to supply or open (pull-up holds the level high) (high likelihood); Interference pulses from poor ground or shielding (medium likelihood); Crankshaft position sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Tone wheel damaged or dirty (gap not recognised) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Misfire, jerking; Engine stalls or starts poorly; Limp mode; Check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0339 – Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0339: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. P0339 means the crankshaft position signal drops out or is disturbed for moments and then recovers. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol engines use it, depending on the engine, instead of P0320 for tooth errors: wrong tooth count after the gap, tooth time outside 30 to 9,000 rpm, gap at an unexpected position, from 500 rpm, detected within 5 s. In Ford's PCM code list (Roush workshop manual) P0339 is listed without check engine light. Saab's 9-3 diesel (T8) counts dropouts: more than 8 within 10 ms over 3 s, or more than 3 in a whole drive cycle. Honda recalled 2023 Accord Hybrids because a mis-machined sensor mounting caused no-start, rough idle, hunting idle and P0017 with P0339. Typical causes are a loose contact, a sensor failing when hot and a wrong air gap. Common causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector or an in-line connector (high likelihood); Sensor dropping out when hot (medium likelihood); Sensor mounting or air gap mechanically wrong (machining error, bracket) (medium likelihood); Electrical interference (low likelihood); Tone wheel slightly damaged (low likelihood). Symptoms: Sporadic jerking or misfire; Brief stalling, hunting idle; Hard starting; Check engine light on (not on all Ford engines). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P033A – Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor D Circuit
text: P033A: Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor D Circuit. The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor D is a fourth sensor on engines with four knock sensors (McLaren 12C V8, Ford's 2020–23 systems). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P033A means the sensor circuit is open or the signal stays below the noise threshold. GM feeds a 20 kHz test signal into the circuit and detects an open circuit when it does not cancel out, setting the code in the first trip; Ford sees any open or short as a knock signal that is too small compared with the speed- and load-dependent noise level (at least 1,500 rpm, 35 % load, warm engine). Common causes: Wiring or connector chafed, broken or corroded (sensor often under the intake manifold) (high likelihood); Knock sensor faulty (cracked piezo, moisture, heat damage) (medium likelihood); Sensor loose or wrongly torqued (medium likelihood); Engine software or diagnostic calibration (low likelihood); Engine module input stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard; Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P033F – Crankshaft/Camshaft Loss Of Synchronization
text: P033F: Crankshaft/Camshaft Loss Of Synchronization. To know which stroke each cylinder is in, the engine module matches the crank angle with the camshaft phase. P033F means this synchronisation is lost while running or cannot be established. It is documented by code only at Ford (2020–2023): P033F, as an alternative to Ford's older own code, stands for a disturbed crank signal without crank/cam synchronisation, and then misfire detection is also impossible. Ford's 2012 description shows the reaction: on a crank sensor fault the module cuts fuel and spark and resynchronises – one revolution to find the gap, one more to confirm cylinder 1 via the camshaft sensor. FCA evaluates the same function in its own cam/crank synchronisation monitor under other codes. Besides the sensors, a jumped timing chain or belt can be behind it. Common causes: Noisy or disturbed crankshaft signal (sensor, air gap, interference) (high likelihood); Disturbed camshaft signal (medium likelihood); Timing chain or belt jumped or heavily stretched (medium likelihood); Wiring or connector (medium likelihood); Tone wheel damaged or loose (low likelihood). Symptoms: Jerking, brief loss of power; Engine stalls, hard starting; Misfire detection inactive; Check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0340 – Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1 or Single Sensor
text: P0340: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1 or Single Sensor. The camshaft position sensor, almost always a Hall sensor, tells the engine module which stroke cylinder 1 is in – one crank revolution alone is ambiguous – and measures the actual cam phase with variable timing. Sensor A is the intake camshaft, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P0340 means no or too few cam pulses arrive while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM sets it after 5.5 s (or 4 s) of cranking without a cam pulse or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, petrol engines after two trips. Ford checks the ratio of cam to crank events from 200 rpm. The engine usually keeps running but starts longer and loses power as cam timing is held. Bulletins: corroded connectors on GM V8s (PIP5335C), moisture in the oil on short trips in Ford hybrids (SSM 48598). Common causes: Camshaft position sensor faulty (heat, moisture) (high likelihood); Connector or wiring corroded or open, 5 V reference disturbed (high likelihood); Tone wheel on the camshaft or phaser damaged, loose or at the wrong distance (medium likelihood); Timing drive jumped or wrongly assembled (medium likelihood); Moisture in the engine oil from short trips (Ford hybrids) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position); Rough idle, occasionally stalling. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0341 – Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 or Single Sensor
text: P0341: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 or Single Sensor. P0341 means the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) delivers pulses, but their number or pattern does not fit the crankshaft. GM counts the pulses while the crank is in sync: 4 to 6 in the first 12 reference events and 398 to 402 per 100 engine cycles on the 4X wheel of the cam phaser; outside that in 8 of 10 checks the code is set after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesel compares the detected segment profile of the cam wheel with the expected one (1.2 s); the Saab 9-4X V6 checks pulses per crank revolution and correlation with crank position. Ford petrol engines use P0344 instead. Result: cam phase uncertain, cam timing switched off, possibly hard starting. GM names corroded connectors at the timing cover as a sporadic cause (PIP5335C). Common causes: Sensor with interference pulses or weak signal, air gap (high likelihood); Tone wheel on the phaser damaged or wrongly fitted (medium likelihood); Connector or wiring fault (corrosion, interference) (medium likelihood); Crankshaft signal disturbed (wrong reference) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position); Rough idle, occasionally stalling. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0342 – Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 1 or Single Sensor
text: P0342: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 1 or Single Sensor. P0342 means the signal of the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) stays at ground level without edges – signal wire shorted to ground, sensor supply missing or the Hall sensor faulty. Ford's 2023 diesel sets it when the signal stays at 0 V over 10 or more crank revolutions (3 s), while cranking or running. On the Saab 9-4X V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, and the code follows after two trips; with the sensor disconnected the signal wire should show 4.8–5.2 V. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) treats low and high together: no connection or short to ground or battery, about 4.5 V at idle, air gap at most 1.5 mm. GM petrol engines 2014–2019 and Ford petrol engines report this under P0340. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); 5 V or 12 V supply of the sensor missing (medium likelihood); Camshaft position sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Connector corroded or wiring chafed (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position); Rough idle, occasionally stalling. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0343 – Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 1 or Single Sensor
text: P0343: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 1 or Single Sensor. P0343 means the signal of the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) stays at supply level without edges. Causes are a signal wire shorted to positive, an open signal wire that the module's pull-up holds at 5 V, a broken sensor ground or a faulty sensor. Ford's 2023 diesel sets it when the signal stays at system voltage over 10 or more crank revolutions (3 s). On the Saab 9-4X V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay high without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, and the code follows after two trips. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) treats low and high together and allows an air gap of at most 1.5 mm. The consequences are as for P0340: longer cranking, cam timing switched off, loss of power. Common causes: Signal wire open or shorted to positive (high likelihood); Sensor ground open (medium likelihood); Camshaft position sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Connector corroded (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position); Rough idle, occasionally stalling. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0344 – Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent Bank 1 or Single Sensor
text: P0344: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent Bank 1 or Single Sensor. P0344 means the signal of the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) is disturbed for moments: edges are missing or appear at an unexpected angle. Ford checks this on the five-tooth wheel used with variable cam timing; if edges appear where none are expected, Ford sets P0344 and switches cam timing off (loss of power and torque), from 200 rpm, detected within 5 s. In Ford hybrids (C-Max, Fusion, MKZ 2013–2020) moisture in the engine oil from short trips caused P0340 and P0344 – remedy: new sensor and oil change (SSM 48598). FCA asks for the cam/crank synchronisation event data to be saved before replacing a cam sensor. The 2010 Saab 9-5 2.0 diesel uses P0344 differently for too few cam pulses. Common causes: Moisture or oil inside the sensor, dropping out when hot (high likelihood); Loose contact or corrosion at the connector (high likelihood); Tone wheel on the phaser damaged or loose (medium likelihood); Interference or chafed wiring (medium likelihood); Crankshaft signal disturbed (wrong reference) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Sporadic loss of power (cam timing off); Jerking, rough idle; Occasionally longer cranking. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0345 – Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 2
text: P0345: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 2. P0345 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0340: the intake camshaft sensor on the side without cylinder 1 – only on V and boxer engines with one cam sensor per bank – delivers no or too few pulses while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM uses the same criteria as for P0340, e.g. on the 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW): 5.5 s or 4 s of cranking without a cam pulse, or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, set after two trips. Ford checks the ratio of cam to crank events from 200 rpm, detected within 5 s. FCA lists P0345 among the cam sensor codes for which the synchronisation event data should be saved before replacing the sensor. Result: cam timing on bank 2 is switched off and power drops; the cam phase usually remains available from the bank 1 sensor. Common causes: Camshaft position sensor bank 2 faulty (high likelihood); Connector or wiring of bank 2 corroded or open (high likelihood); Tone wheel or phaser of bank 2 damaged (medium likelihood); Timing drive of bank 2 jumped (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position); Rough idle, occasionally stalling. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P034A – Crankshaft Position Sensor - Crankshaft Start Position Incorrect
text: P034A: Crankshaft Position Sensor - Crankshaft Start Position Incorrect. Engines with start-stop or hybrid autostart store the crankshaft rest position when the engine stops, so that they can inject and fire correctly at once on restart. This needs a direction-sensing crank sensor, because a cylinder under compression can push the crankshaft backwards after shut-off. On restart the module compares the stored position with the one actually measured after the reference gap. GM sets P034A when they differ by more than 2 teeth in 2 of 3 autostarts or by at least 1 tooth in 4 of 5, after two trips; the diesel already at more than 1 tooth in 1 of 3. The check is suspended while a crank sensor fault is present. Result: start-stop is restricted, restarts take longer with conventional synchronisation, and the autostart may be rough. Common causes: Direction-sensing crankshaft position sensor faulty or aged (high likelihood); Interference pulses in the sensor circuit during shut-off (medium likelihood); Air gap or tone wheel – teeth not detected at low speed (medium likelihood); Engine module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Start-stop restricted or off; Delayed or rough autostart; Rarely stalling after an autostart. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P034B – Crankshaft Position Sensor - Crankshaft Direction Incorrect
text: P034B: Crankshaft Position Sensor - Crankshaft Direction Incorrect. Direction-sensing (bidirectional) crank sensors count the rest position for start-stop even when the crankshaft rocks back after shut-off. In normal running the sensor must never report reverse rotation – if it does, the signal is disturbed. GM sets P034B after at least 3 direction reversals within 10 s at 400 to 2,000 rpm and an airflow of at least 1.5 g/s, after two trips; the diesel uses the same thresholds. GM bulletin 17-NA-317 describes the 3.6 V6 (LFY) in the 2018 Buick Enclave and Chevrolet Traverse: interference in the sensor circuit caused P034B with P0506, low idle or stalling after an autostart, transmission slip above 65 km/h and cruise control dropping out; the remedy was a revised sensor wiring. Result: start-stop disabled, possibly reduced power. Common causes: Interference in the sensor circuit (wiring routed next to switching lines) (high likelihood); Direction-sensing crankshaft position sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Ground or connector fault (medium likelihood); Tone wheel or air gap (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Low idle or stalling after an autostart; Start-stop off, possibly reduced power; Follow-on effects such as transmission slip or cruise control dropping out (GM LFY). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P034C – Ion Sense System Performance
text: P034C: Ion Sense System Performance. With ion current sensing the spark plug serves as a sensor after the spark: a measuring voltage across the gap drives a current through the ions in the flame, from which the module detects combustion, misfire and knock – a Delphi patent describes coils with built-in ion sensing, and Saab's Trionic engines detected misfire this way. P034C means this measuring system works implausibly, so misfire and knock detection are no longer reliable. It is documented on the Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio 2.9 V6 biturbo, where three bulletins fix it mainly with engine software; limp mode is possible. Sooted plugs or a faulty coil with ion circuit are further causes. Common causes: Engine software or calibration (high likelihood); Spark plugs sooted, oily or wrong type or gap (medium likelihood); Ignition coil or cassette with ion circuit faulty (medium likelihood); Wiring or connector of the ion current return line (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Limp mode or reduced power possible; Often nothing noticeable otherwise. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0350 – Ignition Coil Primary/Secondary Circuit/Open
text: P0350: Ignition Coil Primary/Secondary Circuit/Open. P0350 is the general ignition coil circuit code without assignment to a coil: the engine module detects a fault in the primary or secondary circuit of a coil but does not report which one. This typically concerns older systems with a shared output stage or ignition module, or a shared feedback line for all coils. The monitoring works as for P0351 ff – primary-current feedback for each ignition command, or the voltage at the driver. GM and Ford report coil faults individually (P0351 ff, P2300 ff) and do not use P0350; the description follows CARB's output monitoring requirement, which allows one collective code. Common causes: Ignition coil, coil pack or ignition module faulty (high likelihood); Shared supply (fuse, relay, ignition feed) or ground open (medium likelihood); Harness, connector or feedback line to the coils faulty (medium likelihood); Ignition lead or plug connector damaged (secondary side) (low likelihood); Engine module or driver (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Misfire, rough running; Starting problems or stalling if a shared output stage fails. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0351 – Ignition Coil A Primary Control Circuit/Open
text: P0351: Ignition Coil A Primary Control Circuit/Open. Modern engines have one coil-on-plug ignition coil per cylinder, with the output stage either in the engine module or in the coil itself. P0351 monitors the primary control circuit of coil A – the line from the engine module to the coil or its built-in output stage – for an open circuit or high resistance. GM's module measures the voltage with its low-side driver off and flags an open circuit above 30 kΩ in 50 of 63 samples (2018 engines in the first trip, older ones after two); Ford checks continuously within 1 s, expecting a primary-current feedback for every ignition command, and shuts off injection to that cylinder for 30 s at a time. Short circuits and the secondary side have their own codes (P2300 ff). Coil A usually serves cylinder 1, but the assignment is up to the manufacturer. Common causes: Ignition coil A faulty (output stage in the coil or primary winding open) (high likelihood); Connector at the coil corroded, loose or with a spread pin (high likelihood); Control, supply or ground wire open or chafed (medium likelihood); Fuse or relay of the coil supply (then usually several codes) (low likelihood); Driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Misfire and rough running on cylinder 1, often also P0301; Loss of power, jerking under load; Cylinder shut off (injection off), risk to the catalyst if driven on. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0352 – Ignition Coil B Primary Control Circuit/Open
text: P0352: Ignition Coil B Primary Control Circuit/Open. Modern engines have one coil-on-plug ignition coil per cylinder, with the output stage either in the engine module or in the coil itself. P0352 monitors the primary control circuit of coil B – the line from the engine module to the coil or its built-in output stage – for an open circuit or high resistance. GM's module measures the voltage with its low-side driver off and flags an open circuit above 30 kΩ in 50 of 63 samples (2018 engines in the first trip, older ones after two); Ford checks continuously within 1 s, expecting a primary-current feedback for every ignition command, and shuts off injection to that cylinder for 30 s at a time. Short circuits and the secondary side have their own codes (P2300 ff). Coil B usually serves cylinder 2, but the assignment is up to the manufacturer. Common causes: Ignition coil B faulty (output stage in the coil or primary winding open) (high likelihood); Connector at the coil corroded, loose or with a spread pin (high likelihood); Control, supply or ground wire open or chafed (medium likelihood); Fuse or relay of the coil supply (then usually several codes) (low likelihood); Driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Misfire and rough running on cylinder 2, often also P0302; Loss of power, jerking under load; Cylinder shut off (injection off), risk to the catalyst if driven on. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0356 – Ignition Coil F Primary Control Circuit/Open
text: P0356: Ignition Coil F Primary Control Circuit/Open. title: P035A – Ignition E Control Signal Circuit/Open
text: P035A: Ignition E Control Signal Circuit/Open. Ignition E is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P035A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition E to H codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff (open above 30 kΩ) – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst. Common causes: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin) (high likelihood); Ignition module or coil with integrated driver of this group faulty (medium likelihood); Supply or ground of the ignition module faulty (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Misfire, jerking, rough idle; Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off; Additional misfire codes P0300 ff. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0363 – Misfire Detected - Fueling Disabled
text: P0363: Misfire Detected - Fueling Disabled. P0363 is a reaction code: the engine module has detected misfire severe enough to damage the catalyst – through its crankshaft-based misfire monitor – and has therefore shut off injection to the affected cylinder or cylinders. CARB allows exactly this: a vehicle that cuts fuel immediately on catalyst-damaging misfire may turn the check engine light on steadily instead of flashing it, and may switch fuel back on to re-check at most every 30 s. The code names no cylinder; that comes from the accompanying P0301 ff. It is documented by code only at FCA: two reprogramming bulletins for the 2017–2018 Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 turbo list P0363 alongside misfire and mixture codes. Ford reacts in the same way without its own code, VW uses a manufacturer code (P130A) for the hidden cylinder, and GM does not list P0363. Common causes: Ignition coil or spark plug of the affected cylinder faulty (high likelihood); Injector sticking or leaking, or fuel pressure too low (medium likelihood); Engine module software (misfire detection, cold-start mixture) (medium likelihood); Mechanical cause: loss of compression, valve or carbon deposits, vacuum leak (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on steadily instead of flashing; Clearly rough running, one cylinder without power; Loss of power; Jerking or stalling, especially when cold. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0364 – DC/AC Converter Control Module Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0364: DC/AC Converter Control Module Control Circuit Range/Performance. By its J2012 name P0364 means the control circuit to the control module of a DC/AC converter (inverter) behaves implausibly – the command or enable line is present but its signal does not fit what the engine module expects. The code is a late assignment in the P03xx block: older code lists show the slot as reserved, and the other DC/AC converter codes sit in the P2DAx range (P2DA8–P2DAB). Which converter is meant – a traction inverter in a hybrid or a 120/230 V socket inverter – the name does not say, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0364. The description is therefore limited to the code name and CARB's general requirement to monitor electronic powertrain components. Whether the check engine light comes on and what the vehicle restricts depends on the manufacturer. Common causes: Control or enable line to the converter module disturbed (connector, wiring) (medium likelihood); Converter control module faulty internally (medium likelihood); Software of the modules involved (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp depending on the manufacturer; Converter function restricted (for example power socket or hybrid drive). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0365 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
text: P0365: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0365 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM sets it after 4 s of cranking or 5.5 s without a cam pulse, or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, 8 of 10 samples, after two trips; on GM's 3.6-litre V6 (Saab 9-4X) also with no pulse in 800 of 1,000 engine cycles. Ford checks the ratio of crank to cam events from 200 rpm, detected within 5 s, and collects all electrical faults here. The exhaust phaser then goes to its park position; the engine keeps running but cranks longer and loses some power. FCA advises saving the cam/crank synchronisation data before replacing the sensor, as the fault is often elsewhere. Common causes: Exhaust camshaft position sensor faulty (high likelihood); Connector or wiring open or corroded, 5 V reference missing (high likelihood); Oil in the connector from a leaking sensor O-ring (medium likelihood); Tone wheel on the exhaust phaser damaged or loose (low likelihood); Engine module (5 V supply) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power or rough idle (exhaust cam timing in its base position); Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0366 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
text: P0366: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0366 means its pulses arrive, but their number or position does not fit the crankshaft. GM expects 400 pulses per 100 engine cycles and sets the code outside 398–402, or with fewer than 4 or more than 6 pulses in the first 12 reference events at start, 8 of 10 samples, after two trips. On GM's 3.6-litre V6 in the Saab 9-4X the exhaust phaser then goes to its park position and ignition runs from the crankshaft alone; on the 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) the fault must last 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, below 2,520 rpm. Saab's workshop information names a damaged tone wheel, play, foreign matter and too large an air gap. Ford uses the code too but publishes no thresholds. Common causes: Sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet) (high likelihood); Wiring close to ignition coils or solenoids, loose contact (medium likelihood); Tone wheel on the phaser damaged or loose, air gap too large (medium likelihood); Sensor or phaser wrongly fitted after timing drive work (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power or rough idle (exhaust cam timing in its base position); Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0367 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
text: P0367: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. The engine module holds the signal line at about 5 V and the sensor pulls it to ground with each tooth. P0367 means the line stays low without edges – typically a short to ground of the signal wire or a sensor shorted internally. A code-specific manufacturer description exists only from GM: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after more than 10 crank revolutions and below 2,520 rpm, and the code follows after two trips; with the sensor disconnected the signal wire should show 4.8–5.2 V. GM's other engines of 2014–2019 and Ford report such faults under P0365. The consequence is as for P0365: exhaust cam timing in its base position, longer cranking. Common causes: Signal wire chafed through to ground (high likelihood); Sensor shorted internally (medium likelihood); Oil or water in the connector (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power or rough idle (exhaust cam timing in its base position). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0368 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1
text: P0368: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0368 means the signal line stays high without edges. If the signal wire is open, the roughly 5 V the engine module applies to it simply remains; if the sensor's 5 V supply or ground is missing, the sensor never switches and the signal also stays high – and a short to positive has the same effect. A code-specific manufacturer description exists only from GM: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) the signal must stay high without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, and the code follows after two trips; GM lists exactly these causes. GM's other engines of 2014–2019 and Ford report such faults under P0365. The consequence is as for P0365: exhaust cam timing in its base position, longer cranking, some loss of power. Common causes: Connector off or corroded, signal wire open (high likelihood); 5 V reference or ground of the sensor open (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty (output does not switch) (medium likelihood); Signal wire shorted to positive (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking before the engine starts; Loss of power or rough idle (exhaust cam timing in its base position). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0369 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent Bank 1
text: P0369: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent Bank 1. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0369 means its signal is basically present, but now and then a cam pulse arrives at a crank angle where none is expected, or pulses drop out. Ford checks this in its camshaft ignition system test from 200 rpm and decides within 5 s; with this and the other cam timing codes active, Ford also suspends its oxygen sensor monitor. FCA lists P0369 among the cam sensor codes for which the cam/crank synchronisation event data should be read before replacing the sensor. GM does not use the code (2014–2019 only P0365/P0366). Typical causes are a loose contact, interference from ignition wiring and a sensor with metal debris or a borderline air gap. Common causes: Loose contact in connector or wiring (high likelihood); Interference from the ignition (routing, shielding) (medium likelihood); Sensor with metal debris or borderline air gap (medium likelihood); Tone wheel or phaser damaged (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Sporadic jerking or stalling; Occasional starting problems. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P036A – Ignition G Control Signal Circuit/Open
text: P036A: Ignition G Control Signal Circuit/Open. Ignition G is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P036A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition E to H codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff (open above 30 kΩ) – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst. Common causes: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin) (high likelihood); Ignition module or coil with integrated driver of this group faulty (medium likelihood); Supply or ground of the ignition module faulty (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Misfire, jerking, rough idle; Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off; Additional misfire codes P0300 ff. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0370 – Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A
text: P0370: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A. Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal, to time and meter injection precisely – the high resolution signal. GM's 6.5-litre diesel (1997) had an optical sensor in the injection pump that delivers a high resolution track and one cam reference pulse per cylinder; P0370 is set if more than 8 consecutive cam pulses pass without progress on the high resolution counter, in the first trip. The engine then runs on backup fuelling with reduced power, and injection timing control is suspended. On the 2004 Duramax LB7 the injector driver module evaluates the 57X crank signal and reports 'no crank signal' over CAN; from 60 rpm, 100 of 120 samples sets P0370, also in the first trip. Petrol engines practically do not use the code. Common causes: Optical sensor in the injection pump faulty (6.5-litre) (high likelihood); Wiring or connector between pump or sensor and module (medium likelihood); Crankshaft sensor or tone wheel (LB7: 57X signal) (medium likelihood); Injector driver module, engine module or CAN communication (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power (limp-home fuelling); Rough running, hard starting, smoke; Stalling possible. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0371 – Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A Too Many Pulses
text: P0371: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A Too Many Pulses. Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal – the high resolution signal – for precise injection timing and metering. P0371 means signal A delivers more pulses than expected within the reference window – for example more high resolution pulses per reference pulse than the nominal ratio, which on GM's 6.5-litre diesel is 64 ± 4 per cam pulse; the usual cause is interference pulses. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0371: GM's 6.5-litre diesel (optical sensor in the injection pump) reports all faults of its high resolution track under P0370 and the Duramax LB7 uses only P0370 and P0374. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, GM's description of the signal and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. Typically the engine loses power and runs roughly. Common causes: Sensor faulty or dirty (high likelihood); Loose contact or interference in the signal wire (medium likelihood); Sensor disc or tone wheel damaged (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power (limp-home fuelling); Rough running, hard starting, smoke. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P037A – Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit Low
text: P037A: Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit Low. Diesel engines show the driver a wait-to-start lamp while the glow plugs preheat; the engine module switches it with a high-side driver. P037A means the lamp control circuit is too low – in practice a short to ground on the line to the instrument cluster. GM's diesels detect it in the driver itself: about 0.5 Ω to ground with the lamp commanded, only with a lamp configured, ignition on, more than 11 V and not while cranking. The 2015 engines need 3 s of fault, the 2016/2018 engines 10 of 15 samples; the check engine light follows after two trips. The glow plugs keep working; only the indication is missing, so the driver may start too early. CARB requires monitoring of the wait-to-start lamp circuit. Ford reports lamp faults under P0381 and does not use P037A. Common causes: Lamp control wire chafed through to ground between engine module and cluster (high likelihood); Lamp or LED driver in the instrument cluster shorted internally (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the module or cluster connector (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Glow plug light does not come on or stays dim; Check engine light on (GM after two trips); Driver starts too early, possibly poor cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P037B – Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit High
text: P037B: Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit High. P037B is the counterpart of P037A: the control circuit of the wait-to-start lamp is too high, i.e. the line carries voltage although the engine module's driver is off, or the driver sees a short to battery voltage. GM's 2015 diesels check in the off state and set the fault after 1 s with more than 11 V; the 2016/2018 engines evaluate a short of about 0.5 Ω to a voltage source in the driver, 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms. In both cases the check engine light comes on after two trips. The lamp then stays on permanently or cannot be switched off, so the driver no longer gets a usable preheat signal; the driver may protect itself when commanded. There is no limp mode. Ford and Saab do not use P037B; CARB requires monitoring of the lamp circuit and of output components for shorts. Common causes: Lamp control wire chafed against battery or ignition positive (high likelihood); Fault in the instrument cluster feeding voltage back (medium likelihood); Water damage in a connector bridging to a neighbouring pin (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Glow plug light stays on or flickers; Check engine light on (after two trips); No recognisable preheat indication. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P037C – Cold Start Camshaft Profile System Performance
text: P037C: Cold Start Camshaft Profile System Performance. To heat the catalyst quickly after a cold start, some engines select a particular camshaft profile; CARB counts altered valve timing among these cold-start measures and requires components of the cold-start strategy to have their own diagnostics. P037C checks whether the requested profile is actually engaged during this phase. It is documented by code only at GM, on the 2.7-litre turbo four-cylinder (L3B) with a three-step sliding camshaft: while catalyst heating is active, the measured lift state is compared with the cold-start target, and if it is wrong in 100 of 120 cylinder events the code is set in the first trip. Two GM bulletins (19-NA-145 for 2019 Silverado/Sierra 1500 with stalling on remote start below −6 °C, 20-NA-174 for the 2020 Cadillac CT4) trace P037C to a software fault and reprogram the engine module. Common causes: Engine module software (GM L3B, reprogramming) (high likelihood); Profile actuator (sliding cam pin) sticking or not switching (medium likelihood); Actuator circuit (connector, wiring) (medium likelihood); Wrong oil viscosity or low oil level, mechanism stiff when cold (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running or stalling when cold (for example on remote start); Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P037D – Glow Plug Sense Circuit
text: P037D: Glow Plug Sense Circuit. To check the glow plugs, the engine module reads back the voltage or current of the glow plug supply through a sense circuit – CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop, and from model year 2010 the failure of a single plug to be detected. In the J2012 scheme P037D is the general code for this sense circuit, P037E and P037F its low and high counterparts. None of the manufacturer documents available to us uses P037D: GM's 2016/2018 diesels use only P037E/P037F, Ford 2023 its own glow plug codes (P0671 ff, P064C) and Saab reports the feedback of its glow plug control module as P0380/P0382. The description therefore follows CARB and the GM sister codes. Typically glow plug monitoring is inactive; glowing itself can work normally. Common causes: Sense wire open or high resistance, connector corroded (high likelihood); Glow relay or glow plug control module giving an implausible feedback (medium likelihood); Fuse or fusible link of the glow plug supply blown (medium likelihood); Engine module internal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or glow plug light on; Possibly poor cold start if the cause also affects the glow plug supply; Further glow plug codes stored. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P037E – Glow Plug Sense Circuit Low
text: P037E: Glow Plug Sense Circuit Low. P037E means the voltage read back from the glow plug supply is too low. GM's 2016/2018 diesels, whose glow plug output stages sit in the engine module, compare the feedback with the battery voltage while glowing: if it is lower by more than a calibrated, current-dependent threshold – excessive voltage drop or a short to ground of the sense line – a sample counts as faulty, and 60 of 120 samples in a 50 ms grid set the code, roughly 3 of 6 s. The check only runs with the engine running (afterglow), not while cranking, and is suspended if a single plug or the supply already has an electrical fault. GM classes the cause as internal to the module (measuring circuit) and turns on the check engine light after two trips. There is no limp mode; glow plug monitoring is restricted. Common causes: High contact resistance in the glow plug supply (connector, ground, fusible link) (high likelihood); Measuring circuit or output stage in the engine module (medium likelihood); Sense or supply wire shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Weak battery or vehicle voltage at the edge of the enable range (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly hard starting or knocking when cold; Further glow plug codes. Repair difficulty: medium.
