title: P037F – Glow Plug Sense Circuit High
text: P037F: Glow Plug Sense Circuit High. P037F means the voltage read back from the glow plug supply is too high. GM's 2016/2018 diesels set it when the feedback lies above a threshold derived from the run/crank relay voltage, with a feedback above 5.0 V – for example voltage is reported although the plugs are not energised, or the sense line is shorted to positive. The code needs 40 of 80 samples at 50 ms, about 2 of 4 s, only with the engine running, and turns on the check engine light after two trips; GM classes the cause as internal to the module. If there is a real short to positive or a stuck relay or output stage, the plugs can stay energised permanently, overheating them and draining the battery – then also check the single plug codes P0671 ff and P066x. CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop. Common causes: Sense wire chafed against positive or bridged in the connector (high likelihood); Glow relay sticking or output stage shorted (supply stays on) (medium likelihood); Measuring circuit in the engine module (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Glow plugs possibly energised permanently (flat battery, plug damage); Glow plug light implausible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0380 – Glow Plug/Heater Circuit A
text: P0380: Glow Plug/Heater Circuit A. P0380 concerns glow plug circuit A – depending on the manufacturer the first group of plugs, glow relay 1 or feedback line A of the glow plug control module. Saab's 3.0 TiD (9-5, 2002) has two feedback lines from the control module; if line A at the engine module stays above 4.0 V for more than 3 s while glowing, the module is reporting a plug or circuit fault, checked once per drive cycle with the warning lamp on. In Saab's 1.9 TiD (EDC16) the glow plug control module drives two pairs of plugs, monitors them itself and reports faults over a diagnostic line that should switch inversely to the activation line. The 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD sets P0380 for implausible feedback or a missing supply of the module, there without check engine light. Newer GM and Ford diesels report single plugs under P0671 ff instead. Common causes: Glow plug(s) in circuit A burnt out (high likelihood); Glow plug control module or glow relay faulty (medium likelihood); Wiring or connector fault (feedback line, plug connector, supply) (medium likelihood); Missing battery or ignition supply of the control module (fuse) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hard starting when cold, long cranking; White or blue smoke and rough running after a cold start; Glow plug light or check engine light on or flashing. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0381 – Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit/Open
text: P0381: Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit/Open. P0381 monitors the circuit of the wait-to-start lamp for an open circuit or, more generally, for faults that keep the lamp dark when commanded – CARB names a burnt-out bulb as the example, with exemptions for LCD clusters and for engines that only release the starter after preheating. GM's 2015–2018 diesels detect an open circuit in the driver by a high load impedance (about 200 kΩ in 2015), in 0.2 s or 10 of 15 samples, with the check engine light after two trips; on the 2014 Duramax LML P0381 still covered all lamp circuit faults including a short to ground. Ford's 2023 diesels check via the instrument cluster: if it reports the lamp off although on is commanded, P0381 is set within about 1 s at key-on. There is no limp mode; the risk is starting too early in the cold. Common causes: Control wire open or connector fault between engine module and cluster (high likelihood); Lamp or LED in the instrument cluster burnt out (medium likelihood); Instrument cluster faulty or communication problem (Ford) (low likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Glow plug light does not come on at key-on; Check engine light on (GM after two trips); Driver starts too early in the cold. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0382 – Glow Plug/Heater Circuit B
text: P0382: Glow Plug/Heater Circuit B. P0382 is the counterpart of P0380 for glow plug circuit B – depending on the manufacturer the second group of plugs, glow relay 2 or feedback line B of the glow plug control module. A code-specific manufacturer description exists from Saab: the 3.0 TiD V6 diesel in the 9-5 (2002) reads two feedback lines from its glow plug control module, and if line B stays above 4.0 V for more than 3 s while glowing, the module is reporting a fault in the second group of plugs; the check runs once per drive cycle, the warning lamp comes on and there is no further system reaction. Newer GM and Ford diesels report single plugs under P0671 ff and do not use P0382. CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop. The typical consequence is a poor cold start with smoke. Common causes: Glow plug(s) in circuit B burnt out (high likelihood); Glow plug control module or glow relay 2 faulty (medium likelihood); Feedback line B, plug connector or busbar faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Hard starting when cold, long cranking; White or blue smoke and rough running after a cold start; Glow plug light or check engine light on or flashing. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0383 – Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit Low
text: P0383: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit Low. Many diesels have a separate glow plug control module that the engine module commands over a control line. P0383 means this line is too low. In GM's logic for the 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD the engine module drives the module with a PWM signal and holds about 10 V on the line at rest (9.5–10.5 V at the signal terminal); if it reads too little voltage for more than 0.5 s – short to ground, or an open circuit or high resistance – it sets P0383, with ignition on, 9–16 V, once per ignition cycle. In that European version the code does not turn on the check engine light. Without a valid command the module does not glow, so the engine starts poorly when cold. Ford uses P0384 differently and not P0383; GM's 2016/2018 diesels have their output stages in the engine module and no such line. For US vehicles there is no code-specific source. Common causes: Control line between engine module and glow plug module shorted to ground or open (high likelihood); Corroded connector at the glow plug module in the engine bay (medium likelihood); Glow plug control module faulty (input pulls the line down) (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: No preheating, poor cold start; Smoke after a cold start; Warning lamp depending on the manufacturer. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0384 – Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit High
text: P0384: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit High. P0384 is the counterpart of P0383: the control line from the engine module to the glow plug control module is too high, i.e. shorted to positive. In GM's logic for the 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD the signal terminal should show 9.5–10.5 V; a higher voltage for more than 0.5 s, with ignition on and 9–16 V, sets the code, there without check engine light. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) use P0384 differently from the J2012 name, for the supply voltage of the glow plug module: below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or open, detected in about 1 s – today J2012 has P052F for that. So with Ford, check battery, alternator and the module's supply first. The consequence is missing or irregular preheating or a protective shutdown of the module, with a poor cold start. Common causes: Control line chafed against positive or bridged in the connector (high likelihood); Glow plug control module faulty internally (feeding back) (medium likelihood); Ford: supply of the module outside 6.5–16.5 V or open (battery, alternator, fuse) (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: No or irregular preheating, hard starting when cold; Smoke after a cold start; Warning lamp depending on the manufacturer. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0385 – Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit
text: P0385: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit. Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel, which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. P0385 means its signal is missing or does not match. GM's 2004 Northstar 4.6 V8 counts the crank pulses per cam pulse (target 48 ± 1, fault in 8 of 10 tests) and also flags 2 s while cranking or 0.4 s running without a match, after two trips; an active P0385 suspends the cam sensor check. GM's 3.8-litre V6 (2006) sets it when its low resolution track stays silent while the medium resolution track delivers 36 pulses, 40 of 50 samples. The Honda 3.5-litre in the 2004 Saturn Vue Redline sets it when the second crank signal is missing while the first runs, judged after 17 revolutions, in the first trip. The engine usually keeps running on sensor A. Common causes: Crankshaft position sensor B faulty (high likelihood); Connector or wiring open or corroded (high likelihood); Tone wheel or second track damaged (low likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking; Tachometer flickers, rough running; Rarely stalling. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0386 – Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0386: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance. P0386 means the signal of the second crankshaft sensor or second tone wheel track is present but implausible. GM's 2004 Northstar 4.6 V8 sets it after 5 resynchronisations within 10 s, after two trips. GM's 3.8-litre V6 (2006) expects exactly 0 or 6 low resolution pulses per 36 medium resolution pulses and one cam pulse; any other count in 40 of 50 samples sets the code, also after two trips. The Honda 3.5-litre in the 2004 Saturn Vue Redline counts implausible signals of its second crank sensor (target 44 crank pulses per 3 cam pulses, checked every half revolution, the counter dropping by one every 10 s) and sets the code at 30, about 2.2 s at idle, in the first trip. Typical causes are interference pulses, a dirty sensor or a wrong air gap; the result is jerking, misfire or longer cranking. Common causes: Interference pulses (wiring near the ignition, shielding) (high likelihood); Sensor dirty or air gap wrong (medium likelihood); Tone wheel damaged (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Jerking, misfire; Longer cranking. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0387 – Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low
text: P0387: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low. By its J2012 name P0387 means the signal of the second crankshaft sensor stays at a low level – typically a short to ground of the signal wire, a missing or shorted sensor supply, or with an inductive sensor an amplitude that is too small. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0387: the engines with a sensor B that we found (GM Northstar 4.6 and 3.8-litre V6, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline) report its electrical faults under P0385 and implausible signals under P0386. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, the function of sensor B and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. As long as sensor A works, the engine usually keeps running; together with a sensor A fault it may not start. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Sensor supply too low or shorted (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking; Rough running, no start if sensor A also fails. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0388 – Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High
text: P0388: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High. Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel – GM's 3.4/3.5/3.8-litre V6 use the low resolution track of a dual Hall sensor, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline a second sensor – which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. By its J2012 name P0388 means the signal of sensor B stays above its upper limit – with a Hall sensor typically an open signal wire held high by the module's pull-up, or a short to positive. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0388: the engines with a sensor B report its electrical faults under P0385 and implausible signals under P0386. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, these component sources and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. The engine usually keeps running on sensor A; longer cranking is possible. Common causes: Signal wire of sensor B open or connector corroded or loose (high likelihood); Signal wire shorted to positive or reference voltage (medium likelihood); Sensor ground open (medium likelihood); Sensor B faulty internally (medium likelihood); Engine module input (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Longer cranking or starting problems; Possibly rough running or misfire; Often no noticeable symptoms while sensor A takes over. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0389 – Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
text: P0389: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent. Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel – GM's 3.4/3.5/3.8-litre V6 use the low resolution track of a dual Hall sensor, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline a second sensor – which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. By its J2012 name P0389 means the signal of sensor B drops out for moments or becomes erratic – missing or extra edges – without staying permanently low or high. Such faults are typically found by counting pulses against sensor A or the camshaft, as GM's 3.8-litre V6 and the Honda engine do; both, however, report the result under P0385/P0386, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0389. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, these component sources and CARB. Typical causes are a loose contact, a broken wire and interference. Common causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor B connector (high likelihood); Wire break or chafing that appears with engine movement (high likelihood); Electrical interference (add-on devices, routing near ignition or relays) (medium likelihood); Tone wheel damaged or dirty, air gap too large (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty, temperature-dependent (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, possibly only after several trips; Occasional stalling or jerking; Sporadic starting problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P038A – Ignition I Control Signal Circuit/Open
text: P038A: Ignition I Control Signal Circuit/Open. Ignition I is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P038A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition A to J codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst. Common causes: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin) (high likelihood); Ignition module or coil with integrated driver of this group faulty (medium likelihood); Supply or ground of the ignition module faulty (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Misfire, jerking, rough idle; Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off; Additional misfire codes P0300 ff. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0390 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2
text: P0390: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0390 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive from bank 2 while the crankshaft turns. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) sets it after 5.5 s without a cam pulse, 4 s of cranking or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s, after two trips; for GM it collects all circuit faults. GM's 3.6-litre V6 in the Saab 9-4X also counts 800 of 1,000 engine cycles without a pulse. Ford checks the crank-to-cam ratio from 200 rpm within 5 s, and the 2004 Northstar counts missing signal changes up to 16. The bank 2 exhaust phaser then locks in its base position; the engine keeps running on the crank and intake cam sensors. FCA advises saving the synchronisation data before replacing the sensor. Common causes: Connector or wiring of the bank 2 exhaust sensor open or corroded (signal, 5 V, ground) (high likelihood); Camshaft position sensor faulty (high likelihood); Oil contamination or leak at the sensor, sensor loose (medium likelihood); Tone wheel on the phaser damaged or wrongly fitted after timing chain work (medium likelihood); Engine module, or 5 V reference shorted by another sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position); Longer cranking; Rough idle; Higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0391 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2
text: P0391: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0391 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal is present, but the number or position of its pulses does not fit the crankshaft. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) expects 4 to 6 pulses in the first 12 reference events and 398 to 402 per 100 engine cycles on the four-tooth wheel, after two trips; the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) checks pulses per crank revolution below 2,520 rpm. The 2004 Northstar requires each edge within a window of crank teeth, and GM's 2004 3.6-litre V6 (LY7) counts implausible signals over two drive cycles. The phaser then goes to its base position and the engine cranks longer. Mechanical causes – damaged tone wheel, jumped chain – matter more here than with P0390. Common causes: Tone wheel on the bank 2 exhaust phaser damaged, loose or wrongly fitted (high likelihood); Interference or loose contact producing extra edges (medium likelihood); Sensor loose, wrong O-ring or gap, chips on the magnet (medium likelihood); Timing chain stretched or jumped (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position); Longer cranking; Rough idle; Occasional stalling. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0392 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2
text: P0392: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2. Newer GM petrol engines (2015–2020) and Ford report the same fault as P0390. The consequence is as for P0390: cam timing on bank 2 in its base position, loss of power, longer cranking. title: P0394 – Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent Bank 2
text: P0394: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent Bank 2. Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0394 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal now and then appears at a position where it is not expected relative to the crank reference – sporadic extra or missing edges. Ford checks this in its camshaft ignition system test from 200 rpm and decides within 5 s. title: P0395 – Cylinder 1 Pressure Sensor Circuit
text: P0395: Cylinder 1 Pressure Sensor Circuit. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0395 is the general circuit code for this pressure sensor, meant for modules that do not separate open circuits and shorts into low and high. The only manufacturer we found using this code family – GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel, documented in Saab 9-5 workshop information – splits the faults into low and high (P0397, P0398) and does not use P0395; VW's US 2.0 TDI engines with pressure-sensing glow plugs report such faults with their own codes (P13CE ff). The description therefore follows CARB's requirement to monitor input sensors for circuit faults. The sensor has three wires (5 V reference, ground, signal); without it the module drops combustion control for that cylinder. Common causes: Connector at the pressure-sensing glow plug loose or corroded (high likelihood); Reference, signal or ground wire open or shorted (medium likelihood); Sensor electronics in the glow plug faulty (medium likelihood); Engine module (reference voltage or input) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (often after two trips); Usually barely noticeable – combustion control for the cylinder is switched off; Possibly rougher running, more noise or slightly higher consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0396 – Cylinder 1 Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0396: Cylinder 1 Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0396 means the sensor signal is electrically fine but does not fit the expected value. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows how such a check works: in overrun the measured peak pressure is compared with a compression pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the pressure values are also compared with limits and with crankshaft speed fluctuation. GM's European diesel in the Saab 9-5 uses the peak pressure in overrun anyway to find top dead centre. Typical causes are sensor drift from combustion deposits or a glow plug that leaks or is wrongly torqued. CARB requires a two-sided plausibility check of input sensors where feasible. Common causes: Sensor in the glow plug drifting (deposits, ageing) (high likelihood); Glow plug leaking or wrongly torqued (pressure transmitted wrongly) (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in connector or ground (medium likelihood); Actual compression pressure differs (valve, rings) (low likelihood). title: P0399 – Cylinder 1 Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0399: Cylinder 1 Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. title: P039A – Cylinder 1 Pressure Too Low
text: P039A: Cylinder 1 Pressure Too Low. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039A means the pressure measured in the cylinder is lower than expected while the sensor itself is electrically fine. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; GM patents show how such an evaluation works: peak and minimum pressure are compared with limits and with a motoring pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is compared between cylinders. A low value can mean weak combustion or compression – leaking valve, worn rings, leaking glow plug seat, an injector delivering too little – or a sensor drifting downwards. The usual consequence is rough running and more smoke. Common causes: Compression loss (valve, piston rings, leaking glow plug seat) (medium likelihood); Injector delivering too little or coked (medium likelihood); Sensor drifting downwards (deposits) (medium likelihood); Misfire or partial combustion (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power, rough running, possibly misfire on this cylinder; More smoke. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P039B – Cylinder 1 Pressure Too High
text: P039B: Cylinder 1 Pressure Too High. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039B means the pressure measured or calculated for the cylinder is higher than expected. title: P039C – Cylinder 1 Pressure Variation Low
text: P039C: Cylinder 1 Pressure Variation Low. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. title: P039E – Cylinder 1 Combustion Performance
text: P039E: Cylinder 1 Combustion Performance. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039E means the combustion quality in the cylinder, evaluated from the combustion pressure, is abnormal. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows the method: the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is turned into a measure of combustion energy, an inequality index against the neighbouring cylinders in firing order is formed, and a two-sided threshold detects partial combustion, misfire, injector and compression faults. CARB requires engines with a combustion or combustion quality sensor to detect misfire more sharply (5 % in 1,000 revolutions). Typical causes are a coked or leaking injector, compression loss or poor fuel; the engine runs roughly and smokes more. Common causes: Injector coked, leaking or delivering the wrong quantity (high likelihood); Compression loss (valve, rings) (medium likelihood); Partial combustion or misfire (fuel quality, EGR distribution) (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor drifting (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running, vibration; Loss of power, more smoke and consumption. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P03AE – Cylinder 3 Pressure Too Low
text: P03AE: Cylinder 3 Pressure Too Low. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 3. P03AE means the pressure measured in the cylinder is lower than expected while the sensor itself is electrically fine. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; GM patents show how such an evaluation works: peak and minimum pressure are compared with limits and with a motoring pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is compared between cylinders. A low value can mean weak combustion or compression – leaking valve, worn rings, leaking glow plug seat, an injector delivering too little – or a sensor drifting downwards. The usual consequence is rough running and more smoke. Common causes: Compression loss (valve, piston rings, leaking glow plug seat) (medium likelihood); Injector delivering too little or coked (medium likelihood); Sensor drifting downwards (deposits) (medium likelihood); Misfire or partial combustion (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power, rough running, possibly misfire on this cylinder; More smoke. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P03AF – Cylinder 3 Pressure Too High

title: P03B0 – Cylinder 3 Pressure Variation Low

title: P03B2 – Cylinder 3 Combustion Performance
text: P03B2: Cylinder 3 Combustion Performance. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 3. P03B2 means the combustion quality in the cylinder, evaluated from the combustion pressure, is abnormal. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows the method: the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is turned into a measure of combustion energy, an inequality index against the neighbouring cylinders in firing order is formed, and a two-sided threshold detects partial combustion, misfire, injector and compression faults. CARB requires engines with a combustion or combustion quality sensor to detect misfire more sharply (5 % in 1,000 revolutions). Typical causes are a coked or leaking injector, compression loss or poor fuel; the engine runs roughly and smokes more. Common causes: Injector coked, leaking or delivering the wrong quantity (high likelihood); Compression loss (valve, rings) (medium likelihood); Partial combustion or misfire (fuel quality, EGR distribution) (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor drifting (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running, vibration; Loss of power, more smoke and consumption. Repair difficulty: hard.

text: P03C2: Cylinder 5 Pressure Too Low. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 5. P03C2 means the pressure measured in the cylinder is lower than expected while the sensor itself is electrically fine. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; GM patents show how such an evaluation works: peak and minimum pressure are compared with limits and with a motoring pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is compared between cylinders. A low value can mean weak combustion or compression – leaking valve, worn rings, leaking glow plug seat, an injector delivering too little – or a sensor drifting downwards. The usual consequence is rough running and more smoke. Common causes: Compression loss (valve, piston rings, leaking glow plug seat) (medium likelihood); Injector delivering too little or coked (medium likelihood); Sensor drifting downwards (deposits) (medium likelihood); Misfire or partial combustion (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lack of power, rough running, possibly misfire on this cylinder; More smoke. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P03C3 – Cylinder 5 Pressure Too High

title: P03C6 – Cylinder 5 Combustion Performance
text: P03C6: Cylinder 5 Combustion Performance. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 5. P03C6 means the combustion quality in the cylinder, evaluated from the combustion pressure, is abnormal. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows the method: the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is turned into a measure of combustion energy, an inequality index against the neighbouring cylinders in firing order is formed, and a two-sided threshold detects partial combustion, misfire, injector and compression faults. Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running, vibration; Loss of power, more smoke and consumption. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P03C7 – Cylinder 6 Pressure Sensor Circuit
text: P03C7: Cylinder 6 Pressure Sensor Circuit. Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. title: P03E5 – A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
text: P03E5: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1. On some engines the intake cam phaser (camshaft position actuator A) has its own position sensors, which tell the engine module where the phaser actually is; sensor C is the third of them, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P03E5 is the general circuit code for this sensor: the module sees an open circuit or a signal outside its valid window on the supply, signal or ground line. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. GM's 2.7-litre engine monitors comparable position sensors on its sliding camshaft under other codes (P2C05 ff), with an open circuit above 200 kΩ and a short below 0.5 Ω in 4 of 5 samples – only as a comparison. The phaser is then usually held in its base position. CARB requires electronic parts of variable valve timing systems to be monitored as comprehensive components. Common causes: Connector or harness to position sensor C open or corroded (high likelihood); Position sensor C faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or ground disturbed (also by another sensor on the same circuit) (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Cam phasing held in its base position, loss of power; Possibly rough idle or higher consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P03E9 – A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Exceeded Learning Limit
text: P03E9: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Exceeded Learning Limit. Engines with cam profile switching move the intake camshaft between lift profiles with actuators – for example pins that shift a sliding cam – and position sensors report which profile is engaged. The engine module learns reference values of position sensor A, such as its end-position levels or the expected pulse position relative to the crankshaft and camshaft sensors; a Ford patent describes correcting this position for the cam phase. P03E9 means the learned value lies outside the permitted adaptation limit, so profile detection is no longer reliable and the module usually stays in a safe profile. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code or its limits; GM's 2.7-litre sliding cam has no learning-limit code. CARB lists a pin that does not reach its position among the faults to be detected. Common causes: Position sensor A or actuator with integrated sensor worn or faulty (signal drift) (high likelihood); Actuator pin or sliding piece stiff, guide worn, dirty oil (medium likelihood); Actuator not relearned or wrongly fitted after replacement (medium likelihood); Connector or wiring with contact resistance (low likelihood); Engine module software (learning algorithm) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Profile switching disabled: less power at high revs or higher consumption; Possibly further profile actuator or sensor codes. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P03EC – A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
text: P03EC: A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Circuit/Open Bank 1. With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. Actuator C is the third of these actuators – not a profile position. The only known user is GM's 2.7-litre turbo four (L3B, three-step sliding cam, from model year 2019). P03EC means the actuator's control circuit is open: GM checks the circuit with the driver on and sets the code at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more (4 of 5 samples, above 11 V, MIL on the first trip). The actuator can then not shift its cam piece, and lift switching and cylinder deactivation are blocked. Common causes: Actuator connector loose, corroded or pin pushed back (often after valve cover work) (high likelihood); Actuator solenoid open (medium likelihood); Wire broken in the engine harness (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lift switching and cylinder deactivation blocked, higher consumption; Possibly rough running if a cam piece stays in the wrong position. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P03EF – A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
text: P03EF: A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1. With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. Actuator C is the third of these actuators – not a profile position. The only known user is GM's 2.7-litre turbo four (L3B, three-step sliding cam, from model year 2019). P03EF is the function check: in the standard's wording the actuator does not do what is commanded. A Hall sensor in the actuator reports the pin position. GM uses this code for a pin that extends without being commanded (4 of 5 cylinder events, MIL on the first trip); a pin that does not extend on command shows up there through the cam piece position sensors (GM-specific codes P30BE ff). GM bulletins name swapped actuator connectors and actuators fitted to the wrong camshaft after repairs. Common causes: Actuator faulty inside: pin extends uncommanded (weak return spring) (high likelihood); Actuator connectors swapped, or intake and exhaust actuators fitted to the wrong camshaft (medium likelihood); Interference in the Hall feedback signal (ground, connector) (medium likelihood); Cam piece sticking or shift groove worn (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Ticking or rattling at the camshaft carrier; Misfire, rough idle or less power in the wrong lift profile; Lift switching and cylinder deactivation out of service. title: P03F0 – A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Stuck On Bank 1
text: P03F0: A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Stuck On Bank 1. With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. Actuator C is the third of these actuators – not a profile position. The only known user is GM's 2.7-litre turbo four (L3B, three-step sliding cam, from model year 2019). P03F0 means the actuator stays on: its pin remains extended although it was commanded off. GM checks whether the pin returns past its retraction threshold by the end of the engine cycle; a single failure in 5 samples sets the code (MIL on the first trip), because a pin left extended can drag in the groove and shift the piece wrongly. Common causes: Pin sticking in the actuator (sludge, wear) (high likelihood); Return ramp of the shift groove damaged or cam piece sticking (medium likelihood); Solenoid stays energized (control wire shorted to ground) (medium likelihood); Hall feedback faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Ticking or rattling at the camshaft carrier; Misfire, rough idle or less power in the wrong lift profile; Lift switching and cylinder deactivation out of service. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P03F1 – B Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
text: P03F1: B Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Circuit/Open Bank 1. title: P03F6 – B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
text: P03F6: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1. On some engines the exhaust cam phaser (camshaft position actuator B) has its own position sensors, which tell the engine module where the phaser actually is; sensor C is the third of them, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. This is a different family from the sliding-cam position sensors (P2C05 ff). P03F6 is the general circuit code for this sensor: the module sees an open circuit or a signal outside its valid window on the supply, signal or ground line. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code (GM, Ford and FCA tables checked); the intake counterpart P03E5 ff is equally unused. The phaser is then usually held in its base position. Common causes: Connector or harness to position sensor C open or corroded (high likelihood); Position sensor C faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or ground disturbed (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Exhaust cam phasing held in its base position, loss of power; Possibly rough idle or poorer emissions. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P03FA – Ignition K Control Signal Circuit/Open
text: P03FA: Ignition K Control Signal Circuit/Open. Ignition K is one of up to twelve control signal lines (A to L) from the engine module to an ignition coil with integrated output stage or to an ignition module – plausibly the 11th channel, but the code standard leaves the assignment to the manufacturer. The code concerns this logic-level signal, not the coil's primary circuit (coil K has its own codes, P0361 and P2330 ff). P03FA means the control line is open or high-resistance: with its driver switched off the module sees a voltage that indicates a missing load (GM uses more than 30 kΩ for comparable coil drivers). The coil fires wrongly or not at all; the misfire usually also sets P0300 ff, and many modules shut off injection to that cylinder to protect the catalyst. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it would only concern twelve-cylinder engines, whose makers publish no OBD summaries; GM and Ford tables stop at eight and ten cylinders. Common causes: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin) (high likelihood); Coil with integrated output stage or ignition module faulty (medium likelihood); Supply or ground of the coil or module missing (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, may flash with severe misfire; Misfire on the cylinder of this channel, rough running; Loss of power, cylinder possibly shut off. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0400 – EGR A Flow
text: P0400: EGR A Flow. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0400 is the general flow fault of EGR system A, used where the module does not classify the error as too little (P0401) or too much (P0402). Ford petrol engines with a stepper-motor valve open and close the valve at steady part load and compare intake manifold pressure with and without EGR; too small a normalised difference (below 1.0) sets P0400, MIL after two trips. GM diesels use the code differently, for air-mass checks with excessive EGR rate. EGR is then usually switched off. Common causes: EGR passages or valve carboned up (high likelihood); EGR valve stiff or faulty (medium likelihood); Leak in the intake or EGR pipe (medium likelihood); MAP or MAF sensor inaccurate (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Pinging under load or rough idle, depending on direction; Higher NOx, emission test failed. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0401 – EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected
text: P0401: EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0401 means too little exhaust is recirculated. Petrol engines open the valve briefly and expect a rise in manifold pressure (GM 2004 V6, MIL on the first trip); older Ford systems measure the pressure drop across an orifice (DPFE sensor). Diesels balance the air mass: if the meter sees more fresh air than the target EGR rate allows, too little exhaust flows (GM, Ford, Saab, usually MIL after two trips). Diesel causes are mostly a coked valve or cooler, petrol causes blocked passages. Common causes: EGR passages, valve or cooler carboned up (high likelihood); EGR valve faulty or stuck closed (high likelihood); Ford: DPFE sensor or its hoses blocked, cracked or swapped (medium likelihood); Diesel: air mass meter drifting or air leak after the turbo (medium likelihood); Vacuum control of the valve faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Pinging or knocking under load (petrol); Higher NOx, emission test failed; Often no noticeable symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0402 – EGR A Flow Excessive Detected
text: P0402: EGR A Flow Excessive Detected. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0402 means too much exhaust is recirculated, or exhaust flows although the valve should be closed – CARB explicitly requires a leaking valve to be detected. Ford's DPFE check at idle with EGR off expects no pressure difference above the engine-off value; Ford diesels compare the measured EGR rate with the expected one, GM diesels the fresh-air deviation in the opposite direction. Petrol engines idle roughly or stall, diesels smoke and may lose power. Common causes: EGR valve stuck open, dirt under the seat (high likelihood); Ford: DPFE sensor drifting or hose wrong (medium likelihood); Diesel: air leak between air mass meter and turbo, MAF drift (medium likelihood); Valve control opens unintentionally (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle or stalling (petrol); Jerking at part load; Diesel: black smoke, loss of power. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0403 – EGR A Control Circuit/Open
text: P0403: EGR A Control Circuit/Open. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0403 concerns the electrical drive of the EGR valve – solenoid, stepper motor, DC motor or vacuum regulator. The module checks the output and sets the code for an open circuit (GM: above 200 kΩ, MIL after two trips; Ford after 4 s, MIL after two trips). Newer systems report shorts separately as P0489 (low) and P0490 (high); Ford and older GM systems include them in P0403. EGR is then switched off for the rest of the trip. Common causes: Connector at the EGR valve corroded or loose (high likelihood); Broken control or supply wire (medium likelihood); Coil or motor in the EGR valve burnt out (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). title: P0404 – EGR A Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0404: EGR A Control Circuit Range/Performance. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. title: P0407 – EGR Sensor B Circuit Low
text: P0407: EGR Sensor B Circuit Low. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor B is depends on the manufacturer – on systems with a second valve or pressure sensor it is that second sensor. title: P040F – EGR Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
text: P040F: EGR Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation. title: P0410 – AIR System A
text: P0410: AIR System A. After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0410 is the general function code for secondary air system A. Many Bosch-managed engines check it passively: with the pump running, the front oxygen sensor must read lean or the fuel control must react; Pierburg lists P0410 as no lean signal, i.e. no air detected. Saab's Motronic 900, by contrast, uses it for too much air. GM's systems with a pressure sensor use P0411 and P2440 ff instead. The check runs once per trip after a cold start; driving is unaffected. Common causes: Secondary air pump failed (water ingress, seized) (high likelihood); Combination or shut-off valve carboned up or stuck (high likelihood); Vacuum hose or electric changeover valve leaking or faulty (medium likelihood); Pump relay or fuse faulty (medium likelihood); Air ducts in the head carboned up or hose off (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Secondary air readiness not set (emission test); Pump silent after a cold start, or unusually loud; Driving normal, higher cold-start emissions. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0411 – AIR System A Incorrect Flow Detected
text: P0411: AIR System A Incorrect Flow Detected. After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0411 means the measured air flow does not match the expected value. Passive systems judge it from the oxygen sensor or fuel control (Saab 900: less than 12 points of correction within 12 s). GM measures actively with a pressure sensor between pump and valve and compares it with a model while pump and valve are on – from 2018 a deviation above 5.0 kPa or below −4.9 kPa sets the code, MIL after two trips. The test needs a cold engine after a long stop, so short warm trips do not complete it. Common causes: Pump weak or failed (water, filter debris) (high likelihood); Combination valve partly stuck or check valve faulty (high likelihood); Hoses blocked, leaking or off; ducts in the head carboned up (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor port blocked or sensor drifting (pressure-sensor systems) (low likelihood); Pump relay or supply with contact resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Secondary air readiness not set (emission test); Pump silent after a cold start, or unusually loud; Driving normal, higher cold-start emissions. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0412 – AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit
text: P0412: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit. The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0412 is the general electrical fault in the control circuit of valve A, detected by comparing the driver's feedback with its commanded state. GM has used it since about 2015 specifically for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P041F and P044F; older GM systems and Toyota use it for any driver fault. The valve then stays shut, so secondary air is missing and P0411 or P2441 may follow. Common causes: Switching valve A faulty (coil open or shorted, water ingress) (high likelihood); Connector corroded or wire open or chafed (high likelihood); Valve supply missing (fuse, main relay) (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Secondary air inactive; Secondary air readiness not set (emission test); Driving normal. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0414 – AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Shorted

title: P0418 – AIR System Control A Circuit

title: P041F – AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Low
text: P041F: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Low. After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air into the exhaust; switching valve A is the electrically driven valve that opens this path. GM checks the valve circuit in three codes – P0412 open, P041F shorted to ground, P044F shorted to positive – while other makers use P0413/P0414 or P0412 for everything. title: P0420 – Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
text: P0420: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1. The engine module checks whether the catalyst of bank 1 still converts enough. On petrol engines it estimates the oxygen storage capacity by comparing the sensors before and after the catalyst – a good catalyst smooths the rear signal. GM uses a test on overrun (ratio below 0.35 sets the code on the first trip), Ford an index ratio above 0.75 or fuel integration after fuel cut-off. On diesels P0420 concerns the oxidation catalyst, checked by its heat release during filter regeneration (GM Duramax LML, Ford below 45 % of the expected heat). Ford names oil-borne poisoning as the most common cause. Common causes: Catalyst aged or poisoned (oil consumption, silicone, coolant) (high likelihood); Catalyst overheated by misfire or rich running (medium likelihood); Rear oxygen sensor sluggish, dirty or unsuitable (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of or at the rear sensor (medium likelihood); Diesel: oxidation catalyst sooted or poisoned, post-injection faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, otherwise often no change in driving; Emission test failed (higher HC, CO, NOx); Rattling or loss of power if the catalyst has broken up. Repair difficulty: medium.

text: P0421: Catalyst 1 Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1. Catalyst 1 is the first catalyst in the flow direction of bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1) – the close-coupled or warm-up catalyst that lights off first after a cold start; the older wording was Warm Up Catalyst. title: P042E – EGR A Control Stuck Open
text: P042E: EGR A Control Stuck Open. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P042E means the position-controlled EGR valve A is more open than commanded and cannot be closed. GM's diesels of 2016/17 set it when the valve stays too far open despite maximum closing duty (about 1–8 s); the 2018 tables check after switch-off whether it is below 5 % within 2 s – both with MIL on the first trip. Ford petrol engines compare the position with limits for 4 s, Ford diesels a deviation above 15 % for 25 s. Too much EGR causes rough idle, stalling and smoke; EGR control is switched off. Common causes: Valve or disc coked, does not close (high likelihood); Actuator motor, gear or return spring faulty (medium likelihood); Position sensor in the valve reads wrong (medium likelihood); Weak supply to the drive or connector fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (GM after one trip); Rough idle, stalling, starting problems; Loss of power, possibly limp mode; Diesel: smoke, higher soot load. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P042F – EGR A Control Stuck Closed
text: P042F: EGR A Control Stuck Closed. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P042F means EGR valve A does not follow the opening command: its actual position stays more closed than commanded although the actuator works with high opening duty. GM's diesels of 2016/17 set it after about 1–8 s with MIL on the first trip; a GM bulletin covers it on the 2017 Cruze diesel. Ford petrol engines use position limits for 4 s; Ford diesels report both directions under P042E. With too little EGR, NOx rises, petrol engines may knock and P0401 can follow. Common causes: Valve coked or seized in the closed position (high likelihood); Actuator motor or gear weak or faulty (medium likelihood); Position sensor or connector gives a wrong value (medium likelihood); Icing in winter (temporary) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (GM after one trip); Usually no driveability problems; Possibly pinging (petrol) or higher NOx. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0430 – Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2
text: P0430: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2. Like P0420, but for the catalyst of bank 2, so only on V and boxer engines with one catalyst per bank; Y-pipe systems with a shared catalyst report P0420 only. The module compares the oxygen sensors before and after the bank 2 catalyst – a good catalyst smooths the rear signal. GM checks on overrun and sets the code on the first trip if the ratio falls below 0.35; Ford evaluates an index ratio or fuel integration and usually needs several trips. The monitor only runs warm, in closed loop and without misfire, fuel or sensor faults. Common causes: Catalyst aged or poisoned (oil consumption, silicone, coolant) (high likelihood); Catalyst overheated by misfire or rich running (medium likelihood); Rear oxygen sensor sluggish, dirty or unsuitable (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak ahead of or at the rear sensor (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, otherwise often no change in driving; Emission test failed (higher HC, CO, NOx); Rattling or loss of power if the catalyst has broken up. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P043A – Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2
text: P043A: Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2. title: P043E – EVAP System Leak Detection Reference Orifice Low Flow
text: P043E: EVAP System Leak Detection Reference Orifice Low Flow. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Systems with a leak detection pump (Bosch DM-TL at VW, Audi, BMW and Maserati, Denso's canister pump module at Toyota/Lexus) first measure a reference value with the pump working only through a built-in 0.5 mm (0.020 in) orifice; it is the yardstick for the small-leak test that CARB requires. P043E means the reference measurement shows too little flow – the vacuum (or with DM-TL the pressure and pump current) becomes stronger than expected, so the orifice or reference path is partly blocked, often by dirt or liquid after overfilling. GM and Ford do not use the code; Maserati fixed false triggering with software. Common causes: Reference orifice or pump module dirty or blocked by liquid (overfilled tank, splash water) (high likelihood); Leak detection pump faulty (weak or blocking pump, changeover valve stuck) (medium likelihood); Engine module software (false detection) (low likelihood); Pump connector or supply (voltage dip) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EVAP leak test does not run, readiness not set; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0440 – EVAP System
text: P0440: EVAP System. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0440 is the general code for a fault in this system without further narrowing down – leak, purge flow or component. Today most makers use the specific codes instead (P0441 ff, P0455–P0457, P0496); the GM and Ford tables of 2006–2023 do not contain P0440. It appears in VW code lists and in an FCA bulletin for the Alfa Romeo 2.0, fixed by software, where FCA calls it incorrect flow. What sets it is therefore manufacturer-specific; CARB requires purge flow and leaks to be monitored. Common causes: Fuel cap leaking, loose or wrong (high likelihood); Purge valve leaking or sticking (medium likelihood); Leaking or cracked EVAP hoses, canister or vent valve (medium likelihood); Engine module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly slight fuel smell; Readiness or emission inspection not passed; No change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0441 – EVAP System Incorrect Purge Flow
text: P0441: EVAP System Incorrect Purge Flow. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0441 means the actual purge flow does not match the target – too little, or flow although the purge valve is closed. CARB requires a fault when no purge flow is detected. Strategies differ widely: Saab's Trionic T7/T8 sets it for flow with the valve closed (tank pressure falling faster than 27.5–40 Pa/s), VW and Audi check purge flow with the leak detection pump, Honda/Acura for a sticking purge valve. GM and Ford do not use P0441 – they report flow with the valve closed as P0496 or P1450 and missing flow as P0455. Common causes: Purge valve stuck open or not sealing (high likelihood); Purge valve stuck closed, purge line blocked, kinked or off (medium likelihood); Leak detection pump with tolerance fault (VW) (medium likelihood); Canister saturated or damaged, turbo purge check valve faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle or hard start after refuelling (valve stuck open); Fuel smell; Possibly fuel trim codes. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0442 – EVAP System Leak Detected (small leak)
text: P0442: EVAP System Leak Detected (small leak). The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0442 reports a small leak; what size that means depends on the maker. Ford detects 0.040 in (1 mm) with the engine running: the vent valve closes, engine vacuum pulls the tank down, the purge valve closes and a pressure rise above 2.5 inH2O in 15 s sets the code (0.020 in is P0456). GM uses the natural pressure change after switch-off for 0.020 in and averages several tests. Pump systems at VW and Audi compare against a reference leak. A worn or loose fuel cap is the most common cause. Common causes: Fuel cap seal worn, wrong or not clicked in (high likelihood); Cracked or porous EVAP hoses or leaking connections (high likelihood); Purge or vent valve does not seal (medium likelihood); Leak detection pump itself leaking (VW/Audi) (medium likelihood); Filler neck corroded, tank or sender seal leaking (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly slight fuel smell; Readiness or emission inspection not passed; No change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0443 – EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit
text: P0443: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0443 is the electrical check of purge valve A, which the module switches to ground in pulses; it compares the driver's feedback voltage with the commanded state. GM uses it for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P0458/P0459; Ford covers open and short in P0443 (5 s). Purging then stops, the canister is no longer regenerated, and the leak and purge monitors are suspended. Common causes: Purge valve connector corroded, loose or off (high likelihood); Purge valve coil open or shorted (medium likelihood); Control wire broken or chafed, or supply missing (fuse, main relay) (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly fuel smell (no purging); EVAP leak test does not run. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0444 – EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Open

title: P0445 – EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Shorted
text: P0445: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Shorted. title: P0446 – EVAP System Vent Control Circuit
text: P0446: EVAP System Vent Control Circuit. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The vent valve is normally open and closes for the leak test. By its wording P0446 is its control circuit, and Ford uses it that way for open and shorted circuits. GM, however, uses P0446 for vent system performance – a blocked vent path: while purging with the vent valve open, the tank must not build up vacuum; more than 2989 Pa for 5 s before 4 litres have been purged sets the code, MIL after two trips. GM reports vent circuit faults as P0449, P0498 and P0499. A blocked vent makes refuelling difficult. Common causes: Vent valve or filter blocked by dirt, dust or water (GM reading) (high likelihood); Vent valve electrically faulty, coil open or shorted (Ford reading) (medium likelihood); Connector or wire to the vent valve corroded or open (medium likelihood); Canister clogged with charcoal or liquid (overfilling) (medium likelihood); Vent hose kinked or blocked by an insect nest (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Refuelling problems, nozzle clicks off early (blocked vent); Hissing when opening the fuel cap (vacuum); EVAP leak test does not run. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0447 – EVAP System Vent Control Circuit Open
text: P0447: EVAP System Vent Control Circuit Open. title: P0449 – EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit/Open
text: P0449: EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit/Open. title: P044A – EGR Sensor C Circuit
text: P044A: EGR Sensor C Circuit. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor C is depends on the maker: on Ford petrol engines from 2020 it is the DPFE sensor, which measures the pressure drop across an orifice in the EGR pipe (sensor A there is the valve position sensor); GM diesels assign it to the position sensor of a low-pressure EGR valve, but only within fault groups. P044A is the general circuit fault of this sensor. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – Ford splits it into P044C/P044D – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. Without the sensor, EGR flow and cooler checks are suspended. Common causes: Connector or wire to sensor C open or corroded (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or ground disturbed (with other sensor codes) (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving; EGR readiness not set, EGR possibly switched off. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P044F – AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit High
text: P044F: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit High. After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air into the exhaust; switching valve A is the electrically driven valve that opens this path. GM checks the valve circuit in three codes – P0412 open, P041F shorted to ground, P044F shorted to positive – while other makers use P0413/P0414 or P0412 for everything. P044F means the control circuit is shorted to positive or the coil is low-resistance: when the driver switches on, the line stays high. GM sets the code at 0.5 Ω or less to the supply (20 of 25 samples of 250 ms, above 11 V, MIL after two trips). The valve then does not open, secondary air is missing and P0411 may follow. Common causes: Valve coil shorted internally (low resistance) (high likelihood); Control wire chafed against a supply wire (medium likelihood); Water in the connector bridging to the supply (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two trips); No change in driving; Secondary air readiness not set, possibly P0411. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0450 – EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit
text: P0450: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The tank pressure sensor measures small pressures around ambient for the leak tests. Its direction differs by maker – on GM vacuum raises the voltage, on Ford and Bosch pressure does – so low and high refer to the signal voltage only. P0450 is the general circuit fault of tank pressure sensor A; makers that separate the fault use P0452 or P0453. Only Audi (2022/23) is documented with the code, as an electrical fault of the tank ventilation pressure sensor; GM, Ford and Saab do not use it. The leak tests are then suspended. title: P0451 – EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0451: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The tank pressure sensor measures small pressures around ambient for the leak tests. Its direction differs by maker – on GM vacuum raises the voltage, on Ford and Bosch pressure does – so low and high refer to the signal voltage only. P0451 is its plausibility check. GM checks during the engine-off leak test that the signal settles to ambient pressure with the vent open and averages several tests; Ford checks the offset after at least 4–6 hours off (±0.5 kPa). title: P0452 – EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit Low

title: P0455 – EVAP System Leak Detected - Large Leak
text: P0455: EVAP System Leak Detected - Large Leak. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0455 means a large leak or that no vacuum builds up. Ford pulls the closed system down with engine vacuum and expects about −2 kPa within 30 s; after refuelling it sets P0457 instead. GM sets the code if 20 litres have been purged without reaching 2740 Pa tank vacuum (once per cold start, MIL after two trips). Saab's ME9 uses a pressure drop below 525 Pa. Common causes: Fuel cap missing, not clicked in or seal faulty (or capless flap) (high likelihood); Hose off or cracked (canister, filler neck, purge line) (high likelihood); Vent valve stuck open or purge valve stuck closed (medium likelihood); Canister or filler neck cracked or corroded (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (possibly a check fuel cap message); Possibly fuel smell; EVAP readiness or emission inspection not passed. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0458 – EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Low
text: P0458: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit Low. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. title: P045A – EGR B Control Circuit
text: P045A: EGR B Control Circuit. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR B is a second EGR valve next to valve A – on diesels with two EGR circuits the low-pressure valve, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor. GM's diesels of 2016–18 and FCA's 2.2-litre diesel in the Jeep Wrangler use it. P045A is the general electrical fault in the drive circuit of valve B, typically an open circuit (for valve A GM uses 200 kΩ or more). GM lists this code among those that switch off the low-pressure EGR position control, but publishes no thresholds for it; the description follows the comparable valve A checks and CARB, which requires output circuits to be monitored. Low-pressure EGR is then switched off. Common causes: Connector at EGR valve B corroded or loose (high likelihood); Harness chafed or heat-damaged (medium likelihood); Actuator motor in valve B open (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Low-pressure EGR switched off, possibly higher NOx; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0460 – Fuel Level Sensor A Circuit
text: P0460: Fuel Level Sensor A Circuit. The fuel level sensor is a float on a resistor track in the tank unit. It is no emission part, but other monitors depend on it – the EVAP leak tests, for example, need at least 15 % fuel – so CARB requires it to be monitored and the usual exemption from the warning lamp does not apply. P0460 is the general circuit code for sensor A, the main or only fuel level sensor. Ford sets it instead of P0462/P0463 below 5 Ω or above 200 Ω for 30 s and until about 2012 also used it for a stuck sensor (fuel use compared over 100–120 miles); Saab's Trionic T8 uses it for a sensor that does not change. GM does not use P0460. The gauge then shows wrong values or a substitute, and level-dependent monitors do not run. Common causes: Resistor track worn or float arm sticking (high likelihood); Wire or connector at the tank unit open or shorted (corrosion) (medium likelihood); Instrument cluster or gateway sends a wrong value (if the level comes via the bus) (low likelihood); Frequent topping up or overfilling (plausibility test fails without a defect) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Fuel gauge wrong, stuck or jumping; Range display and low-fuel warning wrong; Check engine light (depending on the maker). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0465 – EVAP Purge Flow Sensor Circuit
text: P0465: EVAP Purge Flow Sensor Circuit. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. A purge flow sensor – a heated thermistor in the purge line between purge valve and intake manifold, as described in a Ford patent – measures purge flow directly for the CARB purge monitor. Today indirect methods (fuel trim, tank vacuum) have largely replaced it; no manufacturer document available to us uses these codes. P0465 is the general circuit fault of the sensor (heater supply, signal or ground), which CARB requires to be checked continuously. The purge flow monitor can then not be evaluated. Common causes: Connector or wire at the purge flow sensor (high likelihood); Sensor (heater or thermistor) faulty (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EVAP readiness not set, emission inspection not passed; No change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0469 – EVAP Purge Flow Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0469: EVAP Purge Flow Sensor Circuit Intermittent. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. A purge flow sensor – a heated thermistor in the purge line between purge valve and intake manifold, as described in a Ford patent – measures purge flow directly for the CARB purge monitor. Today indirect methods (fuel trim, tank vacuum) have largely replaced it; no manufacturer document available to us uses these codes. P0469 means the signal jumps or drops out briefly, usually from a loose contact. The purge flow monitor can then not be evaluated. Common causes: Loose contact at the connector (high likelihood); Wire broken by engine movement (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EVAP readiness not set, emission inspection not passed; No change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P046A – Catalyst Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation Bank 1
text: P046A: Catalyst Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation Bank 1. Some engines measure the catalyst temperature with sensors instead of only modelling it. P046A compares catalyst temperature sensors 1 and 2 of bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1): both are electrically valid, but their readings do not match – for example they differ after a long stop, or the difference does not fit the operating state. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; FCA's EcoDiesel has only one such sensor per bank, and most makers handle exhaust temperature sensors and their correlation under EGT codes such as P0544 ff or P24C2. The description follows CARB's plausibility requirement for input components. Common causes: One of the two sensors drifting (soot on the tip, ageing) (high likelihood); Sensors fitted or connected the wrong way round (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at one sensor's connector (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak between the sensors (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving; Diesel: filter regeneration possibly changed. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P046C – EGR Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P046C: EGR Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Which part EGR sensors A and B are depends on the maker: sensor A is usually the position sensor of EGR valve A; GM's Duramax diesels of 2017/18 use sensor B for the coolant temperature sensor at the inlet of the high-pressure EGR cooler, FCA for the position sensor of the low-pressure valve. P046C means the signal of sensor A is electrically valid but implausible. GM's diesels (6.6-litre Duramax LML and others from 2014) set it when the actual valve position deviates from the target by 5 % or more for 8 s, with offset learning completed and at least 11 V (MIL after two trips). Ford uses P0405/P0406/P046D for sensor A instead. EGR is then switched off or limited. Common causes: EGR valve coked and stiff, actual position does not follow (high likelihood); Position sensor worn or offset shifted (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at connector or 5 V supply (medium likelihood); Values not relearned after valve replacement (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EGR switched off, possibly higher NOx; Rarely jerking or lack of power. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P046D – EGR Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P046D: EGR Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. title: P0470 – Exhaust Pressure Sensor A Circuit
text: P0470: Exhaust Pressure Sensor A Circuit. The exhaust pressure sensor measures the pressure ahead of the turbine or in the manifold (Ford: turbine upstream pressure, Cummins: exhaust manifold pressure, older Ford diesels: EBP). The module uses it to calculate EGR flow, to control the variable turbine and engine braking, and to protect against overpressure. P0470 is the general circuit fault of sensor A. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel with a digital SENT sensor sets it when the sensor reports an error status or its raw data leave their limits for 5 s; a loss of communication is U0691 instead. Analogue sensors use it for an open or unspecified circuit fault where low and high are not separated. Common causes: Sensor faulty internally (high likelihood); Connector corroded or heat-damaged near the manifold (medium likelihood); Broken or chafed signal or 5 V wire (medium likelihood); Engine module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EGR and turbo control on a substitute value, possibly reduced power; Exhaust brake or warm-up flap without function. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0471 – Exhaust Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0471: Exhaust Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The exhaust pressure sensor measures the pressure ahead of the turbine or in the manifold (Ford: turbine upstream pressure, Cummins: exhaust manifold pressure, older Ford diesels: EBP). title: P0475 – Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A
text: P0475: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A. The exhaust pressure control valve is a flap in the exhaust: on older Navistar/Ford diesels a warm-up flap that raises back pressure when cold, on Ram and others an exhaust brake, on VW's 2.0 TDI a flap that drives the low-pressure EGR, and on Audi and Bentley a sound flap. P0475 is the general circuit fault of valve A, monitored like any output as CARB requires. VW's 2.0 TDI of 2015 sets it together with P0477/P0478, and the actuator electronics are replaced; Audi uses it for an electrical fault of the sound flap, Bentley for a shorted commutator in the flap motor. On the Navistar warm-up flap, a patent describes control to a target back pressure with the exhaust pressure sensor as feedback. Common causes: Flap actuator (motor or electronics) faulty (high likelihood); Wire or connector at the exhaust damaged or corroded (medium likelihood); Control wire open (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Flap without function: sound unchanged, rattling; Diesel: longer warm-up, exhaust brake weak or EGR faults. Repair difficulty: medium.
