title: P0476 – Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Range/Performance
text: P0476: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Range/Performance. The exhaust pressure control valve is a flap in the exhaust: on older Navistar/Ford diesels a warm-up flap that raises back pressure when cold, on Ram and others an exhaust brake, on VW's 2.0 TDI a flap that drives the low-pressure EGR, and on Audi and Bentley a sound flap. P0476 is the function check: the valve does not reach its target position or the expected back pressure. With the Navistar warm-up flap, the module controls to a target back pressure using the sensor as feedback, so missing pressure despite actuation is a function fault. The only code-specific reference is Ducati's Diavel V4 motorcycle (2023): faulty flap motor movement from a wrongly seated cable bracket, with warning lamp and torque limitation until ignition off. Common causes: Flap stiff, coked or corroded (high likelihood); Linkage, cable or bracket misadjusted (medium likelihood); Actuator (motor, hydraulic or vacuum) weak (medium likelihood); Exhaust pressure sensor or sensing tube giving wrong feedback (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Flap without function: sound unchanged, rattling; Diesel: longer warm-up, exhaust brake weak or EGR faults. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P047F – Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Stuck Open
text: P047F: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Stuck Open. The exhaust pressure control valve is a flap in the exhaust: on older Navistar/Ford diesels a warm-up flap that raises back pressure when cold, on Ram and others an exhaust brake, on VW's 2.0 TDI a flap that drives the low-pressure EGR, and on Audi and Bentley a sound flap. On VW's 2.0 TDI and Audi's A3 TDI of 2009–12 the code appears with P0477, P048A–P048C and P0401: water and road salt corrode the flap shaft so the flap sticks; improved parts were introduced. As the flap drives the low-pressure EGR there, EGR flow is then too low. Common causes: Flap shaft corroded or seized (high likelihood); Soot or carbon on the flap (medium likelihood); Actuator or linkage faulty or unhooked (medium likelihood); Position sensor reports wrongly (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EGR flow too low (P0401), higher NOx; Exhaust brake or warm-up flap without effect, possibly louder exhaust. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0480 – Fan 1 Control Circuit
text: P0480: Fan 1 Control Circuit. The engine module switches the radiator fan either through a relay, whose coil it pulls to ground, or with a PWM signal to a fan control module. The circuit is an output that CARB requires to be checked continuously. P0480 concerns the control circuit of fan 1. GM sets it for an open circuit – 200 kΩ or more with the driver off, 50 of 63 samples, above 11 V, MIL after two trips – and reports a short to ground or positive as P0691/P0692; Saab models on GM technology set it after 5 s (relay) or 1 s (PWM). FCA bulletins also name it with the warning lamp. Ford's OBD summaries do not contain the code. If the fan stops, the engine can overheat in traffic and the air conditioning weakens at standstill. Common causes: Fan relay (coil open) or fan control module faulty (high likelihood); Connector at fan or relay corroded, water ingress or pin pushed out (high likelihood); Control wire open or shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Fan motor or fan assembly faulty (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Radiator fan does not run, or runs constantly; Overheating at standstill or in traffic; Air conditioning weak at standstill. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0481 – Fan 2 Control Circuit
text: P0481: Fan 2 Control Circuit. The engine module switches the radiator fan either through a relay, whose coil it pulls to ground, or with a PWM signal to a fan control module. The circuit is an output that CARB requires to be checked continuously. P0481 concerns the second fan control circuit – depending on the design a second fan or a second speed stage; on GM and Saab, relays 2 and 3 switch the fans in series or parallel for low and high speed. GM sets it for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 50 of 63 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P0693/P0694. Ford's OBD summaries do not contain the code. One fan stage then fails or runs constantly; cooling usually remains partly available. Common causes: Fan relay 2 (or 2/3) faulty (high likelihood); Corrosion or water in relay or fan connector (medium likelihood); Control wire open or shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; One fan stage or fan not working, or running constantly; Temperature rises at standstill. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0482 – Fan 3 Control Circuit
text: P0482: Fan 3 Control Circuit. The engine module switches cooling fan stages through relays, pulling each relay coil to ground. P0482 concerns the control circuit of the third stage or relay: with the driver off the line should sit at battery voltage through the coil, and the internal pull-up level means an open circuit (Saab ME9: more than 1 s, 10–18 V, engine running). On the GM-based Saab 9-5 of 2011 it is relay 3 (medium stage) of a two-fan network, with shorts reported as P0695/P0696. GM tables list P0482 only in fault groups; Ford's OBD summaries do not contain it. One fan stage then fails. Common causes: Fan relay 3 faulty (coil open) or not seated properly (high likelihood); Control wire open or high-resistance, corroded or backed-out pins (high likelihood); Relay coil supply missing (fuse, supply wire) (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; One fan stage fails – temperature rises in traffic or when towing; Air conditioning weaker at standstill. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0483 – Fan Rationality Check
text: P0483: Fan Rationality Check. Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0483 checks the fan's function, not its circuit. With a speed sensor (GM viscous fans) commanded and actual speed are compared: GM's Duramax diesels of 2014–18 set it at more than ±500 rpm for at least 120 s, GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups of 2004–06 at more than 1000 rpm – MIL after two trips. Without a sensor Subaru (and the Saab 9-2X) judges indirectly: if coolant at 100 °C or more does not fall within 5 minutes at idle with the fan on, the code sets after two trips. Ford's OBD summaries do not contain it. Common causes: Viscous clutch worn or leaking, or its solenoid faulty – fan does not reach or leave target speed (high likelihood); Electric fan motor stiff or worn, or fan blocked (medium likelihood); Fan speed sensor or wiring giving a wrong value (medium likelihood); Radiator or condenser clogged, coolant low (Subaru logic) (low likelihood); Drive belt slipping (belt-driven viscous fan) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two trips); Constant fan roar, or temperature rise at standstill; Air conditioning weak at low speed. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0484 – Fan Circuit Current High
text: P0484: Fan Circuit Current High. P0484 monitors the current drawn in the fan's load circuit: if it exceeds a threshold – blocked or stiff motor, shorted turns, a short in the load circuit – the code sets. This is only possible where the fan runs on a current-measuring semiconductor driver or fan module; plain relay circuits do not measure load current. Supplier patents (Bosch and others) describe current limiting or switch-off after a few seconds of overcurrent, ignoring the inrush current. No manufacturer table available to us lists P0484, so thresholds and warning-lamp behaviour remain open; CARB requires output components to be monitored. Common causes: Fan motor stiff (bearing damage) or blocked (foreign object, ice, bent blade) (high likelihood); Shorted turns or worn brushes in the fan motor (medium likelihood); Short in the load circuit (pinched or chafed wire) (medium likelihood); Fan control module faulty (wrong current measurement) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp (depending on the maker); Fan does not run, runs only briefly or at reduced power; Humming or grinding at the fan, possibly blown fan fuse; Overheating at standstill. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0485 – Fan Power/Ground Circuit
text: P0485: Fan Power/Ground Circuit. P0485 monitors the supply or ground path of the fan or its control module – not the control line. It is typical of fans with their own module (PWM or LIN), which can report undervoltage or a missing ground. The high currents involved, often 20–60 A, make contact resistance at ground and supply connections and fuse holders the main cause. No manufacturer table available to us lists P0485, so thresholds and warning-lamp behaviour remain open; CARB requires output components to be monitored. The fan then runs intermittently or not at all. Common causes: Fan or fan module ground loose, corroded or broken (high likelihood); Fan fuse blown or fuse holder overheated or corroded (high likelihood); Relay power contact burnt – voltage drop under load (medium likelihood); Connector at the fan scorched, water ingress (medium likelihood); Fan control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp (depending on the maker); Fan does not run or only intermittently; Overheating at standstill, weak air conditioning; Possibly burnt smell or discoloured connector. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0486 – EGR Sensor B Circuit
text: P0486: EGR Sensor B Circuit. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Which part EGR sensor B is depends on the maker: FCA uses it for the position sensor of the low-pressure EGR valve, GM's Duramax diesels for the coolant temperature sensor at the EGR cooler inlet. P0486 is its general circuit fault without a low or high assignment. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – makers report sensor B as P0407/P0408, P046E and P046F – so the description follows CARB's input component rules. EGR is then switched off or uses a substitute value. Common causes: Connector or harness to sensor B corroded or open (heat at the exhaust) (high likelihood); Sensor B faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or ground disturbed (low likelihood); Engine module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EGR switched off, usually no noticeable change; Higher NOx. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0487 – EGR Throttle Control Circuit A/Open
text: P0487: EGR Throttle Control Circuit A/Open. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The EGR throttle is a regulating flap ahead of the intake manifold on diesels: by closing partly it lowers manifold pressure below exhaust back pressure so that enough exhaust is recirculated, and it also helps filter regeneration and shuts off air at engine stop. It is usually a DC motor with position sensor. GM and Ford report this flap under P02E0 ff; no manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P0487 means its drive circuit is open or has a general circuit fault, detected by the output stage. The flap then stays open, so the EGR rate cannot be raised enough and filter regeneration may be blocked. Common causes: Connector at the flap corroded or loose, wire open (high likelihood); Flap actuator motor faulty (winding open) (medium likelihood); Pneumatic version: vacuum converter faulty (low likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Loss of power or limp mode possible; Shaking when the engine is switched off; Filter regeneration does not complete. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0489 – EGR A Control Circuit Low
text: P0489: EGR A Control Circuit Low. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0489 means the drive circuit of EGR valve A – solenoid, stepper or DC motor – is shorted to ground. The valve is usually switched off; with low-side control a short to ground can keep it energised and open, causing rough idle or stalling. Symptoms: Check engine light on; EGR switched off; Rough idle or stalling if the valve stays open. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P048A – Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Stuck Closed
text: P048A: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Stuck Closed. An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve A is the first such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P048A means valve A is commanded open but its position feedback stays closed. On VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI of 2009–13 water and road salt corrode the shaft of the low-pressure EGR flap so it sticks; the code appears with P047F, P0477, P048B/P048C and P0401. The bulletins advise removing the flap and checking it moves freely, otherwise replacing it; improved parts were introduced. A closed flap keeps back pressure high. Common causes: Flap or flap shaft corroded or coked (stiff) (high likelihood); Flap actuator (motor or gear) faulty or too weak (medium likelihood); Linkage between actuator and flap broken or misadjusted (low likelihood); Position sensor reports wrongly (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Flap without function, exhaust sound changed; VW/Audi TDI: EGR fault P0401 possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P048B – Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit
text: P048B: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit. text: P048E: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High. title: P0490 – EGR A Control Circuit High
text: P0490: EGR A Control Circuit High. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0490 means the drive circuit of EGR valve A is shorted to battery voltage, or its output stage sees overcurrent. GM's Duramax LML sets it at 0.5 Ω or less to the supply for 3 s, GM's 2017 diesels at an H-bridge current above 8 A (160 of 200 samples), Ford diesels after 0.35 s – MIL after two trips. The output stage switches off for protection and the valve falls into its spring position, closed; EGR is off. Common causes: Harness shorted to a supply wire (chafing) (high likelihood); EGR valve with shorted turns (low resistance, overcurrent) (medium likelihood); Moisture in the connector (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). title: P0491 – AIR System Insufficient Flow Bank 1
text: P0491: AIR System Insufficient Flow Bank 1. After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; CARB requires the air flow to be monitored per bank. P0491 means too little air reaches bank 1 (the side with cylinder 1). VW and Audi calculate the injected air mass per bank from the front oxygen sensor's reaction during the cold-start phase; an Audi bulletin names values of 0.4–0.7 on both banks as too little together, often from coked air passages in the cylinder head. On VW/Audi V engines each bank has its own combination valve with a shared pump. Ford assigns the code to the bank 1 secondary air monitor; GM uses P0411 instead. Common causes: Secondary air passages in the cylinder head coked (high likelihood); Combination valve stuck or stiff (high likelihood); Vacuum supply or changeover valve leaking, valve closes too early (medium likelihood); Secondary air pump weak or water in the pump (medium likelihood); Hose between pump and valve leaking or off (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; No change in driving; Secondary air readiness not set (emission test); Possibly no pump noise after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0493 – Fan Overspeed
text: P0493: Fan Overspeed. Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0493 is documented only on GM petrol engines of 2004–06 with a viscous fan: the measured fan speed exceeds a limit that is hardly physically possible (about 6400 rpm), so it is effectively a plausibility check of the speed signal or a seized clutch at high engine speed. Two counts set it, with the warning lamp on the first trip – unlike P0495, which needs two trips. Ford, FCA and GM from 2014 were not found to use it. Common causes: Viscous clutch seized – fan runs rigidly with the belt drive (high likelihood); Interference or faulty signal from the fan speed sensor (medium likelihood); Clutch solenoid or its control stuck at fully engaged (medium likelihood); Engine module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (first trip); Loud fan roar at higher revs; Higher consumption, slightly less power. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0494 – Fan 1 Underspeed
text: P0494: Fan 1 Underspeed. Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0494 means fan 1 turns slower than commanded, judged from the speed reported by a LIN fan module or the clutch's speed sensor. GM's 2.0-litre turbo of 2020 uses a lower limit of about 59 % of the target at 750 rpm, rising to about 76 % at 2750 rpm and above. GM bulletins name an internal fan fault on the Equinox/Terrain 1.5 and water slowing the fan on the Hummer EV; Ford's 6.7-litre Super Duty uses it for the viscous fan and warns against replacing the clutch too quickly. Common causes: Fan motor or fan module faulty or worn (brushes, bearings, electronics) (high likelihood); Fan slowed or blocked (water, snow, ice, foreign object, distorted shroud) (medium likelihood); Viscous clutch slipping or low on fluid, clutch valve faulty (medium likelihood); High-resistance supply or ground, connector problems (medium likelihood); Faulty speed signal (sensor or LIN feedback) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on the maker); Temperature rises at standstill or when towing; Air conditioning weak at standstill. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0495 – Fan 1 Overspeed
text: P0495: Fan 1 Overspeed. Two kinds of cooling fan carry these codes: electric fans switched by relays or driven by a PWM/LIN fan module with speed feedback, and engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch, whose speed a Hall sensor reports – GM calls them EV fans, meaning electro-viscous, not electric vehicle. P0495 mainly concerns viscous fans: with the fan commanded off it turns faster than the permitted drag speed, so the clutch does not release. GM thresholds: Duramax 2016 above 1500 rpm, Duramax 2018 above a calculated drag speed, petrol SUVs of 2004–05 above 1600 rpm without command – all with the warning lamp after two trips; Ford's 6.7-litre Super Duty uses it the same way. On GM's 2020 2.0-litre turbo with a LIN electric fan it means a reported speed above 2900 rpm. title: P0496 – EVAP System High Purge Flow
text: P0496: EVAP System High Purge Flow. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0496 means vapour flows into the intake although the module is not purging – usually a purge valve that leaks or sticks open. GM and Saab seal the system after a cold start with the engine running; if tank vacuum exceeds 2491 Pa for 5 s, the code sets (fuel 10–90 %, MIL after two trips). Ford, which replaced its old code P1450 with P0496, also sets it for excessive vacuum during the leak test, for example with a vent valve stuck closed. Hard starting right after refuelling is typical. Common causes: Purge valve leaking or stuck open (charcoal dust in the seat) (high likelihood); Vent valve stuck closed or vent filter or line blocked (medium likelihood); Vapour line kinked or blocked (low likelihood); Tank pressure sensor reading wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard or long starting right after refuelling; Rough idle, rich fuel trim; Hissing vacuum when opening the fuel cap. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0497 – EVAP System Low Purge Flow
text: P0497: EVAP System Low Purge Flow. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. P0497 is the counterpart of P0496: the module purges but sees too little or no purge flow, judged indirectly from fuel trim, idle control or tank vacuum – CARB requires missing purge flow to be detected. Code-specific use is documented only by Land Rover (5.0-litre V8) and in a GM fault group for systems with a sealed tank (Volt, ELR); standard GM and Ford systems use other codes, such as P0455. The canister is then not purged and saturates. Common causes: Purge valve stuck closed, does not open (high likelihood); Purge line off, kinked or blocked (check valve sticking) (medium likelihood); Canister or vent filter blocked (e.g. after overfilling) (medium likelihood); Vent valve stuck closed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fuel smell around the car; Fuel nozzle clicks off early. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0498 – EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit Low
text: P0498: EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit Low. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The vent valve is normally open and switched to ground by the module; P0449 (open), P0498 and P0499 form the newer code scheme for its circuit, used mainly by GM and Saab models with GM engines, while Ford uses P0446. P0498 means the control wire is shorted to ground: GM sees 0.5 Ω or less to ground with the driver off (20 of 25 samples), Saab below 2.6 V – MIL after two trips. The valve is then permanently energised and closed, so the tank is not vented and refuelling becomes difficult. Common causes: Vent valve control wire chafed against ground (underbody, tank area) (high likelihood); Vent valve coil shorted internally (medium likelihood); Corrosion or water in the connector (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Refuelling difficult, nozzle clicks off; Vacuum noise when opening the fuel cap. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0499 – EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit High
text: P0499: EVAP System Vent Valve Control Circuit High. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. The vent valve is normally open and switched to ground by the module (GM scheme P0449/P0498/P0499; Ford uses P0446). P0499 means the control wire is shorted to positive: with the driver on the output stays high – GM sees 0.5 Ω or less to the supply, Saab above 4.6 V; MIL after two trips. The valve then cannot close, the system cannot be sealed, and the leak tests are suspended because they would otherwise report a large leak. Symptoms: Check engine light on; EVAP readiness not set; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P049A – EGR B Flow
text: P049A: EGR B Flow. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Circuit B is the second EGR path; on diesels with two circuits it is the low-pressure EGR, which takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it in before the turbo compressor (GM diesels 2016–18, FCA's 2.2 and 3.0 diesels). P049A is the general flow fault of circuit B, used where the module does not separate too little from too much; CARB requires low and high flow to be detected, mostly by comparing air mass, manifold pressure or lambda with a model. No manufacturer document available to us uses P049A – GM has only position and actuator codes for its low-pressure EGR, FCA uses P049B. Low-pressure EGR is then switched off. Common causes: Low-pressure EGR valve sooted or sticking (high likelihood); Low-pressure EGR cooler or line blocked or leaking (medium likelihood); Flap creating the pressure difference faulty (medium likelihood); Sensors (air mass, pressure difference, position sensor B) implausible (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EGR switched off, usually no noticeable change; Higher NOx. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P049D – EGR A Control Position Exceeded Learning Limit
text: P049D: EGR A Control Position Exceeded Learning Limit. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P049D checks the learned zero point – the fully closed position – of EGR valve A. The module learns the position sensor voltage with the valve closed, at GM during the after-run following ignition off; if the learned value lies outside a window (GM 2018: 83.5–93.5 % of 5 V, GM 2016: 16.4–25.1 %) or the values scatter too much (GM Duramax LML above 30 %), the code sets – MIL after two trips at GM, immediately after learning at Ford. Usually soot at the seat keeps the valve from closing, or a new valve was not taught in. Common causes: Soot or deposits at the valve seat, valve does not close fully (high likelihood); Position sensor A faulty or characteristic shifted (medium likelihood); New or cleaned valve not taught in, or wrong part (medium likelihood); Position sensor circuit fault as the primary cause (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no driveability effect; EGR possibly switched off, rough idle if the valve stays open. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P049F – Exhaust Pressure Control Valve B
text: P049F: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve B. An exhaust pressure control valve is an electrically driven flap in the exhaust with a position sensor or end-position switch, usually inside the actuator. Valve B is the second such flap; Bentley's V8 assigns A to bank 1 and B to bank 2. Documented uses are the flap behind the particulate filter of VW's and Audi's 2.0 TDI, which raises back pressure for the low-pressure EGR, and the sound flaps of Audi and Bentley. P049F is the general electrical fault of valve B. Audi uses it for sound flap 2 (2017–21, mostly sporadic, with P0475/P0477); on Bentley's Bentayga a commutator short in the flap motor caused by sludge triggers it – if the flap moves freely by hand, the actuator is replaced, otherwise the silencer or pipe. Common causes: Flap actuator faulty (commutator short) (high likelihood); Wire or connector at the actuator damaged (medium likelihood); Control wire open (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Flap without function, exhaust sound changed; VW/Audi TDI: EGR fault P0401 possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04AB – EVAP System Purge Control Valve B Circuit/Open
text: P04AB: EVAP System Purge Control Valve B Circuit/Open. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Purge valve B is a second electric purge valve, usually for the high-load purge line of a turbo engine, which purges to the compressor inlet when there is boost in the manifold (Ford patent). Many makers solve this path with one purge valve and passive check valves instead – Ford tests it as P04F0 – and then have no valve B. CARB requires every purge path to be checked. P04AB means the control circuit of purge valve B is open; the high-load path then does not purge. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the comparable purge valve A checks (for GM P0443/P0458/P0459). Common causes: Purge valve B connector loose or corroded (high likelihood); Coil of purge valve B open (medium likelihood); Supply (fuse, main relay) or control wire open (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; EVAP readiness not set; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P04B0 – Refueling Vapor Control Valve Circuit/Open
text: P04B0: Refueling Vapor Control Valve Circuit/Open. The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Plug-in hybrids and range extenders with a sealed, pressurised tank have an electric valve in the vapour line between tank and canister. It is normally closed and opens before refuelling, so that the tank is depressurised – the filler flap is only released then – and refuelling vapour reaches the canister (Ford patent). title: P04B3 – Refueling Vapor Control Valve Performance/Stuck Open
text: P04B3: Refueling Vapor Control Valve Performance/Stuck Open. title: P04B4 – Refueling Vapor Control Valve Stuck Closed
text: P04B4: Refueling Vapor Control Valve Stuck Closed. Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. When the driver presses the fuel button, the system opens the valve, lets the pressure escape into the canister and only then unlocks the filler door. A switch reports whether the door is open or closed, so that the tank can be sealed again afterwards. P04B4 is the function check of the valve between tank and canister: after the open command the tank pressure must move towards canister or ambient pressure, and if the rate of change stays below a threshold the valve counts as stuck closed (Ford patent). The tank then cannot be depressurised, the door does not unlock or only after a long delay, and during refuelling vapour cannot reach the canister. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. Common causes: Valve mechanically stuck (dirt, fuel in the valve, ice) (high likelihood); Vapour line kinked or blocked, liquid separator blocked (medium likelihood); Canister clogged (charcoal dust, liquid fuel) (low likelihood); Tank pressure sensor sluggish or wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Filler door does not open after pressing the button, or only after a long delay; Nozzle clicks off early when refuelling; Hissing or vapour when opening the cap. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04BB – Fuel Fill Door Lock Control Circuit/Open
text: P04BB: Fuel Fill Door Lock Control Circuit/Open. On plug-in hybrids with a sealed, pressurised tank, pressing the fuel button (open request) starts a refuelling mode: the module opens the tank valve, releases the pressure into the charcoal canister and only then unlocks the filler door via an electric actuator (Ford patent). P04BB concerns the lock circuit: the module detects an open circuit in the output to the door actuator or its relay, which CARB requires for outputs. A separate lock output exists only on actuators that drive actively in both directions; spring-return actuators have only the unlock circuit. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's rules for input and output components and patents on the door actuator. Common causes: Open control wire or connector at the door actuator (high likelihood); Actuator motor or solenoid open internally (medium likelihood); Actuator supply, fuse or relay not working (medium likelihood); Driver in the module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Filler door does not open or lock as commanded; Refuelling system message in the instrument cluster; Possibly check engine light. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04CE – EGR Temperature Sensor C Circuit
text: P04CE: EGR Temperature Sensor C Circuit. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The code standard allows up to four EGR temperature sensors, A to D – for example before and after the cooler, or in the high- and low-pressure circuits; which is which depends on the maker. Sensor C is the third of them, usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. P04CE is its general circuit fault, without separating low and high. FCA lists sensor C codes for its part 68142905A (Ram 2014 6.4 and 3.0 litre, Jeep and Dodge 3.6 Pentastar 2016) together with P040B, P0401 and P2457. Thresholds are not published. Without a valid temperature the EGR flow model is wrong, so the module uses a substitute value or switches EGR off. Common causes: Open or poor contact in signal or ground line (high likelihood); Connector or wire at the sensor corroded or worn by heat and vibration (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (element broken or sooted) (medium likelihood); Engine module input (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving (EGR on a substitute value or off); Possibly EGR flow or cooler codes (P0401, P2457). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04D3 – Exhaust Brake Input Circuit
text: P04D3: Exhaust Brake Input Circuit. The exhaust brake input is the driver's request for the exhaust or engine brake – a button or stalk on diesel pick-ups and trucks. On GM's 6.6-litre L5P, for example, the button must be pressed again after every start. GM uses the exhaust brake status as an enable condition for other emission monitors, which is why CARB requires the input to be checked. No manufacturer table available to us lists P04D3–P04D7; Hino's J08E truck engine checks P04D5 before its exhaust brake function test. P04D3 is the general circuit fault of the request input, used where the module cannot resolve the fault type further – an open circuit or, on bus-connected buttons, an invalid message. Common causes: Exhaust brake button faulty (contact, lighting board) (high likelihood); Open wire or connector between button and module (medium likelihood); Fault in an intermediate module or bus message (low likelihood); Engine module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Exhaust brake cannot be switched on, button lamp off or wrong; Possibly check engine light; More load on the service brakes downhill. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04D8 – Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop EGR Control
text: P04D8: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop EGR Control. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Where EGR is closed-loop controlled – on flow, valve position or pressure difference – CARB requires the control to start within a time set by the maker after starting; otherwise a fault is due, and P04D8 is that code. Typical prerequisites are coolant or cooler temperature, valid sensors and an operating range; Ford diesels, for example, run their EGR monitors only with EGR in closed loop. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04D8 – many monitor the inputs individually instead, as CARB permits. Common causes: Engine reaches release temperature too late (thermostat stuck open, very short trips, cold weather) (high likelihood); Faulty input sensor blocks the release (EGR temperature, air mass, position) (medium likelihood); EGR valve or actuator not ready (stuck, learned value missing) (medium likelihood); Software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no driveability problems; Often together with coolant or sensor codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04D9 – Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too Low
text: P04D9: Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too Low. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04D9 means the EGR control has used up its authority and still gets too little flow – CARB requires this to be detected. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays above 50 points for 20 s. Volvo cars from 2022 also set it after long low-load driving and fix it with a software update and an activation drive; a Mack/Volvo truck bulletin traces it to wrong EGR temperature readings from worn connector contacts. Common causes: EGR cooler, valve or pipes sooted or narrowed (high likelihood); EGR valve sticking or not opening fully (medium likelihood); EGR rate mismeasured (temperature sensor contacts, air mass meter, pressure sensor) (medium likelihood); Software or driving profile with long low-load operation (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no noticeable symptoms; Higher NOx, petrol engines may knock. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04DA – Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too High
text: P04DA: Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too High. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DA is the counterpart of P04D9: the control cannot lower the flow far enough even at the end of its range. CARB requires this for petrol engines from model years 2019–21 and for diesels. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays below −60 points for 20 s with EGR in closed loop. Too much exhaust in the cylinder causes soot, rough running and, on petrol engines, misfire up to stalling at idle. Common causes: EGR valve not closing (soot at the seat, stuck open) (high likelihood); Air mass meter reading too little fresh air (EGR rate calculated too high) (medium likelihood); Position or EGR temperature sensor giving a wrong value (medium likelihood); Intake or exhaust throttle wrong (pressure difference too large) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle, jerking; Smoke or soot (diesel), possibly stalling at idle (petrol). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04DB – Crankcase Ventilation System Disconnected
text: P04DB: Crankcase Ventilation System Disconnected. The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04DB means a disconnection: without the pressure drop the clean-air side is off, without the pulses the crankcase side. GM's LSY uses the product of normalised offset and noise (below 0.63 kPa², MIL after two trips); Ford's EcoBoost checks the dirty side at cranking and the clean side above 5 lb/min of air. Engines without such a sensor may report a disconnection through mixture or load codes, as CARB allows. FCA bulletins cover it on the Alfa Romeo 2.0 turbo and the Ram 3.0 EcoDiesel. Common causes: Ventilation hose off or quick connector not latched (often after intake work) (high likelihood); Hose cracked or porous, or nipple broken (high likelihood); PCV valve stuck closed or oil separator blocked or frozen (simulates a disconnection) (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor in the hose giving a wrong signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hissing, false air, rough idle or lean running; Oil mist or smell in the engine bay. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P04DC – Fuel Fill Door Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance
text: P04DC: Fuel Fill Door Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance. Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. When the driver presses the fuel button, the system opens the valve, lets the pressure escape into the canister and only then unlocks the filler door. A switch reports whether the door is open or closed, so that the tank can be sealed again afterwards. P04DC means the door switch signal is electrically valid but implausible. A GM patent detects refuelling from a rising fuel level at standstill with low tank pressure; if the switch reported open for less than about 20 s, or closed for too long, it is faulty. A Ford patent sets a fault if the fuel level rose and the car drove off without the switch ever reporting open – the valve then stays open and the driver is warned. If the door state is unknown, the system leaves the tank open to the canister as a precaution and suspends the leak tests. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules and patents for the door switch. Common causes: Switch mechanically jammed or misadjusted (reports one state permanently) (high likelihood); Door or actuator damaged or missing (medium likelihood); Signal or connector fault with a valid but wrong level (medium likelihood); Fuel level sensor faulty (refuelling misdetected) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fuel door open message although the door is closed, or missing when it is open; Door may not open or only after a delay; EVAP readiness not set. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P04DD – Cold Start EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected
text: P04DD: Cold Start EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DD monitors EGR A while a cold-start emission reduction strategy is active and commands EGR: if the flow does not react as intended, too little exhaust is recirculated in the warm-up phase. CARB requires separate codes for such cold-start faults, which is why P04DD exists alongside P0401. The only manufacturer reference is a FCA bulletin for a six-cylinder diesel with high- and low-pressure EGR, naming it as a consequence of a failed position sensor (P0407/P0408) – repair that first. Common causes: EGR valve position sensor faulty (follow-on code) (high likelihood); EGR valve sticking or not opening when cold (soot, icing, condensate) (medium likelihood); EGR path or cooler narrowed (medium likelihood); Pressure, temperature or air mass sensor misreading (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms; Higher NOx after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04DE – Cold Start EGR A Flow Excessive Detected
text: P04DE: Cold Start EGR A Flow Excessive Detected. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DE is the counterpart of P04DD: during an active cold-start strategy the flow of EGR A is too high – the strategy calls for little or limited EGR, but the valve lets more through. CARB requires separate codes for cold-start faults. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04DE; FCA uses the neighbouring code P04DD, so its use there is plausible but not documented. Too much exhaust in a cold engine causes rough running, smoke and in extreme cases stalling. Common causes: EGR valve not closing fully (soot, condensate, stuck open) (high likelihood); Position sensor reports a wrong position (medium likelihood); Air mass or pressure difference misreading (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle after a cold start; Smoke or soot after a cold start (diesel), stalling possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04DF – EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Performance/Stuck Open
text: P04DF: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Performance/Stuck Open. Purge valve A is the main EVAP purge valve between charcoal canister and intake manifold (on turbo engines the low-load path); its electrical circuit faults are P0443, P0458 and P0459. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows GM's comparable check P0496, Subaru's valve B counterpart P04AE and CARB's purge flow requirement. P04DF means valve A does not react as commanded or lets vapour through when closed: with the system sealed and the valve not driven, vacuum must not reach the tank. Intake vacuum then draws vapour all the time – rich mixture and hard starting after refuelling are typical. Common causes: Purge valve A leaking or stuck open (charcoal dust or dirt on the seat) (high likelihood); Canister broken down, charcoal dust in the valve (medium likelihood); Tank pressure sensor giving a wrong signal (low likelihood); Hoses swapped or wrongly routed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard starting or stumbling idle right after refuelling; Rough idle, rich fuel trim. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P04E0 – EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Stuck Closed
text: P04E0: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Stuck Closed. Purge valve A is the main EVAP purge valve between charcoal canister and intake manifold (on turbo engines the low-load path); its electrical circuit faults are P0443, P0458 and P0459. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows GM's comparable check P0496, Subaru's valve B counterpart P04AE and CARB's purge flow requirement. P04E0 means valve A does not open although it is driven: no vacuum builds up in the tank and the mixture does not react while purging – CARB requires missing purge flow to be detected. The canister is then not purged and saturates, causing fuel smell and early nozzle shut-off. Common causes: Purge valve A stuck closed (gummed, charcoal dust, spring or armature) (high likelihood); Purge line kinked or blocked (medium likelihood); Canister or vent blocked (low likelihood); Tank pressure sensor faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fuel smell; Nozzle clicks off early when refuelling. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P04E1 – Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Circuit
text: P04E1: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Circuit. The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04E1 is the sensor's general circuit fault, typical of digital sensors with invalid signal patterns or where low and high are not separated. Its circuit diagnosis is a precondition for the disconnection check P04DB. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04E1 itself; GM uses P04E2/P04E3, Ford P051A ff. Common causes: Sensor connector not latched or corroded (high likelihood); Signal, 5 V reference or ground wire open (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Disconnection check P04DB does not run; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P04E5 – EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit
text: P04E5: EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The code standard allows up to four EGR temperature sensors, A to D – for example before and after the cooler, or in the high- and low-pressure circuits; which is which depends on the maker. Sensor D is the fourth of them, usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. P04E5 is its general circuit fault, conceivable on systems with high- and low-pressure EGR and two sensors per circuit. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D – GM, Ford and FCA use at most A to C – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. EGR then uses a substitute value or is switched off. Common causes: Wire or connector fault (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving (EGR on a substitute value or off); Possibly EGR flow or cooler codes (P0401, P2457). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04E6 – EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance

No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E6 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example it differs from other temperatures after a long stop, does not react when EGR opens, or freezes. title: P04EA – EVAP System Small Leak Detected - Fuel Tank Side
text: P04EA: EVAP System Small Leak Detected - Fuel Tank Side. Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EA reports a small leak (0.040 in) in the tank section – tank, filler neck, cap and lines up to the tank valve. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB and the Ford patent. Common causes: Fuel cap or seal leaking or not closed properly (tether trapped) (high likelihood); Filler neck or tank vent line leaking (medium likelihood); Sender or pump flange seal leaking (medium likelihood); Tank valve or tank pressure sensor faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly check fuel cap message or slight fuel smell; No change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04F0 – EVAP System High Load Purge Line A Performance
text: P04F0: EVAP System High Load Purge Line A Performance. Turbocharged engines also purge the charcoal canister under boost, through a high-load line to the compressor inlet via a venturi; check valves keep boost out of the EVAP system, and CARB requires this path to be monitored. P04F0 checks it: Ford (2020–23, replacing P144C) runs the test once per trip under boost with the vent closed and purge open, and sets the code if tank pressure rises faster than 0.5 or 1 inH2O/s or the vacuum rate is out of range, within 5–10 s. VW, Audi and Bentley monitor the line with their own pressure sensor. Common causes: Check valve in the purge line leaking, stuck open, fitted wrongly or missing (high likelihood); High-load purge line to the turbo or venturi off, cracked or blocked (medium likelihood); Purge line pressure sensor wrongly connected or faulty (VW group) (medium likelihood); Purge valve or venturi faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving; Possibly fuel smell, EVAP readiness not set. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04F1 – EVAP System Purge Line Performance
text: P04F1: EVAP System Purge Line Performance. P04F1 is the function check of a purge line that is not the high-load path A – by the wording of another code list the low-pressure path to the intake manifold, counterpart of P04F0. title: P04F2 – Catalyst Heater Supply Voltage Bank 1
text: P04F2: Catalyst Heater Supply Voltage Bank 1. An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04F2 concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code monitors the supply voltage of the heater: if it lies outside its window when heating is requested, the heater cannot deliver its power and is limited or switched off, so the catalyst lights off later. A Subaru patent detects faults in the supply path when the heater is commanded. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part. Common causes: 48 V or high-voltage supply weak (battery, charge, cold, DC-DC converter) (high likelihood); Fuse, relay or power switch faulty (medium likelihood); Contact resistance or corrosion at high-current connector or ground (medium likelihood); Module or voltage measurement faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on the maker); Higher emissions after a cold start; Otherwise usually unremarkable. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04F8 – Catalyst Heater Circuit Intermittent Bank 1
text: P04F8: Catalyst Heater Circuit Intermittent Bank 1. An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04F8 concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code means the heater circuit shows brief or repeated circuit faults that do not persist – typically a loose contact at the high-current connectors or a wire broken by vibration and heat. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part. Common causes: Loose contact at the heater or module connector (high likelihood); Wire broken near the exhaust (medium likelihood); Corrosion at ground or connector (medium likelihood); Internal contact point of the heating disc (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on the maker); Higher emissions after a cold start; Otherwise usually unremarkable. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04FA – EGR A Control Temperature Too High
text: P04FA: EGR A Control Temperature Too High. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04FA is a protective check of the electrically driven EGR valve A (DC motor on an H-bridge with position sensor): the module detects overtemperature or thermal overload of the actuator, modelled from current, actuating work and position behaviour, and limits or switches off EGR. Ford petrol engines from 2020 run it continuously with 4 s to fault above 8.25 V and 400 rpm. Pierburg documents heat damage to VW's 12 V electric EGR valves. EGR then closes, NOx rises. Common causes: EGR valve stiff from coking (motor working against resistance) (high likelihood); High thermal load (full load, poor valve cooling, low coolant) (medium likelihood); Valve motor or H-bridge driver faulty (overcurrent) (medium likelihood); Module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle or jerking if the valve hangs; Loss of power, possibly limp mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04FB – Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Range/Performance
text: P04FB: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Range/Performance. The crankcase ventilation hose connection sensor is a pressure sensor in the PCV line that measures pressure relative to atmosphere; it is the basis for detecting a disconnected hose (P04DB). P04FB is its plausibility check: GM's 2.0-litre LSY checks the zero point with the engine stopped (at least 10 s, coolant 70 °C or more) – a reading outside ±0.63 kPa or a frozen value sets the code in 128 of 160 samples, MIL after two trips. The disconnection check P04DB is then not possible. Common causes: Pressure sensor drifting (zero point error) (high likelihood); Sensor port or line blocked by oil or ice (value frozen) (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in supply, ground or signal (medium likelihood); Residual crankcase pressure after switch-off (blocked ventilation) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; No change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P04FC – Crankcase Ventilation System Performance
text: P04FC: Crankcase Ventilation System Performance. The crankcase ventilation routes blow-by gas into the intake, and CARB requires it to be monitored. P04FC is a general function check: pressure or flow in the system deviates from the model. FCA uses it on the 2.0-litre turbo in the Wrangler and Cherokee (2018–19) and the 3.6 Pentastar in the Challenger (2020), with known false triggers fixed by engine module software; the strategy is not published, a FCA patent evaluates a pressure sensor in the fresh-air line. Common causes: Module software (FCA false trigger) (high likelihood); PCV valve or oil separator blocked or sticking (medium likelihood); Ventilation or fresh-air hose leaking or loose, oil filler cap leaking (medium likelihood); Increased blow-by (piston rings) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly oil consumption or oil in the intake; Whistling from false air. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P04FD – EGR Actuator A Control Processor Performance
text: P04FD: EGR Actuator A Control Processor Performance. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Some EGR actuators have their own electronics (smart actuators), with position control inside the actuator and communication with the engine module by bus or PWM. P04FD means the actuator reports an internal processor or electronics fault, or its self-test failed. CARB does not require such internal faults to be reported, so the code is a voluntary detail. Volvo and Mack trucks with turbocompound document it with false triggers fixed by engine software. The actuator then goes to its default position and EGR is off. Common causes: Engine or actuator software (false trigger) (high likelihood); Electronics in the EGR actuator faulty (heat, moisture) (medium likelihood); Actuator supply or ground unstable (medium likelihood); Valve stiff, causing a control fault in the actuator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Reduced power possible; Higher NOx. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P04FE – Catalyst Heater Circuit Performance Bank 1
text: P04FE: Catalyst Heater Circuit Performance Bank 1. An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04FE concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code is the function check: the circuit is electrically sound but the effect does not fit – for example the energy delivered in a time window after switch-on stays below target, which a Toyota patent evaluates as a ratio, or the catalyst temperature does not rise as modelled. Ageing of the disc raises its resistance. The pure temperature result code is P0424/P0434. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part. Common causes: Heating disc aged (resistance increased, cracks, electrode damage) (high likelihood); Supply drops under load (cold or weak 48 V battery, contact resistance) (medium likelihood); Catalyst or exhaust temperature sensor implausible (low likelihood); Software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on the maker); Higher emissions after a cold start; Otherwise usually unremarkable. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0500 – Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit
text: P0500: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit. The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0500 is the general code for this signal. Ford checks plausibility: the car must be moving (high load, positive torque), yet the signal stays below 1–5 mph for 5 s; Ford diesels flag a missing CAN message after 0.5 s. GM's Saturn ION of 2004 used high load with below 3 mph for 6.2 s (MIL after two trips); GM's 2018 tables use P0502/P0503 instead. Cruise control is then disabled and substitute values are used. Common causes: ABS/ESP module or wheel speed sensor faulty (signal source) (high likelihood); Output speed sensor or vehicle speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet) (high likelihood); Wire or connector open or shorted, corrosion (medium likelihood); CAN communication fault (message missing) (medium likelihood); Wrong tyre or axle data programmed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Speedometer dead or jumping; Cruise control not working; Automatic shifts harshly or wrongly. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0501 – Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0501: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0501 means the signal is present but does not fit the driving state or lies outside the physically possible range. Saab's Trionic T5 sets it above 270 km/h; other makers typically compare it with engine speed times gear ratio, wheel speeds or the transmission output speed. title: P0502 – Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0502: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Low. The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. title: P0503 – Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic/High
text: P0503: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic/High. The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0503 combines three fault patterns: sporadic signal loss, jumping values and a value that is too high. GM detects a sudden signal drop quickly (0.3 s, 5 counts, MIL on the first trip); Subaru sets it at 240 km/h or more for a cumulative 4 s, Saab's diesel above 220 km/h. In limp mode Subaru sets the speed to zero, disables fuel cut-off on overrun and raises the fan. Common causes: Loose contact, chafed wire, corroded connector (high likelihood); Interference from damaged shielding or the ignition (medium likelihood); Sensor with weakened magnet or damaged tone wheel (medium likelihood); ABS/ESP fault (signal source) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Speedometer needle jumps; Cruise control drops out, jerky shifting. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0504 – Brake Switch A/B Correlation
text: P0504: Brake Switch A/B Correlation. The brake pedal switch has two contacts – A usually for the brake lights, B for cruise control and brake information – working in opposite sense, so the module expects opposite states on every brake application. P0504 means they disagree. The signal is used for cruise control cut-off, brake override with electronic throttle, the shift interlock and start-stop. Ford sets it only after more than 25 (petrol) or 40 (diesel) disagreeing brake applications, with the wrench lamp instead of the warning lamp; a NHTSA investigation covers Hyundai brake light switches. Common causes: Brake light switch faulty (burnt or corroded contact) (high likelihood); Switch misadjusted or retaining clip or stop pad worn (high likelihood); Wire, connector or brake light fuse faulty (medium likelihood); Moisture in fuse or junction boxes (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control cannot be switched on; Brake lights stay on or do not come on; Selector lever cannot be moved out of P; Wrench or ESC lamp on. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0505 – Idle Control System
text: P0505: Idle Control System. CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0505 is the general fault of the idle control, used where the maker does not separate too low from too high or the control is at its limit. With an idle valve it is typically sticking or gummed (Saab T5: idle outside 700–1200 rpm); on electronic throttles a Ford investigation shows P0505 from deposits in the throttle body. Ford's 2020–23 engines disable start-stop with P0505–P0507. Warning lamp behaviour depends on the maker. Common causes: Throttle body or idle valve dirty or gummed (high likelihood); False air (hoses, intake gasket, crankcase ventilation) (medium likelihood); Idle valve faulty mechanically or electrically (medium likelihood); Learned values not reset after cleaning (low likelihood). Symptoms: Idle speed fluctuates, too high or too low; Engine stalls at idle or when coasting; Start-stop not working. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0506 – Idle Control System RPM - Lower Than Expected
text: P0506: Idle Control System RPM - Lower Than Expected. CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0506 means the idle speed of the warm engine at standstill stays too low despite fully used control. GM uses more than 91 rpm filtered for 10 s (MIL after two trips), Ford petrol −100 rpm plus a correction above 1 lb/min, Ford diesel −100 rpm for 5 s, Subaru −100 rpm with the correction at its limit for 10 s three times. Typical are deposits, extra load or a restricted intake or exhaust. Common causes: Deposits at the throttle or bypass channel, or gummed idle valve (high likelihood); Extra load: stiff accessory drive, gearbox or converter (medium likelihood); Intake or exhaust restricted (air filter, catalyst) (medium likelihood); Idle valve or throttle actuator faulty, wrong learned value (medium likelihood); Mechanical engine damage (low compression) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Idle too low, engine shakes; Engine stalls when stopping or with A/C on; Check engine light after two trips. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0507 – Idle Control System RPM - Higher Than Expected
text: P0507: Idle Control System RPM - Higher Than Expected. CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0507 means the idle speed stays above target although the control is at its minimum – air bypasses the control or the throttle does not close. GM uses more than 182 rpm filtered (MIL after two trips), Ford petrol +200 rpm, Ford diesel +160 rpm, Subaru +200 rpm for 10 s three times; on the Saab 9-4X three overspeed fuel cut-offs at standstill also set it. False air is the classic cause. Common causes: False air (vacuum hose, intake gasket, brake booster) (high likelihood); Crankcase ventilation leaking or wrongly routed (medium likelihood); Throttle not closing fully (deposits, ice, stop misadjusted) (medium likelihood); Idle valve stuck open (medium likelihood); Wrong throttle learned value after cleaning or replacement (low likelihood). Symptoms: Idle speed too high; Automatic car creeps at standstill; Hissing from false air. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0508 – Idle Air Control System Circuit Low
text: P0508: Idle Air Control System Circuit Low. CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0508 is an electrical fault in the drive circuit of a separate idle valve. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) feeds the valve from the main relay and pulses it to ground; the module counts signal edges and sets P0508 at 8 or fewer in 64 ms instead of about 160 – the output hangs at one level – with the warning lamp at once and limp mode without idle control. Symptoms: Idle fluctuates or is wrong; Engine stalls at idle; Check engine light on at once. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0509 – Idle Air Control System Circuit High
text: P0509: Idle Air Control System Circuit High. CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. title: P050A – Cold Start Idle Control System Performance
text: P050A: Cold Start Idle Control System Performance. After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050A checks whether the raised idle speed or air mass commanded at a cold start is actually reached: Ford sets it when the average deviation between target and actual speed exceeds 200 rpm, with the warning lamp. GM does not use P050A as its own monitor and reports cold-start system faults under its manufacturer code P1400. Common causes: Throttle or idle valve dirty or coked, not enough air when cold (high likelihood); False air or vacuum leak (medium likelihood); Fault in the throttle or idle valve circuit (medium likelihood); Extra load at cold start (alternator, A/C), stiff engine (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Idle after a cold start too low, too high or hunting; Occasional stalling shortly after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P050B – Cold Start Ignition Timing Performance
text: P050B: Cold Start Ignition Timing Performance. After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050B checks the ignition part of the strategy – the retard for catalyst heating; CARB allows checking only the commanded value. Ford sets it when desired and commanded cold-start timing differ by more than 10°, for example because knock, torque or idle control take back the retard. FCA fixed P050B on the 2.0-litre turbo Wrangler of 2018–19 with software. GM has no separate monitor. Common causes: Engine module software or calibration (high likelihood); Idle control takes back the retard because speed would drop (false air, dirty throttle) (medium likelihood); Knock control or knock sensor intervenes (low likelihood); Extra load or alternator at cold start (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable symptoms; Catalyst warms up more slowly after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P050C – Cold Start Engine Coolant Temperature Performance
text: P050C: Cold Start Engine Coolant Temperature Performance. P050C is documented only on Bosch ME9 in the Saab 9-3 V6 2.8 turbo: a cold-start plausibility check of the coolant temperature sensor. After a long stop coolant and intake air must read about the same; the code sets if coolant is more than 10 °C below or 15 °C above intake air, once per trip with the warning lamp. A wrong coolant reading distorts cold-start enrichment and can run the fan on a cold engine. The common reading 'coolant warms up too slowly' does not fit – that is P0125/P0128. GM, Ford and FCA do not use P050C. Common causes: Coolant temperature sensor drifting, wrong characteristic (high likelihood); Contact resistance or corrosion at the coolant or intake air sensor connector (medium likelihood); Intake air temperature sensor reading wrong (medium likelihood); Auxiliary heater or block heater not recognised, very short stop (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough running after a cold start; Radiator fan runs with a cold engine. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P050D – Cold Start Rough Idle
text: P050D: Cold Start Rough Idle. GM's direct-injection petrol engines (from about 2016) split the injection into two pulses and retard the ignition after a cold start to heat the catalyst. P050D counts engine cycles with incomplete combustion via the crankshaft misfire detection during this strategy; if the rate reaches the catalyst-damaging misfire threshold, the code sets – once per trip, while the strategy is active (under 45 s running, coolant up to 66 °C). Mostly MIL after two trips, some calibrations without MIL. Ford and FCA do not use P050D. Common causes: Injector with poor spray pattern or deposits, or injector circuit fault (high likelihood); Spark plug or ignition coil weak (medium likelihood); Engine module software or calibration (medium likelihood); Poor fuel or low fuel pressure (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on calibration); Rough idle or jerking in the first seconds after a cold start; Usually unremarkable when warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P050E – Cold Start Engine Exhaust Temperature Too Low
text: P050E: Cold Start Engine Exhaust Temperature Too Low. After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050E is the system check of the strategy: does enough heat reach the exhaust and catalyst? Ford uses no exhaust temperature sensor but a catalyst temperature model – actual against target – and sets the code when the temperature deficit divided by the target rise exceeds 0.4, with the warning lamp. FCA uses P050E on the 3.0-litre EcoDiesel (Ram 1500, Grand Cherokee 2014), where it concerns heating the oxidation catalyst, fixed by software. GM uses its manufacturer code P1400 instead. Common causes: Idle or air control does not reach the cold-start target (dirty throttle, false air) (high likelihood); Ignition not retarded enough (knock or torque intervention) (medium likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood); Air mass meter reading wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving; Higher cold-start emissions. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P050F – Brake Assist Vacuum Too Low
text: P050F: Brake Assist Vacuum Too Low. GM (from about model year 2017/18) monitors the brake booster with a vacuum sensor: with the pedal at rest and high intake vacuum the booster must hold its vacuum; a loss over time is filtered as a drift ratio, and above a threshold P050F sets, MIL after two trips. It runs with the engine on, during start-stop auto-stops and after switch-off. Without enough brake vacuum the module must throttle, restart the engine from auto-stop or request a pump – which affects idle and start-stop – and brake assistance can drop. Ford and FCA do not use P050F. Common causes: Leaking vacuum hose or check valve (high likelihood); Leaking diaphragm in the brake booster (medium likelihood); Vacuum sensor or its seal faulty (medium likelihood); Electric or mechanical vacuum pump weak (where fitted) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard brake pedal, especially after auto-stop; Hissing at the pedal, start-stop stops less often. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0510 – Closed Throttle Position Switch
text: P0510: Closed Throttle Position Switch. Older engines with a mechanical throttle have a separate idle contact on the throttle or the combined throttle position sensor (Bosch Motronic throttle switch, Nissan and Toyota sensors with idle switch). The module uses it to recognise idle – for idle control, fuel cut-off on overrun and idle ignition timing – and as a substitute if the position sensor fails. P0510 flags an implausible switch: closed with the throttle open, or open at idle. Manufacturer thresholds were not found in accessible documents; with electronic throttle the switch no longer exists. Common causes: Idle switch or throttle sensor misadjusted (high likelihood); Switch contacts worn, dirty or corroded (high likelihood); Wire or connector open or shorted (medium likelihood); Throttle not closing (deposits, sticking cable, stop misadjusted) (medium likelihood); Value not relearned after replacement (low likelihood). Symptoms: Idle too high or fluctuating; Engine stalls when coasting; No fuel cut-off on overrun (higher consumption). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0511 – Idle Air Control Circuit
text: P0511: Idle Air Control Circuit. CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0511 is the general circuit fault of the idle valve – open, short to ground or to positive – without separating low and high, which CARB permits. Ford (up to about 2012, engines with an idle valve) has the output stage report it via a diagnostic status bit, continuously. Valve types are PWM solenoid or rotary valves (two wires) or stepper motors (four wires, typical of GM). Without a working valve the engine runs on a fixed bypass or the mechanical stop and may stall. Common causes: Idle valve faulty (coil open or shorted) (high likelihood); Wire open or shorted (medium likelihood); Connector corroded, pins pushed back (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Idle too high, too low or fluctuating; Engine stalls at idle; Check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.
