title: P0512 – Starter Request Circuit
text: P0512: Starter Request Circuit. The engine module reads a start request – from the ignition switch, a start button via the body module, or start-stop – and drives the starter relay with it. P0512 flags a fault in this signal. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) checks plausibility: if the engine runs above 500 rpm and the start signal stays active for more than 3 minutes, a short or sticking switch is assumed, MIL after two trips. On a Jeep Cherokee diesel a chafed harness caused P0512 with a no-start. The starter then does not crank – or with a short to positive keeps running. Common causes: Ignition or start switch, or start button, faulty or sticking (high likelihood); Harness chafed, short to ground or positive (medium likelihood); Selector or clutch switch in the start path (low likelihood); Starter relay sticking (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine does not start, starter does not crank; Starter keeps running after the start (noise); Check engine light (Subaru after two trips). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0513 – Incorrect Immobilizer Key
text: P0513: Incorrect Immobilizer Key. The engine module receives a secret code from the immobiliser or body module (Chrysler SKIM/SKREEM/RF hub, Saab CIM); if it does not match the stored code, P0513 sets and starting is prevented – Saab cuts fuel and blocks the starter. The most common trigger is a replaced or reflashed engine module that was not taught to the immobiliser (FCA, Saab), less often handshake timing on FCA hybrids or a key not programmed. FCA lists it as invalid SKIM key. It is not emission-related; CARB does not require immobiliser monitoring, and no source documents a warning lamp. Common causes: Engine module replaced or reflashed and not taught to the immobiliser (high likelihood); Key or transponder not programmed or faulty (medium likelihood); Immobiliser, body or RF hub module replaced or faulty (medium likelihood); Software fault in the handshake (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine does not start or stops after 1–2 s; Immobiliser or security lamp flashes; Starter does not crank (Saab). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0514 – Battery Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0514: Battery Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0514 is the plausibility check of the temperature signal. On FCA/Alfa Romeo the temperature comes from the intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal; P0514 means its value is implausible, and several cases on the Alfa Giulia 2.0 were fixed by engine module software. A fixed substitute temperature is then used; CARB requires plausibility faults to have their own code. Common causes: Engine module software (false trigger) (high likelihood); Battery sensor or NTC drifting (medium likelihood); Corrosion at sensor or connector near the battery acid (medium likelihood); Sensor fitted wrongly after a battery change (low likelihood). Symptoms: Possibly check engine light; Charging voltage too high or too low; Start-stop not working. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0516 – Battery Temperature Sensor Circuit Low

title: P0518 – Idle Air Control Circuit Intermittent
text: P0518: Idle Air Control Circuit Intermittent. Older engines without electronic throttle have a separate idle air control valve bypassing the closed throttle; CARB requires its output to be checked but not the fault types to be coded separately. P0518 means its circuit fails sporadically – the signal or current briefly leaves its valid range and returns. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0518; GM and Ford report idle valve faults as P0505–P0507 and P0511. Engines with electronic throttle do not set it. Common causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the idle valve connector (high likelihood); Broken or chafed wire in the harness (medium likelihood); Valve coil with shorted turns (temperature-dependent) (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Fluctuating idle; Engine stalls when coasting or stopping; Check engine light (depending on the maker). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0519 – Idle Air Control System Performance
text: P0519: Idle Air Control System Performance. P0519 means the idle control fails functionally with an electrically sound circuit – the actual idle speed deviates strongly despite fully used control. It is documented only on Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X, electronic throttle, around 2005): idle at least 1000 rpm above target with the control already at zero for 2 or 5 s sets the code with the warning lamp at once, and a fail-safe cuts fuel to cylinders to stop the engine racing. GM and Ford use P0506/P0507 instead; CARB's mandatory limit is +200/−100 rpm. Common causes: False air behind the throttle (intake, gasket, vacuum hose) (high likelihood); Throttle or idle valve stuck open (foreign body, coking) (high likelihood); Throttle actuator motor faulty (follow-on P2101) (medium likelihood); Follow-on fault of other codes (sensors, pedal) (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Idle far above target, engine races; Jerking from cylinder cut-off in limp mode; Check engine light on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P051A – Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit
text: P051A: Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit. The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051A is the sensor's general circuit fault. Ford uses it only for the digital SENT sensor, when the module receives invalid messages or signal patterns (together with U060E for lost communication); analogue sensors report P051B–P051D instead. It is checked continuously with 5 s to fault. Common causes: Connector or supply, ground or SENT signal wire open or corroded (high likelihood); Sensor electronics faulty (medium likelihood); Oil or moisture in the connector (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no change in driving; Disconnection check P04DB suspended. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P051B – Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P051B: Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051B is its plausibility check. Ford flags a zero-point deviation above 0.15 inHg (about 0.5 kPa) from ambient with the engine stopped, and in operation at low air flow a pressure above 5 inHg (about 17 kPa) or below −0.6 inHg – so Ford also reports a real excess crankcase pressure under P051B. Maserati and Alfa Romeo bulletins name blow-by valves or software. Common causes: Sensor zero point drifting (high likelihood); PCV or blow-by valve sticking, ventilation blocked or frozen (real overpressure) (medium likelihood); Engine module software (known false trigger) (medium likelihood); Increased blow-by from engine wear (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly oil leaks or oil mist (real overpressure); Often no change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P051F – PCV Filter Restriction
text: P051F: PCV Filter Restriction. The crankcase ventilation has an oil mist separator or filter element that can clog; the crankcase pressure sensor then sees rising pressure at a given flow. P051F reports this restriction. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – Ford reports high pressure under P051B. BMW and GM bulletins describe the consequences of a blocked separator: oil pushed past seals, oil mist in the intake and charge air cooler, higher oil consumption. CARB requires the PCV system to be monitored. Common causes: Separator or filter clogged with oil, soot or sludge (high likelihood); Icing in the separator or hose on short winter trips (medium likelihood); Oil change intervals exceeded (sludge) (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor reading wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Oil leaks at seals or dipstick; Oil mist in the intake, higher oil consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0520 – Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit
text: P0520: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit. The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0520 is the general circuit fault, used differently: Ford petrol and diesel engines set it for the digital SENT sensor when it reports an internal fault, does not initialise or sends values out of range (lost communication is U0600), after 5 s. GM's 1.4 L turbo with an oil pressure switch sets it when the switch reports pressure although the engine has been off long enough to be pressureless – type C, without warning lamp. Common causes: Sensor or switch faulty internally (high likelihood); Connector corroded or oily (oil creeping through a leaking sensor) (medium likelihood); Signal line open or shorted to ground (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or supply faulty (usually with other sensor codes) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker); Oil pressure gauge or warning wrong; Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly disabled. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0521 – Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Range/Performance
text: P0521: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Range/Performance. The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0521 is the plausibility check. With the engine off the sensor must read about zero (GM: above 40 kPa after 10 s is a fault, Ford diesel above 70 kPa); with it running the value is compared with a model of speed and oil temperature (GM single-stage pump ±50 kPa). GM checks two-stage pumps against limits per stage and calibrates P0521 with the pump valve – so a real pressure fault can also set it. GM type B, two trips. Common causes: Sensor drifting or stuck (offset) (high likelihood); Oil pump control valve or two-stage pump stuck in the wrong stage (medium likelihood); Wrong viscosity, low oil level or foaming oil (medium likelihood); Worn oil pump or bearings (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Oil pressure reading implausible or fluctuating; Cylinder deactivation or cam phasing possibly disabled. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0522 – Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Low
text: P0522: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Low. title: P0524 – Engine Oil Pressure Too Low
text: P0524: Engine Oil Pressure Too Low. P0524 is not a sensor fault but a condition: the measured oil pressure is below a minimum depending on speed, load and temperature (Ford diesel 30–90 kPa) for about 5 s, with the sensor itself plausible. Its purpose is engine protection; Ford petrol engines with mid-lock cam phasers drive them into the locked position. GM's tables do not use it; FCA updated the Ram EcoDiesel software against false setting in the cold. Stop the engine, check the oil level and confirm with a mechanical gauge. Common causes: Oil level too low, oil loss or consumption (high likelihood); Too thin oil, fuel dilution or clogged pick-up screen (medium likelihood); Oil pump or pressure control valve faulty or stuck (medium likelihood); Worn crankshaft or camshaft bearings (low likelihood); False setting by software in the cold (Ram EcoDiesel) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Oil pressure warning and/or check engine light; Engine noise (lifters, timing chain); Possible power reduction. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0525 – Cruise Control Servo Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0525: Cruise Control Servo Control Circuit Range/Performance. P0525 concerns vehicles with a separate cruise control servo – a vacuum or electric actuator on the throttle cable driven by the engine module: the control circuit is electrically sound, but the response does not match the command. With electronic throttle the engine module controls the throttle itself, so the code hardly applies there. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0525. CARB names cruise control as the example of an emission-neutral diagnosis: switching it off as the default reaction suffices, so usually no warning lamp. Common causes: Servo worn or sticking, cable misadjusted (medium likelihood); Vacuum leak at hose or diaphragm (vacuum servo) (medium likelihood); Wiring, connector or fuse to the servo (medium likelihood); Brake or clutch switch interrupting the servo release (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control inoperative or switches off; Speed not held or fluctuating; Usually no check engine light. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0526 – Fan Speed Sensor Circuit
text: P0526: Fan Speed Sensor Circuit. Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0526 means no usable signal although the clutch is driven: GM Duramax below 500 rpm with fan duty at least 36 % for 2 s; the 6.6 L LML distinguishes a level stuck low or high; GM petrol V8s set it when no pulses arrive with the engine running. Type B, two trips. GM also reports a missing signal under P0526. A GM bulletin for 2011–2013 Duramax vans and pick-ups names loud fan noise and weak air conditioning at low speed. Common causes: Hall sensor at the fan clutch faulty (high likelihood); Wiring or connector (chafing at the shroud, corrosion) (medium likelihood); Clutch not turning despite command (medium likelihood); Engine module or supply (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Fan permanently on or off, loud fan noise; Weak air conditioning at low speed, overheating under load. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P052A – Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced Bank 1
text: P052A: Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced Bank 1. Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052A means bank 1 was too far advanced. Outside cold start, P0011 applies. Common causes: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing (high likelihood); Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil (high likelihood); Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged (medium likelihood); Stretched timing chain (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable driving symptoms; Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start; Higher cold-start emissions. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P052E – PCV Regulator Valve Performance
text: P052E: PCV Regulator Valve Performance. P052E is a function fault of the crankcase ventilation pressure regulating valve. Audi's 3.0 TFSI has a diaphragm valve whose torn diaphragm or elbow causes false air and whistling; Mercedes' M270/M274 have a switched part-load ventilation valve that blocks with oil carbon and lets oil into the intake – blue smoke, rough running, lack of power; Mercedes extended the emission warranty on the intake module. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel in the Saab 9-5 uses P052E differently, for PCV heater performance – which J2012 lists as P053D. Common causes: Diaphragm of the regulating valve torn or fatigued (high likelihood); Part-load ventilation valve blocked (oil carbon, sludge) (high likelihood); Elbow or hose at the valve cracked, clamp leaking (medium likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Whistling or hissing in the engine bay; Rough idle, blue smoke or oil consumption, lack of power. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P052F – Glow Plug Control Module 1 System Voltage
text: P052F: Glow Plug Control Module 1 System Voltage. Diesel glow plugs are switched by a separate glow plug control module fed from the battery, with its own ground, a command from the engine module and a diagnostic line back. P052F means its supply voltage is out of range. Ford's 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke set it below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or with an open supply, after about 1 s, continuously. An FCA bulletin shows P052F together with all six glow plug open codes P0671–P0676, because without supply no current flows – check main feed, connector and grounds first. GM does not use it. Common causes: Main feed to the module open or high-resistance (fuse, connector, corroded ring terminal) (high likelihood); Poor ground of the glow plug module (medium likelihood); System voltage too low or too high (weak battery, regulator fault) (medium likelihood); Glow plug module faulty internally (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard cold start, long cranking, white smoke; Several glow plug codes at once. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0530 – A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit
text: P0530: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit. The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008). P0530 is the general circuit fault; GM and the Saab 9-4X use the more precise P0532/P0533 instead. Saab's 2006 9-5 diesel (Bosch EDC16) assigns P0530 differently, to a short to ground below 0.1 V for 0.6 s, switching off the A/C relay. Warning lamp depends on the maker. Common causes: Connector or contacts corroded or loose (high likelihood); Pressure sensor faulty (high likelihood); Wire open or chafed (medium likelihood); 5 V reference shorted by another sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Air conditioning not cooling (compressor off); Radiator fan running permanently; Check engine light (depending on the maker). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0534 – A/C Refrigerant Charge Loss
text: P0534: A/C Refrigerant Charge Loss. P0534 reports too little refrigerant (a leak), not a sensor circuit: the module compares pressure or temperature in the circuit with a model, and the compressor is locked out for protection. FCA's 2020 Ram EcoDiesel sets it with the warning lamp; a software update fixed false setting. In GM's Volt, Spark EV and Lyriq the circuit also cools the traction battery – GM prescribes recovering and weighing the charge (Volt at least 800 of 950 g) and comparing the battery's refrigerant temperature sensors with ambient. Common causes: Refrigerant leak (condenser, joints, compressor shaft seal, service ports) (high likelihood); Pressure or temperature sensor offset (misjudgement) (medium likelihood); Software or calibration (medium likelihood); Traction battery chiller faulty (electric and hybrid only) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Air conditioning weak or not cooling; Compressor not engaging; Check engine light or high-voltage service message (electric). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0535 – A/C Evaporator Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P0535: A/C Evaporator Temperature Sensor Circuit. The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor. P0535 is the general circuit fault; the compressor is usually locked out or run with a substitute value. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules. Common causes: Sensor faulty (high likelihood); Connector corroded by condensate (high likelihood); Wire open or shorted (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Air conditioning not or weakly cooling; Evaporator icing, airflow decreasing; Compressor cycling unusually. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P053A – PCV Heater A Control Circuit/Open
text: P053A: PCV Heater A Control Circuit/Open. The PCV heater is an electric element of a few ohms (Saab: 6–10 Ω) at the junction of the ventilation hose and the intake; it stops water in the blow-by gas from freezing and blocking the ventilation in frost. The module switches it to ground. P053A means its control circuit is open. GM's diesels of 2016 check it with 20 of 40 samples below 90 °C coolant without warning lamp, GM Europe's 2.0 CDTI in the Saab 9-5 with the lamp on the first trip – a difference even within GM. The heater then has no effect, which only matters in hard frost. Common causes: Heating element burnt out (high likelihood); Connector or wire open, corrosion (high likelihood); Fuse of the ignition supply blown (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Often none, except in frost; Check engine light (depending on the maker); In frost: oil leaks or loss of power from frozen ventilation. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P053E – Crankcase Pressure Too High
text: P053E: Crankcase Pressure Too High. P053E is the system code for crankcase pressure above an operating-point limit while the sensor itself is plausible. Normally the crankcase runs at a slight vacuum (GM: −1 to −5 inH2O). No manufacturer document available to us uses P053E – Ford reports the same under P051B (above 5 inHg at idle air flow). Excess pressure pushes oil past seals and the dipstick, carries oil mist into the intake and raises oil consumption. CARB requires the PCV system to be monitored. Common causes: Ventilation or oil separator blocked or frozen (high likelihood); Pressure regulating or PCV valve faulty (medium likelihood); Increased blow-by (piston rings, turbo oil side) (medium likelihood); Leaking vacuum reservoir or pump in the valve cover (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Oil leaks at seals, dipstick pushed out; Higher oil consumption, blue smoke. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P053F – Cold Start Fuel Pressure Performance Bank 1
text: P053F: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Performance Bank 1. Petrol direct-injection engines often inject twice after a cold start, once late in the compression stroke, to heat the catalyst; this needs rail pressure within a window. P053F reports that the window was not reached often enough. Documented only by Ford's EcoBoost: over the whole cold-start phase it compares the time in the window with the phase duration against 0.70, once per cold start, with fuel level at least 15 % and the fuel sensors sound. The module then drops this mode, the catalyst lights off later; warning lamp after two trips. GM does not use P053F. Common causes: High-pressure pump weak or volume control valve sluggish (high likelihood); Low supply pressure (lift pump, filter) (medium likelihood); Rail pressure sensor drifting (medium likelihood); Pump follower or cam lobe worn (low likelihood); Software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no noticeable driving symptoms; Possibly longer cranking or rough cold idle. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0540 – Intake Air Heater A Circuit
text: P0540: Intake Air Heater A Circuit. Some diesels – typically Cummins engines in Ram pick-ups and commercial vehicles, and Iveco – heat the intake air with a grid heater in the intake manifold instead of or alongside glow plugs. It draws very high current through a relay (on recent Ram a solid-state relay) and is switched by the engine module before and after starting; CARB requires cold-start aids to be monitored. Cummins checks it by the manifold temperature rise, Iveco by the battery voltage dip when the relay switches. P0540 is the general circuit fault of heater A without low/high assignment. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM's Duramax LML has an intake heater but reports it under its own codes P154A–P154D. Common causes: Heater relay faulty (contacts welded or burnt, solid-state relay shorted) (high likelihood); Heating grid burnt out (medium likelihood); Power cable or ring terminal corroded or overheated, control connector (medium likelihood); Engine module driver (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard cold start, white smoke, rough cold idle; With welded relay: battery drained, heater stays on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0544 – Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P0544: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1. The exhaust gas temperature sensor is a thermistor in a voltage divider with the module's pull-up resistor; the first one (sensor 1) sits before the turbocharger, the oxidation catalyst or after it depending on the maker. Diesels use it for particulate filter regeneration and component protection; CARB names it explicitly as a monitored input. P0544 is the general fault of bank 1 sensor 1. Ford's 6.7 L diesel uses it not as a circuit fault but for plausibility against an exhaust temperature model: after at least 6 h off it compares sensor and model over 200–400 s, a fault exceeding ±80 °C for 20 s, once per trip. GM's Duramax does not use P0544. The module then runs on a model value and may restrict filter regeneration. Common causes: Sensor aged or drifting, soot on the tip (high likelihood); Cable or connector damaged by heat or vibration (medium likelihood); Exhaust leak before the sensor (low likelihood); Exhaust temperature really deviating (injection fault) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Particulate filter regeneration missing, filter warning; Possible power reduction. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P054A – Cold Start B Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced Bank 1
text: P054A: Cold Start B Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced Bank 1. Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft. During catalyst heating after a cold start some engines set it to a specific position; CARB requires such commanded elements to be monitored with their own codes, separate from the normal cam codes. Ford watches the deviation with an averaged variance index for each direction; GM (Saab 9-4X V6) uses only the retard codes, above 6° for 1 s or 4 s cumulative, type B. The commonest cause is oil pressure building too slowly when cold. P054A means bank 1 was too far advanced. Mercedes (M276) traces it to slow oil pressure – 1 bar should be reached after about 3 s; Audi (Q5 3.2) and VW (Atlas 3.6 and 2.0 T) fixed it by software. Common causes: Oil pressure building too slowly when cold (oil level, viscosity, pick-up, pump) (high likelihood); Exhaust oil control valve sticking or screens clogged (medium likelihood); Module software (threshold too tight) (medium likelihood); Cam phaser defective, locking pin (low likelihood); Timing chain stretched or misassembled (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on, usually without noticeable symptom; Brief rattle on cold start; Rough idle while warming up. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P054E – Idle Control System Fuel Quantity Lower Than Expected
text: P054E: Idle Control System Fuel Quantity Lower Than Expected. Diesel only. At controlled idle the module compares the fuel quantity the idle governor needs for target speed with a model value; CARB sets the limit from 2013 at ±50 % of what a sound engine needs. Ford's diesel sets the codes beyond ±50 % for 5 s at standstill with warm engine and no filter regeneration; GM compares with 0.5 times a minimum map or 1.5 times a maximum map, 200 of 255 samples, type B. P054E means the engine holds idle with much less fuel than expected – more energy arrives than commanded, for example from injectors delivering too much, oil entering combustion or wrong injector correction codes. Common causes: Injectors delivering more than commanded (drift, coking, leaking needle) (high likelihood); Oil entering combustion (turbo seal, crankcase ventilation) (medium likelihood); Rail pressure actually higher than measured (medium likelihood); Wrong injector correction codes after replacement (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough or fluctuating idle; Blue or white smoke, knocking at idle. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0550 – Power Steering Pressure Sensor/Switch Circuit
text: P0550: Power Steering Pressure Sensor/Switch Circuit. Hydraulic power steering has a pressure switch or sensor on the high-pressure line; when the wheel is turned at standstill, pump pressure and engine load rise sharply, so the engine module raises idle air in advance to stop the engine stalling. That makes it an input to idle control under CARB. Switches (Saab, Mitsubishi) ground a pull-up; analogue 5 V sensors (Toyota) give about 0.45 V at zero pressure. GM's and Ford's tables do not use P0550–P0554. P0550 is the general circuit fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses it. Without the signal the engine can drop or stall at full lock, or the module raises idle permanently as a substitute. Common causes: Connector or wire open or corroded (splash zone at the pump) (high likelihood); Sensor or switch faulty, often also leaking (high likelihood); 5 V reference or ground disturbed (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker); Idle drops when steering at standstill, engine may stall; Raised idle (substitute value). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0551 – Power Steering Pressure Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance

title: P0554 – Power Steering Pressure Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent

title: P0555 – Brake Booster Pressure Sensor Circuit
text: P0555: Brake Booster Pressure Sensor Circuit. The brake booster pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal, ground) measures the vacuum in the brake booster. On direct-injection, turbo, stop-start and hybrid engines intake vacuum is scarce, so the engine module watches it and creates vacuum when needed – closing the throttle, suppressing engine stop or running an electric vacuum pump. That makes it an input to idle and throttle control. P0555 is the general circuit fault without low/high distinction. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; GM splits circuit faults into P0557 and P0558. The module then assumes a substitute value and keeps vacuum available as a precaution. Common causes: Connector or wire to the sensor open or corroded (high likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood); 5 V reference disturbed (short at another sensor on the same reference) (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or brake booster warning; Stop-start inactive; Often no change in driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0556 – Brake Booster Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0556: Brake Booster Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. The brake booster pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal, ground) measures the vacuum in the brake booster. On direct-injection, turbo, stop-start and hybrid engines intake vacuum is scarce, so the engine module watches it and creates vacuum when needed – closing the throttle, suppressing engine stop or running an electric vacuum pump. title: P055A – Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit
text: P055A: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit. Oil pressure sensor B is a second sensor, usually in the oil feed to the cam phasers or valve lift switching – on GM's 2.5 L (2014 Impala and Malibu) in the camshaft cover – while sensor A measures the main gallery. title: P055E – Oxygen Sensor Control Module System Voltage
text: P055E: Oxygen Sensor Control Module System Voltage. Some engines use wide-band or NOx sensors with their own evaluation module that reports over CAN. That module measures its supply; outside its working range it sets P055E, and lambda control and the sensor diagnoses are suspended because no valid values exist. No manufacturer document available to us uses P055E – Ford's diesel monitors the comparable supply of its smart NOx/O2 sensor as P220A/P220B, below 8.5 V or above 16.5 V. CARB requires modules delivering emission-relevant signals to be monitored. Common causes: Fuse, relay or supply line to the sensor module (high likelihood); Poor module ground (medium likelihood); Battery or alternator (under- or overvoltage) (medium likelihood); Sensor module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Lambda control in open loop, possibly higher consumption; Further lambda or communication codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P055F – Engine Oil Pressure Out of Range
text: P055F: Engine Oil Pressure Out of Range. P055F is a condition code: the measured oil pressure is above the maximum expected for speed and oil temperature – Ford, which documents it, calls it 'too high' and pairs it with P0524 (too low). Ford checks continuously for 5 s, only with plausible oil pressure, oil temperature and coolant sensors, as engine protection. Background are regulated oil pumps, whose control valve (P06DA ff) defaults to full pressure on failure. An electrically high signal is P0523 or P055D instead. Common causes: Oil pump control valve or variable pump stuck at high pressure (high likelihood); Pump relief valve stuck (medium likelihood); Wrong viscosity, very cold oil (medium likelihood); Sensor A reading high within range (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or oil pressure warning; Possible engine protection or power limit; Possible oil filter or seal leaks. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0560 – System Voltage
text: P0560: System Voltage. The module measures its own supply voltage. CARB allows other monitors to be suspended below 11 V, and above a maker's threshold only if the voltage itself is diagnosed – that is what these codes record. GM's engine modules and Ford's PCM set them without warning lamp. P0560 is the general code without low/high split, used differently: Saab's 2002 9-5 transmission module sets it below 9 V or above 18 V for 1 s and goes into limp mode; Saab's EDC16 diesel only above 17 V (24 V charger or jump start); the GM-built 9-4X as a low-voltage code. GM's and Ford's engine modules use P0562/P0563 instead. Common causes: Battery weak or faulty (high likelihood); Alternator or regulator (under- or overcharging) (high likelihood); Jump start or charger at 24 V (medium likelihood); Corroded or loose battery terminals or ground strap (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Charge warning; Transmission limp mode (Saab); Several modules report codes, starting problems. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0561 – System Voltage Unstable
text: P0561: System Voltage Unstable. The module measures its own supply voltage. CARB allows other monitors to be suspended below 11 V, and above a maker's threshold only if the voltage itself is diagnosed – that is what these codes record. GM's engine modules and Ford's PCM set them without warning lamp. title: P0562 – System Voltage Low

title: P0564 – Cruise Control Multi-Function Input A Circuit
text: P0564: Cruise Control Multi-Function Input A Circuit. Cruise control buttons are almost always a resistor ladder on one or two signal lines, each button giving its own voltage; the module reading it (GM and Saab from about 2010: the body module; FCA: steering column module or PCM) sends the button state to the engine module over CAN. CARB names cruise control as the example of an emission-neutral diagnosis – it is simply switched off – so GM lists all these codes as type C and Ford as non-MIL: no warning lamp, the engine runs normally. P0564 watches signal line A of the ladder: only voltage windows matching a button or no button are valid. GM sets it when the ratio sits in a gap between windows for over 0.5 s (2014: 2.5 s), the body module in the Saab 9-4X and 9-5 after an invalid voltage for 2 s. Cruise control is locked out for the ignition cycle. Common causes: Cruise or steering wheel switch faulty or dirty (moisture, worn contacts) (high likelihood); Clockspring or steering wheel connector with contact resistance (medium likelihood); Supply or signal line to the body module open or shorted (medium likelihood); Body module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control cannot be switched on or switches off; Cruise control locked out; No check engine light, engine runs normally. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P056D – Reductant Control Module System Voltage
text: P056D: Reductant Control Module System Voltage. Diesels with SCR may have a separate module for AdBlue/DEF dosing (pump, heaters, dosing valve) talking to the engine module over CAN. It measures its supply; outside its window no safe dosing is possible, so dosing and SCR diagnoses are suspended and NOx rises, and if it persists the SCR warnings and power limits apply. No manufacturer document available to us uses P056D – Ford's diesel reports the dosing module supply as P21CB below 8.5 V and P21CC above 19 V. CARB requires SCR modules to be monitored. Common causes: Fuse, relay or supply line of the DEF module (high likelihood); Corrosion at module connector or ground (underbody, road salt) (medium likelihood); System under- or overvoltage (medium likelihood); Module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light and DEF warning; Possible countdown to start inhibit or power limit; Further SCR codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P056E – Cold Start Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Performance
text: P056E: Cold Start Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Performance. CARB requires every element commanded by the cold-start strategy to respond measurably in the commanded direction, with its own codes separate from the general monitoring of the same part. During catalyst heating the boost control is positioned deliberately – diesels close the variable turbine for load and heat, petrol engines open the wastegate so heat reaches the catalyst. P056E means boost control A (the first or only charger) did not follow its cold-start target. Its only documented user is Stellantis: the 2025 Ram 3500 cab chassis with 6.7 L Cummins lists it among codes that can light the warning lamp, fixed by a PCM software update; customers noticed hard cold starts and raised cold idle. Ford and GM do not use it. Common causes: Variable turbine or wastegate actuator stiff (coking, cold) (high likelihood); Module software or calibration (medium likelihood); Vacuum or boost hose leaking (medium likelihood); Position or boost sensor faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Hard cold start or rough warm-up; Otherwise usually unremarkable. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0571 – Brake Switch A Circuit
text: P0571: Brake Switch A Circuit. Brake switch A is the brake light switch or its signal to the engine module. The module needs it to cancel cruise control and for brake-throttle override, stop-start, idle control and the shift interlock. As cruise control is simply switched off, CARB treats such faults as emission-neutral – usually without warning lamp. P0571 is the general fault, usually detected by plausibility: Saab's 3.0 TiD (Bosch) sets it when the car brakes three times from over 49 km/h to standstill at 1.6 m/s² or more without a switch signal; Bosch EDC16 then switches cruise control off. NHTSA found Hyundai and Kia setting P0571 with P0504 from misadjusted brake light switches. Ford and GM petrol engines use P0572/P0573 instead. Common causes: Brake light switch misadjusted (high likelihood); Brake light switch faulty (worn contact) (high likelihood); Connector, wire or brake light fuse (medium likelihood); Engine or body module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control cannot be set or switches off; Brake lights not working or permanently on; Possibly ABS/ESC warning (Hyundai/Kia). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0578 – Cruise Control Multi-Function Input A Circuit Stuck
text: P0578: Cruise Control Multi-Function Input A Circuit Stuck. title: P0579 – Cruise Control Multi-Function Input A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0579: Cruise Control Multi-Function Input A Circuit Range/Performance. title: P057A – Brake Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit/Open
text: P057A: Brake Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit/Open. The brake pedal position sensor is an analogue 5 V sensor, usually Hall-type, giving the pedal position continuously instead of a switch – for brake lights, cruise control, stop-start, brake-throttle override and regenerative braking. GM (from about 2012) and Stellantis read it in the engine module, Saab's 9-4X and 9-5 in the body module; its learned rest position (about 1 V) must be relearned after replacement. P057A is the general circuit or open-circuit fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; GM reports an open circuit as P057C or P057D depending on the line, type A with one trip, and sets the pedal position to 0 %. Brake detection then relies on the brake light switch. Common causes: Connector at the sensor loose or corroded, pins pushed back (high likelihood); 5 V reference, signal or ground line open (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); Engine or body module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Cruise control and stop-start inoperative; Possible power reduction. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P057F – Battery A State of Charge Performance
text: P057F: Battery A State of Charge Performance. P057F means the state of charge of battery A behaves implausibly or leaves its expected range – a performance code, not a circuit fault. title: P0582 – Cruise Control Vacuum Control Circuit/Open
text: P0582: Cruise Control Vacuum Control Circuit/Open. Older engines without electronic throttle use a vacuum cruise servo on the throttle cable: a vacuum valve (closed when unpowered) opens the throttle with intake vacuum, a vent valve (open when unpowered) holds or releases it, and a dump valve fed through the brake switch vents it when braking. Where the engine module drives these valves, it checks each circuit and switches cruise off; CARB treats this as emission-neutral, usually without warning lamp. P0582 concerns the vacuum valve circuit: an open circuit, checked with ignition on and cruise control active. Without current the vacuum valve stays closed – the safe state. Common causes: Connector at the servo loose or corroded (high likelihood); Vacuum valve coil in the servo open (high likelihood); Wire between servo and engine module open (medium likelihood); Engine module driver (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control cannot be engaged or switches off; Cruise indicator goes out or flashes (depending on vehicle); Usually no check engine light, code stored only. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P058A – Battery Monitor Module Performance
text: P058A: Battery Monitor Module Performance. The battery monitor module (intelligent battery sensor) sits on the negative terminal of the 12 V battery: a shunt measures current, electronics also measure voltage and temperature and calculate state of charge, health and cranking ability, reporting over LIN. Energy management uses the data for alternator control, idle boost and stop-start release, which is why the engine module diagnoses it. GM sets P058A–P058F in its engine modules from 2016 as type B, warning lamp after two trips. P058A means the module reports an internal fault of its own over LIN. GM checks it every 250 ms above 9 V, without LIN faults and at outside temperatures of −20 to 50 °C. Battery data are then unreliable – stop-start is blocked and the alternator usually runs a fixed substitute voltage. Loss of communication is a separate U code. Common causes: Battery sensor faulty internally (high likelihood); Poor supply or ground at the sensor (loose terminal, corroded connector) (medium likelihood); Sensor not relearned after battery replacement or disconnection (medium likelihood); Module or engine module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Stop-start not available; No driveability problems. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0592 – Cruise Control Multi-Function Input B Circuit Low
text: P0592: Cruise Control Multi-Function Input B Circuit Low. Cruise control buttons form a resistor ladder on one or two signal lines, each button giving its own voltage window. FCA uses two lines with offset windows – signal 1 is input A, signal 2 input B – and both must report the same button; GM evaluates the ratio to the reference. Any fault locks out cruise control; CARB treats this as emission-neutral, and GM and Ford set these codes without warning lamp. P0592 means signal line B is too low: GM (engine variant LGW) at a ratio of 0–0.185 for over 2 s, a short to ground or open circuit; FCA treats signal 2 below 0.784 V as circuit low. Common causes: Line B shorted to ground (steering wheel, clockspring) (high likelihood); Button block faulty or damp (medium likelihood); Corroded connector (medium likelihood); Module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control and distance or mode buttons inoperative; Cruise control locked out; No check engine light. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0594 – Cruise Control Servo Control Circuit/Open
text: P0594: Cruise Control Servo Control Circuit/Open. Older engines without electronic throttle use a vacuum cruise servo on the throttle cable: a vacuum valve (closed when unpowered) opens the throttle with intake vacuum, a vent valve (open when unpowered) holds or releases it, and a dump valve fed through the brake switch vents it when braking. Where the engine module drives these valves, it checks each circuit and switches cruise off; CARB treats this as emission-neutral, usually without warning lamp. P0594 concerns the servo control or supply circuit: an open circuit. Where the servo is fed through the cruise contact of the brake light switch, braking interrupts this supply on purpose, so the brake switch and its wiring are typical causes and brake lights may be affected too. No manufacturer document available to us describes P0594 in detail. Common causes: Brake light switch (cruise contact) faulty or misadjusted (high likelihood); Supply line open or shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Servo connector or servo (medium likelihood); Engine module output (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control cannot be engaged or switches off; Usually no check engine light, code stored only; Possibly brake light problem as well (shared switch). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0597 – Thermostat Heater Control Circuit/Open
text: P0597: Thermostat Heater Control Circuit/Open. A map-controlled thermostat is a wax thermostat with a built-in heating resistor (Valeo: about 10 Ω). Unheated it opens late, for hot running at part load; the engine module heats it by map under full load or towing so it opens earlier. CARB requires the thermostat to be monitored and the heater circuit counts as an output component. GM switches it to ground with a low-side driver and checks it every second, fault after 15 of 30 samples, type B; Hyundai/Kia/Genesis and VW/Audi use the codes as well. P0597 means the heater circuit is open – GM above 200 kΩ with the driver off. The thermostat then only works through its wax and opens late, so coolant runs hotter under load; Audi's 4.2 FSI also limits engine speed. Genesis (G80/G90 3.3 T, 3.8) replaced thermostats from an early production lot. Common causes: Heating resistor in the thermostat open (high likelihood); Connector at the thermostat loose or corroded, coolant in the connector (medium likelihood); Broken wire or missing supply (fuse, relay) (medium likelihood); Engine module driver (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (after two trips); Coolant temperature higher than usual under load; Audi/VW: coolant warning and engine speed limit possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P059A – Active Grille Air Shutter A Position Sensor Circuit
text: P059A: Active Grille Air Shutter A Position Sensor Circuit. The active grille shutter (A = upper or only shutter, B = second) closes louvres to cut drag and speed warm-up and opens them for cooling; CARB names it as an off-cycle CO2 technology and requires its components to be monitored. A separately evaluated position sensor, as these titles assume, is described in Ford patents (Hall sensor on the motor or sensor on the linkage). No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: today the sensor sits inside the LIN actuator, whose faults appear as P059F/P05AE, P05A1/P05B0 or U0284/U0285. Without position feedback the shutter is usually driven open. P059A (shutter A) is the general circuit fault of the position sensor – signal missing or wire open, without low/high split. Common causes: Position sensor in the actuator faulty (replaced as a unit) (high likelihood); Actuator connector corroded or with water ingress (high likelihood); Wire open in the front bumper harness (accident, rodents) (medium likelihood); Engine module or reference voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Shutter stays in one position (usually open) or does not react; Slightly higher consumption, longer warm-up in winter. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P059F – Active Grille Air Shutter A Performance/Stuck Off
text: P059F: Active Grille Air Shutter A Performance/Stuck Off. The active grille shutter (A = upper or only shutter, B = second) closes louvres to cut drag and speed warm-up and opens them for cooling; CARB names it as an off-cycle CO2 technology and requires its components to be monitored. P059F compares commanded and reached position. 'Stuck off' means stuck closed at Toyota (failure type 73) and Nissan; GM and Ford use P059F for any deviation. title: P05A1 – Active Grille Air Shutter A Position Sensor Minimum/Maximum Stop Performance

title: P05A2 – Active Grille Air Shutter A Control Circuit/Open
text: P05A2: Active Grille Air Shutter A Control Circuit/Open. title: P05AE – Active Grille Air Shutter B Performance/Stuck Off
text: P05AE: Active Grille Air Shutter B Performance/Stuck Off. Shutter B is the second active grille shutter – at GM, Ford and Stellantis the lower one in the bumper. Shutters cut drag and speed warm-up when closed and open for cooling; CARB names them as an off-cycle CO2 technology and treats the actuator as an output component. Smart actuators report over LIN (loss of communication: U0285); a fault usually costs fuel and warm-up time, a closed shutter can make the engine run hot under load. P05AE compares commanded and reached position. GM checks in two stages with five clearing attempts, type B, two trips; Ford's 3.0 L diesel at over 6° deviation in operation or 20° when learning open; Stellantis uses it too. GM, Ford and Stellantis do not distinguish the direction. GM bulletins for 2019–21 Silverado and Sierra name stones or ice at the bottom of the lower shutter, often with U0285. Common causes: Debris, stones, ice or snow in the lower shutter (high likelihood); Louvres unhooked or broken, rubbing on bracket or horn, impact damage (high likelihood); Water or corrosion in connector or harness (medium likelihood); Actuator B faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (GM after two trips); Lower shutter not moving or incompletely, possibly U0285 or P059F; Higher coolant temperature under load or slightly higher consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05B8 – Restraint Deployment Signal Circuit/Open
text: P05B8: Restraint Deployment Signal Circuit/Open. After a crash the restraint control module tells the engine module that airbags or belt tensioners have fired; the engine module then cuts the fuel pump (Ford: until the ignition is cycled) and possibly the engine. Depending on the maker the message travels over CAN and/or a dedicated wire with a defined level or voltage drop. P05B8 means the wired signal line is open – no valid rest level arrives. After a real crash the fuel cut-off may then not be triggered via this line. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; it is a safety function, not an emission-relevant monitor, so usually without warning lamp. Common causes: Signal wire or connector between restraint and engine module open (e.g. after accident repair or seat removal) (high likelihood); Corroded or spread pin at either module (medium likelihood); Replacement module not configured (medium likelihood); Restraint module output stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Code stored, driving usually normal; Possibly message that fuel cut-off is unavailable; No check engine light. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05BC – Stop-Start Mode Switch Circuit/Open
text: P05BC: Stop-Start Mode Switch Circuit/Open. The stop-start off switch lets the driver disable automatic engine stop for the current drive. It is read directly or via another module over CAN – on Stellantis' 2025 Ram 1500 it sits in the electronic shifter module. CARB names a stop-start diagnosis as its example of an emission-neutral diagnosis, so no warning lamp is required; stop-start is usually just disabled. P05BC means the switch circuit is open. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; Stellantis documents only its sibling P05BD. Typical are a connector left off after console or dashboard work or an open switch contact. Common causes: Open circuit in switch, connector or wire (high likelihood); Switch faulty (contact or resistor ladder) (medium likelihood); Connector not refitted after console or dashboard work (medium likelihood); Reading module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Stop-start cannot be switched off or stays disabled; Switch indicator not working; Usually no check engine light. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P05C2 – Engine Coolant Pressure Sensor Circuit
text: P05C2: Engine Coolant Pressure Sensor Circuit. An engine coolant pressure sensor (5 V reference, ratiometric signal) measures pressure in the cooling circuit; in a sealed circuit pressure rises with temperature, so deviations reveal leaks or a loose cap – described in Navistar and GE patents for commercial and rail engines. No manufacturer document available to us uses P05C2–P05C6 for passenger cars; CARB requires input components to be checked for circuit faults, range and plausibility. P05C2 is the general circuit fault – signal, reference or ground open, or no communication from a digital sensor. Leak detection is then unavailable. Common causes: Connector corroded or loose, wire open (coolant and heat zone) (high likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); 5 V reference disturbed (low likelihood); Module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or warning (depending on the maker); Coolant pressure or leak warning unavailable; Usually no change in driving. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P05C7 – Economy Mode Switch Circuit/Open
text: P05C7: Economy Mode Switch Circuit/Open. The economy mode switch selects a fuel-saving mode (flatter pedal map, earlier upshifts, sometimes reduced A/C). title: P05CB – Vehicle Hardware Incompatibility
text: P05CB: Vehicle Hardware Incompatibility. P05CB means a control module has found that installed hardware does not match the vehicle configuration – a wrong variant or part number, an unprogrammed replacement module, or messages from another vehicle type. No admissible manufacturer document available to us uses P05CB. CARB requires a calibration verification number showing that emission software is valid for the vehicle, but no hardware code. Ford reports configuration and compatibility faults under P0610 (vehicle options) and P0630 (VIN not programmed or incompatible) instead. Typical cause is a replaced module or battery that was not matched or programmed. Common causes: Replacement module or battery with wrong part number or for another variant (high likelihood); Module not programmed or configured after replacement (high likelihood); Faulty module software level (medium likelihood); Module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Power limitation possible; Wrench or powertrain warning lamp; Further functions possibly disabled. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05CC – Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Performance Bank 1
text: P05CC: Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Performance Bank 1. During catalyst heating after a cold start the engine module commands a specific cam phaser position for more residual gas and exhaust heat; CARB requires this to be monitored under codes separate from the normal cam codes. These 'performance' codes are GM's current form (since about 2015/16; older GM engines and Ford use the direction codes P052A ff and P054A ff): fault when commanded and actual position differ by more than 4° or 6° once the target is stable. P05CC watches intake camshaft A on bank 1 – the cold-start counterpart of P0011. GM's 3.0 L twin turbo sets it above 4°, 60 of 100 samples, type B; the 2.0 L turbo in the Envision above 6° as type A after one trip. A GM bulletin for the 2024–25 Traverse, Enclave and Acadia (2.5 L turbo, electric phaser) names a damaged phaser motor with rattle, together with P0011/P0016. Common causes: Insufficient cold oil supply: wrong viscosity, low level, worn oil (high likelihood); Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged (medium likelihood); Phaser worn or lock pin not releasing; on electric phasers a damaged phaser motor (medium likelihood); Timing chain stretched or skipped (low likelihood); Engine module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on (GM mostly after two trips); Often no noticeable symptoms, possibly rough cold idle; Rattle from the timing drive (GM electric phaser). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05D0 – Driver Mode Select Switch A Circuit
text: P05D0: Driver Mode Select Switch A Circuit. The driver mode select switch (tour, sport, eco, snow, off-road, towing) changes engine and transmission maps such as shift points, pedal map and cylinder deactivation, so CARB requires it to be monitored as an input. GM reads switch A as an eight-position resistor ladder in the body module and sets P05D1–P05D3 in its 2025 tables when a condition is present for 4 s within 5 s, type B with warning lamp after two trips. A fault blocks mode selection; the vehicle stays in its basic mode. P05D0 is the general circuit fault of switch A without low/high assignment. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; GM covers the same switch with the more specific P05D1–P05D3. Common causes: Connector at the switch or control panel corroded or loose (high likelihood); Switch faulty, e.g. liquid in the centre console (medium likelihood); Wire to the reading module open (medium likelihood); Reading module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Drive mode cannot be changed, vehicle stays in normal mode; Mode display missing or jumping back; Check engine light (GM after two trips). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05D8 – PCV Regulator Valve Control Circuit/Open
text: P05D8: PCV Regulator Valve Control Circuit/Open. Some turbo engines have an electrically controlled crankcase ventilation valve that decides when and how much blow-by gas is drawn into the intake (part-load versus full-load path). The engine module monitors its driver output; CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults and the PCV system to be monitored. Nissan's 1.5 L KR15DDT (Rogue 2024–25) sets P05D8/P05D9 with the warning lamp from a severed harness at the valve; Mercedes M270/M274 have such a valve but report it under P052E. P05D8 means the valve control circuit is open – wire, coil or connector; the driver sees no load. Common causes: Harness at the valve connector chafed or severed (high likelihood); Connector not latched or corroded after engine cover or intake work (medium likelihood); Valve coil open (medium likelihood); Engine module driver (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Often no noticeable symptoms; If the valve sticks: oil mist, blue smoke, rough idle. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05DB – Brake Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit/Open
text: P05DB: Brake Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit/Open. Brake-by-wire and hybrid systems use a dual-channel pedal travel sensor; channel B runs opposite to A at Toyota (3.6–4.4 V at rest, falling when pressed), so a common fault of both channels shows up. Symptoms: Brake or regeneration warning light; Check engine light; Regeneration or brake assist reduced, pedal feel changed. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P05E0 – Brake Pedal Position Sensor A/B Correlation
text: P05E0: Brake Pedal Position Sensor A/B Correlation. Brake-by-wire and hybrid systems measure brake pedal travel with a two-channel sensor; the channels often run in opposite directions (Toyota RAV4 hybrid 2024–25: one rises from about 1 V, the other falls from about 4 V). P05E0 means both channels are electrically fine but no longer match each other. Toyota sets it when the relationship is invalid for 0.2 s and lights the lamp at once; Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV adds the regenerative brake warning. Braking falls back to plain hydraulics, so the pedal may feel hard and regeneration is off. GM notes for the CT6, Bolt, Malibu and Volt 2016–18 that the code can also appear without a defect if the driver rests a foot lightly on the brake (1.8–5.6 mm travel) for 60 s while accelerating. Single-channel faults are P057A–P057E and P05DB–P05DF. Common causes: Pedal travel sensor faulty internally (channels drift apart) (high likelihood); Contact resistance or corrosion in the connector or harness of one channel (medium likelihood); Sensor not calibrated after replacement or pedal work (medium likelihood); Foot resting lightly on the brake while accelerating (GM) (medium likelihood); Brake or hybrid control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or service warning; Brake, ABS or stability warning lamp; Hard brake pedal, reduced brake assist; Regenerative braking disabled (hybrid/PHEV). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05E1 – A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P05E1: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. The refrigerant pressure sensor (three wires, 5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) tells the engine module the A/C pressure; it uses it to switch the radiator fan, to block the compressor at too high or too low pressure and to pre-control idle load. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults and plausibility, but they need not light the lamp if they do not affect emissions. 'Intermittent/Erratic' means the signal jumps implausibly fast or briefly leaves its valid range without staying low or high long enough for those codes. Sensor A is usually the high-pressure sensor; GM and Saab report it only as P0532/P0533 (circuit low/high, at GM below 3 % or above 98 % of 5 V) and P0531, so no manufacturer document available to us uses P05E1 itself. Typically the compressor is blocked and the fan runs. GM rates sensor A faults without the lamp, the Saab 9-4X with it. Common causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector (front end, splash water) (high likelihood); Chafed or broken wire (5 V, signal, ground) (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (signal jumps) (medium likelihood); Shared 5 V reference disturbed by another sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: A/C intermittently not cooling (compressor switched off); Radiator fan runs unnecessarily or irregularly; Idle speed fluctuates when A/C engages; Warning lamp depending on the maker. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05E3 – Park Brake Sensor/Switch Circuit
text: P05E3: Park Brake Sensor/Switch Circuit. The engine module reads the park brake status, directly or via another module, because strategies depend on it: a parked diesel filter regeneration only runs with the park brake applied (Navistar), idle shutdown and PTO logic use it, and Ford delays an automatic restart while the electric park brake moves. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored. The only documented user of this code family is Volvo Trucks: since OBD 2021 a second park brake sensor (about 0.5 V applied, 3.5 V released) must agree with the old switch; the engine module reports the fault. No passenger car maker uses it verifiably. P05E3 is the general circuit fault – usually an open circuit or undefined state. Low and high signals are P05E4 and P05E5. Common causes: Broken wire or corroded connector at the park brake switch or sensor (high likelihood); Switch or pressure sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Faulty diode in the switch circuit (Volvo) (low likelihood); Vehicle or brake module delivers a wrong status (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or OBD warning (heavy-duty); Park brake warning in the cluster; Parked regeneration cannot be started; Stop-start or idle shutdown not working. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05E8 – Engine Oil Bypass Valve Control Circuit/Open
text: P05E8: Engine Oil Bypass Valve Control Circuit/Open. The engine oil bypass valve is an electrically switched solenoid that, according to patents (Hyundai/Kia), routes oil around the oil cooler when cold so the engine warms up faster with less friction, and through the cooler once the oil is hot. It is not the purely mechanical oil filter bypass. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. No manufacturer document available to us uses P05E8–P05EA, and no vehicle with these codes was found. If the circuit fails, the valve stays in its unpowered position – depending on design oil may run too hot under load or warm up slowly. P05E8 means the control circuit is open: the driver sees missing voltage or high resistance. Common causes: Connector at the valve loose, corroded or spread (high likelihood); Valve solenoid coil open (medium likelihood); Broken wire in the harness (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (if rated as emission related); Oil too hot under load or slow warm-up, depending on rest position; Usually no noticeable driving symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05EB – Cold Start SCR NOx Catalyst Inlet Temperature Too Low
text: P05EB: Cold Start SCR NOx Catalyst Inlet Temperature Too Low. After a cold start a diesel heats its exhaust actively – retarded and post injection, intake or exhaust throttling, higher idle, EGR cooler bypass – so the SCR catalyst quickly reaches the temperature at which urea dosing can start (around 180–200 °C). P05EB sets when the measured temperature at the SCR inlet stays below the expected or modelled value within a set time after the start: the heating strategy is not working. CARB requires this 'catalyst warm-up' monitor for light-duty diesels from model year 2026 (20 %) to 2028 (100 %); GM 2025 and Ford 2023 tables do not contain the code yet. Volvo Trucks used it on 2016–17 heavy-duty engines and advised a software check instead of replacing parts. The lamp comes on; no power limitation from this code alone is known. Common causes: Engine module software or calibration (false trigger) (high likelihood); Exhaust temperature sensor before the SCR reads low or slow (medium likelihood); Heating measure not effective: throttle, EGR cooler bypass or turbo vanes sticking (medium likelihood); Post or retarded injection not effective (injectors) (low likelihood); Exhaust leak before the sensor or extremely cold conditions (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no driving symptoms; Higher NOx emissions after cold start (not noticeable). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P05EC – Cold Start Injection Timing Performance
text: P05EC: Cold Start Injection Timing Performance. To heat the exhaust after a cold start, a diesel shifts its start of injection, usually later, plus post injections. CARB requires faults of such elements during the cold start strategy to be reported under codes separate from normal operation – hence P05EC. GM's 2025 diesels compare the start of injection requested by the application software with the timing actually scheduled for the injector drivers, during cold start only; a deviation beyond ±4 or ±5 in 88 of 176 or 8 of 16 samples sets the code and the lamp in the first trip. Ford's 2023 diesel instead checks whether the cold start operating mode is really activated when requested (10 s). Mechanical injector timing faults in normal operation are P01CB ff and P020A ff; the petrol counterpart for ignition timing is P050B. Common causes: Engine module software or internal fault (request and execution differ) (high likelihood); Cold start mode blocked by other faults (coolant or fuel temperature, rail pressure) (medium likelihood); Injector driver or injector circuit (low likelihood); Weak battery during cold start (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no driving symptoms; Possibly more white smoke or rougher running after cold start. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P05ED – Reductant Heater Control Module Supply Voltage
text: P05ED: Reductant Heater Control Module Supply Voltage. Some diesels use a separate control module or power stage for the DEF heaters in tank, pump and lines; without heating, frozen fluid cannot thaw in winter and dosing stays blocked. P05ED reports that this module's supply voltage is outside its allowed window – a blown main fuse, an open feed or ground, or system voltage too low or too high. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). Thresholds are not published; GM's L5P monitors the comparable heater supply under its own codes and flags a drop of more than 3 V below battery voltage while heating is requested. Start with fuse, feed, ground and battery or charging system. Common causes: Main fuse or feed wire to the heater module faulty, connector corroded (splash zone) (high likelihood); Poor module ground (medium likelihood); Weak battery or charging fault (system voltage too low or too high) (medium likelihood); Heater control module faulty internally (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart; In cold weather: DEF frozen, dosing blocked, further heater codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05EE – Reductant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
text: P05EE: Reductant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit/Open. The electric supply pump in the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) tank module builds the dosing pressure for the SCR catalyst. Its supply voltage is monitored separately from the pump control circuit (P208A ff); CARB requires SCR components and their outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05EE means the supply circuit is open: when the supply is switched on, no voltage or current reaches the pump branch. Ford's comparable check flags a pump controller voltage below 6 V. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow. Common causes: Connector at the pump or tank module corroded or loose (high likelihood); Open wire in the harness to the tank (medium likelihood); Fuse or relay of the pump supply faulty (medium likelihood); Pump or tank module open internally (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart; Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency. Repair difficulty: medium.

GM's 6.6 L diesel monitors this as P1044 (two trips); Ford flags pump voltage above 16 V or controller voltage above 19 V. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow. Common causes: Pump supply shorted to battery positive in the harness (high likelihood); Overvoltage from the charging system or a jump start (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion causing leakage current in the connector (medium likelihood); Relay or driver does not switch off (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart; Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05F1 – Reductant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit Stuck On
text: P05F1: Reductant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit Stuck On. The electric supply pump in the diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) tank module builds the dosing pressure for the SCR catalyst. P05F1 means the pump supply stays on although the module switches it off – typically detected after the switch-off command, e.g. during after-run, when the feedback still shows voltage. A welded relay or a shorted semiconductor switch is the usual reason. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow. Common causes: Pump supply relay stuck (welded contacts) (high likelihood); Semiconductor driver shorted (medium likelihood); External voltage or short to positive in the harness (medium likelihood); Software or calibration fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart; Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency; Pump keeps running after switch-off, battery drains. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05F3 – Exhaust Aftertreatment Power Relay Control Circuit/Open
text: P05F3: Exhaust Aftertreatment Power Relay Control Circuit/Open. A power relay, switched by the engine module through an output driver, feeds aftertreatment consumers such as the DEF pump, tank and line heaters and possibly NOx sensors or the SCR module. CARB requires such outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F3 means the driver detects an open relay control (coil) circuit. Ford's comparable relay check flags 'driver on but 0 V' or a heater relay current below 0.2 A, within 5 s. Chrysler (FCA) lists this code among those that trigger the DEF inducement: a 'Service DEF System' warning, a countdown after 50 miles and no restart after 150 miles (P241D). If the relay fails, heaters, pump and SCR control drop out and dosing stops. Common causes: Relay missing, coil open or not seated properly (high likelihood); Corroded connector or relay socket (medium likelihood); Harness damaged (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart; Follow-up codes for heaters, pump or NOx sensor supply. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P05F8 – Reductant Heater Control Module Performance
text: P05F8: Reductant Heater Control Module Performance. P05F8 is the function check of the DEF heater control module: its feedback does not match the command – heating current or power, temperature rise, or an internal module fault. The code is documented for Chrysler's 3.0 L EcoDiesel in the 2014 Ram 1500 and Jeep Grand Cherokee: several bulletins list it together with the heater codes P20BA, P20BE and P20C2, and the fix in each case was only reprogramming the engine module – a diagnostic that was too sensitive rather than a hardware defect. It is not on Chrysler's inducement list. Ford checks the same function under heater plausibility codes. Thresholds for P05F8 are not published. If it returns after a software update, check the heater elements in tank and lines and the module supply (P05ED). Common causes: Engine module software (Chrysler 3.0 L 2014: diagnostic revised by reflash) (high likelihood); Heater control module faulty internally (medium likelihood); Heater element or line in tank or hose with abnormal current (medium likelihood); Unstable module supply or ground (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Usually no driveability issue; DEF warning in cold weather, possible heater codes P20BA/P20BE/P20C2. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05F9 – Stop-Start Status Signal Circuit
text: P05F9: Stop-Start Status Signal Circuit. A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB. CARB names stop-start as its example of an 'emissions neutral' reaction: a module that simply disables stop-start when a fault appears may report it without the check engine light, which is what Ford does for its stop-start codes. P05F9 is the general circuit fault or open line. The typical reaction is that stop-start is disabled; the driver-operated stop-start switch has its own codes. Common causes: Open status line or connector problem (high likelihood); Sending module without supply or faulty (medium likelihood); Wrong software or variant coding (stop-start set without hardware) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Stop-start does not work; Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster; Check engine light only with some makers. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P05FC – Cold Start Fuel Pressure Performance Bank 2
text: P05FC: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Performance Bank 2. During a cold start, direct injection petrol engines usually raise rail pressure for finer atomisation with multiple injections while the catalyst heats up. P05FC monitors whether the actual rail pressure of bank 2 stays within the target window during this phase – only engines with separate rails and pressure sensors per bank (V or boxer engines with two high-pressure circuits) can set it. CARB lists fuel pressure as a cold start component that must respond measurably beyond what would happen without the strategy. No manufacturer document available to us uses P05FC; Ford checks the single-rail counterpart P053F and flags a fault when the share of cold start time inside the pressure window is 0.70 or less, and Kia replaced the engine module of the 2018 Stinger 2.0T for P053F with stumbling during warm-up. GM uses P2C1E–P2C20 instead. Common causes: High-pressure pump or volume control valve of bank 2 weak or sticking (high likelihood); Low supply pressure (low-pressure pump, filter) (medium likelihood); Rail pressure sensor of bank 2 inaccurate (medium likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood); Leaking injector or pressure relief on bank 2 (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Stumbling, hesitation or rough idle during warm-up; Poorer cold start; Usually normal once warm. Repair difficulty: hard.
