title: P0635 – Power Steering Control Circuit
text: P0635: Power Steering Control Circuit. P0635–P0637 concern the control or signal circuit between engine module and power steering – depending on the maker the drive of an electro-hydraulic pump or the steering load signal the engine module uses to raise idle. CARB requires power steering components to be monitored only if another diagnostic uses them, so these codes are rare and maker-specific. Mercedes-Benz stores P0635 in the electric steering module itself (no assist after start, software update); no engine module table available to us uses P0635–P0637. P0635 is the general or open-circuit code; output components must be checked for circuit faults, but separate low/high codes (P0636/P0637) are not mandatory. Steering assist may fail or be reduced; without the load signal idle can sag at full lock. The power steering pressure switch family is P0550–P0554. Common causes: Wire or connector between engine module and steering module or pump open or corroded (high likelihood); Software or calibration fault in the steering module (Mercedes) (medium likelihood); Steering module or electro-hydraulic pump faulty (medium likelihood); Undervoltage from weak battery, alternator or poor ground (medium likelihood); Engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Power steering warning, heavy steering; Check engine light (depending on the maker); Idle drops when steering; Fault possibly only after engine start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0638 – Throttle Actuator Control Range/Performance Bank 1
text: P0638: Throttle Actuator Control Range/Performance Bank 1. The electronic throttle motor positions the throttle plate; P0638 means the actuator does not follow its command on bank 1 (or the only throttle): target and actual angle from the two position sensors differ, or the motor needs too much duty cycle to hold the position. Subaru (also sold as Saab 9-2X) sets it at more than 3.5° deviation for 250 ms or over 95 % duty cycle for 2 s, lights the lamp at once and lets the spring set the plate to about 6° – raised idle, almost no power. GM's Saab 9-4X V6 uses more than 80 % duty cycle for over 1 s, lamp in the first trip. Mazda's CX-9 set it after frosty nights when condensation froze the throttle and fixed it with software that moves the plate after switch-off. Ford reports the same function as P2111/P2112. Common causes: Throttle dirty, sooted or stiff (high likelihood); Icing from condensation in frost (medium likelihood); Throttle motor or gears worn (medium likelihood); Resistance in the motor control wires (medium likelihood); Module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or electronic throttle light; Limp mode: much reduced power, raised idle; Delayed or jerky throttle response; Often after a cold start in frost. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0639 – Throttle Actuator Control Range/Performance Bank 2
text: P0639: Throttle Actuator Control Range/Performance Bank 2. P0639 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0638 and only applies to engines with two separate electronic throttles, one per cylinder bank (some V8, V10 and V12 engines with separate intake paths). The module compares target and actual angle and the duty cycle the motor needs; if the plate does not follow, it is de-energised and springs to its rest position, and power is limited. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0639 – this follows P0638 (Subaru: more than 3.5° deviation for 250 ms) and CARB's function check of output components. Ford calls a second throttle 'throttle actuator B' and reports it as P211A ff, its sensors as sensor C (P0225/P0229). Uneven filling of the two banks can also cause a rough idle. Common causes: Bank 2 throttle dirty or stiff (high likelihood); Bank 2 actuator motor or gears faulty (medium likelihood); Icing (low likelihood); Wiring or module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Limp mode, loss of power; Rough idle from uneven bank filling. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P063A – Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A
text: P063A: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A. Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics. P063A is the general or open-circuit code of sense circuit A; range, low and high are P063B–P063D. It differs from the F feedback (P0622/P0625/P0626) and the L line (P0621); the module's own supply voltage is monitored as P0560–P0563. Common causes: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded (high likelihood); Alternator or regulator faulty (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds (medium likelihood); Battery faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Battery warning lamp on; Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery); Flickering lights; Further voltage codes (P0562/P0563). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P063E – Auto Configuration Throttle Input Not Present Bank 1
text: P063E: Auto Configuration Throttle Input Not Present Bank 1. Some modules configure themselves at start-up by detecting which inputs are present. P063E means the module expects a throttle position input for bank 1 but does not detect it. Unlike circuit codes such as P0122/P0123 or P2135, which judge a present but faulty signal, this says the input was not found for the configuration. No manufacturer document or patent available to us describes this check; the explanation is derived from the J2012 wording. CARB requires input components to be checked for circuit continuity and plausibility, and modules with several variants to detect a wrong one. Possible causes are an unplugged throttle body or open wiring, or software meant for a different vehicle. Without a throttle signal an electronic throttle runs in limp mode. Common causes: Throttle sensor or unit not connected, connector or wire open (medium likelihood); Wrong module software or variant for the vehicle (module from another model) (medium likelihood); Faulty throttle unit (low likelihood); Internal module fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Limp mode, reduced power; Rough idle, poor throttle response; Additional throttle circuit codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P063F – Auto Configuration Engine Coolant Temperature Input Not Present
text: P063F: Auto Configuration Engine Coolant Temperature Input Not Present. Some modules configure themselves at start-up by detecting which inputs are present. P063F means the module expects a coolant temperature input but does not detect it during this self-configuration. It differs from the circuit codes P0117/P0118 (signal low/high) and the plausibility codes P0116, P0125 and P0128, which judge a present signal. No manufacturer document or patent available to us describes this check; the explanation is derived from the J2012 wording. CARB requires the coolant temperature sensor to be monitored for circuit, range and warm-up. Possible causes are an unplugged NTC sensor, an open wire or software for a different vehicle. Expect a substitute temperature, a constantly running fan, a dead temperature gauge and poorer cold starts. Common causes: Coolant temperature sensor not connected, connector or wire open (medium likelihood); Wrong module software or variant (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor (low likelihood); Internal module fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Radiator fan runs constantly; Temperature gauge not working; Poor cold start, higher consumption. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0640 – Intake Air Heater Control Circuit
text: P0640: Intake Air Heater Control Circuit. Some diesels (for example GM's 6.6 L Duramax LML and the Cummins in Ram trucks) warm the intake air with a heater grid switched by a relay or semiconductor switch. P0640 reports a fault in its control circuit. GM's LML glow plug module expects a digital feedback from the heater while it is commanded on; if it is missing for 2 s (75 % of 4 s), the code sets and the lamp follows after two trips. Current, voltage and temperature faults run under GM's own codes P154A–P154D. CARB requires intake air heaters to be checked for response, current and voltage drop. The result is poor cold starts, white smoke and rough running after a cold start; a relay stuck on drains the battery – Ram recalled 2021 trucks because a shorted heater relay could overheat. Ford's 2023 diesel does not use P0640. Common causes: Heater relay or switching module faulty (high likelihood); Control wire or connector open or corroded (medium likelihood); Heater grid burnt out or shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Heater main cable or fuse loose or faulty (medium likelihood); Glow plug or engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Poor cold start in low temperatures; White smoke, rough running after cold start; Flat battery if the relay sticks. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0641 – Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit/Open
text: P0641: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit/Open. The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time. P0641 is the general code for circuit A. GM puts everything into this one code: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping (filtered against unfiltered value), 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s in a row, lamp in the first trip; circuits 2–4 are P0651, P0697 and P06A3, and GM does not use P0642/P0643. GM Europe's 2.0 L diesel flags it outside 4.5–5.5 V for 0.5 s with reduced engine power (two trips), the 2.0 L petrol after 1 s or 10 s cumulative (first trip). Because throttle and pedal sensors may be affected, limp mode is common. Common causes: Short to ground or voltage at one of the supplied sensors or its wire (high likelihood); A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage (medium likelihood); Harness damage (chafing, rodent bite, water in connector) (medium likelihood); Module internal (reference regulator) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Limp mode with reduced power; Many codes from several sensors at once; Possibly starting or boost problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0642 – Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit Low
text: P0642: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit Low. title: P0644 – Driver Display Serial Communication Circuit
text: P0644: Driver Display Serial Communication Circuit. P0644 concerns a dedicated serial line on which the engine module sends values or warnings to a driver display or information display – not the general vehicle CAN bus. The module reports missing or invalid communication on that line (open, short, display not answering); CARB requires digital outputs to be checked for communication faults. GM Europe's 2010 Saab, for example, passes engine data such as fuel level over CAN to the body module and on to the instrument unit and information display – where such data runs on the bus, a failure is reported as a U code (e.g. U0155) instead. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. Displays then show missing, frozen or jumping information; the engine runs normally. Common causes: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted (high likelihood); Display or instrument cluster faulty or without supply (fuse, ground) (medium likelihood); Low system voltage during cranking (low likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning message or lamp (depending on the maker); Information in the driver display missing, frozen or jumping; Display stays dark. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0645 – A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit
text: P0645: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit. The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0645 is the general circuit fault of the relay coil control, usually an open circuit. GM Europe's 2011 Saab 9-5 sets P0645/P0646 for an open or short to ground and P0647 for a short to voltage, with the engine running and A/C requested; Ford's commercial trucks report it without the check engine light. Older Saab diesels (Bosch EDC16/PSG16) use a different assignment (P0645 short to voltage, 0.6 s). GM found a no-start with P0645 on the 2002–04 Alero/Grand Am 3.4 L because a shorted compressor clutch coil blew a fuse shared with the engine control; Ford traced warm air with P0645 on the 2020–23 Explorer to spread terminals at the body module. The compressor then does not engage or runs constantly. Common causes: A/C clutch relay faulty (coil open) (high likelihood); Control wire or connector open, terminals spread (high likelihood); Relay or clutch supply fuse blown (e.g. shorted clutch coil) (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: A/C not cooling (compressor does not engage); Compressor runs constantly; Check engine light usually off, code stored only; Rarely no start if a shared fuse has blown (GM 3.4 L). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0646 – A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit Low
text: P0646: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit Low. The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0646 means the voltage at the control output is too low while the driver is off – the control wire is shorted to ground, so the relay can pull in permanently and the compressor keeps running, which can ice up the evaporator. Saab's EDC16 diesels set it after more than 0.6 s with the engine running; GM Europe's 2011 Saab 9-5 also includes an open circuit here. Ford's OBD summaries list P0646/P0647 in a 5 V reference section for Bosch modules – an unusual assignment not covered here. The code is not emission relevant and does not light the check engine lamp at most makers. Common causes: Control wire between relay and module shorted to ground (chafing) (high likelihood); Relay faulty internally (coil, ground) (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: A/C compressor runs constantly, even with A/C off; Evaporator ices up, cooling drops; With an open circuit: no cooling. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0647 – A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit High
text: P0647: A/C Clutch Relay Control Circuit High. The engine module switches the A/C compressor clutch relay through a low-side driver once the climate control requests cooling. P0647 means the voltage at the control output stays too high while the driver switches on (it should pull to ground) – the control wire is shorted to voltage; the driver shuts off for protection and the relay does not pull in, so there is no cooling. GM Europe's 2011 Saab 9-5 uses P0647 only for a short to voltage (check: less than 0.3 V on the control wire with ignition on and the module unplugged); Saab's EDC16 diesels use it for an open circuit instead (0.6 s). title: P0648 – Immobilizer Lamp Control Circuit
text: P0648: Immobilizer Lamp Control Circuit. The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0648 concerns the immobiliser or security lamp where the engine module drives it directly by wire – on GM and Saab systems this lamp shows the immobiliser learn mode and faults. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. The lamp then does not show the immobiliser status, or shows it permanently; the immobiliser itself keeps working, because start authorisation is separate (key faults are P0513/P0633). The immobiliser is not an emission component, so no check engine light is expected. Common causes: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted (high likelihood); Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty (medium likelihood); Instrument cluster (board, connector) faulty (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Immobiliser lamp off, permanently on or flashing wrongly; Code stored; Engine start normally not affected. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0649 – Speed Control Lamp Control Circuit
text: P0649: Speed Control Lamp Control Circuit. The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0649 concerns the cruise control ('speed control') indicator where the engine module drives it by wire. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. CARB names cruise control as an example of a function outside the test cycles, and GM rates its cruise control diagnostics as emission neutral without the check engine light. The indicator then does not work or stays on; whether cruise control is also disabled depends on the maker. Cruise control inputs and switches have their own codes (P0564–P0581). Common causes: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted (high likelihood); Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty (medium likelihood); Instrument cluster faulty (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). title: P064A – Fuel Pump Control Module A
text: P064A: Fuel Pump Control Module A. Demand-controlled fuel systems drive the pump through a separate pump control module; the engine module sets the target and reads its status back. P064A means this module reports an internal fault. Ford petrol engines encode the status as a duty cycle on a monitor line – 30 % (±4 %) means internal driver fault, 20 % invalid data (P025B), no signal U0109 – and set the code after 2–5 s; Ford's 2023 diesel checks the period of the monitor signal (0–1.2 s, 0.5 s). GM's pump module sets P064A when its output stage exceeds 150 °C (3 of 15 samples), with the lamp after two trips; Ford petrol stores it without the lamp. Pump output may be reduced or switched off, so low fuel pressure, stalling or a no-start can follow. A stiff, worn pump drawing high current can overheat the module. Common causes: Pump control module faulty internally (output stage, electronics) (high likelihood); Output stage overheating from a stiff or worn pump or poor module cooling (medium likelihood); Supply or ground fault or corrosion at the module (often on frame or tank) (medium likelihood); Disturbed monitor line, so a wrong duty cycle is read (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM) or stored code only (Ford petrol); Hard start, stumbling or lack of power from low fuel pressure; Stalling or no start if the pump is switched off; Fuel pressure codes as well (e.g. P0087). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P064B – PTO Control Module
text: P064B: PTO Control Module. A power take-off (PTO) drives equipment on trucks and pick-ups – tipper, crane, hydraulic pump or winch – from the engine or transmission. A PTO control module, or the PTO function in the engine module, manages switching, working speed and release conditions; P064B reports a fault of this module or an implausible PTO request. The only manufacturer document found is a Chrysler case for Ram chassis cabs: with the PTO engaged the engine speed hunts and does not rise above about 1100 rpm, P064B sets together with the torque monitoring code P061B and the PTO switches off; the cause was software, so check upfitter installation and programming before replacing parts. CARB defines PTO units and allows monitors to pause while one is active. Thresholds and lamp status are not published; driving is usually normal. Common causes: Engine or PTO module software or calibration (implausible torque or speed request) (high likelihood); PTO equipment installed or programmed incorrectly by the upfitter (medium likelihood); Harness, connector or supply of the PTO module or switches (medium likelihood); PTO control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: PTO switches off or cannot be engaged; Engine speed hunts with PTO active or stays below about 1100 rpm (Chrysler); Warning lamp or stored code; driving usually normal. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P064C – Glow Plug Control Module 1
text: P064C: Glow Plug Control Module 1. On diesels a glow plug control module switches the glow plugs (at Ford also the DEF heaters) with semiconductor switches, diagnoses itself and reports to the engine module. P064C means this module reports an internal fault. GM's 2017–18 Duramax checks for a switch that is commanded on but delivers less than 3.2 A and 0 V at the plug (3.5 s), ROM, RAM and EEPROM checksums, the charge pump of the high-side drivers and reverse polarity; the LML (2011–16) used under 6.6 A for 75 % of 4 s; lamp after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesels flag drivers that do not switch or overheat, a RAM checksum error, supply below 6.5 or above 16.5 V and module temperature above 125 °C, within about 1 s. The glow system then fails partly or completely: hard cold starts, white smoke and higher cold-start emissions. Common causes: Glow plug module faulty internally (switches, memory) (high likelihood); Insufficient supply or ground (battery, corrosion, main fuse) (medium likelihood); Short in a glow plug or wire overloading a driver (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector of the engine-mounted module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking in cold weather; White smoke and rough running after a cold start; Glow plug circuit codes as well. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P064D – Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1
text: P064D: Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1. Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064D means this chip for bank 1 sensor 1 does not work correctly or its messages are invalid. Ford validates the SPI communication continuously and sets P064D/P064E after 10 s at 11–18 V with the sensor heater working; an internal chip fault adds Ford's P1646/P1647. GM (wide-band engines such as the 3.0 L twin turbo, 2018–2025) evaluates two error counters from the chip and sets the code at 128 of 160 samples (about 4 s), more than 20 s after start-up, with the lamp after two trips. Fuel control then runs open loop and oxygen sensor monitors are disabled – fuel consumption and emissions rise. Faults in the sensor or wiring can also push the chip into an invalid state. Common causes: Engine module (lambda chip) faulty (high likelihood); Wiring or sensor fault pushing the chip into an invalid state (short to battery voltage, water in connector) (medium likelihood); Faulty wide-band sensor (e.g. heater-to-signal short) (medium likelihood); Voltage dips or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Higher fuel consumption, rough running (open loop); Failed emissions test; Codes for the bank 1 sensor 1 wide-band sensor. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P064E – Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 2
text: P064E: Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 2. Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064E is the bank 2 counterpart of P064D and only occurs on V and boxer engines with two sensors before the catalysts. Ford sets it when the SPI communication with the bank 2 chip fails (10 s; an internal chip fault adds Ford's P1647); GM uses the same error counters as for bank 1 (128 of 160 samples, lamp after two trips). Fuel control on bank 2 then runs open loop, with higher consumption and emissions. Check the bank 2 sensor 1 wiring and sensor first; if they are fine, the engine module is the likely cause. Common causes: Engine module (lambda chip bank 2) faulty (high likelihood); Wiring or connector fault of the bank 2 sensor 1 (medium likelihood); Bank 2 wide-band sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Voltage dips or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Higher fuel consumption, rough running; Failed emissions test; Codes for the bank 2 sensor 1 wide-band sensor. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P064F – Unauthorized Software/Calibration Detected
text: P064F: Unauthorized Software/Calibration Detected. P064F means the module has found that its software or calibration is not the version released by the manufacturer, or fails an authenticity check (signature, checksum, security keys). CARB requires manufacturers to protect calibrations against changes without special tools and to report calibration IDs and checksums. GM's 2025 engine modules set it when the embedded message authentication table for secured bus messages is invalid, with the lamp in the first trip; chassis modules also check missing key storage or wrong key-slot configuration. Chrysler fixed P064F on the 2017 Ram 3500–5500 chassis cab 6.7 L Cummins by reprogramming – so it is not only about tuning. Typical triggers are tuning software, an interrupted or wrong reflash, a module from another vehicle, or a module replaced without learning its security keys. Programming released software usually clears it. Common causes: Unapproved or tuned software (chip tuning, programmer) (high likelihood); Faulty or interrupted reflash, outdated software (medium likelihood); Used or replaced module without learning the security keys, wrong configuration (medium likelihood); Module faulty internally (key storage) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM in the first trip); Possibly follow-up codes in other modules or communication problems; Driving often normal. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0650 – MIL Control Circuit/Open
text: P0650: MIL Control Circuit/Open. The engine module switches the check engine light (MIL) through a low-side driver – or sends the command over CAN – and monitors the circuit: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V. CARB requires the MIL to light for a bulb check at ignition on with the engine off (at least 15 s since model year 2005). GM's 2018–2025 modules use P0650 only for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, above 11 V, 50 ms) and P263A/P263B for shorts to ground and voltage – stored without lighting the MIL, since a broken MIL cannot report itself; older GM diesels combine all faults in P0650. GM Europe's Saab 9-5 V6 checks only once the MIL has been commanded on and off. The engine runs normally, but emission faults go unseen and inspections fail if the lamp does not light at the bulb check. Common causes: Wire or connector between engine module and instrument cluster open or corroded (high likelihood); MIL bulb burnt out or LED/instrument cluster faulty (high likelihood); MIL supply in the cluster missing (fuse, ignition feed) (medium likelihood); Short in the circuit (at GM reported as P263A/P263B) (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL does not light at the bulb check; MIL stays on (with a short or combined code); Code only visible with a scan tool, engine runs normally; Failed emissions inspection. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0651 – Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit/Open
text: P0651: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit/Open. The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V. P0651 is the general code for circuit B. GM puts all faults into it: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping, 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s in a row, with the lamp in the first trip (2018; GM's 2006 V6 used 10 s and two trips). GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo feeds all four camshaft sensors and pedal sensor 1 from it and also uses P0652/P0653 (1 s or 10 s cumulative). Ford reports reference B only as range/performance P06A7. Expect limp mode if the pedal sensor is affected, and starting problems or stalling if camshaft sensors are. Common causes: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor (camshaft, pedal, pressure) (high likelihood); Chafing or water in harness or connector (medium likelihood); A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage (medium likelihood); Module internal voltage regulator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Several sensor codes at once (camshaft, pedal, pressure); Limp mode, reduced power; Starting problems or stalling. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0652 – Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit Low
text: P0652: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit Low. The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V. P0652 means reference B is too low – usually the 5 V line or a connected sensor is shorted to ground. GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY (2004–05) sets it below 4.7 V for 2 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, each with the lamp in the first trip. Newer GM engines report it under the collective code P0651, and Ford does not use P0652. All sensors on the circuit then read low, with matching codes, limp mode and possibly starting problems. Common causes: 5 V reference wire shorted to ground (chafing) (high likelihood); Sensor on the reference circuit shorted internally (high likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in a connector (medium likelihood); Module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Several 'low' sensor codes at once; Limp mode or reduced power; Starting problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0653 – Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit High
text: P0653: Sensor Reference Voltage B Circuit High. The engine module feeds several sensors (camshaft, pedal, pressure sensors) from separate regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'B' is circuit 2. A short at one sensor pulls the whole reference down, so every sensor on it reports at once – unplug them one by one until the reference returns to 4.8–5.2 V. P0653 means reference B is too high – often a signal wire of a connected sensor has chafed onto a 12 V line, less often the reference wire itself. GM's Duramax LB7/LLY (2004–05) sets it above 5.2 V for 2 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, each with the lamp in the first trip. Newer GM engines report it as P0651, Ford does not use it. Sensor readings then become implausibly high and limp mode follows. Common causes: Reference or sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V line (high likelihood); Faulty sensor feeding in external voltage (medium likelihood); Module voltage regulator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Several 'high' sensor codes; Limp mode; Implausible sensor values in live data. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0654 – Engine RPM Output Circuit/Open
text: P0654: Engine RPM Output Circuit/Open. The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0654 concerns the engine speed output: the module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer and other modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P0654 reports an open circuit or other fault on this output. Saab's EDC16 diesels use P0654 differently (a sensor supply group). No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. The tachometer then reads zero or jumps; devices using the signal may fail, while the engine itself runs normally because the crankshaft input is intact. Common causes: Wire between module and tachometer or receiver open, connector corroded (high likelihood); Output wire shorted (medium likelihood); Instrument cluster or receiving module faulty (input stage) (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Tachometer reads zero or jumps; Functions using the speed signal disturbed (accessories, cruise control, shift indicator); Check engine light depending on the maker. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0655 – Engine Hot Lamp Output Control Circuit
text: P0655: Engine Hot Lamp Output Control Circuit. The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. P0655 concerns the engine hot or coolant warning lamp that the engine module switches by wire from the coolant temperature signal. CARB links overtemperature protection strategies to this lamp: a protective reaction that only starts after the hot lamp lights needs no MIL. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. If the circuit fails, the driver may not be warned of overheating – check it promptly even though the check engine light usually stays off. Actual overheating is P0217; the coolant sensor circuit is P0117/P0118. Common causes: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted (high likelihood); Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty (medium likelihood); Lamp supply missing (fuse) (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Temperature warning lamp does not light at bulb check or when overheating; Warning lamp stays on without overheating; Code stored, check engine light depending on the maker. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0656 – Fuel Level Output Circuit
text: P0656: Fuel Level Output Circuit. The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. Where the engine module reads the fuel level sender itself – it needs the level for the evaporative leak test – it passes the level on to the fuel gauge. GM Europe's 2010 Saab 9-5 reads two senders (0.5–3.5 V), calculates the level in percent and sends it over CAN via the body module to the instrument cluster; there a failure would be a U code. P0656 reports a fault on a hard-wired level output. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. The gauge then reads empty, full or jumps and the low fuel warning is wrong; engine and evaporative test are not affected. Sender input faults are P0460–P0464. Common causes: Wire or connector between module and instrument cluster open or shorted (high likelihood); Instrument cluster (fuel gauge input) faulty (medium likelihood); Output driver in the module faulty (low likelihood); Fuel level sender fault as root cause (low likelihood). Symptoms: Fuel gauge reads empty, full or jumps; Low fuel warning wrong; Range display wrong. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0657 – Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit/Open
text: P0657: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit/Open. Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0657 is the open-circuit code; it is documented at Ford: the high-side switch of the 5R110W and 6R80 automatics feeds all shift solenoids, and the 2023 diesels split them into two supplies (P0657 and P2669), checked continuously. On a fault the solenoids are de-energised and the transmission falls back to a mechanical limp gear with maximum line pressure – harsh shifts and a single forward gear. Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the lamp depending on the variant. GM does not use P0657 and reports opens together with ground faults under P0658. Common causes: Open or connector fault at the transmission pass-through connector or wire to the valve body (high likelihood); Damaged harness (medium likelihood); Internal high-side switch in the engine or transmission module (medium likelihood); Internal transmission harness (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission limp mode (fixed gear); Harsh shifts, no upshift; Check engine light (depending on the variant); Codes for individual shift solenoids. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0658 – Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit Low
text: P0658: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit Low. Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0658 means the supply output is too low with the driver on – a short to ground (0.5 Ω or less). GM's engine module checks its shared high-side driver in 20 of 25 samples; the lamp rating changed from none (2016) via two trips (2017–18) to the first trip (2025). GM's transmission modules include an open circuit here, set it in the first trip and block the solenoid diagnostics, so the gearbox goes into limp mode. On GM Europe's 2.0 CDTI it means the internal 5 V supply is too low – no MIL, and if it recurs, the engine module is replaced. Common causes: Actuator supply wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Actuator (solenoid) shorted internally (medium likelihood); Transmission harness or connector (also open, in transmission modules) (medium likelihood); Module internal (main cause on the Saab diesel) (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission limp mode or fixed gear; Several actuators not working; Check engine light (GM from 2017); Codes for individual solenoids. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0659 – Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit High
text: P0659: Actuator Supply Voltage A Circuit High. Actuator supply A is a high-side switch feeding several actuators together; its use differs by maker (Ford transmission solenoids, GM shared high-side driver, GM Europe 2.0 CDTI internal 5 V supply). P0659 means a short to voltage on the supply output, checked with the driver off – the output should then be dead (GM: 0.5 Ω or less to the supply, 20 of 25 samples; lamp after two trips in 2017–18, none in 2016). The driver can then no longer switch the actuators off; GM's transmission modules block their solenoid diagnostics while P0658/P0659 are active, and limp mode follows. On GM Europe's 2.0 CDTI it means the internal 5 V supply is too high, without MIL – the engine module is replaced. Common causes: Actuator supply wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage (high likelihood); Harness chafed against a 12 V line (medium likelihood); Module (driver shorted; internal on the Saab diesel) (medium likelihood); External voltage fed back through a faulty actuator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM from 2017); Transmission or actuator limp mode; Actuators cannot be switched off; Follow-up codes. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P065A – Generator System Performance
text: P065A: Generator System Performance. Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065A is the function check of the whole charging strategy. Chrysler (Stellantis) explains it as a non-MIL code: the engine module switches off demand-controlled charging and falls back to normal charging because of electrical faults in other modules – returned alternators replaced for P065A were found to be fine. Other Stellantis cases trace it, together with P2503/P2504, to loose B+ or high-current connections, and the Ram 1500 3.0 EcoDiesel Gen 3 received a software update. The result is a constant charging voltage instead of smart charging, possibly with a battery lamp; there is no power limitation. Check codes in other modules and the main battery connections before replacing the alternator. Common causes: Electrical fault in another module (lighting, wipers, blower) disabling smart charging (high likelihood); Loose or corroded B+ or high-current connection (medium likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood); Alternator or regulator faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Battery warning lamp (in some cases); Fluctuating charging voltage reading; No check engine light (Chrysler); Fault codes in other modules. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P065B – Generator A Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P065B: Generator A Control Circuit Range/Performance. Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065B is the plausibility check of the control channel to the alternator regulator (LIN or a dedicated smart-charge line): command and feedback do not match, or the signal is out of range (too low or too high). A manufacturer table published via NHTSA for a gateway with LIN alternator shows the battery lamp and disabled stop-start, notes that jump starting or charging can set it briefly, and says to check P065C (belt) first; Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the lamp depending on the variant. The regulator then falls back to a default target voltage. Circuit faults are P0620; L and F lines are P0621/P0622. Common causes: LIN or control wire between alternator and module (connector, corrosion, open) (high likelihood); Weak battery, jump start or external charging (medium likelihood); Alternator regulator faulty (medium likelihood); Ground or B+ connections (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Battery warning lamp on; Stop-start not working; Battery drains; Usually no check engine light. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P065C – Generator A Mechanical Performance
text: P065C: Generator A Mechanical Performance. Demand-controlled (smart) charging lets the module vary alternator voltage; the charging system is not an emission component, so these codes usually come without the check engine light. P065C points to the alternator's mechanical drive: the alternator does not deliver as commanded or its feedback does not match engine speed, typically because the belt slips. The only manufacturer document found – a table for a gateway with LIN alternator published via NHTSA – shows the battery lamp and disabled stop-start and names checking and adjusting the drive belt tension as the fix, to be checked before P065B. Thresholds are not published. Belt wear or oil contamination, a weak tensioner, a faulty overrunning pulley or a stiff alternator bearing are the obvious mechanical causes. Hybrid starter-generators use other codes. Common causes: Drive belt slipping (tension, wear, oil) (high likelihood); Weak belt tensioner (medium likelihood); Alternator overrunning pulley faulty (medium likelihood); Alternator bearing or rotor stiff (low likelihood). Symptoms: Battery warning lamp; Stop-start disabled; Belt squeal; Low battery voltage. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P065D – Reductant System Malfunction Lamp Control Circuit
text: P065D: Reductant System Malfunction Lamp Control Circuit. The engine module switches this hard-wired output with its own driver and checks the circuit electrically (open, short to ground or voltage) – it cannot see whether the lamp lights; on CAN-based cars such faults appear as U codes. On SCR diesels a separate lamp or symbol warns of low DEF/AdBlue level, poor quality or system faults and announces speed or start restrictions (inducement). P065D reports a fault in the control circuit of this lamp. CARB requires inputs and outputs of the inducement strategy to be monitored on diesels from model years 2019–2021, and US federal rules define the inducement stages; Detroit Diesel, for example, shows the symbol below 1/8 tank and flashes it with a speed limit when empty. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB and the component. Without the lamp the driver may run into an inducement stage without warning; the code itself is not known to trigger one. Common causes: Wire or connector between module and receiver open, corroded or shorted (high likelihood); Bulb/LED or instrument cluster faulty (medium likelihood); Lamp supply missing (fuse) (medium likelihood); Driver in the engine or SCR module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: AdBlue warning lamp does not light at ignition on, or stays on; No early warning of low AdBlue (risk of speed limit or no-restart without notice); Check engine light possible (depending on the maker). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P065E – Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 1
text: P065E: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 1. The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P065E is the function check for bank 1 (or the only valve): the valve does not follow its command. It can be detected with a position sensor or, as a GM patent describes, without one from the intake pressure pulsation in steady running – a closed, tuned manifold pulses more. No manufacturer table available to us uses P065E itself: GM reports the same fault on this valve as P2070/P2071 (end position not reached within 5 s, 320 of 400 samples, two trips), and Ford's valve has no feedback at all. A valve stuck in one position leaves a torque gap in part of the rev range; sooted shafts and broken linkages are typical causes. Common causes: Valve shaft or linkage stiff or sooted (oil mist from crankcase ventilation or EGR) (high likelihood); Plastic lever or ball joint between actuator and shaft broken or detached (medium likelihood); Actuator motor or solenoid faulty (weak, gears) (medium likelihood); Manifold leak or, on vacuum-operated actuators, a leak in the vacuum line (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker); Torque gap in one rev band; Rattling or clicking from the intake manifold; Slightly higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P065F – Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 2
text: P065F: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Performance Bank 2. The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P065F is the function check of the bank 2 valve: it does not follow its command, detected via a position sensor or the intake pressure pulsation (GM patent). Bank 2 codes require a V-engine manifold with two separately switched valves; many V engines use a single central valve between the plenums, and no manufacturer document available to us uses this code, so the description follows bank 1. A stuck valve causes a torque gap in one rev band and can make the banks fill unevenly. Bank 2 circuit faults are P0663–P0665. Common causes: Bank 2 valve or shaft sooted or stiff (high likelihood); Linkage between actuator and valve broken or unhooked (medium likelihood); Bank 2 actuator faulty internally (medium likelihood); Manifold or vacuum leak (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker); Torque gap in one rev band; Noise from the intake manifold. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0660 – Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
text: P0660: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit/Open Bank 1. The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P0660 means the control circuit of the bank 1 (or only) valve is open. GM evaluates the line voltage with the driver off: too low means the supply through the coil is missing (200 kΩ or more). GM's engines with this valve (low-side driver) check with ignition voltage of at least 11 V and the engine above 400 rpm and set the code after 40 of 50 samples (about 0.6 s), with the check engine light after two trips. Ford uses P0660 (older: P1549) as the electrical check of its actuator, which has no position feedback and stays closed and unpowered below about 2600 rpm – without the check engine light (5 s). The valve then stays in its rest position and power at high revs suffers. Common causes: Actuator connector loose, corroded or spread (high likelihood); Actuator coil or motor open internally (high likelihood); Broken or chafed wire (control or supply) (medium likelihood); Supply (fuse, main relay) to the actuator missing (low likelihood); Output driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM after two trips; Ford without); Less power in the upper or middle rev range; Actuator does not click at ignition on or when switching. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0661 – Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit Low Bank 1
text: P0661: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit Low Bank 1. title: P0663 – Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit/Open Bank 2

title: P0666 – Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0666: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit. Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0666 is the general circuit fault of this sensor A. No manufacturer table available to us uses P0666 itself – GM splits the circuit faults into low (P0668) and high (P0669), plausibility is P0667. Expect a warning lamp and, in a transmission module, changed shift quality because a substitute temperature is used. Common causes: Module faulty internally (temperature sensor or measuring circuit) (high likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the module or valve body (medium likelihood); Supply or ground problems of the module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning or check engine light; Changed shift quality (substitute value); Possibly transmission fluid temperature codes. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0667 – Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
text: P0667: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance. Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0667 is the plausibility check: GM compares the module (substrate) temperature with the transmission fluid temperature and the temperature measured at power-up. The Saab 9-4X sets it when, within 5 of 6 minutes, fluid and substrate differ by more than 20–50 °C and power-up and substrate by more than 8–10 °C (two trips); GM's 2019 table uses 3000 of 3750 samples. The module then uses the power-up temperature instead. Check the fluid temperature sensor (P0711) first – it is the comparison partner. Common causes: Transmission module or valve body (internal sensor) faulty (high likelihood); Transmission fluid temperature sensor reads wrong (comparison partner) (medium likelihood); Unusual conditions (long standing in extreme cold or heat, fluid level or condition) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine or transmission warning lamp; Harsher or delayed shifts (substitute temperature); Possibly P0711 as well. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0668 – Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0668: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low. Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0668 means the sensor signal is at the low voltage end: GM converts it into a temperature and treats −249 °C or less – a physically impossible value – for 60 s as a fault, with the lamp after two trips and the power-up temperature as substitute. 'Low' refers to the voltage; depending on the sensor type that need not mean a low temperature. Common causes: Module faulty internally (sensor or measuring circuit shorted) (high likelihood); Moisture or fluid in the electronics of the valve body (medium likelihood); Module supply problem (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp; Changed shift quality (substitute value); Scan tool shows an implausibly low module temperature. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P066A – Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
text: P066A: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low. Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P066A means the circuit to the cylinder 1 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag a circuit impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples at 100 ms) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off, so plug 1 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. A plug shorted internally is the usual cause; a wrong plug type is another. Common causes: Glow plug cylinder 1 shorted internally (element against body) (high likelihood); Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (block, bracket) (medium likelihood); Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating) (low likelihood); Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM 3.0 L 2020) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp; Harder cold start, especially in frost; Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start; Possibly blown glow system fuse. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P066B – Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit High
text: P066B: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit High. title: P0670 – Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit/Open
text: P0670: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit/Open. In today's J2012 meaning P0670 is the electrical check of the activation line from the engine module to glow plug control module 1 for an open circuit; a short to ground is P0383, a short to voltage P0384, and serial communication between the modules P0683/P0684. On Bosch systems (Saab 2.2 TiD and EDC16) the engine module switches this line, detects an open load with the output off and a short to voltage with it on, and also compares the glow module's diagnostic feedback, which must switch inversely – Saab reports all line faults under P0670. GM's LB7/LLY Duramax (2004–05) used P0670 in an older meaning for glow module performance (50 of 100 samples, two trips). No current GM or Ford table uses it. If the line fails, no plug heats: hard or no cold start in frost, smoke and rough running. Common causes: Wire or connector between engine and glow module open or corroded (bent pin, contact tension) (high likelihood); Glow module faulty (input open) or without supply or ground (fuse, terminal 30) (medium likelihood); Control line shorted (makers reporting all line faults under P0670, e.g. Saab) (medium likelihood); Output driver in the engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Glow plug lamp behaves implausibly (stays off or on); Hard or no cold start in frost, since no plug heats; Smoke and rough running after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0671 – Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Circuit/Open
text: P0671: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Circuit/Open. Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P0671 means the load circuit of the cylinder 1 glow plug is open while glowing. Thresholds: GM engine-module drivers 200 kΩ or more (two trips), GM's L5P glow module less than 4.0 A at over 6 V, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke less than 1 A for about 1 s. Older GM systems (LB7/LLY, LML) report open and short under this one code. Chrysler advises checking the main B+ feed and ground of the glow module first when several cylinder codes appear together. Common causes: Glow plug cylinder 1 burnt out (element open) (high likelihood); Plug connector loose or corroded, terminal nut loose, wire broken (medium likelihood); Glow module supply or ground (several cylinder codes at once) (medium likelihood); Glow module or driver faulty, or software (GM 3.0 L 2020) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM also glow plug lamp); Harder cold start in low temperatures; Rough idle, knocking and white or blue smoke after a cold start; Often no symptoms when warm. title: P067A – Cylinder 4 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
text: P067A: Cylinder 4 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low. Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P067A means the circuit to the cylinder 4 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag an impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off and plug 4 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. Common causes: Glow plug cylinder 4 shorted internally (element against body) (high likelihood); Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating) (low likelihood); Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM bulletins) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp; Harder cold start, especially in frost; Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P067B – Cylinder 4 Glow Plug Control Circuit High

title: P0683 – Glow Plug Control Module 1 to PCM Communication Circuit
text: P0683: Glow Plug Control Module 1 to PCM Communication Circuit. Glow plug module 1 reports to the engine module over a feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the activation line) or the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106, Saab as P0380/P1380, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0683/P0684 themselves. P0683 means communication or feedback from the glow module to the engine module is missing or the line is open or shorted. The engine module then no longer receives plug status reports, so the individual plug monitoring fails; depending on design the glow module keeps glowing on its own timing or not at all. The activation line in the other direction is P0670/P0383/P0384. Common causes: Communication or feedback wire between glow and engine module open, chafed or connector corroded (high likelihood); Glow module without supply or ground (fuse, main cable) – does not answer (medium likelihood); Glow module faulty internally (medium likelihood); Glow or engine module software or programming (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (glow plug lamp may flash or stay on); Harder cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough running and white smoke after a cold start; No individual plug reports any more. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0684 – Glow Plug Control Module 1 to PCM Communication Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0684: Glow Plug Control Module 1 to PCM Communication Circuit Range/Performance. Glow plug module 1 reports to the engine module over a feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the activation line) or the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106, Saab as P0380/P1380, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0683/P0684 themselves. P0684 means communication exists but is implausible: wrong level or duty cycle, implausible content or a feedback that does not match the activation state – as in the Saab logic, where the feedback must be the inverse of the command. The engine module can then no longer rely on the glow system status; individual plug faults may go unreported. Contact resistance at the pins and voltage dips at the glow module during high glow currents are typical causes. Common causes: Contact resistance or corrosion at connectors or pins of the communication line (signal distorted) (high likelihood); Supply or ground problem at the glow module (voltage dip at high glow currents) (medium likelihood); Glow module faulty, or software/configuration not matching the engine module (medium likelihood); Engine module input stage faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (glow plug lamp may flash or stay on); Harder cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough running and white smoke after a cold start; No individual plug reports any more. title: P0685 – ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit/Open
text: P0685: ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit/Open. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0685 means the relay control circuit is open: GM measures with the driver off and flags 200 kΩ or more to ground. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo compares commanded and actual state for 2 s, Ford's 2023 diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s. A real open keeps the relay from pulling in – no start; on Saab's V6 there is then no communication with the engine module and the MIL flashes. GM notes P0686 may set alongside. Common causes: Open or corroded control wire between relay coil and module or connector (high likelihood); Relay coil open or relay badly seated (high likelihood); Relay coil supply missing (fuse, battery positive) (medium likelihood); Weak battery or voltage dip (low likelihood); Module driver faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Engine does not start or stalls; No communication with the engine module (Saab); MIL flashes rapidly, other relays click (Saab). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0686 – ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit Low
text: P0686: ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit Low. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0686 means the control line is shorted to ground: with the driver off it should carry battery voltage through the coil, but it sits at ground (0.5 Ω or less). The relay then stays energised and the module can no longer switch it off – after-run and shutdown are disturbed and the battery can drain. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. The former obdex title (the wording of P0685) was a shifted entry; P0686 is the 'low' code. Common causes: Control wire between relay and module chafed to ground (high likelihood); Relay shorted internally or water in the relay carrier (medium likelihood); Module driver shorted internally (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Relay stays on after ignition off, battery drains; Possibly P068B as well. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0687 – ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit High
text: P0687: ECM/PCM Power Relay Control Circuit High. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0687 means the control line is shorted to voltage: when the driver switches on and should pull it to ground, it stays high (0.5 Ω or less to positive) or the driver goes into overcurrent protection, so the relay does not pull in – no supply to the loads, no start or stalling. GM checks with run/crank voltage above 11 V and sets the code after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, with the lamp after two trips. The former obdex title (a sense-circuit wording) was a shifted entry; P0687 is the 'high' code of the control circuit. A high voltage on the sense line is P0690. Common causes: Control wire shorted to positive (harness, external voltage) (high likelihood); Relay coil shorted (very low resistance) (medium likelihood); Module driver faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Engine does not start or stalls; Relay does not click. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0688 – ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit/Open
text: P0688: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit/Open. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0688 means the expected switched voltage does not arrive on the sense line – the line is open, a fuse in the monitored path has blown or the contact does not close. Chrysler (Stellantis) calls the relay 'auto shutdown (ASD) relay'; a service case for intermittent no-starts with P0688 points first to spread or pushed-back terminals in the ASD circuit connector. GM does not use P0688 and reports an open sense line as P0689. The former obdex title (a duplicate of P0690) was a shifted entry. Common causes: Terminal in the sense or ASD circuit connector bent, pushed back or spread (high likelihood); Blown fuse in the monitored load circuit (e.g. shorted ignition coil) (medium likelihood); Relay contact does not close (medium likelihood); Module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Engine cranks but intermittently does not start (Stellantis); Engine stalls while driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0689 – ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Low
text: P0689: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Low. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0689 means the sense voltage is too low although the relay is commanded on – the contact does not close or has high resistance, the sense line is open or grounded, or a fuse in the load circuit has blown. GM sets it at 5 V or less with more than 9 V supply in 5 of 6 samples at 1 s, lamp after two trips; GM Europe's V6 below 6 V for 1 s and the 2.0 L turbo below 5 V, both without the lamp. Common causes: Relay contact burnt or not closing, relay faulty (high likelihood); Fuse in the relay load or sense path blown (medium likelihood); High resistance or corrosion in relay carrier, connector or wire (medium likelihood); Weak battery (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker); Starting problems or no start; Engine stalls or stumbles; Possibly electronic throttle limp mode. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P068A – ECM/PCM Power Relay De-Energized Performance Too Early
text: P068A: ECM/PCM Power Relay De-Energized Performance Too Early. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P068A means the relay dropped out before the module released it. Ford explains it as the non-volatile memory write after ignition off not being completed before the module lost power; the 2023 diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel checks with the engine running for an unexpected loss of relay voltage (no MIL). VW (2017–18 Jetta 1.4 T) and Stellantis (2026 Dodge Charger 3.0 twin turbo) fixed false reports by software updates. Real triggers include disconnecting the battery right after switch-off and loose contacts in the relay supply; learned values may be lost. Common causes: Engine module software (false report) (high likelihood); Battery disconnected during or right after switch-off, or severe voltage dip (medium likelihood); Open, high resistance or short to ground in the relay coil or contact supply (medium likelihood); Relay faulty (drops out with vibration or heat) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (Ford, VW, Stellantis); Often no noticeable symptoms; Lost learned values, rough idle after restart; With a contact fault: stalling or no start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P068B – ECM/PCM Power Relay De-Energized Performance Too Late
text: P068B: ECM/PCM Power Relay De-Energized Performance Too Late. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P068B is the counterpart of P068A: after ignition off and the module's switch-off command the relay voltage remains – the relay drops out late or not at all. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel runs this check from ignition off until the module shuts down and names a control line shorted to ground (coil stays energised), an output line shorted to voltage or a sticking contact as causes, without lighting the MIL. Symptoms: Relay or module stays active after ignition off (fan or pump keeps running); Battery drains; Possibly check engine light (depending on the maker). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P068C – Cylinder 7 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
text: P068C: Cylinder 7 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low. Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P068C means the circuit to the cylinder 7 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag an impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off and plug 7 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. Common causes: Glow plug cylinder 7 shorted internally (element against body) (high likelihood); Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating) (low likelihood); Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM bulletins) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp; Harder cold start, especially in frost; Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0690 – ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit High
text: P0690: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit High. The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0690 means the sense voltage is too high: voltage is present although the relay has been off for 2 s – a welded or sticking contact, or external voltage fed in through a short – or, on some systems, overvoltage above 18 V with the relay on. GM sets it at 4 V or more with the relay off, in 50 of 63 samples at 100 ms, lamp after two trips; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo above 2 V with the relay off or above 18 V with it on, for 2 s, and advises fixing other short-to-voltage codes first. Modules, fans or pumps may keep running after switch-off and the battery drains overnight. Common causes: Relay contact sticking or welded (high likelihood); Short to voltage on the sense or load line (external feed from another component) (medium likelihood); Control wire shorted to ground (relay permanently on) (medium likelihood); Overvoltage from the alternator regulator (where the 18 V limit applies) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Module, fan or pumps keep running after ignition off; Battery drains overnight. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0691 – Fan 1 Control Circuit Low

The former title 'Cooling Fan 1' was shortened to the J2012 wording, as for P0480. Symptoms: Check engine light (GM after two trips); Fan runs constantly or not at all, depending on circuit design; Rising coolant temperature in traffic or with A/C on; A/C may be switched off to protect the engine. title: P0697 – Sensor Reference Voltage C Circuit/Open
text: P0697: Sensor Reference Voltage C Circuit/Open. The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down, so all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. Which sensors hang on circuit C depends on the maker – pedal sensor 2 is common to all: GM 2016–2025 feeds only pedal sensor 2 from it, the Saab 9-4X also the MAP sensor, the Saab 9-5 2.0 L turbo also throttle, crankshaft and A/C pressure sensors, and Bentley's 2026 Bentayga V8 lists its own set. P0697 is the general code for circuit C. GM puts all faults into it: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping, 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s, lamp in the first trip; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo also uses P0698/P0699. Common causes: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor (high likelihood); Chafing or water in harness or connector (medium likelihood); A connected sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); Module internal voltage regulator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Several sensor codes at once (pedal, throttle, pressure); Electronic throttle limp mode, reduced power; Possibly starting problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P069E – Fuel Pump Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
text: P069E: Fuel Pump Control Module Requested MIL Illumination. P069E is not a component fault but a notice in the engine module: the separate fuel pump control module has detected and stored an emission-related fault of its own and requests the check engine light – over serial data or, on older systems, a request line. GM uses it (2014–2019 tables) and lists P069E itself as 'type A, no MIL': the lamp is lit because of the fault in the pump module, not because of P069E. The actual cause must therefore be read from the fuel pump module's own memory – typically pump circuit, fuel pressure sensor, module overheating or supply. On GM diesels (2014) this module also controls the active grille shutters. Clear the code only after repairing the module's fault. Common causes: Fault in the fuel pump circuit (pump, wiring, ground) stored in the pump module (high likelihood); Fuel pressure sensor or its wiring or 5 V reference (medium likelihood); Pump module faulty internally or overheated (corrosion, moisture) (medium likelihood); Insufficient supply or ground of the pump module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Possibly hard start, stumbling or lack of power from fuel supply problems; Further codes stored in the fuel pump module. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P069F – Throttle Actuator Control Lamp Control Circuit
text: P069F: Throttle Actuator Control Lamp Control Circuit. P069F concerns the hard-wired control circuit of the electronic throttle warning lamp (called 'reduced power', wrench or EPC lamp depending on the maker), which lights when the throttle control detects a fault and limits power. The module monitors this output electrically for open circuit and shorts; it cannot see whether the lamp lights. No manufacturer document available to us uses P069F – Ford, for example, switches its wrench lamp via the instrument cluster over the bus, not on its own wire. CARB requires output circuits to be monitored. Without a working lamp the driver is not warned when the engine enters throttle limp mode. The MIL circuit is P0650. Common causes: Open or short in the lamp wire between engine module and cluster (high likelihood); Lamp/LED or its driver in the instrument cluster faulty (medium likelihood); Connector at cluster or module corroded or loose (medium likelihood); Engine module driver faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Throttle warning lamp does not light at bulb check, or stays on; No warning when the engine goes into throttle limp mode; Code stored, engine runs normally. Repair difficulty: medium.
