title: P06A0 – Variable A/C Compressor Control Circuit
text: P06A0: Variable A/C Compressor Control Circuit. Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their swash-plate stroke via an electric control valve: a PWM current sets the crankcase pressure and thus the output. Where the engine module drives this valve (Ford's 'EVDC' compressors 2013–2019), it monitors the circuit; where the climate control module drives it (Hyundai, VW/Audi, GM), faults appear in that module instead. CARB requires monitoring only where the A/C affects engine control. P06A0 is the general circuit fault of the compressor control valve. Ford's service messages for its EVDC compressors (2013–2019) describe it with weak or no cooling, typically from a valve with an open coil or a corroded connector at the compressor; low refrigerant can also mislead the diagnosis. The compressor then runs at minimum stroke or does not cool. Not emission relevant in most cases. Common causes: Compressor control valve faulty (coil open) (high likelihood); Connector at the compressor corroded or loose, wire open (high likelihood); Low or incorrect refrigerant charge misleading the diagnosis (medium likelihood); Engine module driver faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: A/C cools weakly or not at all; Code stored, check engine light usually off; Compressor stays at minimum output. Repair difficulty: medium.

Where the engine module drives this valve (Ford's 'EVDC' compressors 2013–2019), it monitors the circuit; where the climate control module drives it (Hyundai, VW/Audi, GM), faults appear in that module instead. CARB requires monitoring only where the A/C affects engine control. P06A2 means the control valve circuit is too high – a short to voltage, so a low-side driver cannot pull to ground; with low-side drivers an open valve coil can also appear as 'high'. No manufacturer document available to us names P06A2 itself; the description follows P06A0 and the Ford EVDC system. Cooling is then weak or absent. Common causes: Valve control wire shorted to voltage (high likelihood); Valve coil open (seen as 'high' with low-side drivers) (medium likelihood); Connector or harness at the compressor damaged (medium likelihood); Engine module driver faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: A/C cools weakly or not at all; Code stored. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06A3 – Sensor Reference Voltage D Circuit/Open
text: P06A3: Sensor Reference Voltage D Circuit/Open. The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down, so all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. On GM engines (2016–2025) circuit D feeds pedal sensor 1 and both throttle position sensors, on the Saab 9-4X the throttle and pedal sensor 1 – a fault therefore usually means electronic throttle limp mode. P06A3 is the general code for circuit D. GM's petrol engines (2016–2025) and 2018 diesels use it as the only code for this circuit (4.875–5.125 V, lamp in the first trip); the 2014 6.6 L LML used 4.6 V or less for 1 s with two trips. Saab's 9-3 (2012) also reports it. Common causes: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor (high likelihood); Chafing or water in harness or connector (medium likelihood); A connected sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); Module internal voltage regulator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Several sensor codes at once (pedal, throttle, pressure); Electronic throttle limp mode, reduced power; Possibly starting problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06AA – Control Module Internal Temperature B Too High
text: P06AA: Control Module Internal Temperature B Too High. Control modules can carry a second internal temperature sensor (B). In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics, sensor A measures the circuit board (substrate) temperature, sensor B the 'power-up temperature' used as a reference and substitute; both sit inside the transmission module in the valve body, so repairs mean module or valve body. P06AA would report an overtemperature measured by sensor B – the counterpart of P0634 for sensor A (GM: 142 °C, Saab 9-4X: 146 °C with a limp mode in reverse and 5th gear). No manufacturer document available to us uses P06AA itself; GM reports overtemperature via sensor A. Check transmission fluid temperature, cooler and charging voltage first. Common causes: Transmission fluid too hot (cooler, lines, level) (high likelihood); Charging system overvoltage (medium likelihood); Faulty internal sensor or module (medium likelihood); High sustained load (towing, heat) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission limp mode possible; Transmission warning; Often transmission overtemperature as well. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P06AF – Torque Management System Forced Engine Shutdown
text: P06AF: Torque Management System Forced Engine Shutdown. GM uses P06AF for a cross-check between two control modules: the monitored module (engine or transmission module, each with main and secondary processor) sends a fixed answer sequence over CAN only if both its processors work together correctly; the monitoring module (engine, transmission or hybrid control module) sets P06AF if the pattern is wrong or missing. In all GM tables from 2016 to 2025 it is type A – lamp in the first trip – and the torque management may shut the engine down for safety. Typical causes are processor or software faults in one of the modules, communication problems or supply interruptions. Look for further processor codes (P0606, P060A, P060B) and software bulletins. No other manufacturer document available to us uses P06AF. Common causes: Software fault in engine, transmission or hybrid module (high likelihood); Processor fault in one of the modules (medium likelihood); CAN communication disturbance between the modules (medium likelihood); Supply interruption or poor ground of a module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Engine shuts off or does not start; Reduced power; Further processor or communication codes. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P06B0 – Sensor Power Supply A Circuit/Open
text: P06B0: Sensor Power Supply A Circuit/Open. Despite the similar name, 'sensor power supply' is not the 5 V sensor reference (P0641 ff). It is documented in GM hybrid drive motor control modules: a 15 V supply that excites the motor position sensor (resolver) and powers the gate drivers of the inverter transistors, kept separate from the 5 V reference and the 12 V supply. In GM's 2008 Two-Mode hybrid, A and B are the two motor control modules. P06B0 is the general or open-circuit code of supply A. Only Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander bulletin lists this code (as a main code with low/high sub-codes), without thresholds or sensor assignment. Low and high are P06B1/P06B2; GM documents those with thresholds. Check fuses and feeds of the motor control module first. Common causes: Blown fuse or open feed to the module (high likelihood); Internal supply circuit of the motor control module faulty (medium likelihood); Connector or wiring fault (medium likelihood); Short in a supplied component (resolver, gate driver) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light; Electric drive or hybrid mode limited or disabled; Further motor position or inverter codes. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P06B6 – Internal Control Module Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Processor 1 Performance
text: P06B6: Internal Control Module Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Processor 1 Performance. To detect an open knock sensor circuit, GM's engine modules feed a 20 kHz test signal into the sensor circuit and check whether it returns. P06B6 checks the internal test circuit or knock signal processor for sensor 1: it sets when the returned 20 kHz component lies between the open-circuit thresholds, so the module cannot decide 'connected' or 'open'. GM rates it type B (two trips), type A in some 2025 modules; Saab retards ignition timing as a reaction. GM bulletin 22-NA-229 calls for reprogramming only, not part replacement. Ford uses P06B6 for lost communication with its knock chip (more than 200 cylinder events). Knock sensor circuit codes are P0325–P0328. Common causes: Engine module software (GM bulletin) (high likelihood); Internal knock processor or test circuit faulty (medium likelihood); Knock sensor wiring with high resistance or intermittent contact (medium likelihood); Knock sensor faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Retarded ignition, less power and higher consumption; Often no other symptoms. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06B8 – Internal Control Module Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) Error
text: P06B8: Internal Control Module Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) Error. Non-volatile RAM keeps its content without power; among other things it stores the permanent fault codes CARB requires, which cannot be cleared with a scan tool. Ford sets P06B8 when the checksum of this permanent-code memory is wrong; a common companion is P068A (main relay dropped out too early, memory write incomplete). Ford's commercial and propane variants list it with or without the check engine light depending on the vehicle; Ford's 2023 diesel table misprints it as 'P068B'. GM and Saab do not use P06B8. Typical causes are interrupted shutdowns (battery disconnected, voltage dips), software faults and, rarely, a memory defect. After a software check, clearing and an ignition cycle with normal shutdown often resolve it. Common causes: Interrupted shutdown (battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay too early) (high likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood); Weak battery or poor ground (medium likelihood); Memory defect in the module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the vehicle); Often no driving symptoms; Possibly P068A as well. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06B9 – Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Circuit Range/Performance
text: P06B9: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Circuit Range/Performance. The glow module calculates each plug's resistance from voltage and current while glowing. 'Range/performance' means the circuit is electrically intact but the resistance or current lies outside the specified window – typically an aged, high-resistance or wrong plug or contact resistance at the connector. CARB requires a single plug outside specification to be detected from model year 2010. Ford's 2023 6.7 L/3.0 L Power Stroke runs this check during heating after the open and short checks and flags a circuit above 2 Ω after about 3 s. GM does not use this code family. Ram's 6.7 L Cummins (from model year 2025, with glow plugs instead of the grid heater) set these codes falsely; the fix was reprogramming the engine module. On the 2014–15 Ram ProMaster 3.0 L diesel, plugs without an inner O-ring caused it; all plugs were replaced. Common causes: Glow plug cylinder 1 aged or high-resistance (high likelihood); Contact resistance at plug connector or terminal nut (medium likelihood); Wrong plug type or a plug with a manufacturing fault (medium likelihood); Engine or glow module software (Ram 6.7 L from 2025) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp; Harder cold start in frost; Rough running and white smoke after a cold start; Often no symptom when warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06C5 – Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Incorrect
text: P06C5: Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Incorrect. A glow plug has no identification; the control unit recognises its type only from its electrical behaviour – cold resistance at switch-on and how resistance rises during heating (R = U/I). A Beru patent describes how steel and ceramic plugs are told apart this way so the right heating profile is used and a wrong or mixed type is reported. A low-voltage plug on an 11 V control burns out, an 11 V plug on a low-voltage control glows too weakly. GM uses 'incorrect' for any resistance outside the window: the 2025 diesels check 0.22–2.00 Ω (15 of 25 samples, two trips), the L5P glow module a ramp-dependent window. P06C5 reports this for cylinder 1. VW's 2.0 TDI (Jetta, Golf, Passat 2011–13) checks the type 2 s after ignition on – starting during that time caused false codes from the voltage dip, fixed with new glow module software. Common causes: Wrong glow plug type fitted in cylinder 1 (steel/ceramic, voltage rating) (high likelihood); Plug resistance drifted (ageing, damage) (medium likelihood); Glow module software or check during cranking (false report) (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at the plug connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp; Harder cold start or white smoke; Possibly plug burnt out (low-voltage plug on 11 V control); Code after replacing plugs. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06D1 – Internal Control Module Ignition Coil Control Performance
text: P06D1: Internal Control Module Ignition Coil Control Performance. On ignition systems where the coils are driven through a separate driver chip inside the engine module, P06D1 reports that this internal coil control does not work correctly. Ford checks the communication with the coil driver chip continuously and sets the code within 1 s at 200–3200 rpm, positive torque and 11–16 V. GM Europe's V6 (Saab 9-5 2.8 T) reports it as an internal engine module fault with the lamp after two trips. Misfires or rough running can follow if coils are no longer fired correctly. Primary circuit faults of individual coils are P0351–P0360, driver shorts P2300 ff. Check supply and ground, look for software updates; otherwise the module is the likely cause. Common causes: Coil driver chip or internal communication in the engine module faulty (high likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood); Supply or ground problem at the module (medium likelihood); Shorted coil overloading the driver (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Misfires or rough running; Possibly no start. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P06D2 – Sensor Reference Voltage E Circuit/Open
text: P06D2: Sensor Reference Voltage E Circuit/Open. The engine module feeds sensors from several regulated 5 V reference circuits; a short at one sensor pulls the whole circuit down and all its sensors report at once – unplug them one by one to find the culprit. P06D2 is the general code for circuit E. GM uses it as the collective code for its fifth 5 V reference: petrol engines 2015–2019 flag a reference outside 4.875–5.125 V in 19 of 39 samples with the lamp in the first trip, the 6.6 L Duramax LML/LGH 4.6 V or less for 0.1 s with two trips; GM includes it in its 'engine power limited' group. Which sensors are on circuit E is not listed. GM's hybrid control module uses P06D2 for a separate 12 V reference. Common causes: Short in the wire or sensor of a connected sensor (high likelihood); Chafing or water in harness or connector (medium likelihood); A connected sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); Module internal voltage regulator or components (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Several sensor codes at once; Reduced power or limp mode; Possibly starting problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06DA – Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit/Open
text: P06DA: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit/Open. A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DA means the control circuit of this valve is open: it can no longer be powered, so the pump stays at high pressure. GM measures the voltage with the driver off and flags more than 200 kΩ after two trips; some GM modules set P06DB instead. GM checks the low-side driver at 11 V or more relay voltage over 40 of 50 samples (100 ms); Ford's smart driver reports output faults after 5 s with the battery at 11 V or more. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander uses the same code. The engine is not at risk, the pump just can no longer be regulated. Common causes: Connector at the control valve loose or corroded (often at the pump in the oil pan) (high likelihood); Valve coil open or valve broken (medium likelihood); Supply (main relay) or control wire broken (medium likelihood); Engine module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light after two trips; Usually no noticeable symptom, oil pressure permanently high; Slightly higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06DB – Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Low
text: P06DB: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Low. A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DB means the control wire behind the valve is shorted to ground. With a low-side driver the valve is then powered all the time, so the pump stays at the low stage even at high load and speed. That endangers the engine, so GM flags a short below 0.5 Ω after just one trip, unlike open circuit and short to positive. GM checks the low-side driver at 11 V or more relay voltage over 40 of 50 samples (100 ms); Ford's smart driver reports output faults after 5 s with the battery at 11 V or more. A short to positive is P06DC, a pump stuck at low pressure without a circuit fault P06DE. Common causes: Control wire chafing against ground (engine block, oil pan) (high likelihood); Control valve shorted internally (medium likelihood); Oil or moisture in the connector (medium likelihood); Engine module driver stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light at once (GM after one trip); Low oil pressure at high engine speed, possibly oil pressure warning; Possibly reduced power. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06DC – Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit High
text: P06DC: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit High. A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. P06DC means the control wire is shorted to positive: the low-side driver can no longer pull it to ground, so the valve stays unpowered and the pump at high pressure – the safe state. GM checks this with the driver on and flags a short below 0.5 Ω after two trips. GM checks the low-side driver at 11 V or more relay voltage over 40 of 50 samples (100 ms); Ford's smart driver reports output faults after 5 s with the battery at 11 V or more. Apart from slightly higher consumption there are usually no symptoms. An open circuit is P06DA, a short to ground P06DB. Common causes: Control wire shorted to positive (high likelihood); Valve coil shorted (looks like a short to positive at the driver) (medium likelihood); Engine module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light after two trips; Usually no noticeable symptom, oil pressure permanently high; Slightly higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06DD – Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
text: P06DD: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off. A switchable oil pump changes its output via a solenoid valve; unpowered it delivers high pressure. To test it, the module switches the pump between stages (GM up to 15 times, with oil at 50–110 °C and 1350–2500 rpm, expecting more than 100 kPa difference) and watches the oil pressure sensor; Ford checks each switch-over of a two-stage pump within 1 s, or a variable pump over 10 s, from 30 s after start. P06DD means the pressure does not react and stays above the threshold – the pump acts as if the valve were stuck off, at high pressure; GM sets it after two trips. Yet GM bulletins for V8 and 2.5 L engines list P06DD with low oil pressure, too: broken valve tips, unseated valves, a loose pump drive gear or worn tensioners also stop the pressure from changing. Check oil level and pressure before replacing parts. Common causes: Control valve stuck or broken, screen clogged (high likelihood); Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludge (medium likelihood); Mechanical pump or drive damage (tensioner, drive gear, pump face) (medium likelihood); Valve not seated correctly (retaining clip) (low likelihood); Oil pressure sensor inaccurate (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light after two trips; Oil pressure stays high – or, with pump damage, low or fluctuating; Possibly oil pressure warning; Slightly higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P06DE – Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Stuck On
text: P06DE: Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Stuck On. A switchable oil pump changes its output via a solenoid valve; powered it runs at the low stage. To test it, the module switches the pump between stages (GM up to 15 times, with oil at 50–110 °C and 1350–2500 rpm, expecting more than 100 kPa difference) and watches the oil pressure sensor; Ford checks each switch-over of a two-stage pump within 1 s, or a variable pump over 10 s, from 30 s after start. P06DE is the counterpart of P06DD: the commanded high stage is not reached and the pressure stays below the threshold, as if the valve were stuck on. Too little oil pressure at high load endangers the engine, so GM sets it after just one trip; a Ford patent raises idle speed in this case. A short to ground on the control wire (P06DB) has the same effect electrically. An FCA bulletin for the 3.6 L V6 fixes false codes by software. Common causes: Control valve stuck in the powered position (high likelihood); Low oil level, diluted or sludged oil, aeration (medium likelihood); Pump wear or internal leakage (medium likelihood); Engine module software (FCA 3.6 L) (low likelihood); Oil pressure sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light at once; Oil pressure warning at higher engine speed possible; Possibly reduced power or raised idle; Valvetrain or chain tensioner noise from lack of oil. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P06DF – Glow Plug Control Module 1 Memory Checksum Error
text: P06DF: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Memory Checksum Error. A diesel glow plug control module has its own microcontroller. On power-up it forms a checksum over its memory and compares it with the stored value; P06DF means they differ, so the module's program or data cannot be trusted. Ford's 2023 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke list P06DF among the glow module checks, run at power-up and flagged on a RAM checksum mismatch after about 1 s. GM's L5P performs the same check on ROM (4.5 s, two trips) but reports it as P064C. CARB treats the module as a 'smart device' whose internal faults need not be pinpointed, so this is extra diagnosis by the manufacturer. The usual remedy is reprogramming or replacing the module; until then preheating may be missing. Common causes: Glow plug control module faulty internally (memory, controller) (high likelihood); Failed or interrupted programming of the module (medium likelihood); Voltage dip or spike at power-up (weak battery, poor ground) (low likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in module or connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking; White smoke and knocking after cold start; Often no symptoms when warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06E0 – Cylinder 11 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
text: P06E0: Cylinder 11 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low. Diesel glow systems switch each plug through its own power semiconductor and switch off a faulty channel; CARB requires single-plug detection from model year 2010. P06E0 means the circuit to the cylinder 11 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. For cylinders 1–8, GM's engine-module drivers flag below 0.11 Ω to ground after two trips, and Ford's 2023 Power Stroke more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s while heating. The channel is switched off and the plug stays cold; the other plugs keep working. An internally shorted plug or a chafed wire is the usual cause. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it needs at least 11 cylinders, and the only US OBD II diesel above eight, VW's Touareg V10 TDI, has ten; the description follows cylinders 1–8. Common causes: Cylinder 11 glow plug shorted internally (high likelihood); Plug wire chafed through to ground (medium likelihood); Burnt connector or terminal nut, tracking through oil or moisture (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the glow module defective (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM: also glow plug lamp); Harder cold start in frost; Rough cold idle, white smoke after cold start; Cylinder 11 misfire when cold. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06E4 – Control Module Wake-up Circuit Performance
text: P06E4: Control Module Wake-up Circuit Performance. Control modules are woken by a dedicated wake-up line or a network wake-up – at ignition on, when a charging cable is plugged in, or on a timer for engine-off diagnostics and battery management. P06E4 means this wake-up signal is implausible: the module wakes too late or not at all, stays awake, or the line state does not match the network status. In practice the code appears mainly on hybrids: FCA fixes it on the Pacifica plug-in hybrid and the Wrangler 4xe with module software, where it remained as a permanent code that blocked emission inspections; GM's hybrid integration module lists it as a fault bundle. No manufacturer publishes thresholds or timing. Common causes: Module software (false setting, permanent code does not clear) (high likelihood); Wake-up line or connector open or shorted (medium likelihood); Weak 12 V battery, voltage dips at wake-up (medium likelihood); Engine or hybrid control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Permanent code blocks emission inspection; Possibly battery drain (module stays awake). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06E5 – Glow Plug Control Module 1 Performance
text: P06E5: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Performance. P06E5 means glow plug control module 1 does not respond correctly to the glow command: its outputs do not switch or its internal drivers report faults or overheating. Ford's 2023 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke list P06E5 among the glow module checks, run continuously, with a fault after about 1 s when internal drivers for glow plugs, DEF heaters or relays fail to switch or overheat for more than 1 s – Ford does not assign each threshold to a single code. GM files the same check under P064C: on the L5P a plug commanded on but drawing under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s, on the LML a total current under 6.6 A; both after two trips. The plugs then heat partly or not at all, with hard cold starts and white smoke. There is no limp mode. Common causes: Glow plug control module faulty internally (drivers do not switch) (high likelihood); Poor supply or ground of the module (main feed, fuse, ground) (medium likelihood); Module overheating (mounting location, short at a plug) (medium likelihood); Module software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking; White smoke and rough running after cold start; Often stored together with plug codes or P064C/P263C. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06E6 – Sensor Power Supply C Circuit/Open
text: P06E6: Sensor Power Supply C Circuit/Open. 'Sensor power supply' is a separate J2012 family next to the 5 V sensor reference (P0697 ff): an additional supply from the module for sensors or drivers – in GM hybrids a 15 V supply for resolvers and inverter gate drivers, there as supplies A and B. Supply C is a third such circuit. P06E6 is the general or open-circuit code of supply C: the module measures the output of its supply regulator and finds the voltage missing. Low and high are P06E7/P06E8. Only Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander lists P06E6 as a main code with sub-codes for low and high, called internal control module, without thresholds or the sensors fed. All sensors on the circuit then deliver invalid values, so several follow-up codes and limp mode are possible. Common causes: Open circuit or connector problem in the supply circuit (high likelihood); Short in the supply wire or a supplied sensor (medium likelihood); Supply regulator inside the module faulty (medium likelihood); Vehicle under- or overvoltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Several sensor codes at the same time; Limp mode or reduced power possible; Possibly starting problems or rough running. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06E9 – Engine Starter Performance
text: P06E9: Engine Starter Performance. On cars with stop-start or keyless start the engine module operates the starter relay itself and watches the start: if cranking is commanded but the engine does not turn, turns too slowly or the start is aborted, it sets P06E9. CARB counts an engine start from 150 rpm below warm idle. Thresholds for speed and time are not published. Bulletins show both sides: VW traces P06E9 on the Tiguan to dirt inside the starter that opens its contacts intermittently, and on the Atlas has relays, battery and voltage drop checked; Audi's SQ5 and FCA's Jeep Compass need module software instead. Ford lists P06E9 among the starter faults that disable stop-start. Common causes: Starter worn or solenoid contacts intermittently open (high likelihood); Weak battery, voltage drop on main cables or ground (high likelihood); Starter relay or its control (medium likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent no-start or only clicking; Stop-start not working; Check engine light depending on manufacturer (FCA: yes); Long cranking. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06EA – NOx Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
text: P06EA: NOx Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1. A modern NOx sensor is a smart sensor: a ceramic sensing element with pump cells and heater plus its own control unit with a microcontroller, which regulates the pump currents, calculates NOx and oxygen and sends them to the engine module over CAN. P06EA means this control unit of sensor 1 (before the SCR catalyst) reports an internal fault – its self-tests of RAM and ROM or EEPROM checksums fail – so the electronics, not the sensing element, are at fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: Ford's 2023 diesels run exactly these checks continuously, with a fault after 5 s, but report them as P2200; GM uses the P2200 family and U029D/U029E. The NOx value is then invalid, so SCR dosing runs on a model or stops, a warning appears and, depending on market, a countdown to a start lock. Common causes: Faulty electronics in the NOx sensor control unit (high likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in control unit or connector (underbody location) (medium likelihood); Under- or overvoltage or dips in the sensor supply (medium likelihood); Unsuitable replacement sensor or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or emissions warning; Message to check AdBlue/emission system, possibly countdown to start lock; Follow-up codes for SCR efficiency or NOx plausibility; Driveability usually unchanged. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06EC – Fuel Injector Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
text: P06EC: Fuel Injector Control Module Requested MIL Illumination. P06EC is a notice code like P0700: a separate fuel injector control module has stored an emission-related fault of its own and asks the engine module over CAN to switch on the check engine light. The actual fault is stored in that module and must be read there; simple OBD readers show only P06EC. GM uses it on the 2019 Corvette ZR1, whose LT5 engine adds port injection driven by its own module with its own crank and cam inputs; the code runs continuously from key on and is listed as type A without its own MIL – the lamp comes from the module's fault. Older separate injector modules (Ford 6.0 L Power Stroke, GM bi-fuel CNG trucks) report through P0611 or U codes instead. Any limp mode follows the module's fault. Common causes: Emission-related fault in the injector control module or its injectors/sensors (code stored there) (high likelihood); Supply, ground or relay problem of the module (medium likelihood); Internal module fault (memory, processor) (medium likelihood); Software level of engine or injector module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Generic scanner shows only P06EC – details in the injector module; Depending on the fault, power loss, misfire or limp mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06ED – Engine RPM Output Circuit Low
text: P06ED: Engine RPM Output Circuit Low. The engine module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer, transmission or body-builder modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P06ED means this output is too low, typically shorted to ground, so it can no longer switch high. It is the counterpart of P0654 (open circuit) and P06EE (high). CARB requires output circuits to be checked; the signal is emission-relevant only if a receiving module uses it for emission functions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB, the component and P0654. The tachometer then reads zero or jumps, and modules using the signal lose it, while the engine runs normally. Common causes: Speed output wire chafing against ground (high likelihood); Receiver (instrument, add-on device) shorted internally (medium likelihood); Aftermarket tachometer or accessory wired wrongly (medium likelihood); Engine module driver stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Tachometer at zero or jumping; Other modules without speed signal; Engine runs normally. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06EF – Engine Restart Performance
text: P06EF: Engine Restart Performance. P06EF concerns the automatic restart after the system itself has stopped the engine – stop-start or hybrid. The restart, by starter, reinforced stop-start starter or belt starter-generator, takes too long or fails. CARB does not count such a commanded shutdown as a stall. No manufacturer publishes the time limit. VW's Tiguan bulletins list P06EF together with P06E9 and trace both to dirt inside the starter; FCA fixes it on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler with engine-module software and lights the check engine light. Stop-start is then disabled. Besides the starter, a weak stop-start battery or fuel and ignition problems at restart can be the cause. Common causes: Starter or starter-generator worn, contacts intermittently open (high likelihood); Engine module software (medium likelihood); Weak stop-start battery (AGM/EFB) or battery sensor (medium likelihood); Fuel pressure or ignition at restart (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine does not restart or restarts late after stop-start; Stop-start disabled; Check engine light (FCA). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06F0 – Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P06F0: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit. Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F0 is the general circuit fault of this internal sensor: the signal is missing, open or cannot be evaluated. Range, low and high are P06F1–P06F3; the DEF tank temperature sensor is a different part. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow. Common causes: Reductant control module or pump unit faulty (sensor is on the board) (high likelihood); Water ingress or corrosion in the module (DEF crystals, underbody location) (medium likelihood); Supply or ground problems at the module (medium likelihood); Module software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or SCR warning; Message to check AdBlue system, possibly countdown to start lock; DEF heating or pump inactive (no thawing in frost); Driveability usually unchanged. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P06F4 – Stop-Start Mode Lamp Control Circuit
text: P06F4: Stop-Start Mode Lamp Control Circuit. When the engine module switches a lamp through its own wire, it checks the output driver electrically like other lamp outputs: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V – GM's MIL driver, for example, flags an open circuit at 200 kΩ or more. It cannot see whether the bulb lights, and on cars that send the lamp command over CAN such faults appear as U codes. P06F4 concerns the indicator showing that stop-start is active or disabled; the code reports a fault in its control circuit. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; the description follows CARB's output check and other lamp circuits. Only the display is affected – the stop-start function itself has its own codes (P06E9, P06EF). Common causes: Wire or connector to the indicator open or shorted (high likelihood); Indicator or instrument cluster faulty (medium likelihood); Engine module driver stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Stop-start indicator not working or permanently lit; Usually no check engine light. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P06F5 – Glow Plug Control Module 2
text: P06F5: Glow Plug Control Module 2. SAE J2012 provides a complete code family for a second glow plug control module, mirroring module 1 code for code. P06F5 is the general or internal fault of module 2, the counterpart of P064C. For module 1, GM's L5P groups driver faults (under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s) and a ROM checksum error under P064C, after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke lists P064C among the module checks with detection in about 1 s. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P064C). The plugs fed by module 2 then heat poorly or not at all. Common causes: Glow plug control module 2 faulty internally (high likelihood); Poor supply or ground of module 2 (medium likelihood); Module software or configuration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only; Usually no symptoms when warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06F6 – Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit/Open
text: P06F6: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit/Open. P06F6 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is open or has a general circuit fault – the counterpart of P0670 for module 1. The engine module's output driver detects an open load while the driver is off. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0670). Shorts on the same line are P06F7 (to ground) and P06F8 (to positive); the feedback line back to the engine module is P06FC/P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank. Common causes: Line from engine module to glow module 2 open, connector loose or corroded (high likelihood); Input of glow module 2 faulty or module not connected (medium likelihood); Engine module output driver faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only; Usually no symptoms when warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

text: P06F8: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit High. title: P06F9 – Glow Plug Control Module 2 System Voltage
text: P06F9: Glow Plug Control Module 2 System Voltage. P06F9 means the supply voltage of glow plug control module 2 is out of range – the counterpart of P052F for module 1. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke flags below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or an open supply after about 1 s; GM's L5P checks the same under P163C (below 6.0 V with ignition above 9 V, or implausible against ignition voltage, 4 s). An FCA bulletin shows P052F together with the glow plug open codes, because without supply no current flows. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P052F). Check main feed, fuses and ground first. Common causes: Main feed to glow module 2 open or high-resistance (fuse, fusible link, B+ wire) (high likelihood); Weak battery or discharged auxiliary battery (medium likelihood); Module ground corroded (medium likelihood); Charging voltage too high (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only; Usually no symptoms when warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P06FB – Glow Plug Control Module 2 Memory Checksum Error
text: P06FB: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Memory Checksum Error. P06FB means glow plug control module 2 has found a memory checksum error – the counterpart of P06DF for module 1. The module forms a checksum over its memory at power-up and compares it with the stored value. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks the RAM checksum at power-up (about 1 s); GM's L5P checks the ROM checksum (4.5 s, two trips) and reports it as P064C. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P06DF). The usual remedy is reprogramming or replacing the module. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank. Common causes: Glow module 2 faulty internally (memory) (high likelihood); Interrupted programming or faulty software (medium likelihood); Voltage dip at power-up (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only; Usually no symptoms when warm. title: P06FC – Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit
text: P06FC: Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit. P06FC means the feedback or communication from glow plug control module 2 to the engine module is missing, or the line is open or shorted – the counterpart of P0683 for module 1. Depending on design the module reports over a single feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the command line) or over the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106 rather than P0683. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0683). The engine module then loses the plug status reports; implausible messages are P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank. Common causes: Feedback or bus line open or shorted, connector corroded (high likelihood); Glow module 2 without supply (does not transmit) (medium likelihood); Glow module 2 or engine module interface faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only; Usually no symptoms when warm. title: P06FD – Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit Range/Performance
text: P06FD: Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit Range/Performance. P06FD means signals or messages from glow plug control module 2 arrive at the engine module but are implausible – wrong duty cycle or pattern, feedback not matching the command, or single messages timing out. It is the counterpart of P0684 for module 1; Saab's Bosch-based diesels, for example, expect the feedback signal to be inverse to the command line. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0684). A missing signal or open line is P06FC, a lost bus link usually U0106. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank. Common causes: Loose contact or contact resistance in the feedback or bus line (high likelihood); Ground offset between module and engine module from glow currents (medium likelihood); Software mismatch between modules or module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp; Hard cold start, long cranking in frost; Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only; Usually no symptoms when warm. title: P06FE – Cold Start Diesel Intake Air Flow Control Performance
text: P06FE: Cold Start Diesel Intake Air Flow Control Performance. 'Diesel intake air flow control' is the diesel's electric intake throttle with position sensor (P02E0 ff). During cold start many diesels close it partly: the extra load raises exhaust temperature so the catalysts light off sooner. CARB requires such cold start elements to be monitored, with their own codes separate from normal operation. P06FE means the throttle does not reach its target position while the cold start strategy is active – it is not the intake air heater. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06FE: GM's 2025 diesels run this check under P2957 (deviation above 16 % or 10 %, two trips), Ford's 2023 diesels under P02E4 in cold start mode. Cold start emissions rise; driveability usually stays normal. Common causes: Intake throttle coked with soot and oil (EGR, crankcase ventilation) (high likelihood); Throttle motor or gear stiff, position sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Ice or condensate in the intake in frost (low likelihood); Contact resistance in connector or wiring, low voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, usually after two trips; Hardly any change in driveability; Possibly more smoke or smell while warming up; Further throttle codes (P02E1/P02E4/P02E5) possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0700 – Transmission Control System (MIL Request)
text: P0700: Transmission Control System (MIL Request). P0700 is a notice code: the separate transmission control module has stored an emission-related fault of its own and asks the engine module to switch on the check engine light. The actual fault – a sensor, solenoid, ratio or speed sensor code – is stored in the transmission module and must be read with a tool that can address it; simple OBD readers often show only P0700. GM's engine module reads the request message from 3 s after start; Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) light the MIL at once and clear it after three fault-free cycles. Ford's engine modules with integrated transmission control do not use P0700. Any limp mode comes from the transmission fault, not from P0700. Common causes: Actual fault stored in the transmission module (sensor, solenoid, ratio, speed sensor) (high likelihood); Wrong transmission fluid level or condition causing slip or ratio codes (medium likelihood); Harness or connector at the transmission corroded or damaged (medium likelihood); Low system voltage or weak battery (low likelihood); Transmission module or software faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, possibly transmission warning; Depending on the transmission fault: limp mode, harsh or delayed shifts; Often no symptoms if the fault was intermittent; Simple OBD reader shows only P0700. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0701 – Transmission Control System Range/Performance
text: P0701: Transmission Control System Range/Performance. P0701 means the transmission control system works outside its expected range or its function is implausible – without a circuit fault. What exactly is checked is up to the manufacturer; no GM, Ford, Saab or bulletin document available to us describes the strategy. The only manufacturer evidence is Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks, where P0701 is stored without the check engine light. Typically the control cannot plausibly achieve the requested gear, pressure or torque, and the transmission goes into limp mode. Individual components have their own codes (P0705 ff range sensor, P0715 ff speed sensors, P0750 ff solenoids). Common causes: Transmission control faulty internally or software (medium likelihood); Implausible input signals (speed or range sensor) without own circuit fault (medium likelihood); Wrong fluid level or quality – hydraulics do not respond (medium likelihood); Harness or connector with contact resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning (at Ford no check engine light); Limp mode with fixed gear or missing gears; Harsh or irregular shifts. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0702 – Transmission Control System Electrical
text: P0702: Transmission Control System Electrical. P0702 reports an electrical fault in the transmission control system as a whole – typically the supply of the transmission actuators (solenoid supply, transmission relay, supply switch in the module) or a circuit fault not assigned to a single component. No manufacturer document available to us describes it in detail; Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks stores it without the check engine light. If the solenoid supply is lost, transmissions usually fall back to a hydraulic limp gear. Individual solenoids have their own codes (P0750 ff); actuator supply is P0657 ff. Common causes: Transmission actuator supply interrupted (fuse, relay, ground) (high likelihood); Harness or connector at transmission or module damaged, corroded or oil-soaked (medium likelihood); Transmission module output stage or supply switch faulty (medium likelihood); Low or fluctuating system voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission limp mode with fixed gear; Transmission warning; check engine light depending on the maker; No or harsh shifts, further solenoid codes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0703 – Brake Switch B Circuit
text: P0703: Brake Switch B Circuit. Brake switch A is usually the brake light switch, B a second, redundant contact or signal used to cancel cruise control, release the converter clutch, check 'brake before throttle' and for stop-start. Since about 2014 GM receives it as a CAN message from the body module and checks its integrity (rolling counter, protection value: 3 of 10 faulty in 2014, 9 of 17 in 2025) without the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) check the circuit electrically during stops and starts and light the MIL after two trips. An NHTSA investigation of Hyundai and Kia brake light switches lists P0703 with a brake light that stays on. Brake switch A codes are P0571–P0573, disagreement between A and B is P0504. Common causes: Brake light or double switch worn, corroded or misadjusted (high likelihood); Wiring or connector at the pedal damaged, fuse blown (medium likelihood); CAN message from the body module disturbed (GM: software, bus fault) (medium likelihood); Aftermarket LED lamps or trailer module distorting the circuit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control cannot be engaged or drops out; Brake light stays on or does not work; Selector cannot be moved out of P (shift lock); Check engine light depending on the maker. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0704 – Clutch Switch Input Circuit
text: P0704: Clutch Switch Input Circuit. Only on cars with a clutch pedal: the clutch switch tells the engine module that the clutch is depressed, used to cancel cruise control, smooth load changes when shifting and for stop-start. The check is a plausibility test over driving events rather than a voltage check: Saab's Trionic T8 expects a change of state every time the car pulls away from 3 to 50 km/h (four misses in a row), the EDC16 diesel at gear changes (25 in a row, above 35 km/h and 1500 rpm), and Ford compares its two clutch switches continuously. None of them lights the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Separate clutch pedal switch codes are P0830–P0835. Common causes: Clutch switch faulty or misadjusted (does not switch or too late) (high likelihood); Connector or wiring at the pedal box damaged or corroded (medium likelihood); Floor mat or pedal stop shifted, switch bracket broken (medium likelihood); Driving style (pulling away or shifting without fully depressing the clutch) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control not working or not cancelling when declutching; Jerks or rev hang when shifting; Stop-start inactive; Usually no check engine light. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0705 – Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit (PRNDL Input)
text: P0705: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit (PRNDL Input). The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0705 is the circuit or pattern fault: the module receives a combination that matches no valid position. Ford flags an invalid pattern after 5 s (digital sensor) or 200 ms (4-bit sensor), checking continuously with the check engine light; Saab's 9-5 (9600) detects an impossible combination of its four contacts and goes into limp mode with the gearbox warning. The transmission no longer knows the range reliably – limp mode, start interlock or reversing light may be affected. Check the harness for shorts to ground before replacing the sensor. Common causes: Range sensor worn, dirty or with oil or water ingress (high likelihood); Sensor misadjusted or selector cable out of adjustment (medium likelihood); Harness or connector at the transmission damaged, short to ground (medium likelihood); Transmission or engine module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp; Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts; Starting problems in P/N or start interlock; Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0706 – Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0706: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0706 means the signal is present but implausible. Ford uses it per transmission: for its PWM sensor when the frequency leaves 100–175 Hz (nominal 125 Hz), for the 6F digital sensor when it stays in the transition zone between two positions. Saab's 9-5 (9650), whose sensor sits in the transmission module, flags a sum of the two opposing channels more than 0.29 V away from 5 V, with the lamp in the first trip; adaptations are frozen, the gearbox holds 2nd gear in D and the engine may not restart after switch-off. Common causes: Range sensor or transmission module with integrated sensor faulty (high likelihood); Selector cable or sensor misadjusted (position between two ranges) (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in sensor supply or ground (medium likelihood); Moisture or oil in harness or connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp; Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts; Starting problems in P/N or start interlock; Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0707 – Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0707: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Low. The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0707 means the sensor A signal is too low – usually a short to ground or lost supply. 'Low' refers to the signal, not to a gear. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing at the transmission case) (high likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); Sensor supply missing (5 V reference, fuse) (medium likelihood); Connector corroded or oil in the connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp; Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts; Starting problems in P/N or start interlock; Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working. title: P0708 – Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0708: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit High. title: P0709 – Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0709: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0709 means the sensor A signal jumps briefly to invalid values or drops out without being permanently low or high. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0709 – Ford catches short invalid states under P0705 and P0706 instead – so the description follows the sibling codes. Sliding contacts in older selector switches are a typical source; the transmission may briefly lose the range and go into limp mode. Common causes: Loose contact or corrosion in the range sensor connector (high likelihood); Worn sliding contacts in the selector switch (medium likelihood); Harness chafing on transmission or bracket, breaking when moved (medium likelihood); Misadjusted sensor or selector cable (position at the limit) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent transmission warning or check engine light; Gear indication flickers, brief shift jolts; Occasional starting problems in P/N; Occasional limp mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P070A – Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit
text: P070A: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit. Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070A is the general circuit fault of this sensor (open or fault in the signal circuit). Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is not a P070A fault. Range, low, high and intermittent are P070B–P070E; fluid temperature has its own codes (P0710 ff). Common causes: Fluid level sensor faulty (high likelihood); Wire or connector to the sensor (often through the sump or transmission connector) open or oil-soaked (medium likelihood); Transmission module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning or 'check fluid level' message; Fluid level display missing; Usually no driveability problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P070B – Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P070B: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070B means the signal is present but implausible – it does not change, does not fit temperature or operating state, or lies outside the physically possible range. Such checks only make sense within the valid measuring window. A truly wrong oil level (overfilled, underfilled) or the wrong fluid can also appear as an implausible signal. The circuit fault is P070A. Common causes: Fluid level sensor drifting or dirty (wear debris, sludge) (high likelihood); Fluid level actually wrong (over- or underfilled) or wrong fluid (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in connector or wire (medium likelihood); Faulty tilt or temperature compensation (fluid temperature sensor fault) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning or message about transmission fluid level; Fluid level display implausible or unavailable; Usually no driveability problems. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P070C – Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Low
text: P070C: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Low. Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070C means the sensor signal is below its lower limit – typically the signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor shorted internally. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is P070F. Common causes: Signal wire to the level sensor shorted to ground (chafing, transmission connector) (high likelihood); Level sensor faulty internally (medium likelihood); Transmission connector soaked in oil or corroded (medium likelihood); Module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Fluid level display missing or warning to check transmission fluid; Usually no driveability problems; Transmission warning lamp depending on manufacturer. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P070E – Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P070E: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070E means the level signal drops out briefly or jumps unrealistically – usually a loose contact or a wire breaking under movement. Sloshing and tilt also make readings vary, which is why valid measurements need the vehicle at rest. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. Common causes: Loose contact in transmission connector or harness (high likelihood); Sensor with internal contact fault (medium likelihood); Contaminated or foaming fluid at the sensor (low likelihood). title: P070F – Transmission Fluid Level Too Low
text: P070F: Transmission Fluid Level Too Low. P070F is not a circuit fault but a condition: a working fluid level sensor reports a level below the target band. In the Allison patent the module compares the measured height in millimetres with a tilt-dependent band and reports at least a quart too little or too much – only with the vehicle at rest, fluid above about 30–40 °C and low input speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. Take it seriously: real fluid loss leads to slipping, overheating (P0218) and ratio errors. Leaks at the pan gasket, seals or cooler lines and wrong filling after service are the usual causes. Common causes: Leak (pan gasket, shaft seals, cooler lines) (high likelihood); Underfilled after fluid change or repair (medium likelihood); Level sensor reading wrong (drift) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning: transmission fluid level low; Slipping gears, delayed engagement; Transmission overheating; Oil spots under the vehicle. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0710 – Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0710: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit. The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0710 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not separate low and high. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag 0.1 V or less or 4.7 V or more, light the MIL after two consecutive trips and use 80 °C as substitute. Ford's 2023 diesels use P0710 alongside P0712/P0713 for open and short circuits, without MIL, after 5–12 s, substituting coolant temperature. GM uses only the split codes. With the substitute value the shift quality suffers: harsh shifts and a late converter clutch. Common causes: Fluid temperature sensor faulty (often part of the internal harness or valve body) (high likelihood); Transmission connector leaking or corroded, oil in the connector (medium likelihood); Wire open or shorted (medium likelihood); Transmission or engine module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh or late shifts; Torque converter clutch applies late or not at all; Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer; Implausible fluid temperature in the scan tool. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0711 – Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0711: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. P0711 means the fluid temperature signal is electrically valid but implausible. Manufacturers check three things: the fluid does not warm up as expected (GM 2025 still below 15 °C after the calibrated warm-up time, Saab's AF40 below 20 °C after 10 minutes of driving), the value is stuck (Ford: within ±2 °F for about 2.5 minutes below 70 or above 225 °F), or it jumps unrealistically. GM's 6T70 compares it with the module's internal temperature. The MIL rating varies: GM's newer modules after two trips, Saab AF40 none, Ford none; a 2013 Ram 6.7 bulletin moved P0711–P0714 from one to two trips. A substitute value then limits adaption and converter clutch control. Common causes: Fluid temperature sensor drifting or stuck (high likelihood); High contact resistance in connector or harness (oil, corrosion) (medium likelihood); Very cold weather or short trips (fluid does not reach warm-up threshold) (medium likelihood); Outdated module software (low likelihood); Fluid cooler thermostat faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh or late shifts; Torque converter clutch applies late or not at all; Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer; Implausible fluid temperature in the scan tool. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0712 – Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0712: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low. The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0712 means the signal is too low – the sensor reads extremely hot, or the signal wire is shorted to ground. GM's 2025 transmission modules flag below 13.5 Ω for 5 of 6 s after two trips; the 2018 LT4 engine module below 17.88 Ω (over 150 °C) without MIL; the 2007 Allison 1000 150 °C or more for 2.5 s; Saab's AF40 over 200 °C; Ford below 0.05 V for 5–12 s without MIL. The module substitutes a value (coolant temperature, 80 °C or a hot mode) and may shift with hot-fluid strategy. Real overheating with a good sensor is P0218. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (internal harness, chafing) (high likelihood); Sensor shorted internally (medium likelihood); Transmission actually severely overheated (low likelihood); Control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission in hot mode (early converter clutch, changed shift points); Harsh shifts; Extremely high fluid temperature shown; Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer. title: P0713 – Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0713: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit High. The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. title: P0714 – Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0714: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0714 means the signal drops out or jumps briefly – not long enough for P0712 or P0713. Ford's 2012 6R80 transmission names P0714 among its fluid temperature checks for open, short and in-range faults. A loose contact in the transmission connector or a chafing internal harness is the usual cause. title: P0715 – Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit
text: P0715: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit. The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0715 is the general circuit code. Ford uses it for 'no signal' too: the vehicle is moving under power (engine above converter stall speed, output speed plausible) but the sensor reports under 200 rpm for 5–30 s; Ford's DPS6 dual-clutch sets it for a hardware-detected fault of input shaft sensor 1. Subaru-based systems flag an open or shorted circuit, Saab's Aisin box no input signal while the output sensor works, substituting output speed. GM does not use P0715. Limp mode, harsh shifts and a disabled converter clutch follow. Common causes: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted) (high likelihood); Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector) (high likelihood); Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel (medium likelihood); Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp; Limp mode with fixed gear, harsh shifts; Torque converter clutch does not apply; Input speed shows 0 or implausible in the scan tool. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0716 – Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0716: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0716 means a signal is present but implausible: too high, or dropping suddenly without recovering. GM's 2025 modules count drops of more than 650 rpm between 25 ms samples and fail after more than three; the 6T70 in the Saab 9-4X flags a 1350 rpm drop for 1 s; the 2007 Allison 1000 also detects noise and swapped sensor wires; all after one trip. Ford's 6R80 flags turbine speed above 7700 rpm. The 6T70 then runs only reverse and fifth gear, with maximum line pressure and no converter clutch. Common causes: Loose contact or chafing in the sensor circuit (high likelihood); Sensor faulty, wrong air gap or metal debris (medium likelihood); Reluctor wheel or clutch drum damaged (medium likelihood); Sensor wires swapped after repair or interference (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp; Limp mode with fixed gear (6T70: reverse and fifth only); Harsh or delayed shifts; Torque converter clutch locked out. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0717 – Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit No Signal
text: P0717: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit No Signal. The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0717 means there is practically no input speed signal although the vehicle is driving under power. GM's 2025 modules flag under 200 rpm for more than 4 s with torque applied, the 6T70 under 50 rpm for 5 s, the Allison 1000 under 61 rpm with output above 500 rpm; Ford under 200 rpm for 5–30 s; all after one trip. GM calls it 'circuit low voltage', but means missing frequency. On GM's 10-speed both input and output sensors share a supply – P0717 together with P0722 points to that supply rather than two sensors. Common causes: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted) (high likelihood); Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector) (high likelihood); Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel (medium likelihood); Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp; Limp mode with fixed gear, harsh shifts; Torque converter clutch does not apply; Input speed shows 0 or implausible in the scan tool. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0718 – Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0718: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0718 means the signal is present but jumps or drops out briefly. Ford's petrol modules from 2012 to 2023 count 200 turbine speed spikes above 400 rpm with at most 1.5 s between them in a forward gear. GM's Honda-built five-speed of 2006 flags jumps of more than 3 mph per 10 ms three times in 500 ms, after two trips; GM's own transmissions file such jumps under P0716 instead. Loose contacts and electrical interference are the usual causes; shifts become erratic and limp mode may follow at times. Common causes: Loose contact, corroded connector or chafing (high likelihood); Electrical interference (shielding, ground, added consumers) (medium likelihood); Metal debris on the sensor or loose mounting (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty internally (temperature-dependent) (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Occasional harsh or unexpected shifts; Warning lamp; Converter clutch applies and releases unevenly; Limp mode at times. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0719 – Brake Switch B Circuit Low
text: P0719: Brake Switch B Circuit Low. Brake switch B is the brake signal to the transmission module or a second brake switch channel, used to release the converter clutch, adapt shift strategy on grades and cancel cruise control. Low and high describe the signal voltage, and what that means depends on polarity: GM's converter clutch brake switch is closed at rest (12 V), while Saab's Trionic 8 sees 12 V when braking. Detection is always a plausibility check against driving: the brake reads applied during accelerations or never applied during decelerations. P0719 means the signal stays low. For GM that reads as brake applied: 2006 transmission modules flag it after eight accelerations without the brake releasing, without MIL. Saab's Trionic 8 flags the brake light signal not changing during four decelerations from 40 to 3 km/h and disables cruise control. The opposite is P0724. Common causes: Brake light switch faulty or misadjusted (high likelihood); Wire to the module open (GM) or shorted to ground (Saab T8) (medium likelihood); Connector at the pedal box corroded (medium likelihood); Brake light circuit fuse blown (low likelihood). Symptoms: Cruise control cannot be activated or switches off; Unusual shifting, converter clutch behaviour changed; No downshift on uphill grades (Subaru); Brake lights stay off or on. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P071A – Transmission Mode Switch A Circuit
text: P071A: Transmission Mode Switch A Circuit. A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071A is the general circuit fault of mode switch A: its state is invalid or implausible. The transmission then usually stays on its normal schedule. Low and high are P071B/P071C, switch B has P071D–P071F; the range sensor (PRNDL) is P0705 ff. Common causes: Mode switch A faulty (selector lever or console) (high likelihood); Wiring or connector in the console damaged (spilled drinks, chafing) (medium likelihood); Resistor coding drifted (analog buttons) (low likelihood); Control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Mode A cannot be selected or stays active; Mode indicator missing or flashing; Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule. Repair difficulty: easy.
