title: P0720 – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit
text: P0720: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit. The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0720 is the general circuit code. Ford also uses it for 'no signal': while engine and turbine speed show the vehicle moving, the sensor reports under 100–200 rpm for 5–30 s; ZF's 6HP26 in Ford vehicles flags an open or short after 0.6 s. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag an impossible 255 km/h or 0 km/h while driving and light the MIL after two trips, substituting the other sensor. GM does not use P0720 but P0722. Speedometer and cruise control may fail, often with a vehicle speed code as well. Common causes: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted) (high likelihood); Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector) (high likelihood); Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel (medium likelihood); Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Speedometer drops out or jumps; Warning lamp, limp mode or fixed gear; Harsh shifts, cruise control not working. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0721 – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0721: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0721 means the output speed is present but implausible: too high (Ford 6R80 above 7450 rpm), not matching wheel or input speed in the engaged gear (ZF 6HP26 more than 200 or 250 rpm apart, Ford's F21 more than 15 % for 10 s), or jumping (Allison 1000: 500 rpm within 0.15 s). On GM's 10-speed with a direction-sensing sensor, P0721 means the reported direction of rotation does not fit – since 2025 after two trips, earlier after one. Wrong tyre sizes or a faulty wheel speed sensor can also falsify the comparison. Common causes: Output speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris) (high likelihood); Contact problems or interference in the sensor circuit (medium likelihood); Wrong tyre size or axle ratio, faulty wheel speed sensor (medium likelihood); Reluctor wheel damaged or sensor mounted wrongly (low likelihood). Symptoms: Speedometer jumps; Warning lamp; Wrong shifts, limp mode; ABS/ESP warning possible if wheel speed is affected. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0722 – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit No Signal
text: P0722: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit No Signal. The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0722 means the output speed signal is missing while the vehicle is driving. title: P0723 – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0723: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Intermittent. The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0723 means the output speed drops or jumps briefly. GM's 2006 tables flag road speed falling below 61 rpm while driving; the 2019–2025 modules count sudden drops (for example 700 rpm) and fail after more than five, after one trip. In Ford vehicles the ZF 6HP26 flags a drop of more than 1000 rpm with the converter clutch locked, the CFT30 more than 6000 rpm per second. title: P0725 – Engine Speed Input Circuit
text: P0725: Engine Speed Input Circuit. The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0725 is the general fault of this input; with CAN it means the engine module marks its speed value as invalid. Saab's Aisin transmissions and a 2006 GM table set it after about 4 s, the GM table with immediate MIL. A Saab bulletin notes that behind P0725 there is always a crankshaft or camshaft sensor code in the engine module (P0016, P0335–P0339) – so read the engine module first. Limp mode follows; a completely missing CAN message is U0100. Common causes: Crankshaft or camshaft sensor fault in the engine module (speed invalid there) (high likelihood); CAN fault between engine and transmission module (wiring, termination, connector) (medium likelihood); Engine module software or fault (low likelihood); Transmission module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning lamp, possibly check engine light; Torque converter clutch locked out; Harsh shifts or limp mode; Often an engine code (crankshaft sensor) as well. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0729 – Gear 6 Incorrect Ratio
text: P0729: Gear 6 Incorrect Ratio. The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0729 concerns sixth gear. Saab's Aisin six-speed also checks whether the actual ratio matches fourth or fifth – the sixth gear clutch is not holding and the box drops into another gear. Ford stores it only if the fault does not fit a particular solenoid (otherwise P0751 ff). On GM manual transmissions (LT4) it checks the gear position sensor instead. Common causes: Fluid level too low or fluid worn or contaminated (high likelihood); Clutch for sixth gear worn (linings, piston seal) (high likelihood); Sticking shift or pressure valve, leaking valve body gasket, blocked passages (medium likelihood); GM manual transmissions only: gear position sensor faulty or not learned (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Slipping or flare in sixth gear, engine speed higher than expected; Harsh or delayed shifts; Limp mode (Aisin: second gear and reverse only), transmission warning; Check engine light depending on manufacturer. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P072A – Stuck in Neutral
text: P072A: Stuck in Neutral. Ford's DPS6 dry dual-clutch transmission moves its gears with two electrically driven shift drums whose position is read by Hall sensors: drum A shifts 1st, 3rd and 5th, drum B reverse, 2nd, 4th and 6th. Ford's 2012 summary lists 'stuck in gear' codes for each drum: the module commands the drum out of a gear, but the gear stays engaged. It gives no thresholds or MIL rating. P072A means the transmission stays in neutral although a gear is commanded – no drive. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the DPS6 reports drum position faults under its own codes. On dual-clutch or automated manuals a drum or fork would fail to engage a gear, on planetary automatics clutch pressure would be missing. The opposite is P073D. Common causes: Shift fork or synchronizer for this gear sticking (medium likelihood); Shift drum A motor, Hall position sensing or driver faulty (medium likelihood); Transmission module (low likelihood); On planetary automatics: clutch or brake not releasing (sticking valve) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission stays in one gear, no further shifts; Limp mode, transmission warning; Clunking or blocking when shifting. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0730 – Incorrect Gear Ratio
text: P0730: Incorrect Gear Ratio. P0730 reports a wrong transmission ratio without assigning it to a gear. Two uses are documented. Older Aisin-type automatics (a 2006 GM table, Saab's 9-5 of 2002) set it when fourth or fifth gear shows the ratio of third – a shift solenoid (Saab: S3) is not switching; GM lights the MIL at once, Saab enters limp mode. GM's continuously variable transmissions of 2023 and 2025 use it when the pulleys do not reach the commanded variator ratio – the belt or chain slips or clamping pressure is too low – after one trip. Ford and newer GM step automatics use gear-specific or clutch valve codes instead. Check fluid level and condition first. Common causes: Fluid level or quality (CVT fluid or ATF) (high likelihood); Shift solenoid or pressure control valve sticking or faulty (high likelihood); Clutch or brake wear, or worn variator belt, chain or pulleys (medium likelihood); Faulty speed sensor signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Slipping, engine speed rises without drive; Wrong gear or missing upper gears, limp mode; Check engine light (GM) or transmission warning; CVT: judder, weak acceleration. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0731 – Gear 1 Incorrect Ratio
text: P0731: Gear 1 Incorrect Ratio. The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0731 concerns first gear. A 2006 GM table uses a tighter 4 % limit here and caps output speed at 1260 rpm; Saab's 2002 9-5 flags 3 % with the brake released. With a one-way clutch in first, slip shows as slipping when pulling away. On GM manual transmissions it checks the gear position sensor instead. Common causes: Fluid level too low or fluid worn or contaminated (high likelihood); Clutch or brake for first gear worn (linings, piston seal) (high likelihood); Sticking shift or pressure valve, leaking valve body gasket, blocked passages (medium likelihood); GM manual transmissions only: gear position sensor faulty or not learned (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Slipping or flare in first gear, engine speed higher than expected; Harsh or delayed shifts; Limp mode (Aisin: second gear and reverse only), transmission warning; Check engine light depending on manufacturer. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0736 – Reverse Incorrect Ratio
text: P0736: Reverse Incorrect Ratio. title: P0737 – TCM Engine Speed Output Circuit
text: P0737: TCM Engine Speed Output Circuit. Some transmission modules pass an engine speed signal on to other devices such as a tachometer over a wire of their own. CARB requires output circuits to be checked. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0737–P0739 – engine speed is shared over CAN today; the description follows CARB and the engine module's own speed output (P0654), which sends, for example, two pulses per revolution. P0737 is the general circuit fault of this output; low and high are P0738/P0739. Not to be confused with the engine speed input at the transmission module (P0725 ff). A tachometer or dependent display then reads wrong or nothing, while driving is usually unaffected. Common causes: Wire to the receiver open or shorted (high likelihood); Receiver (e.g. instrument cluster) shorted internally (medium likelihood); Connector corroded (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the transmission module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Tachometer or dependent display not working or wrong; Warning lamp depending on manufacturer; Usually no effect on driving. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P073A – Stuck in Gear 5
text: P073A: Stuck in Gear 5. Ford's DPS6 dry dual-clutch transmission moves its gears with two electrically driven shift drums whose position is read by Hall sensors: drum A shifts 1st, 3rd and 5th, drum B reverse, 2nd, 4th and 6th. title: P073D – Unable to Engage Neutral
text: P073D: Unable to Engage Neutral. P073D means neutral is commanded but not reached or not held. GM uses it on vehicles with electronic gear selection (shift-by-wire, e.g. Cadillac XT4): the selector or engine module compares commanded and actual range from the range sensor and flags it after 1.8–2 s in the selector module or 10 s in the engine module, after two trips. For Ford's 6F35 the supplier Sonnax describes a mechanical cause: a forward or direct clutch dragging in neutral, visible as turbine speed staying only 200–400 rpm below engine speed. The car may creep in N; range changes may be locked. The opposite, stuck in neutral, is P072A. Common causes: Ford 6F35: forward or direct clutch dragging (balance piston, plates, seal) (high likelihood); Shift-by-wire: range actuator or park module, range sensor or its calibration (medium likelihood); Valve body (manual valve, missing check ball, sticking solenoid) (medium likelihood); CAN communication or control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle creeps in N or engine is loaded when shifting to N; N selection not accepted, warning message; Harsh engagement N to D/R (6F35); Check engine light after two trips (GM). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P073E – Unable to Engage Reverse
text: P073E: Unable to Engage Reverse. P073E means reverse is commanded but not reached. Two uses are documented. With electronic gear selection (shift-by-wire) GM compares the commanded range with the actual range reported by the transmission and flags it if reverse is not reached within 1.8–3 s in the selector or diesel engine module, or 10 s in petrol engine modules, after two trips; GM bulletins name a range actuator centred wrongly (LaCrosse, XT5) and software after an over-the-air update (2025 Equinox/Terrain). On dual-clutch transmissions (2020–23 Corvette, Maserati MC20) it means the reverse gear cannot be engaged. Stuck in reverse is P072B, slip in reverse P0736. Common causes: Range actuator or park module centred wrongly or faulty (shift-by-wire) (high likelihood); Module software (e.g. after an over-the-air update) (medium likelihood); Range sensor reports the wrong actual range (medium likelihood); Reverse clutch or brake, valve or shift fork (DCT) (medium likelihood); Fluid level or system pressure (low likelihood). Symptoms: No reverse, or R not accepted; Transmission warning, check engine light after two trips (GM); Display shows R but the vehicle does not reverse. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P073F – Unable to Engage Gear 1
text: P073F: Unable to Engage Gear 1. 'Unable to engage' means the transmission does not reach the commanded gear – the opposite of 'stuck in gear', where a gear cannot be disengaged. Documented users are dual-clutch transmissions, whose shift forks are moved hydraulically and watched by travel sensors: GM's 8-speed in the 2020–23 Corvette, Maserati's MC20 and – for the odd gears only – Acura's RLX Sport Hybrid, whose 'odd gear monitor' is part of an emission recall with permanent codes. No manufacturer publishes thresholds. P073F means the first gear, on the odd sub-gearbox, cannot be engaged; a gear that will not disengage is P072C, slip in an engaged gear P0731. GM's bulletin first runs a learn procedure and cleans valves only if system pressure codes are present; Maserati checks system pressure (20–30 bar). If neither helps, the mechanics are at fault. Common causes: Shift fork valve or solenoid in the mechatronic unit sticking (dirt, wear) (high likelihood); System pressure unstable or too low (pressure valve, pump, fluid level) (medium likelihood); Shift fork, sleeve, synchronizer or dogs damaged (medium likelihood); Learned shift fork or clutch values lost or wrong (medium likelihood); Module software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Gear 1 skipped or not engaged; Transmission warning or check engine light, possibly limp mode with one sub-gearbox locked out; Jerking, delayed pulling away or shifting. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0740 – Torque Converter Clutch Circuit/Open
text: P0740: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit/Open. The torque converter clutch (lock-up) connects pump and turbine mechanically; a solenoid – on/off, pulse-width modulated or proportional – moves a control valve in the valve body. Slip is engine speed minus turbine speed. Manufacturers do not use P0740–P0744 uniformly: Ford uses P0740 for open, P0742 for short to ground and P0744 for short to power, and reports stuck on as P2758. P0740 concerns the control circuit of the converter clutch solenoid. Ford flags an open circuit when the driver feedback line disagrees with the command for 0.5–5 s, with MIL; a 2006 GM table checks 0/12 V with more than 43 of 50 failed counts after two trips – newer GM units use P2761/P2763/P2764. FCA's Ram 6.7 reads P0740 as converter slip out of range and moved it to two trips by software in 2013. The clutch is then switched off: higher engine speed when cruising, more fuel, hotter fluid. Common causes: Open or corroded harness or transmission pass-through connector (high likelihood); Converter clutch solenoid coil open (medium likelihood); Internal transmission harness or mechatronic unit (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the module faulty (low likelihood); FCA: actual converter slip (clutch wear, fluid) or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or transmission warning; No lock-up: engine speed about 100–300 rpm higher when cruising; Higher fuel consumption, hotter transmission fluid. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0741 – Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
text: P0741: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Performance/Stuck Off. P0741 means the converter clutch does not lock although commanded – slip stays too high while the circuit is electrically fine. Thresholds: GM's T43 at least 130 rpm for 5 s twice, the 6T70 50 rpm for 5 s three times, Saab's Aisin AF40 over 100 rpm for 2 s, all after two trips; Ford over 100–200 rpm or a speed ratio below 0.93 over five lock-up events; Subaru engine speed more than 9/8 of target for 10.2 s. The module then locks out the clutch, sometimes the top gear, and uses a hot-mode shift pattern. Low or burnt fluid, a worn control valve in the valve body and a glazed converter clutch are the usual causes; Hyundai's 8-speed bulletin calls for a new converter. Common causes: Fluid level too low, old or burnt fluid (high likelihood); Converter clutch control valve worn or sticking, bore worn (high likelihood); Lock-up clutch in the converter worn or glazed (medium likelihood); Solenoid mechanically sluggish (electrically fine) (medium likelihood); Leaking turbine shaft seals or pump (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or transmission warning; Higher engine speed when cruising, 'rubber band' feel; Higher consumption, rising fluid temperature; Possibly shudder when the clutch applies. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0742 – Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Stuck On
text: P0742: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Stuck On. P0742 means the converter clutch stays applied although commanded off – there is almost no slip. GM's T43 flags −50 to +13 rpm for 1.5 s six times and the 6T70 −20 to +30 rpm for 2.5 s, both after one trip; Allison and Saab's Aisin AF40 after two trips, the AF40 also when the engine stalls without slip. Typical is the engine stalling when stopping or when selecting D or R, plus jerking at low speed. Note the different uses: Ford's P0742 is a short to ground in the clutch solenoid circuit (stuck on is P2758 there), and Saab's 9-3 of 2003 uses it for a mechanical lock-up fault. Common causes: Converter clutch control valve sticking in the applied position (high likelihood); Solenoid stuck open (or short to ground with low-side control) (medium likelihood); Lock-up clutch seized in the converter (medium likelihood); Wrong fluid level or contaminated fluid (medium likelihood); Engine or turbine speed signal implausible (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine stalls when stopping or selecting D/R; Jerking or bucking at low speed; Check engine light or transmission warning. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0745 – Pressure Control Solenoid A
text: P0745: Pressure Control Solenoid A. Pressure control solenoid A sets line or clutch pressure by current; most are 'normally high', so with no current – as in limp mode – maximum pressure applies. 'A' is usually the line pressure valve, on GM clutch-to-clutch transmissions (6T, 8L, 9T) the pressure valve of clutch 1. Ford does not use P0745–P0749 but P0960–P0963. P0745 is the general code for this valve; the sub-codes P0746–P0749 follow. It is documented on Mitsubishi CVTs as a current plausibility check: at most 400 mA while 750 mA or more is commanded for 5 s, or 1.34 A or more for 1 s. A failure usually leaves the valve unpowered, so pressure goes to maximum: harsh shifts and, depending on the transmission, limp mode in a fixed gear. Common causes: Pressure control solenoid (coil) faulty (high likelihood); Transmission harness or connector (high likelihood); Contaminated fluid, valve sluggish (medium likelihood); Transmission module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh shifts or engagement (maximum pressure); Limp mode in a fixed gear; Transmission warning or check engine light. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P074A – Unable to Engage Gear 2
text: P074A: Unable to Engage Gear 2. 'Unable to engage' means the transmission does not reach the commanded gear – the opposite of 'stuck in gear', where a gear cannot be disengaged. Documented users are dual-clutch transmissions, whose shift forks are moved hydraulically and watched by travel sensors: GM's 8-speed in the 2020–23 Corvette, Maserati's MC20 and – for the odd gears only – Acura's RLX Sport Hybrid, whose 'odd gear monitor' is part of an emission recall with permanent codes. No manufacturer publishes thresholds. P074A means the second gear, on the even sub-gearbox, cannot be engaged; a gear that will not disengage is P072D, slip in an engaged gear P0732. GM's bulletin first runs a learn procedure and cleans valves only if system pressure codes are present; Maserati checks system pressure (20–30 bar). If neither helps, the mechanics are at fault. Common causes: Shift fork valve or solenoid in the mechatronic unit sticking (dirt, wear) (high likelihood); System pressure unstable or too low (pressure valve, pump, fluid level) (medium likelihood); Shift fork, sleeve, synchronizer or dogs damaged (medium likelihood); Learned shift fork or clutch values lost or wrong (medium likelihood); Module software or calibration (low likelihood). Symptoms: Gear 2 skipped or not engaged; Transmission warning or check engine light, possibly limp mode with one sub-gearbox locked out; Jerking, delayed pulling away or shifting. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0750 – Shift Solenoid A
text: P0750: Shift Solenoid A. A shift solenoid is an electrically switched valve in the valve body. Manufacturers use these codes differently: Ford reports an open circuit with the base code and shorts separately, newer GM units have separate low/high codes, and the letter is not tied to a valve number (Saab's 9-5: A = valve S2). P0750 is the general code for solenoid A and is used in practice for an open circuit: Ford's step automatics (2012–2023) set it when the smart driver feedback disagrees with the command for 0.5–5 s, with shorts to ground and power as P0973/P0974; Ram's 6.7 L with Aisin transmission calls it 'control circuit open', and a 2023 bulletin traces it to a leaking capacitor in the engine module. GM does not use P0750. With the solenoid unpowered the transmission falls back to a hydraulic default gear with maximum pressure. Common causes: Open or corroded wire or transmission pass-through connector (high likelihood); Solenoid coil open or shorted (medium likelihood); Internal harness or electronic module in the transmission (medium likelihood); Module driver faulty or valve supply missing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning lamp; Limp mode in a fixed gear, no upshifts; Harsh shifts from maximum line pressure. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0751 – Shift Solenoid A Performance/Stuck Off
text: P0751: Shift Solenoid A Performance/Stuck Off. A shift solenoid is an electrically switched valve in the valve body; together the solenoid states select the gear, and the module checks the result by gear ratio, slip or a pressure switch – the pattern of wrong gears shows which solenoid hangs off or on. P0751 means solenoid A is commanded on but valve, clutch or gear do not follow. GM's 6T70 flags a ratio of 1.34–1.48 with slip of 400 rpm for 0.3 s eight times and locks out first gear; GM 4-speeds recognise the pattern 2-2-3-3; both after two trips. Allison checks its pressure switch for 5 s after one trip. Ford's 'functionally failed off' covers the whole clutch circuit, and its 10R80 and 8F35 bulletins show purely mechanical causes such as a leaking clutch cylinder. Common causes: Shift spool in the valve body sticking (dirt, debris) (high likelihood); Internal leak or clutch fault in the circuit (medium likelihood); Solenoid mechanically sluggish or screen clogged (medium likelihood); Fluid level or quality wrong (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Gears missing or skipped; Pulling away in the wrong gear, weak acceleration; Limp mode or gear lock-out; Check engine light. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0752 – Shift Solenoid A Stuck On

title: P075A – Shift Solenoid G
text: P075A: Shift Solenoid G. Shift solenoid G only exists on transmissions with seven or more solenoids. Ford's 10R80 and 8F35 use solenoids A–F, GM's 9- and 10-speeds report clutch pressure valve codes, the Allison 1000 uses three; the only documented user of the G block is Hyundai/Genesis' 8-speed, which assigns P075A and P075D to its on/off solenoids. Hyundai's bulletins for the Genesis, Equus and G80/G90 (2012–2018) use P075A for the on/off solenoid 'SS-A' – on the G80/G90 in connection with the park lock – and treat it as a circuit fault: replace valve and electronic module, then load the valve data. That 'SS-A' is Hyundai's own numbering, not solenoid A in the J2012 scheme. Common causes: On/off solenoid faulty (high likelihood); Electronic module or internal harness (medium likelihood); Connector or wiring (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Limp mode or shift problems; With shift-by-wire possibly a park lock fault. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P075F – Transmission Fluid Level Too High
text: P075F: Transmission Fluid Level Too High. P075F is not a circuit fault but a condition: a working fluid level sensor reports a level above the target band – the counterpart of P070F. In the Allison patent the transmission module reports 'too high, drain a quart or more', measuring only with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid and low input speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. Overfilling makes rotating parts churn the fluid, which foams, pressure control becomes unsteady, fluid escapes at the vent and temperature rises; an FCA bulletin traces poor shifting after repairs to overfilling. Automatic transmission fluid level depends strongly on temperature – topping up cold often overfills. Common causes: Overfilled at fluid change or repair (wrong check temperature or procedure) (high likelihood); Level sensor drifting (reads too high) (low likelihood); Measured under poor conditions (slope, cold fluid) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission fluid level warning; Fluid escaping at the transmission vent; Foaming fluid, unsteady or harsh shifts; Transmission overheating. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0760 – Shift Solenoid C
text: P0760: Shift Solenoid C. A shift solenoid is an electrically switched valve in the valve body. title: P0761 – Shift Solenoid C Performance/Stuck Off
text: P0761: Shift Solenoid C Performance/Stuck Off. title: P076F – Gear 7 Incorrect Ratio
text: P076F: Gear 7 Incorrect Ratio. P076F means the ratio in seventh gear is wrong: input speed divided by output speed does not match the commanded gear, so a clutch slips or another gear is engaged. It only exists on transmissions with seven or more gears. Ford's 10-speed 10R80 and 10R140 list it in bulletins together with the other ratio codes and the check engine light – causes include a migrating sleeve on a clutch cylinder causing hydraulic leaks and sticking valve body valves. Ford's ratio check elsewhere flags more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times. On GM's Corvette with seven-speed manual gearbox, P076F is a plausibility check of the gear position sensor instead (ratio window 0.41–0.50), after one trip. Common causes: Hydraulic leak at the seventh gear clutch (Ford 10R80: clutch cylinder sleeve) (high likelihood); Sticking valves in the valve body or solenoid (medium likelihood); Fluid level or condition (medium likelihood); Gear position sensor implausible or not learned (GM manual only) (medium likelihood); Turbine or output speed sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Slipping or flaring engine speed in seventh gear; Harsh or delayed shifts; Check engine light, transmission warning, possibly limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0775 – Pressure Control Solenoid B
text: P0775: Pressure Control Solenoid B. Pressure control solenoids are current-controlled proportional valves, and what B and C mean depends on the design: on GM's clutch-to-clutch automatics they are the pressure valves of clutches 2 and 3, on GM's CVT B is primary pulley pressure and C line pressure, on Jatco CVTs B is the secondary pressure valve, on Saab's AF40 B and C are clutch valves SLC1/SLC2. P0775 is the general code for valve B. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; the trade journal MOTOR names it as a performance code of line pressure valve B on Ford's 5R55, set together with ratio codes after a broken overdrive servo. Sub-codes for performance, stuck on, electrical and intermittent follow (P0776–P0779). Common causes: Valve body or pressure valve B worn or dirty (high likelihood); Line pressure wrong (load signal, main regulator) (medium likelihood); Fluid condition (medium likelihood); Circuit or coil (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh or slipping shifts; Limp mode; Check engine light. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0776 – Pressure Control Solenoid B Performance/Stuck Off
text: P0776: Pressure Control Solenoid B Performance/Stuck Off. title: P0777 – Pressure Control Solenoid B Stuck On
text: P0777: Pressure Control Solenoid B Stuck On. title: P0778 – Pressure Control Solenoid B Electrical
text: P0778: Pressure Control Solenoid B Electrical. title: P077A – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Loss of Direction Signal
text: P077A: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Loss of Direction Signal. Some transmissions use an output shaft speed sensor that also reports direction of rotation: in a GM patent two offset Hall elements send one pulse per tooth whose width encodes forward or reverse. The direction is needed to detect rolling back on a hill (a Hyundai patent raises idle speed then), for hill hold, stop-start and the forward/reverse change. P077A means the sensor still delivers speed pulses but no usable direction information – the pulse width stays outside the direction windows or one Hall element has failed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM checks direction coherence under P0721. Hill hold, auto hold or stop-start may then be disabled and the forward/reverse change runs in a substitute mode. Common causes: Output speed sensor faulty (one Hall element or direction channel failed) (high likelihood); Contact resistance in connector or wiring distorts the pulse (medium likelihood); Wrong replacement sensor without direction function (medium likelihood); Reluctor wheel damaged or air gap too large (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning or check engine light depending on manufacturer; Hill hold, auto hold or stop-start unavailable; Rolling back on a hill not caught. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P077B – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Direction Error
text: P077B: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Direction Error. Some transmissions use an output shaft speed sensor that also reports direction of rotation: in a GM patent two offset Hall elements send one pulse per tooth whose width encodes forward or reverse. The direction is needed to detect rolling back on a hill (a Hyundai patent raises idle speed then), for hill hold, stop-start and the forward/reverse change. P077B means the sensor reports a direction that does not fit – for example reverse while a forward gear is engaged and the input and intermediate shaft sensors confirm forward motion. GM's transmission modules list P077B as a blocking condition for other checks, but run the actual check under their own codes: direction contradicts the gear for 2.5 s above 500 rpm, after one trip. Speed and direction are then unreliable: hill hold and the park and reverse logic fall back to substitute modes. Common causes: Output speed sensor faulty (direction evaluation disturbed) (high likelihood); Wrong or incorrectly fitted sensor (orientation to the wheel) (medium likelihood); Reluctor wheel damaged, metal debris on the sensor (medium likelihood); Faulty reference (input or intermediate shaft sensor) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or transmission warning; Hill hold off; Limp mode possible; Speedometer or cruise control unreliable. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P077C – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Low
text: P077C: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Low. GM's transmission modules from 2019 to 2025 (9- and 10-speeds) also read the active output speed sensor's line voltage as an analog value. P077C means this voltage is below 0.25 V – a short to ground of under about 0.5 Ω between signal and module ground – for more than 0.05 s with the system above 10 V; GM rates it after one trip. GM then blocks the no-signal and ratio checks so that P0722 is not set instead of the actual short. Without output speed the transmission enters limp mode and road speed may be missing. On GM's 10-speed input and output sensors share a supply. Common causes: Signal or supply wire shorted to ground (chafing at the case) (high likelihood); Sensor shorted internally (medium likelihood); Oil or moisture in the connector, corrosion (medium likelihood); Module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light at once (GM); Limp mode or fixed gear; Speedometer or cruise control failed; Harsh shifts, no converter lock-up. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P077D – Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit High
text: P077D: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit High. GM's transmission modules from 2019 to 2025 (9- and 10-speeds) also read the active output speed sensor's line voltage as an analog value. title: P077E – Transmission Fluid Temperature Measurement System Multiple Sensor Correlation
text: P077E: Transmission Fluid Temperature Measurement System Multiple Sensor Correlation. P077E is a plausibility check between several fluid temperature readings – for example sensors A and B, sump and valve body, or the module's internal temperature. If they differ by more than allowed after a settling time, such as a long stop, the code sets, without being able to blame a single sensor. No manufacturer document available to us uses it: GM checks each sensor alone (P0711, with the module temperature on the 6T70), and Ford has no multi-sensor check. A substitute value then limits converter clutch and shift adaption. Common causes: One temperature sensor drifting (aged NTC) (high likelihood); Contact resistance at a sensor connector or wire (medium likelihood); Fluid level too low (sensor not wetted) (low likelihood); Module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning, possibly check engine light; Converter clutch applies late or not at all; Harsh cold shifts. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P077F – Reverse 2 Incorrect Ratio
text: P077F: Reverse 2 Incorrect Ratio. P077F checks the ratio in a second reverse gear: input speed divided by output speed lies outside the tolerance band around the target ratio – a slipping clutch, a wrong gear or a sensor fault. Only transmissions with two reverse ratios need it, such as Mercedes' 7G-Tronic (−3.42 and −2.23, with the second reverse kept in limp mode) and its 5G-Tronic predecessor; GM's 9- and 10-speeds, Ford's 10R and ZF's 8HP have one. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the check works like the other ratio codes such as P0736. Common causes: Slipping clutch or brake in the second reverse power path (high likelihood); Fluid level low or fluid worn (medium likelihood); Solenoid or pressure regulator sticking (medium likelihood); Faulty input or output speed sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Reverse slips or engages late; Limp mode; Transmission warning or check engine light. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0780 – Shift Error
text: P0780: Shift Error. Shift codes are a functional check of the gear change itself: the module compares the commanded shift with the speed trace and flags a shift that takes too long, is too short or abrupt, does not happen, flares or ties up. Ford does not use P0780–P0784 (its shift completion check feeds the solenoid codes), nor do GM's 2018–2025 tables. P0780 is the collective code when the faulty shift is not assigned to a gear. GM's 2006 Aisin-type five-speed counts five shifts that are too long, too short or tied up with fluid above 60 °C and lights the MIL at once; GM's Honda-built unit flags a 3–4 shift that stays in the lower ratio after two trips; Saab's 2010 Aisin six-speed counts ten faulty shifts without MIL, limits torque and keeps second and reverse. Nissan fixed P0780 on the 2021 Rogue CVT with new software. Common causes: Fluid level wrong, fluid worn or contaminated (high likelihood); Valve body, shift or pressure valve sticking (high likelihood); Worn clutches or bands (mechanical damage) (medium likelihood); Module software or shift adaption (medium likelihood); Faulty speed sensor signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh, delayed or missing shifts; Engine flare during shifts; Warning lamp; Limp mode with fixed gear, reduced power. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0785 – Shift Timing Solenoid A
text: P0785: Shift Timing Solenoid A. 'Shift timing solenoid' means different parts: on GM's 4L60-E the 3-2 downshift solenoid that times the band apply on that downshift, on Aisin five-speeds (GM, Saab) the linear valve SLS that sets clutch pressure during the shift, and on the 2017–18 Genesis G80/G90 with shift-by-wire the on/off solenoids that engage drive (A) and reverse (B). P0785 is the general circuit code for solenoid A. GM's 2006 tables use it for the 3-2 downshift solenoid circuit (more than 43 of 50 failed counts, after one trip); Saab's 2002 Aisin box for an open or short in the SLS circuit with warning lamp and limp mode; Hyundai's Genesis bulletins for the drive solenoid, replacing valve and electronic module and then the module if it returns. Limp mode, harsh 3-2 downshifts or – on the Genesis – no drive follow. Common causes: Solenoid coil open or shorted (high likelihood); Connector or wire at the transmission (oil, corrosion) (medium likelihood); Electronic module or transmission module driver (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp; Limp mode; Harsh 3-2 downshift (GM) or rough shifts (Aisin); Genesis shift-by-wire: drive cannot be engaged. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P078E – Shift Timing Solenoid B Intermittent
text: P078E: Shift Timing Solenoid B Intermittent. 'Shift timing solenoid' means different parts: on GM's 4L60-E the 3-2 downshift solenoid that times the band apply on that downshift, on Aisin five-speeds (GM, Saab) the linear valve SLS that sets clutch pressure during the shift, and on the 2017–18 Genesis G80/G90 with shift-by-wire the on/off solenoids that engage drive (A) and reverse (B). Only Hyundai/Genesis is documented using solenoid B, and only with the base code P078A. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows solenoid A (P0789: an intermittent circuit fault). A loose contact is the likely cause; the warning lamp comes and goes. Common causes: Loose contact (high likelihood); Coil with thermal dropouts (low likelihood). Symptoms: Occasional warning lamp; Shift jolts at times. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P078F – Transmission Mode Switch C Circuit
text: P078F: Transmission Mode Switch C Circuit. P078F is the circuit fault of a third transmission mode switch (C), after A (P071A–P071C) and B (P071D–P071F): its state is invalid or implausible. GM's transmission modules of 2023 and 2025 list the number only as a blocking condition for another check, without a description of their own; GM reports its drive mode selector today under P05D0–P05D3 (8-step resistor ladder, two trips). No manufacturer document available to us describes P078F itself. The mode then cannot be selected and the transmission stays on its normal schedule. Common causes: Switch or button faulty or sticking (high likelihood); Wire or connector open or shorted (medium likelihood); Moisture or dirt in the centre console (medium likelihood); Control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Drive mode (sport, winter, tow) cannot be selected; Mode indicator missing; Transmission stays on the normal program. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0790 – Normal/Performance Switch Circuit
text: P0790: Normal/Performance Switch Circuit. P0790 is the circuit fault of the normal/performance (sport or power program) selector of an automatic transmission – the older single code that preceded the mode switch codes P071A ff; the early J2012 list still called it 'circuit malfunction'. The switch is usually a button to ground or a resistor ladder; a fault is an invalid level, a permanently pressed button or an open circuit. No manufacturer document available to us describes it; GM uses P05D0–P05D3 for its drive mode selector today. The sport program is then unavailable or permanently on. Common causes: Button faulty or sticking (high likelihood); Wire or connector open or shorted (medium likelihood); Liquid in the console (medium likelihood); Control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Sport or performance program unavailable or always on; Mode indicator missing or flashing. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0791 – Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit
text: P0791: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit. The intermediate shaft speed sensor measures a shaft between input and output – a countershaft on Toyota's U760 six-speed, the intermediate shaft behind the overdrive set on Ford's 5R110W. Together with turbine and output speed it lets the module check each gear stage and control clutch slip. Ford uses P0791 as its only intermediate shaft code, for 'no or too little signal': while the vehicle drives under power (turbine at least 1500 rpm, output at least 650 rpm or 15 mph), the sensor reports below 250 rpm for 5 s – in the 2012 and 2020–23 summaries, with MIL. A Toyota bulletin for the U760 (Highlander, Venza, Camry 2009–10) replaces the countershaft sensor for P0791/P0793. GM's 10-speed has two such sensors but uses its own codes. Limp mode and harsh shifts follow. Common causes: Intermediate shaft speed sensor faulty (high likelihood); Connector or wire at the transmission (oil, corrosion, chafing) (medium likelihood); Reluctor wheel damaged or debris on the sensor (medium likelihood); Control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Limp mode or fixed gear; Harsh or delayed shifts; Follow-up pressure control codes (Toyota). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0792 – Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0792: Intermediate Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The intermediate shaft speed sensor measures a shaft between input and output – a countershaft on Toyota's U760 six-speed, the intermediate shaft behind the overdrive set on Ford's 5R110W. Together with turbine and output speed it lets the module check each gear stage and control clutch slip. P0792 means a signal is present but implausible: intermediate shaft speed does not match turbine or output speed for the detected gear stage, exceeds a maximum or jumps unrealistically. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford uses only P0791, Toyota's bulletin P0791/P0793, GM its own codes; the logic follows GM's range checks for input and output sensors (P0716/P0721). Symptoms: Check engine light or transmission warning; Shift problems; Limp mode possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0795 – Pressure Control Solenoid C
text: P0795: Pressure Control Solenoid C. Pressure control solenoids are current-controlled proportional valves, and what B and C mean depends on the design: on GM's clutch-to-clutch automatics they are the pressure valves of clutches 2 and 3, on GM's CVT B is primary pulley pressure and C line pressure, on Jatco CVTs B is the secondary pressure valve, on Saab's AF40 B and C are clutch valves SLC1/SLC2. P0795 is the general code for valve C. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; GM's 8-speed uses only P0796/P0797 for its clutch 3 valve, Saab's AF40 only P0798 for valve SLC2. Sub-codes for performance, stuck on, electrical and intermittent follow (P0796–P0799). Common causes: Valve body or pressure valve C (high likelihood); Fluid or line pressure (medium likelihood); Circuit or coil (low likelihood). Symptoms: Shift problems; Limp mode; Check engine light. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P079A – Transmission Friction Element A Slip Detected
text: P079A: Transmission Friction Element A Slip Detected. The 'friction element slip' codes monitor a clutch that is commanded locked in a power-split hybrid transmission: the module calculates its slip from electric motor, engine and output speeds (target 0 rpm) and flags slip above a threshold for a minimum time, with sufficient line pressure and clutch torque; from 2016 GM also flags a calculated friction energy threshold at once. The letter matches the manufacturer's clutch number. P079A concerns clutch 1. On GM's Two-Mode SUVs and pickups (2008–13) that is the hybrid low/1-2 clutch, flagged above 200 rpm for 3 s after one trip; GM bulletins link it to a clogged line pressure orifice and the auxiliary oil pump. The Volt flags above 200 rpm in three attempts, Malibu Hybrid and Volt from 2016 190 rpm for 0.6 s or 8003 J. Chrysler's Pacifica PHEV fixes P079A by software, as a permanent code with MIL. Common causes: Clutch A plates worn or glazed (high likelihood); Too little line pressure: low or aged fluid, filter, auxiliary oil pump or blocked pressure orifice (medium likelihood); Pressure or shift valve of clutch A or valve body sticking (medium likelihood); Module software (false setting) (low likelihood); Faulty speed signals (motor resolver, output) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or 'service hybrid system' message; Limp mode with reduced power or restricted drive mode; Slipping, engine speed rises without drive; Jolt when the engine starts or stops. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07A2 – Transmission Friction Element A Performance/Stuck Off
text: P07A2: Transmission Friction Element A Performance/Stuck Off. Each friction element (clutch or brake) has three functional codes: slip while commanded locked (P079A ff), performance/stuck off – it does not apply or applies too weakly – and stuck on – it does not release. P07A2 concerns clutch A. Ford's DPS6 PowerShift dry dual-clutch (Fiesta, Focus) uses it for clutch A – input shaft 1 with gears 1, 3 and 5 – as 'functionally stuck off', next to the electrical codes of its electric clutch actuator; Ford publishes no thresholds. A GM bulletin for the 2017 LaCrosse and 2017–19 XT5 lists P07A2 as 'transmission clutch 1 performance' together with ratio codes, caused by a misaligned range actuator. GM's hybrids do not use it. Common causes: Clutch A plates worn or piston seal leaking (high likelihood); Too little apply pressure (fluid, pump, valve) (medium likelihood); Clutch actuator or valve sticking (DCT: electric actuator) (medium likelihood); Module software or lost adaption (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or transmission warning; Gear missing or slipping, weak acceleration; Limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07A3 – Transmission Friction Element A Stuck On
text: P07A3: Transmission Friction Element A Stuck On. Ford's DPS6 uses P07A3 for clutch A 'functionally stuck on'. Symptoms: Check engine light or 'service hybrid system' message; Jolt or tie-up on mode or gear changes; Engine stalls or drags when stopping; Limp mode with reduced power. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07B2 – Transmission Park Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit/Open
text: P07B2: Transmission Park Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit/Open. With electronic gear selection the park position sensor/switch reports the park request or position. On GM's shift-by-wire selectors (2017 LaCrosse, XT4/XT5, Bolt EV, later SUVs and pickups) it is the P button, read by two redundant analog sensors A and B with separate 'released' and 'pressed' voltage zones. P07B2 means the circuit of sensor A is open: the module sees a missing or undefined signal. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM covers an open analog circuit under its low and high codes (P07B3/P07B4), which CARB allows when an open cannot be told apart from an out-of-range value. Park may then not be selectable by button. Common causes: Wire or connector to the selector open (high likelihood); Connector not latched (medium likelihood); Sensor faulty (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light, 'service transmission' or 'unable to shift' message; Park cannot be selected by button, or the car will not shift out of P; P button illumination off. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07BF – Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P07BF: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Low. These low/high codes are a purely electrical check of the sensor's signal voltage at the module and run even with the vehicle at rest – unlike the circuit, range, no-signal and intermittent codes, which evaluate speed while driving. Low means a short to ground, high a short to supply or, depending on the circuit, an open. GM's transmission modules from 2019 (9-speed, 10-speed) flag below 0.25 V or above 4.75 V – a short of under 0.5 Ω – for more than 0.05 s with the system above 10 V for 5 s, after one trip. P07BF is the low side: a short to ground of the input sensor. A GM bulletin for 2019 nine-speed models (Enclave, Equinox, Malibu, XT4 and others) traces intermittent P07BF/P07C0 together with P0717 to an open inside the input speed sensor. Common causes: Signal or supply wire shorted to ground (chafing at the case) (high likelihood); Sensor shorted internally (medium likelihood); Oil or moisture in the connector (medium likelihood); Module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM after one trip); Limp mode, harsh shifts, no converter lock-up; Adaption frozen. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07CB – Transmission Fluid Thermostat Performance
text: P07CB: Transmission Fluid Thermostat Performance. Many automatics have a thermostat in the fluid cooler circuit or a coolant-to-oil heat exchanger: a BMW patent describes a wax thermostat that bypasses the cooler until about 76 °C, a Ford patent a heat exchanger that warms transmission fluid from the coolant after a cold start. P07CB means this thermostat does not work as expected: fluid warms up too slowly (stuck open) or overheats (stuck closed). No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM checks fluid warm-up under the temperature sensor code P0711 (below 15 °C after the warm-up time, two trips). The check works like CARB's engine thermostat monitor (P0128). Slow warm-up raises consumption and delays converter lock-up; overheating ages fluid quickly. Common causes: Transmission fluid thermostat stuck open or closed (high likelihood); Fluid temperature sensor drifting (medium likelihood); Cooler lines or heat exchanger blocked or leaking (medium likelihood); Very cold weather or short trips (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning lamp; Converter clutch applies late, higher consumption; Fluid overheating warning. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07CC – Transmission Mode Switch C Circuit Low
text: P07CC: Transmission Mode Switch C Circuit Low. Transmission mode switches select alternative shift programs such as sport, winter or tow/haul; the J2012 family runs from A (P071A–P071C) and B (P071D–P071F) to C (base code P078F), D and E. No manufacturer document available to us uses switches C to E; GM reads its analog mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, two trips) and newer drive mode selectors under P05D0–P05D3. P07CC means the signal of mode switch C is below its lower limit – a short to ground or a button stuck against ground. The opposite is P07CD. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Button stuck pressed (switching to ground) (medium likelihood); Moisture or dirt in the button (medium likelihood); Control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Mode C cannot be selected or stays active; Mode indicator missing or flashing; Transmission stays on the normal program. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P07D7 – Stuck in Gear 8
text: P07D7: Stuck in Gear 8. P07D7 means gear 8 cannot be disengaged: the module commands a shift out of 8th, but the transmission stays in it. It is the counterpart to P07D8, where gear 8 cannot be engaged. The only documented user is Maserati's eight-speed dual-clutch gearbox in the MC20 (from model year 2023), whose bulletin lists it next to the other 'Stuck in Gear' codes: hydraulic actuators move the shift forks, and a fork that does not reach neutral is reported. The repair path there first runs a service fast-learn with valve flushing and new adaptation, then records system pressure – it should hold 20–30 bar; drops below 5 bar point to the mechatronic unit, a stable pressure to the gearbox itself. No thresholds or trip counts are published. Common causes: Shift fork actuator or shift valve sticking (contamination) (high likelihood); System pressure low or unstable (mechatronic pressure valve) (medium likelihood); Shift fork, synchronizer or gear damaged (medium likelihood); Fluid or filter contaminated (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission stays in gear 8 and will not downshift; Weak take-off after stopping; Transmission warning, limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07D8 – Unable to Engage Gear 8
text: P07D8: Unable to Engage Gear 8. 'Unable to Engage' means the transmission does not reach the commanded gear – here 8th. Documented users are eight-speed dual-clutch gearboxes with hydraulically moved, position-monitored shift forks. A GM bulletin for the 2020–23 Corvette lists it with the MIL on, caused by a solenoid or internal switch sticking from debris: valve cleaning is only advised when system pressure codes are present as well, otherwise a service fast-learn; if that fails, the mechanics are damaged. Maserati's MC20 lists it with a pressure check of 20–30 bar. On a dual-clutch box the half carrying the even gears may be locked out. No published thresholds or trip counts. Common causes: Sticking solenoid or shift valve in the mechatronic unit (high likelihood); System pressure too low or unstable (medium likelihood); Adaptives lost or wrong after software or parts work (medium likelihood); Shift fork or synchronizer damaged (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Gear 8 skipped or never reached, higher rpm at cruise; Check engine and transmission warning lamp; Jerky shifts, possibly loss of one half of a dual-clutch gearbox. title: P07D9 – Gear 8 Incorrect Ratio
text: P07D9: Gear 8 Incorrect Ratio. A ratio code compares input or turbine speed divided by output speed with the ratio of the commanded gear; a slipping clutch or the wrong gear trips it. Ford's summaries describe the check (over 30 rpm off for more than 1.8 s, three times) for gears 1–6 only; its 10-speed bulletins show gears 7–10 as P076F, P07D9, P07F6 and P07F7. P07D9 covers 8th gear. Ford's 10R80 (F-150, Mustang, Ranger, Expedition and others) and 10R140 (2020 Super Duty) list it in bulletins on harsh or delayed shifts, caused by adaptive learning, sticking valve-body valves or a migrating sleeve in a clutch cylinder. Nissan's nine-speed Frontier and Titan set it with the MIL on; a Stellantis bulletin pairs it with P0731 on low-mileage vehicles with wrong factory adaptives. Hyundai's eight-speeds and GM's 10-speed do not use it. Common causes: Clutch slipping or hydraulic leak (Ford 10R: migrating sleeve in the CDF clutch cylinder) (high likelihood); Shift adaptives wrong or not learned (high likelihood); Sticking valve in the valve body (medium likelihood); Fluid level low or fluid degraded (medium likelihood); Turbine or output speed sensor signal wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Slipping or flaring engine speed in gear 8; Harsh or delayed shifts; Check engine or transmission warning lamp; Gear 8 locked out, higher rpm at cruise. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07DA – 6-7 Shift
text: P07DA: 6-7 Shift. Shift codes check the gear change itself: the module compares the commanded change with the speed trace and flags a shift that takes too long, does not happen, flares or binds up two clutches. They continue the series P0781 '1-2 Shift' to P0784 '4-5 Shift'. No manufacturer document available to us uses P07DA or P07DB: Ford's Diesel summary checks shift completion (speed must drop by more than 30 rpm on an upshift, flare above 300 rpm) without a gear-specific code, Ford's 10R80 feeds the solenoid function codes and GM the clutch valve codes. P07DA names the change between 6th and 7th gear, in either direction, as faulty; it exists only on transmissions with seven or more gears. Flags and thresholds follow the manufacturer's own logic. Common causes: Shift or clutch valve sticking (medium likelihood); Worn clutch or hydraulic leak on the clutches involved (medium likelihood); Shift adaptives wrong (medium likelihood); Fluid level or condition (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh, delayed or missing 6-7 shift; Engine speed flares during the shift; Transmission warning, possibly MIL. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07DC – Incorrect Shift from Gear 1
text: P07DC: Incorrect Shift from Gear 1. The series 'Incorrect Shift from Gear N' (P07DC–P07E3 for gears 1–8, P07FA and P07FD for 9 and 10) covers a shift that leaves the starting gear but lands in a gear other than the commanded target – a skipped or overshot gear. A module can see this after the shift because the measured ratio matches the wrong gear. No manufacturer document available to us uses the series: Ford assigns such patterns to the shift solenoid that caused them (P0751 ff), newer GM automatics report clutch pressure valve codes. P07DC starts from gear 1. It differs from P0731 (wrong ratio while in gear 1, a slipping clutch), P072C (gear 1 cannot be left) and P0781 (the shift itself takes too long or flares). Detection, MIL and trip count therefore follow only by analogy from CARB's functional check and Ford's ratio and shift completion checks. Common causes: Shift or pressure control valve sticking in the valve body (high likelihood); Clutch or brake pack worn or leaking (medium likelihood); Fluid low or contaminated (medium likelihood); Wrong adaptives or software (medium likelihood); Turbine or output speed signal wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Wrong or skipped gear when shifting out of gear 1; Harsh shift or engine speed jump; Transmission warning, possibly limp mode in a fixed gear. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07E4 – Unable to Engage Park
text: P07E4: Unable to Engage Park. With shift-by-wire or park-by-wire, P, R, N and D are requested electrically (buttons, rotary selector, automatic park on shutdown) and an actuator moves the selector shaft or the park pawl; the module compares the requested with the range actually reached. P07E4 means park is not reached or not held within the allowed time. GM gives thresholds: 2 s in 2018 tables and the ICCM of its electronic range selector (2000 ms), 6–10 s in later tables, type B with the MIL after two trips; a 2018 bulletin for LaCrosse and XT5 blames a misaligned coupling of the range control module. Ford sets it with the wrench lamp instead of the MIL – on the 2020 Escape and Corsair a misrouted park release cable, on the Mach-E software – and applies the electric parking brake. Ram 1500 (2019) sets the MIL; Stellantis names a used manual park release as the most common cause. Common causes: Manual park release cable misrouted or actuated (high likelihood); Range actuator misaligned or its coupling offset (medium likelihood); Control module software (medium likelihood); Park lock actuator or its ground faulty (medium likelihood); Range or park position signal wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Park cannot be selected, 'Park not available' message; Electric parking brake applies automatically; Wrench lamp (Ford) or MIL (GM, Ram); Vehicle may roll away if not secured. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07E5 – Unable to Engage Drive
text: P07E5: Unable to Engage Drive. With shift-by-wire or park-by-wire, P, R, N and D are requested electrically (buttons, rotary selector, automatic park on shutdown) and an actuator moves the selector shaft or the park pawl; the module compares the requested with the range actually reached. P07E5 means drive is requested but not reached in time. Only GM documents it: its electronic range selector (LaCrosse, XT5, XT4, 2025 Equinox and Terrain) allows 10 s in most tables, 3 s in the 2018 Diesel table and 2000 ms in the selector module, type B with the MIL after two trips. A 2018 bulletin blames a misaligned range control module coupling, its 2019 revision adds ratio codes; on the 2025 Equinox and Terrain it can appear after an over-the-air update and clears after a ten-minute rest. The car does not move forward or falls back to neutral. Common causes: Range control actuator misaligned or faulty (high likelihood); Software or after-effect of an over-the-air update (medium likelihood); Range sensor signal wrong (medium likelihood); Forward clutch or line pressure missing (low likelihood). Symptoms: No drive in D; 'Service Transmission' message, MIL; Range falls back to N or P. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07E6 – Stuck in Park
text: P07E6: Stuck in Park. With shift-by-wire or park-by-wire, P, R, N and D are requested electrically (buttons, rotary selector, automatic park on shutdown) and an actuator moves the selector shaft or the park pawl; the module compares the requested with the range actually reached. P07E6 means park cannot be left: the pawl stays engaged or its position feedback keeps reporting P. Ford documents it on the HF45 hybrid transmission (2023–24 Escape, 2022–24 Maverick), where the inverter control module monitors the park actuator – the P on the rotary selector flashes, the wrench lamp comes on and an internally failed actuator is replaced (about 13–14 h) – and on the 2024–25 Mach-E, where a high resistance in the park motor ground is fixed with new software and a ground harness. Maserati lists it for the MC20 dual-clutch gearbox. Ford keeps it off the MIL; GM tables do not list it. Common causes: Park lock actuator failed internally (high likelihood); High resistance at the park motor ground (medium likelihood); Control module software (medium likelihood); Low system voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle stays in P and cannot be driven away; P flashes on the selector, P in the cluster dark; Wrench lamp or 'Service vehicle soon'. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07E7 – Stuck in Drive
text: P07E7: Stuck in Drive. With shift-by-wire or park-by-wire, P, R, N and D are requested electrically (buttons, rotary selector, automatic park on shutdown) and an actuator moves the selector shaft or the park pawl; the module compares the requested with the range actually reached. P07E7 means drive cannot be left: after a request for P, N or R the transmission stays in D. It is the counterpart to P07E5, where drive cannot be engaged, and to P07E6 for park. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; GM's range selector module checks requested against reached range in the same way for P07E4 and P07E5 (2000 ms, two trips). With shift-by-wire the fault matters for safety, because the car cannot be put into park or neutral. Typical causes would be a sticking range actuator or selector shaft, a range sensor wrongly reporting D, or the selector or its software. Common causes: Range actuator or selector shaft sticking (medium likelihood); Range sensor wrongly reporting D (medium likelihood); Selector sensor or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Range stays in D despite the selector request; P or N cannot be reached, warning message; Warning lamp (depends on manufacturer). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07E8 – Transmission Range Control A Circuit/Open
text: P07E8: Transmission Range Control A Circuit/Open. Despite its name, 'Transmission Range Control A' is not the range actuator motor – that has its own codes, P272A and P272B – but the sensor circuits of an electric shift-by-wire selector. The only documented user is Mitsubishi's 2022 service manual for a CVT with electric shift (very likely the 2022–23 Outlander): the lever carries eight position sensors whose on/off pattern encodes R, N, home, D and M. P07E8 is the open-circuit check of these sensor lines: if one sensor input is pulled above 4.5 V for 2.4 s with the ignition on, the code sets. Mitsubishi lists it with the MIL but without a fail-safe reaction, because the remaining sensors still identify the position. Low and high are P07EA/P07EB. GM and Ford use their own codes for their selectors. Common causes: Wire or connector between selector and shift module open (high likelihood); Position sensor in the selector faulty (medium likelihood); Shift module input faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Electric shift or check engine warning; Usually no noticeable restriction; Further sensor faults lead to P07EC/P07ED. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07E9 – Transmission Range Control A Circuit Performance

title: P07EC – Transmission Range Multi-Function Select Circuit
text: P07EC: Transmission Range Multi-Function Select Circuit. 'Transmission Range Multi-Function Select' is the multi-bit code of the shift-by-wire selector position: each position produces a fixed pattern of sensor states, and the module checks the pattern for logic errors. Mitsubishi's 2022 CVT with electric shift uses eight sensors (R: 1–2 on, N toward R: 1–5, home: all, N toward D: 4–8, D/M: 7–8). P07EC sets when a single bit does not change as the lever moves through its positions – it is stuck on or off. The other bits still identify the position, but the decision takes at least a second. Mitsubishi shows only the yellow electric-shift warning, without the MIL. Two or more stuck bits are P07ED. Common causes: One position sensor in the selector faulty (high likelihood); One sensor wire open or shorted (medium likelihood); Dirt or sticking mechanism in the selector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Yellow shift warning or message; Selected range taken over with a delay of a second or more; No MIL (Mitsubishi). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07ED – Transmission Range Multi-Function Select Circuit Stuck
text: P07ED: Transmission Range Multi-Function Select Circuit Stuck. 'Transmission Range Multi-Function Select' is the multi-bit code of the shift-by-wire selector position: each position produces a fixed pattern of sensor states, and the module checks the pattern for logic errors. Mitsubishi's 2022 CVT with electric shift uses eight sensors (R: 1–2 on, N toward R: 1–5, home: all, N toward D: 4–8, D/M: 7–8). P07ED is the step after P07EC: at least two bits are stuck, so the position can no longer be decoded reliably. Mitsubishi then puts the drive in neutral and blocks changes between P, R, N and D, lights the MIL and the red or yellow shift warning; the car cannot be driven and has to be towed. Common causes: Selector sensor board faulty (high likelihood); Selector connector corroded or loose (several pins) (medium likelihood); Liquid spilled into the center console (low likelihood). Symptoms: No range can be selected, vehicle in neutral; MIL and red or yellow shift warning; Vehicle cannot be driven (tow). Repair difficulty: medium.

text: P07EF: Transmission Range Multi-Function Select Circuit Low. 'Transmission Range Multi-Function Select' is the multi-bit code of the shift-by-wire selector position: each position produces a fixed pattern of sensor states, and the module checks the pattern for logic errors. Mitsubishi's 2022 CVT with electric shift uses eight sensors (R: 1–2 on, N toward R: 1–5, home: all, N toward D: 4–8, D/M: 7–8). P07EF is the low state of the whole pattern: all eight bits report off, which is no valid code – typically a disconnected selector plug or a missing common supply or ground. Mitsubishi detects it already at standstill after about 10 s with the ignition on, puts the drive in neutral and lights the MIL. Common causes: Selector plug disconnected or its supply or ground open (high likelihood); Selector sensor board faulty (medium likelihood); Electric shift module (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle in neutral, no range selectable; MIL and shift warning; Fault appears right after switching the ignition on. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07F0 – Transmission Range Multi-Function Select Circuit High
text: P07F0: Transmission Range Multi-Function Select Circuit High. 'Transmission Range Multi-Function Select' is the multi-bit code of the shift-by-wire selector position: each position produces a fixed pattern of sensor states, and the module checks the pattern for logic errors. Mitsubishi's 2022 CVT with electric shift uses eight sensors (R: 1–2 on, N toward R: 1–5, home: all, N toward D: 4–8, D/M: 7–8). P07F0 would be the high counterpart of P07EF: the position code reports a high state that matches no valid position, for example signal levels pulled up by a short to the supply. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – on Mitsubishi's selector 'all on' is the valid home position, so a high state cannot be told apart there. By analogy to P07EF a module would block range changes or select neutral. Common causes: Selector signal wires shorted to the supply (medium likelihood); Selector faulty (medium likelihood); Shift module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Shift warning or MIL (depends on manufacturer); Range selection blocked or neutral. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07F1 – Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor C Circuit
text: P07F1: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor C Circuit. P07F1 is the general circuit code of a third input or turbine shaft speed sensor, after sensor A (P0715) and B (P2765); low and high for sensor C are P07C3 and P07C4. No production use could be found in GM tables from 2015 to 2025, Ford's summaries of 2012 and 2020–23, Mitsubishi's code index or manufacturer bulletins; such a sensor would make sense on transmissions with three input shafts or a hybrid input. The check would follow P0715: no plausible signal while driving or an open circuit. The module then uses a substitute value, keeps the converter clutch open and shifts more harshly; with emissions impact CARB requires the MIL. Common causes: Sensor wire or connector open (medium likelihood); Speed sensor faulty (medium likelihood); Control module or software (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine lamp (expected); Harsh shifts, converter clutch stays open; Limp mode possible. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P07F2 – Transmission Range Control Module Communication Circuit
text: P07F2: Transmission Range Control Module Communication Circuit. The transmission range control module is the separate shift-by-wire control unit that reads the selector and drives the range actuator. P07F2 reports a fault in its communication. Mitsubishi's 2022 CVT with electric shift sets it when the module's start-up CAN check fails and blames the module itself; it switches to neutral only if the CVT or the whole system is affected too, and one of its two entries carries no MIL. GM (U18AA, U2409) and Ford (U101F, without MIL) report the same function under their own U codes. Common causes: Shift-by-wire module faulty or its software (high likelihood); Communication wire or connector (medium likelihood); Weak battery during start-up (low likelihood). Symptoms: Shift warning; Usually no restriction; neutral if the transmission is affected too; U codes in other modules possible. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07F3 – Transmission Range Control Module Communication Circuit Low
text: P07F3: Transmission Range Control Module Communication Circuit Low. The transmission range control module is the separate shift-by-wire control unit that reads the selector and drives the range actuator. P07F3 is the electrical low check of its communication line: the line is shorted to ground and stays at a low level. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; the code fits a dedicated signal or redundancy line between selector, range control module and transmission or engine module rather than a CAN bus. GM handles a bus short under its own U2409 (bus off for 1 s, two trips). The module may block range changes or select neutral. Common causes: Communication wire shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Module output stage faulty (low likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Shift warning; Possible shift lock or neutral (depends on manufacturer). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07F5 – Transmission Range Control Module System Voltage Low
text: P07F5: Transmission Range Control Module System Voltage Low. The transmission range control module is the separate shift-by-wire control unit that reads the selector and drives the range actuator. P07F5 means its supply voltage is too low. No manufacturer document available to us uses the generic code, but GM checks exactly this under its own P17B0: battery voltage at the range control module at or below 9 V for 5 s within a 6 s window, type C without MIL. With too little voltage the actuator may not set the range or park pawl reliably; GM also suspends further checks of the module. A weak battery or a resistance in the module's fuse, supply or ground is the usual cause. Common causes: Weak battery or charging system (high likelihood); Fuse, supply or ground wire of the module with high resistance (medium likelihood); High actuator motor current on a weak supply (low likelihood). Symptoms: Shift warning; Range or park lock reacts late or not at all; Often together with battery voltage codes. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P07F6 – Gear 9 Incorrect Ratio
text: P07F6: Gear 9 Incorrect Ratio. A ratio code compares input or turbine speed divided by output speed with the ratio of the commanded gear; a slipping clutch or the wrong gear trips it. Ford's summaries describe the check (over 30 rpm off for more than 1.8 s, three times) for gears 1–6 only; its 10-speed bulletins show gears 7–10 as P076F, P07D9, P07F6 and P07F7. P07F6 covers 9th gear. Ford's 10R80 bulletins from 2023 to 2025 (F-150, Mustang, Ranger, Explorer, Transit, Expedition) list it with the other ratio codes; the causes are adaptive learning, the valve body and a migrating clutch cylinder sleeve. The 10R140 bulletin of 2021 does not mention it. Nissan's nine-speed Frontier and Titan set it with the MIL on; the repair check drives each gear 1–9 for at least 10 s in manual mode. Common causes: Clutch slipping or hydraulic leak (Ford 10R: migrating sleeve in the CDF clutch cylinder) (high likelihood); Shift adaptives wrong or not learned (high likelihood); Sticking valve in the valve body (medium likelihood); Fluid level low or fluid degraded (medium likelihood); Turbine or output speed sensor signal wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Slipping or flaring engine speed in gear 9; Harsh or delayed shifts; Check engine or transmission warning lamp; Gear 9 locked out, higher rpm at cruise. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07F7 – Gear 10 Incorrect Ratio
text: P07F7: Gear 10 Incorrect Ratio. A ratio code compares input or turbine speed divided by output speed with the ratio of the commanded gear; a slipping clutch or the wrong gear trips it. title: P07F8 – Stuck in Gear 9
text: P07F8: Stuck in Gear 9. P07F8 means gear 9 cannot be disengaged: the transmission stays in 9th despite the command to leave it. No manufacturer document available to us uses it. The family is documented only for 8th gear on eight-speed dual-clutch gearboxes (Maserati MC20: P07D7 and P07D8; Corvette 2020–23: P07D8), where hydraulic actuators move shift forks under position monitoring. Nine- and ten-speed planetary automatics from Ford, GM and Nissan report faults in 9th gear as a ratio code (P07F6) or through solenoid and clutch valve codes. The description follows the J2012 scheme and CARB's functional check of transmission outputs. Common causes: Shift fork actuator or shift valve sticking (contamination) (high likelihood); System pressure low or unstable (mechatronic pressure valve) (medium likelihood); Shift fork, synchronizer or gear damaged (medium likelihood); Fluid or filter contaminated (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission stays in gear 9 and will not downshift; Weak take-off after stopping; Transmission warning, limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P07F9 – Unable to Engage Gear 9
text: P07F9: Unable to Engage Gear 9. P07F9 means the transmission does not reach the commanded 9th gear – the counterpart to P07F8, where 9th cannot be left. No manufacturer document available to us uses it. 'Unable to Engage' is documented only for eight-speed dual-clutch gearboxes, for example the 2020–23 Corvette (P07D8, MIL on, sticking solenoid from debris). Nine- and ten-speed planetary automatics from Ford, GM and Nissan report faults in 9th gear as a ratio code (P07F6) or through valve codes. Common causes: Sticking solenoid or shift valve in the mechatronic unit (high likelihood); System pressure too low or unstable (medium likelihood); Adaptives lost or wrong after software or parts work (medium likelihood); Shift fork or synchronizer damaged (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Gear 9 skipped or never reached, higher rpm at cruise; Check engine and transmission warning lamp; Jerky shifts, possibly loss of one half of a dual-clutch gearbox. title: P07FA – Incorrect Shift from Gear 9
text: P07FA: Incorrect Shift from Gear 9. P07FA belongs to the series 'Incorrect Shift from Gear N' (P07DC–P07E3 for gears 1–8, P07FA for 9, P07FD for 10): when leaving 9th gear, the transmission ends up in a gear other than the commanded target, or the shift out of 9th goes wrong. No manufacturer document available to us uses it. Ten-speed users such as Ford's 10R family and GM's 10L report such faults through ratio or valve codes; Ford's Diesel summary checks shift completion without a gear-specific code. Possible causes are a sticking shift or clutch valve, a worn or leaking clutch, or wrong adaptives. Common causes: Shift or clutch valve sticking (medium likelihood); Worn clutch or hydraulic leak on the clutches involved (medium likelihood); Shift adaptives wrong (medium likelihood); Fluid level or condition (low likelihood). Symptoms: Wrong gear or harsh downshift out of 9th; Transmission warning, possibly limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.
