title: P089F – Gear Lever Y Position Sensor 2 Circuit
text: P089F: Gear Lever Y Position Sensor 2 Circuit. Gear lever position sensor 2 is the redundant second sensor of an electronic selector lever, next to sensor 1 (P0821 ff), for the X or Y axis. The only documented user is GM's electronic range selection with PWM Hall sensors, as in the Cadillac XT4, and only for range, low and high. Following GM's patent, an invalid sensor is dropped and the other carries on; with both invalid the module can request park. P089F, the general circuit fault of Y sensor 2, is used by no maker found; GM reports that sensor under P08A0 to P08A2. In GM's patent a sensor counts as invalid as a whole once its X or Y value fails. Common causes: Wire or connector at the selector module open (high likelihood); Sensor 2 faulty (medium likelihood); Corrosion from liquid in the console (low likelihood). Symptoms: Gearbox or selector warning in the cluster; Range selection delayed or limited; Usually still drivable, sensor 1 takes over. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08A0 – Gear Lever Y Position Sensor 2 Circuit Range/Performance
text: P08A0: Gear Lever Y Position Sensor 2 Circuit Range/Performance. Sensor 2 is the redundant second Hall sensor that reports the Y-axis travel of an electronic selector lever as a PWM duty cycle. GM uses it in its electronic range selection (ECM and ICCM tables 2019–2025, Cadillac XT4 among them). P08A0 is set when sensor 2 reports a lever path outside the shifter gate (tolerance 5.5 %, ICCM 6–11 % of duty cycle), its frequency check fails, or it disagrees with Y sensor 1 by more than 12 %. Debounce is 3 of 4 samples at 25 ms (2025: 10 of 12). Type B, MIL after two trips. Low/High of the same sensor are P08A1/P08A2. GM's patent lets the other sensor carry on; only when both are invalid may the module ask for park. Common causes: Sensor 2 in the selector assembly drifting or faulty (high likelihood); Selector mechanism worn, bent or binding, lever leaves its nominal path (medium likelihood); Loose contact or interference on the PWM signal line (medium likelihood); Spilled liquid in the centre console (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light after two drives; Shift lever message or occasional unaccepted range selection; Usually still drivable, sensor 1 takes over. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08A1 – Gear Lever Y Position Sensor 2 Circuit Low

title: P08A3 – Gear Lever Y Position Sensor 2 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P08A3: Gear Lever Y Position Sensor 2 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. This code covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal of the second, redundant Y-axis sensor of an electronic selector lever. No manufacturer documents P08A3 publicly. GM, the only proven user of this sensor family, uses only range/performance, low and high (P08A0 to P08A2) in all OBD tables from 2016 to 2025 and catches an unsteady PWM signal through the frequency check inside P08A0. GM's patent on two redundant lever sensors explains why a second sensor exists: if one becomes invalid, the other keeps range selection alive. Expect loose contacts in the console harness; the MIL status depends on the maker. Common causes: Loose or fretting contact at the selector connector (high likelihood); Harness chafed by console or lever movement (medium likelihood); Sensor 2 with intermittent internal fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Stored fault that comes and goes, often without driver complaint; Occasional shifter warning message; Possibly check engine light, depending on the manufacturer. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08A6 – Gear Lever Position Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation
text: P08A6: Gear Lever Position Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation. Here the module compares the combined gear lever position information with other evidence and finds no consistent picture. Two makers document it. FCA/Stellantis sets P08A6 in the PCM of 6-speed manual Jeeps such as the Wrangler JL as the all-gear-sensor check: the sensed gear is compared with a learned top-gear engine-to-road-speed ratio, so larger tyres trigger it until that ratio is relearned in sixth at 40–80 mph; a 4Low issue and software updates are also known, with MIL. Maserati's electronic shift module stores P08A6-64 for signal plausibility, leaving no gear selectable. Unlike P08A4/P08A5 it concerns the whole sensor system, not one sensor pair. Common causes: Tyre size changed without relearning the top-gear ratio (FCA manual) (high likelihood); Control module software needing an update (medium likelihood); Modified transfer case gearing, fault only in 4Low (low likelihood); Internal fault or connector problem of the electronic shift module (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Start-stop and gear indicator disabled, clutch overheat or service transmission message; On shift-by-wire, no gear can be selected. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08A7 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit/Open
text: P08A7: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit/Open. Sensor A is the analog or PWM sensor that reports how far the clutch pedal of a manual car is pressed; the engine controller needs it for start-stop, cruise control, gear detection and starter release. P08A7 is the general circuit or open-wire fault of that sensor. No manufacturer documents this code publicly: GM folds an open circuit into its low-signal code P08A9, and Ford lists only P08A9/P08AA for sensor A. Saab's 2012 9-3 used the older P0806 as a comparable circuit fault (Check Engine, cruise control off). Range/performance, low, high and erratic faults have their own codes P08A8–P08AB. Expect a warning lamp and disabled start-stop or cruise control until the wiring or sensor is repaired. Common causes: Loose connector or broken wire at the pedal sensor (pedal box wiring flexes with every clutch stroke) (high likelihood); Internal fault in clutch pedal position sensor A (medium likelihood); Missing 5 V reference or sensor ground (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input in the engine control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp on; Start-stop and cruise control unavailable; Engine may not crank if the starter release relies on the sensor. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P08A8 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P08A8: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. P08A8 flags a clutch pedal sensor whose signal is electrically valid but contradicts how the car is actually driving. GM uses it on manual cars since model year 2018 (before: P0806), e.g. the LV7 1.4 L engine and the 2019 Corvette ZR1 (LT5): when engine speed to output shaft speed shows that a gear is engaged and transmitting torque, but the pedal reads as pressed, the filtered position error must stay below 4 %. Enabled above 4.3 mph (LT5: 5.6 mph), not in 4WD low, torque above a table, no circuit, crank or speed sensor faults; Type A, MIL after one trip. Circuit faults are P08A9/P08AA. Typical result: start-stop and cruise control off, and the engine computer may misjudge clutch state. Common causes: Sensor loose or misaligned on the pedal bracket, so its reading no longer matches pedal travel (high likelihood); Worn or drifting sensor track giving an offset signal (medium likelihood); Driver resting a foot on the clutch pedal, or a floor mat holding it down (medium likelihood); Corroded connector adding resistance to signal or ground (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp on; Start-stop and cruise control switched off; Rev-matching or hill-start functions may be disabled. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08A9 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P08A9: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit Low. The sensor is designed with dead bands at both ends, so a signal near 0 V can only come from a fault. GM sets P08A9 when the signal stays below 4 % of the 5 V reference (low voltage or open circuit) for 400 of 500 samples taken every 12.5 ms, with the engine not cranking and system voltage above 9 V (10 V in some 2018 tables); Type A, MIL after one trip. GM used P0807 for this before 2018 and lists P08A9 for the LV7, the 2019 Corvette ZR1 and its 2018 OBDG04 engines. Ford's 2020–23 gasoline summary uses P08A9 for cars with dual PWM pedal sensors or a single analog sensor plus switches, detected in under a second. The high-side counterpart is P08AA; sensor B low is P08B6. Common causes: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground in the pedal area (high likelihood); Open signal wire or missing 5 V reference (connector off, broken wire) (high likelihood); Failed clutch pedal position sensor A (medium likelihood); Shared 5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same circuit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip; Start-stop and cruise control unavailable; Engine may refuse to crank on vehicles that release the starter via the sensor. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P08AA – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit High
text: P08AA: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit High. P08AA is the mirror image of P08A9: the pedal sensor signal climbs into the upper dead band that a healthy sensor never reaches. It replaced GM's pre-2018 P0808 and appears in the LV7, 2019 Corvette ZR1 and 2018 OBDG04 tables. Ford's 2020–23 gasoline summary lists P08AA for both its dual PWM and single analog clutch pedal sensor layouts, flagged in under a second. A lost sensor ground or a signal shorted to the reference are the usual triggers. Sensor B high is P08B7; the driver mostly loses start-stop and cruise control. title: P08AB – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P08AB: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P08AB is meant for a clutch pedal sensor A signal that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than a foot could move the pedal, without staying out of range long enough for the low or high codes. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's published tables for the same sensor use only P08A8, P08A9, P08AA and P08AC, and its low/high checks need 400 of 500 bad samples, so short dropouts would go unnoticed there; Ford names only low, high and A/B correlation. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults and plausibility. In practice the cause is usually a loose connector or a wire that breaks inside its insulation as the pedal moves. Start-stop and cruise control may cut out intermittently. Common causes: Loose or worn terminals in the pedal sensor connector (high likelihood); Wire breaking inside its insulation where the harness flexes with the pedal (high likelihood); Worn sensor track causing signal dropouts at certain pedal positions (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the footwell connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Start-stop or cruise control cutting out intermittently; Warning lamp that comes and goes; Erratic clutch pedal value in scan tool data while the pedal is held still. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08AC – Clutch Pedal Position Not Learned
text: P08AC: Clutch Pedal Position Not Learned. The engine controller has to know at which pedal position the clutch is fully released or disengaged. GM teaches the fully applied position at the factory and then adapts it over time to clutch wear. P08AC is set when this learned value falls outside a window (LV7 1.4 L: 7–33 %, 2019 Corvette ZR1: 9–36 % of travel) or when the manufacturer's enable counter shows the learn was never completed; 250 ms loop, Type A, MIL after one trip. Before 2018 GM used P080A. After replacing the sensor, pedal parts, clutch or ECM, a relearn with a scan tool is needed; FCA, for example, issued a Renegade bulletin calling for a clutch pedal sensor learn. Circuit faults (P08A9/P08AA) must be cleared first. Common causes: Relearn not performed after replacing the sensor, clutch parts or engine control module (high likelihood); Learned position drifted out of the allowed window (worn clutch, wrong pedal stop, air in hydraulics) (medium likelihood); Learn procedure aborted, for example by low battery voltage (medium likelihood); Faulty or misaligned clutch pedal sensor preventing a valid learn (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp on; Start-stop, cruise control or automatic parking brake release not working as expected. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08AD – Neutral Position Sensor B Circuit/Open
text: P08AD: Neutral Position Sensor B Circuit/Open. A neutral position sensor tells the engine module whether a manual gearbox is in neutral, which start-stop, remote start and rev matching rely on. Sensor B is a second sensor or channel next to sensor A (P086A ff). P08AD flags an open or otherwise faulty sensor B circuit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Audi (sender G701) and GM (Corvette LT5) are only known to use the A codes. A GM patent shows why a B channel exists: two Hall sensors on the shift shaft give a PWM signal, and in neutral both must read the same. CARB 1968.2 (e)(15) requires circuit monitoring of such inputs. Expected effect: start-stop stays off; MIL status depends on the maker. Common causes: Wire to the sensor broken or stretched by shift shaft movement (high likelihood); Connector at the gearbox loose or corroded (medium likelihood); Sensor B open internally (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Start-stop no longer switches the engine off; Start system warning in the cluster; Driving normally unaffected. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08B4 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit/Open
text: P08B4: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit/Open. title: P08B6 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit Low
text: P08B6: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit Low. P08B6 means the signal of the second clutch pedal sensor has dropped below its valid range. Ford lists it in the 2020–23 gasoline OBD summary under dual PWM clutch sensors, together with P08A9/P08AA for sensor A, P08B7 for sensor B high and P08B9 for the A/B comparison; monitoring runs continuously and needs less than one second to flag a fault. Ford does not mark the code as non-MIL, unlike its clutch switch codes. For a PWM sensor, low usually means the output is stuck at ground (no pulses or 0 % duty cycle), caused by a short to ground, a lost supply or a dead sensor. GM's published tables have no sensor B. The driver mainly notices a warning lamp and missing start-stop. Common causes: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Lost supply voltage to sensor B (open wire, connector off) (medium likelihood); Failed clutch pedal position sensor B (medium likelihood). title: P08B7 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit High
text: P08B7: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit High. P08B7 is set when the second clutch pedal sensor reports a value above its valid range. Ford uses it on vehicles with two PWM clutch pedal sensors, as listed in its 2020–23 gasoline OBD summary next to P08B6 (sensor B low), P08A9/P08AA (sensor A) and P08B9 (A/B correlation); the check is continuous and decides within one second. The clutch switch codes on the same page are marked non-MIL, the sensor codes are not. With a PWM output, high typically means the line is held at its pull-up level (100 % duty cycle), which points to an open signal or ground wire or a short to voltage. GM's published tables cover sensor A only. Effect for the driver: warning lamp, start-stop locked out. Common causes: Open signal or ground wire of sensor B, leaving the input at its pull-up level (high likelihood); Sensor B signal shorted to a voltage source (medium likelihood); Failed clutch pedal position sensor B (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp on; Start-stop disabled; Sensor B reading pinned at maximum in scan tool data. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P08B8 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P08B8: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P08B8 is intended for a second clutch pedal sensor whose signal drops out briefly or jumps without staying out of range. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB requires circuit and plausibility monitoring of such inputs. Likely culprits are worn connector terminals or a wire fatiguing where the harness moves with the pedal. Sensor A's counterpart is P08AB. Drivers may see start-stop drop out now and then. Common causes: Loose or worn terminals in the sensor B connector (high likelihood); Wire fatiguing where the harness flexes with pedal movement (medium likelihood); Sensor B producing glitches internally (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Start-stop dropping out intermittently; Warning lamp that comes and goes. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08B9 – Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A/B Correlation
text: P08B9: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A/B Correlation. P08B9 is stored when two independent measurements of the clutch pedal disagree. Ford uses it in two ways per its 2020–23 gasoline OBD summary: with dual PWM sensors it compares sensor A with sensor B and decides within a second; with a single analog sensor plus two clutch switches it covers an in-range rationality fault or any switch-related mismatch, the switch part being judged over about 40 clutch cycles at different speeds. FCA patented a similar cross-check of the pedal sensor against the clutch interlock switch, which disables electronic stop-start on a mismatch and cannot always tell which part failed. Circuit faults of each sensor have their own codes (P08A9/P08AA, P08B6/P08B7). Common causes: One of the two sensors drifting or worn so the channels no longer agree (high likelihood); Sticking or misadjusted clutch switch on systems with one sensor plus switches (medium likelihood); Corroded connector or wiring adding resistance to one channel (medium likelihood); Sensor assembly or pedal stop misaligned after repairs (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp on; Start-stop disabled; Cruise control unavailable. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P08BA – Pressure Control Solenoid L
text: P08BA: Pressure Control Solenoid L. Base code for the twelfth pressure control solenoid of an automatic transmission; which valve carries the letter L is up to the manufacturer. Toyota is the one documented user: bulletin T-SB-0094-24 for the 2024 Tacoma and Tacoma Hybrid lists it as P08BA71, actuator stuck, next to the stuck faults of solenoids A, C, D, G and H and a torque converter clutch stuck off. Because Toyota reports the fault type through the suffix, the stuck valve sits under this base code rather than under P08BB/P08BC. The MIL comes on. For trucks built before the production change Toyota's fix is a new transmission with torque converter, on the hybrid also the hybrid module. GM's Corvette dual clutch tables contain no L code. Common causes: Solenoid or its control valve sticking inside the valve body (high likelihood); Internal transmission fault from production, debris spreading through the hydraulics (medium likelihood); Contaminated or wrong transmission fluid (medium likelihood); Connector or harness fault at the solenoid (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Harsh, delayed or missing shifts; Transmission may hold a substitute gear. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08BB – Pressure Control Solenoid L Performance/Stuck Off
text: P08BB: Pressure Control Solenoid L Performance/Stuck Off. Set when pressure control solenoid L is commanded but the pressure or shift element it serves does not respond, i.e. the valve acts as if it were stuck in its off state. CARB requires such functional checks for transmission solenoids. P08BC is the opposite fault, P08BF to P08C2 cover the circuit. The driver notices missing or harsh shifts. Common causes: Valve spool held closed by debris or varnish (high likelihood); Low fluid level or weak supply pressure to the valve (medium likelihood); Leaking seal or circuit downstream of the valve (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Missing, slipping or delayed shifts; Possible substitute gear operation. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08BC – Pressure Control Solenoid L Stuck On
text: P08BC: Pressure Control Solenoid L Stuck On. Set when pressure control solenoid L keeps applying pressure although the control module has commanded it off, so the element it feeds stays loaded. No manufacturer publishes this code. Toyota, the only documented user of letter L, files a stuck valve under P08BA71 instead. GM's P08C5 for solenoid M of the Corvette dual clutch shows how such a check can work: after a selector valve change the module watches the shift rods, and unexpected movement of one rod or relaxation of another within 200 ms points to a valve that keeps pressure on. CARB lists transmission solenoids as monitored output components. P08BB is the stuck off counterpart. For the driver this means shift shock, binding or a fallback gear. Common causes: Valve spool held open by debris (high likelihood); Worn bore in the valve body letting pressure through (medium likelihood); Output stage or wiring keeping the solenoid energised (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Harsh engagement or binding during shifts; Transmission locked in a fallback gear. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08BD – Pressure Control Solenoid L Electrical

title: P08BE – Pressure Control Solenoid L Intermittent
text: P08BE: Pressure Control Solenoid L Intermittent. Reports a fault of pressure control solenoid L that comes and goes, typically a circuit that drops out briefly or a valve response that is only occasionally implausible. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and in earlier packages the intermittent codes of the other pressure control solenoids also proved unused. Toyota, the one documented user of letter L, publishes only P08BA71. GM's circuit tests for the comparable solenoid M confirm a fault only after it persists for 150 ms, which is why brief dropouts tend to surface as a stored circuit code instead. CARB requires transmission solenoids to be monitored. Loose pins and chafed wires are the likely causes; symptoms are occasional shift flare or a short-lived fallback mode. Common causes: Loose or spread terminal at the solenoid or transmission connector (high likelihood); Chafed wire touching ground intermittently (medium likelihood); Debris making the valve hang only now and then (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes; Occasional harsh or flaring shift. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08BF – Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit/Open
text: P08BF: Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit/Open. Points to an open control circuit of pressure control solenoid L: the module sees no load where the coil should be. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Toyota, the only known user of letter L, has published just P08BA71. GM's open-load test for the analogous solenoid M (P08C8) shows the method: with the low-side driver switched off, the coil should pull the sense pin up to battery voltage; if the driver chip can hold it between roughly 1.7 and 3 V with a tiny current, the circuit is open. Confirmation takes 150 ms. P08C1 and P08C2 are the short to ground and short to power. Typical results are a fallback gear and the warning light. Common causes: Connector loose, unplugged or corroded (high likelihood); Broken wire in the internal or external harness (medium likelihood); Solenoid coil burnt open (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Transmission in fallback gear. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08C0 – Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P08C0: Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit Range/Performance. Set when the control circuit of pressure control solenoid L is electrically intact but its behaviour is implausible, for example the current through the coil does not match the commanded value. title: P08C1 – Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit Low
text: P08C1: Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit Low. Reports a control circuit voltage of pressure control solenoid L that is too low, usually a short to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Toyota, the one documented user of letter L, has published only P08BA71. GM's equivalent for solenoid M (P08CA) illustrates the check: while the low-side driver is switched on, the sense pin is examined and a value below about 1.7 V is read as a short to ground, confirmed after 150 ms with battery voltage between 8.75 and 18 V. Depending on the wiring, a ground short can energise the valve permanently or make it uncontrollable. P08C2 is the high counterpart, P08BF the open circuit. Expect a fallback gear and the warning light. Common causes: Control wire chafed through to ground (high likelihood); Shorted turns in the solenoid coil (medium likelihood); Fluid or moisture in the connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Transmission in fallback gear. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08C2 – Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit High
text: P08C2: Pressure Control Solenoid L Control Circuit High. Reports a control circuit voltage of pressure control solenoid L that is too high, typically a short to battery voltage or to a neighbouring output. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Toyota, the one documented user of letter L, has published only P08BA71. GM's equivalent for solenoid M (P08CB) uses two tests: with the low-side driver on, a sense voltage above 0.7 to 1.1 V, depending on supply voltage, means a short to power; at shutdown each output is also switched on in turn to detect a short to a neighbouring output, which is then stored and reported at the next start. A shorted valve usually cannot be switched off. P08C1 is the low counterpart, P08BF the open circuit. Common causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage (high likelihood); Short between adjacent solenoid wires in the internal harness (medium likelihood); Defective output stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Transmission in fallback gear. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08C3 – Pressure Control Solenoid M
text: P08C3: Pressure Control Solenoid M. Base code for the thirteenth pressure control solenoid; the letter is assigned by the manufacturer. GM uses letter M in the Tremec eight-speed dual clutch of the Corvette (RPO M1L/M1M): its 2023–2025 TCM tables name the part synchronizer actuation valve 1, which serves the odd-gear shaft, while valves 2 to 5 report under P27B9 onwards. If it appears, the module has seen a non-specific fault of this valve; the driver typically notices the warning light and rough or missing gear changes on that shaft. Common causes: Valve sticking from debris in the valve body (high likelihood); Fault in the solenoid wiring or connector (medium likelihood); Worn or failed solenoid (low likelihood). title: P08C4 – Pressure Control Solenoid M Performance/Stuck Off
text: P08C4: Pressure Control Solenoid M Performance/Stuck Off. GM sets this code on the Corvette's Tremec dual clutch when synchronizer actuation valve 1, the valve for the odd-gear shaft, is hydraulically stuck off. The test runs inside a synchronizer recovery or integrity routine, started after a shift-related fault or when the stored gear does not match the sensed gears at start-up: the shift rods are moved slightly, and if a rod travels 100 µm or less where the valve should move it, a current profile check of the valve has to fail three times before the fault is confirmed. Type A, MIL at once. Bulletin 21-NA-033 blames debris; the fix is GDS valve cleaning three times, service clean and fast learn, and a new control valve body only if it returns. Common causes: Valve stuck closed by debris in the control valve body (high likelihood); Debris from a dislodged snap ring in the direct clutch assembly (bulletin 23-NA-197) (medium likelihood); Low system pressure or fluid level (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Odd gears not engaged or engaged late; Noise from the transmission area. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08C5 – Pressure Control Solenoid M Stuck On
text: P08C5: Pressure Control Solenoid M Stuck On. GM uses this code on the Corvette's Tremec dual clutch when synchronizer actuation valve 1, serving the odd-gear shaft, keeps pressure on although it is commanded off. The check runs whenever the selector pilot valve changes position: a valve stuck on keeps pushing a shift rod, so after the switch the pressure is routed elsewhere. If within 200 ms one rod moves unintentionally by 1000 µm or more while another relaxes by 125 µm or more, and both position sensors are electrically fine, the fault is set. Type A, monitored continuously. Bulletins 21-NA-033 and 23-NA-197 list it with the other valve codes; debris in the control valve body is the main cause. P08C4 is the stuck off counterpart. Common causes: Valve held open by debris in the control valve body (high likelihood); Debris from a dislodged snap ring in the direct clutch assembly (bulletin 23-NA-197) (medium likelihood); Worn valve bore in the control valve body (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Clunks or unwanted gear engagement on the odd shaft; Noise from the transmission area. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08CB – Pressure Control Solenoid M Control Circuit High

title: P08CC – Shift Solenoid J
text: P08CC: Shift Solenoid J. Base code for the tenth on/off shift solenoid of an automatic transmission; which valve gets the letter J is decided by the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford's gasoline OBD summary ends its shift solenoid list at SS E, the Genesis 8-speed bulletin stops at solenoid F, and GM and Toyota label their later valves as pressure control or clutch solenoids, so J stays unused in the known sources. CARB requires automatic transmission solenoids to be checked for functional response and circuit faults. A manufacturer reporting the fault type through a DTC suffix, as Toyota does for pressure control solenoid L, would store such faults under this base code instead of P08CD to P08D4. Expect harsh, missing or substitute-gear shifts. Common causes: Shift solenoid J faulty (coil or valve) (high likelihood); Contaminated or degraded transmission fluid restricting the valve (medium likelihood); Connector or harness fault between TCM and solenoid (medium likelihood); Transmission control module output fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Harsh, delayed or missing shifts; Transmission may hold a substitute gear. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08CD – Shift Solenoid J Performance/Stuck Off
text: P08CD: Shift Solenoid J Performance/Stuck Off. Set when shift solenoid J is switched on but the gear or clutch it controls does not respond, so the valve behaves as if stuck in its off position. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest documented analogue is GM's P0751 on the 6-speed transmissions: the TCM commands first gear and flags shift solenoid A stuck off when slip reaches 400 rpm with the gear ratio out of window, a two-trip fault. Ford sets P0751 to P0771 when the obtained gear or shift pattern shows a solenoid functionally failed off after three solenoid events. CARB requires this kind of functional check. P08CE is the opposite fault, P08CF and P08D1 to P08D4 cover the circuit. The driver notices slipping, flare or a missing gear. Common causes: Solenoid or its shift valve held in the off position by debris or varnish (high likelihood); Low fluid level or weak supply pressure to the valve (medium likelihood); Worn clutch pack or leaking seal in the circuit served by the valve (medium likelihood); Solenoid coil too weak to move the valve (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Engine flare or slipping during or after a shift; A gear is missing or skipped; Transmission may hold a substitute gear. title: P08CE – Shift Solenoid J Stuck On
text: P08CE: Shift Solenoid J Stuck On. Set when shift solenoid J is switched off but its clutch or shift valve stays applied, so the valve behaves as if stuck in its on position. Ford sets its stuck-on codes P0752 to P0772 from the gear or shift pattern actually reached. CARB requires such functional monitoring. P08CD is the opposite fault. Because an applied clutch can tie up the gearbox, drivers may feel a wrong gear, a harsh engagement or limp mode. Common causes: Solenoid or its shift valve held in the applied position by debris or varnish (high likelihood); Contaminated transmission fluid after internal wear (medium likelihood); Control circuit shorted so the solenoid stays energised (low likelihood); TCM output driver does not switch off (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Wrong gear or harsh engagement, possible binding feel; Transmission goes into limp mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08D0 – Shift Solenoid J Intermittent
text: P08D0: Shift Solenoid J Intermittent. Reserved for a shift solenoid J fault that comes and goes instead of being present continuously, typically brief circuit dropouts or erratic valve response. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and the intermittent codes of the earlier shift solenoids, such as P0754 for solenoid A, are not used in the GM and Ford sources checked either; those makers report dropouts through their open, short or functional codes. Ford runs its solenoid electrical checks continuously with 0.5 to 5 second filters, so short interruptions are caught there. CARB requires circuit monitoring of transmission output components in general. P08CF and P08D1 to P08D4 are the permanent electrical faults. Drivers notice occasional harsh shifts or a passing warning light. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector losing contact under vibration or heat (high likelihood); Chafed harness with intermittent short or break (medium likelihood); Valve sticking now and then due to contaminated fluid (medium likelihood); Solenoid coil failing only when hot (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes; Occasional harsh or delayed shifts; Sporadic limp mode that clears after restart. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08D2 – Shift Solenoid J Control Circuit Low
text: P08D2: Shift Solenoid J Control Circuit Low. Set when the TCM sees too little voltage on the control line of shift solenoid J, typically because the line or the coil is shorted to ground. Common causes: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Solenoid coil with internal short (medium likelihood); Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame (medium likelihood); Faulty output stage in the TCM (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Transmission holds a substitute gear; Harsh or missing shifts. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08D3 – Shift Solenoid J Control Circuit High
text: P08D3: Shift Solenoid J Control Circuit High. Which reading applies to J therefore depends on the maker. CARB requires the circuit check. P08D2 is the low-side counterpart, P08D4 the dedicated open-circuit code. A valve that cannot be driven correctly leads to wrong or missing gears. Common causes: Control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying conductor (high likelihood); Open solenoid coil (on systems that report opens as high) (medium likelihood); Moisture in the transmission connector bridging pins (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Wrong gear or harsh engagement; Possible limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08D4 – Shift Solenoid J Control Circuit/Open
text: P08D4: Shift Solenoid J Control Circuit/Open. Dedicated code for an open control circuit of shift solenoid J: the TCM drives the valve but no current flows through wire, connector or coil. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford detects such electrical faults when driver feedback disagrees with the command for 0.5 to 5 seconds. CARB requires open and short checks on transmission outputs. P08D2 and P08D3 are the short-circuit codes. An unpowered valve rests in its default state, so a gear may be missing or locked. Common causes: Broken control wire or loose terminal (high likelihood); Burnt-out solenoid coil (medium likelihood); Transmission connector not fully seated after service (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; One gear missing or transmission stuck in one gear; Harsh shifts. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08D5 – Shift Solenoid K
text: P08D5: Shift Solenoid K. Base code for shift solenoid K, the eleventh on/off shift valve in SAE's lettering. title: P08D6 – Shift Solenoid K Performance/Stuck Off
text: P08D6: Shift Solenoid K Performance/Stuck Off. Indicates that shift solenoid K was commanded on but the gear or clutch behind it never engaged, as if the valve stayed in its off position. Ford infers a solenoid failed off from the obtained gear or shift pattern over three solenoid events. CARB requires this functional check. The reverse fault is P08D7. Typical signs are engine flare during shifts and a skipped gear. Common causes: Valve or shift spool held in rest position by debris or varnish (high likelihood); Low fluid level or weak line pressure (medium likelihood); Leaking seal or worn clutch pack in the circuit fed by the valve (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Engine flare or slipping during shifts; A gear is skipped or missing. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08DB – Shift Solenoid K Control Circuit Low
text: P08DB: Shift Solenoid K Control Circuit Low. title: P08DD – Shift Solenoid K Control Circuit/Open
text: P08DD: Shift Solenoid K Control Circuit/Open. title: P08DE – Shift Solenoid L
text: P08DE: Shift Solenoid L. Base code for shift solenoid L, which in SAE's lettering would be the twelfth on/off shift valve of an automatic transmission. title: P08DF – Shift Solenoid L Performance/Stuck Off
text: P08DF: Shift Solenoid L Performance/Stuck Off. Typical causes are a valve jammed by debris, low line pressure or a leaking clutch circuit rather than wiring. CARB requires the check. P08E0 is the stuck-on fault. Expect flare or a missing gear. Common causes: Shift spool jammed by debris (high likelihood); Low line pressure or low fluid level (medium likelihood); Leak in the clutch circuit fed by the valve (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Engine flare between gears; Gear missing or skipped. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08E0 – Shift Solenoid L Stuck On
text: P08E0: Shift Solenoid L Stuck On. Functional fault of shift solenoid L in the opposite direction: although switched off, the valve keeps its circuit applied, leaving engaged a clutch that should be released. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB requires such functional checks. Electrical causes are rare here; a seized spool or an output stage that never switches off is more likely. P08DF is the stuck-off fault. Possible effects are tie-up, harsh shifts and limp mode. Common causes: Shift spool seized in applied position (high likelihood); Contaminated fluid after clutch or bearing wear (medium likelihood); TCM output stage does not switch off (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Drivetrain binding or harsh shifts; Limp mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P08E7 – Drive Motor A Clutch Enable Circuit
text: P08E7: Drive Motor A Clutch Enable Circuit. Covers the enable line with which a drive motor control module activates the actuator of a clutch that couples or uncouples electric drive motor A from the wheels. The code sets when the module sees an electrical fault on that line, typically an open circuit or an implausible state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest known hardware is the front electric drive unit of the 2024 Corvette E-Ray, which has a disconnect clutch actuator, a clutch pawl and a position switch; GM lists separate faults there, such as P08ED and a lost-communication code for the actuator. CARB requires circuit checks on such output components. P08E8 and P08E9 are the low and high variants. The driver usually loses electric assist on that axle. Common causes: Enable wire open or connector at the clutch actuator not seated (high likelihood); Internal electronics fault in the disconnect clutch actuator (medium likelihood); Corroded or water-damaged connector near the drive unit (medium likelihood); Faulty enable driver in the drive motor control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or hybrid system warning on; No electric drive or assist from the affected axle; All-wheel-drive or electric-only modes unavailable. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08EA – Drive Motor A Clutch Pawl Position Circuit
text: P08EA: Drive Motor A Clutch Pawl Position Circuit. Concerns the sensor or switch that reports where the pawl of the drive motor A disconnect clutch sits, i.e. whether the form-locking clutch is engaged or released. The code sets when the control module finds an electrical fault in that signal circuit, such as an open line or a signal outside its valid states. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM fits a drive motor disconnect clutch switch to the front drive unit of the Corvette E-Ray and blames it for P08ED; pawl clutches with dedicated position sensors are described in supplier patents such as one from Means Industries. Symptoms: Check engine light or hybrid system warning on; Electric drive or all-wheel drive unavailable; Reduced acceleration in hybrid modes. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P08ED – Drive Motor A Clutch Pawl Position Performance
text: P08ED: Drive Motor A Clutch Pawl Position Performance. title: P0904 – Gate Select Position Circuit A
text: P0904: Gate Select Position Circuit A. Circuit A of the gate select position sensor tells the control module of an automated manual gearbox where the shift mechanism stands in the select direction, i.e. which gate (for example 1-2, 3-4, 5-6 or reverse) is lined up. This generic circuit code sets when the module sees an electrical fault on that signal that is not covered by the more specific low, high or intermittent variants. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. Aisin AI and Isuzu patents describe such select stroke or select position sensors working next to an electric or hydraulic select actuator, and CARB requires circuit checks on transmission inputs of this kind. P0905 to P0908 are the siblings, P09A2 and P09A6 the same signal on circuits B and C. Without a valid gate signal the gearbox usually stops shifting or holds one gear. Common causes: Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at the gate select sensor or actuator unit (high likelihood); Chafed or broken sensor wiring near the gearbox (medium likelihood); Faulty gate select position sensor (often integrated in the shift and select actuator) (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input or reference supply in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Gearbox stops shifting or stays in one gear; Neutral indicator flashes or vehicle will not pull away. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0905 – Gate Select Position Circuit A Range/Performance
text: P0905: Gate Select Position Circuit A Range/Performance. Plausibility fault of the gate select position signal on circuit A in an automated manual gearbox. No manufacturer documents this code in freely citable material. title: P0906 – Gate Select Position Circuit A Low
text: P0906: Gate Select Position Circuit A Low. title: P0908 – Gate Select Position Circuit A Intermittent
text: P0908: Gate Select Position Circuit A Intermittent. Points to a gate select position signal on circuit A that drops out or jumps for short moments in an automated manual gearbox, too briefly or too irregularly for a steady low or high fault. Loose terminals, a damaged harness that moves with the engine, or moisture in the connector at the shift and select actuator are the usual reasons. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. An Aisin AI patent explains why even short sensor dropouts matter: if a stroke sensor fails while driving, the controller can no longer confirm the engaged gear and must switch to a fallback strategy. CARB requires circuit and rationality checks on such inputs. P0904 to P0907 are the steady faults of the same circuit. Drivers often notice occasional neutral drops or refused shifts that vanish again. Common causes: Loose or spread terminals at the sensor or actuator connector (high likelihood); Harness damage that only opens or shorts under engine movement (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector near the gearbox (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes; Occasional drop to neutral or refused shift; Fault often disappears after restarting the engine. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0909 – Gate Select Control Error
text: P0909: Gate Select Control Error. Set when the control module of an automated manual gearbox commands the select actuator to a new gate, but the measured select position does not reach the target within the allowed time and tolerance. Sensor and actuator circuits may be electrically fine; the fault lies in the closed loop as a whole. Typical reasons are a jammed or stiff select shaft or shift head, a worn or weak select motor, or a sensor offset. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. An Aisin AI patent describes select control with target and actual gates, and a Hyundai/Kia patent detects jammed or stuck shift actuators from motor current. CARB requires functional checks on such outputs. P0910 to P0913 are the actuator circuit faults, P0919 the same error in the shift direction. The gearbox may refuse gears or stay in neutral. Common causes: Stiff or jammed select shaft, shift head or internal selector mechanism (high likelihood); Worn select motor (brushes, gears) with too little force (medium likelihood); Select sensor offset or gate positions not relearned (medium likelihood); Weak battery or voltage drop on the actuator supply (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Certain gears cannot be engaged or gearbox stays in neutral; Clicking or whirring from the actuator without a gear change. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P090A – Clutch B Actuator Control Circuit/Open
text: P090A: Clutch B Actuator Control Circuit/Open. title: P0910 – Gate Select Actuator Circuit/Open
text: P0910: Gate Select Actuator Circuit/Open. Concerns the drive circuit of the gate select actuator, the motor or valve that moves the shift mechanism of an automated manual gearbox sideways from gate to gate. title: P0916 – Gear Shift Position Circuit A Low
text: P0916: Gear Shift Position Circuit A Low. title: P0917 – Gear Shift Position Circuit A High
text: P0917: Gear Shift Position Circuit A High. Set when the gear shift position signal on circuit A of an automated manual gearbox stays above its highest valid value for longer than a calibrated time. The signal line may be shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage, the sensor ground may be open, or the sensor itself may be faulty. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi patents show the shift stroke or shift position sensor as the feedback that confirms an engaged gear; with a reading above the valid band the controller can no longer tell neutral from an engaged gear. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P0916 is the opposite low fault, P091D and P095D are the high faults of circuits B and C, P0919 a shift movement that misses its target. Shifting is usually locked. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage (high likelihood); Open sensor ground or corroded ground pin (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the shift position sensor (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Gearbox stays in one gear or in neutral; Warning message about the transmission on the dashboard. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0918 – Gear Shift Position Circuit A Intermittent
text: P0918: Gear Shift Position Circuit A Intermittent. Flags a gear shift position signal on circuit A that drops out or jumps for short moments in an automated manual gearbox. The module sees implausible steps or brief losses that are too short or too irregular for a lasting low or high fault. Typical triggers are terminals that lose contact under vibration, a chafed harness moving with the powertrain, or moisture at the actuator connector. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi show the shift stroke sensor as the feedback that confirms an engaged gear. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0914, P0916 and P0917 are the steady electrical faults of circuit A, P0915 the plausibility fault. Shifts may abort or the gearbox may briefly fall back to neutral. Common causes: Connector at the shift sensor or actuator unit losing contact under vibration (high likelihood); Chafed or partially broken sensor wire near the gearbox (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (medium likelihood); Shift position sensor with an internal contact or track fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light comes and goes; Gear changes abort now and then or the gearbox drops to neutral; Fault often appears on rough roads or in wet weather. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0919 – Gear Shift Position Control Error
text: P0919: Gear Shift Position Control Error. Set when the control module of an automated manual gearbox drives the shift actuator towards a gear, but the measured shift position does not reach the target within the allowed time and tolerance. Sensor and actuator circuits can be electrically intact; the fault concerns the closed loop as a whole. Usual reasons are a stiff or jammed shift rail or synchroniser, a weak actuator, low hydraulic pressure on hydraulic units, or a sensor offset. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Hyundai/Kia patent detects jammed shift actuators from motor current, and an Isuzu patent controls the shift motor by stroke ranges using a shift stroke sensor. CARB requires functional checks on such outputs. P0909 is the same error in the select direction, P0920 to P0927 the actuator circuits. Gears may not engage. Common causes: Stiff or jammed shift rail, shift fork or synchroniser (high likelihood); Worn shift motor or leaking shift cylinder that no longer delivers full force (medium likelihood); Low pressure in the hydraulic supply on hydraulically actuated units (medium likelihood); Shift positions not relearned after actuator or module replacement (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning light on; Gear does not engage or engages only after a delay; Gearbox remains in neutral or locks in one gear. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P091A – Gear Shift Position Circuit B
text: P091A: Gear Shift Position Circuit B. Circuit B is a second channel reporting the shift position of an automated manual gearbox, for instance a redundant sensor track or a separate sensor on another shift rail. This general circuit code sets on an electrical fault on that signal that matches none of the more specific B variants. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, and which physical sensor carries the letter B depends on the design. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi describe shift stroke sensors as the feedback for gear engagement, an Aisin AI patent also covers the fallback when a stroke sensor fails. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P091B to P091D are the B siblings, P0914 and P095A the same signal on circuits A and C. Shifting may be restricted. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector at the shift position sensor (high likelihood); Damaged signal, supply or ground wire of sensor circuit B (medium likelihood); Faulty shift position sensor B (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission or engine warning light on; Slower or restricted gear changes in fallback mode; Gearbox may hold a gear or stay in neutral. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P091B – Gear Shift Position Circuit B Range/Performance
text: P091B: Gear Shift Position Circuit B Range/Performance. Plausibility fault of the shift position signal on circuit B in an automated manual gearbox. The voltage stays within its electrical limits, yet the value does not fit: it disagrees with circuit A, does not change while the shift actuator moves, or does not match the learned gear positions. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Nissan/Aichi patent notes that sensor mountings on shift parts can deform under vibration and falsify the reading, and an Aisin AI patent describes how the control continues when a stroke sensor is no longer trusted. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P091A, P091C and P091D are the electrical faults of circuit B, P0915 the same check on circuit A. Gear changes may be limited. Common causes: Worn or drifting shift position sensor, channels A and B disagree (high likelihood); Bent sensor bracket or displaced magnet on the shift rail (medium likelihood); Gear positions not relearned after actuator or module replacement (medium likelihood); Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning light on; Harsh or aborted gear changes; Fallback mode with fewer available gears. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0920 – Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit/Open
text: P0920: Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit/Open. Concerns the drive circuit that moves the shift mechanism of an automated manual gearbox in the forward shift direction. Depending on design this is one of two solenoid valves on a double-acting shift cylinder or one rotation direction of an electric shift motor. The code sets when the module finds this output open or electrically faulty, e.g. no current while the driver is on. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. A ZF patent feeds each chamber of a double-acting cylinder through its own 3/2 solenoid valve, an Isuzu patent turns the shift motor forward or reverse by shift direction. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0921 to P0923 are the siblings, P0924 the reverse direction. Gears in this direction can no longer be engaged. Common causes: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the shift actuator or valve (high likelihood); Broken drive wire between module and actuator (medium likelihood); Open solenoid coil or motor winding in the actuator (medium likelihood); Faulty driver stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning light on; Some gears cannot be selected, the gearbox skips them or stays in neutral; Vehicle may only move off in a limited set of gears. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0921 – Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0921: Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit Range/Performance. Plausibility fault in the drive circuit of the forward shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox. The circuit is neither open nor shorted, but current, voltage or the resulting movement do not fit the command, for example a current that is too high for the requested stroke or a shift position that hardly changes. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Hyundai/Kia patent explains that jamming raises the motor load of a shift actuator and must be caught early, and a ZF patent shows double-acting shift cylinders with one solenoid valve per chamber. CARB requires functional checks on such outputs. P0920, P0922 and P0923 are the clear electrical faults, P0925 the reverse direction, P0919 the missed target. Forward shifts become slow or fail. Common causes: Sticking shift valve, worn shift motor or stiff shift linkage (high likelihood); Solenoid or motor resistance out of specification (medium likelihood); Increased contact resistance in connector or wiring (medium likelihood); Insufficient hydraulic pressure on hydraulic units (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning light on; Slow, harsh or aborted gear changes in one direction; Fallback mode with fewer available gears. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0922 – Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit Low
text: P0922: Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit Low. Set when the drive circuit of the forward shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox shows a voltage that is too low for the current switching state. This usually points to a short to ground on a valve or motor line, or to an internal short in the actuator. Many controllers then switch the output off to protect the driver stage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A ZF patent drives each chamber of a double-acting shift cylinder through its own solenoid valve, and an Isuzu patent runs an electric shift motor in both directions, so a fault can affect one shift direction only. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0923 is the opposite high fault, P0920 the open circuit, P0926 the reverse direction. Gears in this direction are blocked. Common causes: Drive wire chafed through and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Internal short in solenoid coil or shift motor (medium likelihood); Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning light on; Certain gears can no longer be engaged; Gearbox may stay in neutral or hold one gear. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0923 – Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit High
text: P0923: Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit High. Set when the drive circuit of the forward shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox shows a voltage that is too high for the current switching state. Typical reasons are a valve or motor line shorted to battery voltage, or a driver stage in the module that no longer switches off; depending on circuit design an open load can also read high. A ZF patent describes double-acting shift cylinders whose chambers each have a 3/2 solenoid valve, and an Isuzu patent drives a shift motor forward or reverse by shift direction. An actuator that stays energised can hold or force a gear, so shifting is usually locked. Common causes: Drive wire shorted to battery voltage (high likelihood); Driver stage in the control module stuck on (medium likelihood); Open coil or winding read as high on some circuit designs (low likelihood). Symptoms: Transmission warning light on; Gearbox locks in one gear or refuses to shift; Possible grinding when a gear is pushed unintentionally. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0928 – Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A/Open
text: P0928: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A/Open. The module that drives the shift lock (brake transmission shift interlock, BTSI) sees no continuity on control circuit A, so it cannot reliably release the selector from Park. FCA/Chrysler uses the code as P0928-00 BTSI Control: bulletin 08-072-14 (2013-14 Ram 1500, 2014 Durango with 8-speed) and 21-034-15 (2015 Chrysler 300 rotary shifter) name it when the selector will not leave Park or the knob turns without the brake applied; the cure there is a new electronic shifter. P0929 is the plausibility fault, P0930 and P0931 the low and high faults of circuit A, P092A the same open fault on circuit B. The driver usually cannot shift out of Park until the fault clears or the manual release is used. Common causes: Internal fault in the electronic shifter module, often logged together with P0607 (documented by FCA) (high likelihood); Shift lock solenoid coil open (medium likelihood); Broken wire, poorly crimped or pushed-out terminal on the shift lock circuit (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Selector lever will not move out of Park even with the brake pressed; Problem may disappear after the ignition is switched off and the modules go to sleep; Rotary or electronic shifter can be moved without the brake applied; Shift position flashes or a message asks to return the selector to Park. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0929 – Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A Range/Performance
text: P0929: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A Range/Performance. Set when the shift lock actuator on circuit A is electrically present but does not respond as commanded, for example it fails to reach the locked or released position. Ford stores it in the gear shift module (GSM): SSM 51057 and 53039 list P0929:77 (commanded position not reachable) on Mach-E, Escape, Bronco Sport, Maverick and Transit, fixed by GSM software or replacement; TSB 25-2045 adds P0929:00, :07 and :9A on 2021-24 F-150 together with a selector that will not leave or enter Park, and checks pin 3 of connector C211. Ford shows the wrench lamp, not the MIL. P0928, P0930 and P0931 are the pure electrical faults of circuit A, P092B the same fault on circuit B. Common causes: Gear shift module software that misjudges the actuator position (Ford reprogramming bulletins) (high likelihood); Worn or binding lock actuator inside the shifter assembly (medium likelihood); Poor pin fit or damaged pin at the shifter connector (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Wrench or transmission warning lamp on; Selector will not leave Park or will not go back into Park; Clicking from the shifter or a selector that does not stow or unstow. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P092A – Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B/Open
text: P092A: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B/Open. Reports an open on control circuit B of the shift lock. P0928 is the same open fault on circuit A, P092B the plausibility fault, P092C and P092D the low and high faults of circuit B. Expect a lever that is locked in a position or no longer locked. Common causes: Broken wire or loose terminal on circuit B at the shifter (high likelihood); Open coil in the second lock solenoid (medium likelihood); Shifter connector not fully seated after console work (low likelihood). Symptoms: Selector lever locked in one position although the brake is pressed; Lock no longer engages, lever moves freely without brake; Warning message about the shifter or transmission. title: P092B – Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B Range/Performance
text: P092B: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B Range/Performance. title: P0931 – Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A High
text: P0931: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A High. The control module reads a voltage on shift lock circuit A that is higher than the commanded state allows. title: P0932 – Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit
text: P0932: Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit. General electrical fault in the circuit of the sensor that reports hydraulic pressure in the gearbox, usually line pressure in an automatic or system pressure in an automated manual or dual-clutch unit. The module sees a signal it cannot use at all, without a clear low or high pattern. Chrysler names it Line Pressure Sensor Circuit Fault; an ALLDATA case on a 2003 Grand Cherokee 4.7 automatic shows it together with P0935, caused by an open line pressure solenoid in the solenoid pack. CARB requires circuit checks on such transmission inputs. P0934 and P0935 are the low and high faults, P0933 the plausibility fault, P0936 the intermittent one. Expect harsh shifts, often with line pressure forced to maximum. Common causes: Fault in the solenoid pack or valve body module that carries the pressure sensor (open solenoid, internal lead frame) (high likelihood); Poor crimp or solder joint at the sensor connector terminals (medium likelihood); 5 V reference or sensor ground interrupted (medium likelihood); Transmission or powertrain control module fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light or transmission warning on; Harsh engagements and firm shifts from maximum line pressure; Possible limp mode with limited gears. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0933 – Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
text: P0933: Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Range/Performance. The pressure reading is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state. Chrysler RFE, RLE and TES transmissions set it when measured line pressure is more than 25 psi (172 kPa) above the commanded value while staying below the highest pressure ever used in that gear; Sonnax notes that a maximum-pressure condition from an open pressure control solenoid circuit can trigger it and mislead toward the sensor. Ferrari lists P0933 on its DCT as an invalid hydraulic pressure sensor signal, read in the NCR gearbox ECU. Neighbours: P0932, P0934 and P0935 are circuit faults, P0936 intermittent, P0869 a true high line pressure. The driver notices firm or harsh shifts. Common causes: Open circuit or fault in the line pressure control solenoid causing real excess pressure (high likelihood); Pressure sensor drifting or reading offset (medium likelihood); Worn or sticking valves in the valve body (medium likelihood); Wrong fluid level or degraded fluid (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh or firm engagements and shifts; Warning light on; Shift quality does not adapt and may stay rough. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0934 – Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0934: Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit Low. The pressure sensor signal sits below its valid window. Chrysler RFE transmissions feed the line pressure sensor with a 5 V reference and expect 0.35 to 4.75 V; P0934 sets when the signal stays at or below 0.35 V for 0.18 s, monitored continuously with the engine running. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a failed sensor. Ferrari also uses P0934 on its DCT, described as hydraulic pressure sensor signal too low. P0935 is the opposite high fault, P0932 the general circuit fault, P0933 plausibility and P0936 intermittent. Without a usable pressure signal the control usually raises pressure to a safe maximum, so shifts turn harsh. Common causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); 5 V reference open or shorted (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor or the solenoid pack carrying it failed (medium likelihood); Control module fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light on; Harsh shifts due to default maximum pressure; Possible limp mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0935 – Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit High
text: P0935: Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit High. The pressure sensor signal sits above its valid window. On Chrysler RFE transmissions the line pressure sensor normally reads between 0.35 and 4.75 V; P0935 sets when the signal stays at or above 4.75 V for 0.18 s with the engine running. That pattern points to a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, an open sensor ground or a sensor failed internally. An ALLDATA case on a 2003 Grand Cherokee logged it with P0932. Ferrari lists P0935 on its DCT as hydraulic pressure sensor signal too high. P0934 is the low counterpart, P0932 the general circuit fault, P0933 plausibility, P0936 intermittent. Expect harsh shifts and possibly a limp mode. Common causes: Sensor ground open or poor terminal contact (high likelihood); Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage (medium likelihood); Pressure sensor or solenoid pack failed internally (medium likelihood); Control module fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light on; Harsh shifts and engagements; Possible limp mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0936 – Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0936: Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent. The hydraulic pressure signal drops out or jumps for short periods, too briefly or irregularly for a lasting low or high fault. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The underlying sensor is the same one Chrysler uses for line pressure on RFE units and Ferrari for system pressure on its DCT, where the steady faults appear as P0934 and P0935. Gears Magazine names poor solder joints and crimps at the sensor terminals as a frequent source of intermittent pressure sensor codes. CARB requires circuit checks on such transmission inputs. P0932 to P0935 cover the general, plausibility, low and high faults. The driver may see a warning that comes and goes and occasional harsh shifts. Common causes: Poor crimp or solder joint at the sensor connector (high likelihood); Chafed harness making intermittent contact (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (medium likelihood); Sensor with an internal intermittent fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light comes and goes; Occasional harsh or erratic shifts. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0937 – Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P0937: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit. General electrical fault in the circuit of the temperature sensor for the hydraulic fluid of an automated gearbox, without a clear low or high pattern. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Ferrari shows where such a sensor sits: its DCT carries a radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor reported under P0938 to P0940 in the NCR gearbox ECU. The control needs this value to correct pressure and clutch fill for viscosity. CARB requires circuit checks on transmission sensors. P0938 is the plausibility fault, P0939 and P0940 low and high, P0941 intermittent; P0711 to P0713 cover the main transmission fluid temperature sensor. Shift quality may suffer and a warning appears. Common causes: Connector at the temperature sensor loose, corroded or oil-soaked (high likelihood); Damaged sensor wiring near the gearbox or cooler lines (medium likelihood); Temperature sensor failed (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Gearbox warning light on; Rougher shifts or clutch engagement, especially when cold. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0938 – Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
text: P0938: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Range/Performance. By J2012 wording the hydraulic oil temperature reading is electrically valid but implausible, for example frozen, rising too slowly after a cold start or disagreeing with other temperature values. Ferrari uses P0938 on its DCT for the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor, but describes it in its bulletin as no signal, an electrical fault rather than a plausibility check; the code is read in the NCR gearbox ECU. CARB asks for rationality checks on temperature inputs. P0937 is the general circuit fault, P0939 and P0940 the low and high faults, P0941 intermittent. A wrong temperature value leads to poorly matched clutch and shift pressures and may limit the cooling strategy. Common causes: Temperature sensor drifting or reacting sluggishly (high likelihood); Signal lost through connector or wiring fault (as in Ferrari's no-signal case) (medium likelihood); Real temperature anomaly from a cooler or thermostat fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Gearbox warning light on; Shift and clutch quality inconsistent with operating temperature. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0939 – Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0939: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit Low. The hydraulic oil temperature sensor signal sits below its valid window. With the usual NTC thermistor, a low voltage corresponds to an implausibly hot reading and typically comes from a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor shorted internally. Ferrari uses P0939 on its DCT for the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor, described as signal too low and read in the NCR gearbox ECU. CARB requires out-of-range checks on transmission sensors. P0940 is the high counterpart, P0937 the general circuit fault, P0938 plausibility and P0941 intermittent. Because the module believes the oil is very hot, it may reduce torque, change shift strategy or show an overheat warning. Common causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Temperature sensor shorted internally (medium likelihood); Control module input fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Gearbox warning or overheat message; Reduced performance or altered shift behaviour. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P093A – Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Circuit/Open
text: P093A: Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Circuit/Open. The control circuit of the solenoid that opens or locks a hydraulic accumulator in the gearbox is open. Such accumulators store pressurised fluid, for example to keep clutches applied during engine stop-start, as GM's patents on a stop-start accumulator and an accumulator with solenoid valve describe. No manufacturer documents P093A publicly. GM uses its own P171A for the same fault on the surge accumulator solenoid: failed if circuit impedance exceeds 200 kOhm in 32 of 40 samples, Type B with MIL after two trips. P093B and P093C are the low and high faults, P093D the performance fault. Stop-start is usually disabled, and the first restart may engage with a jolt. Common causes: Accumulator solenoid coil open (high likelihood); Connector unplugged or wire broken between module and solenoid (medium likelihood); Fault in the internal transmission harness or lead frame (medium likelihood); Output driver in the control module failed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light on (after repeated detection); Engine stop-start no longer active; Jolt or slip when driving off after an engine restart. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P093B – Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Circuit Low
text: P093B: Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Circuit Low. The control circuit of the hydraulic accumulator solenoid reads low, usually a control wire shorted to ground or a coil with very low resistance. No manufacturer documents P093B publicly. GM covers the same fault on its surge accumulator solenoid with P171B: failed short to ground when circuit impedance drops below 0.5 Ohm in 32 of 40 samples, Type B with MIL after two trips. The accumulator holds pressurised fluid so clutches stay applied during an engine auto-stop, as GM's stop-start accumulator patent explains. P093A is the open-circuit fault, P093C the high fault and P093D the performance fault. A grounded control line can leave the valve permanently energised, and stop-start is typically switched off. Common causes: Solenoid control wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Solenoid coil shorted internally (medium likelihood); Output driver in the control module failed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light on (after repeated detection); Engine stop-start no longer active; Harsh engagement after restart. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P093C – Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Circuit High
text: P093C: Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Circuit High. The control circuit of the hydraulic accumulator solenoid reads high, typically a control wire shorted to battery voltage so the driver cannot switch the valve as commanded. No manufacturer documents P093C publicly. GM covers the same fault on its surge accumulator solenoid with P171C: failed short to voltage when the circuit impedance criterion of 0.5 Ohm is met in 6 of 8 samples, Type B with MIL after two trips. GM's patent on an accumulator with solenoid valve shows how the valve holds or releases the stored fluid. P093A is the open circuit, P093B the low fault and P093D the performance fault. Stop-start is usually disabled; a valve that never closes cannot keep the accumulator charged during an auto-stop. Common causes: Solenoid control wire shorted to battery voltage (high likelihood); Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame (medium likelihood); Output driver in the control module failed (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light on (after repeated detection); Engine stop-start no longer active; Jolt when pulling away after a restart. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P093D – Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Performance
text: P093D: Hydraulic Accumulator Solenoid Performance. The accumulator solenoid circuit is electrically sound, but the accumulator system does not deliver the expected hydraulic result. No manufacturer documents P093D publicly. GM's comparable P171D on the 9-speed transmission watches turbine speed during an engine auto-start: if it exceeds a predicted value because holding clutches slip from too little stored pressure, it counts a failure, enabled between 0 and 110 °C transmission fluid temperature, Type B. Gears Magazine names a solenoid stuck open or closed, a leaking accumulator piston, clutch or valve body leakage and misplaced check balls as causes. P093A to P093C are the electrical faults. Stop-start is disabled and the restart may feel like a bang. Common causes: Accumulator solenoid stuck open (drains) or closed (no fill) (high likelihood); Accumulator piston or bore leaking (medium likelihood); Leakage at clutch seals or a worn valve body (medium likelihood); Missing or misplaced check ball after a rebuild (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine stop-start disabled; Lurch or bang when the engine restarts; Firm shifts with adaptive learning frozen. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0940 – Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit High
text: P0940: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit High. The hydraulic oil temperature sensor signal sits above its valid window. With an NTC thermistor this matches an extremely cold reading, typically from an open circuit, an unplugged connector, a broken ground or a short to a voltage source. Ferrari uses P0940 on its DCT for the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor, described as an electrical fault with signal too high, read in the NCR gearbox ECU. CARB requires out-of-range checks on transmission sensors. P0939 is the low counterpart, P0937 the general circuit fault, P0938 plausibility and P0941 intermittent. With a substitute value the gearbox works on, but clutch and shift pressures are no longer matched to the real oil temperature. Common causes: Open signal or ground wire, or connector unplugged (high likelihood); Temperature sensor open internally (medium likelihood); Signal wire shorted to a voltage source (low likelihood). Symptoms: Gearbox warning light on; Shifts or clutch engagements feel rough once warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0941 – Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0941: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent. The hydraulic oil temperature signal jumps or drops out briefly, too short or irregular for a lasting low or high fault. Since fluid temperature changes slowly, a sudden step is a clear sign of an electrical problem rather than a real temperature change. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ferrari's DCT bulletin shows the related sensor at the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet, with its steady faults under P0938 to P0940. CARB requires circuit checks on transmission sensors. P0937 is the general circuit fault, P0938 plausibility, P0939 and P0940 low and high. For the driver this means a warning that may come and go and shift quality that changes from one moment to the next. Common causes: Loose contact at the sensor connector under vibration or heat (high likelihood); Chafed wiring near hot gearbox or cooler parts (medium likelihood); Sensor with an intermittent internal fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light comes and goes; Shift quality varies unpredictably. Repair difficulty: medium.
