title: P0993 – Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0993: Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit Range/Performance. Pressure sensor or switch F is electrically intact, but its reading does not match what the module expects from the commanded clutch state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest documented logic is GM's for switch E (TFP switch 5, 6T70/6T75): the module checks after each clutch release whether the switch returns to its exhausted state and counts failures, at 50 kPa or less commanded pressure for the low case. A sixth switch would be checked the same way, plausibility against commanded pressure and gear, which CARB requires for transmission inputs. Typical causes are sticking regulator valves, debris and worn switch films rather than wiring. P0992 is the plain circuit fault, P0994/P0995 are low and high. Common causes: Sticking clutch regulator valve feeding the switch (high likelihood); Worn or delaminated switch film, debris in the switch (medium likelihood); Low or contaminated transmission fluid (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh or flared shifts; Shift adaptation frozen; Warning light depending on calibration. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0994 – Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit Low
text: P0994: Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit Low. The signal of pressure sensor or switch F stays low. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. With a normally closed switch as described by Sonnax for GM's valve body modules, low means the contacts stay closed, so the module sees no pressure where pressure should be, or the signal wire is shorted to ground. GM's equivalent for switch E, P0989, flags a low signal when commanded pressure is 50 kPa or less and handles it as Special No Trip without MIL; Saab's 9-4X text gives 0 V as the low state and 12 V as high. For an analogue sensor, low would mean a voltage below its valid range. CARB requires such out-of-range checks on transmission inputs. P0995 is the high counterpart. Common causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Switch stuck closed by debris or damaged film (medium likelihood); Clutch circuit not reaching pressure (valve or seal leak) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh or delayed shifts; Shift adaptation frozen; Possible limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0995 – Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit High
text: P0995: Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit High. GM's matching switch E code P0990 is a Special No Trip without MIL; Saab's 9-4X text treats an open and a short to voltage alike as high. CARB requires such checks on transmission inputs. P0994 is the low side. title: P0996 – Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit Intermittent
text: P0996: Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch F Circuit Intermittent. The signal of pressure sensor or switch F drops out or flickers for short moments without staying low or high. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and no transmission with a sixth pressure switch was found: GM's six-speeds end at switch 5 (E), Mitsubishi's 2019 six-speed uses letters B, D and E. Because such switches are thin film-and-piston units inside the valve body module, as Sonnax shows, debris or a delaminated film can make the contact chatter, and connector or harness faults do the same electrically. CARB requires transmission inputs to be checked for circuit faults; an intermittent code is the slot for faults too short to set P0994 or P0995. Expect occasional rough shifts, often without a warning light. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector contact (high likelihood); Debris or delaminated film making the switch chatter (medium likelihood); Chafed harness shorting or opening under vibration (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Stored fault, often without warning light; Occasional rough or flared shift. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0997 – Shift Solenoid F Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0997: Shift Solenoid F Control Circuit Range/Performance. The drive circuit of shift solenoid F works electrically but its measured current or voltage does not fit the command. No manufacturer was found to document this code. The users of the F block, Nissan's RE0F11A CVT and a 2019 Mitsubishi six-speed, list only P0998 and P0999. FCA's nine-speed bulletin 21-019-17 (2015 Chrysler 200 and Jeep Cherokee) shows how the slot is used for solenoids 2 to 5, with P0975, P0978, P0981 and P0984 for control circuit performance, but stops before a sixth solenoid. Genesis reports an electrical fault of its solenoid F under P2709 instead. CARB requires transmission outputs to be checked for proper function. P097F is the open circuit, P0998/P0999 low and high. Common causes: Solenoid coil resistance out of specification (high likelihood); High-resistance connector or harness contact (medium likelihood); Weak driver stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light depending on calibration; Missing or harsh shifts into gears using this solenoid; Possible limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0998 – Shift Solenoid F Control Circuit Low
text: P0998: Shift Solenoid F Control Circuit Low. Low-voltage fault, typically a short to ground, in the control circuit of shift solenoid F. Two makers document it. Mitsubishi's 2019 service manual for a six-speed automatic names P0998/P0999 the low clutch shift solenoid valve system and counts it among faults that can cause gear ratio errors. CARB requires transmission outputs to be checked for circuit faults. P0999 is high, P097F open. Common causes: Solenoid or valve body (control valve) internal fault (high likelihood); Control wire shorted to ground in harness or connector (medium likelihood); Transmission control module driver fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; Limp mode or loss of a gear range; Harsh engagement or flare when shifting. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P099B – Shift Solenoid G Control Circuit Low
text: P099B: Shift Solenoid G Control Circuit Low. Low-voltage fault, usually a short to ground, in the control circuit of shift solenoid G. Mitsubishi's 2019 service manual for a six-speed automatic uses it for the low-reverse brake shift solenoid: with transmission relay voltage at 2 V or more and the solenoid commanded on, the module sets P099B if the actual voltage stays below 3.7 V for 0.5 s. The check runs continuously; the solenoid is normally energised only in reverse and first-gear coasting. Nissan lists P099B as shift solenoid G in bulletin NTB15-037 for the 2012–2017 Versa, Versa Note and Sentra with the RE0F11A CVT and replaces the control valve when diagnosis confirms it. P099C is the high side, P09A0 the generic open. Common causes: Control wire shorted to ground in harness or connector (high likelihood); Shorted solenoid inside the valve body (medium likelihood); Transmission control module driver fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light; No reverse or no engine braking in first gear (Mitsubishi); Limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P099C – Shift Solenoid G Control Circuit High
text: P099C: Shift Solenoid G Control Circuit High. High-voltage fault in the control circuit of shift solenoid G. Mitsubishi's 2019 six-speed uses P099C for an open circuit of the low-reverse brake shift solenoid: with the solenoid commanded off and transmission relay voltage of 2 V or more, a reading of 3.7 V or more for 0.5 s sets the code. Causes named are the harness, connectors, the TCM and the solenoid in the valve body. Nissan lists P099C as shift solenoid G for the 2012–2017 Versa, Versa Note and Sentra with the RE0F11A CVT, with control valve replacement as the fix. P099B is the low side, P099A performance. Symptoms: Check engine light; No reverse or harsh reverse engagement (Mitsubishi); Limp mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A2 – Gate Select Position Circuit B
text: P09A2: Gate Select Position Circuit B. General electrical fault on the second gate select position signal (circuit B) of an automated manual gearbox. The published designs from Isuzu (one select potentiometer) and Aisin AI (one select stroke sensor) show only a single sensor, so it is not documented whether B is a redundant second track of that sensor or a separate sensor. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P09A4 and P09A5 are the more specific low and high faults of circuit B, P09A3 its plausibility fault; unlike circuit A (P0908) there is no intermittent variant. P0904 and P09A6 cover circuits A and C. Expect shifting to be restricted. Common causes: Loose, corroded or wet connector at the select sensor or actuator unit (high likelihood); Chafed or broken signal wire of circuit B near the gearbox (medium likelihood); Faulty select sensor, often integrated in the shift and select actuator (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage for circuit B in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Gearbox shifts slowly or locks out certain gears; Gearbox stays in one gear or neutral. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A3 – Gate Select Position Circuit B Range/Performance
text: P09A3: Gate Select Position Circuit B Range/Performance. Plausibility fault of gate select circuit B: the signal is electrically valid but does not match what the module expects. That could be the reading of circuit A, the learned gate positions, or the target gate the module has commanded, as in the Aisin AI select control that compares actual and target gate. Which comparison applies depends on whether B is a redundant track or a separate sensor, and no manufacturer publishes that or uses this code in citable material. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P09A2, P09A4 and P09A5 are electrical faults of B, P0905 and P09A7 the same check on circuits A and C. A fallback mode with limited shifting is likely. Common causes: Worn or drifting select sensor, signal B no longer agrees with the reference (high likelihood); Gate positions not relearned after actuator, clutch or module replacement (medium likelihood); Contact resistance at connector pins distorting signal B (medium likelihood); Sluggish or worn select mechanism so the measured gate lags the commanded one (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Wrong gate selected or gears refused; Slow, jerky shifting in fallback mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A4 – Gate Select Position Circuit B Low
text: P09A4: Gate Select Position Circuit B Low. Set when the gate select signal on circuit B stays below its lowest valid value for longer than a calibrated time. Likely causes are a signal line shorted to ground, a lost sensor supply or an internal sensor short; with potentiometer sensors like the select position sensor in an Isuzu patent, an open signal wire often reads low too. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, nor whether B is a second track or another sensor. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A5 is the opposite fault, P09A2 the general circuit fault, P0906 and P09A8 the low faults of circuits A and C. If A and B are both low, look for a shared supply or ground. Common causes: Signal wire of circuit B chafed through and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Sensor reference supply interrupted or shorted (medium likelihood); Internal short or broken wiper in the select sensor (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Gear changes blocked or limited to a few gears; Transmission warning message in the instrument cluster. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A5 – Gate Select Position Circuit B High
text: P09A5: Gate Select Position Circuit B High. Indicates that the gate select signal on circuit B has stayed above its highest valid value for longer than allowed. Typical reasons are a short of the signal wire to the sensor supply or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or a defective sensor. No manufacturer publishes how it uses this code or what circuit B physically is. An Aisin AI patent shows the consequence of losing select feedback: warning, request to stop, then a limp-home in first gear. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A4 is the low counterpart, P09A2 the general fault, P0907 and P09A9 the high faults of circuits A and C. A gearbox that can no longer confirm its gate restricts shifting. Common causes: Signal wire of circuit B shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage (high likelihood); Open sensor ground or corroded ground pin (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the select sensor (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Gearbox stays in one gear or in neutral; Limp-home mode with very limited gear choice. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A6 – Gate Select Position Circuit C
text: P09A6: Gate Select Position Circuit C. Electrical fault on a third gate select position signal (circuit C) that fits none of the more specific C codes. Public AMT designs show far fewer channels: Aisin AI and Isuzu use one select sensor, and a Mannesmann Sachs patent combines motor encoders with an extra neutral position sensor. What a third channel is in practice remains open. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P09A7 to P09A9 are the plausibility, low and high faults of C; as with circuit B there is no intermittent variant. P0904 and P09A2 cover circuits A and B. Gear changes may be limited. Common causes: Loose, corroded or wet connector at the select sensor or actuator unit (high likelihood); Damaged signal wire of circuit C in the gearbox harness (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor supplying signal C (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage for circuit C in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Delayed or missing gear changes; Vehicle reluctant to pull away. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A7 – Gate Select Position Circuit C Range/Performance
text: P09A7: Gate Select Position Circuit C Range/Performance. Rationality fault on gate select circuit C: the value is electrically valid, yet it disagrees with the other select channels, the learned gate positions or the commanded movement. A Mannesmann Sachs patent shows why several select signals can exist: when one sensor fails, the remaining ones still allow controlled positioning before an emergency mode based on stored drive times takes over. No manufacturer documents this code or the role of circuit C publicly. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P09A6, P09A8 and P09A9 are electrical faults of C, P0905 and P09A3 the same check on A and B. The driver usually notices slower or restricted shifting. Common causes: Drifting or worn sensor so signal C disagrees with the other channels (high likelihood); Select positions not relearned after repair work on the actuator or gearbox (medium likelihood); Loose sensor mounting or magnet shifting the measured position (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in the connector of circuit C (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Slower or hesitant gear changes; Some gears no longer offered. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A8 – Gate Select Position Circuit C Low
text: P09A8: Gate Select Position Circuit C Low. The module stores this code when the gate select signal on circuit C remains below its valid range for a calibrated time. Common triggers are a signal wire shorted to ground, a missing sensor supply or an internal sensor fault; depending on the sensor type, a broken signal wire can read low as well. No manufacturer documents this code publicly or explains what circuit C measures. Patents from Isuzu and Aisin AI show the select sensor as the feedback the module needs to line up the right gate. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A9 is the high counterpart, P09A6 the general C fault, P0906 and P09A4 the low faults of A and B. Common causes: Signal wire of circuit C shorted to ground (high likelihood); Sensor supply for circuit C missing or pulled down (medium likelihood); Internal short in the sensor delivering signal C (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Gearbox holds one gear or drops to neutral; Transmission warning message in the instrument cluster. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P09A9 – Gate Select Position Circuit C High
text: P09A9: Gate Select Position Circuit C High. Logged when the gate select signal on circuit C sits above its highest plausible value for longer than a calibrated time. Usual suspects are a short to the sensor supply or battery voltage, an interrupted sensor ground, or a sensor with an internal fault. No manufacturer publicly documents this code, and the physical meaning of circuit C is not published either. An Aisin AI patent describes the fallback once select feedback is lost: warning, stop request and a limp-home in first gear. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P09A8 is the low counterpart, P09A6 the general C fault, P0907 and P09A5 the high faults of A and B. Shifting is usually curtailed. Common causes: Signal wire of circuit C shorted to supply or battery voltage (high likelihood); Open or corroded sensor ground (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the sensor delivering signal C (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage in the transmission control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning light on; Limp-home mode, often in a single low gear; Gear changes refused while driving. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A00 – Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0A00: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit. General circuit fault on temperature sensor A in the separate coolant loop that cools the inverter and other drive electronics of a hybrid or electric vehicle. The module flags it when the sensor signal cannot be used at all, without a more specific low, high or plausibility verdict; those cases have their own codes P0A01 to P0A04. No manufacturer documents P0A00 publicly. GM's Two-Mode hybrid trucks monitor the same sensor only through P0A01 to P0A03, and CARB requires every input of the inverter thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. Without a valid reading the control unit usually limits electric drive power to protect the electronics. Common causes: Corroded or loose connector at the sensor in the inverter coolant loop (high likelihood); Temperature sensor element failed (medium likelihood); Damaged signal or reference wire between sensor and hybrid control module (medium likelihood); Fault in the input stage of the hybrid or inverter control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning light; Reduced electric drive power; Inverter coolant pump or radiator fan running constantly as a precaution. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A01 – Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A01: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. The sensor delivers a value inside its electrical range, but it does not fit the other temperatures in the vehicle. GM uses this code on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado and Sierra as a cold-start test: after the vehicle has stood for more than 28,800 s (8 h), the power electronics coolant temperature at power-up may differ from engine coolant temperature by no more than 30 °C, provided engine coolant and intake air agree within 15.75 °C. A failure is a Type B code with MIL after two trips. Nissan describes a similar comparison between inverter coolant and power element temperatures. Hard electrical faults are P0A02 and P0A03. Common causes: Sensor characteristic drifted, reading offset against the other temperature sensors (high likelihood); Added resistance at a corroded connector shifting the reading (medium likelihood); Low coolant or air pocket at the sensor in the electronics loop (medium likelihood); Fault actually in the engine coolant or intake air sensor used for comparison (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light after two trips; Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour; Electric drive power limited when the electronics are hot. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A02 – Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0A02: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low. The signal voltage of the coolant temperature sensor in the electronics loop sits below its valid window. Because the sensor is an NTC thermistor, a low voltage means an implausibly hot reading, typically a short to ground. GM uses P0A02 on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado and Sierra: the converted temperature reaches the 162.1 °C limit in 30 of 50 samples taken every 100 ms, after more than 10 s of propulsion active and with no intake air sensor fault (P0112, P0113) present. It is a Type B code with MIL after two trips. The opposite fault is P0A03. Expect a warning light and possibly reduced electric power. Common causes: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Internal short in the thermistor (medium likelihood); Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging signal to ground (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light; Displayed electronics temperature extremely high although the system is cool; Cooling fans and pump running at full output, drive power limited. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A03 – Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0A03: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High. The sensor signal voltage is above its valid window, which for an NTC thermistor reads as an impossibly cold coolant temperature. Typical reasons are an open circuit in the sensor or its wiring, or a short to a voltage source. GM monitors this on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado and Sierra with a limit of -59.1 °C, counted as 30 failures in 50 samples at 100 ms intervals once propulsion has been active for over 10 s and the intake air sensor codes P0112 and P0113 are clear; Type B, MIL after two trips. P0A02 covers the reverse case. Because the system cannot see real heat any more, it often reduces electric power as a precaution. Common causes: Connector unplugged, loose or with a pushed-back terminal (high likelihood); Broken signal or ground wire of the sensor (medium likelihood); Thermistor element open internally (medium likelihood); Signal wire shorted to a voltage supply (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light; Electronics temperature shown far below ambient; Reduced electric drive power as a safeguard. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A04 – Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A04: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. The temperature signal from the drive electronics coolant loop jumps or drops out for short moments, then returns to normal. Coolant temperature changes slowly, so a sudden step that the physics cannot explain points to a loose contact rather than a real temperature change. No manufacturer documents P0A04 publicly. GM's Two-Mode hybrids check the same sensor only for steady faults (P0A01 to P0A03), and a Nissan patent shows how an inverter coolant sensor is compared with the power element temperature to catch implausible readings. CARB requires such inverter cooling inputs to be monitored. The driver may see a warning light that comes and goes, with occasional power reduction. Common causes: Loose or fretting terminal at the sensor or module connector (high likelihood); Partly broken wire that opens under vibration or heat (medium likelihood); Sensor with an internal intermittent contact (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning light that appears and disappears; Short, unexplained drops in electric drive power; Stored code with no steady fault on re-test. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A05 – Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit/Open
text: P0A05: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit/Open. The electric pump that circulates coolant through the inverter, converter and drive motor loop is driven by a control line from the hybrid module. P0A05 means that line shows an open circuit or a fault the driver cannot classify further. No manufacturer documents P0A05 publicly. GM's Chevrolet Volt tables cover the same pump under P0CE9, set when the control line is open or shorted in 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms, Type B with MIL after two trips. CARB requires inverter cooling outputs to be checked, and Toyota patents describe how pump faults are told apart from other cooling faults. Low and high faults are P0A06 and P0A07; pump B is P0B38. Without circulation the electronics heat up quickly and power is cut. Common causes: Pump connector loose or corroded, often from road splash at the low-mounted pump (high likelihood); Broken control wire between module and pump (medium likelihood); Failed electronics or open winding inside the pump (medium likelihood); Blown pump fuse or missing supply, so the control input sees no load (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine light; Electric drive power reduced, especially in warm weather or under load; Follow-up inverter overtemperature codes such as P0A93. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A06 – Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low
text: P0A06: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low. The control line of pump A in the drive electronics coolant loop sits at a voltage below what the module expects for the commanded state, usually because the line or the pump input is shorted to ground. Depending on the driver design, the pump then runs uncontrolled or not at all. No manufacturer documents P0A06 publicly; GM's Volt reports a short of the comparable pump control line under P0CE9 (16 of 20 samples at 250 ms, Type B). CARB requires circuit checks of inverter cooling outputs, and Toyota patents show why a failed pump must be separated from radiator or fan faults. P0A05 is the open case, P0A07 the short to voltage. A failing pump soon leads to power reduction. Common causes: Control wire chafed against the body and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Internal short at the pump's control input (medium likelihood); Water or coolant in the pump connector (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine light; Electronics temperature rising quickly, power limited; Pump silent when commanded on, or running continuously. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A07 – Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High
text: P0A07: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High. The module measures a voltage on the pump A control line that is higher than the commanded state allows, typically because the line touches a supply wire or the pump input has failed internally. The pump in the inverter and motor cooling loop may then be stuck on or never receive a valid command. No manufacturer documents P0A07 publicly. GM's Volt flags a short to voltage on its equivalent pump line as P0CE9, with 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms and a two-trip MIL. CARB requires inverter cooling outputs to be monitored for such circuit faults; Toyota patents describe pump speed and coolant flow checks for the same loop. P0A05 and P0A06 cover open and short to ground. Common causes: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition supply wire (high likelihood); Pump control electronics failed, pulling the input high (medium likelihood); Output driver in the control module damaged (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine light; Pump running all the time, even with the vehicle off; Possible power limitation if cooling cannot be confirmed. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A08 – DC/DC Converter Status Circuit
text: P0A08: DC/DC Converter Status Circuit. General fault on the status line through which the DC/DC converter reports its condition to the hybrid control module. The converter replaces the alternator: it steps the traction battery voltage down to charge the 12 V battery. When its self-diagnosis detects an internal problem it signals this back, and the controller reacts. P0A08 is the broad verdict for an unusable or implausible status signal; a signal stuck low or high has its own codes P0A09 and P0A10. No manufacturer documents P0A08 publicly in an official source. Toyota's Prius c recall shows the consequence of a dead converter: warning lights, then a draining 12 V battery that can shut the hybrid system down. Drivers should not keep driving for long. Common causes: Internal fault in the DC/DC converter reported by its self-diagnosis (high likelihood); Damaged or corroded status line or connector between converter and hybrid control module (medium likelihood); Converter overheating due to a fault in the inverter/converter coolant loop (low likelihood); Faulty input stage in the hybrid control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system, battery or master warning light on; 12 V battery is no longer charged and voltage drops while driving; Electrical consumers fail and the hybrid system may finally shut down. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A09 – DC/DC Converter Status Circuit Low
text: P0A09: DC/DC Converter Status Circuit Low. The status signal that the DC/DC converter sends to the hybrid control module stays below its expected range, typically from a short to ground, an open line read as low, or a converter that pulls its status output down because of an internal fault. Mitsubishi uses P0A09 on the 2012-2013 i-MiEV for a DC-DC converter fault; its bulletins tie it to a failed on-board charger that blows the high-voltage fuse feeding the converter, after which the 12 V battery and drive battery stop charging. That usage predates the current split into P0A08, P0A09 and P0A10. Siblings: P0A08 covers the general circuit fault, P0A10 a signal stuck high. Expect warning lights and a 12 V battery that slowly runs flat. Common causes: Blown high-voltage fuse feeding the converter, e.g. after an on-board charger failure (Mitsubishi i-MiEV) (high likelihood); DC/DC converter internal fault pulling the status output low (medium likelihood); Status line shorted to ground or chafed harness (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage in the hybrid/EV control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Power unit, battery or hybrid warning light on; 12 V battery not charged, voltage drops; On EVs the drive battery may also stop charging. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A0A – High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A
text: P0A0A: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A. The high-voltage interlock loop (HVIL) is a low-voltage signal loop routed through every HV connector, the service disconnect and component covers. If it opens, the control module opens the main contactors so no one can touch live parts. P0A0A is the general circuit fault on loop A. Stellantis sets P0A0A-00 on the Jeep Wrangler and Grand Cherokee 4xe when an HV connector is torqued but not fully seated after repair, and on the 2024-2025 Pacifica Hybrid it was traced to battery pack control module software; there the car will not start on either power source. Mercedes logs P0A0A00 in the DC converter of model line 243. CARB counts the HVIL as a safety-only system, so MIL behaviour varies. Low, high, performance and intermittent faults use P0A0B to P0A0E. Common causes: HV connector or service disconnect not fully seated after repair (high likelihood); Spread, bent or corroded interlock pins or damaged connector seals (medium likelihood); Interlock wiring chafed or cut (medium likelihood); Battery pack control module software fault (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid 2024-2025) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle will not start or go into ready mode; Check engine and hybrid system warning on; High-voltage system switched off while the 12 V system still works. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A0B – High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Performance
text: P0A0B: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Performance. The interlock loop A responds electrically, but its behaviour does not match what the module expects – for example a loop resistance outside the window, a signal that does not follow the commanded test pattern, or two modules on the same loop disagreeing. Mercedes-Benz logs P0A0B00 in the battery management system, the DC converter and the on-board charger of model line 243 when the vehicle will not start; its listed causes include oxidised interlock pins in the low-voltage connectors, twisted or chafed harnesses and bent pins on HV components. Patent literature explains why voltage-based loops are prone to false alarms from contact resistance and interference. Unlike P0A0C/P0A0D this is not a clear short. Expect the HV system to stay off. Common causes: Oxidised interlock pins in low-voltage connectors raising loop resistance (high likelihood); Improperly connected HV connector or bent interlock pins on an HV component (medium likelihood); Twisted or chafed interlock harness rubbing on the body (medium likelihood); Faulty interlock driver or receiver in a control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle cannot be started; High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster; Several modules store interlock codes at the same time. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A0C – High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Low
text: P0A0C: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Low. The voltage sensed on interlock loop A is too low while the module drives the loop – typically an opened loop or a short to ground. GM documents it codegenau: in its 2016 HPC2 table P0A0C sets when the sensed interlock voltage stays below 30 % of the 5 V test signal in 2 of 2 samples (12.5 ms each) with the 12 V supply above 10.2 V; it is Type A, so the MIL lights after one trip. The 2011 Volt tables used a 10 % threshold. Mercedes-Benz model line 243 stores P0A0C00 in the DC converter and on-board charger as a short to ground in the interlock circuit. The opposite fault is P0A0D. Since the loop guards against live HV parts, the system drops the contactors and the car will not drive on electric power. Common causes: HV connector, cover or service disconnect open, interrupting the loop (high likelihood); Interlock wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed at a module or the body (medium likelihood); Corroded or pushed-back interlock pins (medium likelihood); Faulty interlock source or sense stage in the battery or hybrid module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light (GM Type A) and hybrid/EV warning; No ready mode, electric drive unavailable; Charging may be blocked. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A0D – High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A High
text: P0A0D: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A High. The voltage sensed on interlock loop A is higher than expected – most often a short to a voltage source, or the loop not being pulled down when the module expects it. GM checks both states: in the 2016 HPC2 table P0A0D sets when the sensed voltage exceeds 24 % of 5 V with the source switched off (5 of 8 samples) or 44 % with it switched on (4 of 6 samples), Type A with MIL after one trip. Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid 2011-2015 bulletins send P0A0D straight to the HEV safety plug, alongside high-voltage path and relay codes, with check engine light and no ready mode. Mercedes model line 243 stores P0A0D00 in the battery management as a short to positive. P0A0C is the low-side counterpart; both leave the HV system switched off. Common causes: Service/safety plug not fully inserted or with poor contact (Hyundai Sonata Hybrid) (high likelihood); Interlock wire shorted to a 12 V or reference voltage (medium likelihood); Damaged interlock harness or connector after body or battery work (medium likelihood); Faulty interlock stage in the battery or hybrid control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: No ready mode or ready light blinking; Check engine and charging warning lights on; Vehicle cannot be started. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A0E – High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Intermittent
text: P0A0E: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Intermittent. The interlock loop A signal drops out or jumps for short moments and then recovers, so the module sees an unstable loop rather than a lasting open or short. Typical are connectors with loose or spread contacts, harness sections that move with the body or drivetrain, and moisture in seals. No manufacturer documents P0A0E publicly; the GM tables only list P0A0C and P0A0D for the same loop. Reference designs and patents on interlock monitoring describe the loop as a current or voltage path through each HV connector and point out that contact resistance and interference can cause brief false trips. CARB treats the HVIL as a safety-only system. For the driver this means sudden HV shutdowns or no-starts that come and go; static faults use P0A0A to P0A0D. Common causes: Loose or spread interlock contacts in an HV or low-voltage connector (high likelihood); Harness section with a broken strand that opens under vibration (medium likelihood); Moisture entering through a damaged connector seal (medium likelihood); Electrical interference on the interlock line or a weak module input (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid/EV warning that appears and disappears; Occasional loss of ready mode or sudden shutdown of electric drive; Intermittent no-start, often after rough roads or rain. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A0F – Engine Failed to Start
text: P0A0F: Engine Failed to Start. The control module commanded an engine start – by the hybrid system or an automatic start/stop restart – but the combustion engine did not reach a self-sustaining run within the allowed attempts. The code describes the result, not the cause. Toyota sets P0A0F with MIL on the 2010-2013 Prius and Prius v when a separated purge VSV/PCV hose leans out the mixture, often with P3190, P3191 and P0171. Kia traced P0A0F on the 2017-2018 Niro hybrid to an A/C pressure sensor harness chafed by an idler pulley, which disturbs the engine ECU 5 V reference. Audi sets P0A0F00 on 2019 A6/A7 3.0 mild hybrids after the second failed automatic restart, with a drive system warning. Look at fuel, air, ignition and engine sensor faults first. Common causes: Vacuum leak, e.g. separated purge VSV/PCV hose at the throttle body (Toyota Prius) (high likelihood); Shorted sensor harness pulling down the engine ECU 5 V reference (Kia Niro) (medium likelihood); Fuel delivery or ignition fault preventing combustion (medium likelihood); Failed automatic restart of a mild hybrid with a cold engine (Audi A6/A7 2019) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light and hybrid or drive system warning; Engine does not start, or runs briefly and stops; Reduced power because the vehicle runs on the battery only. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A10 – DC/DC Converter Status Circuit High
text: P0A10: DC/DC Converter Status Circuit High. The status signal from the DC/DC converter to the hybrid control module sits above its valid range, typically because the line is shorted to a voltage source, its ground or pull-down path is open, or the converter drives the output high after an internal failure. The converter supplies the 12 V system from the traction battery, and its self-diagnosis reports problems over this status path. No manufacturer documents P0A10 publicly in an official source; older lists that call it a hybrid battery voltage sense circuit are wrong for today's J2012. Siblings: P0A08 is the general status fault, P0A09 the low signal. A converter that stops working shows up as warning lights and a falling 12 V voltage until the hybrid system shuts down. Common causes: Status line shorted to 12 V or another supply (medium likelihood); Open ground or signal return at the converter connector (medium likelihood); DC/DC converter internal fault driving the status output high (medium likelihood); Faulty input stage in the hybrid control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or battery warning light on; 12 V battery voltage falls while driving; Possible shutdown of the hybrid system if the 12 V battery runs flat. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A11 – DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit/Open
text: P0A11: DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit/Open. General or open-circuit fault on the enable line with which the hybrid or battery control module tells the DC/DC converter that it may deliver power to the 12 V system. In typical designs a high enable level permits converter output, and a CAN message carries the same permission in parallel, so the two can be cross-checked. If the line is open, the converter cannot be switched on reliably and the 12 V battery is no longer charged. No manufacturer documents P0A11 publicly in an official source; Honda's hybrid recall shows what follows when the converter shuts down: charging warning, discharged 12 V battery, possible loss of drive. Low and high faults on the same line are P0A12 and P0A13; status line faults are P0A08 to P0A10. Common causes: Broken enable wire or unplugged connector between control module and converter (high likelihood); Corroded or pushed-out terminal at the converter enable pin (medium likelihood); Faulty enable output driver in the control module (low likelihood); Faulty enable input inside the DC/DC converter (low likelihood). Symptoms: Battery or charging warning light on; 12 V battery is not charged and runs down; Vehicle may lose motive power after a while. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A12 – DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit Low
text: P0A12: DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit Low. The enable line to the DC/DC converter reads low when the control module is commanding it on. Because a low enable level usually means converter output is not permitted, the converter stays off and the 12 V system loses its charging source. Typical causes are a short to ground on the enable wire, a weak output driver in the module, or an input stage in the converter that loads the line. Older lists name this code DC/DC converter communication; today's J2012 wording is enable circuit low. No manufacturer documents P0A12 publicly in an official source, so the description rests on CARB and on patent descriptions of hard-wired enable lines. P0A11 covers an open line, P0A13 a line stuck high. Drivers see a charging warning and a draining 12 V battery. Common causes: Enable wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Weak or failed enable output driver in the control module (medium likelihood); Converter enable input internally shorted (low likelihood). Symptoms: Charging or battery warning light on; 12 V voltage drops, electrical consumers misbehave; Hybrid system may shut down when the 12 V battery is flat. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A13 – DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit High
text: P0A13: DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit High. The enable line to the DC/DC converter reads high when the control module expects it low, for example while the converter should be switched off. The usual reasons are a short to battery voltage on the enable wire, a stuck output driver, or a missing pull-down. Since a high enable level normally permits converter output, the converter may keep running when it should not – during shutdown, a fault or high-voltage disconnection – which the module treats as a safety and battery-drain risk. No manufacturer documents P0A13 publicly in an official source; the explanation relies on CARB and on patents describing hard-wired DC/DC enable lines cross-checked against a CAN request. P0A11 is the open line, P0A12 the low fault; status-side faults are P0A08 to P0A10. Common causes: Enable wire shorted to 12 V or another supply (high likelihood); Enable output driver in the control module stuck on (medium likelihood); Open pull-down or ground reference at the converter input (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or battery warning light on; 12 V battery drains while the vehicle is parked; Converter-related functions disabled as a precaution. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A14 – Engine Mount A Control Circuit/Open
text: P0A14: Engine Mount A Control Circuit/Open. Some vehicles use switchable or active engine mounts that the powertrain or a mount control unit changes between soft and firm, or drives with an actuator against vibration. P0A14 reports an open or undefined fault in the control circuit of mount A. Ford lists it in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary as the active mount circuit check: the low-side driver reports the fault and it matures after about 5 seconds; mount B uses P0AB6 to P0AB8. Honda's active control engine mounts, for example on the 2008 Pilot V6, use P0A14 for the front mount actuator and P0AB6 for the rear. P0A15 and P0A16 cover low and high faults. The car stays drivable, but vibration may increase. Common causes: Mount actuator connector loose, corroded or unplugged after engine work (high likelihood); Open coil in the mount actuator or switching solenoid (medium likelihood); Wire broken where the harness flexes with engine movement (medium likelihood); Fault in the engine or mount control unit output (low likelihood). Symptoms: More vibration at idle or during cylinder deactivation; Warning light, depending on manufacturer; Shudder that feels like a torque converter problem. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A15 – Engine Mount A Control Circuit Low
text: P0A15: Engine Mount A Control Circuit Low. The control circuit of switchable or active engine mount A shows a voltage or current below the expected level, which usually points to a short to ground on the line or inside the actuator. Ford uses P0A15 in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary for the active mounts: the low-level driver reports the fault and the PCM matures it after about 5 seconds; the partner mount B has P0AB7. Honda's active control engine mount system on the 2008 Pilot V6 assigns P0A15 to the front mount actuator and P0AB7 to the rear. Ford engineers describe these mounts as switched between a damping and a stiffening mode, so a stuck mount is felt as vibration. The open circuit is P0A14, the high fault P0A16. Common causes: Control wire chafed on the engine or subframe and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Shorted coil in the mount actuator or solenoid, often after fluid leakage (medium likelihood); Moisture in the mount connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Noticeable vibration at idle or low speed; Warning light, depending on manufacturer; Cylinder deactivation may be suppressed. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A16 – Engine Mount A Control Circuit High
text: P0A16: Engine Mount A Control Circuit High. The module sees a higher voltage on the control circuit of engine mount A than it should for the commanded state, usually a short to a supply line or a failed actuator input. The mount can then no longer be switched or driven as intended. Ford lists P0A16 in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary under the active mount circuit check, matured after about 5 seconds once the driver reports the fault; mount B uses P0AB8. On Honda's active control engine mounts, such as the 2008 Pilot V6, P0A16 belongs to the front mount actuator and P0AB8 to the rear one. A Ford patent shows the mounts are toggled between soft and firm, so a fault means either harsh idle or more movement. See P0A14 and P0A15. Common causes: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition supply (high likelihood); Mount actuator or solenoid failed with an open low side (medium likelihood); Driver stage in the engine or mount control unit damaged (low likelihood). Symptoms: Harsh idle or more engine movement on take-off; Warning light, depending on manufacturer; Vibration during cylinder deactivation. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A17 – Motor Torque Sensor Circuit
text: P0A17: Motor Torque Sensor Circuit. Some electric drive units measure the torque on the motor or generator shaft directly, for example with a magnetostrictive sensor inside a hollow motor shaft as described in Honda patents for hybrid drive systems. The control unit uses that value to check the torque it commands. P0A17 is the general circuit fault of this sensor, set when the signal is missing or cannot be evaluated at all. No manufacturer documents P0A17 publicly. CARB requires a monitoring plan for drive motor faults that affect propulsion or emission strategies, which covers such feedback sensors. Plausibility is P0A18, low and high P0A19 and P0A20, intermittent P0A21. Expect reduced electric power and a hybrid warning. Common causes: Loose or corroded sensor connector at the drive unit (high likelihood); Damaged sensor wiring between drive unit and control module (medium likelihood); Torque sensor or its excitation electronics failed, often only replaceable with the drive unit (medium likelihood); Input stage of the hybrid or motor control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Electric drive power limited or electric drive disabled; Higher fuel consumption because the engine runs more often. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A18 – Motor Torque Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A18: Motor Torque Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. The motor torque sensor delivers an electrically valid signal, but the torque it reports does not match what the control unit expects from the commanded motor current, speed and operating state. Typical checks compare measured and estimated torque or look for an offset when no torque is applied. Honda patents show such a sensor mounted inside the hollow output shaft of a traction motor, where electromagnetic noise is a known accuracy issue. No manufacturer documents P0A18 publicly. CARB requires approved monitoring of drive motor faults that impair propulsion. P0A17 is the plain circuit fault; P0A19 and P0A20 are out of range low and high. The drive system usually limits electric torque. Common causes: Sensor offset or gain drifted, reading off against the torque model (high likelihood); Electrical interference on the signal from damaged shielding or ground (medium likelihood); Missing or outdated calibration after module or drive unit replacement (medium likelihood); Mechanical fault in the drive unit that changes the real torque (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Reduced or uneven electric assistance; Engine runs more often, fuel use rises. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A19 – Motor Torque Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0A19: Motor Torque Sensor Circuit Low. The control unit watches the voltage of a torque sensor that measures load directly on the traction motor shaft, such as the magnetostrictive sensor in a hollow motor shaft shown in a Honda patent. P0A19 sets when the signal stays below its valid window for a calibrated time, typical of a short to ground, a broken supply or an open signal line pulled low. No manufacturer documents P0A19 publicly; CARB only requires an approved drive motor monitoring plan. P0A20 is the opposite fault, P0A18 a plausible voltage with wrong torque, P0A21 dropouts. The driver usually sees a hybrid warning and reduced electric drive power. Common causes: Sensor signal or supply line shorted to ground (high likelihood); Sensor reference or excitation supply missing (medium likelihood); Corroded or loose connector at the drive unit (medium likelihood); Torque sensor electronics failed, often replaced with the drive unit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Reduced electric drive power or electric drive disabled; Engine runs more often, higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A1A – Generator Control Module
text: P0A1A: Generator Control Module. P0A1A reports a fault of the electronics that control the generator, either inside a hybrid inverter or in a belt starter-generator. Toyota lists P0A1A for the 2010-2015 Prius and 2012-2017 Prius V together with P0A94, P324E and P3004 as a malfunction inside the inverter assembly with converter; the repair can mean replacing the MG ECU, IPM transistors or the whole inverter. Audi stores P0A1A00 in the engine control unit of 2025 models with a Valeo 48 V starter-generator, paired with a 48 V system fault, and blames starter-generator software. CARB requires monitoring of the generator system. Effects range from a MIL to lost charging or no hybrid drive. Common causes: Internal failure of the inverter or generator control electronics (high likelihood); Control software fault, fixed by an update where the maker provides one (medium likelihood); Supply, ground or bus connection to the module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on; Battery no longer charged, start-stop or hybrid drive unavailable; Vehicle may not reach ready state. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A1B – Drive Motor A Control Module Performance
text: P0A1B: Drive Motor A Control Module Performance. P0A1B flags a self-test failure of the processor that controls drive motor A, usually inside the inverter. In GM hybrid tables (2016) it sets when the processor fails an inhibit path test at power-down, three or more times, proving it could not take the system to a safe state; in 2011 tables internal SPI, RAM or cache faults in 28 of 32 samples count. Both are Type A, MIL on the first trip. Land Rover sets P0A1B in the inverter of 2024-25 PHEVs at start-up, VW lists P0A1B00 for the ID.4 front drive. Toyota uses subtype P0A1B-1F on the 2023-24 Corolla Hybrid. Drive motor B is P0A1C. Expect a red loss-of-drive warning. Common causes: Control software fault, several makers resolve it by reprogramming (high likelihood); Internal processor or memory fault in the inverter control board (medium likelihood); Weak 12 V supply during start-up or shutdown (low likelihood). Symptoms: Loss of drive warning and MIL; Vehicle cannot be driven electrically or not at all; Fault may vanish after a full sleep cycle while the code stays stored. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A1C – Drive Motor B Control Module Performance
text: P0A1C: Drive Motor B Control Module Performance. P0A1C is the counterpart of P0A1B for the second electric machine, drive motor B, and reports that its control processor is no longer trustworthy. GM hybrid tables use it for the motor control processor B: in 2016 calibrations the code sets when an inhibit path test at power-down fails three or more times, in 2011 calibrations internal processor integrity faults such as SPI, RAM or cache errors are counted. Both are Type A with MIL on the first trip. The code concerns the control electronics, not a phase current sensor; those faults use their own codes. Expect a hybrid warning and loss of the affected motor function. Common causes: Internal processor or memory fault on the motor B control board (high likelihood); Calibration or software fault in the inverter (medium likelihood); Unstable 12 V supply or ground to the inverter electronics (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning and MIL; Reduced drive power or no electric drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A1D – Hybrid/EV Powertrain Control Module A
text: P0A1D: Hybrid/EV Powertrain Control Module A. The hybrid powertrain control module coordinates engine, motors and battery. P0A1D says this module has reported an internal failure or is no longer working reliably. In GM hybrid tables (2013) the engine control module stores P0A1D when a message from motor control processor A signals a hybrid controller status failure in 3 of 4 counts, as a Type B code with MIL after two trips. GM 2016 tables list P0A1D among codes that limit engine power. Subaru warns for the 2014-16 Crosstrek Hybrid that generic OBD readouts may store P0A1D from a scan tool communication error; replace the module only if the code returns. P0E43 covers module B. Common causes: Internal fault of the hybrid control module (high likelihood); Code stored by a scan tool communication error, not by a real defect (medium likelihood); Supply, ground or network fault at the module (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid warning on; Engine power reduced; Hybrid functions limited or unavailable. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A1E – Starter/Generator Control Module
text: P0A1E: Starter/Generator Control Module. Mild and full hybrids often start the engine and recharge the battery with a belt-driven starter-generator that has its own control electronics. P0A1E means that controller has reported a fault or works incorrectly. Audi stores P0A1E00 in the starter-generator control module of the 2020-2022 Q3 mild hybrid and cures it with a software update. Ford logs P0A1E in the engine control module of 2021-2023 F-150 PowerBoost and 2020-2026 Explorer and 2020-2023 Aviator hybrids; its bulletins name a loose connection at the belt integrated starter-generator or its software. Drivers notice a wrench or MIL lamp, no start-stop and no electric-only driving. Common causes: Loose wiring connection at the starter-generator (high likelihood); Starter-generator software fault, fixed by update (high likelihood); Starter-generator with integrated electronics failed (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Wrench lamp or MIL on, electrical system warning; Auto start-stop disabled; Electric-only driving unavailable. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A1F – Battery Energy Control Module A Performance
text: P0A1F: Battery Energy Control Module A Performance. The battery energy control module supervises cell voltages, current and temperatures of the high-voltage pack. P0A1F reports that this module failed its own integrity checks. In GM hybrid tables (2011) a single reset of the module by its software watchdog is enough, and the code sets in one trip. GM told dealers for the 2011-2012 Chevrolet Volt not to replace the module for P0A1F but to install a new calibration. FCA lists subtype P0A1F-09, internal component failure, on the 2018 Jeep Wrangler with eTorque and also fixes it by reflashing the battery pack control module. Lost communication with the module is U0111. Expect a MIL and limited hybrid function. Common causes: Module software fault, fixed by a new calibration (high likelihood); Internal hardware fault of the battery control module (medium likelihood); Unstable 12 V supply causing module resets (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or service engine soon light on; Battery or hybrid warning, limited electric operation; Start-stop may be disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A20 – Motor Torque Sensor Circuit High
text: P0A20: Motor Torque Sensor Circuit High. This code covers the upper electrical limit of a torque sensor fitted to the traction motor shaft, for example the magnetostrictive design inside a hollow output shaft described in a Honda patent. The control unit sets P0A20 when the sensor voltage remains above the valid range for a calibrated time, which points to a short to the supply voltage, an open ground return or a sensor output stuck high. No manufacturer documents P0A20 publicly; CARB requires an approved drive motor monitor. Siblings: P0A19 low, P0A18 implausible torque, P0A21 intermittent, P0A17 general circuit. Expect a hybrid warning and limited electric torque. Common causes: Signal line shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage (high likelihood); Open sensor ground return (medium likelihood); Sensor electronics output stuck high (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Electric drive torque limited; Reduced acceleration in electric mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A21 – Motor Torque Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A21: Motor Torque Sensor Circuit Intermittent. Here the torque sensor on the traction motor shaft delivers a signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing permanently. Such shaft sensors, as in the Honda patent with a sensor inside a hollow motor shaft, sit in an area with strong electromagnetic fields and vibration, so loose terminals, chafed wires and interference are the usual suspects. P0A21 sets when the control unit counts too many implausible signal changes. No manufacturer documents P0A21 publicly; CARB demands an approved drive motor monitor. Steady faults would show as P0A19 or P0A20. The warning may come and go. Common causes: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector (high likelihood); Chafed sensor wiring that shorts briefly under vibration (medium likelihood); Damaged shield letting inverter noise into the signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning that appears and disappears; Brief loss of electric assist. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A22 – Generator Torque Sensor Circuit
text: P0A22: Generator Torque Sensor Circuit. In series or power-split hybrids a separate electric machine runs as generator, driven by the combustion engine. A Honda patent claims a torque sensor inside the hollow shaft of either the traction motor or this generator. P0A22 is the general circuit fault of the generator torque sensor: the control unit receives no usable signal at all, without a more specific low, high or intermittent pattern. No manufacturer documents P0A22 publicly; CARB requires an approved monitoring plan for the generator system. Related: P0A23 plausibility, P0A24 low, P0A25 high, P0A26 intermittent. Charging and engine-driven power generation may be limited. Common causes: Sensor connector at the generator unplugged, loose or corroded (high likelihood); Open circuit in the sensor harness (medium likelihood); Generator torque sensor or its electronics failed (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Reduced battery charging by the engine; Limited system power. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A23 – Generator Torque Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A23: Generator Torque Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. The generator torque sensor sends an electrically valid voltage, but the torque it reports does not fit the generator current, speed and engine load the control unit knows. Typical checks compare the measured value with a torque model or look for an offset while the generator is idle. Such a sensor can sit in the hollow generator shaft, as a Honda patent claims, where magnetic noise and ageing shift the reading. No manufacturer documents P0A23 publicly; CARB requires approved monitoring of generator faults. Pure wiring faults appear as P0A22, P0A24 or P0A25. The system tends to cap generator torque. Common causes: Sensor zero point or gain drifted (high likelihood); Electromagnetic interference from the generator or inverter (medium likelihood); Contact resistance in the connector skewing the signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Generator output limited, battery charges slowly. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A24 – Generator Torque Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0A24: Generator Torque Sensor Circuit Low. P0A24 is stored when the voltage from the generator torque sensor stays under its lower diagnostic limit for a calibrated time. Electrically this means the line is pulled toward ground, the sensor supply is missing or the signal wire is broken. The sensor measures torque on the shaft of the engine-driven generator; a Honda patent describes such a sensor inside a hollow generator or motor shaft. No manufacturer documents P0A24 publicly; CARB requires an approved generator monitoring plan. The upper limit is P0A25, implausible but valid readings are P0A23, short dropouts P0A26. Electric generation may be cut back. Common causes: Signal line shorted to ground (high likelihood); Sensor supply voltage missing (medium likelihood); Sensor electronics failed with output stuck low (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Reduced charging and system power. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A25 – Generator Torque Sensor Circuit High
text: P0A25: Generator Torque Sensor Circuit High. With P0A25 the control unit sees the generator torque sensor signal above its permitted upper limit for longer than the calibrated debounce time. The common electrical explanations are a short from the signal line to the supply or battery voltage, an interrupted sensor ground, or a sensor output stuck at its maximum. The sensor belongs to the engine-driven generator of a hybrid; a Honda patent shows torque sensing inside a hollow generator or motor shaft. No manufacturer documents P0A25 publicly; CARB only demands an approved generator monitor. Opposite fault: P0A24; plausibility: P0A23; intermittent: P0A26. Generator torque is usually limited. Common causes: Signal line shorted to supply or battery voltage (high likelihood); Open sensor ground (medium likelihood); Sensor output stuck high (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Generator output limited. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A26 – Generator Torque Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A26: Generator Torque Sensor Circuit Intermittent. P0A26 points to short interruptions or jumps in the generator torque sensor signal rather than a constant fault. The control unit counts implausible signal changes or brief out-of-range events and sets the code once a calibrated limit is exceeded. Because the sensor works next to the generator, as in the Honda patent with a sensor in a hollow generator or motor shaft, heat cycles, vibration and inverter noise favour loose contacts and chafed wires. No manufacturer documents P0A26 publicly; CARB requires an approved generator monitor. Permanent faults show as P0A24 or P0A25. Symptoms often appear only on rough roads. Common causes: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector (high likelihood); Chafed wiring near the generator housing (medium likelihood); Shield or ground damage letting inverter noise in (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning that comes and goes; Brief drop in charging or system power. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A27 – Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit
text: P0A27: Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit. P0A27 covers the circuit that tells the high-voltage battery to drop off the bus, i.e. the command path that opens the main contactors at key-off, after a fault or after a crash signal. Patents describe such a path as a dedicated hardware line in addition to CAN, so the contactors open within milliseconds. The code sets when commanded and actual state disagree. Honda lists P0A27 as High Voltage Contactor Stays Activated on the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid, where it is one of the codes that call for replacing the motor power inverter. P0A28 and P0A29 are the low and high voltage faults of the same line. The driver may see a hybrid warning and the car may refuse to start or power down. Common causes: Contactor or its driver does not release when power-off is commanded (high likelihood); Internal fault in the inverter/power unit that controls the contactors (Honda Civic Hybrid) (medium likelihood); Damaged wiring or loose terminal on the hardwired power-off line (medium likelihood); Crash or emergency shutdown signal stored or still active (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine light; Vehicle will not enter ready mode or shuts down while driving; High-voltage system does not power down after key-off. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A28 – Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit Low
text: P0A28: Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit Low. The control unit watches the voltage on the line that commands the high-voltage battery to disconnect. P0A28 sets when that signal stays below its valid window for a calibrated time, typical of a short to ground or a lost supply on the line. No manufacturer documents P0A28 publicly; GM only lists it as a search keyword in a general pin-fit bulletin. Patents show the power-off path as a hardwired line next to CAN that opens the contactors within milliseconds; CARB requires hybrid components that can affect emissions to be monitored. P0A29 is the opposite fault, P0A27 a mismatch between command and contactor state. Expect a hybrid warning and, depending on strategy, no ready mode. Common causes: Power-off signal line shorted to ground (high likelihood); Poor terminal fit or corrosion at the battery or control module connector (medium likelihood); Missing supply or blown fuse feeding the power-off circuit (medium likelihood); Faulty driver stage in the battery or hybrid control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Vehicle does not reach ready mode; Electric drive disabled, engine runs constantly. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A29 – Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit High
text: P0A29: Hybrid/EV Battery Power Off Circuit High. P0A29 is stored when the voltage on the hybrid battery power-off line sits above its plausible range for longer than allowed, which points to an open line pulled up internally or a short to a supply voltage. No manufacturer explains P0A29 publicly; GM merely names it as a keyword in a generic bulletin on terminal fit. The circuit itself is the hardwired disconnect path that patents describe beside the CAN crash message, and CARB 1968.2 requires monitoring of hybrid components relevant to emissions. Related: P0A28 for a signal too low, P0A27 when the contactors do not follow the command. A stuck-high line can keep the system from powering up or from shutting down correctly. Common causes: Open power-off line or unplugged connector (high likelihood); Power-off line shorted to battery voltage (medium likelihood); Spread or corroded terminals at the connectors (medium likelihood); Faulty input or driver stage in the control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; Vehicle does not reach ready mode; High-voltage system stays active after switching off. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A2A – Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0A2A: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit. A thermistor in the stator of traction motor A reports winding temperature so the inverter can cut torque before the insulation overheats. P0A2A is the general circuit fault; the failure type sits in the extension byte. McLaren uses P0A2A1C on the Artura when a short or broken wire drives the sensor voltage out of range and P0A2A29 for an invalid signal. GM instead splits the electrical faults into P0A2C and P0A2D. Siblings: P0A2B plausibility, P0A2C low signal (hot), P0A2D high signal (cold or open), P0A2E dropouts, P0A2F real overheating; P2DAC is the same fault on a second sensor B. Hyundai shows the sensor sits inside the transaxle. Expect a hybrid warning and reduced electric power. Common causes: Broken or shorted sensor wire between motor and inverter (high likelihood); Loose or corroded connector at the drive unit (medium likelihood); Thermistor failed inside the motor or transaxle (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input in the inverter/motor control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine light; Reduced electric drive power; Implausible motor temperature in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A2B – Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A2B: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. This is the rationality check: after a long soak, motor A's temperature should match other temperatures in the drive. GM compares it with the average inverter module temperature on its 2013 two-mode trucks and sets P0A2B, Type B, if they differ by more than 28 °C after at least 360 minutes off; the 2011 table uses 20 °C against coolant and transmission fluid, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid 25 °C. Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid bulletin lists the code with resistance specs for the NTC; Audi pairs it on the A7 e quattro with P0A2E and a worn connector. McLaren also files over-temperature under P0A2B98. P0A2C/P0A2D are hard electrical faults, P0A2F real heat. Expect reduced electric power. Common causes: Thermistor drifted out of its resistance curve (high likelihood); Added resistance from a worn or corroded connector (Audi A7 e quattro) (medium likelihood); Fault in a reference temperature such as inverter or fluid temperature (low likelihood); Motor cooling problem that makes a real temperature look implausible (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine light; Electric drive power limited; Motor temperature far off from other temperatures after a cold soak. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A2C – Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0A2C: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low. The motor A sensor is an NTC thermistor, so its signal voltage falls as the winding heats; Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid bulletin gives about 11 to 13 kOhm at 20 °C for 2014-15 units. P0A2C means the voltage is too low, which the module reads as an impossibly hot motor: GM sets it on 2013 two-mode trucks above 230 °C (near 0 V), Type B, two trips; the 2011 table uses 184 °C, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid 236 °C. The usual cause is a signal wire shorted to ground or a shorted sensor. P0A2D is the opposite fault, P0A2F a real over-temperature that only counts while the sensor is in range. Hyundai reports a stuck 417 °F reading as a circuit fault. The driver sees a warning and derated electric drive. Common causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Thermistor internally shorted (often only with transaxle or motor) (medium likelihood); Chafed extension harness between drive unit and inverter (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input in the inverter/motor control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine light; Motor temperature shows a very high fixed value in live data; Electric drive power reduced or disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A2D – Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0A2D: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit High. With an NTC thermistor, a high signal voltage stands for a cold motor, and a voltage close to the 5 V pull-up means the circuit is open. GM sets P0A2D on its 2013 two-mode trucks when the reading falls below -40 °C, Type B over two trips; if the fault is already present at start-up it waits until the motor has warmed up under load for at least 1.5 minutes. The 2011 table uses -41 °C, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid -48 °C with torque above 10 Nm. Typical causes are a broken signal or ground wire, an unplugged connector or an open sensor. Hyundai checks the sensor resistance at the transaxle connector. P0A2C is the low-voltage counterpart. Motor protection is lost, so electric power is limited. Common causes: Open signal or ground wire of the motor temperature sensor (high likelihood); Connector unplugged or terminal pushed out, often after drive unit work (medium likelihood); Thermistor open inside the motor or transaxle (medium likelihood); Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine light; Motor temperature shows about -40 degrees in live data; Electric drive power limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A2E – Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A2E: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. P0A2E flags short jumps or dropouts in the motor A temperature signal that are too brief or too erratic for the low/high checks. Bentley documents it for the Bentayga PHEV and Flying Spur Hybrid 2020-23: the resistance in the sensor crimp changes suddenly at high temperature, and only the sensor has to be replaced, although the engine and gearbox come out to reach it. Audi lists it on the 2021-22 A7 e quattro together with P0A4000 and/or P0A2B00, caused by contact wear in a coupling connector, fixed with new gold-plated pins. Siblings: P0A2C/P0A2D for a steady out-of-range signal, P2DB0 for sensor B. The car shows a MIL or HV warning and may limit electric drive. Common causes: Worn contacts in a coupling connector of the sensor line (Audi A7 e quattro) (high likelihood); Resistance jumps in the sensor crimp at high temperature (Bentley hybrids) (medium likelihood); Chafed or loosely routed sensor wire with intermittent contact (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or high-voltage warning in the cluster; Fault comes and goes, often after hard driving; Gearbox or electric drive warning on some models. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A2F – Drive Motor A Over Temperature
text: P0A2F: Drive Motor A Over Temperature. Unlike its siblings, P0A2F reports a real thermal problem: the sensor works, but motor A stays too hot. GM sets it on 2013 two-mode trucks when the temperature exceeds 200 °C and does not fall below the 135 °C reset level, Type B, provided no circuit or plausibility fault is active. The 2011 table uses 159 °C; on the 2013 MGU mild hybrid the limit is 165 °C, and torque is already cut linearly from 100 % to zero between 155 and 165 °C. Hyundai lists the code in its Sonata Hybrid sensor bulletin, so a skewed sensor can mimic it. McLaren handles over-temperature under P0A2B98 and points to the dielectric cooling circuit. Expect a warning and sharply reduced electric power. Common causes: Motor cooling failure such as a weak pump, low fluid or blocked cooler (high likelihood); Sustained high load such as towing or long climbs in electric mode (medium likelihood); Temperature sensor reading too high while still within range (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning; Electric drive power drops sharply or is cut; Engine runs more often to support the drive. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A30 – Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P0A30: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit. P0A30 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor in the second traction motor (motor B). It is meant for faults the control unit can see on the sensor line but cannot classify as too low, too high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0A30 publicly; GM two-mode hybrids and Mitsubishi (rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV) use the specific codes P0A31 to P0A33 for the same sensor instead. CARB 1968.2 requires hybrid components whose failure can affect emissions to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid winding temperature the motor cannot be protected against overheating, so the system usually cuts electric drive power and lights a hybrid warning. Common causes: Loose, corroded or damaged connector between motor B and its control module (high likelihood); Chafed or broken sensor wiring at the drive unit (medium likelihood); Thermistor in the motor winding failed (often only replaceable with the motor) (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input in the motor control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine light; Reduced electric drive power; Motor B temperature missing or implausible in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.
