title: P0A31 – Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A31: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. P0A31 checks whether the motor B temperature reading makes sense, typically after a long rest when all parts should be close to the same temperature. GM compares it with other temperatures: the 2011 tables flag a gap above 20 °C to the average of power-electronics coolant and transmission fluid after 6 h without propulsion (Type A); the 2013 two-mode trucks allow 28 °C against the inverter module after 360 min key-off (Type B, two trips). Mitsubishi (2023 Outlander PHEV rear motor) compares two coil sensors after 5,400 s soak and sets it at 13 °C difference. P0A32 and P0A33 cover hard circuit faults; P0A35 is only judged while this test passes. Expect a hybrid warning and limited electric drive. Common causes: Motor B thermistor reading drifted out of tolerance (high likelihood); Corroded terminals adding resistance in the sensor circuit (medium likelihood); Comparison sensor (inverter, coolant or fluid temperature) is wrong (low likelihood); Uneven cooling of the drive unit, e.g. low fluid level (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning light after a cold start; Motor B temperature differs clearly from other temperatures after a long rest; Electric drive limited as a precaution. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A32 – Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0A32: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Low. P0A32 means the motor B temperature signal sits below its valid voltage range. GM uses an NTC thermistor, so a voltage near 0 V reads as an impossibly hot winding: the 2011 hybrid tables set it above 184 °C (Type A, one trip), the 2013 two-mode trucks above 230 °C (Type B, two trips). Mitsubishi sets it on the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the sensor voltage is 0.065 V or less for 0.5 s. A signal wire shorted to ground or a shorted thermistor is the typical cause. P0A33 is the opposite fault, P0A31 the plausibility check, and P0A35 a real over-temperature that GM only evaluates while no out-of-range fault is active. The system derates electric drive and warns the driver. Common causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Thermistor shorted inside the motor (medium likelihood); Chafed harness between drive unit and motor control module (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input in the motor control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning or check engine light; Motor B temperature shows an extremely high fixed value; Electric drive reduced or switched off. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A33 – Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit High
text: P0A33: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit High. P0A33 is stored when the motor B temperature signal stays above its valid voltage range. With GM's NTC thermistor a voltage near 5 V reads as an impossibly cold motor: GM sets it below -41 °C in the 2011 tables (Type A) and below -40 °C on the 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips). Mitsubishi flags the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the voltage reaches 4.761 V or more for 0.5 s. That pattern points to an open sensor circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to a voltage source. P0A32 is the low-side fault, P0A31 the rationality check, P0A35 the over-temperature code. Because winding temperature is unknown, the system limits electric drive power and shows a warning. Common causes: Open sensor circuit or unplugged connector (high likelihood); Spread or corroded terminals at the motor or module connector (medium likelihood); Thermistor open inside the motor (medium likelihood); Signal wire shorted to a voltage source (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning or check engine light; Motor B temperature shows about -40 °C regardless of conditions; Electric drive power limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A34 – Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A34: Drive Motor B Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent. P0A34 covers a motor B temperature signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing permanently. A winding temperature cannot change by tens of degrees within milliseconds, so such steps point to a loose contact, a chafed wire or a cracked solder joint. No manufacturer documents P0A34 publicly; GM and Mitsubishi only list the permanent faults P0A32 and P0A33 for this sensor, with debounce times of a few hundred milliseconds to seconds that a brief dropout may not meet. CARB 1968.2 requires circuit monitoring of emission-relevant hybrid components. The fault often comes and goes with vibration or heat, and the hybrid system may limit electric drive while it is active. Common causes: Loose or fretting terminal in the sensor connector (high likelihood); Wire insulation chafed through at a moving harness section (medium likelihood); Cracked joint at the thermistor leads inside the motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning that appears and clears on its own; Motor B temperature jumps in live data; Occasional loss of electric drive power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A35 – Drive Motor B Over Temperature
text: P0A35: Drive Motor B Over Temperature. Unlike the sensor codes, P0A35 reports that motor B is actually too hot according to a working sensor. GM's 2011 hybrid tables set it above 149 °C (Type A, one trip); the 2013 two-mode trucks use 200 °C, clear it only below 135 °C and run it only while P0A31 is not active (Type B). Mitsubishi sets it on the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the coil reaches 177 °C for one second and names the motor assembly, electric water pump, EV cooling circuit and radiator fan as suspects. Sustained heavy load, towing or a cooling fault are the usual triggers. P0A2F is the same check for motor A, P0A3D for the motor B inverter. The system cuts motor B torque until it has cooled down. Common causes: Electric coolant pump of the drive cooling circuit failed or weak (high likelihood); Low coolant or transmission fluid in the motor cooling path (medium likelihood); Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked (medium likelihood); Extended high load such as towing or long climbs (low likelihood). Symptoms: Noticeable loss of electric drive power; Hybrid system overheat or warning message; Engine runs more often to compensate. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0A36 – Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P0A36: Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit. P0A36 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor in the hybrid generator, the machine that is mainly driven by the engine to produce electricity. It covers faults the module detects on the sensor line without classing them as low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0A36 publicly; Mitsubishi (2023 Outlander PHEV) monitors its generator coil sensor with the specific codes P0A37 to P0A39 instead. CARB 1968.2 requires circuit monitoring for hybrid components that can affect emissions. With the generator temperature unknown, the system cannot protect the windings, so it usually restricts generator output and series operation and shows a hybrid warning. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector between generator and its control unit (high likelihood); Damaged sensor wiring near the transaxle (medium likelihood); Generator coil thermistor failed (usually replaced with the generator) (medium likelihood); Faulty input in the generator control unit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning or check engine light; Generator output or battery charging restricted; Generator temperature missing or implausible in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A37 – Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A37: Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. P0A37 tests whether the generator temperature reading is believable. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: once per drive cycle, after at least 5,400 s of soak and with the inverter switched off, the generator W-phase coil temperature is compared with the front motor coil and with the oil temperature. A gap of 26 °C to the motor or 22 °C to the oil, held for 0.8 s, sets the code. Suspects are the power drive unit, the coil sensor inside the generator and the wiring. P0A38 and P0A39 are hard voltage faults of the same sensor, P0A3B the real over-temperature. Mitsubishi is the only manufacturer found that documents P0A37 publicly. The driver sees a warning and generator use may be limited. Common causes: Generator coil sensor reading out of tolerance (high likelihood); Corroded connector or damaged harness in the sensor circuit (medium likelihood); Fault in the power drive unit that evaluates the sensor (medium likelihood); Comparison sensor (motor coil or oil temperature) reads wrong (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning after the first start of the day; Generator temperature differs from oil temperature after a long rest; Generator operation possibly restricted. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A38 – Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0A38: Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit Low. P0A38 means the generator temperature signal has fallen below the range a healthy sensor can produce. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the voltage of the generator W-phase coil sensor is 0.1 V or less for at least 0.5 s while the generator control unit has at least 8 V supply. Such a low voltage usually comes from a signal wire shorted to ground or a shorted sensor; Mitsubishi lists the power drive unit, the generator coil sensor and damaged wiring or connectors as suspects. P0A39 is the matching high fault, P0A37 the plausibility check and P0A3B a genuine over-temperature. Mitsubishi is the only manufacturer found that documents P0A38. Expect a hybrid warning and restricted generator use. Common causes: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Generator coil sensor shorted internally (medium likelihood); Damaged connector or harness between generator and power drive unit (medium likelihood); Faulty sensor input in the power drive unit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning or check engine light; Generator temperature shows an implausibly high fixed value; Battery charging by the engine restricted. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A39 – Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit High

title: P0A3A – Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A3A: Generator Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent. P0A3A flags a generator temperature signal that is interrupted or jumps only briefly. Since the thermal mass of a generator winding rules out sudden steps, such behaviour indicates a contact or wiring problem rather than a real temperature change. No manufacturer documents P0A3A publicly; Mitsubishi (2023 Outlander PHEV) only lists the permanent faults P0A38 and P0A39 for its generator coil sensor, each needing at least 0.5 s outside the valid voltage before it sets, so short dropouts would not trigger them. CARB 1968.2 calls for circuit monitoring of emission-relevant hybrid parts. Symptoms come and go, often with heat, vibration or moisture, and generator use may be restricted while the fault is present. Common causes: Loose or fretting terminal in the generator sensor connector (high likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the connector (medium likelihood); Harness chafed against the transaxle housing (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning that appears now and then; Generator temperature jumps in live data; Occasionally restricted battery charging by the engine. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A3B – Generator A Over Temperature
text: P0A3B: Generator A Over Temperature. P0A3B reports that the hybrid generator itself has become too hot, with the temperature sensor working correctly. Mitsubishi documents it as generator coil temperature high on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the monitor runs continuously and sets the code when the W-phase coil temperature criterion of 199 °C is met for one second. Mitsubishi's checks cover higher-priority codes, the radiator fan, and the EV oil cooling circuit that cools the generator; if those are fine, the generator is replaced. P0A37 to P0A39 are the sensor faults that must be ruled out first, P0A3E the over-temperature of the generator inverter. No other manufacturer documents P0A3B publicly. The system restricts generator output, which can cut charging and series-mode power. Common causes: Fault in the oil cooling circuit of the generator (low oil, leak, pump) (high likelihood); Radiator fan not working (medium likelihood); Internal generator fault such as damaged winding insulation (medium likelihood); Power drive unit commanding excessive generator current (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or overheat message; Reduced charging and power when the engine drives the generator; Battery state of charge drops during driving. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A3C – Drive Motor A Inverter Over Temperature
text: P0A3C: Drive Motor A Inverter Over Temperature. P0A3C reports overheating of the inverter that powers drive motor A, usually measured at its IGBT power switches. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the front motor control unit reads 166 °C or more at the U-phase upper IGBT for 0.12 s; other switch positions have their own P30xx codes. Honda calls it motor control module overheating and lists it among the codes caused by a cracked solder joint in the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid motor power inverter, covered by a warranty extension. On the 2023-25 Accord Hybrid and 2025-26 Civic Hybrid, Honda links it to a PCU radiator damaged by road debris. P0A78 is the general inverter performance code, P0C11 to P0C13 are phase-specific. Power is cut to protect the inverter. Common causes: PCU or inverter radiator damaged or leaking (Honda Accord/Civic Hybrid) (high likelihood); Internal inverter defect such as a cracked solder joint (Honda Civic Hybrid 2012-15) (medium likelihood); Low coolant or failed electric pump in the inverter cooling circuit (medium likelihood); Radiator fan not running (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and check engine light; Strongly reduced drive power; Coolant loss from the inverter circuit. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A3D – Drive Motor B Inverter Over Temperature

title: P0A3E – Generator Inverter Over Temperature

title: P0A3F – Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit
text: P0A3F: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit. The rotor position of a traction motor is read by a resolver: one excitation coil and two pickup coils that return sine and cosine signals. P0A3F is the basic circuit code for motor A and mostly means the signal is gone. GM sets it when the sine or cosine amplitude drops below 2.3 V (Type A, one trip in the 2011 and 2016 tables); Mitsubishi (2023 Outlander PHEV front motor) watches the excitation voltage and fails it outside 1.0 to 2.86 V for 0.14 s. Field causes: a spread terminal at the X2 connector of the Chevrolet Bolt, low 12 V supply on the 2014 Subaru XV Crosstrek Hybrid (software fix), Stellantis Pacifica Hybrid. P0A40 covers a degraded signal. Expect lost propulsion or no electric drive. Common causes: Spread or poorly seated terminal at the resolver connector (documented on the Chevrolet Bolt) (high likelihood); Open or shorted excitation, sine or cosine wire between motor and inverter (medium likelihood); Low 12 V auxiliary battery voltage disturbing the motor control module (Subaru, fixed by reprogramming) (medium likelihood); Resolver coil failed inside the motor (low likelihood); Faulty resolver excitation or input stage in the inverter/motor control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Sudden loss of propulsion, sometimes normal again after a restart; MIL and hybrid/EV system warning on; Vehicle will not enter ready mode or electric drive is disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A40 – Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A40: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. P0A40 means the resolver of motor A still delivers a signal, but its quality is poor or implausible. P0A3F is the hard signal loss. Expect a drive system warning or no start. Common causes: Rotor position sensor (resolver) delivering a degraded signal, e.g. Audi G713 (high likelihood); Worn, loose or contaminated contacts in the resolver connectors (Audi, Bentley) (high likelihood); Sensor wires pinched or misrouted on the gearbox housing after a repair (medium likelihood); Faulty resolver evaluation in the inverter/motor control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Drive system fault message in the instrument cluster; Vehicle cannot be started or will not enter ready mode; Electric drive disabled or torque jerks while driving. title: P0A41 – Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0A41: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Low. P0A41 reports that a resolver signal of motor A sits below its permitted range, as happens with a sine, cosine or excitation wire shorted to ground, a shorted coil or a broken line pulled down by the input circuit. Kia documents it on the 2011-13 Optima Hybrid: an intermittent MIL or hybrid service lamp with P0A41 in the motor control unit, traced to internal shorts or poor pin fit in the sub-harness between the hybrid power control unit and the motor, checked against resistance specs. Bosch patents describe telling a short to ground from a short to supply by the offset of the coil lines. P0A42 is the high side, P0A3F the general loss of signal, P0A40 a degraded signal. Expect a warning lamp and possibly no electric drive. Common causes: Internal short in the resolver sub-harness between power control unit and motor (Kia Optima Hybrid) (high likelihood); Poor pin fit at the resolver connectors (high likelihood); Shorted resolver coil inside the motor (low likelihood); Faulty resolver input stage in the motor control unit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent MIL or hybrid service lamp; Electric drive temporarily disabled; Code returns after clearing, often with vibration or heat. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A42 – Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit High
text: P0A42: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit High. P0A42 is the counterpart to P0A41: a resolver line of motor A reads above its allowed range. Typical triggers are a sine, cosine or excitation wire shorted to a supply voltage, or an open coil whose line is pulled up by the bias resistors of the input circuit, which drives the converter into clipping. Kia covers it in the same Optima Hybrid 2011-13 bulletin as P0A41: intermittent MIL or hybrid service lamp, fixed by inspecting the HPCU-to-motor sub-harness for internal shorts and pin fit. Bosch patents explain why clipping alone is not enough and how the line offset reveals a short to supply or an open line. P0A3F is the general circuit fault. Expect a warning lamp and reduced or no electric drive. Common causes: Resolver wire shorted to a supply voltage inside the sub-harness (Kia Optima Hybrid) (high likelihood); Open sine or cosine line pulled high by the input circuit (medium likelihood); Poor pin fit or corrosion at the resolver connectors (medium likelihood); Faulty resolver input stage in the motor control unit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent MIL or hybrid service lamp; Electric drive disabled or vehicle not ready; Reduced power until the fault clears. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A43 – Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A43: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent. P0A43 is set when the motor A resolver signal drops out or jumps only briefly, so that neither a steady low, high nor a lasting loss is confirmed. No public set threshold exists. GM's Bolt bulletin shows how a slightly spread connector terminal causes such short dropouts. P0A3F, P0A41 and P0A42 cover permanent faults. Expect a warning that may vanish after a restart, sometimes with a short loss of drive. Common causes: Loose or spread terminal in the resolver connector, losing contact under vibration (high likelihood); Hybrid control or inverter software needing an update (Stellantis) (medium likelihood); Chafed resolver wiring making intermittent contact (medium likelihood); Intermittent fault in the power inverter module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or MIL that comes and goes; Brief loss of propulsion, normal again after restart; Code stored as history without current symptoms. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A44 – Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Overspeed
text: P0A44: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Overspeed. P0A44 reports that the speed derived from the motor A resolver is above the highest speed the motor may run. Mitsubishi uses it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV front motor: set at 15,500 rpm or more for 0.5 s with module supply above 8 V, judged only when the position sensor itself is fault-free; the guided fix after other codes are ruled out is a new front motor. GM covers the same check under its own code P1B0D (above 11,500 rpm, Type A) instead of P0A44. A true overspeed can come from a slipping drivetrain or a mechanical fault; a false one from a corrupted speed signal. P0A3F to P0A43 cover the sensor circuit. The system cuts motor torque to protect the rotor. Common causes: Mechanical fault in the front motor or its drivetrain (Mitsubishi replaces the motor) (medium likelihood); Real overspeed from wheel spin or a slipping coupling (medium likelihood); Disturbed resolver signal producing a false speed value (medium likelihood); Motor control module calculating speed incorrectly (low likelihood). Symptoms: Electric drive torque cut during acceleration or high speed; Hybrid/EV system warning and MIL; Reduced top speed in limp mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A45 – Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit
text: P0A45: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit. P0A45 is the general circuit code for the resolver of the second traction motor (B), usually meaning its signal is missing. GM sets it like P0A3F when sine or cosine amplitude falls below 2.3 V (Type A, one trip). Mitsubishi uses it for the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV: both sine and cosine below 0.12 V for at least 0.18 s; the resolver is part of the rear motor assembly, which is replaced. Toyota fixes P0A45 on 2016-18 RAV4 Hybrid models built before a production change with a new frame wire harness, and Stellantis lists it for the Pacifica Hybrid. P0A46 to P0A49 split out degraded, low, high and intermittent signals. Expect a hybrid warning, MIL and loss of the motor B drive. Common causes: Damaged or faulty frame/body wire harness to the rear motor (Toyota RAV4 Hybrid) (high likelihood); Poor contact at the motor B resolver connector (medium likelihood); Resolver or control unit inside the rear motor assembly failed (Mitsubishi) (medium likelihood); Hybrid control software needing an update (Stellantis) (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning message; Loss of rear-axle electric drive or all-wheel drive; Reduced power or vehicle not ready. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A46 – Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A46: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. P0A46 reports that the motor B resolver still delivers a signal, but one that is degraded or not plausible. title: P0A4A – Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit Overspeed
text: P0A4A: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit Overspeed. P0A4A reports that the speed calculated from the motor B resolver exceeds the motor's permitted maximum. title: P0A4B – Generator Position Sensor Circuit
text: P0A4B: Generator Position Sensor Circuit. P0A4B covers the resolver that tells the inverter where the generator rotor stands; without a valid angle the generator cannot be commutated. Mitsubishi (Outlander PHEV 2023) runs the check continuously once the generator control unit has at least 8.0 V and sets P0A4B when its internal status flags stay failed for 0.23 s or 0.28 s; low and high signal levels go to separate codes there. Volvo lists P0A4B in the inverter generator module of its 2022-23 plug-in hybrids, as permanent or intermittent fault, with no-start complaints, and fixed false detections by software only. P0A4C is the plausibility check, P0A4D/P0A4E the low and high signal, P0A4F a sporadic signal, P0A50 overspeed. The driver sees a hybrid warning and may lose electric drive or engine start. Common causes: False detection in the inverter monitor software (Volvo, fixed by update) (medium likelihood); Damaged resolver wiring or connector between generator and inverter (high likelihood); Generator resolver defective (medium likelihood); Resolver evaluation in the power drive unit faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and MIL; Engine does not start or crank in hybrid mode; Electric drive or charging by the generator disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A4C – Generator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A4C: Generator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. P0A4C means the generator resolver delivers signals that are electrically present but implausible, so the computed rotor angle cannot be trusted. Mitsubishi documents the exact limits for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the sine or cosine winding voltage must stay between 2.1 and 2.9 V; if either leaves that window for 0.28 s, or an internal status fault persists for 0.31 s, the generator control unit stores P0A4C. Typical triggers are a corroded or loose resolver plug, a chafed shield picking up noise, a winding that has drifted, or a faulty input stage in the power drive unit. P0A4B is the general circuit fault, P0A4D and P0A4E the hard low and high signal, P0A4F a sporadic dropout. Expect a hybrid warning, reduced power and possibly no engine start via the generator. Common causes: Corroded or loose resolver connector (high likelihood); Damaged shielding letting interference onto the sine/cosine lines (medium likelihood); Resolver winding drifted out of tolerance (medium likelihood); Faulty resolver input stage in the power drive unit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and MIL; Reduced drive power or engine-only operation; Engine start via the generator not possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A50 – Generator Position Sensor Circuit Overspeed

title: P0A51 – Drive Motor A Current Sensor Circuit
text: P0A51: Drive Motor A Current Sensor Circuit. P0A51 reports a fault in the circuit of the current sensor that measures the phase current of drive motor A. The inverter needs this value for torque control and overcurrent protection. No manufacturer documents P0A51 publicly with its criteria. A Toyota patent shows the principle: a control sensor and a monitoring sensor measure the same motor current, and if the control sensor sits in its ground-short range or the two differ beyond a threshold over several cycles, the system flags the sensor and opens the main relays, because a wrong reading could drive the inverter into overcurrent. CARB requires circuit checks of hybrid input components. P0A52 covers plausibility, P0A53/P0A54 low and high; P0A55 is motor B. The hybrid system usually shuts down drive motor A. Common causes: Current sensor in the inverter assembly failed (high likelihood); Sensor supply or signal line interrupted inside the inverter (medium likelihood); Evaluation circuit on the motor control board faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and MIL; Drive motor A disabled, vehicle may not move or runs on engine only. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A52 – Drive Motor A Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A52: Drive Motor A Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. P0A52 means the current sensor of drive motor A delivers values that are electrically valid but do not fit the operating state. Typical checks compare the reading at zero current with its expected offset, or compare redundant sensors with each other. No manufacturer documents P0A52 publicly. A Hyundai patent describes compensating the sensor offset while no current flows and declaring the compensation abnormal when the offset leaves its allowed band; a Toyota patent compares a control sensor with a monitoring sensor and flags a lasting difference. CARB requires rationality checks of hybrid input components. P0A51 is the general circuit fault, P0A53 and P0A54 the hard low and high signal. A wrong current reading can cause torque errors, so the system limits or disables drive motor A. title: P0A59 – Generator Current Sensor Circuit
text: P0A59: Generator Current Sensor Circuit. P0A59 is the general circuit fault of the current sensor on the hybrid generator, the electric machine driven by the engine that charges the battery and often starts the engine. Its inverter uses the current reading to control generator torque. No manufacturer documents P0A59 publicly with criteria. Patents describe the same sensing on generators: Toyota for a motor that also works as an engine-driven generator, Hyundai for the hybrid starter-generator, where two phases are measured and the third is calculated, and Caterpillar for generator and traction motor sensors. CARB requires circuit checks of hybrid input components. P0A5A is plausibility, P0A5B/P0A5C low and high. Without a valid reading the generator is disabled, so charging and engine start can be affected. Common causes: Generator current sensor failed (usually inside the inverter) (high likelihood); Sensor supply or signal line interrupted or shorted (medium likelihood); Evaluation circuit on the generator control board faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning and MIL; Engine runs constantly or the high-voltage battery is no longer charged; Vehicle may not enter ready mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A5B – Generator Current Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0A5B: Generator Current Sensor Circuit Low. title: P0A5C – Generator Current Sensor Circuit High

title: P0A5D – Drive Motor A Phase U Current

title: P0A66 – Drive Motor B Phase U Current
text: P0A66: Drive Motor B Phase U Current. P0A66 is the general fault code for the current in phase U of drive motor B, the second electric machine of a two-motor hybrid or an electric rear-axle motor. CARB requires circuit and rationality monitoring of electric drive components. P0A67 and P0A68 are the low and high variants, P0A69 and P0A6C cover phases V and W, P0A5D is the same code on motor A. Motor B is normally shut off. Common causes: Phase U current sensor of motor B failed (inside the inverter) (high likelihood); Phase U high-voltage cable or terminal between inverter and motor B faulty (medium likelihood); Internal fault in the motor B power stage (medium likelihood); Winding fault in phase U of drive motor B (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and MIL; Motor B switched off, less power or no electric all-wheel drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A68 – Drive Motor B Phase U Current High
text: P0A68: Drive Motor B Phase U Current High. P0A67 is the low side, P0A6B and P0A6E cover V and W. Motor B is shut down. Common causes: Winding short or insulation breakdown in phase U of motor B (e.g. coolant ingress) (high likelihood); Shorted power switch in the phase U leg of the inverter (medium likelihood); Phase U current sensor reading too high (gain or offset fault) (medium likelihood). title: P0A70 – Generator Phase U Current Low
text: P0A70: Generator Phase U Current Low. P0A70 means phase U of the hybrid generator carries or reports too little current while the generator is loaded, typical of an open phase or a sensor stuck near zero. No manufacturer documents P0A70 publicly. The closest published test is GM's open-phase check for the drive motors (P0A67 and siblings), which compares the peak current near each phase axis against a 9 A threshold; GM publishes no such test for the generator. A Caterpillar patent identifies a failed phase sensor by a reading close to zero while the currents no longer sum to zero. CARB requires circuit monitoring of electric drive components. P0A71 is the high side, P0A73 and P0A76 phases V and W, P0A6F the general code. Engine start and charging can be affected. Common causes: Open circuit in the generator phase U lead or terminal (high likelihood); Generator phase U current sensor stuck near zero (medium likelihood); Phase U switch in the generator inverter not conducting (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning and MIL; Engine runs rough at start or battery charge level keeps dropping. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A71 – Generator Phase U Current High
text: P0A71: Generator Phase U Current High. P0A71 is set when the current in phase U of the hybrid generator exceeds its permitted level. No manufacturer documents P0A71 publicly. The Toyota patent on current sensor monitoring applies directly, since its machine also runs as an engine-driven generator and starts the engine: a sensor stuck too low makes the controller push the real current far above command, and an overcurrent through the inverter can damage its switches, so the relays are opened. A real overcurrent can also come from a winding or insulation short in the generator or a shorted switch. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A70 is the low side, P0A74 and P0A77 phases V and W, P0A6F the general code. The hybrid system usually shuts down. Common causes: Shorted power switch in the generator phase U leg (medium likelihood); Winding or insulation short in generator phase U (medium likelihood); Faulty phase U current sensor or its evaluation in the inverter (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL; Hybrid system shuts down; vehicle may not move or restart. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A72 – Generator Phase V Current
text: P0A72: Generator Phase V Current. P0A72 reports a fault in the phase V current of the hybrid generator. Toyota uses it: a field report filed with NHTSA covers a 2006 Highlander Hybrid with the MIL on and P0A72 stored together with P0A75 for generator phase W, P0A60 and P0A63 for drive motor A, and inverter performance codes including P0A78; after checking connector fit and the resistance of the three-phase cables, the inverter/converter assembly was replaced. The pairing of V and W codes fits inverters that measure two phases and calculate the third, as a Hyundai patent describes for its starter-generator. P0A73 and P0A74 are the low and high cases, P0A6F and P0A75 phases U and W. Expect a hybrid warning and possibly no drive. Common causes: Internal fault in the inverter/converter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid) (high likelihood); Generator phase V current sensor failed (medium likelihood); Poor pin fit or damaged three-phase cable to the generator (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and master warning, several hybrid codes at once; Vehicle may not move or enter ready mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A73 – Generator Phase V Current Low
text: P0A73: Generator Phase V Current Low. P0A73 indicates that phase V of the hybrid generator delivers or reports too little current under load. No manufacturer documents P0A73 publicly. On inverters that measure only phases V and W, a low V reading has a knock-on effect: the calculated U current is wrong as well, so the generator torque control loses accuracy. A Caterpillar patent shows the logic for three-sensor systems, where a near-zero reading plus a violated zero-sum identifies the failed sensor; a Toyota patent compares a control sensor with a monitoring sensor and the current command. CARB requires circuit monitoring of electric drive components. P0A74 is the high side, P0A70 and P0A76 phases U and W, P0A72 the general code. Charging and engine start can suffer. Common causes: Generator phase V current sensor reading near zero (high likelihood); Generator phase V lead or terminal open (medium likelihood); Phase V switch in the generator inverter not conducting (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning and MIL; Engine runs more often, battery charge does not recover. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A74 – Generator Phase V Current High
text: P0A74: Generator Phase V Current High. P0A74 appears when phase V of the hybrid generator shows more current than its limit allows. No manufacturer documents P0A74 publicly. A drifting sensor zero point is one candidate: a Hyundai patent covering both the traction motor and the starter-generator corrects phase sensor offsets and flags a fault when the correction fails. Real overcurrent is the other, for example from a winding or insulation short or a power switch that no longer turns off; a Toyota patent explains why the inverter then shuts down quickly. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A73 is the low side, P0A71 and P0A77 phases U and W, P0A72 the general code. The hybrid system typically stops, and in power-split hybrids the car may lose drive entirely. Common causes: Phase V sensor offset drifted or offset correction failed (medium likelihood); Power switch in the generator phase V leg not turning off (medium likelihood); Winding or insulation short in generator phase V (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL; Hybrid system shutdown, possibly no propulsion. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A75 – Generator Phase W Current
text: P0A75: Generator Phase W Current. P0A75 stands for a fault in the phase W current of the hybrid generator. Toyota documents it in practice: in a field report from an NHTSA investigation of 2006 Highlander Hybrid inverters, P0A75 appeared next to P0A72, the drive motor phase codes P0A60 and P0A63 and inverter performance codes, and the root cause was inside the inverter/converter, which was replaced. A sudden cluster like this points more to the shared inverter than to the generator winding. A Toyota patent shows how a control and a monitoring current sensor are cross-checked so that a defective sensor is caught before it causes overcurrent. P0A76 and P0A77 are the low and high variants, P0A6F and P0A72 phases U and V. Ready mode or drive may be lost. Common causes: Internal fault in the inverter/converter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid) (high likelihood); Generator phase W current sensor failed (medium likelihood); Generator phase W cable or connector faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and master warning, usually with other hybrid codes; Vehicle will not become ready or will not move. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A76 – Generator Phase W Current Low
text: P0A76: Generator Phase W Current Low. P0A76 signals that phase W of the hybrid generator conducts or reports too little current while the generator should be producing or absorbing torque. No manufacturer documents P0A76 publicly. Physically, the generator phase leads run from the inverter into the transaxle or engine bay, so a loose bolted terminal, a cracked lead or a corroded connector can open the W path; electrically, a sensor fixed near zero gives the same reading. A Caterpillar patent separates both: a sensor fault is assumed when one phase reads about zero while the sum of the three no longer balances. A Hyundai patent shows separate generator phase sensors in the inverter. CARB requires circuit monitoring. P0A77 is the high side, P0A70 and P0A73 phases U and V. Common causes: Loose terminal, cracked lead or corroded connector in generator phase W (high likelihood); Generator phase W current sensor stuck near zero (medium likelihood); Open phase W winding in the generator (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning and MIL; Engine start harsh or delayed, charging reduced. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A77 – Generator Phase W Current High
text: P0A77: Generator Phase W Current High. P0A77 is the excess-current code for phase W of the hybrid generator. No manufacturer documents P0A77 publicly. When the engine drives the generator hard, for instance while charging or during engine start, a short between turns, a breakdown to the housing or a switch that fails closed can let the W current climb beyond its limit; a sensor with too much gain produces a similar picture without real overcurrent. A Toyota patent, whose machine also works as generator, describes stopping the inverter and opening the relays when current runs away; a Caterpillar patent checks the zero-sum of the phase currents to unmask a bad sensor. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A76 is the low side, P0A71 and P0A74 phases U and V. Common causes: Turn-to-turn short or insulation breakdown in generator phase W (medium likelihood); Power switch in the generator phase W leg failed closed (medium likelihood); Generator phase W current sensor with excessive gain (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL; Hybrid system shuts down during charging or engine start. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A78 – Drive Motor A Inverter Performance
text: P0A78: Drive Motor A Inverter Performance. P0A78 means the inverter stage feeding drive motor A has reported a power-switch fault. GM explains the check in its hybrid OBD tables: the IGBT module watches each phase for desaturation, a sign of a short between the upper and lower switch; if that status persists for about 2 ms the code sets as Type A, MIL on the first trip. Stellantis replaced the power inverter module on 2021 Jeep Wrangler 4xe with P0A78 and P0A79, which ran on engine power only, and refreshed hybrid control software on the 2017 Pacifica Hybrid. Land Rover logs P0A78 in the inverter converter of 2024-25 Range Rover models and asks not to clear it before diagnosis. P0A79 is motor B, P0A7A the generator inverter, P0A3C overheating of inverter A. Expect a warning and loss of electric drive. Common causes: IGBT desaturation or short in the inverter power stage (high likelihood); Power inverter module defective (replaced on Jeep Wrangler 4xe) (high likelihood); Hybrid control software requiring update (medium likelihood); Shorted winding or phase cable of drive motor A (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or high-voltage warning; No electric drive, engine-only operation; Stop safely warning on some models. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A79 – Drive Motor B Inverter Performance
text: P0A79: Drive Motor B Inverter Performance. P0A79 is the drive motor B counterpart of P0A78: the inverter stage for motor B has detected a power-switch fault. In GM hybrid OBD tables the IGBT module reports a desaturation status on a high or low side switch of any phase; persisting for about 2 ms it sets P0A79 as Type A with MIL on the first trip. Stellantis documents P0A79 several times: on the 2021 Jeep Wrangler 4xe together with P0A78 and an engine-only limp mode, fixed by a new power inverter module; on the 2017 Pacifica Hybrid with improved hybrid control software, and with a loose high-voltage cable at the inverter terminal that also caused loss of propulsion. P0A78 is motor A, P0A7A the generator inverter, P0A3D overheating of inverter B. The driver loses electric drive. Common causes: IGBT desaturation or short in the motor B power stage (high likelihood); Power inverter module defective (high likelihood); Loose high-voltage cable at the inverter terminal (Pacifica Hybrid) (medium likelihood); Hybrid control software requiring update (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning; No electric drive, engine-only operation; Loss of propulsion in severe cases. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A7A – Generator Inverter Performance
text: P0A7A: Generator Inverter Performance. P0A7A reports that the inverter stage driving the generator has signalled a fault, for example overcurrent or a failed power switch. Toyota uses the code across its hybrids and splits it with information codes. Bulletin T-SB-0142-16 covers 2012-2016 Avalon, Camry and RAV4 Hybrid with MIL on and P0A7A plus information code 122, a generator inverter fail signal caused by overcurrent; the repair replaces inverter and transaxle. A Toyota field report filed with NHTSA describes a 2006 Highlander Hybrid with P0A7A sub code 325, master warning, MIL and Check Hybrid System, traced to a fault inside the inverter assembly. P0A78 and P0A79 are the drive motor inverters, P0A3E generator inverter overheating, P0A92 generator performance. Common causes: Internal generator inverter fault with overcurrent (Toyota information code 122) (high likelihood); Inverter assembly defective (high likelihood); Fault in the generator inside the transaxle (medium likelihood); Insufficient inverter cooling stressing the power stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL, master warning and Check Hybrid System message; Reduced power or vehicle will not enter ready mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A7B – Battery Energy Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
text: P0A7B: Battery Energy Control Module Requested MIL Illumination. P0A7B is a request code: the battery energy control module, which has found an emissions-relevant fault of its own, asks the engine control module to switch on the MIL, and the engine controller stores P0A7B. The actual cause sits in a separate code in the battery module. GM documents this on the 2024-25 Corvette E-Ray: P0A7B in the K20 engine controller appears together with P0E3C in the battery module, caused by air trapped around the battery coolant pump after a repair; purging the air is the fix. Subaru reports P0A7B in the engine controller of the 2014 XV Crosstrek Hybrid alongside battery and drive motor codes after a frozen power relay. Diagnose the battery module codes first. P0AC4 is the matching request from the hybrid control module. Common causes: Emissions-relevant fault stored in the battery energy control module (high likelihood); Air trapped at the battery coolant pump (Corvette E-Ray, with P0E3C) (medium likelihood); Frozen power supply relay of the drive motor control module (Subaru Crosstrek Hybrid) (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on; Additional codes stored in the battery control module. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A7C – Motor Electronics Over Temperature
text: P0A7C: Motor Electronics Over Temperature. P0A7C reports that the electronics controlling the hybrid motors, mainly the inverter, have run hotter than allowed. Ford uses the code on its hybrids and stores it in the PCM. A Ford bulletin for 2010-11 Fusion and Milan Hybrid and 2011 MKZ Hybrid built up to 9 September 2010 describes a wrench light with no drivability concern and P0A7C, cured by a PCM software update. Ford warranty statistics supplied to NHTSA list P0A7C as a recurring code on 2010-12 Escape, Tribute and Mariner Hybrid. Common physical causes are a failed coolant pump of the motor electronics cooling loop, low coolant, air in the loop or a blocked radiator. CARB requires monitoring of inverter thermal management. P0A3C and P0A3D cover the individual inverters. Power is reduced to protect the electronics. Common causes: Coolant pump of the motor electronics cooling loop failed (high likelihood); Low coolant or air in the electronics cooling loop (medium likelihood); PCM calibration triggering the code without real overheating (Ford Fusion Hybrid) (medium likelihood); Blocked electronics radiator or faulty cooling fan (low likelihood). Symptoms: Wrench or hybrid warning light; Reduced power, especially under high load or heat. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A7D – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack State of Charge Low
text: P0A7D: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack State of Charge Low. The battery controller watches whether the traction or mild-hybrid pack stays inside its usable state-of-charge (SOC) window. GM sets P0A7D (Type B, two trips) when SOC stays below a program threshold (30 % or 10.5 %) for more than half of a drive cycle longer than 50 km, after allowing generator time to recover. Ford reports it on 2020 Escape/Explorer Hybrid after a deep discharge from long standing or crank/no-start, and Audi on 48 V systems whose protection relays open at low SOC. Unlike P0A7F/P0A80 the pack itself is not judged worn; it is simply too empty. Expect no EV mode, weak assist or, in severe cases, a no-start until the pack is recharged. Common causes: Pack discharged by long standing time or repeated crank/no-start attempts (high likelihood); Generator, DC/DC or charging path not replenishing the pack (medium likelihood); 48 V battery in low-voltage protection state (relays open) (medium likelihood); Weak or self-discharging cell modules (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning; No electric driving or reduced motor assist; Engine runs longer to recharge the pack; Vehicle may not start or reach ready mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A7E – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Over Temperature
text: P0A7E: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Over Temperature. The pack controller compares the hottest module temperature with a protection limit. GM sets P0A7E, mostly as Type A (MIL after one trip), when the maximum module temperature exceeds a program limit between about 61 and 73.5 °C, unless a temperature sensor fault is active. Subaru documents it on the 2014–16 Crosstrek Hybrid, where too strict logic for heat after shutdown cut assist and auto start-stop; GM links it on eAssist cars to a cooling fan that stops at low system voltage; Porsche saw it with implausible sensor signals on the 911 GTS T-Hybrid. Sensor circuit faults have their own codes (P0A9B–P0A9E). The car limits charge and discharge power to protect the cells. Common causes: Battery cooling fan inoperative or intake/filter clogged (high likelihood); Battery controller software logic (update released by Subaru, Porsche) (medium likelihood); Low 12 V system voltage stopping the cooling fan (medium likelihood); Aged cells with high internal resistance heating up (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and check engine light; Reduced electric assist and regeneration; Auto start-stop no longer works; In rare cases warning with no-start. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A7F – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Deterioration
text: P0A7F: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Deterioration. This is the state-of-health monitor that CARB requires for hybrid storage systems. GM compares the calculated pack power capability with an end-of-life table at mid state of charge and sets P0A7F as Type B (two trips) when it falls short. Honda reports it as battery module deterioration on the 2009 Civic Hybrid and as serious capacity deterioration on the 2014 Accord Plug-In; Mercedes uses it when the 48 V module reaches its health limit, partly fixed by software. Toyota bulletins for Prius, Prius v and Camry Hybrid name a clogged battery cooling fan as a trigger. P0A80 is the harder replace-pack verdict. Drivers notice weaker assist, more engine running and higher fuel use. Common causes: Pack capacity or power capability lost through ageing (high likelihood); Dust or debris in the battery cooling fan or filter overheating cells (medium likelihood); Battery controller software misjudging health (Honda, Mercedes) (medium likelihood); Individual weak modules pulling the pack down (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or hybrid/IMA warning light; Weak acceleration assist, especially from a stop; Engine runs more often, higher fuel consumption; Shorter electric range on plug-in models. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A80 – Replace Hybrid/EV Battery Pack
text: P0A80: Replace Hybrid/EV Battery Pack. The battery controller has concluded that the pack is at end of life. In GM tables this is a resistance test: the maximum cell or pack resistance, measured from current and voltage swings, exceeds a temperature-dependent end-of-life threshold, and the code sets as Type A after one trip. Toyota bulletins for Prius (2004–09, 2013–15), Prius v and Camry Hybrid report P0A80, often together with P0A7F, caused by dust in the battery cooling fan; cleaning the fan comes first. Honda recalled the 2018 Accord Hybrid because software wrongly set this code as a permanent fault after pack replacement. Compared with P0A7F it is the final verdict; assist and economy drop and the MIL stays on. Common causes: Cell or module resistance above end-of-life limit (high likelihood); Clogged battery cooling fan or intake filter (Toyota) (medium likelihood); Controller software misreading a replaced pack (Honda Accord Hybrid 2018) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine and hybrid system warning on; Noticeably weaker electric assist; Higher fuel consumption, engine runs more. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A81 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit/Open
text: P0A81: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit/Open. The controller watches the output that drives battery cooling fan 1 for an open circuit. In the 2016 GM table the fan is commanded at low duty (under 10 %) and the circuit voltage sits between about 1.6 and 5.85 V instead of being pulled low; 16 failures in 20 samples set it as Type B. An older GM program used it as a general fan unit fault judged by a monitor voltage. Ford found P0A81, often with P0A96 for fan 2, in the battery control module of 2005–12 Escape and Mariner Hybrids and replaced both fans; drivers usually noticed nothing. Low and high faults have their own codes (P0A84, P0A85). Without airflow the pack heats up and power may be limited. Common causes: Fan motor or its internal electronics open (high likelihood); Loose or corroded fan connector, broken control wire (medium likelihood); Blown fan supply fuse (medium likelihood); Faulty output stage in the battery control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning, often no other complaint; Battery cooling fan does not run when commanded; Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A82 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Performance/Stuck Off
text: P0A82: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Performance/Stuck Off. This code covers a fan 1 that is electrically intact but does not deliver the requested cooling, up to standing still. No manufacturer publishes code-exact criteria; CARB requires a functional check of battery cooling where feasible. Typical methods: GM compares commanded and fed-back fan speed (filed under its own sense code P0BC8), Toyota flags a fan whose feedback-corrected duty deviates too far from the expected value, and Honda compares expected and measured battery temperature rise. Causes are mostly mechanical: dust on the blades, a clogged intake filter, worn bearings. Circuit faults use P0A81/P0A84/P0A85; the stuck-on case is P0A83. The pack runs hotter and power may be limited. Common causes: Dust or debris on fan blades or in the duct (high likelihood); Clogged or covered battery air intake or filter (high likelihood); Worn or seized fan motor bearings (medium likelihood); Faulty fan speed feedback signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid warning or check engine light; Fan audibly weak or silent under load; Reduced electric assist in warm weather. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A83 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Stuck On
text: P0A83: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Stuck On. P0A83 means battery cooling fan 1 keeps turning although the controller has switched it off. No manufacturer publicly documents this exact code. CARB asks for fan outputs to be checked for proper response to commands. GM shows the method under its sense code P0BC8: with the fan off for more than 20 s, a reported speed above 120 rpm counts as a fault. Likely causes are a control wire shorted to supply, a welded fan relay (GM files that as P0BC1) or a fan controller that ignores the command. The pack stays cool, but the fan drains the 12 V battery when parked and stays loud. Do not confuse it with P0A82 (fan too weak or off) or the circuit codes P0A81/P0A84/P0A85. Common causes: Fan control wire shorted to supply voltage (medium likelihood); Welded fan relay keeps power applied (medium likelihood); Fan's internal speed controller ignores off command (medium likelihood); Battery control module output stuck active (low likelihood). Symptoms: Battery fan heard running with the vehicle off or idle; Discharged 12 V battery after parking; Hybrid or check engine warning. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A84 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit Low
text: P0A84: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit Low. The controller detects a short to ground on the control output of battery cooling fan 1. GM tests it while the fan is commanded at low duty: a circuit voltage below about 0.26 V counts as a failure, and 16 fails in 20 samples at 250 ms set a Type B code (MIL after two trips). Another GM hybrid program detects it through the output stage status flag (20 of 25 samples). Mitsubishi lists P0A84 in the BMU and PHEV ECU of the 2018–20 Outlander PHEV among codes caused by a frozen battery heater relay, so meaning can differ by maker. Open and high faults are P0A81 and P0A85. With the output pulled low the fan may not respond, the pack warms up and power can be reduced. Common causes: Fan control wire chafed and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Internal short in the fan's control input (medium likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the fan connector (low likelihood); Defective output stage in the controller (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning after two trips; Battery cooling fan does not follow commands; Reduced hybrid power when the pack gets warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A85 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit High
text: P0A85: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit High. The controller detects a short to voltage on the control output of battery cooling fan 1. GM runs the test while the fan is commanded between 11 % and 100 % duty: a circuit voltage above 9 V counts as a failure, and 16 fails in 20 samples set a Type B code with MIL after two trips. GM tables from 2013, 2016, 2018 and 2019 hybrid programs carry it, partly via the output stage status flag. Depending on the circuit, the fan may run constantly at full speed or not respond. The low and open counterparts are P0A84 and P0A81; a fan that keeps running without a circuit fault is P0A83. Common causes: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage (high likelihood); Fan control input internally open or shorted to its supply (medium likelihood); Corroded connector creating leakage to supply (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning after two trips; Battery fan runs constantly or not at all; Possible 12 V battery drain when parked. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A86 – 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit
text: P0A86: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit. The 14 volt power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network of a hybrid or electric vehicle from the high-voltage battery; GM calls it the Accessory Power Module (APM). Current sensor A measures the current flowing through this converter. P0A86 is the general circuit code for that sensor, used when the controller recognises a fault in the sensor circuit without classifying it as low, high, implausible or intermittent (P0A87 to P0A8A). No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's published tables for the same APM input sensor use only the low/high codes P0A88 and P0A89. With an untrustworthy current reading the hybrid controller may limit or switch off the converter, so the 12 V battery can run down over time. Common causes: Current sensor inside the 14 V power module faulty (usually not replaceable separately) (high likelihood); Damaged wiring or corroded connector between module and hybrid controller (medium likelihood); Software fault in the module or hybrid controller (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or charging system warning lamp on; 12 V battery discharges, low-voltage warnings; Possibly no other noticeable change in driving. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A87 – 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0A87: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. This code means the current sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter, GM: APM) delivers values that are electrically valid but implausible. GM's 2016 eAssist tables (hybrid control processor HPC1) describe a stuck-in-range test: once per key cycle, while the high-voltage contactors are open and then move to precharge, the converter should be off, so the averaged input current must be near zero. If the average is 0.50 A or more, P0A87 sets as a Type B code, so the MIL comes on after two failed trips. The test is skipped while P0A88 or P0A89 is active. Unlike those circuit low/high codes, the wiring is usually intact here; a sensor with offset drift is the typical finding. Common causes: Current sensor zero-point drift inside the power module (high likelihood); Converter actually conducting current when it should be off (internal module fault) (medium likelihood); Ground or reference fault distorting the sensor signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two drive cycles; Usually no driveability change; Possible reduced 12 V charging if the converter is limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A88 – 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0A88: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Low. P0A88 reports that the current sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter feeding the 12 V system) reads too low while the converter should be delivering power. GM documents it for the Accessory Power Module: in the 2013 eAssist tables the input current must stay below 0.5 A for 1.5 s within a 2 s window while calculated output power is 0.25 to 1.5 kW; the 2016 tables use 0.50 A or less in 640 of 800 samples, enabled only when the APM is on, the hood is closed and the 12 V target is reached. Both rate it Type B, two trips to MIL. A short to ground, an open signal line or a dead sensor are typical; P0A89 is the opposite high fault, P0A87 the plausibility check. Common causes: Sensor signal shorted to ground or open (high likelihood); Current sensor in the power module failed (medium likelihood); Corroded or loose module connector (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid/charging warning; 12 V battery not charged properly; Start/stop function may be disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A89 – 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0A89: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit High. P0A89 is set when the current sensor of the 14 V power module reports more current than the converter can physically carry. GM's eAssist tables show how: in 2013 the APM input current reading had to exceed 22.5 A for 1.5 s while calculated output power was 1.5 kW or less; in 2016 the limit is 45.25 A or more in 200 of 250 samples (about 5 s) with the APM commanded on and 9 to 32 V supply. Both versions classify it Type B, so the MIL lights after the second failing trip. Typical causes are a signal short to voltage or an internal sensor fault. P0A88 is the low counterpart, P0A87 the in-range plausibility test, and the APM output sensor has its own codes (P0C9E/P0C9F). Common causes: Sensor signal shorted to supply voltage (high likelihood); Current sensor in the power module failed (medium likelihood); Open sensor ground pulling the signal high (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid/charging warning; Converter output limited, 12 V voltage drops; Start/stop function may be disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A8A – 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
text: P0A8A: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent. P0A8A covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal of the current sensor in the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter that charges the 12 V battery in hybrids and EVs. The signal is valid most of the time but briefly leaves its range or changes faster than physically possible. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's APM tables only show the hard limits for the same sensor (P0A88 below 0.5 A, P0A89 above 22.5 A or 45.25 A), which indicates what the intermittent check guards against. Loose terminals, chafed wiring near the module and vibration are the usual suspects. Compared with P0A88/P0A89 the fault often clears and returns, which makes freeze-frame data valuable. Common causes: Loose or fretted terminals at the module connector (high likelihood); Chafed wiring with intermittent short or open (medium likelihood); Intermittent internal fault of the current sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes; Occasional 12 V voltage fluctuations. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A8B – 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage
text: P0A8B: 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage. The 14 V power module (DC/DC converter) regulates the voltage of the 12 V network in hybrid and electric vehicles. P0A8B is the general code for a fault in the voltage this module produces or senses, without the more specific labels unstable, low, high or performance (P0A8C to P0A8F). No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist tables show how the sibling codes are used for the same function: the APM low-voltage sensor is checked against fixed limits and against the separately measured run/crank voltage. A fault here means the 12 V system may no longer be supplied reliably, so the 12 V battery and consumers should be checked before the module is condemned. Common causes: Internal fault of the DC/DC converter (medium likelihood); Loose or corroded 12 V output cable or ground connection (medium likelihood); Weak 12 V battery distorting the system voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Charging or hybrid system warning; Electrical consumers behave erratically; 12 V battery discharged. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A8C – 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage Unstable
text: P0A8C: 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage Unstable. P0A8C indicates that the output voltage of the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter supplying the 12 V network of a hybrid or EV, fluctuates beyond what the control strategy accepts instead of settling at its target. Possible reasons include a poor 12 V connection, an aged 12 V battery that no longer buffers the network, or a regulation problem inside the converter. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's APM tables only cover low, high and performance faults of the same voltage (P0A8D, P0A8E, P0A8F). For the driver, flickering lights, resets of electronic units or start/stop being disabled are typical. Unlike P0A8D/P0A8E the average voltage may still be normal. Common causes: Loose or corroded 12 V battery terminal or ground strap (high likelihood); Aged 12 V battery no longer buffering the network (medium likelihood); Unstable regulation inside the DC/DC converter (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Flickering lights or display resets; Charging or hybrid system warning; Start/stop disabled. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A8D – 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage Low
text: P0A8D: 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage Low. P0A8D reports too low a voltage at the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter feeding the 12 V network). GM uses it in its 2013 eAssist tables as the circuit-low check of the APM low-voltage sensor: if that sensor reads below 1 V for 1.5 s within a 2 s window while ignition voltage is 9 to 32 V, the code sets; it passes again above 1.5 V. It is Type B, two trips to MIL. Because a real 12 V network cannot be at 1 V with the ignition on, GM's version really points to an open or shorted voltage sense line or a failed sensor, not a flat battery. Other makers may apply the code to genuine undervoltage. P0A8E is the high counterpart, P0A8F the correlation check. Common causes: Voltage sense line open or shorted to ground (high likelihood); Voltage sensor inside the power module failed (medium likelihood); Converter not delivering output (fuse, output cable) (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and charging/hybrid warning; 12 V battery discharges; Start/stop disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A8E – 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage High
text: P0A8E: 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage High. P0A8E signals too high a voltage at the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter supplying the 12 V side. In GM's 2013 eAssist tables it is the circuit-high check of the APM low-voltage sensor: a reading above 20 V for 1.5 s within a 2 s window, with ignition voltage 9 to 32 V, sets the code, and it passes below 19.5 V. GM rates it Type B, so the MIL comes on after two failing trips. Since the network should sit around 14 V, a reading over 20 V usually means a sense line shorted to a higher potential or a faulty sensor; a genuinely over-regulating converter would also threaten bulbs and modules. P0A8D is the low counterpart, P0A8F compares the sensor with the ignition voltage. Common causes: Voltage sense line shorted to a higher potential (high likelihood); Voltage sensor inside the power module failed (medium likelihood); Converter regulating its output too high (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and charging/hybrid warning; Very bright lights or failing bulbs if overvoltage is real; Converter may be shut down. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A8F – 14 Volt Power Module System Performance
text: P0A8F: 14 Volt Power Module System Performance. P0A8F means the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter for the 12 V network) does not perform as expected even though its signals are electrically in range. GM's 2013 eAssist tables use it as a correlation test: with the APM commanded on and ignition voltage 9 to 32 V, the APM's own low-voltage reading and the run/crank voltage measured by the controller must agree within 4.5 V. A larger difference over 3.75 s in a 5 s window sets the code as Type B, two trips to MIL. A high resistance in the 12 V output path or ground, a drifting sensor or a converter that cannot hold its target can all cause this. P0A8D and P0A8E cover sensor circuit low/high faults. Common causes: High resistance in 12 V output cable, fuse link or ground (high likelihood); Drifting voltage sensor in the module (medium likelihood); Converter unable to hold its target voltage (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and charging/hybrid warning; Low or fluctuating 12 V voltage. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A90 – Drive Motor A Performance
text: P0A90: Drive Motor A Performance. P0A90 reports that electric drive motor A does not behave as commanded. In GM's eAssist mild hybrid the motor/generator is belt-driven from the crankshaft, so GM uses P0A90 to detect a slipping or broken belt: the motor speed is compared with the engine speed. In 2013 a difference above 1000 rpm for 1.5 s, or repeated smaller slips above 500 rpm on two key cycles, set it; the 2016 tables use more than 1500 rpm for about 5.6 s or repeated 1000 rpm slip events. GM rates it Type A, MIL on the first trip. In full hybrids the generic definition applies to speed or torque deviations of the traction motor. P0A91 is the equivalent for motor B, P0A92 for the generator. Common causes: Slipping, worn or broken drive belt on belt-driven motor/generators (high likelihood); Faulty belt tensioner or contamination on the belt (medium likelihood); Motor, position sensor or inverter fault in full hybrids (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning; Belt squeal or auto-stop/start not working; Reduced electric assist or limp mode. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A91 – Drive Motor B Performance
text: P0A91: Drive Motor B Performance. P0A91 is set when the second electric drive motor (motor B) of a hybrid or electric vehicle does not deliver the expected speed or torque, although no electrical circuit fault is detected. Motor B exists only on systems with two traction motors, such as power-split or dual-motor layouts. CARB requires hybrid OBD systems to monitor electric motor performance. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's tables describe the motor A equivalent P0A90 as a comparison between motor speed and a reference speed, which illustrates the approach. Causes range from inverter or resolver faults to mechanical damage. The vehicle usually limits power or enters a reduced mode. P0A79 covers inverter B performance. Common causes: Inverter B fault limiting motor current (medium likelihood); Motor position sensor (resolver) signal error (medium likelihood); Mechanical damage to motor B or its gearing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid/EV system warning and MIL; Reduced power or limp mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A92 – Hybrid Generator Performance
text: P0A92: Hybrid Generator Performance. P0A92 indicates that the generator of a hybrid system, the electric machine mainly used to convert engine power into electrical energy, does not reach the expected output, speed or torque. CARB requires manufacturers to describe how they monitor the generator so that faults preventing it from working are detected. FCA documents the code for the 2020 Jeep Compass and Renegade plug-in hybrids (bulletin 08-057-21): it appears together with drive motor phase current sensor codes, and the fix is a software update of the hybrid control processor and power inverter module. A turtle (limp home) lamp may accompany it. P0A90/P0A91 cover the drive motors; P0A3F and similar codes cover generator position sensing. Common causes: Hybrid controller or inverter software needing update (documented by FCA) (high likelihood); Inverter phase current sensing fault (medium likelihood); Internal generator fault (winding, bearing, position sensor) (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning; Limp home (turtle) lamp, reduced power; Reduced charging of the high-voltage battery. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A93 – Inverter A Cooling System Performance
text: P0A93: Inverter A Cooling System Performance. The power inverter of a hybrid has its own coolant circuit with an electric pump, radiator and fan, separate from engine cooling. P0A93 is set when this circuit does not cool as intended. CARB lists inverter thermal management among the components that hybrid OBD must monitor. Hyundai documents the code for the 2011 Sonata Hybrid (bulletin 14-HC-001), assigning it, like P0C73, to the electric water pump; symptoms include a hybrid warning, no EV mode and poor acceleration. Toyota recalled 2004–2009 Prius models (12V-536) because the inverter water pump could fail and cause a stall; that notice does not name a code. A leaking or air-locked circuit should also be checked. Common causes: Electric inverter coolant pump failed or seized (high likelihood); Low coolant or air in the inverter circuit (medium likelihood); Pump wiring, fuse or relay fault (medium likelihood); Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and MIL; No EV mode, reduced power; Vehicle may not start or may stall. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0A94 – DC/DC Converter A Performance
text: P0A94: DC/DC Converter A Performance. P0A94 reports that a DC/DC converter in the high-voltage system does not perform as commanded. In Toyota hybrids this is the boost converter inside the inverter assembly, which raises the battery voltage before it reaches the motor inverters. Toyota documents P0A94 for 2010–2015 Prius and 2012–2017 Prius v together with P0A1A, P324E and P3004 (bulletin T-SB-0003-21): the cause is damage in the inverter with converter, and the repair depends on the detail code. Recalls 14V-053 and 18V-684 address transistors in the intelligent power module that could overheat; the car then enters a fail-safe mode with reduced power. Not to be confused with the 14 V power module codes P0A86 to P0A8F. Common causes: Damaged power transistors in the boost converter / inverter assembly (high likelihood); Thermal stress from insufficient inverter cooling (medium likelihood); Outstanding recall or software update not performed (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL, hybrid system and other warning lamps; Fail-safe mode with greatly reduced power; Vehicle may stop and not restart. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A95 – High Voltage Fuse A
text: P0A95: High Voltage Fuse A. P0A95 means the battery management detects that a fuse in the high-voltage circuit has opened, usually by comparing the voltage before and after the fuse. Several makers document it: Jaguar for the I-PACE battery energy control module, where a shorted high-voltage auxiliary component blows fuses in the junction box and battery module; Porsche for the Taycan as the main high-voltage fuse with a vehicle that will not become ready to drive; Volvo, whose procedure compares the voltage after the fuses with pack voltage; and Audi, which found an intermittent false entry in hard cornering fixed by software. P0E2F and P0E30 cover fuses B and C. Mostly the car cannot be driven until the cause is found. Common causes: Short circuit in a high-voltage auxiliary component (e.g. compressor, heater) (high likelihood); Fuse opened after overload or ageing (medium likelihood); Faulty voltage measurement or software misdetection in the battery control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle not ready to drive, propulsion warning; MIL or yellow warning lamp; Climate compressor or heater inoperative. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0A96 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit/Open
text: P0A96: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit/Open. Some packs use two cooling fans; P0A96 reports an open or general fault in the control circuit of the second one. Ford documents it code-exact: on 2005–12 Escape Hybrid and 2006–11 Mariner Hybrid the traction battery control module may store P0A96, often together with P0A81 for fan 1, and the repair is to replace both high-voltage battery fans with a kit (about 3 hours, pack removal included). Ford notes the code alone usually causes no noticeable symptom. CARB requires the electronic outputs used for battery thermal management to be monitored. Short-circuit faults on fan 2 are P0A99 and P0A9A. If one fan fails, cooling capacity drops and power may be limited in heat. Common causes: Fan 2 motor or electronics failed (Ford replaces both fans) (high likelihood); Loose connector or broken wire to fan 2 (medium likelihood); Blown fan fuse (low likelihood). Symptoms: Code found during other diagnosis, often no complaint; Check engine or hybrid warning; Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions. Repair difficulty: shop_only.
