Siblings are P0AD9 (open) and P0ADB (low). A short to power can energize the coil unintentionally, so the contactor may not open when it should. Symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning light; High-voltage system disabled, vehicle not ready; Possible related stuck-closed codes. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0ADD – Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit/Open
text: P0ADD: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit/Open. The negative main contactor closes the return path of the traction battery; P0ADD reports an open in its coil drive circuit. Without this contactor the HV system stays off. title: P0ADE – Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0ADE: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance. title: P0AE0 – Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit High
text: P0AE0: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit High. title: P0AE1 – Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit
text: P0AE1: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit. Before the main contactors close, a precharge contactor routes battery current through a resistor so the inverter capacitors fill slowly instead of drawing a damaging inrush. P0AE1 is the general fault of this precharge path when it is not split into stuck closed (P0AE2), stuck open (P0AE3) or a driver fault (P0AE4 to P0AE7). Honda lists P0AE1 as a bypass contactor malfunction in bulletins 20-030 (2012-15 Civic Hybrid) and 20-021 (2013 ILX Hybrid); there a cracked solder joint in the motor power inverter is the cause and the whole inverter is replaced. Mercedes-Benz names P0AE173 on the G 580 with EQ technology after unplugging the AC charger too early. Expect no ready mode or no charging. Common causes: Defective solder joint in the motor power inverter (Honda IMA) (high likelihood); Precharge contactor or precharge resistor failed (medium likelihood); Fault logged by battery controller software after an interrupted charging sequence (low likelihood); Wiring or connector fault in the contactor circuit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning in the cluster; Vehicle does not become ready to drive; Charging not possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AE2 – Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
text: P0AE2: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed. P0AE2 means the precharge path conducts although it should be open, for example welded contacts or a precharge switch that no longer turns off. GM's 2011 Volt table checks it once per precharge event: if the bus voltage already exceeds 80 % of pack voltage before precharge begins, the precharge FET is judged stuck closed, 4 of 4 samples, Type A with MIL after one trip. Mitsubishi lists P0AE2 as charging contactor seizure on the 2012 i-MiEV (TSB-12-54-014). Audi names it for the 2022 e-tron GT with a software fix, and Dodge and Jeep list P0AE2-00 for the 2025 Charger EV and 2024 Wagoneer S, where a battery pack replacement may be required. The car may refuse to start. Common causes: Precharge contactor contacts welded or precharge switch shorted (high likelihood); Battery controller software sets the code falsely (Audi, Stellantis bulletins) (medium likelihood); Contactor driver held on by a short to power (low likelihood); Bus voltage not discharged before the next precharge (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle does not become ready to drive; MIL and hybrid or EV warning on; Wrench symbol or service message in the cluster. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AE3 – Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
text: P0AE3: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Open. P0AE3 is set when the precharge path does not conduct after it has been commanded closed, so the bus voltage fails to rise and the main contactors are not allowed to close. GM documents several cases: preliminary information PIC6165A for the 2016-17 Chevrolet Volt describes a rare P0AE3 in cool weather right after a completed charge, without driveability effects; parts should not be replaced, a new calibration followed, and the MIL goes out after three clean drive cycles. GM bulletin 23-NA-151 lists P0AE3 among high-priority codes on Ultium EVs that call for battery stability checks. Audi includes P0AE300 for the 2022 e-tron GT. Unlike P0AE2, the contacts stay open; a slow precharge is P0C78. Common causes: Battery controller calibration sets the code under certain conditions (GM Volt, Audi) (high likelihood); Precharge contactor contacts burnt or coil not pulling in (medium likelihood); Precharge resistor or its fuse open (medium likelihood); Internal fault in the battery disconnect unit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle does not become ready to drive; MIL or service engine soon light on; No battery charge level shown after switching on. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AE4 – Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit/Open
text: P0AE4: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit/Open. P0AE4 concerns the circuit that drives the coil of precharge contactor A, not its contacts. title: P0AE5 – Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0AE5: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance. P0AE5 reports that the precharge function works electrically but does not deliver the expected result, so the controller judges the circuit implausible. Ford documents it in special service message SSM 47129: 2013-18 C-MAX and Fusion Hybrid and Energi models and the MKZ Hybrid may not start, with P0AE5 stored in the battery energy control module. When pinpoint tests show that the DC/DC converter, the cabin coolant heater or the A/C compressor has a low internal resistance on its high-voltage side, Ford replaces only that component, not the battery junction box. A load that drags the bus down keeps the precharge from reaching its target. Open, low and high driver faults are P0AE4, P0AE6 and P0AE7. Common causes: High-voltage consumer with low internal resistance (DC/DC converter, coolant heater, A/C compressor) (high likelihood); Precharge resistor degraded or wrong value (medium likelihood); Precharge contactor responding slowly or with high contact resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle does not start or become ready; Red warning triangle or hybrid warning in the cluster; Possible additional codes from the faulty high-voltage consumer. title: P0AE8 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit
text: P0AE8: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit. Battery temperature sensor D is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the matching codes as temperature sensor 4 of nine. P0AE8 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller finds an electrical fault without classifying it as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables report the more specific siblings P0AE9 to P0AEC instead. CARB requires temperature inputs of hybrid batteries to be monitored for circuit faults. With one value missing, the controller has a gap in its temperature picture and usually limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits on a module or sensing board inside the pack, so checks require high-voltage safety procedures. Common causes: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor D and sensing board (high likelihood); Temperature sensor D failed (medium likelihood); Fault in the battery controller input stage (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning; Reduced electric power and regeneration; Further battery sensor codes may be stored. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AE9 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0AE9: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance. P0AE9 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor D, GM's sensor 4: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. In GM's 2016 and 2019 tables it fails when the value is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use more than 15 °C in 90 of 100; the eAssist table 13OBDG05C allows 8.55 °C after a long module off time; GM's 2018 table uses 20 °C for 5 s within 6.7 s. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 counts P0AE9 among sensor codes that set falsely in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming. Otherwise a drifting sensor or a real hot spot in one module is the likely cause. Common causes: Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342) (medium likelihood); Temperature sensor D drifting out of tolerance (medium likelihood); Genuine local temperature difference in one battery module (low likelihood); Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips; Battery Too Cold message despite mild weather (Volt); Reduced charge and electric drive power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AEA – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
text: P0AEA: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low. P0AEA means the voltage of battery temperature sensor D is below its valid range. GM uses NTC thermistors with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an extremely hot cell, usually from a short to ground. Thresholds vary: above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples in the 2016 and 2019 tables; above 95 °C in 30 of 40 on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids; below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 in the eAssist table 13OBDG05C; above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s in a 2018 controller. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists P0AEA among codes that can set falsely and calls for a software update first. A genuinely hot pack would trip lower limits earlier, so treat it as electrical. Common causes: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Temperature sensor D internally shorted (medium likelihood); Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342) (medium likelihood); Moisture or damage on the battery sensing board (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips; Charge and drive power strongly limited; Battery cooling running more than usual. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AEB – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
text: P0AEB: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit High. P0AEB reports that battery temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensors this reads as extreme cold, pointing to an open wire, a backed-out pin at the sensing board or a cracked thermistor. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids below -45 °C in 30 of 40, the eAssist table 13OBDG05C above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10, and a 2018 controller below -40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; all Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links such codes to a Battery Too Cold message above -25 °C ambient and prescribes reprogramming. A pack the controller believes frozen gets strict charge and power limits. Common causes: Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor D (high likelihood); Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342) (medium likelihood); Temperature sensor D open internally (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips; Battery Too Cold message (Volt); Charging and electric drive restricted. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AEC – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0AEC: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0AEC flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor D: the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables. The controller sums the absolute changes of the sensor value across a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips. GM applies the same logic to sensors A to C. The older two-mode and eAssist tables list no erratic code for sensor D. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a partly broken wire or a connector not fully latched after pack service. If several sensors jump at once, suspect the sensing board rather than the individual thermistor. Common causes: Loose terminal or connector not fully latched at sensor D (high likelihood); Partly broken or chafed sensor wire (medium likelihood); Fault on the battery sensing board (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips, may go out again; Jumping battery temperature in live data; Occasional power limitation. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AED – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0AED: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit. The inverter of an electric drive motor carries thermistors near its power switches so the controller can derate before the IGBTs overheat. In GM's hybrid tables, inverter temperature sensor A is the phase U sensor of the inverter for motor A. P0AED is the general circuit code for it, used for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the specific siblings P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensors for circuit faults. Without a valid inverter temperature the controller has to assume the worst and usually limits motor torque. The sensor is built into the power inverter module, so repair often means replacing that unit. Common causes: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module (medium likelihood); Software fault in the motor control processor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp; Reduced electric drive power; Possible loss of electric drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AEE – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0AEE: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. P0AEE checks whether inverter temperature sensor A reads sensibly. GM's 2016 to 2019 tables compare it after a cold soak with an average temperature of the vehicle; more than 20 °C apart sets Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors (20 °C, Type A), the 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off (15 °C), eAssist with module and MGU temperatures (20 °C). GM bulletin PIC6303A notes that on Volt, Malibu and LaCrosse with 5ET50 the code alone triggers no remedy; the inverter is only replaced with P0AC4. Audi fixes P0AEE00 on Q5 and A7 e quattro by software, and Honda lists it among inverter faults of the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid with extended warranty. Common causes: Controller software error (Audi Q5/A7 e quattro bulletin) (medium likelihood); Inverter temperature sensor A drifting out of tolerance (medium likelihood); Failing power inverter module (e.g. Honda MPI solder joints) (medium likelihood); Uneven inverter cooling after soak (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp, often without drivability change; Drive system fault warning (Audi); Vehicle may not start in hybrid mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AEF – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0AEF: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low. P0AEF means the signal of inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. GM describes it as an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an impossibly hot inverter, usually a short to ground or an internal sensor fault. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 150 °C on eAssist; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. Stellantis lists P0AEF-11 for the 2026 Jeep Compass PHEV outside the US among codes behind an Electric Traction System Fault and a no-start, repaired by replacing the inverter. Common causes: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present (medium likelihood); Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Electric drive power cut back strongly; Vehicle may not start (Jeep Compass PHEV). Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF0 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
text: P0AF0: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit High. P0AF0 reports a signal from inverter temperature sensor A above its valid range, which for an NTC sensor reads as an extremely cold inverter: open wire, lost ground or a broken sensor. GM's 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables set it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only after at least 90 s of inverter warm-up at 20 Nm or more, so a really cold car does not trigger it; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), eAssist below -70 °C and the two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). Kia's 2025 Sorento Hybrid bulletin lists P0AF0 with P0A3C and P1B77 after intermittent motor operation during engine clutch learning and fixes it with a motor control unit update. Common causes: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Motor control unit software (Kia Sorento Hybrid 2025) (medium likelihood); Loose or corroded connector at the inverter (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Reduced electric drive power; Traction motor noise or inoperative A/C (Kia). Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF1 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0AF1: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0AF1 is meant for an inverter temperature sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of failing permanently. Inverter heat sinks are liquid-cooled and change temperature smoothly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or an internal fault in the sensing circuit. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables cover sensor A only with the plausibility, low and high codes P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0. GM's method for erratic battery sensors, such as P0AEC, sums signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, which shows how such a check usually works. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for this kind of fault. Freeze-frame data help, since the fault often comes and goes. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module (high likelihood); Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module (medium likelihood); Electrical interference on the sensor signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes; Brief power reductions while driving; Jumping inverter temperature in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF2 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
text: P0AF2: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit. Inverter temperature sensor B is, in GM's hybrid tables, the phase U thermistor of the second inverter, the one that drives motor B in two-motor systems. P0AF2 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables report the specific siblings P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensor circuits. Without a valid temperature the controller cannot protect the power switches of inverter B and usually limits that motor's torque. Whether a vehicle uses sensor B at all depends on its layout, so read the full code list and check the inverter connectors. Common causes: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module (medium likelihood); Software fault in the motor control processor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp; Reduced electric drive or generator power; Higher fuel consumption in hybrid operation. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF3 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0AF3: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance. P0AF3 is the plausibility test for inverter temperature sensor B, the phase U sensor of GM's motor B inverter. In the 2016 to 2019 tables the sensor is compared after a cold soak with a calculated average vehicle temperature; a difference above 20 °C sets the code, Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors at 20 °C, Type A, and the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off at 15 °C, Type B. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0AF3 with P0AEE and the other inverter thermistor codes on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal with the 5ET50 drive: alone they cause no noticeable effect, and the inverter is replaced only if P0AC4 set at the same time. Common causes: Inverter temperature sensor B drifting out of tolerance (medium likelihood); Failing power inverter module (medium likelihood); Uneven inverter coolant flow after soak (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips; Often no noticeable drivability change; Further inverter temperature codes may be stored. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF4 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
text: P0AF4: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low. P0AF4 reports a signal of inverter temperature sensor B below the valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up, so a low voltage reads as an inverter far hotter than possible, usually from a short to ground or an internal sensor fault in the motor B inverter. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. A genuine overheat is reported separately as an over-temperature code such as P0A3D or P0C14. Because the sensor sits inside the inverter, the fix is usually the inverter assembly. Common causes: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present (medium likelihood); Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Motor B power strongly limited; Reduced hybrid assist and regeneration. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF5 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
text: P0AF5: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High. P0AF5 means inverter temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely. In GM's 2016 to 2019 tables the code sets below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only once the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more, which rules out a genuinely cold start; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C with Type A, one trip; the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks use below -40 °C, Type B. Until the value is valid, the controller protects inverter B with substitute values and may reduce motor B power. Check connectors at the inverter before condemning the unit. Common causes: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter (medium likelihood); Lost sensor ground (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips; Reduced motor B power; Implausibly cold inverter temperature in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF6 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0AF6: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0AF6 targets an inverter temperature sensor B signal that jumps or drops out briefly. Since the heat sink of the motor B inverter is liquid-cooled and warms or cools gradually, abrupt changes in the reading indicate a contact problem or an intermittent fault in the sensing circuit rather than real temperature. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables only list P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 for sensor B. For erratic battery temperature sensors such as P0AEC, GM sums the signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, a likely model for this check. CARB requires sensor inputs of hybrid systems to be checked for erratic behaviour. Watch live data while gently moving the inverter harness. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module (high likelihood); Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module (medium likelihood); Electrical interference on the sensor signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes; Brief reductions of motor B power; Jumping inverter temperature in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF7 – 14 Volt Power Module Internal Temperature Too High
text: P0AF7: 14 Volt Power Module Internal Temperature Too High. The 14 V power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery in hybrids and EVs. P0AF7 reports that its internal temperature has exceeded the protection limit, a real overheat rather than a sensor circuit fault. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist table shows how the same module is watched: its Accessory Power Module has two temperature sensors with their own circuit codes, and the separate code P0C32 compares sensor 1 with a thermal model and fails if they differ by more than 15 °C. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components. Common causes are a blocked cooling path, a weak coolant pump or fan, or a constantly high 12 V load. The module then derates its output, so the 12 V battery may run down. Common causes: Restricted cooling, weak coolant pump or failed cooling fan (high likelihood); Sustained high 12 V load or weak 12 V battery (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the DC/DC converter (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp or 12 V charging warning; Low 12 V voltage, flickering lights; Comfort consumers switched off. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF8 – Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage
text: P0AF8: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage. P0AF8 compares the battery pack voltage reported by the battery controller with an independent measurement on the high-voltage bus. GM calls it system voltage correlation: with the contactors closed, the 2019 tables fail it when the pack reading differs from the inverter bus voltage by more than 13.95 V, or from the charger bus voltage by more than 14.95 V, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A. The 2011 Volt table uses 12 V and Type A, the 2013 eAssist table 5.77 V against the motor controller, Type B. GM's Saturn Vue Hybrid PIP4005A links P0AF8 with P0AFB to a loose negative battery cable, and Volt PIC6089B mentions it with low 12 V system faults. P0AFA and P0AFB judge the voltage level itself. Common causes: Loose or arcing high-voltage battery cable connection (high likelihood); Pack or bus voltage sensing circuit inaccurate (medium likelihood); Low 12 V supply or loose 12 V power fuse affecting the measuring modules (medium likelihood); High resistance in a pack fuse or main contactor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on; Battery saver or low battery message; Intermittent no crank or reduced hybrid power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AF9 – Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Unstable
text: P0AF9: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Unstable. P0AF9 is meant for a traction battery voltage that fluctuates more than load changes can explain, for example through a loose terminal, an intermittent contactor or a cell group that collapses under load. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, covers system voltage with P0AF8 (correlation), P0AFA and P0AFB (low and high), and reports uneven cell groups as P0BBE pack voltage variation, which bulletin 19-NA-117 ties to degraded cells in the Volt and ELR. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored for circuit and rationality faults. Typical effects are intermittent power limits and warnings; check high-voltage connections and cell voltages under load. Common causes: Loose high-voltage terminal or busbar connection (high likelihood); Degraded cell group collapsing under load (medium likelihood); Main contactor with intermittent contact (low likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent hybrid or EV warning; Sudden power reductions while driving; Code may come and go without lasting symptoms. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AFA – Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Low
text: P0AFA: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Low. P0AFA protects the traction battery from deep discharge: the pack voltage, or in some versions any cell voltage, has fallen below a temperature-dependent limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it after 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack or 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch it so that only a technician command can clear it. GM bulletins name causes: degraded cell groups in 2011-15 Volt and ELR (19-NA-117), a blown fuse in the Bolt EV manual disconnect lever (18-NA-225), cell contamination in the 2015 Spark EV (17-NA-131) and repeated cranking that empties the Malibu Hybrid pack (PIC6229). A Ram eTorque parts notice names it for the 48 V power pack. Expect a no-start. Common causes: Degraded or self-discharging cell groups (high likelihood); Pack drained by repeated failed engine starts or long standing (medium likelihood); Open high-voltage fuse or manual disconnect (medium likelihood); Loose or high-resistance ground on 48 V systems (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle does not start; restart blocked while the code is latched; Reduced or lost propulsion before the no-start; Plug-in charging not possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AFB – Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage High
text: P0AFB: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage High. P0AFB guards against overcharging: the pack voltage, or a single cell, exceeds a temperature-dependent upper limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables use 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack and 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch the code until a technician clears it by command; the 2011 Volt table also uses Type A. On the 2007-09 Saturn Vue Hybrid, GM's PIP4005A finds P0AFB together with P0AF8 caused by a loose negative battery cable. Mercedes-Benz uses P0AFB00 on 48 V starter-alternator systems for an on-board voltage that is too high, with software fixes for M256 engines, S-Class and GLE/GLS. Toyota's Prius Prime tech tip uses P0AFB11 with a current sensor text. Common causes: Loose or arcing battery cable causing voltage spikes (medium likelihood); Control unit software allows overvoltage (Mercedes 48 V bulletins) (medium likelihood); Cell imbalance so that one cell overcharges (medium likelihood); Faulty voltage sensing reporting too high a value (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system or MIL warning; Start-stop or regenerative braking disabled; Possible no crank on mild hybrids. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AFC – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Sensor Module
text: P0AFC: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Sensor Module. Some hybrid packs carry a separate sensor module that measures block voltages and passes them to the battery controller; Toyota calls it the battery voltage sensor or battery smart unit. P0AFC reports a fault of this module itself, such as a failed self-check or disturbed data transfer. Toyota documents it for the 2012-2015 Camry Hybrid in tech tip T-TT-0359-15 (repair manual entry P0AFC-123): an aftermarket antenna in the trunk, for example for CB radio, can set the code, and relocating it is the first step before following the regular diagnosis. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored. Without valid block voltages the hybrid system usually shuts down or limits power. Common causes: Radio interference from an aftermarket antenna near the battery (Toyota Camry Hybrid) (high likelihood); Battery voltage sensor module internally defective (medium likelihood); Supply or communication wiring of the sensor module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and check hybrid system warning on; Hybrid drive disabled or reduced; Code may return when the radio transmitter is used. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AFD – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Temperature Too Low
text: P0AFD: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Temperature Too Low. P0AFD indicates that the traction battery is colder than its permitted operating range. At very low temperatures cell resistance rises and charging risks lithium plating, so the controller restricts or blocks charging and discharging. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. As a related case, GM's bulletin 18-NA-342 describes a Chevrolet Volt showing Battery Too Cold, Plug in to Warm above -25 °C because of faulty temperature sensor readings, fixed by reprogramming. CARB requires hybrid battery temperature inputs and their plausibility to be monitored. Distinguish a genuinely cold pack, which warms up on the charger or through the battery heater, from a sensor or heater fault; sensor circuit faults have their own codes. Common causes: Vehicle parked unplugged in extreme cold (high likelihood); Battery heater or coolant heater not working (medium likelihood); Temperature sensor reading too cold (sensor or software) (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Battery too cold message in the cluster; Reduced electric power or electric drive unavailable; Charging slow or not possible until the pack warms up. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0AFE – Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Up Conversion
text: P0AFE: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Up Conversion. Many hybrids raise the battery voltage with a step-up (boost) converter before it reaches the inverters; Toyota's second-generation Hybrid Synergy Drive, for example, boosts a pack of around 200 V to 500 V or more. The converter needs a minimum input voltage to reach its target without excessive current. P0AFE is set when the battery-side voltage is below that minimum, so the converter cannot boost properly. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires hybrid components such as converters to be monitored for functional faults. A deeply discharged or weak pack, a high-resistance connection or a voltage measurement fault are the obvious suspects. Expect reduced electric assist; a low pack voltage is reported separately as P0AFA. Common causes: Pack deeply discharged or weak under load (high likelihood); High-resistance connection between battery and converter (medium likelihood); Converter input voltage measured too low (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning; Reduced acceleration and electric assist; Engine runs more often than usual. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0AFF – System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Down Conversion
text: P0AFF: System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Down Conversion. A step-down (buck) DC/DC converter, often called the accessory power module, supplies the 12 V system from the high-voltage or 48 V bus. To regulate its output it needs an input voltage above a minimum. P0AFF is set when the input system voltage is too low for this conversion, so the converter cannot hold its 12 V output. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM monitors the related function in its 2013 eAssist table: P0CA2 flags a step-down failure of the 14 V power module after a shoot-through fault in its switching device, one trip, Type A. CARB requires such hybrid components to be monitored. Expect a charging system warning and a slowly draining 12 V battery. Common causes: High-voltage or 48 V bus voltage too low (discharged pack, open contactor) (high likelihood); High-resistance input connection or fuse of the DC/DC converter (medium likelihood); DC/DC converter internal measuring fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Battery or charging system warning light; 12 V battery discharges, electrical consumers fail; Hybrid or start-stop functions restricted. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B00 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current
text: P0B00: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current. P0B00 is the general fault for phase U of the three-phase motor that drives the electric auxiliary transmission fluid pump, the pump that keeps line pressure while the engine is stopped. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM, which runs such pumps on the Volt, ELR, Spark EV and CT6, monitors phase U instead with the low-side code P0B01 and catches overcurrent on any phase with P0C28. A Hitachi patent for an idle-stop sub-oil pump shows that the inverter often derives every phase current from one DC-bus shunt, so a U fault may come from the shared sensor rather than the phase itself. Expect a warning lamp, a stopped pump and, depending on design, no engine auto-stop or a no-start. P0B01/P0B02 are the low and high variants, P0B03 and P0B06 phases V and W. Common causes: Loose, corroded or unlatched phase U connection at the pump motor (high likelihood); Current sensing in the pump inverter faulty (shunt or phase sensor) (medium likelihood); Power stage of phase U in the pump control module faulty (medium likelihood); Winding fault in phase U of the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or hybrid/transmission warning message; Engine auto-stop disabled or no electric drive mode; Delayed engagement or harsh restart after a stop. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B01 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current Low
text: P0B01: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current Low. P0B01 means the pump inverter sees almost no current in phase U of the auxiliary fluid pump motor, typically an open phase. GM documents the check for the Volt motor control processor (2016) and its hybrid tables of 2018 and 2019: with the drive state in Run, the inverter in normal PWM above 50 V and a squared current command above 5 A2 (2016) or 14.97 A2 (2018), the peak current on the U axis is compared while the rotor is within 30 degrees of it; below 1 A for 0.4 s of a 0.6 s window, the code sets as Type A, MIL on the first trip. On the 2014-15 Chevrolet Spark EV, GM bulletin PI1433 links P0B01, P0B04 or P0B07, Service Vehicle Soon and reduced propulsion to an unlatched pump connector. P0B04/P0B07 are phases V and W, P0B02 the high side. Common causes: Pump motor connector not fully seated or latched (Chevrolet Spark EV) (high likelihood); Open circuit in the phase U lead or terminal of the pump motor cable (medium likelihood); Phase U switch in the pump inverter not conducting (medium likelihood); Open winding of phase U in the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Service Vehicle Soon light and MIL; Propulsion Power Reduced or Vehicle Speed Limited message. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B02 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current High
text: P0B02: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase U Current High. P0B02 reports excessive current in phase U of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor, an overcurrent condition that the pump inverter must cut off to protect its switches. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM handles the same case differently: on the Volt and later hybrids it sets P0C28 when the absolute current of any phase exceeds 35 A for a few milliseconds, Type A. A phase-specific high code therefore points to a shorted U lead, a shorted winding, a jammed pump or a U current sensor reading too high. The Hitachi idle-stop pump patent shows phase currents being reconstructed from one bus shunt, which makes a sensing error a real candidate. The pump usually stops; auto-stop or electric driving is blocked. P0B01 is the low side, P0B05 and P0B08 the same fault on V and W. Common causes: Phase U lead shorted to another phase or to ground (high likelihood); Pump binding mechanically, raising motor current (medium likelihood); Current sensing in the pump inverter reads too high (medium likelihood); Shorted turns in phase U of the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and transmission or hybrid warning; Auxiliary pump shuts down, auto-stop disabled; Harsh or delayed engagement after an engine stop. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B03 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current
text: P0B03: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current. P0B03 covers a general current fault in phase V of the brushless motor of the electric auxiliary transmission fluid pump. No manufacturer publicly describes a monitor for it. GM's 2013 eAssist (BAS Plus) tables name P0B03 only once, as a code that must be inactive before another speed check runs, without a description of its own. In GM's Volt and CT6 tables phase V is watched by the low-side code P0B04, and any overcurrent goes to P0C28. A GM, BMW and Daimler patent on a hybrid transmission pump explains why the pump matters: it must hold transmission pressure when the engine is stopped, otherwise gear engagement can be lost. The general code is a catch-all for implausible V current that fits neither low nor high. P0B04/P0B05 are the low and high variants, P0B00 and P0B06 phases U and W. Common causes: Poor contact in the phase V lead or pump connector (high likelihood); Current sensing in the pump inverter faulty (medium likelihood); Phase V power stage in the pump control module faulty (medium likelihood); Winding fault in phase V of the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or transmission/hybrid warning; Engine auto-stop or electric mode no longer available. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B04 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current Low
text: P0B04: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current Low. P0B04 indicates that phase V of the auxiliary fluid pump motor carries too little current, usually because the phase is open somewhere between inverter and winding. GM tests it on the Volt (2016) and in the 2018 and 2019 hybrid tables like its U and W siblings: in Run, with normal PWM, more than 50 V on the inverter and a minimum squared current command, the V current is sampled while the rotor sits within 30 degrees of the V axis. Under 1 A for 0.4 s out of 0.6 s (0.08 s windows in 2019) sets a Type A fault. GM bulletin PI1433 for the 2014-15 Spark EV names P0B04 with Service Vehicle Soon and reduced propulsion and points to the pump connector not being latched. P0B01 and P0B07 are phases U and W, P0B05 the high side, P0B03 the general V code. Common causes: Pump motor connector not fully seated or latched (Chevrolet Spark EV) (high likelihood); Open circuit in the phase V lead or terminal (medium likelihood); Phase V switch in the pump inverter not conducting (medium likelihood); Open winding of phase V in the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Service Vehicle Soon light and MIL; Reduced propulsion power or limited vehicle speed. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B05 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current High
text: P0B05: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase V Current High. P0B05 flags overcurrent in phase V of the electric auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor. No manufacturer publicly documents this specific code. GM monitors the same physical fault without naming the phase: P0C28 trips when any of U, V or W exceeds 35 A for about 10 ms within a 62 ms window, and a 2018 Cadillac CT6 plug-in service update shows how a faulty pump restart routine alone can push the current over that limit. Likely triggers for a V-specific high code are a short in the V lead, shorted turns, a seized or contaminated pump, or a restart against a stalled rotor. The Hitachi patent on sub-oil pump drives shows the phase currents come from a shared sensor. Auto-stop is usually blocked. P0B04 is the low side, P0B02 and P0B08 phases U and W. Common causes: Phase V lead shorted to another phase or to ground (high likelihood); Pump seized or contaminated, motor draws excess current (medium likelihood); Pump restart logic in the inverter software causing overcurrent (medium likelihood); Shorted turns in phase V of the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and transmission or hybrid warning; Loss of propulsion or no-start in severe cases. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B06 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current
text: P0B06: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current. P0B06 is the general current fault for phase W of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor. No manufacturer publishes a monitor description for this exact code. GM covers phase W in its Volt, ELR and CT6 calibrations with the low-side code P0B07 and treats overcurrent on any phase as P0C28. CARB requires hybrid and transmission components whose failure affects emissions or other monitors to be checked for circuit faults and rationality, which is why manufacturers can use the general code for implausible readings. The Hitachi sub-oil pump patent describes a sinusoidal drive whose W current is calculated from a single bus shunt, so wiring, sensing and the power stage are all suspects. The pump stops and auto-stop is blocked. P0B07/P0B08 are the low and high variants, P0B00 and P0B03 phases U and V. Common causes: Poor contact in the phase W lead or pump connector (high likelihood); Current sensing in the pump inverter faulty (medium likelihood); Phase W power stage in the pump control module faulty (medium likelihood); Winding fault in phase W of the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or transmission/hybrid warning; Engine keeps running at stops, no auto-stop. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B07 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current Low
text: P0B07: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current Low. P0B07 means phase W of the auxiliary fluid pump motor carries less current than commanded, the typical sign of an open W path. GM uses it on the Volt and later hybrids: below 1 A peak W-axis current for 0.4 s of 0.6 s, with the inverter in normal PWM above 50 V, sets a Type A fault. A GM service update for the 2017-18 Cadillac CT6 plug-in shows the code had been calibrated off; a W phase loss then shut the car down or prevented starting with no code and no MIL, until reprogramming of the drive motor power inverter module enabled P0B07 as Type A. On the 2014-15 Spark EV, bulletin PI1433 ties P0B01, P0B04 or P0B07 to an unlatched pump connector. P0B01 and P0B04 are phases U and V, P0B08 the high side, P0B06 the general W code. Common causes: Pump motor connector not fully seated or latched (Chevrolet Spark EV) (high likelihood); Open circuit in the phase W lead or terminal (medium likelihood); Outdated inverter software (Cadillac CT6 plug-in, service update 18199) (medium likelihood); Open winding of phase W in the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and Service Vehicle Soon light; Loss of propulsion, vehicle shutdown or no-start. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B08 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current High
text: P0B08: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Phase W Current High. P0B08 is set when the current in phase W of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump motor rises above the permitted limit. No manufacturer documents this exact code in public sources. In GM's 2016 Volt calibration the equivalent protection is P0C28, which fails on any phase above 35 A or on a d-axis current below a temperature-dependent limit, both within milliseconds to protect the IGBTs. A W-specific high code points to a short in the W lead or winding, a binding pump or a sensing error; the Hitachi patent shows the W value may be calculated rather than measured directly. CARB requires such output drivers to be monitored for circuit faults. The pump shuts down, so start-stop and electric driving are restricted. P0B07 is the low side, P0B02 and P0B05 phases U and V. Common causes: Phase W lead shorted to another phase or to ground (high likelihood); Pump binding mechanically, raising motor current (medium likelihood); Current sensing in the pump inverter reads too high (medium likelihood); Shorted turns in phase W of the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and transmission or hybrid warning; Auxiliary pump shuts down, auto-stop disabled. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B09 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
text: P0B09: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit/Open. P0B09 concerns the power feed of auxiliary pump A's motor: the controller sees no valid supply voltage, usually because the circuit is open. GM documents it for its 2012-13 eAssist mild hybrids (BAS Plus): the hardware input reports an out-of-range voltage flag on the auxiliary pump circuit, enabled with ignition voltage above 9 V; failing for at least 0.375 s within a 1.2 s sample sets P0B09 as Type B, MIL after two trips. A related GM check, P2797, verifies during auto-stops that the pump draws power and that turbine speed does not flare on restart. A Hitachi patent on a battery-fed sub-oil pump shows the controller inhibits engine auto-stop when pump current behaves abnormally. Typical results: no auto-stop and a lamp. P0B0A/P0B0B are the low and high variants. Common causes: Blown fuse or open relay in the pump supply (high likelihood); Open supply wire or loose terminal at the pump connector (high likelihood); Poor ground connection of the pump motor (medium likelihood); Voltage sensing input in the controller faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine auto-stop no longer occurs; MIL after two drive cycles; Shift flare or delayed drive engagement on restart. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0B0A – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
text: P0B0A: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit Low. P0B0A means the supply voltage measured at the motor of auxiliary pump A is lower than expected while the pump should be running. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's eAssist tables only cover the open-circuit case as P0B09. A Mikuni patent shows why the controller measures this voltage at all: it combines motor current, supply voltage and speed to judge the hydraulic load, so a sagging supply also falsifies pump diagnosis. Causes are high resistance in the feed or ground, a weak 12 V battery, a failing DC/DC converter or a voltage drop when the pump starts. CARB requires circuit checks on such outputs. The pump runs slowly or not at all and start-stop is usually inhibited. P0B09 covers an open circuit, P0B0B a supply that is too high, P0562 low system voltage in general. Common causes: Corroded terminal or high resistance in the pump feed or ground (high likelihood); Weak 12 V battery or poor charging (medium likelihood); DC/DC converter or alternator output too low (hybrid) (low likelihood); Voltage sensing input in the controller faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Start-stop function inactive; MIL or transmission warning; Jerky drive-off after an engine stop. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0B0B – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit High
text: P0B0B: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit High. P0B0B reports a supply voltage at the motor of auxiliary pump A that is above the expected range. Subaru documents it on the 2014-15 XV Crosstrek Hybrid (bulletin 16-94-15R), together with P172A: a leaking O-ring at the electric oil pump relief valve can let CVT fluid into the pump motor. The check removes the three U, V and W cables at the oil pump inverter and reads AC voltage across them with the engine held at 1800 rpm in Park; 0.5 V or more means the drive motor and case assembly with the damaged seal must be replaced, less means the cause lies elsewhere. Subaru adds that P0C79, drive motor inverter voltage too high, appears only together with these codes and does not mean the inverter is faulty. P0B09 and P0B0A are the open and low variants. Common causes: CVT fluid entering the pump motor via a leaking relief valve O-ring (Subaru XV Crosstrek Hybrid) (high likelihood); Supply circuit shorted to a higher voltage source (medium likelihood); Oil pump inverter or its voltage sensing faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp on, hybrid or CVT function restricted; Possibly P0C79 stored at the same time. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B0C – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Hydraulic Leakage
text: P0B0C: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Hydraulic Leakage. P0B0C says the circuit fed by auxiliary pump A loses pressure through a leak, so the pump cannot hold the demanded pressure. Stellantis documents it as P0B0C 7A for the 2023-26 Jeep Avenger and 2026 Compass with hybrid dual-clutch transmission outside the US (TSB 21-061-26): an internal leak at the parking pawl locking piston causes jerking and power loss and may stop the engine from restarting after a stop; with P07E4 or P07E6 present and more than 5 km on the clock, the piston or the transmission is replaced. How a controller can see a leak shows a Nidec patent: after a speed change the pump current keeps falling instead of recovering, and the pump is stopped. P0B0B and P0B09 cover the supply, P2797 a pump that does not deliver. Common causes: Internal leak at the parking pawl locking piston (Jeep Avenger/Compass hybrid DCT) (high likelihood); Worn seal or valve leaking inside the hydraulic circuit (medium likelihood); External leak and low transmission fluid level (medium likelihood); Internal wear of the auxiliary pump (low likelihood). Symptoms: Jerking and loss of power while driving; Engine fails to restart after a stop; Transmission warning, possibly with P07E4 or P07E6. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B0D – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Control Module
text: P0B0D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Control Module. P0B0D is an internal fault of the module that drives the auxiliary pump motor. GM documents it for the auxiliary transmission pump controller (ATPC) in its 2011 and 2014 hybrid tables and for the 2016 Cadillac ELR: it checks processor integrity, such as SPI hardware faults or a wrong seed and key between processors, with more than 9.5 V supply; 28 failures out of 32 samples in a 6.25 ms loop, detected within about 200 ms, set a Type A fault. Stellantis lists P0B0D-00 on the 2021-25 Jeep Wrangler 4xe and 2022-25 Grand Cherokee 4xe with the 8P75PH plug-in transmission (TSB 21-038-25, revised 21-041-26): MIL and limp mode, sometimes with U0287; the fix is a new in-pan electric pump. U0287 is lost communication with the pump module, P0C23 to P0C25 its circuit. Common causes: Electric pump with integrated control electronics failed (Jeep 4xe 8P75PH) (high likelihood); Processor or memory fault inside the pump control module (medium likelihood); Supply voltage dips or poor ground at the module (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on; Transmission in limp mode; Possibly lost communication with the pump module (U0287). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0B0E – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit
text: P0B0E: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit. Many packs measure current with two channels or two sensors so the controller can cross-check them; sensor B is the second channel next to sensor A (P0ABF to P0AC3). P0B0E is its general circuit code. Toyota uses it as the base of internal codes on the 2020-25 RAV4 Hybrid: the sensor sends a voltage rising with current on channel IB0 (sensor A) and an inverse one on IB1 (sensor B). P0B0E11 (IB1 too low) and P0B0E15 (IB1 too high or open) are reported to a generic scan tool as P0B10 and P0B11, one trip, MIL on. GM monitors its fine-range channel B with P0B10, P0B11 and the A/B correlation P0B13. CARB requires circuit monitoring. State of charge then becomes uncertain. Common causes: Signal or ground wire of channel B damaged or connector loose (high likelihood); Current sensor or junction block with integrated sensor defective (medium likelihood); Sensor supply voltage faulty (low likelihood); Battery ECU input defective (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning on; Battery power limited, less electric assist; Implausible state-of-charge display. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B0F – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0B0F: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance. P0B0F flags a current sensor B signal that is electrically in range but implausible, for example an offset at zero current or a value that does not match the other measurement. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM handles comparable faults differently: on its dual-range sensor, the 2019 table P0B13 compares sensors A and B and fails when they differ by more than 10 A while both read between -20 and 20 A, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A; offset errors of sensor A are P0AC0. CARB requires rationality checks for hybrid battery inputs. A drifting current reading corrupts the state-of-charge calculation, so the controller tends to narrow the usable battery window. Common causes: Current sensor B offset drift or ageing (high likelihood); Ground offset or high resistance in the sensor wiring (medium likelihood); Sensor displaced on the busbar or magnetic interference (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning, MIL possible; State of charge jumps or drifts; Reduced battery power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B10 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Low
text: P0B10: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Low. P0B10 means the output of current sensor B lies below its valid range. GM uses a dual-range Hall sensor whose channel B covers small currents with high resolution: the 2019 battery energy control module table sets P0B10 when this fine current reads below -24 A (ADC count under 82) for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip; the 2011 Volt table uses -23 A for 175 ms within 250 ms, one trip. Toyota reports P0B10 for the 2020-25 RAV4 Hybrid when the inverse channel IB1 voltage is excessively low (internal code P0B0E11), one trip, MIL on immediately. A short to ground or a lost sensor supply is typical. The high-side code is P0B11. Common causes: Sensor B signal line shorted to ground (high likelihood); 5 V supply of the current sensor missing (medium likelihood); Current sensor or junction block with integrated sensor defective (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning on; Battery charge and discharge power limited; Engine runs more often, fuel use rises. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B11 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit High
text: P0B11: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit High. P0B11 is set when current sensor B delivers a signal above its valid range. In GM's dual-range design, channel B is the fine channel for small currents: the 2019 battery energy control module table fails it above +24 A (ADC count over 4013) for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip, and the 2011 Volt table above +23 A for 175 ms within 250 ms, one trip. Toyota maps its internal code P0B0E15, excessively high or open IB1 channel voltage, to P0B11 on the 2020-25 RAV4 Hybrid, with one-trip logic and immediate MIL. An open ground, a signal shorted to the supply or a failed sensor are typical. The low-side code is P0B10, the sensor A equivalent P0AC2. Common causes: Open signal or ground wire of sensor B (high likelihood); Signal line shorted to the sensor supply or 12 V (medium likelihood); Current sensor or junction block with integrated sensor defective (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning on; Battery power limited, less electric driving; Implausible state-of-charge display. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B12 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0B12: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0B12 covers a current sensor B signal that jumps or drops out in a way real current cannot, typically from a loose connector, a chafed signal wire or noise on the sensor ground. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM monitors its sensor B channel with the range limits P0B10 and P0B11 and compares it with sensor A through P0B13, which fails above a 10 A difference in 400 of 500 samples, Type A; an erratic channel often shows up there first. CARB requires circuit and rationality monitoring for hybrid battery inputs. Because the fault comes and goes, the code may be the only trace, but during dropouts the controller can still cut battery power or light a warning. Common causes: Loose connector or poor terminal contact at the current sensor (high likelihood); Chafed signal or ground wire (medium likelihood); Electrical noise on the sensor ground (low likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent hybrid or EV warning; Short power reductions during dropouts; Code stored without lasting symptoms. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B13 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A/B Correlation
text: P0B13: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A/B Correlation. P0B13 compares the two pack current readings, sensor A and sensor B, and sets when they disagree. On the Chevrolet Volt GM pairs a coarse and a fine channel: the code fails when they differ by more than 10 A while both read between -20 and 20 A, for example 10 s within a 12.5 s window (2016) or 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms (2019), Type A, one trip. Bulletins show P0B13 on the GM Lyriq, Hummer EV and BrightDrop Zevo after suspect public chargers, and on the Audi Q5 PHEV and e-tron GT, where software of the battery controller caused it. Single-sensor faults use P0ABF to P0AC3 and P0B0E to P0B12. The driver sees a high-voltage warning and reduced power. Common causes: Battery controller software fault, fixed by update (Audi, GM) (high likelihood); Disturbance from an external charging station during charging (medium likelihood); Offset drift of one of the two current channels (medium likelihood); Internal communication fault between switching unit and current sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid/EV system warning on; Red battery or Service High Voltage message, request to stop safely; Battery power limited, reduced electric drive or assist; Charging interrupted or refused. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B14 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit
text: P0B14: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit. SAE J2012 reserves up to four pack voltage measurements, A to D; voltage sense B is the second one. P0B14 is its general circuit code: the battery controller sees an electrical fault on this input, typically an open or implausible raw signal. Which tap a manufacturer calls B is not standardised. No manufacturer documents P0B14 publicly. For the comparable channel A GM checks pack-side voltage against fixed limits and against the sum of cell voltages (P0ABB to P0ABD). CARB requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be monitored like any input component. Range, low, high and erratic faults have their own codes, P0B15 to P0B18. The system usually limits or blocks high-voltage operation. Common causes: Voltage sense lead or its fuse open inside the pack (high likelihood); Sense connector at the battery controller loose or corroded (medium likelihood); Measurement input of the battery controller defective (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid/EV system warning on; Battery power limited, reduced electric drive or assist; Vehicle may not reach Ready or may shut down the high-voltage system. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B15 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0B15: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit Range/Performance. P0B15 marks pack voltage measurement B as electrically valid but implausible: the value lies within the sensor range yet does not match a reference, typically the sum of the cell voltages or another pack measurement. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM shows the principle on channel A: P0ABB fails when pack voltage and summed cell voltages differ by more than 12 V, 20 of 25 samples at 25 ms, Type A, one trip. CARB demands rationality checks for battery voltage sensors of the hybrid storage system. Hard circuit faults of channel B are P0B14, P0B16 and P0B17. Because state of charge and cell protection rely on this value, the controller restricts power or charging. Common causes: Drift or calibration error of measurement channel B (high likelihood); Faulty cell voltage acquisition distorts the reference sum (medium likelihood); Increased contact resistance at sense terminals (medium likelihood); Battery controller software needs an update (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid/EV system warning on; Battery power limited, reduced electric drive or assist; Implausible state-of-charge or range display. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B16 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit Low
text: P0B16: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense B Circuit Low. P0B16 sets when pack voltage measurement B reports a value below its plausible minimum, usually an electrical cause such as a sense lead shorted to ground or an open input that pulls the reading down. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM uses the same logic on channel A: on its BECM P0ABC sets when the pack-side voltage drops below 24 V for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip. CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of battery voltage sensors in hybrid storage systems. The opposite fault is P0B17, implausible but in-range values are P0B15. title: P0B23 – Hybrid/EV Battery A Voltage
text: P0B23: Hybrid/EV Battery A Voltage. title: P0B24 – Hybrid/EV Battery A Voltage Unstable
text: P0B24: Hybrid/EV Battery A Voltage Unstable. Some of these Jeeps would not start or reported low 12 V batteries. Ford names P0B24 in the BECM of the 2025 Mustang Mach-E Extended Range, shown with the wrench lamp and fixed by reprogramming. Hardware causes are loose busbar or sense contacts. Common causes: Battery controller software (Jeep 4xe BPCM/HCP, Ford BECM updates) (high likelihood); Loose busbar, terminal or sense contact in battery A (medium likelihood); Cell with rising internal resistance in battery A (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on; Hybrid/EV system or high-voltage battery warning on; Vehicle may not start (Jeep 4xe); Warning comes and goes, fault often stored as intermittent. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B25 – Hybrid/EV Battery A Voltage Low
text: P0B25: Hybrid/EV Battery A Voltage Low. P0B25 sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery A drops below the window the controller expects. Bentley uses it in two different systems. Symptoms: Bentley Dynamic Ride fault warning, roll control inactive; MIL on; Hybrid/EV system or high-voltage battery warning on; Battery power limited, less electric drive or assist. title: P0B2E – Hybrid/EV Battery C Voltage High
text: P0B2E: Hybrid/EV Battery C Voltage High. P0B2E is set when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery C exceeds its upper limit. It pairs with P0B2D for undervoltage; P0B2C covers unstable readings and P0B2B the general fault. No manufacturer publishes a description of P0B2E. GM's comparable monitor for the complete pack is P0ABD, which fails above 479 V and is Type A, so the MIL comes on at once. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid battery voltage sensors and cells and dedicated codes for the replaceable unit. An overvoltage reading usually comes from a cell group that ended up overcharged because balancing failed, or from a drifting measurement channel. The controller then blocks or reduces charging and regenerative braking; plugging in may be refused. Common causes: Cell group in battery C charged too high, balancing ineffective (medium likelihood); Drifting voltage measurement channel or sense lead fault (medium likelihood); Battery controller software fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid/EV system or high-voltage battery warning on; MIL on; Charging or recuperation restricted; External charging refused. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B2F – Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage
text: P0B2F: Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage. P0B2F is the general voltage fault of hybrid/EV battery D, the fourth and last sub-battery in this code family. The controller reports with it that the voltage of unit D is implausible, without specifying unstable (P0B30), low (P0B31) or high (P0B32). Only packs that the manufacturer splits into four separately monitored units can set it, and no manufacturer documents P0B2F publicly. For orientation, GM checks the whole pack with P0ABB to P0ABD, including a comparison of the pack voltage with the sum of all cells. CARB requires voltage sensors and cells of hybrid storage systems to be monitored, with codes pointing to the smallest replaceable unit. The driver sees a hybrid or battery warning and reduced power. Common causes: Weak or failing cells or module in battery D (medium likelihood); Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of battery D (medium likelihood); Battery controller software or internal measurement fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid/EV system or high-voltage battery warning on; MIL on; Battery power limited, less electric drive or assist; Charging or recuperation restricted. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B30 – Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage Unstable
text: P0B30: Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage Unstable. P0B30 reports an unstable voltage of hybrid/EV battery D: the measured value fluctuates beyond the limit the controller allows. It differs from P0B31 and P0B32, which stand for a lasting low or high voltage, and from the general fault P0B2F. No manufacturer documents P0B30 publicly. The sibling codes for batteries A and B show the typical background: Stellantis and Ford corrected P0B24 and P0B28 by updating the battery controller software, and Jeep even blocks starting after 49 days with P0B28. CARB requires the hybrid storage voltage sensors to be monitored. Apart from software, poor contact at busbars or sense terminals and cells with high internal resistance make the reading of unit D jump. Common causes: Loose busbar, terminal or sense contact in battery D (medium likelihood); Battery controller software (pattern known from P0B24/P0B28) (medium likelihood); Cell with rising internal resistance in battery D (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid/EV system or high-voltage battery warning on; MIL on; Warning comes and goes, fault often stored as intermittent; Battery power limited, less electric drive or assist. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B31 – Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage Low
text: P0B31: Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage Low. P0B31 is stored when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery D stays below the expected range. High voltage of the same unit sets P0B32, fluctuation P0B30 and an unspecified deviation P0B2F. No manufacturer publishes a definition of P0B31; Bentley's P0B25 for battery A is the closest documented example, with the energy store replaced once the cell spread reaches 0.5 V. GM uses P0ABC for an undervoltage of the whole pack (below 24 V). CARB asks for monitoring of cells and voltage sensors in hybrid storage and for fault codes that single out the replaceable unit. Typical is a module in unit D that has aged faster or self-discharged during standstill. Discharge power and electric range drop, and the controller may stop electric driving. Common causes: Aged cells with lost capacity in battery D (high likelihood); Deep discharge or self-discharge after standstill (medium likelihood); Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid/EV system or high-voltage battery warning on; MIL on; Battery power limited, less electric drive or assist; Reduced electric range. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B32 – Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage High
text: P0B32: Hybrid/EV Battery D Voltage High. P0B32 sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery D goes above its permitted maximum. It is the high counterpart of P0B31; P0B30 covers unstable readings and P0B2F the general fault. No manufacturer documents P0B32 publicly; Bentley's P0B26 for battery A, cured by replacing the 48 V super capacitor, shows the same fault type on another unit. GM's analogous whole-pack monitor is P0ABD (above 479 V, Type A, MIL at once). CARB requires hybrid storage voltage sensors and cells to be monitored and codes to identify the replaceable unit. Causes are an overcharged cell group when balancing fails, a defective module or a measuring error. Charging and recuperation are cut back, and the contactors may open to protect the pack. Common causes: Cell group in battery D charged too high, balancing ineffective (medium likelihood); Defective module in battery D (medium likelihood); Voltage measurement fault in the controller or sense leads (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid/EV system or high-voltage battery warning on; MIL on; Charging or recuperation restricted; Battery power limited, less electric drive or assist. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B33 – High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit
text: P0B33: High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit. The high-voltage service disconnect is the removable plug, usually fused, that splits the traction battery for safe servicing. A low-voltage detection loop runs through the plug, and the battery controller reads it to know whether the plug is seated; patents from Ford and Lear describe this loop, which opens before the main contacts part. P0B33 is the general circuit code for this detection input. No manufacturer documents P0B33 publicly. CARB requires such hybrid components to be monitored like any input. Performance, low, high and open have their own codes, P0B34 to P0B37; the separate high-voltage interlock loop uses P0A0A ff. Expect contactors to stay open: no ready mode, no charging. Common causes: Service disconnect plug not fully seated or locked after service (high likelihood); Chafed, open or shorted detection loop wiring between plug base and battery controller (medium likelihood); Corroded or spread terminals in the plug or its base (medium likelihood); Battery controller input fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle does not enter ready mode or will not start; High-voltage system warning and MIL on; Charging not possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B34 – High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit Performance
text: P0B34: High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit Performance. P0B34 covers a plausibility fault of the service disconnect detection: the signal is electrically within limits but does not match what the controller expects, for example a plug reported as removed while the high-voltage bus still shows voltage, or a state that changes without a matching event. Audi lists P0B3400 in the controller at address 008C of the 2025 Q5 e-hybrid, together with U029A00 and U059B00, and asks technicians to log the case in its pending service database; no threshold is published. CARB requires hybrid components to be checked for rationality as input devices. Pure circuit, low, high and open faults are P0B33, P0B35, P0B36 and P0B37. The car may refuse ready mode or charging. Common causes: Battery controller software fault (Audi case under investigation) (medium likelihood); Loose plug or worn contacts giving an implausible detection state (medium likelihood); Increased resistance in the detection loop (medium likelihood); Communication fault between battery controller and other modules (low likelihood). Symptoms: Electrical system or high-voltage warning; No ready mode or charging interrupted; Related network codes stored at the same time. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B35 – High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit Low
text: P0B35: High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit Low. P0B35 sets when the service disconnect detection signal stays below its lower limit. Where the loop is coded with a resistor in the plug, as in a Lear patent, a reading near zero typically points to a short to ground in the loop wiring; the exact meaning depends on how the manufacturer powers the input. Ford traced an intermittent short to ground in the low-voltage interlock wiring as the cause of its open-loop code P0B37 on the C-Max Energi, which shows how chafed harnesses act here. No manufacturer documents P0B35 publicly. CARB treats such signals as monitored hybrid inputs. High, open and performance faults are P0B36, P0B37 and P0B34. The contactors usually stay open. Common causes: Detection loop wire chafed and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Moisture or corrosion in the plug base bridging to ground (medium likelihood); Coding element in the plug shorted (low likelihood); Battery controller input stage fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: No ready mode or stall with a stop-safely message; MIL and high-voltage warning on; Charging not possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B36 – High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit High
text: P0B36: High Voltage Service Disconnect Circuit High. P0B36 sets when the service disconnect detection signal stays above its upper limit. With a pulled-up input this usually means a short to a voltage source or a missing coding element in the plug; on some designs an open loop also reads high, so manufacturers separate it with P0B37 only where they can tell the cases apart. Patents from Ford and Lear show the detection loop as a low-voltage circuit that closes through the plug and is read by a battery or vehicle controller. No manufacturer documents P0B36 publicly. CARB requires such hybrid inputs to be monitored for out-of-range values. Low and performance faults are P0B35 and P0B34. The high-voltage system normally stays switched off. Common causes: Detection loop wire shorted to a supply voltage (high likelihood); Open loop or missing contact read as high signal (medium likelihood); Wrong or damaged service disconnect plug without proper coding (low likelihood); Battery controller input stage fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Vehicle not ready to drive; MIL and high-voltage warning on; Charging blocked. Repair difficulty: shop_only.
