title: P0B90 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit
text: P0B90: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit. P0B90 is stored when the battery controller concludes that the tap of sense R, the eighteenth cell channel, is open or too resistive. GM's 2019 battery energy control module runs seven cases for it: neighbouring cells 1.3 V or more apart, a reading under 36 mV while the balancing gate is on, or splice voltages above 0.1 V (0.5 V at a busbar splice). The fault has to be present for 0.8 s within a 1.6 s window and is Type A. The 2016 Volt and ELR use the same cases with a 0.6 s window. Oddly, GM's first-generation Volt tables of 2011 to 2015 contain no P0B90 at all, although they list the circuit codes of S to V. Range, low and high faults of R are P0B91 to P0B93. Common causes: Loose, corroded or broken tap of sense lead R (high likelihood); Excessive resistance at a splice or busbar joint feeding channel R (medium likelihood); Faulty measuring or balancing input on the cell monitoring board (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL with service hybrid or EV system warning; Reduced propulsion power or no ready mode; Charging interrupted or refused. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B91 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0B91: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Range/Performance. Here the wiring of sense R is intact, but its value does not behave like a real cell. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain processor demands that cell R moves at least 0.005 V in the same direction whenever the cell average shifts by more than 0.022 V; 35 failures out of 40 samples at 100 ms give a Type A fault. The 2016 Volt allows 7 s of failure in an 8 s window, the ELR 20 of 40 samples at 200 ms. On the 2012 two-mode trucks R is nickel-metal hydride block 18: blocks 18 and 19 are each multiplied by twenty, and if both estimates miss the pack voltage by more than 70 V in 160 of 170 samples, P0B91 is set as Type B. A frozen measuring channel or controller software is the usual suspect. Common causes: Measuring channel R reporting a stuck value (high likelihood); Outdated battery controller or hybrid processor software (medium likelihood); Block 18 or 19 voltage drifting on two-mode NiMH packs (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on, vehicle often drives normally; Less electric assist or regenerative braking. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B92 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Low
text: P0B92: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Low. P0B92 stands for an implausibly low reading on sense R. In GM's lithium-ion battery controllers of 2016 and 2019 the limit is 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s inside a 2 s window, Type A; the test is suspended while an open sense line fault is active, so a broken lead appears as P0B90 rather than P0B92. Programmes with a separate battery sensor module (GM 16OBDG02) use under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples. The eAssist mild hybrid applies 1.4 V, 7 of 10 samples, Type B. In the 2012 two-mode trucks R is NiMH block 18, and blocks 18 and 19 must both read under 2 V in 15 of 20 samples (Type B). A short of the sense lead to ground or to a lower cell is the classic cause. Common causes: Sense lead R chafed through and touching ground or a lower cell (high likelihood); Failed input for channel R on the cell monitoring board (medium likelihood); Cell or block on channel R genuinely collapsed (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV system message; Propulsion limited, possibly no restart. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B93 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit High
text: P0B93: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit High. A reading on sense R above anything a healthy cell could produce sets P0B93. GM's lithium-ion battery controllers of 2016 and 2019 use 4.8 V or more, held 1.4 s within 2 s, as a Type A fault. The 16OBDG02 programme with its own battery sensor module draws the line at 4.90 V, 14 of 18 samples. GM's eAssist mild hybrid already reacts above 4.65 V (7 of 10 samples, Type B). On the 2012 two-mode trucks the channel is nickel-metal hydride block 18, which must exceed 23 V in 15 of 20 samples, Type B. Because a cell this high would be dangerous, an electrical fault is far more likely: a sense lead touching a higher potential, or a damaged measuring input on the monitoring board. Common causes: Sense lead R in contact with a higher cell potential (high likelihood); Damaged measuring input for channel R (medium likelihood); Cell on channel R actually overcharged (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning; Charging or regeneration cut back; Reduced power mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B94 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0B94: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. No manufacturer documents P0B94 publicly. The code is reserved for a sense R signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing steadily. GM monitors channel R in six table sets between 2011 and 2019, but every one of those tables stops at the circuit, range, low and high monitors; an intermittent test does not appear. The legal basis is CARB 1968.2, which requires the voltage sensors of a hybrid energy storage system to be monitored like any other input and wants fault codes that point to the smallest replaceable unit. In practice such a fault would come from a connection that opens under vibration or heat, for instance a cracked crimp or a hairline crack in a flexible circuit. Common causes: Crimp or terminal of lead R opening under vibration (high likelihood); Hairline crack in the flexible circuit carrying channel R (medium likelihood); Moisture or contamination in the monitoring board connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning appears and disappears between trips; Short power reductions, normal after restart. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B95 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit
text: P0B95: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit. P0B95 reports that the sense S lead, channel nineteen, no longer connects its cell reliably to the monitoring electronics. GM programmes with a separate battery sensor module (16OBDG02) measure this directly: after each normal reading the balancing gates switch in a test pattern, current flows through the sense wires and the voltage drop is turned into a line resistance. Above 30.00 (the table gives no unit) in 7 of 9 samples at 100 ms, the code sets as Type A. GM's eAssist mild hybrid instead needs lines N and N-1 both under 1.4 V plus a jump of more than 0.5 V in 200 ms, 7 of 10 samples, Type B, and stays quiet while P1B37 is active. The 2019 lithium-ion controller uses its seven cases with 0.8 s in 1.6 s. Common causes: High resistance in sense lead S from corrosion or a loose terminal (high likelihood); Sense lead S broken at the cell connector (medium likelihood); Defective input of the battery sensor module for channel S (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV warning; Vehicle may refuse ready mode; Cell balancing no longer effective. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B96 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0B96: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Range/Performance. P0B96 is a plausibility code: the voltage of sense S looks electrically valid but fails to track the rest of the pack. GM's eAssist mild hybrid requires cell S to move at least half as much as the other cells once the average changes by more than 0.045 V, judged over 20 of 40 samples at 200 ms, Type B. The 16OBDG02 programme accepts a trend of 0.002 V and sets Type A after 35 of 40 evaluations, while the 2019 hybrid processor wants 0.005 V. On the 2012 two-mode trucks S is block 19, and the check scales blocks 19 and 20 by twenty and compares them with the pack voltage, with more than 70 V deviation in 160 of 170 samples leading to Type B. Circuit, low and high faults of S are excluded first. Common causes: Measuring channel S frozen or lagging behind the other cells (high likelihood); Battery controller calibration requiring a software update (medium likelihood); Block 19 or 20 out of step with the pack on two-mode NiMH batteries (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL with little or no change in driving; Electric assist reduced at times. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B97 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Low
text: P0B97: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Low. With P0B97 the controller sees sense S pulled close to zero. In the 2012 two-mode trucks, where S is the nickel-metal hydride block 19, the battery pack control module only sets it when block 19 and block 20 are both below 2 V in 15 of 20 samples, Type B, with the 12 V system between 9 and 18 V. GM's lithium-ion packs work cell by cell: 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s in 2 s on the 2016 Volt and the 2019 controller, Type A, and under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples in the 16OBDG02 programme. The eAssist mild hybrid sets it below 1.4 V, 7 of 10 samples, Type B. An open sense line fault takes priority, so P0B97 points more to a short than to a broken lead. Common causes: Sense lead S shorted to ground or to the next lower cell (high likelihood); Defective channel S input on the monitoring board (medium likelihood); Cell or NiMH block on channel S actually discharged (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV warning message; Restricted power, engine may run more often on hybrids. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B98 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit High
text: P0B98: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit High. P0B98 marks a sense S value that is too high to be a cell voltage. The thresholds vary with the battery chemistry and controller: GM's 2016 Volt and 2019 battery controllers flag 4.8 V or more after 1.4 s in 2 s (Type A), the 16OBDG02 programme 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples (Type A), and the eAssist mild hybrid more than 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples with the 12 V supply above 8.8 V (Type B). On the 2012 two-mode trucks S is NiMH block 19 and its limit is 23 V, 15 of 20 samples, Type B. Like the low test, the high test waits until open sense line faults are ruled out. The fix is usually wiring or the monitoring board; a truly overcharged cell is rare but must be excluded. Common causes: Sense lead S shorted to a higher cell or busbar (high likelihood); Measuring chip reading channel S incorrectly (medium likelihood); Real overvoltage of the cell or block on channel S (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and service hybrid system message; Charging and regeneration limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B99 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0B99: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0B99 is the erratic variant within the sense S group. A public manufacturer description does not exist. GM's tables cover channel S from the 2011 Volt via the 2012 two-mode trucks and eAssist to the 2019 controllers, yet only with circuit, range, low and high codes (P0B95 to P0B98). CARB 1968.2 obliges manufacturers to monitor battery voltage sensors of a hybrid storage system for circuit and rationality faults and to separate the fault codes by replaceable unit, which is why J2012 reserves this slot. Should a vehicle set it, the technician would look for a sense S connection that works most of the time but breaks briefly, typically a fretting terminal or a cracked solder joint on the board. Common causes: Fretting corrosion on the terminal of sense lead S (high likelihood); Cracked solder joint for channel S on the monitoring board (medium likelihood); Harness chafing that only shorts under movement (low likelihood). Symptoms: Sporadic hybrid warning without a pattern; Code often stored as history, hard to reproduce. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B9A – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit
text: P0B9A: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit. P0B9A is the open-circuit code for sense T, the twentieth cell channel. GM uses it only on lithium-ion packs. The 2011 Volt compares adjacent cells for a difference above 1 V and checks the busbar cap voltage against 0.7 V; the 2016 Volt and ELR raise the adjacent-cell limit to 1.3 V, add a balancing-gate test below 36 mV and decide within 0.6 s, and the 2019 controller keeps those values but stretches the window to 0.8 s of 1.6 s, Type A in both cases. The 2012 two-mode trucks also have a channel T, their last nickel-metal hydride block 20, yet their tables carry range, low and high codes for it and no circuit code. A genuinely open lead usually means opening the high-voltage pack. Common causes: Open sense lead T at the cell tab or connector (high likelihood); Poor busbar or splice joint in the channel T path (medium likelihood); Monitoring board input for channel T failed (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL, hybrid or EV system warning; Ready mode or charging blocked. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B9B – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0B9B: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Range/Performance. On the 2012 two-mode trucks sense T is block 20, the last of their twenty nickel-metal hydride blocks, and P0B9B shows how GM handles the missing neighbour: block 20 alone is multiplied by twenty and compared with the pack voltage, and a gap above 70 V in 160 of 170 samples sets the code as Type B. All other channels there use a pair of blocks. On lithium-ion packs the code means that cell T does not follow the pack average: the 2019 hybrid processor demands 0.005 V of movement when the average shifts by more than 0.022 V (35 of 40 samples, Type A), the 2016 Volt the same with a 7 s in 8 s window, and eAssist half the average movement in 20 of 40 samples, Type B. Common causes: Channel T measurement stuck or sluggish (high likelihood); Block 20 voltage diverging from pack voltage on two-mode NiMH packs (medium likelihood); Faulty pack voltage reference used for the comparison (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL, drivability usually unchanged; Hybrid assist or EV range slightly reduced. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B9C – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Low
text: P0B9C: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Low. P0B9C signals that sense T reads too low. Open sense line faults are evaluated first. For the driver the result is a warning and reduced power until the cause is repaired. Common causes: Sense lead T shorted to ground or a lower potential (high likelihood); Weak or discharged NiMH block 20 on two-mode packs (medium likelihood); Failed measuring input for channel T (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid warning; Reduced power, engine may not shut off on hybrids. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B9D – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit High
text: P0B9D: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit High. If sense T reports more voltage than its cell can hold, the battery controller stores P0B9D. GM documents it on several systems. Most such readings come from wiring touching a higher potential or a faulty measuring input. Common causes: Sense lead T shorted to a higher cell or busbar (high likelihood); Measuring input for channel T drifting high (medium likelihood); Cell or block T genuinely overcharged (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and service hybrid or EV system message; Charging power reduced. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B9E – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0B9E: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0B9E would describe a sense T signal that flickers. It lacks any public manufacturer documentation. Even the 2012 two-mode trucks, whose last NiMH block is channel T, monitor it only for range, low and high, and GM's lithium-ion controllers add a circuit test but no intermittent one. The requirement behind the whole code family comes from CARB 1968.2: battery voltage sensors of a hybrid energy storage system are monitored components, and manufacturers must store separate codes that lead to the smallest part replaceable in service. A technician facing this code would wiggle-test the channel T wiring while watching the cell voltage live and look for a reading that dips or spikes for a fraction of a second. Common causes: Loose or spread terminal in the channel T connector (high likelihood); Connection that opens with temperature changes (medium likelihood); Electrical interference coupling into sense lead T (low likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent warning lamp; Occasional brief loss of electric drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0B9F – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit
text: P0B9F: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit. P0B9F covers an open or high-resistance sense U lead, channel twenty-one. From U onward the 2012 two-mode trucks drop out, as their pack has only twenty blocks, so this code is a lithium-ion matter at GM. In the eAssist mild hybrid the test is the familiar one, lines N and N-1 both under 1.4 V with a change above 0.5 V within 200 ms in 7 of 10 samples, Type B, but it is now blocked by P1B38 instead of P1B37. The 16OBDG02 programme measures the sense line resistance and sets above 30.00 in 7 of 9 samples, Type A. The 2016 Volt and ELR decide in 0.6 s, the 2019 controller in 0.8 s of 1.6 s, both on adjacent-cell differences of 1.3 V and splice checks. Common causes: Sense lead U interrupted or detached from its cell (high likelihood); Corroded terminal raising the resistance of lead U (medium likelihood); Fault in the balancing circuit used for the channel U test (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning; No start or ready mode on some vehicles; Charging not possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BA0 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BA0: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Range/Performance. P0BA0 tells the technician that channel U gives a number, but the number does not move with the pack. GM checks this rationality only on lithium-ion systems, since the two-mode NiMH trucks end at block 20. The Cadillac ELR of 2016 reacts to the smallest movement: when the average cell voltage changes by more than 0.006 V, cell U must follow, and 20 failures in 40 samples at 200 ms set a Type A fault. The Volt of the same year looks at 0.022 V of average movement and a 7 s in 8 s window, the 2019 hybrid processor at 0.005 V with 35 of 40 samples, and eAssist at half the average movement, Type B. Circuit, low and high faults are excluded before the test runs, so wiring is less likely than the controller. Common causes: Measuring channel U holding a fixed value (high likelihood); Software or calibration issue in the battery controller (medium likelihood); Cell U behaving differently from its neighbours due to ageing (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL, often without driver-noticeable change; Electric range may be reduced. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BA3 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BA3: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. Within the sense U group, P0BA3 is the slot for a signal that is present but unsteady. CARB 1968.2 demands monitoring of the hybrid storage system's voltage sensors and separate codes per repairable unit, and SAE reserves the intermittent code so that a manufacturer could report unstable sensing separately from a hard open or short. Physically this points to a connection that breaks for milliseconds, such as a fatigued crimp, a loose screw at a busbar tap or vibration damage to a flexible printed circuit. Repair follows the same path as for the circuit code. Symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes; Brief reduced-power events. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BA4 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit
text: P0BA4: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit. P0BA4 reports an open or poorly connected sense V lead, the twenty-second channel and the last before W begins at P0BA9. Without a good sense lead the pack cannot balance or protect that cell. Common causes: Broken or unplugged sense lead V (high likelihood); High-resistance splice or busbar joint on channel V (medium likelihood); Cell monitoring board fault on channel V (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning; Vehicle may not become ready to drive; Charging blocked. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BA6 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Low

title: P0BA7 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit High
text: P0BA7: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit High. P0BA7 is the high-voltage plausibility code for channel V. The battery controller compares the measured value against a ceiling no healthy cell should reach: 4.8 V for 1.4 s within 2 s in GM's 2016 Volt and ELR and in the 2019 battery energy control module (Type A), 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples of 100 ms in the 16OBDG02 programme (Type A), and 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples in the eAssist mild hybrid (Type B). Each of these checks waits for the open sense line monitor to pass. A high reading usually comes from a sense lead V pressed against a higher cell tab or busbar, or from a measuring chip that has lost its reference, and only rarely from a cell actually overcharged. Common causes: Sense lead V touching a higher cell tab or busbar (high likelihood); Measuring chip with faulty reference reading channel V high (medium likelihood); Cell V really overcharged (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV warning; Charging and regeneration reduced. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BA8 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BA8: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0BA8 completes the five codes of channel V and is meant for an unstable rather than a failed sense V signal. title: P0BA9 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit
text: P0BA9: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit. P0BA9 opens the W group, the twenty-third cell voltage channel, and flags a sense lead that is open or badly connected. The 2016 Volt module uses a 0.6 s window instead. GM's eAssist mild hybrid needs readings under 1.4 V on lines N and N-1 plus a change of more than 0.5 V within 200 ms in seven of ten samples, Type B. With the lead lost, the cell behind it can neither be balanced nor protected. Common causes: Broken, chafed or unplugged sense lead W (high likelihood); High-resistance busbar or splice joint at channel W (medium likelihood); Failed input on the cell monitoring board for W (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL with hybrid or EV system warning; Reduced propulsion power or no ready mode; Charging interrupted or refused. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BAA – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BAA: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Range/Performance. Here the W reading is not missing but implausible: it fails to follow the rest of the pack. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 watches for the average cell voltage to move more than 0.022 V between samples and then expects channel W to trend at least 0.005 V in the same direction; 35 failures in 40 samples at 100 ms give a Type A fault. The 16OBDG02 programme applies the same logic with 0.002 V. The eAssist system is more tolerant and only asks the cell to move half as far as the others once the average shifts more than 0.045 V, 20 of 40 samples, Type B. In the 2011 Volt tables W appears as sensor 23 of the rationality check. Drivers often notice nothing beyond the warning lamp. Common causes: Measuring input for W frozen at a fixed value (high likelihood); Battery controller software needing an update (medium likelihood); Cell W reacting differently to load because of ageing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp with little change in driving; Possibly limited regeneration or electric assist. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BAB – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Low
text: P0BAB: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Low. A W channel reading at or near zero sets P0BAB. How low is too low depends on the battery: GM's lithium-ion modules of 2016 and 2019 react to 0.2 V or less held for 1.4 s within a 2 s window, Type A, and the 16OBDG02 programme to under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples at 100 ms. The eAssist mild hybrid already fails below 1.4 V, seven of ten samples, as long as the 12 V supply exceeds 8.8 V and P1B38 is not active; that fault is Type B. All of these tests stand down while an open sense line fault is present, so a simply broken lead shows up as P0BA9. P0BAB on its own suggests a short towards a lower potential, a dead measuring input or a deeply discharged cell. Power and charging are usually restricted. Common causes: Sense lead W shorted to a lower cell potential (high likelihood); Measuring input for W on the monitoring board failed (medium likelihood); Cell W deeply discharged or internally shorted (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning and MIL; Reduced power output; Charging limited or blocked. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BAC – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit High
text: P0BAC: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit High. P0BAC is the upper counterpart to P0BAB: channel W reports more voltage than a single cell can plausibly hold. GM sets the limit at 4.8 V or more for 1.4 s within 2 s in the 2011 and 2016 Volt battery modules, which makes it a one-trip fault. The 16OBDG02 programme fails at above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, Type A, while the eAssist battery is stricter with more than 4.65 V in seven of ten samples, Type B. A high reading usually comes from a lead touching the potential of the next cell up or from a faulty input, less often from a genuinely overcharged cell. Because overcharging is a safety risk, the controller typically cuts charging and regeneration until the cause is found. Common causes: Sense lead W in contact with a higher cell potential (high likelihood); Monitoring board input for W reading too high (medium likelihood); Cell W actually overcharged after a balancing fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and battery system warning; Charging and regeneration stopped; Possible reduced power mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BAE – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit
text: P0BAE: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit. Channel X, number twenty-four, starts with P0BAE, the open-lead code. The first-generation Volt of 2011 already detected it through several cases: two neighbouring readings more than 1 V apart, a busbar sense voltage above 0.7 V combined with an implausible cell voltage, or adjacent cells differing by more than 0.5 V on a shared supply line. GM's later 16OBDG02 programme measures the sense line resistance directly and fails it above 30.00 in seven of nine samples, Type A; the unit is not printed. In the 2019 battery energy control module the familiar 1.3 V and 36 mV criteria apply with 0.8 s in 1.6 s. Whichever method is used, the controller loses sight of one cell and normally restricts the battery. Common causes: Sense lead X broken or disconnected (high likelihood); Loose busbar fastener at the X sensing point (medium likelihood); Sense harness X damaged during earlier battery work (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and service message for the high-voltage system; Vehicle may stay out of ready mode; Charging stops early. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BAF – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BAF: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Range/Performance. P0BAF covers a sense X signal that is electrically present yet does not behave like a real cell. For model year 2016 GM documents two versions in the same booklet. The Volt controller fails it when X moves in a different direction from the pack average, or by less than 0.005 V while that average moves more than 0.022 V, for 7 s within 8 s, Type A. The ELR variant samples every 200 ms, needs average movement above 0.006 V and fails after 20 of 40 samples, one trip. The eAssist hybrid asks for at least half of the average change, Type B over two trips, and GM's 2019 processor uses a 0.005 V trend test. Since the check pauses during circuit, low or high faults, P0BAF points to a stuck measurement rather than a broken wire. Common causes: Sense X value stuck while the pack voltage changes (high likelihood); Calibration of the battery controller requiring reprogramming (medium likelihood); Cell X with deviating internal resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL without obvious driving change; Reduced electric range in some cases. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BB0 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Low
text: P0BB0: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Low. When channel X reads too low, P0BB0 is stored. In GM's eAssist mild hybrid the battery interface module sets it below 1.4 V in seven of ten samples at 200 ms, provided the 12 V system is above 8.8 V and the group fault P1B38 is not active, as a two-trip Type B fault. The 2011 Volt and the 16OBDG02 programme work with a far lower limit of about 0.2 V, the latter in 14 of 18 samples at 100 ms, Type A. That difference reflects the cell chemistry and how much voltage a healthy cell can lose. Because an open lead is caught first by P0BAE, a stand-alone P0BB0 is more often a short in the sense harness, a failed input or a cell that has collapsed. Expect reduced power and blocked charging. Common causes: Short between sense lead X and a lower potential (high likelihood); Defective measuring channel X in the monitoring electronics (medium likelihood); Cell X collapsed or internally shorted (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and MIL; Electric assist or propulsion reduced; Charging not possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BB1 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit High
text: P0BB1: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit High. P0BB1 means the battery controller sees too much voltage on sense X. In GM's 2019 battery energy control module the threshold is 4.8 V or more, held for 1.4 s within a 2 s window, and the code is Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. The 16OBDG02 programme allows up to 4.90 V and needs 14 failing samples out of 18, while the eAssist battery treats anything above 4.65 V in seven of ten samples as a Type B fault. These tests are suppressed while an open sense line or a lost communication with the cell monitoring slave is active. A real cell at that voltage would be dangerously overcharged, so a wiring fault towards the neighbour cell or a defective input is the more frequent finding. Common causes: Sense lead X shorted to the next higher cell (high likelihood); Measuring input X drifting high (medium likelihood); Cell X genuinely over voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL in the first trip; Charging and regenerative braking disabled. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BB2 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BB2: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. Of the five X codes, P0BB2 is the only one without any public manufacturer description. It is intended for a sense X signal that flickers, drops out briefly or jumps between values. GM's Volt tables of 2011 and 2016 list channel X with circuit, range, low and high monitors, P0BAE to P0BB1, and no intermittent check. The code therefore rests on the J2012 structure and on CARB 1968.2, which requires hybrid battery voltage sensors to be monitored and the fault to be isolated to the smallest replaceable unit. In practice a technician would look for a contact that opens under vibration, moisture in a connector or a harness rubbing against the module housing. title: P0BB3 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit
text: P0BB3: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit. P0BB3 reports that the sense lead of channel Y, the twenty-fifth cell group, is no longer properly connected. GM's 16OBDG02 programme does not wait for odd voltages but calculates the resistance of the sense line and fails it above 30.00 in seven of nine samples, which is a one-trip Type A fault; the unit is missing in the table. The 2019 battery energy control module instead looks at the cell voltages themselves, for example 1.3 V between neighbours or a reading below 36 mV while that cell is being balanced, with 0.8 s of failure in 1.6 s. The eAssist mild hybrid sets it as a Type B fault when lines N and N-1 both read under 1.4 V and jump by more than 0.5 V. Low and high monitors for Y are blocked while P0BB3 is active. Common causes: Open circuit in sense lead Y (high likelihood); Corroded or loose terminal raising line resistance at Y (medium likelihood); Cell monitoring slave board fault on input Y (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and high-voltage system warning; Vehicle may not start in electric mode; Charging aborted. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BB4 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BB4: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Range/Performance. P0BB4 is a plausibility code: the controller compares how the Y reading changes over time with the behaviour of all other cells. In the 16OBDG02 programme a sample counts as failed when the pack average moves by more than 0.022 V but Y has not trended at least 0.002 V the same way; 35 such results in 40 evaluations set a one-trip Type A fault. The 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 uses the same frame with a 0.005 V trend. For the 2016 Volt the window is 7 s in 8 s. A frozen analogue input or a software problem in the battery controller are the typical findings, while a real cell defect is rarer. Unlike P0BB3, the signal is present, so the car usually keeps driving. Common causes: Analogue input Y frozen at one value (high likelihood); Battery controller software fault (medium likelihood); Weak cell Y with sluggish voltage response (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL, vehicle still drivable; Battery power occasionally limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BB5 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Low
text: P0BB5: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Low. P0BB5 stands for a sense Y voltage below the plausible minimum. GM's 2016 Volt module and the 2019 battery energy control module both use 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s inside a 2 s window and flag it as Type A. title: P0BB6 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit High
text: P0BB6: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit High. The battery controller logs P0BB6 when the Y channel climbs above a level no healthy cell reaches. title: P0BB7 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BB7: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0BB7 would describe an unstable sense Y signal, one that is mostly correct but drops out or jumps from time to time. Diagnosis would focus on connectors, crimps and solder joints that react to movement or heat. title: P0BB8 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit

title: P0BB9 – Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BB9: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Range/Performance. Should it appear, contacts that fail under vibration or heat cycling are the logical starting point. title: P0BBD – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Variation Exceeded Limit
text: P0BBD: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Variation Exceeded Limit. P0BBD means the spread between cells or blocks of the pack has grown beyond what the controller accepts. GM used it on the two-mode hybrids, where a difference of more than 1.5 V between adjacent block voltages in three of three samples at 1 s, with battery current above 0.2 A, set a Type B fault labelled as end-of-life deviation. On the Chevrolet Bolt EV, bulletin 22-NA-151 links it to reduced propulsion and charging capped at 30 % and names cases induced by driving style that need reprogramming, otherwise a pack replacement. Volkswagen reports it on the ID.4 from cells with increased self-discharge, Audi on the Q4 e-tron with a drive system that cannot be activated, and Stellantis on the Wrangler 4xe. Common causes: Cells or modules with increased self-discharge or capacity loss (high likelihood); Controller software or cell capacity adaptation needing an update (medium likelihood); Aged battery pack at end of life (medium likelihood); Cell balancing unable to equalise the pack (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or electrical system warning; Reduced propulsion power and capped state of charge; Reduced electric range; Drive system cannot be activated in severe cases. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BBE – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Variation
text: P0BBE: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Variation. P0BBE watches the gap between the highest and the lowest cell voltage in the pack. GM's first-generation Volt sets it when that difference exceeds 0.3 V in 50 of 245 samples taken every 100 ms, provided the cell voltage rationality fault is not active; it is a one-trip Type A fault. Stellantis lists the code on the Jeep Grand Cherokee 4xe and Wrangler 4xe together with P0B24, P0DAB and a state-of-health code, where updated battery pack control module software is the remedy and an unresolved case can end in a no-start. Chrysler's warranty extension for the 2017 to 2021 Pacifica Hybrid replaces the whole high-voltage pack for this code. Its companion P0BBD reports a spread that has exceeded a set limit. Common causes: Cells drifted apart beyond what balancing can correct (high likelihood); Battery pack control module software needing an update (medium likelihood); Defective or aged high-voltage battery pack (medium likelihood); Faulty cell voltage measurement simulating a spread (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning; Reduced electric range or propulsion; Vehicle may not start. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BBF – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
text: P0BBF: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit/Open. Air-cooled hybrid packs draw cooling air through a 12 V blower that is fed through a fuse and often a relay; the controller watches the voltage reaching the fan, and Toyota even uses that measured supply voltage to correct the fan duty. P0BBF means this feed is open or missing while the fan should be powered. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's Two-Mode hybrid monitors the same feed but reports only the high case, a welded relay, as P0BC1. CARB requires the electrical inputs and outputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. Low and high faults are P0BC0 and P0BC1, faults in the fan's own control line P0A81 to P0A85. Without power the fan stops, the pack warms up and the controller limits power. Common causes: Blown fuse in the battery fan feed (high likelihood); Fan relay contacts not closing or relay coil open (medium likelihood); Open supply wire or loose terminal at the fan connector (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or MIL on; Battery fan silent when it should run; Reduced electric assist in hot weather or under load. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0BC0 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit Low
text: P0BC0: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit Low. P0BC0 reports that the voltage feeding the battery cooling fan is lower than expected while the fan is switched on. A short to ground downstream of the fuse, a corroded connector or a relay with burnt contacts drops the voltage, so the fan turns slowly or not at all. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Toyota's hybrid controller measures the fan supply on the auxiliary battery side and raises the duty when it is low, which shows why a sagging feed matters for cooling. CARB asks for circuit monitoring of all battery thermal management parts. The open case is P0BBF, the high case P0BC1 (GM: welded relay). A weak 12 V battery can cause a sag too, so check it first. Expect reduced power when the pack heats up. Common causes: Fan supply wire chafed and shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Burnt fan relay contacts or corroded terminals causing voltage drop (medium likelihood); Weak 12 V auxiliary battery or poor ground (medium likelihood); Seizing fan motor pulling excessive current (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or MIL on; Battery fan runs slowly or noticeably weaker; Reduced electric assist when the pack is warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0BC1 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit High
text: P0BC1: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit High. P0BC1 flags voltage on the battery fan feed when there should be none, or more than expected. It is Type B, MIL after two trips. A stuck relay keeps the fan running with the vehicle off and drains the 12 V battery. The open and low cases are P0BBF and P0BC0; a fan that keeps turning without this fault is P0A83. Common causes: Fan relay contacts welded closed (high likelihood); Fan feed shorted to a constant battery voltage wire (medium likelihood); Relay control output in the module stuck on (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Battery fan keeps running after the vehicle is switched off; Discharged 12 V battery after standing. Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P0BC2 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit
text: P0BC2: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit. Battery temperature sensor E is the fifth thermistor in the high-voltage pack; GM's Chevrolet Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the E codes as temperature sensor 5 of nine. P0BC2 is the general circuit code, used when the controller detects an electrical fault without classing it as low, high or erratic. GM's hybrid tables report only the specific siblings P0BC3 to P0BC6. NHTSA's summary of an Audi pending service solution for 2027 Q6 and A6 e-tron models names P0BC2 with a failure type byte among implausible temperature sensor errors. CARB requires battery temperature sensors to be monitored for circuit faults. With one value missing the controller limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits inside the pack, so checks call for high-voltage safety procedures. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector of sensor E at the sensing board (high likelihood); Failed thermistor E (medium likelihood); Faulty input on the battery sensing board or module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL; Reduced power or charging rate; Battery cooling running more than usual. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BC3 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BC3: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance. P0BC3 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor E, GM's sensor 5: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors, which should agree closely. GM's 2016 hybrid table fails it when E is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the 2018 CT6 plug-in table more than 20 °C for 5 s within 6.7 s; the eAssist mild hybrid (13OBDG05C) allows only 8.55 °C, and only after the module has been off for more than six hours. All are Type B, two trips. The check is suspended while circuit codes are active, so it points to a sensor that reads wrongly but in range, or to a real hot spot. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 counts it among codes that set falsely in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming. Common causes: Sensor E drifting or poorly seated on its cell group (medium likelihood); Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt) (medium likelihood); Real local hot spot from a weak cell group or blocked airflow (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Battery too cold or reduced power message; Limited charge and discharge power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BC4 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low
text: P0BC4: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low. Sensor E is an NTC thermistor with a pull-up resistor, so its voltage falls as it gets hotter; a short to ground therefore looks like an extremely hot cell group. GM's 2016 table sets P0BC4 when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the 2011 Volt table and GM's 2019 battery module table use above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; the eAssist mild hybrid flags a sense voltage under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 5 circuit low voltage. Its counterpart is P0BC5 (open circuit, reads very cold); a genuinely overheated pack is reported as P0A7E. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts charge and discharge power and may run cooling at full speed. Common causes: Sensor E signal wire shorted to ground inside the pack (high likelihood); Internally shorted thermistor E (medium likelihood); Moisture or contamination on the sensing board (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Implausibly high temperature for sensor E on the scan tool; Reduced power and battery fan or cooling at full speed. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BC5 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit High
text: P0BC5: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit High. P0BC5 reports that battery temperature sensor E delivers a voltage above its valid range. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links these codes to a Battery Too Cold message at ambient temperatures above -25 °C and prescribes reprogramming. Its counterpart is P0BC4. A pack the controller believes frozen gets strict charge and power limits. Common causes: Open sensor E wire or backed-out pin at the sensing board (high likelihood); Cracked or open thermistor E (medium likelihood); Module software misreading in the cold (GM Volt, reprogramming) (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Battery too cold, plug in to warm message; Very limited power or charging. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BC6 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BC6: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0BC6 flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor E: the reading jumps far faster than the heavy battery mass could warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 18OBDG02). Sampling every 100 ms, the controller adds up the absolute changes of the sensor value over a 10-sample window; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips, provided system voltage is above 10.2 V. The same logic covers the other pack sensors. The older Volt, Two-Mode and eAssist tables list no erratic code for sensor E. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a cracked wire or a connector not fully latched after pack work; if several sensors jump at once, suspect the sensing board. Common causes: Loose terminal or unlatched connector of sensor E (high likelihood); Cracked or chafed sensor wire breaking contact intermittently (medium likelihood); Sensing board fault affecting several temperature inputs (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Sensor E value jumping on the scan tool; Occasional power reduction. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BC7 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit/Open
text: P0BC7: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit/Open. Many battery cooling fans report their actual speed back to the controller as a pulse signal; Toyota patents describe a rotation sensor on the fan motor whose measured speed is compared with the target. P0BC7 means this feedback line for fan 1 is open or carries no usable signal. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables cover the same feedback only through P0BC8, P0BC9 and P0BCA. CARB requires the electrical inputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. The fan may still turn, but the controller can no longer confirm it and usually limits power to protect the pack. Faults in the drive circuit are P0A81 to P0A85; fan 2 feedback has its own codes P0D5F to P0D63. Common causes: Open feedback wire or loose pin at the fan connector (high likelihood); Failed speed sensor or electronics inside the fan unit (medium likelihood); Faulty feedback input in the controlling module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or MIL on; Reduced electric assist or charging power; Fan audible even though the code reports no feedback. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0BC8 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Range/Performance
text: P0BC8: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Range/Performance. P0BC8 compares the speed fed back by battery cooling fan 1 with what the controller commanded. GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables run two checks. With the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 11 s, the filtered difference between commanded and reported speed must stay inside calibrated limits; large errors fail within seconds, small ones after up to 43 s. With the fan off for more than 20 s, a reported speed above 120 rpm fails in 24 of 32 samples at 250 ms. It is Type B, two trips, and waits while drive or sense circuit codes are active. A dusty or worn fan that cannot reach its speed is the usual cause; a fan turning while commanded off points to a stuck drive. The circuit cases are P0BC7, P0BC9 and P0BCA. Common causes: Dust-clogged impeller, blocked intake or worn fan bearing (high likelihood); Fan keeps running while commanded off (stuck drive or relay) (medium likelihood); Fan electronics reporting a wrong speed (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Weak airflow or unusual fan noise from the battery intake; Reduced electric assist when the pack warms up. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0BC9 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Low
text: P0BC9: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Low. P0BC9 means the speed feedback of battery cooling fan 1 is implausibly low while the fan is running. A frequency near zero comes either from a fan that is not turning or from a feedback line shorted to ground or interrupted. The high case is P0BCA, a speed that is merely too far from the target is P0BC8, and drive circuit faults are P0A81 to P0A85. Expect power limits when the pack warms up. Common causes: Fan seized, blocked or without power (high likelihood); Feedback wire shorted to ground or interrupted (medium likelihood); Failed speed sensor inside the fan unit (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; No airflow from the battery cooling fan; Reduced power when the battery gets warm. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0BCA – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit High
text: P0BCA: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit High. P0BCA means the speed feedback of battery cooling fan 1 is implausibly high. GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables count a failure when the feedback frequency exceeds 290 Hz with the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 8 s and system voltage above 10.2 V; 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms set it as Type B, two trips. No real fan reaches that frequency, so the cause is electrical: noise coupled into the feedback line, a line shorted to another signal or to voltage, or fan electronics sending garbage. Check wire routing and grounds before replacing the fan. The low case is P0BC9, speed errors within range P0BC8, an open line P0BC7. While the feedback is untrusted the controller may limit power. Common causes: Electrical noise on the feedback line from poor routing or a bad ground (medium likelihood); Feedback wire shorted to voltage or another signal (medium likelihood); Fan electronics sending an invalid speed signal (medium likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Implausible fan speed reading on the scan tool; Possible power reduction. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0BCB – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BCB: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0BCB flags a speed feedback from battery cooling fan 1 that drops out or jumps in a way no rotating fan can, typically a loose contact in the feedback line. title: P0BCC – Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0BCC: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit. In a two-machine hybrid one inverter feeds the traction motor and a second one the generator, the machine that is mainly driven by the engine to charge the battery or start it. Its power switches carry thermistors so the controller can cut current before they overheat. P0BCC is the general circuit code for sensor A of that generator inverter, used for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires hybrid components and their sensor inputs to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid reading the controller limits generator power, which can reduce charging and hybrid performance. The sensor normally sits inside the inverter assembly. Common causes: Fault of the sensor or its circuit inside the inverter assembly (high likelihood); Loose or corroded connector at the inverter (medium likelihood); Software fault in the inverter or hybrid control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp; Reduced generator output and battery charging; Engine runs more often or hybrid mode limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BCD – Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BCD: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance. P0BCD flags a generator inverter temperature sensor A whose signal is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example a value stuck at one temperature or far from the other temperatures after a long soak. Ford documents this exact code: on 2020 Lincoln Aviator 3.0L hybrids built up to 18 July 2020, P0BCD stored in the inverter system controller (SOBDMC) lights the MIL and is caused by software; the fix is reprogramming that module. Patents by Hino and Mitsubishi Electric describe how such checks work, comparing heat generated in the inverter with the measured temperature change or detecting a stuck sensor. Circuit faults go to P0BCE or P0BCF instead. Common causes: Inverter controller software (Ford SSM 49120, Lincoln Aviator 2020) (high likelihood); Sensor drifting or stuck at one value (medium likelihood); Uneven inverter coolant flow distorting the comparison (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp; Often no noticeable change in driving; Hybrid system warning message possible. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BCE – Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
text: P0BCE: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low. P0BCE means the signal of generator inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. Inverter thermistors are usually NTC types with a pull-up resistor, as GM's tables describe for the drive motor inverter sensors: a short to ground or a shorted element pulls the voltage down, which the controller reads as an impossibly hot inverter. GM sets the comparable drive motor codes at roughly 125 to 170 °C, depending on generation. No manufacturer documents P0BCE itself publicly; CARB requires this circuit monitoring for hybrid sensor inputs. The controller then protects the generator inverter with a substitute value and limits generator power. A real overheat is reported separately as P0A3E. Common causes: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the inverter assembly (high likelihood); Signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present (medium likelihood); Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Generator power strongly limited; Battery charge drops, engine runs more. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BD0 – Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BD0: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. A liquid-cooled inverter changes temperature slowly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or to interference: a Hitachi patent on inverter systems explains that the small sensor signal can pick up noise from the high-voltage main circuit and has to be filtered statistically. No manufacturer documents P0BD0 itself publicly; CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be checked for such faults as well. Permanent faults are reported as P0BCE or P0BCF. Symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes; Brief drops in generator or hybrid power; Jumping inverter temperature in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BD2 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BD2: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance. text: P0BD8: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low. GM sets it above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt, above 159 °C, Type A, in a 2019 table, above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt and above 125 °C, two trips, in the 2012 table. Stellantis lists P0BD8-11 for the 2026 Jeep Compass 1.6 PHEV outside the US among the codes behind a no-start with the message Electric Traction System Fault; the repair is the traction inverter of the hybrid dual-clutch transmission. Common causes: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the inverter (Jeep Compass PHEV bulletin) (high likelihood); Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present (medium likelihood); Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Vehicle does not start, Electric Traction System Fault (Jeep); Electric drive power strongly limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BD9 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
text: P0BD9: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit High. P0BD9 means inverter temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor in the motor B inverter that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely. GM checks only after the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more, so a real cold start is excluded. The 2016 Volt then sets it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, Type B, two trips; a 2019 table uses -50 °C with Type A; the 2011 Volt below -58 °C, Type A; the 2012 table below -40 °C, two trips. Until the value is valid the controller uses substitute values and may limit motor B. Check the inverter connectors before replacing the unit. Common causes: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter (medium likelihood); Lost sensor ground (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on model after two trips; Reduced motor B power and regeneration; Implausibly low inverter temperature in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BDA – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BDA: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0BDA covers an inverter temperature sensor D signal that changes in steps or drops out briefly. Real temperatures of a liquid-cooled inverter move smoothly, so such jumps suggest a contact problem or interference from the high-voltage switching, which a Hitachi patent on inverter systems names as a typical disturbance of the small sensor signal. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables cover sensor D, the second sensor of the motor B inverter, only with P0BD7, P0BD8 and P0BD9. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for erratic behaviour as well. Because the fault comes and goes, freeze-frame data and live data during a wiggle test are the most useful clues. Common causes: Loose or corroded contact at the inverter module (high likelihood); Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module (medium likelihood); Interference from the high-voltage circuit on the sensor signal (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes; Brief power reductions while driving; Jumping inverter temperature in live data. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BDB – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit
text: P0BDB: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit. Which thermistor counts as inverter temperature sensor E is set by the manufacturer. In GM's hybrid tables it is the third sensor of the motor A inverter (PIM sensor #3), assigned to phase W in the 2016 to 2019 tables. Without a valid reading the controller cannot protect the phase W power switches and usually limits motor torque. The sensor is built into the inverter, so the repair is often the inverter assembly. Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning; Reduced electric drive power; Further inverter temperature codes stored at the same time. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BDC – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BDC: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance. P0BDC checks whether inverter temperature sensor E, GM's phase W sensor in the motor A inverter, agrees with the vehicle after a long stand. A 2019 table uses the same 20 °C as Type A. The 2011 Volt compares it with power electronics coolant temperature (20 °C, Type A); the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks use 15 °C after at least 360 minutes off (Type B). GM bulletin PIC6303A says that on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal the code has no remedial action; the inverter is replaced only together with P0AC4. Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two drives, often without any drivability change; Code found during inspection without customer complaint. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BDF – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BDF: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0BDF flags an unstable signal from inverter temperature sensor E: the reading jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying out of range, typically from a loose connector, a cracked solder joint or an ageing thermistor. In GM's hybrid tables sensor E is the phase W sensor of the motor A inverter, but GM does not list this erratic code; no manufacturer documents P0BDF publicly. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be checked for circuit faults, which includes intermittent signals. Unlike P0BDD and P0BDE, the value returns to plausible levels between faults, so the code may come and go. Because the controller cannot trust the sensor, it usually reduces motor power while the fault is present. Common causes: Loose, corroded or vibrating connector at the inverter (high likelihood); Cracked solder joint on the inverter sensing board (medium likelihood); Ageing thermistor with unstable resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes; Occasional loss of electric drive power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BE2 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low
text: P0BE2: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low. P0BE2 is set when the voltage from inverter temperature sensor F, the phase W thermistor in GM's motor B inverter, drops below the valid window. Common causes: Shorted thermistor or signal line inside the power inverter module (high likelihood); Signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where the design has any (medium likelihood); Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Power of drive motor B strongly limited; Engine runs more often in hybrid operation. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BE4 – Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0BE4: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0BE4 stands for brief dropouts or jumps in the signal of inverter temperature sensor F, which GM's hybrid tables place at phase W of the motor B inverter. The reading returns to normal between events, which separates it from the steady low and high faults P0BE2 and P0BE3. GM does not list this code, and no other manufacturer documents P0BE4 publicly. Typical sources are a connector with poor contact, a cracked solder joint or a thermistor whose resistance has become unstable. While the signal is distrusted, the controller tends to cut motor B power, and the fault can disappear before the workshop sees it. title: P0BE5 – Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
text: P0BE5: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit. The inverter of drive motor A measures the current in each motor phase with a current sensor; the controller needs these values for torque control and overcurrent protection. P0BE5 is the general circuit code for the phase U sensor, used for an electrical fault that is not classed as offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables (2011 Volt through 2019) only use the siblings P0BE6, P0BE7 and P0BE8, and CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a reliable phase U reading the inverter typically switches to a reduced or alternate control mode, so motor A loses power. The sensor sits inside the inverter, which usually means inverter replacement. Common causes: Failed phase U current sensor inside the inverter (high likelihood); Supply or signal fault on the inverter's sensor board (medium likelihood); Software fault in the motor control processor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and malfunction indicator lamp; Reduced power from drive motor A; Possible loss of electric drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BE6 – Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BE6: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. GM uses P0BE6 as the offset check of the phase U current sensor in the motor A inverter. At every start, while no current flows, the controller learns the sensor's zero offset; if it exceeds 30 A (2011 Volt and 2016 tables, Type A; 2012 two-mode trucks, Type B) or 35 A (2019 table, Type A), the code sets. In GM's BAS Plus (eAssist) table a fault of this sensor makes current control switch to an alternate mode that does not use the current sensors. Jeep lists P0BE6 with the other phase current codes on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV for Europe, with the turtle and Service 4WD lights, and fixes it by reprogramming the hybrid control processors. Common causes: Hybrid control processor software (Jeep bulletin 08-056-21/08-057-21) (high likelihood); Zero offset of the phase U current sensor drifted beyond the limit (medium likelihood); Faulty sensing electronics in the power inverter module (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp; Turtle (limp home) light and Service 4WD light (Jeep); Reduced electric drive power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BE7 – Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0BE7: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low. P0BE7 means the output of the phase U current sensor in the motor A inverter has fallen below its valid range. GM converts the sensor voltage into amps and compares it with a limit: below -700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s in the 2016 tables and 0.1 of 0.15 s in a 2019 table, both Type A; below -700 A, Type B, on the 2012 two-mode trucks; below -440 A, Type B, two trips, in the BAS Plus (eAssist) table; the 2011 Volt uses 800 A limits for these sensors. Such values are far beyond real phase currents, so the cause is electrical, typically a sensor signal pulled toward ground. GM's eAssist controller then runs current control without the sensors, which costs motor A performance. Common causes: Failed phase U current sensor inside the inverter (high likelihood); Sensor signal or supply pulled to ground on the sensor board (medium likelihood); Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Reduced power or no assist from drive motor A; Possible shutdown of electric drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BF0 – Drive Motor A Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High
text: P0BF0: Drive Motor A Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High. P0BF0 is the high-signal fault of the phase W current sensor in the motor A inverter. GM sets it above 700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s in the 2016 tables or 0.1 of 0.15 s in a 2019 table, Type A, one trip; above 700 A, Type B, two trips, on the 2012 two-mode trucks; above 440 A, Type B, in the BAS Plus (eAssist) table; the 2011 Volt uses 800 A limits for this sensor family. A value this high without matching battery current points to the sensor, its supply or an open reference rather than to real overcurrent, which GM reports separately (P0C01). With P0BF0 active, GM's eAssist logic switches to sensorless current control and suspends P0BFD, so motor A is limited until repair. Common causes: Failed phase W current sensor inside the inverter (high likelihood); Sensor signal shorted to the sensor supply voltage or open reference ground (medium likelihood); Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Reduced power from drive motor A. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BF1 – Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
text: P0BF1: Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit. On hybrids with two electric machines, the inverter of drive motor B carries its own set of phase current sensors, which the motor control processor uses for torque control and to protect the power switches. P0BF1 is the general circuit code for the phase U sensor of motor B, meant for an electrical fault that is not classified as offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly: GM's tables for the 2011 Volt, the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks and the 2016 to 2019 models list only P0BF2, P0BF3 and P0BF4 for this sensor. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a valid phase U value, motor B is usually limited or switched off. Common causes: Failed phase U current sensor in the motor B inverter (high likelihood); Supply or signal fault on the inverter's sensor board (medium likelihood); Software fault in the motor B control processor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning and malfunction indicator lamp; Reduced power or no contribution from drive motor B; Engine runs more often because electric drive is limited. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BF2 – Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0BF2: Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. GM runs P0BF2 as the offset test of the phase U current sensor in the motor B inverter. title: P0BF3 – Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0BF3: Drive Motor B Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low. P0BF3 is stored when the phase U current sensor of the motor B inverter reports a value below its valid range. GM converts the sensor voltage into amps and sets the code below -800 A on the 2011 Volt (Type A, 4 of 6 samples), below -700 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips), and below -700 A for 0.05 of 0.1 s in the 2016 tables or 0.1 of 0.15 s in a 2019 table (Type A, one trip). No real phase current of motor B reaches such values, so the reading reflects an electrical defect, typically a sensor output pulled toward ground or a dead sensor. The offset check P0BF2 covers a shifted zero instead. Motor B is then restricted or shut off. Common causes: Failed phase U current sensor in the motor B inverter (high likelihood); Sensor signal or supply pulled to ground on the sensor board (medium likelihood); Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Reduced power or no contribution from drive motor B; Possible shutdown of electric drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BF5 – Drive Motor B Phase V Current Sensor Circuit
text: P0BF5: Drive Motor B Phase V Current Sensor Circuit. P0BF5 stands for a general circuit fault of the phase V current sensor in the motor B inverter, an electrical problem the controller does not narrow down to offset, low or high. title: P0BF7 – Drive Motor B Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0BF7: Drive Motor B Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low. P0BF7 reports that the phase V current sensor of the motor B inverter outputs a signal below its valid range. title: P0BF9 – Drive Motor B Phase W Current Sensor Circuit
text: P0BF9: Drive Motor B Phase W Current Sensor Circuit. P0BF9 is reserved for a general circuit fault of the phase W current sensor in the drive motor B inverter, outside the offset, low and high categories that have their own codes. The sensor sits inside the inverter, so repair usually means replacing the inverter assembly. Common causes: Failed phase W current sensor in the motor B inverter (high likelihood); Supply or signal fault on the inverter's sensor board (medium likelihood); Software fault in the motor B control processor (low likelihood). title: P0BFD – Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation
text: P0BFD: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation. In a three-phase motor without a neutral connection the three phase currents must add up to roughly zero. P0BFD checks this for drive motor A: if the absolute sum of the U, V and W readings exceeds a limit, at least one sensor is wrong. GM's limits: 156 A on the 2011 Volt and 110 A on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks (Type A, one trip), 110 A for 0.0032 of 0.0038 s in the 2016 and 2019 tables (Type A). GM's BAS Plus (eAssist) uses another balance, motor DC current plus accessory module current versus battery current, above 40 A, Type B, blocked while a phase sensor code is active. Jeep lists P0BFD on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV (EMEA), fixed by a software update. Common causes: Hybrid control processor software (Jeep bulletin 08-056-21/08-057-21) (high likelihood); One motor A phase current sensor reading wrong but still within its own limits (medium likelihood); Faulty current sensing electronics in the power inverter module (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning; Turtle (limp home) light and Service 4WD light (Jeep); Reduced power from drive motor A. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0BFE – Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation
text: P0BFE: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation. P0BFE applies the phase balance test to drive motor B: the controller adds the U, V and W current readings, which should cancel out, and sets the code when the absolute sum stays above a limit. Jeep lists P0BFE on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV (EMEA) with the turtle and Service 4WD lights; reprogramming the hybrid processors is the fix. title: P0BFF – Drive Motor A Current
text: P0BFF: Drive Motor A Current. P0BFF is the general code for the current flowing through drive motor A, the electric machine the manufacturer labels A. It covers a current fault that is not classed as too low (P0C00) or too high (P0C01). No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. CARB requires hybrids to monitor electric motor performance. The closest documented check is GM's P0C01, which compares the sensed phase current with a fixed limit, and Stellantis lists P0C01 on the 2026 Wagoneer S with damaged three-phase cabling as the cause. A stored P0BFF means the motor controller no longer trusts the motor current, so it usually reduces electric drive power. Check the three-phase connections, the motor windings and the inverter. Common causes: Loose, corroded or damaged three-phase cable joint between inverter and motor A (medium likelihood); Fault in the motor A inverter or its current measurement (medium likelihood); Damaged stator winding of drive motor A (low likelihood); Motor control software fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning; Reduced electric drive power or limp mode; Other drive motor A current or phase codes stored. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C00 – Drive Motor A Current Low
text: P0C00: Drive Motor A Current Low. P0C00 reports that the current of drive motor A is lower than the controller expects for the commanded torque, the counterpart of P0C01 (current high). No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM and Stellantis use only P0C01 from this group. CARB requires hybrids to monitor electric motor performance. Symptoms: Weak or missing electric drive torque; Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning; Vehicle runs on the engine only or in limp mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C01 – Drive Motor A Current High
text: P0C01: Drive Motor A Current High. P0C01 is the overcurrent check of drive motor A, meant to protect the inverter's IGBTs. A fast and a slow counter catch sudden and intermittent faults; Type A, one trip. GM PIP5246 links it on Volt and ELR to a damaged motor 1 stator. Stellantis lists it on the 2018/19 Wrangler eTorque (motor generator unit) and on the 2026 Wagoneer S and Cherokee, there caused by cross-threaded three-phase cable bolts. Expect limp mode. Common causes: Damaged or improperly torqued three-phase cable joints (Stellantis S2608000006) (high likelihood); Damaged stator winding of motor A (GM PIP5246) (medium likelihood); Outdated hybrid control software (Jeep TSB 08-144-23) (medium likelihood); Failing power switch or current measurement in the inverter (low likelihood). title: P0C02 – Drive Motor B Current
text: P0C02: Drive Motor B Current. title: P0C05 – Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
text: P0C05: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open. P0C05 detects an open or missing phase between the inverter and drive motor A. Common causes: Loose or open three-phase terminal between inverter and motor A (high likelihood); Software fault, cured by update (Jeep TSB 08-144-23) (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the motor generator unit or open stator winding (medium likelihood); One-off event that does not return after clearing (Volvo TJ 36863) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Propulsion system performance message or warning lamp; Reduced electric drive power; Loss of 12 V charging or noise from the motor generator on mild hybrids. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C06 – Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
text: P0C06: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit Low. P0C06 belongs to the phase circuit group of drive motor A and reports that a U, V or W phase line sits too low, typically a short to the negative high-voltage rail or to chassis ground. P0C05 covers an open or missing phase, P0C07 the opposite high state. No manufacturer documents P0C06 for a drive motor publicly; GM's hybrid tables use only P0C05 from this trio. CARB requires hybrid input and output components to be monitored for circuit faults. Such a short usually also trips the inverter's overcurrent protection, so P0C01 or insulation faults may appear alongside. The motor controller shuts down motor A, which leaves the driver with reduced or no electric drive and a warning lamp. Common causes: Phase cable or winding shorted to ground or housing (medium likelihood); Shorted low-side power switch in the motor A inverter (medium likelihood); Insulation damage from heat, moisture or chafing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Electric drive shut down with warning lamp; Overcurrent or insulation codes stored at the same time. Repair difficulty: shop_only.
