title: P0C07 – Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit High
text: P0C07: Drive Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit High. P0C07 is the high member of the drive motor A phase circuit group: a U, V or W phase line reads higher than it should, most likely through a short to the positive high-voltage rail or a power switch that stays on. Its siblings are P0C05 for an open phase and P0C06 for a phase pulled low. No manufacturer documents P0C07 publicly; among these three, GM uses only P0C05, which watches for missing phase current. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid input and output components. Because a stuck high phase drives uncontrolled current, the inverter normally disables motor A at once. The driver sees a warning lamp and loses some or all electric propulsion until the shorted part is replaced. Common causes: Shorted high-side power switch in the motor A inverter (medium likelihood); Phase cable shorted to the positive high-voltage path (medium likelihood); Faulty gate driver holding a switch on (low likelihood). Symptoms: Immediate shutdown of electric drive with warning lamp; Reduced performance or engine-only operation. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C08 – Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
text: P0C08: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open. P0C08 is the open-phase check for drive motor B, the motor B twin of P0C05. GM runs it on the 2011 Volt and the 2012 two-mode trucks: each phase is checked as the rotor passes its axis, and a phase axis current below 9 A while at least 23 A is commanded, with the rotor within 30 degrees and over 35 V on the inverter, counts as a miss. Around 200 failed samples set it, Type A, one trip. Later GM tables up to 2016 keep the same logic. GM's eAssist has only one machine and no P0C08. The usual causes are a loose three-phase terminal, an open stator winding or an inverter stage that does not conduct. Motor B then delivers no torque, the MIL lights and drive power is reduced. Common causes: Loose or open three-phase terminal between inverter and motor B (high likelihood); Open stator winding in drive motor B (medium likelihood); Inverter stage for motor B not conducting (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive; Reduced propulsion power; Engine running more often than usual. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C09 – Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
text: P0C09: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit Low. P0C09 marks a U, V or W phase line of drive motor B that is pulled low, for example by a short to the negative high-voltage rail, to ground or by a power switch that conducts when it should not. It is the motor B twin of P0C06; the siblings P0C08 and P0C0A cover an open phase and a phase stuck high. No manufacturer documents P0C09 publicly, and GM's hybrid tables use only P0C08 for motor B phase circuits. CARB requires circuit fault monitoring of hybrid components. A low phase usually causes overcurrent too, so P0C04 or insulation codes often accompany it. The motor controller switches motor B off; the vehicle continues with reduced power and a warning lamp. Common causes: Phase cable or winding of motor B shorted to ground or housing (medium likelihood); Shorted low-side power switch in the motor B inverter (medium likelihood); Insulation damage from heat, moisture or chafing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Motor B shut down with warning lamp; Overcurrent or insulation codes stored at the same time. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C0A – Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit High
text: P0C0A: Drive Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit High. P0C0A reports that a phase line of drive motor B reads too high, typically a short to the positive high-voltage rail or a high-side power switch that stays on. It mirrors P0C07 for motor A and completes the motor B trio with P0C08 (open) and P0C09 (low). No manufacturer documents P0C0A publicly; GM only uses P0C08 for motor B phase circuits, based on missing phase current. CARB requires hybrid components to be monitored for circuit faults. A phase stuck high leads to uncontrolled current, so the inverter switches motor B off immediately and P0C04 may be stored as well. For the driver this means a warning lamp, reduced propulsion and, on electric all-wheel drive, loss of the driven axle. Common causes: Shorted high-side power switch in the motor B inverter (medium likelihood); Phase cable of motor B shorted to the positive high-voltage path (medium likelihood); Faulty gate driver holding a switch on (low likelihood). Symptoms: Immediate shutdown of motor B with warning lamp; Reduced performance or loss of electric all-wheel drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C0B – Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit/Open
text: P0C0B: Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit/Open. P0C0B flags a lost or interrupted supply inside the motor A inverter. GM reads it from the IGBT module status: when the gate drive supply falls below its threshold, the module reports a bias fault; on eAssist the 5 V rail below 3.5 to 4.3 V or the 15 V rail below 10.4 to 12.6 V counts, with run/crank above 7 V. The 2012 trucks enable it between 9.5 and 18 V; the 2016 to 2019 tables need 0.002 to 0.168 s of fault within short windows, Type A, one trip. Mercedes applies the code to the high-voltage supply of the inverter in the belt starter-alternator of P3 hybrids (subtypes 16 and 17) and replaces that unit. Expect loss of electric drive or engine start. Common causes: Failed gate-drive power supply inside the motor A inverter (high likelihood); Low 12 V feed, blown fuse or poor ground to the inverter control board (medium likelihood); Open high-voltage feed to the inverter, e.g. in a belt starter-alternator (Mercedes LI15.40-P-077947) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive; Electric drive or motor generator unavailable; Engine cannot be started, only electric driving possible (Mercedes P3 hybrids). Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C0C – Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit Low
text: P0C0C: Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit Low. P0C0C reports that the supply voltage of the motor A inverter is present but too low, while P0C0B covers a lost or open supply and P0C0D a supply that is too high. Which supply is meant depends on the maker: GM ties its sibling P0C0B to the gate-drive supply of the IGBTs, Mercedes to the high-voltage feed. Audi documents P0C0C on the 2025 and 2026 A6 and Q6 e-tron family: stored in the electric drive modules together with P0E8D, it comes with a red high-voltage fault warning to stop safely, and the bulletin calls for replacing the affected front or rear power electronics. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid components. Without a stable supply the inverter cannot switch, so drive power is cut. Common causes: Internal fault of the drive power electronics (Audi TSB 2081725) (high likelihood); Weak 12 V supply, poor ground or high-resistance connector at the inverter (medium likelihood); Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC converter output (low likelihood). Symptoms: Red high-voltage system warning asking to stop safely; Loss of drive power or vehicle will not get ready to drive. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C0D – Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit High
text: P0C0D: Drive Motor A Inverter Power Supply Circuit High. P0C0D reports that the supply of the motor A inverter is above its permitted range, while P0C0B stands for a lost or open supply and P0C0C for a supply that is too low. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's tables for the sibling P0C0B show what the supply is: the gate-drive rails of the IGBT module, on eAssist a 5 V and a 15 V rail that are each watched against limits. A rail running too high stresses the driver stage and can falsify the switching of the power transistors. CARB requires hybrid components to be monitored for circuit faults. Expect the inverter to shut down or derate, with reduced or no electric drive. Common causes: Faulty voltage regulation of the gate-drive supply inside the motor A inverter (high likelihood); Excessive 12 V system voltage from the DC/DC converter or a charger (medium likelihood); Supply or sense line shorted to a higher voltage in the harness (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp, hybrid system warning; Reduced or no electric propulsion from motor A; Engine runs more often or the vehicle enters limp mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C0E – Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit/Open
text: P0C0E: Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit/Open. P0C0E is the motor B counterpart of P0C0B: the inverter for the second motor has lost the supply of its gate-drive board. GM documents it on the Volt and the two-mode trucks. The IGBT module reports a bias fault through its status line when the supply of phase A, B or C fails. The 2011 Volt checks with high voltage above 100 V, the 2012 trucks with run/crank voltage between 9.5 and 18 V, both after one count, Type A. The 2016 Volt needs 0.002 s of fault in a 0.024 s window, the 2018 table 0.02 s, the 2019 table 0.168 s, always Type A, one trip. P0C0F and P0C10 cover low and high supply. Motor B can no longer be driven, so propulsion is reduced. Common causes: Failed gate-drive power supply inside the motor B inverter (high likelihood); Weak 12 V feed, blown fuse or poor ground at the inverter control board (medium likelihood); Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the power inverter module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive; Reduced propulsion message, motor B unavailable; Engine runs continuously instead of electric driving. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C0F – Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit Low
text: P0C0F: Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit Low. P0C0F means the supply of the motor B inverter is present but below its permitted range. P0C0E covers a lost or open supply, P0C10 a supply that is too high, and P0C0C is the same fault on motor A. No manufacturer documents P0C0F publicly. GM's tables for P0C0E name the supply in question: the power feed of the gate-drive board, checked phase by phase with run/crank voltage between 9.5 and 18 V on the 2012 trucks. A sagging rail can no longer switch the power transistors fully, so the inverter protects itself. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid components. The driver typically sees a warning and loses the electric drive of motor B. Common causes: Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC converter output feeding the inverter electronics (high likelihood); Corroded connector or poor ground raising resistance in the inverter supply (medium likelihood); Failing internal gate-drive power supply in the motor B inverter (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp, hybrid system warning; Reduced propulsion, motor B unavailable; Fault appears mainly with low 12 V voltage, e.g. after standing. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C10 – Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit High
text: P0C10: Drive Motor B Inverter Power Supply Circuit High. P0C10 flags a supply of the motor B inverter that is above its permitted range. Its siblings are P0C0E for a lost or open supply and P0C0F for a low one; P0C0D is the motor A version. No manufacturer documents P0C10 publicly. GM uses only the open-circuit code P0C0E for this supply and describes it as the power feed of the gate-drive board, monitored through the status line of the IGBT module. An overvoltage on that rail can damage the driver circuits, so the controller shuts the inverter down. CARB requires hybrid components to be checked for circuit faults. Expect a warning lamp and loss of the electric drive provided by motor B. Common causes: Faulty voltage regulation of the gate-drive supply inside the motor B inverter (high likelihood); Excessive 12 V system voltage from the DC/DC converter or an external charger (medium likelihood); Supply or sense line shorted to a higher voltage in the harness (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp, hybrid system warning; Reduced propulsion, motor B unavailable; Vehicle limited to engine or reduced-power operation. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C11 – Drive Motor A Inverter Phase U Over Temperature
text: P0C11: Drive Motor A Inverter Phase U Over Temperature. P0C11 is a protective code: the temperature sensor at phase U of the motor A inverter reads a valid but excessive value. GM uses it across its hybrids. The 2011 Volt reads PIM sensor A against 98 °C, the 2012 two-mode trucks against 88 °C with a reset at 85 °C, both Type A; the 2016 Volt sets it above 126 °C for 1.2 s within 2 s, the 2019 table above 128 °C, Type A, one trip. On eAssist the single inverter code P0C11 sets above 118.2 °C as Type B, two trips. Sensor faults such as P0AEE block it. Phase V and W are P0C12 and P0C13. GM advises finding the cause of poor cooling. The inverter cuts power to protect itself. Common causes: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics cooling loop (high likelihood); Failed or weak electric coolant pump of the inverter loop (high likelihood); Clogged power electronics radiator or inoperative cooling fan (medium likelihood); Sustained heavy load such as towing uphill in high ambient heat (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp, often with a hybrid system overheat message; Reduced propulsion power until the inverter cools down; Electric drive unavailable, engine runs continuously. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C12 – Drive Motor A Inverter Phase V Over Temperature
text: P0C12: Drive Motor A Inverter Phase V Over Temperature. P0C12 sets when the inverter for motor A measures an excessive temperature at phase V while its sensor itself is plausible. In GM's 2011 Volt table that is PIM sensor C above 98 °C; the two-mode trucks of 2012 use 88 °C with an 85 °C reset, the 2016 Volt 126 °C for 1.2 s out of 2 s and the 2016 ELR 102.5 °C, all Type A, one trip. The sensor circuit codes of that thermistor, such as P0BD1 and P0BD2, have their own numbers and must be ruled out first. P0C11 and P0C13 are phases U and W, P0C15 is phase V on motor B. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists these overheat codes as a sign of insufficient cooling. Power is reduced while the inverter is hot. Common causes: Low coolant level or trapped air in the inverter cooling loop (high likelihood); Inoperative electric coolant pump of the power electronics (high likelihood); Blocked low-temperature radiator or failed cooling fan (medium likelihood); Degraded thermal contact or failing power stage inside the inverter (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive; Propulsion power reduced, especially under load or in hot weather; Hybrid system overheat or service message. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C13 – Drive Motor A Inverter Phase W Over Temperature
text: P0C13: Drive Motor A Inverter Phase W Over Temperature. P0C13 covers phase W of the motor A inverter: the controller sees a credible sensor reading that exceeds the overtemperature limit. GM's 2011 Volt uses PIM sensor E with 98 °C, the 2012 two-mode trucks 88 °C, the 2016 and 2018 tables 126 °C for 1.2 s within a 2 s window and the 2019 table 128 °C for 1.5 s, always Type A, one trip, so the MIL comes on at once. The check is blocked while circuit or performance faults of the thermistor are active. Siblings are P0C11 for phase U and P0C12 for phase V; P0C16 is phase W on motor B. Because the code reports a real heat condition, the cooling system of the power electronics is the first place to look; output stays limited. Common causes: Coolant loss or air pocket in the power electronics loop (high likelihood); Electric coolant pump for the inverter stopped or running slow (high likelihood); Debris on the low-temperature radiator or cooling fan not running (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp immediately after the fault; Reduced propulsion until temperatures drop; Engine runs more often, little or no electric driving. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C14 – Drive Motor B Inverter Phase U Over Temperature
text: P0C14: Drive Motor B Inverter Phase U Over Temperature. P0C14 is the motor B counterpart of P0C11: phase U of the second inverter has become too hot while its temperature sensor reads plausibly. GM documents it on the Volt and the two-mode trucks. The 2011 Volt compares PIM sensor B with 98 °C, the 2012 trucks use 88 °C with a reset at 85 °C, the 2016 Volt 131 °C for 1.2 s in 2 s and the 2019 table 131 °C for 1.5 s, all Type A, one trip. Sensor circuit codes such as P0AF2 or P0AF3 point to the thermistor instead and are checked first. P0C15 and P0C16 cover phases V and W. GM bulletin PIC6303A sends technicians to the cooling system when inverter overheat codes appear. Power from motor B is limited meanwhile. Common causes: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics cooling loop (high likelihood); Failed electric coolant pump of the inverter loop (high likelihood); Clogged low-temperature radiator or failed cooling fan (medium likelihood); Long periods of high load on motor B, e.g. towing or steep climbs (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive; Reduced propulsion power, especially under load; Hybrid system overheat message. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C15 – Drive Motor B Inverter Phase V Over Temperature
text: P0C15: Drive Motor B Inverter Phase V Over Temperature. P0C15 reports overtemperature at phase V of the motor B inverter, based on a sensor reading that is valid but above the limit. GM applies it on the Volt and the two-mode trucks: PIM sensor D above 98 °C on the 2011 Volt, 88 °C on the 2012 trucks, 102.5 °C on the 2016 ELR, 131 °C for 1.2 s within 2 s on the 2016 Volt and in the 2018 table, every time Type A with one trip. It is a protective diagnosis, not a wiring check; the thermistor's own codes P0BD6 and P0BD7 handle sensor faults. Phase U and W are P0C14 and P0C16, phase V on motor A is P0C12. GM bulletin PIC6303A names P0C15 among the overheat codes that call for a cooling diagnosis. Motor B output is restricted. Common causes: Coolant loss or air in the inverter cooling loop (high likelihood); Electric coolant pump of the power electronics not working (high likelihood); Blocked radiator for the power electronics or fan failure (medium likelihood); Poor heat transfer or ageing power stage inside the inverter (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive; Reduced propulsion until the inverter has cooled; Engine runs more often than usual. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C16 – Drive Motor B Inverter Phase W Over Temperature
text: P0C16: Drive Motor B Inverter Phase W Over Temperature. P0C16 is set by the motor B inverter when phase W runs too hot and the temperature sensor itself shows no fault. GM's tables give PIM sensor F above 98 °C for the 2011 Volt, above 88 °C with an 85 °C reset for the 2012 two-mode trucks, and 131 °C for 1.2 s within 2 s for the 2016 Volt, with 1.5 s in the 2019 table; each is Type A, one trip. Thermistor circuit codes such as P0BE0 and P0BE1 take priority and block the check. P0C14 and P0C15 are phases U and V, P0C13 is phase W on motor A. CARB allows some protective overtemperature strategies to run without MIL, but GM lights it here. Look for weak cooling first; until then motor B is derated. Common causes: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics loop (high likelihood); Electric coolant pump of the inverter failed or blocked (high likelihood); Dirty low-temperature radiator or inoperative fan (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive; Reduced propulsion, notably at high load or high ambient temperature; Hybrid system overheat message. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C17 – Drive Motor A Position Sensor Not Learned
text: P0C17: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Not Learned. P0C17 means the controller has no valid learned offset for the resolver of motor A, which it needs to align rotor position with the stator field. GM runs the learn at key-off and sets the code if it fails without a stored value: motor speed above 50 rpm, DC voltage below 192 V (200 V on the 2016 Volt), phase current below 15 A or a learn time over 1.4 s. The Volt is Type A, the 2012 two-mode trucks Type B. GM bulletin 21-NA-218 links it to missing high voltage or three-phase current, loose phase terminals or stator damage on Volt and ELR. Mazda requires the speed sensor learn on CX-90 and CX-70 PHEV after inverter or motor replacement. P0C4E reports a learned value out of range. Common causes: Offset learn not performed after replacing the inverter, motor or resolver (high likelihood); High voltage not reaching the inverter during the learn, e.g. contactor or HV cable fault (medium likelihood); Loose three-phase ring terminals after a repair (medium likelihood); Damaged motor stator winding (GM 21-NA-218) (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine starts and stalls or will not start after a repair; Malfunction indicator lamp with reduced propulsion message; Electric drive unavailable. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C18 – Drive Motor B Position Sensor Not Learned
text: P0C18: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Not Learned. P0C18 is the motor B version of P0C17: the resolver offset of the second motor has not been learned and no valid earlier value is stored. GM performs the learn at key-off; it fails if motor speed exceeds 50 rpm, DC voltage stays below 192 V, phase current stays below 15 A or the learn takes longer than 1.4 s. The Volt tables rate it Type A, one trip, the 2012 two-mode trucks Type B, two trips. GM bulletin 21-NA-218 notes that when P0C17 and P0C18 set together, a programming event is needed to allow a wide position sensor learn, and that missing high voltage at the drive motor control module can be the reason. P0C4F reports a learned value beyond its limit. Common causes: Offset learn not completed after replacing the inverter, motor B or its resolver (high likelihood); No high voltage at the drive motor control module, e.g. contactor fault or disconnected HV cable (medium likelihood); Control module needs reprogramming to enable a wide position sensor learn (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after a repair or module programming; Reduced propulsion or vehicle will not enter ready mode; Motor B unavailable for driving or charging. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C19 – Drive Motor A Torque Delivered Performance
text: P0C19: Drive Motor A Torque Delivered Performance. P0C19 is a plausibility check: the torque that motor A actually delivers, calculated by the motor control processor, does not follow the slewed torque command. GM sets it when the difference exceeds 123 Nm for 0.1875 s within 0.2 s on the 2016 and 2018 tables, Type A, one trip; eAssist uses 36 Nm as Type B, two trips. The 2012 two-mode trucks check whether the sum of the three phase currents exceeds 110 A for 200 ms. Stellantis lists P0C19 on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe and the Wagoneer PHEV with P1B03, a resolver rationality fault, and cures it by reflashing the power inverter module. The electric drive shuts down and the engine takes over. Common causes: Outdated power inverter module software (Stellantis 08-059-25, 08-231-24) (high likelihood); Implausible rotor position signal from the motor A resolver or its wiring (medium likelihood); Faulty phase current sensing distorting the calculated torque (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the inverter power stage or motor winding (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp; Electric drive shuts off and the engine takes over; Engine stop-start no longer works or a service hybrid system warning appears. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C1A – Drive Motor B Torque Delivered Performance
text: P0C1A: Drive Motor B Torque Delivered Performance. P0C1A compares the torque command for motor B with the torque the motor control processor calculates as actually delivered. GM's 2016, 2018 and 2019 tables set it when the difference exceeds 132 Nm for 0.1875 s in a 0.2 s window, Type A, one trip, and only while listed resolver and motor control faults are inactive. The 2011 Volt and 2012 two-mode tables also list it, the trucks with a three-phase current sum above 110 A. Chrysler documents it on the 2017 to 2023 Pacifica Hybrid: with resolver codes P0A3F, P0A43 or P0A45 it points to a short in the internal wiring connector of the eFlite transmission, which is replaced. P0C19 is motor A. Expect limp mode. Common causes: Short in the internal transmission wiring connector (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid 21-008-23) (high likelihood); Implausible rotor position signal from the motor B resolver (medium likelihood); Hybrid control or inverter module software requiring an update (medium likelihood); Faulty phase current sensing for motor B (low likelihood). Symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp; Vehicle in limp mode with reduced propulsion; Hybrid system warning, engine runs more often. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C1B – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Too High
text: P0C1B: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Too High. P0C1B is a protection code: the electronics that drive the auxiliary transmission fluid pump measure a valid but excessive internal temperature. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM shows the same function on the 2016 Cadillac ELR pump controller under its own code P1E37, an in-range overtemperature above 98 °C that could damage the inverter, checked only when the sensor itself is plausible. A Honda patent for a CVT pump explains the reaction: once the board temperature passes a limit, the control unit opens the pump relay and keeps the pump off until the fluid has cooled. The pump then stops, so start-stop and pressure support are lost. P0C1C to P0C1F cover faults of the temperature sensor itself and must be excluded first. Common causes: High transmission fluid temperature from heavy load, towing or a weak fluid cooler (high likelihood); Pump running against high resistance (binding, clogged filter) and heating its driver (medium likelihood); Poor heat transfer from the module (mounting, contamination) or internal module fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Engine auto-stop temporarily unavailable; Transmission or hybrid warning, MIL depending on manufacturer; Harsh engagement when driving off after a stop. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C1C – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit
text: P0C1C: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit. P0C1C is the general circuit fault of the temperature sensor inside the auxiliary pump control module, used when the signal is invalid without fitting the low, high or range checks. No manufacturer documents it publicly. GM's 2016 ELR pump controller monitors its inverter sensor with own codes P1E34 to P1E36 instead, and the Honda CVT pump patent shows why the reading matters: it is the basis for switching the pump off before the board overheats. Without a valid value the controller cannot protect itself, so the pump usually runs restricted or stays off. CARB requires such sensors to be checked for circuit faults. Because the sensor is on the circuit board, the fix is normally the module or the pump assembly. P0C1D to P0C1F are the specific variants. Common causes: Temperature sensor or its measuring circuit on the module board faulty (high likelihood); Unstable supply or ground of the pump module distorting the sensor reading (medium likelihood); Moisture or fluid inside the module housing (low likelihood). Symptoms: Warning lamp or transmission message; Start-stop function inactive. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C1D – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0C1D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance. P0C1D means the internal temperature sensor of the auxiliary pump module delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit the other temperatures in the vehicle. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's comparable check on the 2016 ELR pump controller, own code P1E36, runs after at least 6 hours of inactivity: the inverter reading is compared with the average of the power electronics coolant and transmission fluid temperatures, and a difference above 20 °C fails, Type B, MIL after two trips. A sensor that reads too low would let the board overheat unnoticed, which is why the Honda pump patent bases shutdown on this value. P0C1E and P0C1F cover voltage out of range, P0C1B real overtemperature. Common causes: Board temperature sensor drifted or measuring circuit out of tolerance (high likelihood); Reference value wrong because the transmission fluid or coolant temperature sensor is faulty (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the pump control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL after repeated detection; Start-stop restricted or unavailable. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C1E – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
text: P0C1E: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Low. P0C1E reports that the signal voltage of the module's internal temperature sensor is below its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor, low voltage corresponds to a very high temperature, so a short to ground looks like an overheated board. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM shows the scale on the 2016 ELR pump controller with its own code P1E35, labelled circuit low: a reading above 130 °C, near 0 V, for 250 of 350 samples at 10.4 ms sets a Type B fault, MIL after two trips. The Honda CVT pump patent uses this board value to cut the pump relay, so a shorted sensor can stop the pump although nothing is hot. P0C1F is the high side, P0C1B a genuine overtemperature. Common causes: Board temperature sensor or its signal path shorted to ground inside the module (high likelihood); Measuring circuit of the pump control module faulty (medium likelihood); Fluid or moisture on the module board (low likelihood). Symptoms: Pump switched off as if overheated, auto-stop unavailable; MIL after two drive cycles. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C1F – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit High
text: P0C1F: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit High. P0C1F means the internal temperature sensor of the auxiliary pump module delivers a voltage above its valid range, which for an NTC thermistor reads as an implausibly cold board and usually indicates an open sensor path. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's ELR pump controller of 2016 shows the matching case under its own code P1E34, labelled circuit high: below -58 °C, near 5 V, for 250 of 350 samples sets the fault, Type B in the ELR tables. With such a value the controller loses its overtemperature protection; the Honda CVT pump patent shows that this protection is what keeps the driver board alive, so the pump is typically restricted. P0C1E is the low side, P0C1D the plausibility check, P0C1B real overtemperature. Common causes: Board temperature sensor open or its solder joint cracked (high likelihood); Measuring circuit of the pump control module faulty (medium likelihood); Ground offset at the pump module shifting the sensor voltage (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL after two drive cycles; Start-stop restricted, pump in protective mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C20 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
text: P0C20: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open. P0C20 means at least one of the three motor phases of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump carries no current, typically an open lead, terminal or winding. GM uses it in the pump controller of the Chevrolet Volt (2011-15 tables) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR: with the inverter in Run, high voltage above 35 V and the rotor within 30 degrees of a phase axis, the peak current of that phase is checked; below 1 A for 200 counts sets the code, Type A, MIL on the first trip. Each phase is tested in turn as the rotor turns. The pump cannot build torque, so pressure support and electric operation are lost. Later GM tables split the check into the per-phase codes P0B01, P0B04 and P0B07; P0C21/P0C22 are the low and high variants. Common causes: Motor connector of the pump not fully seated, or loose phase terminal (high likelihood); Open phase lead between pump inverter and motor (medium likelihood); Power switch of one phase in the pump inverter not conducting (medium likelihood); Open winding in the pump motor (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and Service Vehicle Soon message; Reduced propulsion or no electric drive mode; Engine restart harsh or delayed. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C21 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
text: P0C21: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit Low. P0C21 reports a low condition on the phase U, V or W circuits of the auxiliary pump motor, usually a phase lead shorted to ground or a voltage at a phase terminal that stays below what the inverter commands. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM watches the same wiring on the Volt and ELR with the open-circuit code P0C20 and catches shorts through overcurrent on P0C28 and its own phase current sensor codes P1E2A to P1E32. The Hitachi idle-stop pump patent shows that the inverter often reconstructs all phase currents from one DC-bus shunt, so a ground short and a sensing fault can look alike. The pump usually shuts down, auto-stop is blocked. P0C20 is the open circuit, P0C22 the high side, P0B01 to P0B08 the per-phase current codes. Common causes: Phase lead chafed through and shorted to ground or the transmission case (high likelihood); Transmission fluid or water in the motor connector creating a leakage path (medium likelihood); Low-side switch or phase sensing in the pump inverter faulty (medium likelihood); Motor winding shorted to the stator core (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and transmission or hybrid warning; Auxiliary pump off, no engine auto-stop. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C22 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit High
text: P0C22: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit High. P0C22 reports a high condition on the U-V-W phase circuits of the auxiliary pump motor, for example a phase lead shorted to the supply or a phase voltage that stays high while the inverter should pull it down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. In GM's Volt tables the closest monitors are P0C28, which trips above 35 A on any phase within a few milliseconds to protect the IGBTs, and its own phase sensor codes P1E2B, P1E2E and P1E31 for readings above 30 A. The Hitachi sub-oil pump patent shows that phase currents are often calculated from a shared bus shunt, so a sensing error must be ruled out before the wiring is condemned. The pump stops and auto-stop is blocked. P0C21 is the low side, P0B02, P0B05 and P0B08 the per-phase high codes. Common causes: Phase lead shorted to supply voltage or to another phase (high likelihood); High-side switch of the pump inverter stuck conducting (medium likelihood); Phase current sensing in the inverter reads too high (medium likelihood); Shorted turns in the pump motor winding (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid or transmission warning; Pump shuts down, harsh engagement after stops. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C23 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit/Open
text: P0C23: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit/Open. P0C23 is set by the controlling module, usually the PCM, TCM or hybrid controller, when the circuit to the auxiliary pump control module is open. J2012 does not name the line further; in practice it is the command or enable wire. Ford's 2016 F-150 2.7L bulletin shows such a command: the PCM drives the pump with a duty cycle that a scan tool can vary from 20 to 90 percent. GM's ELR pump controller only runs its phase tests while a wake-up signal is on. No manufacturer publicly documents P0C23 itself. With the line open the pump gets no command and stays off, so auto-stop is disabled and pressure support is missing. P0C24 and P0C25 are the low and high variants, P0C2B to P0C2E the feedback line in the other direction. Common causes: Open command or enable wire between controller and pump module (high likelihood); Pushed-out or corroded terminal at the pump module or controller connector (medium likelihood); Input stage of the pump control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: Start-stop no longer works; MIL or transmission warning; Harsh engagement after an engine stop. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C24 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit Low
text: P0C24: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit Low. P0C24 means the circuit from the controlling module to the auxiliary pump control module is held low, typically a short to ground on the command line. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. How the line is used is visible in Ford's 2016 F-150 2.7L bulletin, where the PCM commands the start-stop pump by duty cycle and the technician checks the pump by sweeping that command from 20 to 90 percent. A grounded line leaves the pump without a valid command or, depending on logic, permanently off. GM's ELR pump controller likewise depends on its wake-up signal to run. CARB requires output circuits of such components to be monitored. P0C23 is the open circuit, P0C25 the high side, P2796 to P2798 the classic pump control circuit codes. Common causes: Command wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed at the transmission case (high likelihood); Fluid or corrosion in the pump connector pulling the line low (medium likelihood); Output stage in the PCM/TCM or input of the pump module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: No engine auto-stop; MIL or transmission warning. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C25 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit High
text: P0C25: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit High. P0C25 reports that the circuit from the controlling module to the auxiliary pump control module sits high, for instance a command wire shorted to battery voltage or an output that cannot pull the line down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Ford's 2016 F-150 2.7L bulletin shows the type of signal involved: a PCM duty-cycle command that can be swept from 20 to 90 percent to prove pump operation. A line stuck high can be read as a constant full command or rejected as invalid, so the pump may run continuously or be shut off. GM's ELR pump controller also uses a separate wake-up line as enable. CARB requires circuit monitoring of such outputs. P0C23 is the open circuit, P0C24 the low side, P0C2E the high fault on the feedback line. Common causes: Command wire shorted to battery or another supply voltage (high likelihood); Output stage in the PCM/TCM stuck high (medium likelihood); Input stage of the pump control module faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or transmission warning; Pump runs continuously or start-stop is disabled. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C26 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current
text: P0C26: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current. P0C26 is the general motor current fault of auxiliary pump A: the current drawn does not match what the commanded operating point should need, without clearly being too low or too high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Its siblings show what is monitored: Ford stores P0C27, current too low, on 2014-16 Fusion and 2015-16 Edge with the 6F35 start-stop transmission when air enters the pump supply tube, and GM sets P0C28 on the Volt and ELR when any phase exceeds 35 A. CARB requires such components to be checked for rationality. A general current code therefore points to aeration, low fluid, a binding pump or current sensing errors. The pump may be switched off and auto-stop blocked; P0C27 and P0C28 are the specific variants. Common causes: Low or aerated transmission fluid at the pump intake (high likelihood); Pump binding or contaminated, changing the motor load (medium likelihood); Current sensing in the pump driver implausible (medium likelihood); Outdated control software of the pump or controlling module (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or transmission warning; Harsh engagement after an auto-stop; Start-stop deactivated. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C27 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current Low
text: P0C27: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current Low. P0C27 means motor A of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump draws less current than expected, a sign that the pump is not loaded, for example because it sucks air or turns without delivering. Ford documents it twice. TSB 16-0111 covers 2014-16 Fusion and 2015-16 Edge with the 6F35 transmission and start-stop: MIL, P0C27 in the PCM and a harsh engagement after an auto-stop, caused by air entering the pump supply tube on transmissions built up to 26 February 2016; a new tube with a check ball fixes it. TSB 18-2282 for the 2013-17 Fusion Energi and C-Max Energi lists P0C27 and/or P0C28 and calls for reprogramming the PCM and hybrid module. P0C28 is the high side, P0C26 the general code, P0C2A a stalled motor. Common causes: Air entering the pump supply tube (Ford 6F35, new tube with check ball) (high likelihood); Calibration of PCM and hybrid module (Ford Fusion/C-Max Energi) (medium likelihood); Low transmission fluid level letting the pump draw air (medium likelihood); High resistance or open circuit in the pump motor wiring (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on; Harsh transmission engagement after a start-stop event. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C28 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current High
text: P0C28: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current High. P0C28 is the overcurrent protection of auxiliary pump motor A. GM uses it on Volt, ELR and later hybrids: the inverter trips when any of the U, V or W phases exceeds 35 A, in 2016 within about 4 ms of a 62 ms window, or when the d-axis current falls below a stator temperature limit, Type A, MIL on the first trip. GM service update 18199 for the 2018 Cadillac CT6 plug-in traces P0C28 to a faulty pump restart logic in the software. Ford's TSB 18-2282 lists P0C27 and/or P0C28 on the 2013-17 Fusion Energi and C-Max Energi, fixed by reprogramming the PCM and hybrid module; Ford also reports P0C28 in the SOBDMC of the 2024-25 Mustang Mach-E LFP, solved by software. P0C27 is the low side. Common causes: Pump control software faulty (Cadillac CT6 update 18199, Ford Energi TSB 18-2282) (high likelihood); Pump seized, contaminated or running against blocked flow (medium likelihood); Short between motor phases or to ground (medium likelihood); Current sensing or power stage in the pump inverter faulty (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or service wrench lamp; Auxiliary pump shuts down, no auto-stop or electric mode. Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P0C29 – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Driver Circuit Performance
text: P0C29: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Driver Circuit Performance. P0C29 means the driver stage of auxiliary pump A does not behave as commanded, for instance the pump does not reach its target or the activation is reported as implausible. Volkswagen Group documents it on the 7-speed DSG 0GC (DQ381): VW lists P0C29 for the 2018 Golf R as implausible activation of auxiliary hydraulic pump 1 (V475), often with clutch and gear actuator codes as consequences; Audi's bulletin for the 2017-18 A3, A3 Cabriolet and S3 with gearbox dated up to 26 September 2017 calls for replacing the auxiliary hydraulic pump when only P0C29 remains. The customer sees a Gearbox Malfunction warning. VW improved the pump from October 2017 production. P0C2A is a stalled motor, P0C26 to P0C28 current faults. Common causes: Auxiliary hydraulic pump V475 of early production faulty (VW/Audi 0GC) (high likelihood); Poor contact at the pump electrical connection (medium likelihood); Transmission control software not updated per service action (low likelihood). Symptoms: Gearbox Malfunction warning in the instrument cluster; Consequential clutch or gear actuator codes, limp mode. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C2A – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Stalled
text: P0C2A: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Stalled. P0C2A means motor A of the auxiliary pump is commanded but does not turn, or turns far slower than required. Ford documents it in TSB 17-2056 for the 2016 F-150 2.7L with start-stop built from 1 May 2016: with the fluid above 38 °C the technician commands the pump through the PCM at duty cycles from 20 to 90 percent; if it runs, the PCM gets new software, if not, the auxiliary pump is replaced. GM shows how a stall is detected on the ELR pump controller, under its own code P1E3A: commanded minus actual speed above 200 rpm while more than 6.8 Nm is requested, Type A. Sensorless pumps cannot measure speed directly, so a stall shows up as a speed or current mismatch. P0C29 covers the driver stage, P0C28 overcurrent. Common causes: Auxiliary pump seized or jammed by debris (Ford F-150 2.7L replaces the pump) (high likelihood); PCM calibration causing false stall detection (Ford TSB 17-2056) (medium likelihood); Very cold, thick fluid or wrong fluid type raising drag (low likelihood); Open phase so the motor cannot develop torque (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on; Start-stop inactive, harsh engagement after stops. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C2B – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal
text: P0C2B: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal. P0C2B concerns the status signal the auxiliary pump control module sends back to the controlling module. GM uses it on the Two-Mode hybrid trucks and SUVs (Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado, Sierra, 2ML70): the hybrid controller expects a complete fault status message from the pump controller every 1.5 s; if it is missing or incomplete for 9.75 s with the vehicle in Run or Crank, the code sets as Type B, MIL after two trips. GM preliminary information PIP4751G stresses that P0C2B, with or without P2797, rarely means a bad pump: check the wiring, replace the pump control module if its date code is 089-11 or older, and note that a key held in Crank during a no-start can set it. P0C2C to P0C2E are the specific variants. Common causes: Wiring or terminal tension fault between hybrid controller and pump control module (high likelihood); Early pump control module (GM date code 089-11 or older) (medium likelihood); Key held in crank for a long time during a no-start (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL after two drive cycles; Bumps, lulls or surges around auto-stops. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C2C – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Range/Performance
text: P0C2C: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Range/Performance. P0C2C means the feedback signal from the auxiliary pump control module is present and electrically valid but does not make sense, for example a reported speed or status that contradicts the command. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Its siblings show the signal: on GM's Two-Mode trucks P0C2B watches a fault status message expected every 1.5 s, and on the 2021-23 Chevrolet Bolt EV and 2022 Bolt EUV GM bulletin 21-NA-148 pairs P0C2D with the pump performance codes P2797 and P2798, caused by bad solder joints in the low-voltage pump. CARB requires rationality checks for such inputs. Implausible feedback usually points to the pump electronics themselves. P0C2B is the general code, P0C2D and P0C2E the low and high variants. Common causes: Electronics of the pump module reporting wrong status or speed (high likelihood); Intermittent contact on the feedback line distorting the signal (medium likelihood); Pump not following the command mechanically, so feedback and command differ (low likelihood). Symptoms: Service Vehicle Soon or MIL; Reduced propulsion power or no start-stop. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C2D – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Low
text: P0C2D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Low. P0C2D reports that the feedback signal from the electric transmission fluid pump module stays low, below its valid range. GM documents it for the 2021-23 Chevrolet Bolt EV and 2022 Bolt EUV in bulletin 21-NA-148: the driver sees Propulsion Power is Reduced and a Service Vehicle Soon lamp, with P0C2D, P2797 or P2798 stored. The cause is a part quality spill in the low-voltage electric transmission fluid pump on the driver side of the drive unit, where a soldering process was out of specification; the motor is not serviceable, so the complete pump is replaced. In this EV the pump supplies fluid for cooling and lubricating the drive unit. P0C2B is the general feedback code, P0C2C the plausibility and P0C2E the high variant. Common causes: Faulty solder joints in the electric transmission fluid pump (Chevrolet Bolt, GM 21-NA-148) (high likelihood); Feedback line shorted to ground (medium likelihood); Corroded or loose pump connector (low likelihood). Symptoms: Propulsion Power is Reduced message; Service Vehicle Soon lamp. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C2E – Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal High
text: P0C2E: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal High. P0C2E means the feedback line from the auxiliary pump control module sits above its valid range, for example shorted to supply voltage or no longer pulled down by the module. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's use of the siblings shows what the line carries: on the Two-Mode hybrids P0C2B watches a status message from the pump controller every 1.5 s, Type B, and on the Chevrolet Bolt EV and EUV bulletin 21-NA-148 links the low variant P0C2D to bad solder joints inside the pump. A stuck-high line can hide real pump faults, so the controller usually stops relying on the pump. CARB requires circuit checks for such signals. P0C2D is the low side, P0C2C the plausibility check, P0C25 the high fault on the command line. Common causes: Feedback line shorted to supply voltage (high likelihood); Output stage of the pump control module no longer switching (medium likelihood); Lost ground at the pump module letting the line float high (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or Service Vehicle Soon lamp; Start-stop or electric drive restricted. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C2F – Internal Control Module Drive Motor/Generator - Engine Speed Sensor Performance
text: P0C2F: Internal Control Module Drive Motor/Generator - Engine Speed Sensor Performance. P0C2F is an internal plausibility check of the hybrid control processor: the engine speed it reads through its own sensor path must match other speed information. In GM's Two-Mode truck tables (12OBDG06, 13OBDG06) the HCP compares its SPI-sensed engine speed with the calculated transmission input speed and with the engine speed received over CAN; a deviation beyond 250 rpm above 1500 rpm, with a wider band at lower speed, in 160 of 320 samples sets it as Type A, MIL after one trip. Ford uses it on the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E as P0C2F:92 in the secondary OBD module C, paired with a 1 Pedal Drive fault message; bulletin 24-2187 fixes it by reprogramming the powertrain modules. Real sensor circuit faults have their own codes. Common causes: Control module software flagging the comparison falsely (Ford Mach-E, fixed by reprogramming) (high likelihood); Speed signals disagree because of a faulty input or a disturbed CAN signal (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the hybrid control module (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL or hybrid system warning; One pedal drive or regenerative functions switched off (Ford Mach-E); Reduced hybrid assist or limited power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C30 – Hybrid/EV Battery Pack State of Charge High
text: P0C30: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack State of Charge High. P0C30 is the counterpart of P0A7D: the battery controller finds that the state of charge of the high-voltage pack stays above its usable window. CARB requires hybrid OBD to flag a state of charge that can no longer be kept inside the manufacturer's range. GM's 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 describes the method: the SOC is checked once per drive cycle, the controller first allows time for the motor to draw the charge back down, then counts the distance driven with excessive SOC; if that share exceeds half of a trip longer than 50 km, at speeds above 15 km/h and pack temperature at least −10 °C, the code is stored as Type B, two trips. No other manufacturer documents it publicly. The car limits regeneration and charging to protect the cells, so braking feel and fuel economy can change. Common causes: Wrong SOC estimate from a drifting pack current or voltage measurement (medium likelihood); Battery or hybrid control software not drawing the charge down as intended (medium likelihood); Electric assist blocked by another fault, so the pack cannot discharge (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL after two trips; Reduced or no regenerative braking; Changed brake pedal feel and higher fuel consumption. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C31 – Inverter B Cooling System Performance
text: P0C31: Inverter B Cooling System Performance. P0C31 reports that the cooling circuit of a second power inverter does not remove heat as expected; inverter A has its own code, P0A93. Vehicles with two separately cooled power electronics units, for example a front and a rear drive unit, need this second code. CARB requires hybrid OBD to monitor the parts used for inverter thermal management and, where feasible, to check the cooling performance itself. No manufacturer documents P0C31 publicly. For the analogous P0A93, Hyundai's 2011 Sonata Hybrid bulletin 14-HC-001 points to the electric water pump, and coolant pump faults of the B circuit are reported as P0B38 or P0C74. To protect the semiconductors the controller limits motor power. A low coolant level or trapped air is worth checking first. Common causes: Low coolant level or air trapped in the inverter B circuit (high likelihood); Weak or failed electric coolant pump of the circuit (medium likelihood); Clogged radiator or inoperative cooling fan (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL; Reduced drive power, especially under load or in heat; Coolant level low in the electronics reservoir. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C32 – Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System A Performance
text: P0C32: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System A Performance. P0C32 is the functional check of the battery thermal system that CARB asks for. GM tunes it per vehicle: the 2012 Volt (12OBDG01A) fails it when the average pack temperature stays above 40 °C in active cooling or below −17 °C in active heating, after 4200 s or 9000 s, Type A, one trip. The Two-Mode trucks (12OBDG06) compare the hottest module with a limit that rises with inlet temperature, from 45 °C to about 65 °C, Type B. The air-cooled eAssist (13OBDG05C) models the power pack temperature after six hours off and fails above 15 °C deviation, Type B. GM bulletin PIP4992C links P0C32 on 2012–2016 eAssist cars to a pack fan that stops at low 12 V voltage and calls for reprogramming and fan replacement. B and C circuits use P2D3F and P2D40. Common causes: Battery cooling fan stopping at low 12 V system voltage (GM eAssist) (high likelihood); Low coolant, air or a weak pump in a liquid-cooled pack circuit (medium likelihood); Blocked cooling air intake or ducts of an air-cooled pack (medium likelihood); Failed pack heater or chiller valve (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning; Reduced electric range or assist; Charging system or battery warning message (eAssist). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0C33 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit
text: P0C33: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit. Battery temperature sensor F is the sixth thermistor in the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the F codes under temperature sensor 6 of nine. P0C33 is the general circuit code for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly: GM's hybrid tables use only the more specific siblings P0C34 to P0C37. CARB requires battery temperature sensors to be monitored for circuit faults and, where possible, separate codes that point to the smallest replaceable part. With one temperature missing the controller has to assume the worst and limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits inside the pack, so checks need high-voltage safety procedures. Common causes: Loose or corroded connector of sensor F at the sensing board (high likelihood); Failed thermistor F (medium likelihood); Faulty input on the battery sensing board or module (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL; Reduced power or charging rate; Battery cooling running more than usual. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C34 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
text: P0C34: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance. P0C34 checks whether sensor F, GM's sensor 6, agrees with the rest of the pack. The controller compares its reading with the average of the other battery temperature sensors. GM's 2016 hybrid table fails it above 25 °C difference in 50 of 67 samples; the Volt and plug-in tables of 2016 to 2019 use 20 °C, in 2018 for 5 s within 6.7 s; the air-cooled eAssist (13OBDG05C) allows only 8.55 °C and tests only after more than six hours with the module off. All are Type B, two trips. Active circuit codes suspend the test, so P0C34 means a sensor that reads wrongly but within range, or a real local hot or cold spot. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 6 performance among codes that set in cold weather without a hardware fault. Common causes: Sensor F drifting or poorly seated on its cell group (medium likelihood); Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt) (medium likelihood); Real local temperature difference from a weak cell group or uneven cooling (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL on after two trips; Battery too cold or reduced power message; Limited charge and discharge power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C35 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low
text: P0C35: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low. Sensor F is an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so its voltage drops as temperature rises; a short to ground looks like an extremely hot cell group. Low refers to the signal, not to the temperature. GM's 2016 table sets P0C35 when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the Volt battery tables of 2016 to 2019 use above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; the eAssist mild hybrid flags a sense voltage under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 calls it sensor 6 circuit low voltage. The opposite fault is P0C36; a pack that is really too hot is reported as P0A7E. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts power and may run the cooling hard. Common causes: Sensor F signal wire chafed and shorted to ground (high likelihood); Internally shorted thermistor F (medium likelihood); Faulty input on the battery sensing board (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL after two trips; Battery cooling running at high speed; Strongly reduced charge and drive power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C36 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit High
text: P0C36: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit High. P0C36 means the voltage from battery temperature sensor F sits above its valid range. With GM's NTC thermistor and pull-up, an open circuit, a broken wire or an unplugged connector pulls the input up and reads as an impossibly cold cell group. GM's 2016 table fails it below −69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the Volt battery tables of 2016 to 2019 below −40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s, and the eAssist table above 4.63 V, about −45 °C, in 7 of 10 samples, each as Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 6 circuit high voltage and links the F group to a Battery Too Cold message. The counterpart for a short to ground is P0C35. Expect limited power and possibly pack heating that is not needed. Common causes: Open circuit or unlatched connector of sensor F (high likelihood); Thermistor F open internally (medium likelihood); Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt) (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL after two trips; Battery too cold, plug in to warm message; Reduced electric power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C37 – Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0C37: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic. P0C37 targets a sensor F signal that jumps instead of following the slow temperature change of a heavy battery. GM documents the logic in its 2016 to 2018 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 17OBDG02, 18OBDG02): every 100 ms the controller adds up the absolute changes of the sensor value over a window of 10 samples; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 set the code as Type B, two trips, with system voltage above 10.2 V and no communication fault active. The Volt, Two-Mode and eAssist tables have no erratic code for this sensor. Unlike P0C35 and P0C36, the signal stays inside its valid range, so the cause is usually a loose terminal or a cracked wire. If several sensors jump at once, the sensing board is the likelier suspect. Common causes: Loose terminal or connector of sensor F not fully latched after pack work (high likelihood); Cracked sensor wire with intermittent contact (medium likelihood); Faulty battery sensing board, often with several sensors affected (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL after two trips; Intermittent hybrid warning, often on rough roads; Temporarily reduced power. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C38 – DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
text: P0C38: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Circuit. The DC/DC converter steps the high-voltage battery down to the 12 V system and replaces the alternator in hybrids and EVs. Its power stage carries temperature sensors so the controller can derate before the semiconductors overheat. P0C38 is the general circuit code for sensor A. Hyundai documents it on the 2027 Palisade Hybrid as P0C381C (failure type 1C, voltage out of range): the hybrid warning light comes on after the car has been parked for a long time, and bulletin 26-01-071H and campaign 9D8 cure it with an HPCU software update that improves the detection logic, so the sensor itself is usually fine. CARB requires the converter's inputs to be monitored as comprehensive components. Low, high and erratic signals have their own codes P0C3A to P0C3C. Common causes: Control unit software misjudging the sensor after long parking (Hyundai Palisade Hybrid) (high likelihood); Fault in the circuit of sensor A inside the converter or power control unit (medium likelihood); Internal fault of the DC/DC converter requiring replacement (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid system warning light; 12 V charging reduced or switched off; Code appearing after the car has stood for a long time. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C39 – DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
text: P0C39: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance. P0C39 is the plausibility check of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A: its reading lies within the electrical range but does not fit the converter's operating state or a second sensor. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid, where the code is called temperature sensor 1 performance. Bulletin 08-037-21 updates the HCP software and changes this code from a two-trip to a one-trip DTC, so the MIL can come on after a single fault. Sensor B, sensor 2 at Ram, has the matching code P0C3E. CARB requires rationality checks for such inputs. A drifting sensor or poor thermal contact is typical; outright circuit faults are reported as P0C38, P0C3A or P0C3B instead. Common causes: Outdated hybrid control software (Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21) (medium likelihood); Sensor A drifting or with poor thermal contact to the power stage (medium likelihood); Uneven cooling of the converter making the readings disagree (low likelihood). Symptoms: MIL, after one trip with updated Ram software; Mild hybrid assist or 12 V supply reduced. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C3A – DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Low
text: P0C3A: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Low. P0C3A means the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. Low refers to the signal voltage: with an NTC thermistor and pull-up, as GM uses for its hybrid temperature sensors, a short to ground or a failed element reads as extreme heat. No manufacturer documents P0C3A publicly. Mercedes-Benz shows the opposite case for the same sensor, P0C3B as a short to positive, on the EQB and the G-Class, and Ram the plausibility code P0C39. CARB requires the converter's inputs to be checked for out-of-range values. Because the controller must assume an overheated power stage, it limits or stops the converter output; the 12 V battery then supplies the car alone and a low-voltage warning may follow. The sensor is usually built into the converter. Common causes: Sensor A signal shorted to ground inside the converter or its harness (high likelihood); Shorted temperature element A, usually requiring converter replacement (medium likelihood); Converter really overheated due to a cooling fault (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning; 12 V battery warning, system voltage dropping; Reduced power or restricted functions. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C3B – DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A High
text: P0C3B: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A High. P0C3B reports a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A above its valid range, typically a short to positive or an open circuit pulled up by the input. Mercedes-Benz documents it on series 243 (EQB) and 465 (G-Class, including the electric G 580): information LI54.10-P-079533 describes P0C3B00 as a short circuit to positive of temperature sensor A, stored together with P0E9700, P0E5400 and P0C4000 after faulty wake-up behaviour of the converter. Drivers see a red 12 V battery message and white or yellow HV warnings. The remedy is a converter check in XENTRY, clearing the fault memory and a converter reset; parts are not replaced first. The low-signal sibling is P0C3A, sensor B's high code is P0C40. Common causes: Faulty wake-up behaviour of the converter putting it into an error state (Mercedes 243/465) (high likelihood); Open circuit or short to positive in the sensor A circuit (medium likelihood); Internal defect of the DC/DC converter (low likelihood). Symptoms: Red 12 V battery warning in the cluster; White or yellow high-voltage system warning; 12 V battery no longer charged while driving. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C3C – DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
text: P0C3C: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic. P0C3C covers a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A that drops out or jumps for short moments while staying mostly within range. The heat sink of a converter warms and cools slowly, so fast jumps point to the signal path rather than to real temperature changes. No manufacturer documents P0C3C publicly. The method is known from GM's hybrid tables for comparable thermistors, such as P0C37 for battery sensor F: the controller adds up signal changes in short windows and fails the test when several windows exceed a limit. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored for faults. Typical causes are a loose terminal, vibration damage or moisture at the converter connector. Unlike P0C3A and P0C3B, the fault may vanish between tests, so a wiggle test helps. Common causes: Loose terminal or moisture at the converter connector (high likelihood); Harness damaged by vibration with intermittent contact (medium likelihood); Intermittent fault inside the converter (low likelihood). Symptoms: Intermittent hybrid or EV warning; Occasional 12 V charging interruptions. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C3D – DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
text: P0C3D: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Circuit. P0C3D is the general circuit code for the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter, which turns high-voltage battery power into 12 V supply. Converters with two sensors watch separate parts of the power stage or cross-check one sensor against the other. No manufacturer documents P0C3D publicly. Sensor B itself appears in bulletins: Mercedes-Benz lists P0C4000, a short to positive of sensor B, on the EQB and the G-Class, and Ram the plausibility code P0C3E as temperature sensor 2 on the 2021 1500 eTorque. Sensor A uses P0C38 for the same fault class. CARB requires such converter inputs to be monitored. A circuit fault makes the controller limit or stop the converter, so the 12 V battery may run down and warnings follow. Common causes: Connector or wiring fault in the sensor B circuit (high likelihood); Failed temperature element B inside the converter (medium likelihood); Converter or hybrid control software misjudging the sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning; 12 V battery warning. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

title: P0C3E – DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance
text: P0C3E: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance. P0C3E flags DC/DC converter temperature sensor B as electrically valid but implausible, for instance when it disagrees with sensor A or with what the converter load should produce. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid under the name temperature sensor 2 performance. Bulletin 08-037-21 reflashes the hybrid control processor and changes P0C3E, together with P0C39 for sensor 1, from a two-trip to a one-trip code, so one failed test can light the MIL. CARB requires rationality checks for converter inputs. Typical causes are a drifting element, poor thermal contact or outdated software. Circuit faults of sensor B are reported as P0C3D, P0C3F or P0C40; a converter that is really too hot sets P0D32 instead. Symptoms: MIL, after one trip with updated Ram software; Mild hybrid assist or 12 V supply reduced. Repair difficulty: shop_only.

Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location. Common causes: Wire shorted to ground (high likelihood); Coil internal short (medium likelihood); Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance (low likelihood). Symptoms: EV/hybrid system warning light on; Reduced power output or limp mode; Charging may fail or be slowed; Reduced electric range. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P0E70 – Control Pilot Signal Frequency Too Low
text: P0E70: Control Pilot Signal Frequency Too Low. The control pilot PWM frequency from the EVSE is too low. SAE J1772 requires 1 kHz +/- tolerance. The on-board charger negotiates voltage, current and safety with the EVSE; a fault interrupts charging or limits it to AC slow-charge despite a DC fast charger being attached. Common causes: EVSE PWM below 1 kHz spec (high likelihood); Filter capacitor too large (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Charge status indicator shows fault; Charging may not start or interrupts; Slower-than-expected charge rate. Repair difficulty: medium.

text: P2000: NOx Adsorber Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1). The lean NOx trap (LNT) on bank 1 is no longer storing or releasing NOx within the required efficiency window. title: P2004 – Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open (Bank 1)
text: P2004: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open (Bank 1). The intake manifold runner control (IMRC) flap on bank 1 is stuck in the open position. title: P20E0 – Reductant Pressure Too Low
text: P20E0: Reductant Pressure Too Low. The pressure in the SCR reductant (AdBlue/DEF) line is below the calibrated minimum. title: P2187 – System Too Lean at Idle (Bank 1)
text: P2187: System Too Lean at Idle (Bank 1). Fuel trim on bank 1 hits the lean limit only at idle, while trim returns to normal at higher load. title: P218F – Reductant No Flow Detected
text: P218F: Reductant No Flow Detected. The DEF dosing system commands flow but the pressure or flow sensor reports no actual delivery — typically a fully blocked dosing nozzle, a frozen line, or a dead pump. title: P2190 – System Too Rich at Idle (Bank 2)
text: P2190: System Too Rich at Idle (Bank 2). Fuel trim on bank 2 hits the rich limit only at idle. Often a leaking injector dribbling fuel at low load, a sticky purge valve dumping fuel vapour, or fuel pressure regulator that fails to relieve pressure when intake vacuum is high. Common causes: Leaking injector at idle on bank 2 (high likelihood); Purge valve stuck open (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Increased fuel consumption; Black smoke from exhaust on acceleration; Smell of unburned fuel, fouled spark plugs. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P2191 – System Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 1)
text: P2191: System Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 1). Bank 1 fuel trim hits the lean limit only at higher engine load. Pattern points to a fuel-supply restriction — failing fuel pump, blocked filter, or weak injectors — rather than a vacuum leak (which would dominate at idle). Common causes: Fuel pump weak under load (high likelihood); Fuel filter clogged (medium likelihood); MAF reads low at high airflow (medium likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light on; Rough idle, possible stalling; Hesitation or hard cold start; Power loss under load. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P2195 – O2 Sensor Signal Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 1)

title: P219A – Bank 1 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
text: P219A: Bank 1 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance. Diesel cold-start uses adapted injection timing per cylinder to limit white smoke and noise; deviation typically points at a worn injector or faulty crank/cam correlation. Common causes: Injector flow-rate aged (high likelihood). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P21C2 – Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit/Open
text: P21C2: Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit/Open. The control circuit for the relay that powers the DEF heaters is open — main DEF heating supply path interrupted. Common causes: Relay coil open (high likelihood); Pin pushed back out of connector body (low likelihood); Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or NOx warning on; AdBlue/DEF level or quality warning; Possible no-start countdown after ignore period; Failed emissions inspection (NOx). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P21C3 – Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit Low
text: P21C3: Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit Low. DEF heater relay control line stuck low — short to ground. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location. Common causes: Short to ground (high likelihood); Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance (low likelihood); Harness chafing through insulation (low likelihood). Symptoms: Check engine light or NOx warning on; AdBlue/DEF level or quality warning; Possible no-start countdown after ignore period; Failed emissions inspection (NOx). Repair difficulty: medium.

A flow-deviating injector throws off cylinder balance — adjacent cylinders run leaner/richer to compensate, often masking the root cause until the trim limit is hit. Common causes: Short to ground (high likelihood); Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance (low likelihood); Harness chafing through insulation (low likelihood). Repair difficulty: hard.

title: P21F4 – Fuel Control System B Too Lean Off Idle (Bank 1)
text: P21F4: Fuel Control System B Too Lean Off Idle (Bank 1). The secondary fuel control loop B on bank 1 reports a lean condition outside idle. title: P2200 – NOx Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)
text: P2200: NOx Sensor Circuit (Bank 1). The NOx sensor on bank 1 — typically upstream of the SCR catalyst — does not communicate or sends an invalid signal. Symptoms: Check engine light or NOx warning on; AdBlue/DEF level or quality warning; Possible no-start countdown after ignore period; Failed emissions inspection (NOx). Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P2278 – O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 3 / Bank 2 Sensor 3
text: P2278: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 3 / Bank 2 Sensor 3. The PCM detects that the O2 sensor signals from bank 1 sensor 3 and bank 2 sensor 3 are swapped — typically a wiring crossover after sensor replacement. title: P2279 – Intake Air System Leak
text: P2279: Intake Air System Leak. The ECU has detected a discrepancy between commanded throttle/intake conditions and the resulting MAP/MAF that points to unmetered air entering after the throttle body. On turbocharged engines this often means a cracked or disconnected boost pipe between turbo and intake; on naturally aspirated engines, a hole in the intake manifold or hose. Common causes: Boost pipe disconnected or cracked (high likelihood); Intake hose split (high likelihood). Repair difficulty: easy.

title: P22FF – SCR NOx Catalyst Inlet Temperature Too Low
text: P22FF: SCR NOx Catalyst Inlet Temperature Too Low. The temperature sensor at the SCR catalyst inlet reports a value below the threshold needed for efficient ammonia conversion. Below roughly 180-200 °C the SCR cannot reduce NOx and reductant injection is suspended; if this is detected continuously the ECU sets the fault. Symptoms: Check engine light on; Failed emissions inspection; Possibly slightly increased fuel consumption; Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load. Repair difficulty: medium.

title: P230A – Cylinder 1 Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance Adjustment At Limit During Balance
